M. THIERS has brought up his Report from the Commission on the Deputies on the Education Bill as fashioned by the Peers. It is a grand tractate, which occupied nearly three hours in the reading, and requires seven or eight columns of the journals. There is much of verbiage, sciolism, false social philosophy, pretension, and rhetoric in this work of a professor, anti-christian design. The alterations proposed in the bill reverse the work of the Peers, and re-establish the University monopoly and privileges. Frequent were the plaudits of the Deputies, a majority of whom belong to the school of Voltaire. During the recitation, the Monarchy betrayed their chagrin at the success of one who stands perpetually in their van or rear as a premier candidate or leader of the most formidable of their adversaries. THIERS, observes a Legitimist oracle, is Voltairean, Revolutionary, Imperialist, Monarchist, Doctrinaire, Radical—head of none. The Jansenist journal of Public Instruction will come from his incubator. GUIZOT took up a small share of the debates, space is consumed by the serial report of a criminal trial at Auch, in the extreme South, which lasted eight days, and in which the accused and distant nearly two hundred leagues from Paris. The case is of a beautiful and opulent widow accused of poisoning her husband with arsenic; it teems with romantic circumstances quite as congenial for the French temperament as those of the Suire-de-Boissy. All the reporters from the capital announced that they would have reporters at Auch, and receive the stimulating matter by special couriers; the details in the newspapers are devoured; and the avidity with which they are grasped at the reading rooms equals at least any interest connected with the Education bill. Count MOLÉ made a sage to excite any where in the Union. I enclose a summary of the accusation; the whole story is a drama of real life. Gravity, dignity, high tone, scandal, and forensics were never more remarkably mixed and exhibited. There is not a suspect proof of guilt—no conclusive presumption—but God knows, only an impressionable jury could convict. In the Court of Appeal of Paris, the bar of the Royal Court having resigned, a new election took place on the 14th instant. Their Spanish candidate, M. BRESSON, received 217 votes out of their brethren entitled to vote. The number of these was five hundred and one, and the whole body is not as pleased by that number and with six votes, greater by ninety-six than any poll on the records of the bar. Octogenary judges and councilors, aged from sixty to eighty-five years, had long ceased to practise claimed the right of suffrage; particular homage was paid to BERRYER; the Council is twenty-eight in full, contemporary and friend of the GERBIERS and TRONSON DU COUDRAY. They are directly related to professors, and the lecturers who have succeeded them in jurisprudence in the Colleges, bustled in the suite. Animosity exists in some measure between this bar and arriere-ban of the Council—this professional clanship shown in the resurrection of so many antique and decrepit bodies; the old bar was ended the batonnier (staffman) of the Council delivered an address, in which he congratulated the Elders and his colleagues on the success of their activity, their perseverance, and their pecuniary sacrifices for the dignity and independence and the moral influence of the profession. To the Count, he repeals the strife will be between the esprit de corps of the bar and that of the magistracy. Three rounds of applause followed the address. Up to this date the result of the Cabinet conference at Barcelona is the dissolution of the Cortes so long suspended, and the convocation of a new assembly, to be opened and organized, and the convocation of the Spanish electors college in their proper districts, on the 10th October. You may judge how fair and regular the elections may prove; and, nevertheless, it is quite possible that NARVAEZ & Co. may not be unable to control the new body and be quickly brought to the alternative of another suspension or a dictatorship. A letter of July 3d, from Madrid, called from London, resigned because he would have proceeded without Cortes: NARVAEZ appointed himself in his stead, and now holds the double office of Minister of War, Minister of Foreign Affairs, Commander-in-chief of the Army—a political dictator, pure and simple. The press has not reprinted the prate of the farce of constitutional freedom after the tragedy of military despotism; and for this look at the remonstrance of the British Minister, who with drugs from his bed and consigned to the stomach ... How fine and sincere the language of Lord ABERDEEN, in his reply to Lord CLANRICARDE'S question concerning the proposals of DON CARLOS to marry his son to the young Queen of Spain! His Lordship said:

"He would just observe that if the question in Spain were only one between a Carlist contender, and a Carlist princess, that proposed, if adopted by the Spanish people, might be regarded as an eligible means of terminating differences and putting an end to civil war; but if it were proposed to change the nature of the affair had completely changed; it was no longer a question of a Carlist pretender, but of a pretender to Government—a question between a constitutional Government and absolute rule."

Such a division in favor of the Narvaez party and Moderado system rivals the declaration from the same source of French favorite-ship and French concurrence in the insurrection against the ESPARTERO Regency. A Barcelona decree of the 4th instant, countermanded the tax-abatement and privileges for the Basque provinces according to the ancient fueros. This measure precludes national concord, but tends to strengthen the cause of the Pretender's Government against the Carlists, who have relied chiefly on those provinces.

In Switzerland the split is temporizing, and seems willing to see realized in the federal concerns the French notion: "In general the most vexed questions decide themselves natively." The No. 234 Athens was disturbed and alarmed by a mob crying, "Down with the Ministers and Constitution!" the Emeute was quelled by the troops, not without much effusion of blood: the elections in the interior of Greece have been generally and very contentious for the present Cabinet: lately, in our own Chamber of Deputies, Mr. GUIZOT related that the French Plenipotentiary at Athens had, conformably to his instructions, exerted himself to maintain the original coalition in the National Councils of the Metaxist party and Coletti party—the English and French; but the rupture came, and no control could be attempted. Greece is too crude as a nation, and foreign influence too strong for a regular, familiar, to allow firm and steady management of the representative system. The Paris Commerce of yesterday has an article on the French Navy in the Pacific, occasioned by the news by the Burgundy from New York. That anti-Ministerial sheet is charged by the Commerce with instigating Mexico to her warlike "armor and attitude," and French Admirals to usurp authority and act at discretion either on the Mexican or American side. The Commerce is said to have passed into the hands of the Press party—the Conservative anti-Guizot party—led by Messrs. DE TOCQUEVILLE, DE BEAUMONT, and LANGUINAIS. The recall of Admiral DE MOGES, who is replaced by Admiral LAPLACE on the Antilles station, forms a ground of Opposition complaint. DE MOGES mediated between the Dominican Republic and Negro Hayti, and favored or welcomed the overture of the Spanish party for French protectorate. A Conservative journal supposes the French Cabinet to apprehend that Great Britain would claim the protectorate of the North of the island—far the most valuable, and the true French portion. Admirals, continues the journal, must not be allowed to anticipate, with regard to Saint Domingo or Tahiti, the proper work of Cabinets. Those of London and Paris are blamed for employing themselves in the detection and frustration of the conspiracies and enterprises against the Governments of Italy. A natural fellow-feeling prompts them. Their success has not been great, for it seems that some forty political zealots and adventurers was more preposterous and not more lucky than M. MAZZINI'S band of 1833. The two Cabinets have reached arrangements for terminating the quarrel of Mexico with Texas, and guaranteeing Texas independence, on condition that Texas will not annex to any other party. French affairs at Montevideo afford plentiful ammunition to the Paris Opposition in the Chamber of Deputies.

The Revue des Deux Mondes, issued to-day, contains an article of fifty pages, entitled Texas and the United States, and signed A. CAUCHY. It refers mainly to the question of annexation. The editor gave read, in manuscript, to M. DE TOCQUEVILLE, Colonel BUTLER, General HOUSTON, Mr. VAN BUREN, Mr. CLAY, Mr. ADAMS, with MEXICO, &c. TEXAS, in regard to English policy and designs. He condemns them all as Machiavelian; he relates the proceedings of Mr. TYLER, and the formation, management, and ultimate defeat of the Annexation treaty. He gives the purport, with quotations, of each principal document; he exhibits, as he understands them, the agents, their spirit and aims, as well as the political chiefs; he dwells on the respective interests and views of the South and the North, and the British Government, the latter and the United States; of Great Britain with respect to Texas; he exposes the late treaty as the offspring of President TYLER'S treaty and the approaching Presidential election; the whole abolition strife is explained and analyzed. Touching the policy of France in the matter, Monsieur CAUCHY thinks that she should insist, as far as possible, against the revival of the Mexican claim, or that, at least, the independence of Mexico should be permanently secured from the encroachments and institutions of the slaveholders who possess Texas, provided Texas remain an independent State with England in obtaining from the U. States a certain absolute guaranty of Mexican independence. The author of the essay had, from his personal acquaintance of the writer with events, persons, publications, documents, and publications of every description, representing all the views. In the body of this essay has an extract from an American paper of last December—the correspondence between Captain ELLIOT and the Texan Government—which has engaged my attention on account of the identity of some of its statements and inferences with our impressions here.

The Journal du Havre tells us that Edward CONROY, Esq., specialized as British Consul, has embarked for the United States at that port. Our morning papers say that the telegraph reports the acquittal of M. DE BRUGEQ, at Paris, charged with breach of the criminal calendar. Curiosity is still alive in Paris about the results of the inquiry by the secret committee of the British House of Lords touching the Government prerogative and practice of opening letters. Let us leave, observes the Constitutionnel, Lord RADNOR, BANNERMAN, and DUNCOMBE to search the internal system of Cabinet noirs. We may smile at such pharisaism. The houses of the Duke of MORNY and M. ROUL, and M. DE LAGRANGE have just been thoroughly searched—all papers found (letters, wills) were duly opened; and, if you enter any coffee-house with a political turn of mind, domiciliary visits and arrests are performed, you may learn a little, and of the legal formalities too, of the system. M. DUNCOMBE got the proceedings of the Peers yesterday afternoon.

"VISCOUNT DEROUCHAGE referred to the certain prevention of small-pox by the vaccine matter, and stated that M. Charbonnier de la Guesnerie, who had been brought from the prison of Saint Lazare to the Civil Tribunal of Paris, and afflicted with acute rheumatism, was kept for ninety-six hours in a damp cell...

"THE MINISTER OF PUBLIC INSTRUCTION begged leave to say that the noble peer was greatly mistaken in supposing that the police of Paris acted...

records.full_text:
From St. Domingo.—We learn from Capt. Wilson of the brig Republic, just arrived from Port au Prince, that on the 12th of March the Haytien man of war Herard, in the schr. La Granada, had been seen off the South side of the Island, five miles off, by five gun boats. The whole coast was guarded by vessels of war, to prevent the ex-President and his adherents from landing. The government called out all the militia, and the whole of that part of the Island belonging to the Haytien government was under martial law. Several of the adherents of Herard had been taken and shot, and there was a great excitement throughout the Island. Coffee was very scarce and high on account of all the country men having been taken for soldiers, and no persons left to bring the Coffee to market. The markets were glutted with American produce.

Although numerous arrests were made in different parts of the Republic, among whom were some of the journalists, there was no general sympathy for Herard, who was viewed as an ambitious usurper, and by all parties of government, that his attempts to revolutionize the country would prove abortive.

It was rumored at Port Republican, that a revolution had taken place at St. Domingo, which had resulted in the expulsion of Gen. Santana from the Presidency, and in the elevation to that office of Major Moru, a mulatto of splendid character, and the respectable family of the Alvares of Zagnate (Saint Domingo.) If true, this change of government in the Dominican Republic would be the triumph of an enlightened policy over military rule, and demagogism personified in Santana and Bobadilla.

We have received more recent accounts from the island of Hayti than the "Charleston Patriot" gives above. They are contained in the following extract of a letter received in Washington, from Cape Haytien, September 24:

"The authorities of the Haytien part of this island are making great preparations for a naval force. It may, therefore, be interesting to you to have a statement of the present force of the Haytien navy, as near as can be ascertained.

"I can present the following list of their armed vessels:

"A frigate, (coppered)—about 600 tons, formerly a slaver, carrying 14 18-lb. carronades.

"A square schooner—Port au Prince—formerly American built, carrying 6 long 6-pounders.

"A vessel at Jacmel, (part coppered,) of 145 tons, American built, has not received her armament.

"A topsail schooner—La Mouche—about 70 tons, Haytien built, carrying 3 guns.

"A topsail schooner—Le Sucriere—about 70 tons, Haytien built, carrying 3 guns.

"A topsail schooner—La Signora—about 70 tons, a prize from the Dominicans, carrying 3 guns.

"A fore-and-aft schooner, — about 60 tons, Haytien built, carrying 3 guns.

"This latter schooner is at or near Port-au-Prince. La Mouche and Le Sucriere are at the cape. La Signora is at Jacmel, and the others are under repairs at Port-au-Prince, fitting out for service.

"The Haytiens have vessels sufficient for four times the number of sailors they can command; and those now in service are unskillful seamen, and not accustomed to naval discipline. From defective knowledge of naval usage in the commanders of these vessels, some fears may be entertained that, inflated by pride at sudden elevation to the command of armed vessels, they may annoy foreign commerce in these seas, by firing at merchant vessels, or arresting them in their course, as was the case lately with respect to an American vessel.

"The whole fleet has been at sea once, captured the Dominican schooner, (now the Surprise,) and returned to Port-au-Prince.

"The President, Pierrot, who makes this city his residence, has given orders for an immediate and vigorous descent on the Spanish part, with all his available force, which is to move in three columns from this time.

"This island is assuming every day a new interest in the eyes of the people of the United States. About two years since, the Spanish portion of the island declared their independence of the French or black part of the island. These (called the Dominicans) have had a continued struggle with the Haytiens. They have been engaged in several battles on land and by sea—principally marauding parties of black race, in which the Dominicans have generally been successful. This contest becomes very important to us; for upon its result depends the destiny of this rich but neglected island, so susceptible of improvement, and so productive of the most valuable articles, including coffee, cotton, rich minerals, and fine timber. It is an interesting question to which side it must yield, when, in consequence of the insurrection in St. Domingo, it fell under the ruthless sway of the ignorant and barbarous black race. The Dominicans, however, are reviving from the slumber which has reigned for several years—improving their towns, and cultivating their farms. If they were perfectly free from the ferocious assaults of the Haytiens, they would gradually extend their settlements, and establish a government, like the people of the United States. France is unwilling to recognize their independence, and has not probably abandoned the idea of recovering this long-lost island. The policy of England is probably opposed to the Dominicans, because it would be too much in favor of the Dominicans as the people of the United States. We shall probably have it in our power in a few days to lay before our readers some commercial statistics, showing the value of the trade which we might carry on with the white and mixed breed Dominicans in the Spanish portion of this rich and beautiful island."

The article noted that the Dominicans received sympathy as representatives of Columbus's first American colony, though it claimed their incompetency for self-government had been proven and an impending revolution might restore the island. Additionally, the newspaper reported a Cabinet rumor that Mr. Buchanan would remain in his position, and noted an occurrence from the *Turk's Island Gazette* of October 23 regarding a man named Benjamin Lightbourn who was killed by a wild bull at Salt Rock, Caicos.

La nota observaba simpatías hacia los dominicanos por encarnar el primer asentamiento colombino en América, si bien argüía su supuesta impericia para el régimen autónomo y vaticinaba un vuelco revolucionario capaz de reconfigurar la isla. Por añadidura, recogía el comentario ministerial de que el Sr. Buchanan permanecería en su secretaría y transcribía un hecho de la *Turk's Island Gazette* del 23 de octubre concerniente a Benjamin Lightbourn, muerto por una res bravía en Salt Rock, Caicos.

records.full_text:
Advices which have been received here go to show that the Haytians are making another great contest with the Dominicans, and that they are becoming tired of it. Against the Haytians, the blacks were always powerful and successful, by the aid of their climate. All they had to do was to lay waste the coast and retreat to the mountains, leaving their climate and its diseases to do the rest. But, against the whites, who, like themselves, are inured to the climate, and who, as if by a miracle which will reverse all moral and physical laws, have shown a courage in battle that has, in all conflicts with other colors, been resisted; Hayti must fall in the end. Besides, the English journals invoke the interference of their government to put a stop to this waste of humanity. They suggest the idea of giving independence to both parties.

Cart-loads of petitions have been, from time to time, sent to Congress, for the recognition of the independence of Hayti; but their prayer has not yet been granted. Should this government interfere at all, it will, I presume, be by the recognition of the independence of the Dominican Republic.

What course England and France may take as to the affairs of St. Domingo since they have set up a sort of joint protectorate as to Texas affairs, is not known, though we have had some vague and contradictory rumors on that subject.

The Dominicans receive some sympathy from the fact that they are the representatives of the white race in Hayti, but it is somewhat singular that the first settlement of Europeans in Hayti, by Columbus, was the first to come under the dominion of the African race. That predominance for the African race has been short, and another revolution seems to be beginning which will, without the interference of foreign powers, restore this fertile island to the dominion of the white race in the new world.

We have now a new and correct version of the Cabinet rumor. Mr. Buchanan is to remain in the Cabinet—it was never his intention to resign.

records.summary_en: The *Mobile Register and Journal* reported on the geography, population demographics, and government structure of the island, noting that the Spanish (Dominican) portion features a republican government, good racial relations, and a Catholic majority alongside Protestant churches. The excerpt further stated that the Dominican military possesses approximately 35,000 to 40,000 regular and National Guard troops, and predicted that the Dominicans would inevitably conquer the entire island. Additionally, it mentioned that the negro part of the island owes about 12 million dollars to France, that English and French mutual jealousies exist regarding influence, and that the true interest of Spain, France, the United States, and England is to aid and countenance the region.

El pasaje puntualizaba que el ejército dominicano reunía de 35.000 a 40.000 combatientes entre tropa de línea y Guardias Nacionales, augurando el sometimiento inexorable de la totalidad de la isla. Indicaba además que el sector negro registraba un débito aproximado de doce millones de duros con Francia, constataba los recelos hegemónicos anglo-franceses y juzgaba conforme a la conveniencia de España, Francia, Estados Unidos y Gran Bretaña respaldar e impulsar aquel territorio.

records.full_text:
Correspondence of the Journal of Commerce.
THE DOMINICAN REPUBLIC. — This the Republic of the larger part of the Island of Hayti, the recognition of its de facto government, no one can doubt who will take the trouble to look into the case with an unprejudiced eye.
The course taken by Mr. Calhoun as to this island, we trust, will be followed by the present and the South American Governments. Prior to their recognition, the U. S. should, as they have done, send commissioners, to inquire into and report upon their condition.
The same course seems to have been taken by the British government, as to the Dominican Republic.
The Island of St. Domingo is situated in the Gulf of Mexico, and is 400 miles in length from East to West, and from 60 to 120 miles in breadth. Its circumference is about 1000 miles.
It is the most central and important of all the West India islands. It lies only 30 miles from Porto Rico, 60 miles from Cuba, 120 from Jamaica, and about 3 days sail from the Spanish Main and Yucatan. It is 1000 miles South of Charleston, and 1700 from New-York. The soil and climate of the Spanish part are much better than those of the French part; three-fourths of the inhabitants are Spaniards, or, as now called, Dominicans; the rest French. The white population is about 130,000; mixed, 70,000; black, 30,000. In the Spanish or Dominican part of the Island there exists a good feeling towards the white races. The Spanish language and laws have been established. The Catholic religion prevails, but other denominations are tolerated.
The Government is Republican, consisting of a President with a Senate and House of Representatives; there is a Supreme Court, three Judges, a Secretary of the Interior; and a Judiciary, consisting of a Supreme Court, with a Chief Justice and four deputies, and inferior Courts, for the interior and commercial cities of the coast.
The military strength of the Dominicans is about 15 or 20 to 30,000 regular troops, and about 40,000 stand of arms, and 300 cannon, principally brass. The island is now well fortified throughout the whole island. The negro part of the Island is mostly governed by France, although nominally free. The English are opposed to the extension of the influence of the French, and also of the Spanish. The true interest of the great powers, Spain, France, the United States, and England, is to aid and assist the growth and prosperity of the Dominican Republic. The thing once done, that interesting section of the West Indies coming in favor, should be rendered independent and rich, and would present an extensive field for the enterprise of the American merchant. The population of the Spanish portion of the Island has increased since 1822, while on the other hand, the negro population has rapidly diminished. This undoubtedly has been the case of late, and results from the almost entire absence of the institution of marriage, and the consequent loose habits of the people, and degeneracy between the sexes. This, together with other causes of importance, would soon prove the entire incapacity of the blacks for self-government. If the French part of the Island is not soon settled and blood-shed, are beyond conception or belief. At all events, the white portion of the Island must and will increase by victories, as the strongest inducement is held out to the white race to settle there. Thank God, the whites are victorious, and this will be a great measure owing to the influence and value of the white women, who fought themselves for their homes.
Great commercial advantages would accrue to the United States by the recognition of the independence of the Dominicans.
There are great numbers of the old French families, who have become identified with this country, whose possessions would derive great advantage from the recognition of their right and just claim. All that is now wanted is a stable government, and a policy on the part of the United States, to aid and assist in the independence of the Dominicans.

records.summary_en: The newspaper reported that the remaining old Spanish white population of the island did not exceed 10,000 souls, casting doubt on recently reported figures of 130,000 whites. It detailed the island's fertile agricultural capacity and export staples—principally coffee, along with cocoa, tobacco, and mahogany—and noted specific import and export figures for the United States and Hayti between 1833 and 1844. It adds that in 1825 Boyer concluded a treaty with France recognizing independence and guaranteeing payment of 150,000,000 francs for French colonists' losses, later reduced by France to 60,000,000 francs.

Añade que en 1825 Boyer concluyó un tratado con Francia que reconocía la independencia y garantizaba el pago de 150.000.000 de francos por las pérdidas de los colonos franceses, reducidos después por Francia a 60.000.000 de francos.

records.headline: The Dominican Republic
records.summary_en: In 1845, the newspaper reported that Mr. Calhoun, while in the State Department, dispatched Mr. Hogan to investigate the resources of the Dominican Republic following a petition to have the United States acknowledge its independence. Hogan subsequently returned with a satisfactory account of the commonwealth. The publication advocated for the U.S. recognition of the Dominican Republic, citing racial sympathies with the white population struggling against Hayti, commercial interests in the West Indies, and strategic concerns regarding European monarchies holding territory in the region.
records.summary_es: Hacia 1845, el rotativo informó que el Sr. Calhoun, hallándose al frente del Departamento de Estado, comisionó al Sr. Hogan con el propósito de evaluar la potencialidad de la República Dominicana a raíz de una solicitud tendiente al reconocimiento de su soberanía por Estados Unidos. Hogan retornó consecuentemente con un balance favorable de aquella comunidad política. La publicación instaba a que Estados Unidos reconociese al Estado dominicano invocando afinidades de raza con la población blanca en conflicto contra Haití, conveniencias mercantiles en las Antillas e inquietudes de seguridad ante enclaves soberanos de coronas europeas en el área.

records.chapter_es: Una república en busca de reconocimiento
records.full_text:
Few of our readers are aware that a new Republic has been formed under this name in the island of St. Domingo. Yet such is the fact. Within two years past a revolution has been made, and successfully maintained against the negro government of Hayti. Our purpose is to give some new idea of this new Republic and its resources.
The Island of St. Domingo is the most flourishing and fertile of the West India Islands. There are two political divisions of the island. The formerly French portion is now the Haytien Republic, as it is called. From this nation are exported coffee, cotton, mahogany, dye wood, &c. The formerly Spanish portion of the island, or now the Dominican Republic, exports mahogany, the wood fustic, cotton, cocoa, honey, hides, gum guaiacum, and tobacco, equal to the best Havana in quality. Sugar is also raised. It unquestionably contains mineral wealth, as gold and copper mines have been discovered.
The climate of the island is that of the tropics—warm and damp. The heats, however, are tempered by the sea breeze, which sets in about 10 o'clock, A. M., and lasts until night, when it is followed by the land breeze. The soil of the island is exceedingly fertile.
The east end of the island of St. Domingo, formerly was known as the Spanish Possession, now forms the Dominican Republic. Its extent is 33,000 square leagues of 25 to a degree. This Republic has been formed by the white portion of the island rising in rebellion against the black Government of Hayti. For twenty years and upwards, the whites have submitted to a most humiliating oppression. In February, 1844, they successfully made a stand against the black government, and have since gallantly and efficiently maintained their independence. They sent commissioners to this country during the administration of Mr. Calhoun in the State Department, for the purpose of having the government of the United States take measures to acknowledge the independence of the Republic. Mr. Calhoun at once favored the idea, and despatched Mr. Hogan, of this State, to investigate the resources of the country. Mr. Hogan having faithfully executed his important trust, has returned and given, we hear, a most satisfactory account of the rising commonwealth.
We trust that steps will be taken to acknowledge the independence of the Dominican Republic. The sympathies of our race, Caucasian as it is, must be with the whites of the Dominican Republic struggling with the African race of Hayti.—The interests of the United States should also prompt us to feel a deep interest in this new nation, as our object is to extend our commercial relations with every country, but particularly with the West India islands. We wish to cultivate friendship with this new and rising Republic. We cannot be insensible to the fact that England has her naval depots in one of these West India islands. That France has her foot—or is to—that these little ocean gems of islands belong to European monarchies, except St. Domingo, (where a black government, with which we can have no sympathies, and certainly they have none for us,) rules with despotic sway. Does not our interest prompt us to cherish the effort of a white people to create an independent Republic in one of these islands? In case of a war with any European power, we should have a friendly naval power in the West Indies whose feelings, sympathies and government were all republican, and certainly more in favor of our system than any other power? The Dominican Republic has several fine harbors—good timber for ship building. Is it not right we should look for a refuge for our naval force in time of trouble?
The population of the Republic is about 220,000, and the country is capable of sustaining a population ten times beyond that which it now has.
There is very little doubt of the ability of the Dominican Republic to maintain its independence. It has cannon, military stores, about 7000 military men, and can in an emergency raise 25,000 capable of bearing arms. It also has a small naval force. There is reason to believe that the Haytiens will find it a difficult matter to attack the Dominicans. The negroes (Haytiens) are in disunion and incapable of making a vigorous assault on the whites of the Dominican Republic. We hope our Congress now in session will take early steps to acknowledge the independence of the Dominican Republic.

records.headline: Important News from St. Domingo—Progress of General Annexation.
records.summary_en: According to the *New York Herald*, documents including a memorial presented to the U.S. government by a San Domingo agent and letters to U.S. agent Mr. Hogan indicate that the United States is pursuing a policy toward San Domingo similar to the one that led to the annexation of Texas. Mr. Hogan was sent to San Domingo by Secretary of State Mr. Calhoun to investigate the island's resources and capabilities, while the ongoing war between San Domingo and Hayti reportedly nears an end.
records.summary_es: Conforme al *New York Herald*, pliegos que comprenden una memoria cursada al gobierno norteamericano por un comisionado de Santo Domingo y comunicaciones libradas al delegado estadounidense Sr. Hogan evidencian que Estados Unidos aplica hacia Santo Domingo una directriz análoga a la que precedió a la incorporación de Texas. El Sr. Hogan fue acreditado ante Santo Domingo por el secretario de Estado Sr. Calhoun para indagar sus facultades y renglones económicos, en tanto el enfrentamiento sostenido entre Santo Domingo y Haití se aproxima presumiblemente a su término.

records.chapter_es: Una república en busca de reconocimiento
records.full_text:
The news which we have received here, during the last two days, by two vessels from different ports of the Island of San Domingo, or Hayti, in the West Indies, and which will be found in this day's paper, is of the highest importance to this country for all time to come.

Through the energy and industry of a special agent and correspondent, whom we sent to San Domingo, last summer, we have received, exclusively, copies of several documents and diplomatic correspondence which have already passed between the government of the United States and that of San Domingo, preparing the way for the great measure of the recognition of the latter republic by the former, according to the same policy or plan, which was pursued towards Texas, and which has, in a few years, terminated in the absorption or annexation of the latter into this great republic of the North. These documents consist of a memorial presented to the United States government at Washington, by the agent of San Domingo, about a year ago, together with copies of highly interesting letters, written by certain public agents sent to San Domingo, during last summer—one of them by Mr. Hogan, the agent of the United States, then in San Domingo, to which island he was sent by Mr. Calhoun, then Secretary of State, in order to investigate the resources, and ascertain the disposition and capabilities of that new republic in the West Indies.

Thus far, the movement has been highly prosperous and successful. The war between San Domingo and Hayti, is fast drawing to a close, and it is highly probable that the black and bloody republic will be overcome by the white and more civilized race of San Domingo. As soon as that object shall have been accomplished, there will come other movements, leading to the natural termination of the negotiation, already begun, in annexation to the United States.

We have long perceived that the diplomatic correspondence which we give, only comes up to the period at which Mr. Hogan, the United States agent, left the island, during last summer; but what Mr. Hogan, the United States agent, has already made to the Secretary of State at Washington, or the action of our government on that information, has not transpired. What the present President or his Secretary of State may have in contemplation on this subject, we know not; but we have reason to believe that the present President has not failed to take notice of the diplomatic movement of Mr. Calhoun, or the reports of Mr. Hogan, which he has so auspiciously begun in the annexation of Texas.

Looking around, we see, that the United States, favored by God and nature, is surely marching, with a step as regular as the eternal laws of nature, to its destined and ultimate extent; that there is her to fulfil—that is, the union and incorporation, in one great and mighty system, or one immense confederacy of regular republics, the whole of the continent of North America, with the islands around it, of which Hayti is one. We see that, at any rate, in Canada, the spirit has been awakened that will, in the course of a few years, lead to the republic of the Great North; and we see that the differences between England and the United States, respecting the 49th parallel in the Oregon Territory, in a short time will terminate in a manner long since contemplated and begun in reference to other portions of this continent, but as yet not united to this republic. Our government ought, in our view, to quietly settle that question by giving England all she asks or desires in the North—and a quarter of a country, all Oregon will, like a ripe fruit, fall into the lap of the United States, along with every other state or island of the North. The desirable end of all prosperity, peace and stable government in San Domingo, in Mexico and in the neighboring countries, will be reached by the coming events that already cast their shadows over the present and the future, and make the monarchies of the Old World look aghast.

The next news from San Domingo will be highly interesting, and we wait for it, through our special agent and correspondent, now in that island, with every probability of its being decisive of great events. With our special agents, both in San Domingo, in Cuba and in Mexico, we have already dispatched special correspondents to both these countries, to gather information and transmit news of great importance, even in advance of our own government at Washington.

records.headline: Highly Important from Hayti.
records.summary_en: Based on the provided excerpt, the newspaper reported on historical events involving the eastern part of the island of Hispaniola, detailing a January 6, 1801 convention between Governor Don Joaquin Garcia and a black general that allowed entry into St. Domingo. It described how the eastern inhabitants remained under French dominion through the commands of Generals Kerverseau and Ferrand while avoiding the massacres in other regions. Additionally, the excerpt noted that Dessalines's 1806 expedition to seize St. Domingo failed, meaning the eastern part was excluded from the subsequent Haitian constitution of 1806.

Consignó que los moradores del este permanecieron bajo soberanía francesa a órdenes de los generales Kerverseau y Ferrand, eludiendo las matanzas padecidas en otros parajes. Asentó por fin que la tentativa de Dessalines en 1806 para sojuzgar Santo Domingo resultó infructuosa, por cuya razón dicha banda no quedó comprendida en la subsecuente carta constitucional haitiana de 1806.

records.full_text:
Highly Important from Hayti.

The barque Hecia, Capt. Hoyt, from Port au Prince, arrived here on Saturday, from Port au Plata, with advices from each place to the 6th inst., have arrived in the last two days.

The intelligence received by them from our correspondents at St. Domingo City and Port au Prince, is of a very interesting and important character.

It appears by what we learn from Capt. Lake, of the Clara, that extensive preparations continued to be made at Port au Prince for the long expected final conflict. It was the opinion of the Captain and General Pierrot, that St. Jago must decide the issue in its results. Either the black or white race must soon rule the island of Hayti. It is impossible for both to live together as one nation.

This aspect of affairs assumes an additional importance from the fact that there is likely to be some difficulty with the Haytien government, owing to an indignity offered to a commercial agent of the U. S.

All the intelligence, however, that we have received by these arrivals, perhaps the most important and exciting is that relative to the Dominicans and the course of Mr. Hogan, our agent, and his very attentive correspondents. This intelligence is not only important to us whether or not the island of Hayti shall fall into the power of Hayti, but as affecting our own relations with France, and perhaps with another power in Europe.

Among other documents which have been furnished to us, are several containing a great many highly interesting facts connected with the mission of Mr. Hogan to St. Domingo. We present three or four of these papers, because they bear the marks of authenticity, and well merit the perusal of all our readers. It will be recollected that about a year ago, or more, we mentioned the arrival here of two agents from St. Domingo to our government, relative to the acknowledgment, by the United States, of the independence of the Dominican Republic. Our government, in consequence of that movement, induced Mr. Calhoun to despatch Mr. Hogan to St. Domingo, to examine into the condition and resources of that part of Hayti. It is not yet known what Mr. Hogan has returned home from his mission, but we have reason to believe that he has made his report to our government, and that the President and his Cabinet are deliberating in the matter, in order to ascertain the best course to pursue.

We give three of the documents which we have received:

The first is an abstract of a statement made by Mr. Hogan to our government. The second paper is a sketch of the Dominican Republic, written by a highly intelligent Dominican to Mr. Hogan, after his arrival at St. Domingo; and the third is a brief history of Hayti, sent to Mr. Hogan by a member of the Haytien Legislature.

Takes in all points of view, these papers open an important issue in our relations with Europe, and the future affair of the American continent. The island of Hayti is the most fertile of any in the Atlantic, and its value is considered so great, that France, having once owned the island to the French, they have been devising plans for some time back to gain a colony to them too valuable to lose; and we are looking by for its probable re-occupancy by France. Commercial men, belonging to France, who have been, for some time, residing in different parts of the island; and one has lately been seen foreignly lodged by the Dominicans for modeling a new flag; and this may afford a pretext for France to strike a blow, which may at once be subversive of the Haytien Republic. All this, however, we shall see, will, perhaps, be proper for the United States to be a sort of protector to one person at least of that island, in order to promote the easy growth of power on this continent. The mission of Mr. Hogan may enable our executive to place the Dominican Republic in such a strong and favorable light to our government, as to lead to its recognition of the independence of Hayti; and if we be the first in this recognition, that Republic will, of course, apart from her republican feelings and instincts, look up to the United States in preference to any other nation. This gives the whole matter an importance that it would not otherwise have. It is expected that, considering the great probabilities of the present war against the Haytiens, the whole island will fall into the American Union, and thus become one great Republic—the Island Republic of the world.

It is necessary, in this view of the news we have received, for our government to act decisively in the matter. It is necessary for us to prevent any intervention on the part of France, or any European nation, in the affairs of Hayti, as in the case of the Republic of Texas. There is no time to lose.

An Abstract of a Memoir delivered to the Secretary of State of the United States, by the Political Agent of the Dominican Republic, near the government at Washington.

WASHINGTON, Jan. 8, 1845.
To the Hon. JOHN C. CALHOUN,
Secretary of State of the United States.
Sir—The undersigned has the honor to address you, as Political Agent, for information respecting the Republic of Do-mingo.
2. The former Spanish part of St. Domingo remained under the Spanish dominion till the 30th of November, 1821, when it declared its independence of the mother country, which then occupied the western part of the island. On the 9th of February, 1822, the President of Hayti and Spanish part took occasion on the 27th February, 1844, by separating themselves from the Haytiens, and taking possession of the fortified places, where they established a government, under the name of the Central Junta, who directed the army, and commanding the district and the Haytien forces, who, a few days after, was obliged to evacuate the country.
3. The Dominicans took up their headquarters at Sabana Buey, on the river Ocoa, and erected two redoubts at the pass of El Numro to restrain the march of the aggressors, who would not venture to advance further; and on the 7th of July, at St. Jago, they were encountered and driven back with great loss.
4. The President of Hayti, Herard Riviere, and General Pierrot, on the 3d of March, near the city of Santiago de los Caballeros, when they were met by the Dominicans at Azua, while only one was wounded on the Dominican side. On the 7th of July, 1844, Gen. Riviere retreated to Azua, and on the 9th to Port au Prince, and the President of Hayti to Port au Prince, since which time no further aggressions have been committed.
5. The Dominican territory was then invaded through the south by the President of Hayti, Charles Riviere, under General Herard Riviere, who arrived at Azua, with 10,000 men. The Dominicans met them with 2,500 men, under command of Gen. Pedro Santana, of 2,500 men and three cannons. The battle began on the 19th of March, 1844, and lasted three hours. The Dominicans lost three killed, while more than 1,000 Haytiens were left dead on the field.
6. The Dominicans then took up their head quarters at Sabana Buey, on the river Ocoa, and erected two redoubts at the pass of El Numro to restrain the march of the aggressors, who would not venture to advance further; and on the 7th of July, at St. Jago, they were encountered and driven back with great loss.
7. The President of Hayti, Herard Riviere, and General Pierrot, on the 3d of March, near the city of Santiago de los Caballeros, when they were met by the Dominicans at Azua, while only one was wounded on the Dominican side. On the 7th of July, 1844, Gen. Riviere retreated to Azua, and on the 9th to Port au Prince, and the President of Hayti to Port au Prince, since which time no further aggressions have been committed.
8. On the 12th of May, 1844, the declaration of the independence and the response of the Dominicans were considered at a meeting of all the towns, and a central government then engaged in calling on the people to elect deputies to frame a constitution. The deputies met at St. Christoval on the 24th of September, 1844, and framed a constitution which consecrated those social principles which secure civil and political rights, as well as the admission of foreigners to civil and political rights.
9. On the 14th of November, 1844, the 13th of the month of November, Senor DON PEDRO SANTANA was inaugurated President, and Senores Manuel Cabral y Baez, Minister of War; Senores Bobadilla, Foreign Relations and Justice; Don Manuel Jimenes, Minister of Finance; and sentence of banishment passed against Juan Pablo Duarte, and General Don Manuel Jimenes, of War and Marine.
10. The people then elected members of the Senate and Chamber of Deputies.
11. All the public functionaries are elected for a fixed period.
12. The state owns own property, or are licensed to carry on some industry. The state owns the public domain, the officers of the civil and navy, are entitled to vote.
13. The legislative power is vested in two bodies, periodical electors, who constitute an electoral college in each province, who elect the members of the legislative power. In case of no majority, Congress elects the members.
14. The President and Vice President are appointed for four years by the Executive.
15. The Dominican territory is divided into five provinces: St. Domingo, Azua, Vega, and Santiago, with the island, extending from Lasbon, on Massacre river, to the mouth of the river Pedernales, both falling into the sea; the latter to the windward (west) of Beate island.
16. The country fertile in the productions of the West Indies, and contains gold, iron, and coal. Two great bays, which form ideal anchorages and can anchor in security, viz. the Bay of Samana, and the latter admitting the whole navy of Samana on the north, the latter admitting the whole world as well as pearl fishery.
17. The principal ports and places of trade are St. Domingo, Puerto de Plata, Azua, Samana, and Monte Christi.
18. A constant trade is kept up with the islands of St. Thomas, Curacoa, Jamaica, and also with England and Germany, whether is transported a large amount of mahogany, and nearly two-thirds of their hides.
19. A sufficient supply of sugar is made for the people, and could be made an article of export.
20. The principal articles of export are mahogany, lignum vitae, fustic, and other woods of dye, tobacco, hides, yellow and white wax, gum guacum, honey, and a small quantity of coffee.
21. St. Domingo is surrounded by walls and fortifications, with the necessary artillery, as well as the city of Santiago; the city of Puerto de Plata is also fortified, sufficiently. The cities of Azua are in progress, and fortifications are being made at other points on the frontier, towards the enemy. At all passages between the two countries, there are posts of observation and troops to prevent aggression.
22. St. Domingo has plenty of cannon and ammunition, and other articles of war, with an arsenal well supplied, and a navy of ten vessels, carrying from three to fifteen guns each, two schooners of large size, also four armed vessels; viz: one brig and three schooners, of 12 guns each.
23. The revenues from imports, &c., is sufficient to cover the expenses of the government, and the republic has no debt, except that of its own paper money, which it has put means in the mining operation, and after the cessation of the war.
24. The population is over 200,000, half of which are white, and the other half colored. They are intelligent, industrious, and good citizens. Those of the whites, whom are landed proprietors or old mechanics; are well off; their manners are European, and those of color, who are negroes, most of whom are free born. Slavery was abolished in 1822, and never after re-established.
25. The government is anxious to encourage foreign immigration, and will make grants of land to immigrants, and give great security, thus augmenting and attract the white population. The Dominicans will never consent to a union with Hayti, nor will they consent to live with the white Dominicans who emigrated in 1822. Those who have taken up arms against the country, and their government has not confiscated; this will be restored, and if they return to their country, without prejudice to the injury of the present heirs.
26. The Dominican Republic presents actual capacity to fulfill the obligations of an independent nation, as well as every claim to the sympathy of the United States, as well as every other with nations that may grant it their sympathy.
27. The Dominican Republic is an object of interesting case for contemplation. Its cause is noble, just and holy; it is defending itself against the barbarous invasions, especially those of the American continent. It is a war of extermination, carried on by Hayti, to prevent the vengeance of the Haytiens, who count half a million, and the Dominicans 200,000; the white population, consequently, from their superior numbers and force, would be massacred or driven from the country, and all those massacres and conflagrations must ensue, if not supported by foreign powers.
28. The fear of another invasion, ought not to prevent the acknowledgment of the Dominican Republic, because the Haytiens are not able to execute it, and humanity dictate the preservation of the Dominican State from destruction, as an act sanctioned by philanthropy and religion.
29. The Dominican Republic, ought to be recognized, a rights to a place among the family of nations, in consequence of its being the first city built by European colonists from magnanimous and Christian nations: from Spanish ancestors, who are justly considered, for their heroic traits, by all lovers of independence, as the founder of real liberty in the new world.
30. Without the assistance of foreign nations, the Republic of Dominica would be respected, and the vigor of its people will protect it.
31. This recognition may be resolved affirmatively, as there is no obstacle in the treaty of 1825, between France and Hayti, which never comprehended Dominican territory, as Spanish Santo Domingo was never recognized by the United States, as it never had legal possession, and could not be transferred by France to Hayti.
32. The Republic of Dominica should not be left in her present state, as her position is dangerous to the continent of America, whose independence has been recognized.
DOCTOR J. M. CAMINERO.

AN ABSTRACT OF A NOTE TO THE HON. C. A. CLINTON, POLITICAL AGENT OF ST. DOMINGO.
WASHINGTON, Jan. 25, 1845.
TO THE HON. C. A. CLINTON—
Sir:—
1. An addenda to his note of the 9th inst to show that the Dominican territory was never comprehended under the name of Hayti, nor under that of the Haytien Republic.
2. The Spanish part of the island remained under the dominion of Spain till 1821, when it took the title of Spanish Hayti, night of which Dr. Jose Nunez de Caceres, Lieutenant Governor, and Auditor of War, took command of St. Domingo.
3. A few days afterwards, Brigadier General Don Tomas Portes, with his officers, officers, embarked for Spain, Porto Rico and Cuba.
4. President Boyer, in 1822, under the pretext that the rest of the republic of Hayti, contributed to restrain and maintain the tranquility of Spanish Hayti, invaded it with a force of 12,000 men, for the purpose of subjugating the country and changing the French part. The political change had been effected without bloodshed, and in consequence of the popular mind was not made up on the question, and in a state of surprise and unprepared, Boyer conquered the country. The Spanish flag was then only flying in the north side, which was fomented by European Spaniards; Boyer marched from Monte Christi and Santiago, and entering into relations with Spanish Hayti, entered St. Domingo.
5. The President, Nunez, in December, communicated with Boyer, and stated that the towns had yielded to his terms for a treaty of alliance, offensive and defensive. Boyer replied that he was not coming as an enemy, but as a friend, and would be at St. Domingo; and on the 9th of February, styled Nunez, in Azua, General, Chief of the Spanish Haytien Republic, and stated his hopes had been disappointed, and caused the utmost consternation among the inhabitants.
6. In this state of things all the civil and military authorities submitted to Boyer, who took possession of Spanish Hayti. Spanish Hayti retained all its former laws, and sent to submit to the outrageous oppression, baseline, and tyranny of Boyer for 22 years. Spanish Hayti was, on the 27th of February, 1844, when the Dominicans again marched into St. Domingo, on the 12th of May following, the independent republic of Spanish Hayti was declared.
7. On the following day he caused his constitution to be proclaimed, which has not existed since 1816, for the Spanish part, which had never taken part in it, nor was represented in its formation. Spanish Hayti was completely different in character and customs from those of the Spaniards, while that of Spanish Hayti was European, or rather Spanish, as shown by posterior acts, and by the general spirit of independence, was displayed, and the same spirit and energy which took place in 1821, was displayed by certain numbers of this class.

ST. DOMINGO, June 10, 1845.
JOHN HOGAN, Esq., Commissioner of the United States, St. Domingo:
DEAR SIR—I have to acknowledge the receipt of your favor letter of the 20th inst. I must first thank you for your kind wishes for my health, and your congratulations on my safe arrival, and assure you that I shall be happy to serve you or your republic, and give you my opinion concerning the several questions you have submitted to me:
1st. What is the political and moral condition of that portion of the island?
2d. What is the nature of its constitution, laws, and government?
3d. What is the population of the Republic?
1st. What is the political and moral condition of that portion of the island?—In order to answer this question, I must give you a short sketch of our former condition. We have been since the discovery of this island, Spanish subjects, and consequently have partaken of the spirit, character and habits of Spanish nations. Under the Spanish government, although Spanish policy did not tend to improve the country, yet we enjoyed the protection of the laws, and were under a moral influence, which maintained order, and made the inhabitants respectful to the laws, and attached to the soil. We had also a large clerical body, which maintained religion, and formed the morals of the people. St. Domingo was an Arch-episcopate, and the Archbishop had five suffragan bishops. It was also a primate of the Indies. We had a university, which produced men of great learning and talents; we had also many convents of both sexes, and many primary schools. Religious orders were established, and parish churches were erected in every parish. I must give you a list of our churches and their present state:
1. The Cathedral of St. Domingo, with 32 priests.
2. The church of St. Miguel, with a curate.
3. The city of Bayaguana, with its curate living in the town.
4. In the city of Monte Plata, a church with its curate, and a curate in Boya.
5. A church, very handsome, in the village of Boya, under the care of the curate of Monte Plata. It has a blessed image of Holy Virgin, with its church, very handsome, much frequented by travelers, under the particular protection of Our Lady of Grace, to whom all uneducated parish pay homage.
6. The city of the Holy Cross of Seibo, with a splendid church, and its curate, living in the town, and a curate in Higuey.
7. A country seat with a church and a curate, dedicated to the Lady of Altagracia.
8. The town of Salvaleon, with its curate and church, tied to the Lady of Merced.
9. The city of Hato Mayor, with its curate and church, living in the town.
10. Church belonging to the same parish.
11. The city of St. Antonio de Guerra, a curate.
12. The town of San Jose de los Llanos, a curate, and St. Charles, of Teneriffe, with a curate, who is, for want of a church, officiating in the chapel of St. Lazaro, being in repairing the damage caused in the church by, as is said, an earthquake.
13. The city of San Christoval, with a curate.
14. Bani, with its church and its curate—a person who was educated in Spain.
15. The town of Compostella, of Azua, with its church and curate, who also officiates in the parish of Neyba.
16. Neyba, with its church and curate.
17. San Juan de Maguana.
18. The convent of St. Francis, fronting a church, newly repaired by the people.
19. San Jose de Ocoa, a new parish, the church of which was injured by the earthquake now being repaired.
20. The city of La Vega, with a curate and handsome church, which was built after the earthquake of 1842.
21. The City of Conception, with its curate—out of the town—the church was destroyed by the earthquake of 1842.
22. The city of Santiago de los Caballeros, with a large and splendid church, which was destroyed by the earthquake, but the people, by their own subscriptions and labor, have built a temporary church. The church of Altagracia, which was destroyed by the earthquake, but the neighborhood have always supplied some means for repairing the damage.
23. The city of Santiago and its districts are destroyed, and their churches in ruins, with the exception of the church of St. Jago, which has a curate. The districts of Sabaneta, Guayubin, San Jose de las Matas, and Altabacoa, and risings of cattle—consequently rich in livestock, and producing mahogany and tobacco; with the exception that were known as the large convent and the little convent, with their curates.
24. The city of St. Philip of Puerto Plata, with its curious and splendid church, which has a curate; but, being in ruins, they have been obliged to build a temporary one; also the parish of Monte Christi, which is in ruins, and its curate, two leagues from that a hermitage.
This was the state of things when Boyer invaded us, and although he declared that he would respect our rights, he forced the clergy to leave the country, by taking away their property, and giving them a small pittance, which would not support them; so that our population was left without a priest, without religious instructions, and without schools. Our clergy were reduced to six or eight priests, and these were aged men, and could not visit the parishes. Boyer, seeing the consequence of his conduct, permitted some foreign priests to enter, but they were men without morals and without learning; and, taking advantage of the ignorance of the people, they committed the most disgraceful acts; but now our government has taken measures to remedy these evils, and has sent a mission to His Holiness the Pope to obtain priests, and has also established primary schools in all the towns, and we have now a college in this city, where the youth are instructed in all the branches of education.
Under the Haytien government, the spirit of religion was destroyed, and the people fell into a state of total indifference and opposition of the government has been broken, and the people have returned to their former habits. It is true that our churches are in a very bad state, owing to account of political motions, and the famous earthquake of 1842, when almost all of them were destroyed or damaged; and those that were repaired, were, during the revolution, cost uselessly, owing to the Haytiens using them for barracks; but the government, although poor, has appropriated a sum of money to repair some of these buildings for synagogues; and nothing was left for our churches. The Haytiens did not encourage any movement of divine worship; but on the contrary, to throw obstacles in the way of the Catholic religion, and to favor the See of Rome. It appears that the intention was to destroy our religion, and to establish the Haytien religion, which is a mixture of African superstitions, and it was the design of the Haytien part, to have missionaries and other sects of religion to establish themselves in the country, and the Pope who had no right there except the executive itself, to interfere with the religious affairs.
With this in trust I have given you information with regard to the first part of your letter. It is true that the people of this part of the island have been brought up in the habit of having religion in its purity, and its pastors to be aquin with their flock, and to give them good advice, and although they have been left without priests, yet they retained their superstitions rites, with some exterior forms of our religion; and, since our independence, they have returned to their former habits. My opinion is that the people of this country are capable of being led to a high state of civilization, if they have a good government, and good priests to instruct them, and I am happy to inform you, that since our independence, our government has taken measures to promote education and religion, and I hope that in a short time we shall see the fruits of their labors.
I remain, dear sir, &c.,
Your most obt. servant,
DR. JOHN H. FRELIGH, Member of the Legislature of St. Domingo.

2d. What is the nature of its constitution, laws, and government?—I have already spoken of the spirit of independence which existed in the Spanish part of St. Domingo. It was this spirit which induced the people to throw off the Spanish yoke in 1821, and to declare their independence. It was the same spirit which led them to resist the invasion of Boyer in 1822, and although they were obliged to submit to superior force, they never lost sight of their independence. During the long period of twenty-two years, they were subjected to the most oppressive tyranny, and were deprived of all their rights; but their spirit was not broken, and when the revolution of 1843 broke out in Hayti, they availed themselves of the opportunity, and declared their independence on the 27th of February, 1844.
After having declared their independence, they formed a provisional government, which was called the Central Executive Junta. This junta was composed of eleven members, chosen from the different provinces, and was charged with the government of the country until a constitution could be formed. The junta immediately took measures to organize the army, and to defend the country against the Haytiens, who were preparing to invade it. They also issued a decree for the election of deputies to a constituent assembly, which was to frame a constitution for the republic.
The constituent assembly met at San Cristobal on the 24th of September, 1844. It was composed of twenty-four members—six from the Santo Domingo province, six from Azua, six from La Vega, and six from Santiago. The assembly elected its officers, and appointed a committee to draft a constitution. The committee presented its report, and after a long and animated discussion, the constitution was adopted on the 6th of November, 1844.
This constitution is framed on the model of that of the United States, with such modifications as were thought necessary to adapt it to the circumstances of the country. It establishes a representative, republican, and democratic government, divided into three branches—the legislative, executive, and judicial. The legislative power is vested in a congress, composed of a senate and a chamber of deputies. The senate is composed of five members—one from each province—who are elected for six years, one-third of the number being renewed every two years. The chamber of deputies is composed of fifteen members—three from each province—who are elected for four years, one-half of the number being renewed every two years. The congress meets annually on the 1st of February, and its sessions last for three months.
The executive power is vested in a president, who is elected for four years by the electoral colleges of the provinces. He is assisted by a council of ministers, composed of four secretaries of state—one of war and marine, one of foreign relations and justice, one of finance, and one of the interior and public instruction. The president is the commander-in-chief of the army and navy, and is charged with the execution of the laws and the administration of the government.
The judicial power is vested in a supreme court of justice, and in such inferior courts as may be established by law. The supreme court is composed of a president and four judges, who are appointed by the senate on the nomination of the president. The judges hold their offices during good behavior.
The constitution also contains a bill of rights, which guarantees to all the inhabitants of the republic civil and political liberty, equality before the law, security of person and property, the liberty of the press, the right of petition, and the free exercise of religion. It also abolishes slavery forever, and declares that all persons born in the republic, or who may be naturalized, are citizens.
Having given you a short sketch of our constitution, I will now speak of our laws and government. Under the Spanish government, the laws of Spain were in force in the country, and after our independence in 1821, those laws were continued in force until they were modified or repealed by the legislature. Under the Haytien government, the French codes were introduced, and were continued in force until our independence in 1844. The present government has appointed a commission to revise and codify the laws, and in the meantime, the French codes, with such modifications as have been made by our legislature, continue to be the law of the land.
The government of the republic is now fully organized, and is administered with wisdom and firmness. The president, General Pedro Santana, is a man of great energy and talent, and possesses the confidence of the whole nation. He has succeeded in restoring order and tranquility in the country, and in organizing the army and navy, so as to be prepared for any emergency. The finances of the republic are also in a prosperous condition, and the revenue is sufficient to meet all the expenses of the government.

3d. What is the population of the Republic?—In the absence of an official census, it is difficult to give the exact number of the population of the republic; but from the best information I have been able to obtain, I think it may be estimated at about 200,000 souls, divided as follows:
White population . . . 100,000
Colored population . . . 100,000
Total . . . 200,000
The white population is composed of descendants of Spanish colonists, and of European immigrants who have settled in the country at different periods. The colored population is composed of mulattoes and blacks, most of whom are free born, slavery having been abolished in 1822. The people of both races live together in harmony, and enjoy the same civil and political rights.
In conclusion, I will add a few words respecting the whole island of Hayti. The island was formerly divided between France and Spain, the western part belonging to France, and the eastern part to Spain. In 1795, by the treaty of Basle, Spain ceded her portion of the island to France, and the whole island became a French colony. In 1801, Toussaint Louverture, Commandant of the province and regional chief of the north, under pretext of executing the treaty of Basle, set out from St. Jago in the northern part, to march against the east with 10,000 men. A convention held between him and the Governor, Don Joaquin Garcia, the 6th of January, 1801, permitted the black General to enter St. Domingo 30 days after. This is how France became master of all the island. At the time of the war of independence the eastern part of the island took no part in it. The expedition of Le Clerc had placed before the capital of Hispaniola Gen. Kerverseau, who was well received...

[The article proceeds with a detailed historical account of Haytien and Dominican rulers, including Dessalines, Christophe, Petion, Boyer, and Santana, outlining political developments, constitutional changes, legislative structures, military forces, and population breakdowns for the whole island.]

The population is found divided:
North . . . 250,000
West . . . 100,000
South . . . 90,000

records.full_text:
To the Hon. John C. Calhoun, Secretary of State of the United States.
1. An addenda to his note of the 8th inst. to show that the union of the Spanish part, in 1822, with Hayti, was not voluntarily, but forcibly produced.
2. The Spanish part of the Island remained under the government of Spain until the 30th Nov. 1821, on the night of which Dr. Jose Nunez de Caceres, Lieutenant Governor, raised the standard of independence in St. Domingo.
3. A few days afterwards, Brigadier General Don Pasqual Real, together with his officers, embarked for Spain, Porto Rico and Cuba.
4. The inhabitants of Spanish Hayti, perceiving soon that the republic of Hayti, contributed to restrain and even check the progress of a people far superior to those occupying the French part. The political change had not been brought about by them; because, in fact, the popular mind was not made up on the question; and in a few days after, national independence was proclaimed in several towns on the north side, which was fomented by European Spaniards, assisted by the inhabitants, starting at the same time from St. Raphael, Monte Cristi and Santiago, and entering into relations with the Spanish authorities.
5. The President, Nunez, in December, communicated to President Boyer certain ideas of the people, and made overtures to him for a treaty of alliance, offensive and defensive, and for commercial and other relations; to which the latter replied, that he would never tolerate, in the newly styled Republic of Hayti, the government of Dr. Nunez, in 1822, political chief of the Spanish part, and the other authorities, and that he meant to hoist the Haytian flag, with threats in case of refusal.
6. The Spanish part appealed to France, after all her hopes had been disappointed, and caused the utmost consternation in the public mind.
7. In this state of things all the civil and military authorities, being convinced of their inability to resist the Haytian army, which was then on the frontier, and being hesitant to submit to the unpropitious union, thus forced upon them, the Haytian flag was hoisted, and President Boyer made his entrance into St. Domingo, on the 12th of February, 1822, at the head of 12,000 men, without resistance.
8. On the following day he caused his constitution to be proclaimed, which had existed since 1816, for the French part only. By that constitution, and by the laws which followed, the laws and customs of a people different in character and customs from those of the Spaniards, were forced upon the inhabitants of the Spanish part, as shown by posterior acts, and by the general spirit of the people, which was always to separate and expel the Haytians forever from the Dominican territory.
9. The Haytians, from the first moment of their entry, took possession of the property of the Spanish part; that they have always been the masters of the soil; that they have destroyed the property of the inhabitants of the territory, to which they are accustomed from their infancy; and that this state of things has been the constant cause of opposition to throw off the yoke of the Haytians, and in the end, the inhabitants of the Spanish part, with the same resolution, and displayed the same spirit and desire to recover their independence, as they did in the certain numbers of this class.
