ject of my first letter. But on arriving and making various inquiries, relative thereto, and after carefully looking over the state of the country, I was thoroughly satisfied of the perfectly tranquilized state of this city and its inhabitants, which had been represented to me as being in a state of siege. A very intelligent merchant, and one who had a considerable stake in the issue of events, said to me, the plot did not give them four-and-twenty hours uneasiness.

The principal facts concerning it are briefly the following, which I have gathered on the spot, and from authentic sources. On the 21 of December last, the President, receiving information through several individuals, that a conspiracy was on foot in this city to throw off the Haitian yoke. He immediately summoned a cabinet council of the principal officers of state, to take measures to secure the city and put it in a state of defence; and measures were forthwith taken to disarm the troops and the citizens who volunteered with them, and a number of the principal citizens were arrested at the command of the military authorities.

On the morning of the 22d, on the reassembly of the cabinet, the officer in command of the garrison, the officer charged with making the inquiries, relative thereto, reported that no plot existed, as the result of them thus far, the discoveries made, showed that no plot existed. He then present in the council, and who had officially issued or countersigned the order for these very measures, and measures were forthwith taken which he had called for, was at the head of the conspiracy. He was immediately arrested, with several others, and conveyed away to prison. A brother of his, who was also arrested, and four or five several others, to the number of about nine, were brought to trial before a military commission, composed of members of congress, judges of the court, officers of the army, and private citizens; and four of the number, including the two brothers, were convicted of the crime of high treason, and condemned to death. They were accordingly executed on the morning of the 23d instant. Several of the others were subsequently banished the country.

Such was the end of the affair. The firmness, energy, and decision with which the government acted on the occasion, at their first discovery, and meeting the emergency, inspired all, I believe, and with good reason, with a thorough conviction of its ability to maintain its authority. Towards evening the consternation was great and universal. Every preparation had been made to resist an attack, which, in such cases, rumor, with its thousand surmises, had magnified into a formidable one. The foreign traders, merchants, all armed to sustain the government, and preserve their property from the plunder with which they were threatened. But the lapse of a very few hours brought back order and tranquility; and though business was somewhat paralyzed by the event, it soon recovered its former tone as far as these had disturbed it.

The effect of the plot, however, will still continue to be felt, and with for some time to come. Besides the cost of the military force, which had mostly been sent to the city, the government paper fell about fifty per cent. in value, causing a necessity, for apart for the purpose of encouraging and effecting foreign immigration, the withdrawal of much of the rural population--sparse and scanty at best--from their agricultural avocations, to serve as additions to the army, caused a necessity for the interruption to that branch of domestic industry, and a consequent diminution in the corresponding productions, together with a proportionate advance in the price of the necessaries of subsistence; a calamity, of course, to a country that imports a very large proportion of these necessaries.

As regards the state of the currency--which after all is the pulse of the political system--so far as affected by these disturbances, I will briefly refer to it. During the early part of the first two months of my absence, which included that in which the affair took place, the currency depreciated only about as much as it had done during the three preceding months, or about five per cent; and stayed there, and during the last two or three months has recovered its former position.

Thus much, by way of anticipation. The history, political organization, the condition and prospects of the Dominican Republic, will form the subject of the remainder of this letter, and of the succeeding ones.

For about a century and a half after the first discovery of Spanish colony, Columbus had founded the first settlement in the island, until the buccaneers--that hybrid race of adventurers, who have so often been written, and written about, but whom so little is correctly known--commenced their incursions into the north and west portions of the island in quest of the cattle which ran wild in immense herds over its rich plains; and finally formed settlements at the western end.

As these adventurers were mostly French, that nation began to regard them as a colony of her own; and in the treaty of Ryswick, she obtained from Spain, the cession of that portion of the island, comprising nearly one-third of its whole extent. The two colonies came thus to be posssessors, and at long intervals, and remained so separate and distinct, the one a dependence of Spain, the other of France, until 1795, which, so at the period of the memorable revolt of the blacks, and massacre of the whites, in the French part, in 1791. At that period, the latter colony had attained a high degree of prosperity, while the Spanish colony, of which this city was the capital, which had been languishing for nearly two centuries under a very partial and inefficient system of practiced agriculture. Slavery existed in this as well as in the French part of the island; but the condition of the slaves, towards the end of the present century, were there still existing in Spanish colony, was far different from the severe, forced labor, which in the other part produced those immense crops of sugar, coffee, and indigo, for the revolt which in the other part resulted in the independence of the black population, and white race, did not extend to this portion, or, at least, to any such extent or degree as to affect the relative position of the different races.

Meanwhile the year 1795, France, which was still at war with Spain, obtained by treaty the cession of the Spanish colony, on the island, by maintaining a desperate struggle to retain possession of her own colony in the island, obtained by cession from Spain the nominal possession of Spanish colony also. But, on the final triumph of the blacks in the former, and the establishment there of the Haitian governments (of which there were at first two), the Spanish population, who had ever preserved, as they still do, their separate position and ancient social and political institutions against the claims and attempts of the black governments of the west. With the loss of her own colony, France lost all foothold on the island thenceforward, with the exception of one or two years' occupation of this city in the early part of this century.

Here he remained until the winter of 1843-4, when the Spanish portion of the inhabitants of this city, who had often sought in vain for an opportunity to throw off the Haitian yoke, suddenly found a favorable one, on occasion of the main body of the Haitian troops being withdrawn for some domestic purpose to the other end of the island, only a few hundred being left in the fort to guard and hold the city. This juncture gert on the unsuspicious garrison, besieged it within the fort, after gaining possession of the city and which they compelled it to capitulate, allowing it to return home.

From this period, the existence of the republic, or, to speak more accurately, its style and duties were assumed by the central junta, or committee, of this city, consisting of its president, vice, president, and eight members, which had organized and nurtured the revolutionary movement. On the 16th of January, 1844, this body published a manifesto setting forth the grievances and oppressions they had suffered under the Haitian rule, they expressed their determination to submit to them no longer, incline their enemies to a just and reasonable settlement of the difficulty, but to avoid the effusion of blood and the horrors of a calamitous war, expressing their readiness to defend their rights, which, if begun, shall, if the case calls for it, be several of the succeeding ones.

On the 9th of March following, the same executive body, in an address to the inhabitants, accompanied with a respectful and dignified address, to the President of the republic of Haiti. In this address, they speak as the organs of the "people of the Spanish part of the island," and reiterate the sentiments of devotion to the existing mating that they thus notify him of their determination, so far as the Dominican people are concerned, that he may act as the occasion may seem to require. On the 15th of March, the junta, in the month, published an address to the resident foreigners, assuring them of their intention of respecting the inviolability of their persons and property, and assuring them of protection under the new government. These guarantees have never, I believe, been violated in the cast of their persons or legitimate rights.

In April, 1844, the Haitian government, disposed to relinquish their former possession without a struggle, sent a force of 15,000 to 20,000 men, an army to the frontier, where it found the Dominicans prepared for them, and eager to defend their presents to the foreign press. Towards the middle On the 11th of the month of March, in which the Dominicans were successful, and forced them to retreat against great numerical odds. The issue of these battles was so far satisfactory to them, and though the war still nominally continues, and has since that time, keeping a considerable force ment along the frontier, as a measure of security, very little fighting has occurred.

The independence, or separation, as it is more properly termed, took place on the 27th of February, 1844; and the name assumed by the new state was that of the Dominican Republic.

Subsequently to the victories which secured the quiet possession of the country, and after order had had been commanded on the frontier, and under whom the government had been conducted, the inhabitants, without distinction of color, had triumphed over their oppressors, sending out of a faction opposed to the Provisional government re-established the authority of the Republic.

The duty of drafting a constitution for the new state, was committed to a convention, which when completed, was published with great solemnity, and ceremony on the 24th of November, 1844.

Having thus brought down the history of the domination of Haitians, the people of the old Spanish part of St. Domingo, have asserted their independence, and sought to assume a place among nations. And as the political position of this island will, most assuredly, some day, and that, probably, not very distant, awaken the attention of our people and government, I shall, besides, in my next, give an outline of the Constitution, and of some of the organic laws enacted to carry out its provisions.

COUPEUR.

records.summary_en: *The New York Herald* detailed provisions of the Dominican constitution regarding foreigners, citizenship, and civil rights. Foreigners of non-hostile nations who practiced useful industries were granted civil rights and could gain residency, with requirements reduced for those marrying Dominican citizens or establishing agricultural estates worth at least $12,000. records.chapter_es: Una república en busca de reconocimiento
records.full_text:
As promised in my last, I now proceed to give a sketch of the constitution of the Dominican Republic, embracing an occasional reference to laws subsequently enacted to carry out some of its provisions. This instrument, the essential features of which seem to have been derived in part from the constitution of the United States, and in part from the French charter of 1830, declares, in the first place, that the Dominicans erect themselves into a free, independent, and sovereign nation, under a government essentially civil, republican, popular, representative and responsible; and defines the extent of the national territory, which, it states, embraces the Spanish part of the island of St. Domingo and its adjacent isles—to be identical with those which in 1793 divided it on the west from the French part. That is, embracing about seventy-five-hundredths (75-100) of the whole area of the island.
All persons are declared to be citizens who were born in the territory, and were residents at the time of the drafting of the constitution; so also the children of all Spanish Dominican absentees and their descendants, who, not having borne arms against the new State, return to reside within its limits. These are declared capable of becoming citizens—first, who acquire in the republic real estate of the value of six thousand dollars; and secondly, those who, by their personal labor, form in the republic agricultural establishments, under the title of proprietors, or owners. But foreigners commissioned in these last two classes cannot enjoy political rights until after a residence of six years in the territory. This period, however, is reduced to three years—first, in favor of those foreigners who marry a Dominican wife; and secondly, of those who form agricultural establishments, the value of which amounts to at least twelve thousand dollars. All foreigners not belonging to a hostile nation are declared to be admissible into the territory of the republic, if they profess any art, science, or useful industry, or possess any capital; and they are, from the time of being declared to be under the safeguard of the nation, to enjoy all civil rights from the moment they step upon the soil of the republic.
The Dominicans are declared to be free, and to remain free, and equal in right, slavery being forever abolished; and all are eligible to public offices and employments. Individual liberty is secured. No one can be prosecuted except in conformity with a pre-existing law, and in the manner it prescribes. Nor can any one be imprisoned, unless taken in the criminal act, except by the order of a judge, setting forth the cause of the arrest; and this must be made known to the party arrested at once, or at latest within the space of forty-eight hours. The confiscation of property can never be imposed as a punishment for, or consequence of, crime; nor can private property be taken from its owner, except where the public good requires it, in which case he is to be indemnified its value, to be ascertained by a just appraisement.
The residence or dwelling-house of every citizen is declared to be sacred and inviolable asylum, and no domiciliary visits are to be allowed, except in cases provided for by law, and with the formalities it prescribes. No censorship of the press is to be allowed. All Dominicans are permitted to print and publish freely whatever they think proper, being responsible solely for the abuse of the right to the laws.
A subsequent law has defined what shall constitute such an abuse, and limits it to five classes of cases, namely—publishing maxims or doctrines that tend directly to destroy or subvert the religion of the State, or the constitution of the republic; publishing maxims or doctrines intended to excite rebellion, or cause any disturbance of the public tranquility; making an insult to the character of any law or legitimate authority, or instigating to this violation by invective or satire; publishing obscene writings, or such as are contrary to good morals; injuring any individual or individuals by infamous libels, stigmatising his or their private character, or wounding their honor or reputation. The author or editor of such impure matter is allowed, in exculpation, to offer in evidence the truth of his charges. Allegations against public functionaries are embraced within the same provision.
The constitution proceeds to declare that no person can be compelled to do what the law does not command, nor prevented from doing what it does not forbid. Public instruction is to be established, common to all the citizens, and gratuitous in all the elementary branches. Schools for this purpose are to be established throughout the territory of the republic. The details in regard to those elementary branches, as well as the higher ones, are to be regulated by law. To carry out this provision of the constitution, the Congress passed a law the following year, establishing one elementary school in each of the communes (or parishes) of the republic, and two in each provincial capital. These last can be transformed into higher schools, if expediency suggests it. In these elementary schools are to be taught the principles of religion, the Castilian grammar, and the other usual branches of a common school education. The law places the general supervision of education under the Minister of Public Instruction.
The Dominicans are declared to possess the right of forming associations—of peaceably assembling, without arms—and of petition to the President, or to the National Congress, as individuals, one or many, but not in the name of a collective or corporate body. No law can be made to have a retroactive effect; nor can any be enacted that is contrary to the spirit or letter of this constitution. In cases of doubt the latter is to prevail.
The Apostolic Roman Catholic religion is declared to be religion of the State; its ministers, in whatever pertains to the exercise of the ecclesiastical ministry, are dependent solely on the properly constituted authority. The article stops here, nor does the constitution say anything whatever on the subject of religious toleration, or make any allusion to other forms or doctrine of religious faith. I shall again advert to this subject in the latter part of this letter.
The sovereignty is declared to reside in the universal body of the citizens, and is to be exercised by three delegated powers, corresponding to the three co-ordinate branches of our own government. The members of both houses of the national congress are chosen for six years. The upper house, or as it is called the conservative council, consists of five members, one for each province of the republic, and is renewed integrally every six years. The lower house, or tribunate, is composed of fifteen members, apportioned by law according to the population of each province. Both bodies are again chosen by vote of the people in their primary assemblies. The qualifications of a voter are citizenship and the possession in fee of real estate, or in place of the last, the exercise of some public office or employment, the profession of some science, art, or useful industry, or the proprietorship of land for years of an agricultural establishment in active cultivation. In these primary assemblies are likewise chosen the members of the Ayuntamientos (or town councils) of each commune. Each of these last mentioned bodies is presided over by the alcalde, who is chosen by the body from among its members.
The national mercantile colors designated, and now used, are blue and red, placed in diagonal squares, separated from each other by a white cross. The military colors bear besides, in their centre, the arms of the republic, which are a cross, at the foot of which is an open volume of the gospels, and both of these rising from amidst a trophy of arms, with the emblem of liberty on winged with a laurel, and under the following device, Dios, Patria y Libertad, Republica Dominicana. (God, our country and liberty, Dominican Republic.)
There are four national festivals, one commemorating the separation; two, important victories; and the fourth, the publication of the present constitution.
Under the article on religion, I remarked that I should again allude to that subject.
The assembly who framed the constitution were divided in opinion in regard to religious toleration; some being in favor of it, but the majority opposed to such a concession, and in favor of inserting in the article on religion a clause prohibiting the public exercise of any other religion than that adopted as the state religion. The former, on the other hand, wished to have inserted an express declaration of religious freedom. Now this question deeply interested a portion—though a very small one—of the citizens, namely, the naturalized people of color, of whom I shall speak in a subsequent communication. These were Protestants, and had never failed to see, that in the Haitian supremacy, under an express guaranty, thus far sacredly kept, of toleration they possessed a right to fear for their faith and its public exercise. The discussion of the question of toleration in the assembly awakened their apprehensions, and many, if not most of them, were about making up their minds to fly to the other part of the island—as many of their fellow-countrymen had already done on the breaking out of the revolution—from a conviction that fear, later, the same cause being applied, their own rights of person and property derived from them, would no longer be respected. On more sober consideration, however, better assurances were given them that the old guaranties, given to them favor by the late government, would be religiously respected by the new one. Soon after, therefore, an assuring that the article on religion had been inserted in its present shape—which I mentioned in giving the sketch of the constitution to acquiesce in—they again took the alarm; but their apprehensions were now finally allayed by their being referred to a previous article, which declared, as has been seen, that no person could be compelled to do what the law did not command, nor prevented from doing what it did not forbid; although the article certainly does not cover, in terms, the whole ground, since the word "law," which might be legitimately interpreted to mean any future as well as present enactment, is used in it, and not the term "constitution." But though this circumstance might be thought to afford advantage ground, and justify the alarm in the enemies of toleration, if any such now exist in any number, it is too late to take any advantage of it, it being but justice to state that it is well understood and acknowledged on all hands that religious toleration is a fundamental law of the republic, though nowhere expressed so to be, within the writer's knowledge, in written terms; and no guaranty of the kind can anywhere be relied upon as more sacred and irrevocable than this.
In regard to this matter, I might have entered much further into minute, and, in some respects, instructive as well as curious details, having at my command well-accredited materials for this purpose; for the peculiar facility and faculty of getting into the secrets of cabinets, councils, and conclaves, not apparent to the uninitiated, is not confined to your home correspondents; though it certainly is to be hoped that it is there only they are used to get impressions for it. His sole reason for not doing so is, that his motives might be brought in to question by persons of whom he does not entertain.
The writer would further and finally remark on this topic, that so far as he has been able to observe and judge, a tone of sentiment and a degree of liberality exist, both throughout the different branches of the government and among the better informed portions of the community at least, such as we are not accustomed to look for, or suppose to exist in American governments and communities south of our own country.
CELERES.

Affairs in the Dominican Republic.
CITY OF ST. DOMINGO, May 16, 1848.

As promised in my last, I now proceed to give a sketch of the constitution of the Dominican Republic, embracing an occasional reference to laws subsequently enacted to carry out some of its provisions. This instrument, the essential features of which seem to have been derived in part from the constitution of the United States, and in part from the French charter of 1830, declares, in the first place, that the Dominicans erect themselves into a free, independent, and sovereign nation, under a government essentially civil, republican, popular, representative and responsible; and defines the limits of the national territory, which, it states, embraces the Spanish part of the island of St. Domingo and its adjacent isles—to be identical with those which, in 1793, divided the east from the West from the French part. That, is embracing about two-thirds—perhaps a little more—of the whole area of the island.

Citizenship is declared to belong to citizens who were born in the territory, and were residents at the time of the drafting of the constitution; as also the children of all Spanish Dominican absentees who have returned, or who, not having taken arms against the new State, return to reside within its limits. There are two classes of aliens becoming citizens—first, who require a residence of two years in the state, if they acquire real estate; and secondly, those who, by their personal labor, farm or set up agricultural establishments, under the title of proprietors, or owners. But the descendants of any part of the African classes cannot enjoy political rights until after a residence of six years in the territory. This exception was, it is said, introduced in favor of those foreigners who marry a Dominican woman, or bring into the republic capital or cultural establishments, the value of which amounts to a certain sum—a privilege denied to those who, not belonging to a hostile nation are declared to be citizens at the end of two years, provided they profess any art, science, or useful industry, or possess real estate or capital—foreigners generally being declared to be under the safeguard of the national honor from the moment they step upon the soil of the republic.

The Dominican people are declared to be equal in rights, and equal in right, slavery being forever abolished, as also all hereditary titles, offices and employments. Individual liberty is protected. No one can be prosecuted except in conformity with rules of law, nor in any other form than it prescribes. Nor can any one be imprisoned, unless taken in the flagrant act, except on the order of a judge, setting forth the cause of the arrest; and this must be made known to the party arrested at once, or at least within the space of forty-eight hours. The confiscation of property can never be imposed as a punishment for political offenses, nor can any portion of property be taken from its owner, except where the public good requires it, in which case he must be indemnified its value, to be ascertained by a just standard.

The residence or dwelling-house of every citizen is declared to be a sacred and inviolable asylum, and no domiciliary visits are to be allowed, except in cases provided for by law, and with all formalities it prescribes. No censorship of the press is to be allowed. All Dominicans are permitted to print and publish freely whatever they think proper, being responsible solely for the abuse of that right to the laws.

A subsequent law has defined what shall constitute abuse of the press, and limits it to five classes of cases, namely—publishing maxims or doctrines that tend directly to destroy or subvert the religion of the State, or the constitution of the republic; publishing maxims or doctrines intended to excite rebellion, or cause any disturbance of the public tranquility; inciting hatred to the person of any law or legitimate authority, or inciting to this violation by invective or satire; publishing obscene writings, or such as are contrary to good morals; injuring any individual or individuals by infamous libels, stigmatizing his or their private character, or wounding their honor or reputation. The author or editor of such writings must be sentenced, in exculpation, to offer in evidence the truth of his charges. Allegations against public functionaries are embraced within the same provision.

The constitution proceeds to declare that no person can be compelled to do what the law does not command, nor prevented from doing what it does not forbid. Public instruction is to be established, common to all the citizens, and gratuitous in all the elementary schools. Schools for this purpose are to be established throughout the territory of the republic. The details in regard to those elementary schools, as well as the higher ones, are to be regulated by law. To carry out this provision of the constitution, the Congress passed a law the following year, establishing one elementary school in each of the communes (or parishes) of the republic, and two in each provincial capital, with the permission to convert these into higher schools, if expediency suggests it. In these elementary schools are to be taught the principles of religion, the Castilian grammar, and the other usual branches of a common school education. The law places the general supervision of public education under the Minister of Public Instruction.

The Dominicans are declared to possess the right of forming associations of peaceably assembling, without arms—and of petition to the President, or to the National Congress, as individuals, or one many, but not in the name of a collective or corporate body. No law can be made to have a retroactive effect; nor can any be enacted that is contrary to the spirit or letter of this constitution. In cases of doubt the letter is to prevail.

The Apostolic Roman Catholic religion is declared to be the religion of the State; its ministers, enjoying a salary from the public treasury, or an ecclesiastical stipend, are dependent solely on the prelate canonically appointed. The article stops here, nor does the constitution say anything whatever on the subject of freedom of worship, or make any allusion to other forms or doctrine of religious faith. I shall again revert to this subject in the latter part of this letter.

The sovereignty is declared to reside in the universal body of the citizens, and is to be exercised by three delegated powers, corresponding to the three co-ordinate branches of our own government. The members of both houses of the national congress are chosen for six years. The upper house, or as it is called the conservative council, consists of five members, one for each province of the republic, and is renewed integrally every six years. The lower house, or tribunal, is composed of fifteen members, apportioned by law bodies are again chosen by the vote of people in their primary assemblies. The qualifications of a voter are citizenship and the possession in fee of real estate, or in place of the last, the exercise of some public office or employment, the profession of some science, art, or useful industry, or the possession of a lease for a farm or an agricultural establishment in active cultivation. In these primary assemblies are likewise chosen the members of the Ayuntamientos (or town councils) of each commune. Each of these last mentioned bodies is presided over by the alcalde, who is chosen by the body from among its members.

The national mercantile colors designated, and blue and red, distributed in four alternate squares, separated from each other by a white cross. The military colors bear besides, in their centre, the arms of the republic, which are a cross, at the foot of which is an open volume of the gospels, and both of these rising from amidst a trophy of arms, with the emblem of liberty entwined with a riband that bears the following device, Dios, Patria y Libertad, Republica Dominicana "God, our country and liberty, Dominican republic."

There are four national festivals, one commemorating the separation; two, important victories; and the fourth, the publication of the present constitution.

Under the article on religion, I remarked that I should again allude to that subject.

The assembly that framed the constitution were divided in opinion in regard to religious toleration; there being of those in it, but the minority, opposed to such a concession, and in favor of inserting in the article in question a clause prohibiting the public exercise of any other religion than that adopted as the national one. The former, on the other hand, wished to have inserted an express declaration of religious freedom. Now this question deeply interested a portion of the Dominican people—one of the citizens, namely, the naturalized American people of color, of whom I shall speak in a subsequent communication. These were Protestants, and brought with them their faith; and if Italian supremacy, under an express guaranty, thus prevailed, it might be converted into a weapon in regard to their faith and its public exercise. The discussion of the subject, it would seem, had possibly awakened their apprehensions, and many, under the influence of it, took early measures to sell their property, to return to the U. S. or pass over to the other part of the island—as many of them did—and those that remained, done on the breaking out of the revolution—from a suspicion, that being no longer allowed or compelled, their own rights of person and property derived from them, would no longer be respected, if a strictly Roman Catholic provision was inserted—were given terms that the old guarantees, so far as their freedom of worship was concerned, would be religiously respected by the new one. Soon after, however, on framing the constitution, no religion had been inserted in its press shape—which had been done to calm the fears of that portion to acquiesce in—they again took the alarm; for that, this omission was now finally allayed by their being referred to a previous article, which commanded the government, on its responsibility, to compel to do what the law did not command, or to refrain from doing what it did not forbid; although the article certainly does not cover, in effect, the whole ground, since the word "law," which might be legitimately interpreted to mean any future as well as present enactment, is used in it, and leaves room for future enactments. Under this circumstance it might be thought to afford advantage to the present or future government, in the matter of religious, if any such now exist in any member of the government, to use that article; it being but justice to state that it is well understood and acknowledged on all hands that religious toleration is a fundamental law of the republic, though nowhere expressed so to be, within the writer's knowledge, in written terms; and no guarantee of the form of toleration in the U. S. is more sacred and irrevocable than this.

In regard to this matter, I might have entered much further into minute, and, in some respects, instructive as well as curious details, having at my command well-accredited materials for this purpose; for the peculiar facility and facility of getting into the secrets of cabinets, councils, and conclaves, not apparent to the uninitiated, is not destitute of interest; but for obvious reasons, it certainly is to be hoped that it is there the only reason—and looking to the future, my sole reason for not doing so is, that his motives might be such as the majority of the present congress would not entertain.

In order to provide against such a contingency, I will further remark, that so far as he has been able to observe the article in question does not, and cannot, do much for the general cause of religious liberty exist, both throughout the different branches of the government and among the better informed portions of the community at least, such as we are not accustomed to look for, or suppose to exist in American governments and communities south of our own country.
CELERES.

CITY OF ST. DOMINGO, May 22, 1848.

I will now give a cursory glance at the currency, trade, and commerce of this republic, and present your readers with a few details in regard to its revenue and finances; closing with some remarks on the civil administration.

In order to provide for the new state of things consequent on the separation from Hayti, the new government resorted to the expedient usual in such cases—a paper issue. I have not by me the documents to show the whole amount issued from the beginning. In the second fiscal year of the republic (1845-6) there was issued in paper and in copper coin, the sum of $1,128,886, and in the third and last reported year (1846-7), in same, the sum of $771,830, making an aggregate of nearly two millions of dollars. The whole amount in circulation is probably not far from three millions. This issue was based on the credit of the government, and, like that of most others, has gradually depreciated. A year ago it was worth eight cents to the dollar, and now it is worth a little over six and a half, showing a depreciation, during that period, of about eighteen per cent., as I have been in some previous ones of its short existence. Its value has remained quite stationary for several months past. The government is now directing its attention to the devising of some means whereby to avoid the necessity of making any further issues. The only other circulating medium heretofore, and the principal one still, has been the Spanish or South American gold coins, though now, silver, in the form of Mexican and American dollars, is getting into use.

There are four ports of entry in the republic, though this one on the south, and Puerto Plata ed, in the year 1845-6, to $118,755 43, hard money, and $360,944 22, national currency; and in 1846-7, to $69,493 10, hard money, and $703,708 38 national currency; which shows a falling off in the hard money receipts of about one-half. This arose, not from a corresponding diminution of imports, from which it is chiefly derived, but from the fact that the tariff of duties on importation was, by a law of the first mentioned year, reduced about one-half.

The relative proportions of the revenue derived from the principal classes—the last year's alone, having the documents before me—was, from duties, to $44,630 38, and tonnage $15,735 46, hard money, and from the export duties in the national currency, to about $11,827 63 hard money, taking the national currency at six and a half cents; so that date, July 1, 1847; the two first items of which are payable in hard money, yielded most of the revenue; the whole for that year, reducing the paper in the same manner, being $98,623 88 hard money.

The expenditures of the government for the same year were $32,942 32, hard money, and $1,345,217 87 paper money—or $120,381 48 hard money—being, before the two, about, in hard money, to the sum of $21,757 60; the principal part of the expenditures over the legitimate receipts of the government, being for the army, which amounted to $100,500 hard dollars,—a sum not quite equal, however, to that which would have been derived from the reduction made in the tariff of imports.

These details show, to your readers, omitting the items of government emissions of paper and payments, the real financial state of the republic, only those which compose the actual revenue. I have been thus particular in order to show the actual resources of the government, as compared with its current expenses.

To devise the means of bringing the receipts of the amount up to the expenses of the government, which were considerably within the national estimates for the last year, has occupied the earnest attention of the government during the present year. The President in his annual message recommended an export duty upon several articles, principally mahogany, and tobacco which measure, indeed, main reason. We have grown up with the future, while the Congress has been warmly discussing the matter, no measure on the subject of anything has yet been decisively acted upon. Measures, to be sure, sufficiently marked. But we are, as a sury, resulting from the extraneous sources of receipts; but no steps have yet been taken, that I am aware of, for the purpose.

I pass to a few observations on the general administration of the several departments of the government. In doing so, as I have had occasion to, I may remark that their proceedings are characterized by a degree of wisdom and parliamentary system and regularity, which under all the circumstances, could not but be expected. The proceedings are discussed in it with as great a degree of order and dignity as in those of older nations, under the circumstances. For it is to be considered—and I write not for the purpose of eulogy, and art of legislation, since there do not exist—those elements from which to form it—their hereditary ideas, so to speak, of the character and model of the government under which they were brought up, centuries in the story of colonial dependence—present, as has been remarked in a previous letter, a singular subject of speculation. In this view of the case, one cannot but be struck with the advancement in the science of legislation as their acts and proceedings show. Not possessing, in common with our own, or our State legislatures, the contrast is, in many respects, highly favorable to the Dominican nation, much more. Nor yet is the this only, or even the principal, cause of the difference between our systems and practices; or rather, they are the result of all those differences in race, character, and social and national education; they, or their ancestors, have never had any experience in such associations, and grow with our growth, not formed from our own system—our peculiar social and political system. Here the ease is otherwise in each of these respects. This machinery of legislation which belongs to an advanced political state, exists here as an exotic. It is not indigenous to the soil, the habits and associations of the Dominican people. Not indigenous, its idea has been seized upon, introduced and attached to the body politic here, by a few intelligent men, who, by a long course of reading and study at home, have grasped the ideas of rational liberty and republican institutions, and machinery, and transplanted them to their own country, and have done so much, and continue to do so, to the condition, wants and character of the Dominican people, so far as their ultimate success time alone can disclose. Mean time, it will not be out of place to observe, that this series of letters to illustrate this experiment, of particular nations originate, of the fruit of the tree of liberty, and thrives to so perform, and flourish in this home—transplanted from its native soil—transplanted to this island-home—blossom within the tropical seas, fanned by its soft breezes, and created by nature, as it would seem, in one of her most prodigal moods

The remarks to which my allusion to the legislative department has drawn me out, are equally applicable to every department of the administration. In the judicial department, with the previous letter, the civil and criminal codes of the Dominican Republic, are of French origin—growing out of the character, condition, and wants of a people essentially different from those of Spanish origin, the offspring of a very different state of society, and are still clothed in the unnatural garb of a foreign language. All these circumstances render it often a matter of perplexity and difficulty for the judges to expound the laws. The consequence is, that their decisions, being founded, as they necessarily are, upon such laws, and inbred ideas and associations do not come in aid of their decisions, as is the case where, as in the case under the common law, or even those modified systems of the civil law which the wants and habits of a people have demanded, so that the judiciary are, so far as the writer's professional knowledge extends, far from satisfactory, or rather to form an opinion, as a body, upright and intelligent men, as could be expected from such an instance, a tardy and imperfect administration of justice. These, as well as the administrative imperfections and difficulties have attracted the attention of the government and of the national congress. The President has recently called the attention of the national Congress to the subject; and the minister who presides over this department, closes his remarks on the subject by recommending such an alteration in the system of laws as will "adapt them to the capacity of those who administer them, and of those who are to obey them."

Affairs in the Dominican Republic.
CITY OF ST. DOMINGO, May 16, 1848.
As promised in my last, I now proceed to give a sketch of the constitution of the Dominican Republic, embracing an occasional reference to laws subsequently enacted to carry out some of its provisions. This instrument, the essential features of which seem to have been derived in part from the constitution of the United States, and in part from the French charter of 1830, declares, in the first place, that the Dominicans erect themselves into a free, independent, and sovereign nation, under a government essentially civil, republican, popular, representative and responsible; and defines the territory of the republic as consisting of what it states, embraces the Spanish part of the island of St. Domingo and its adjacent isles—to be identical with those bounds which, in 1793, divided the west from the French part. That is embracing, also, a capacity, at some future period, of the whole area of the island.

Citizenship is limited to be citizens who were born in the territory, and were residents at the time of the drafting of the constitution; as also the children of all Spanish Dominican absentees who have not taken up national citizenship, or borne arms against the new State, return to reside within its limits. There are three ways of foreign born becoming citizens—first, who acquire the requisite amount of real estate, after a two years' residence; dollars; and secondly, those who, by their personal labor establish agricultural or industrial establishments, under the title of proprietors, or owners, after three years' residence. A third and fourth classes cannot enjoy political rights until after a residence of six years in the territory. This period, however, is reduced to two, in both cases, in favor of those foreigners who marry a Dominican female. All foreigners belonging to nations of cultural establishments, the value of which amounts to or exceeds one thousand Dominican national dollars; not belonging to a hostile nation are declared to be under the protection of the republic, while they profess any art, science, or useful industry, or work as day laborers; while those so belonging being declared to be under the safeguard of the public faith from the moment they step upon the soil of the republic.

Dominicans are all equal in the eye of the law; remain free, and equal in right, salary being given for public service; and are all equally eligible to offices and employments. Individual liberty is guaranteed, so that no one can be prosecuted except in conformity with the forms, and in the cases which it prescribes. Nor can any one be imprisoned, except under the authority of a written order of a judge, setting forth the cause of the arrest; and this must be made known to the party arrested at once, or at least within the space of twenty-four hours. Right of property—property can never be imposed as a punishment —can only be taken when the public good requires property be taken from its owner, except where the public good requires it, and then only for a previous indemnified value to be ascertained by a just standard.

The residence or dwelling-house of every citizen is guaranteed to be inviolable, and search warrants and no domiciliary visits are to be allowed, except in cases provided for by law, and with the formalities it prescribes. No censorship of the press is to be established. All Dominicans are permitted to print and publish their thoughts, or cause them to be printed and published, without previous censorship, being responsible only for the abuse of that liberty in cases provided by law.

A subsequent law has defined what shall constitute abuse of this liberty, and limits it to five classes, namely—publishing maxims or doctrines that tend directly to destroy or subvert the religion of the State, or the constitution of the republic; publishing maxims or doctrines intended to excite rebellion, or cause any disturbance of the public peace; publishing maxims or doctrines to subvert any law or legitimate authority, or inciting to this violation by invective or satire; publishing obscene writings, or such as are contrary to good morals; injuring any individual or individuals by infamous libels, stigmatising his or their private character, or wounding their honor or reputation. The author or editor of such writings must be allowed, in exculpation, to offer in evidence the truth of his charges. Allegations against public functionaries are embraced within the same provision.

The constitution proceeds to declare that no person can be compelled to do what the law does not command, nor prevented from doing what it does not forbid. Public instruction is to be established, common to all the citizens, and gratuitous in all the elementary schools. Schools for this purpose are to be established throughout the territory of the republic. The details in regard to those elementary branches, as well as the higher ones, are to be regulated by law. To carry out this provision of the constitution, the Congress has enacted the law of the present year, establishing one elementary school in each of the communes (or parishes) of the republic, and two in each provincial capital, with a power in the government to add to the number, or change elementary into higher schools, if expediency suggests it. In these elementary schools are to be taught the principles of religion, the Castilian grammar, and the other usual branches of a common school education. The law places the general supervision of education under the Minister of Public Instruction.

The Dominicans are declared to possess the right of forming associations, of peaceably assembling, without arms—and of petition to the President, or to the National Congress, as individuals, one or many, but not in the name of a collective or corporate body. No law can be made to have a retroactive effect; nor can any be enacted that is contrary to the spirit or letter of the constitution. In cases of doubt the letter is to prevail.

The Apostolic Roman Catholic religion is declared to be the religion of the State; its ministers, enjoying a salary from the national treasury as ecclesiastical ministry, are dependent solely on the prelates canonically appointed. The article stops here, nor does the constitution say any thing whatever on the subject of freedom of conscience, or make any allusion to other forms or doctrine of religious worship. I shall revert to this subject in the latter part of this letter.

The sovereignty is declared to reside in the universal body of the citizens, and is to be exercised by three delegated powers, corresponding to the three co-ordinate branches of our own government. The members of both houses of the national congress are chosen for six years. The upper house, or as it is called the conservative council, consists of five members, one for each province of the republic, and is renewed integrally every six years. The lower house, or tribunal, is composed of fifteen members, appointed by law bodies are again chosen by vote of the people in their primary assemblies. The qualifications of a voter are citizenship and the possession in fee of real estate, or in place of the last, the exercise of some public office or employment, the practice of some science, art, or useful industry, or the occupation of a farm, with a given length of establishment in active cultivation. In these primary assemblies are likewise chosen the members of the Ayuntamientos (or town councils) of each commune. Each of these last mentioned bodies is presided over by the alcalde, who is chosen by the council itself.

The national mercantile colors designated, and described to be a blue and red background, in four squares, separated from each other by a white cross; the national flag, to have, in the centre, the arms of the republic, which are a cross, with two spears on each side, with national colors, grouped, and both of these rising from amidst a trophy of arms, with the emblem of the gospel, open in the centre, and bearing the following device, Dios, Patria y Libertad, Republica Dominicana. The military colors are the same as the republic.

There are four national festivals, one commemorating the separation; two, important victories; and the fourth, the publication of the present constitution.

In concluding this part of my letter, I promised to again make an allusion to that subject.

When the constitution was under discussion, a division of opinion in regard to religious toleration; a large majority of the convention was opposed to such a concession, and in favor of inserting in the constitution a clause prohibiting the public exercise of any other religion than that adopted as that of the state. The minority, on the contrary, wished to have inserted an express declaration of religious freedom. Now this question deeply interested the foreign residents of the island, and one—of the citizens, namely, the naturalized american, whose name I have had occasion to mention in a subsequent communication. These were Protestant, and wished to have secured to them, if Haytian supremacy, under erran guarantees, such as they had enjoyed under the former regime, in regard to their faith and its public exercise. The zeal of the majority, on the other hand, had reasonably awakened their apprehensions, and many, under the impression that the government had minds to fly over the other part of the island—as it was then very generally believed would be done on the breaking out of the revolution—from a fear that their religious privileges would be imperilled, their own rights of person and property derived from them, would no longer be respected, resolved to quit the island. Under these circumstances were given them that the old guarantees, so long enjoyed by them, would continue to be religiously respected by the new one. Soon after the constitution was adopted, a law on religion had been inserted in its present shape—as a peace-maker, and to allay the irritation to acquiesce in—they again took the alarm; but were again quieted, and are now finally allayed by their being referred to a previous article, which leaves the whole matter where it was, and which compelled to do what the law did not command, indeed, main reason. We have grown up with although the article certainly does not cover, in terms, the whole ground—or indeed much of it—which might be legitimately interpreted to mean any future as well as present enactment, is used in the article in question. My own opinion is, that this circumstance might be thought to afford advantage ground to press for a clause prohibiting the toleration of duties, if any such now exist in any future revision of the constitution. It might be fitting but justice to state that it was well understood and acknowledged on all hands that religious toleration is a fundamental law of the republic, though not expressly so to be, within the writer's knowledge, in written terms; and no guarantee for its continuation can be relied upon as more sacred and irrevocable than this.

In regard to this matter, I might have entered much further into minute, and, in some respects, instructive as well as curious details, having at my command well-accredited materials for this purpose; for the peculiar facility and facility of getting into the secrets of cabinets, councils, and conclaves, not apparent to the uninitiated, is not as we are not accustomed to look for, or suppose certainly to be hoped that it is there only they exist; and the writer's sole reason for not doing so is, that his motives might be misunderstood, a misconstruction he certainly does not entertain.

In order to provide for it, I might here remark this topic, that so far as he has been able to observe and judge of the subject of religious, or rather liberality exist, both throughout the different branches of the government and among the better informed portions of the community at least, such as we are not accustomed to look for, or suppose to exist in American governments and communities south of our own country.
CELSUS.

CITY OF ST. DOMINGO, May 22, 1848.
In order to provide for the new state of things consequent on the separation from Hayti, the new government resorted to the expedient usual in such cases—a paper issue. I have not by me the documents to show the whole amount issued from the beginning. In the second fiscal year of the republic (1845-6) there was issued paper and in copper coin, the sum of $1,128,886, and in the third and last reported year (1846-7), in same, the sum of $771,830, making an aggregate of nearly two millions of dollars. The whole amount in circulation is probably not far from three millions. This issue was based on the credit of the government—and like all similar expedients—has gradually depreciated. A year ago it was worth from eight to ten dollars for one, and for a little over a six and a half, showing a depreciation, within a year, of upwards of thirty per cent, as I have been in some previous ones of its short existence. Its value has remained stationary for several months past. The government is now directing its attention to the devising of some means whereby to avoid the necessity of making any further issues. The only other circulating medium heretofore, and the principal one still, has been the Spanish or South American gold coin, though now, silver, in the form of Mexican and American dollars, is getting into use.

There are four ports of entry in the republic, though this one only on the south, and Puerto Plata ed, in the year 1845-6, to $118,755 43, hard money, and $369,944 22, national currency; and in 1846-7, to $69,493 10, hard money, and $703,708 38 national currency; which showing a falling off in the hard money receipts of about one-half. This arose, not from a corresponding diminution of imports, from which it was chiefly derived, but from the fact that duties on importations was, by a law of that year, made payable three-fourths in paper money.

The proportions of the revenue derived from the principal classes—the last year's alone—were from duties on importations, national currency to $44,630 38, and tonnage from $15,735 46, hard money; while from exportations, it only amounted to, or about $11,827 68 hard money, take it altogether, is little more than half the first mentioned date, July 1, 1847; the two first items of which are for the year 1845-6. The expenditures of the government for the same year were $32,942 32, hard money, and $1,345,217 87 paper money; leaving a balance against it, for the year, before, two amount, in hard money, to the sum of $143,158 52, hard money, and paper, after deducting the receipts over the receipts of the year—taking the paper at the same rate, thirty-six dollars for one, of three dollars—a sum not quite equal, however, to the excess of paper issued over the former reduction made in the tariff of imports.

These statements will show, at a glance, omitting the items of government emission of paper and the small amounts derived from other sources than only those which compose the actual revenue. It will also be seen how inadequate are the present actual resources of the government, as compared with its current expenses.

To devise the means of bringing the receipts of the treasury up to its expenditures, (which it is to be remembered, were considerably within the estimates for the last year,) has occupied the earnest attention of the government during its present session. The President in his annual message recommended an increase of the export duty on the staples, namely, mahogany and tobacco; which measure, indeed, main reason. We have grown up with future, while the Congress has been warmly discussing the policy of an export duty on mahogany—a thing which has yet been decidedly acted upon. Measures, to be sure, sufficiently marked. But we are, as a result, suffering from the extraneous sources of revenue; and, indeed, main reason. We have grown up with of; but no steps have yet been taken, that I am aware of, to carry them into effect.

I pass to a few observations on the general administration of the several departments of the government. In doing so, and omitting those of a occasionally attended, I may remark that their proceedings have been conducted, on the whole, with decorum and parliamentary system and regularity, and with a degree of ability and intelligence, which, to be sure, sufficiently marked. But we are, as a result, under the circumstances. For it is to be consider—the people—on the contrary, they are of trans-atlantic origin, and still clothed in the unnatural duties, if any such now exist in any future revision of the constitution. It might be fitting but justice to state that it was well understood and acknowledged on all hands that rel-it is not indigenous to the soil. This has been in its country; this has been remarked in a previous letter; and it has been grown up with another, and the product of a different state of social and national education; they, or their national political existence, state here as an exotic. It is not indigenous to the soil, the habits and associations of the country, and are still clothed in it; its ideas have been seized upon, introduced and attached to the body politic here, by a few intelligent men, who, having received their own education or study at home, have grasped the ideas of rational political existence, as they exist in more advanced machinery, and transplanted them to their own country; where, if time be given to them to do so, to the condition, wants and capacities of the people, they may, in time, take root, and ultimate success time alone can disclose. Mean-time, it will be one of the principal objects of this series of letters to illustrate this experiment, and to show how far the offshoot, transplanted from the tree of liberty and thrives, is likely to flourish, or if it will wither and die under the influence of the tropical sun, fanned by its soft breezes, and created by nature, as it would seem, in one of her most prodigal moods

The remarks to which my allusion to the legislative department of the government has led, are equally applicable to every department of the administration of the country. The constitution, the various letter, the civil and criminal codes of the country, are all, with few exceptions, having their spring out of the character, condition, and wants of the people—on the contrary, they are of trans-atlantic origin, the offspring of a very different state of society, and still clothed in the unnatural garb of a foreign language. All these circumstances render it often a matter of perplexity and difficulty for the judges to expound the laws. The consequence of all this is, that trans-atlantic ideas and inbred ideas and associations do not come in aid of the judge in the performance of his duties, as is the case under the common law, or even those modified systems of the civil law which the wants and experience of a country have suggested. Thus the judiciary are, so far as the writer's professional knowledge enables him to form a judgment, as well to form an opinion, as a body, upright and intelligent; but there is, nevertheless, as might be expected in such a case, a degree of uncertainty, and a lack of uniformity, and a want of firmness, which all these circumstances tend to produce. The President has recently called the attention of the national Congress to the subject; and the minister who presides over this department, closes his remarks on the subject by recommending such an alteration in the system of laws as will "adapt them to the capacity of those who administer them, and of those who are to obey them."

records.headline: Interesting from the Dominican Republic.
records.summary_en: The newspaper reported that the Spanish colony of St. Domingo was never primarily agricultural, as early colonists were drawn instead by gold mining. Due to a lack of agricultural enterprise, industry, and the departure of enterprise toward Mexico, the colony became isolated and stagnated. Consequently, the higher and richer classes lost their energy and ambition, sinking into intellectual and physical sloth while agriculture and wealth declined.
records.summary_es: El órgano noticioso refirió que la colonia española de Santo Domingo jamás tuvo un carácter preponderantemente agrícola, atrayendo más bien a los primeros pobladores la explotación aurífera. A consecuencia de la desatención del cultivo, el desmayo industrial y la emigración de hombres activos hacia México, la colonia quedó aislada y estancada. En consecuencia, las clases encumbradas y acomodadas perdieron el empuje y la ambición, sumiéndose en la incuria intelectual y material al compás de la postración del campo y la pérdida de caudales.

records.headline: Affairs in the Dominican Republic.
records.summary_en: Based on the provided excerpt, *The New York Herald* reported on a constitutional provision empowering the Dominican President to freely organize military forces, mobilize the National Guards, and issue defense-related decrees without responsibility during the war with the Haytian republic. Additionally, the newspaper noted that the gold, copper, and potential silver mines of St. Domingo had long remained unwrought due to government fears of stimulating the cupidity of enemies and foreign nations, though a recent act of Congress addressed these matters.
records.summary_es: Con base en el pasaje reproducido, *The New York Herald* expuso un precepto constitucional que facultaba ampliamente al presidente dominicano a ordenar las fuerzas militares, convocar las Guardias Nacionales y promulgar decretos defensivos exento de responsabilidad durante las hostilidades con la república haitiana. El periódico añadía que los veneros de oro, cobre y potenciales vetas de plata de Santo Domingo yacieron largo tiempo inexplotados por el recelo gubernamental de incitar la codicia de adversarios y naciones extranjeras, habiendo dictado el Congreso medidas recientes sobre la materia.
