records.chapter_es: Una república en busca de reconocimiento
records.full_text:
IN THE NAME OF THE MOST HOLY TRINITY.
Her Majesty the Queen of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland, and the President of the Dominican Republic, being desirous to consecrate the formal recognition of the independence of the same, and to conclude a treaty of peace and friendship, and to regulate thereby the commercial intercourse between the dominions and subjects of her Majesty, and the territories and citizens of the Republic, they have for this purpose named as their respective Plenipotentiaries, that is to say:—
Her Majesty the Queen of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland, Sir Robert Hermann Schomburgk, Doctor of Philosophy, Knight of the Royal Prussian Order of the Red Eagle, of the Royal Saxon Order of Merit; of the Legion of Honor of the French Republic; Her Consul to the Dominican Republic;
And the President of the Dominican republic, Senor Jose Maria Medrano, Minister Secretary of State for the departments of police and the interior, and charged with those of Justice, Public Instruction, and Foreign Affairs;
Who, after having communicated to each other their respective full powers, found in good and due form, have agreed upon and concluded the following articles:—
Art. 1. There shall be perpetual peace and friendship between her Majesty the Queen of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland, her heirs and successors, and the Dominican republic, and between their respective subjects and citizens.
Art. 2. There shall be reciprocal freedom of commerce between the British dominions and the Dominican republic. The subjects of her Britannic Majesty may reside in and trade to any part of the territories of the republic, to which any other foreigners are or shall be admitted. They shall enjoy full protection for their persons and properties. They shall be allowed to buy from and sell to whom they like without being restrained or affected by any monopoly, contract, or exclusive privilege of sale or purchase whatever; and they shall moreover enjoy all other rights and privileges which are or may be granted to any other foreigners, subjects or citizens of the most favored nation.
The citizens of the Dominican republic shall, in return, enjoy similar protection and privileges in the dominions of Her Britannic Majesty.
Art. 3. No tonnage, import or other duties or charges shall be levied in the Dominican republic on British vessels, or on goods imported or exported in British vessels, than are or may be provided to be levied on national vessels, or on the like goods imported or exported in national vessels; and in the same manner, no tonnage, import, or other duties or charges shall be levied in the British dominions on vessels of the republic, or on goods imported or exported in those vessels, beyond what are or may be levied on national vessels, or on the like goods imported or exported in national vessels; or from the ports upon the commerce, without prejudice whatever to the provisions of the fourth article, exclusively reserved to national vessels of each of the the two countries respectively.
Art. 4. Merchandise or goods coming from the British dominions in any vessels, or coming from British vessels from any country, shall not be prohibited in the Dominican republic, nor be subjected to higher duties than are levied on the same kinds of merchandise or goods, coming from any other foreign country, or imported in any other vessels.
All articles, the produce of the republic, may be exported therefrom by British subjects and British vessels, on as favorable terms as by the subjects and citizens and vessels of any other foreign country.
Art. 5. The protection of the government of the republic shall be afforded to all British vessels, their crews and goods. If any British vessel should be wrecked on the coast of the republic, the local authorities shall afford them aid, and secure them from plunder, and shall cause all articles saved from the wreck to be restored to their lawful owners. The amount of salvage dues in such cases shall be settled, in case of dispute, by arbitrators chosen by both parties.
Art. 6. It being the intention of the two contracting parties to bind themselves by the present treaty, to treat each other on the footing of the most favored nation, it is hereby agreed between them, that any favor, privilege, or immunity whatever in matters of commerce and navigation, which either contracting party has actually granted, or may hereafter grant, to the subjects or citizens of any other State, shall be extended to the subjects or citizens of the other contracting party, gratuitously, if the concession in favor of that other State shall have been gratuitous, or in return for a compensation as nearly as possible of proportionate value and effect, to be adjusted by mutual agreement if the concession shall have been conditional.
Art. 7. Each contracting party may appoint Consuls for the protection of its trade, in the dominions or territories of the other; but no such Consul shall enter upon the exercise of his functions until he shall have been admitted and approved, in the usual form, by the government of the country to which he is sent.
The respective agents and Consuls of each of the two contracting parties residing within the dominions or territories of the other, shall enjoy the same rights, immunities, privileges and exemptions which are or may be granted to the diplomatic agents or Consuls of equal rank, of the most favored nation.
Art. 8. The subjects of her Britannic Majesty residing in the Dominican republic shall not be disturbed, persecuted, or annoyed on account of their religion, but they shall have perfect liberty of conscience therein, and exercise their creed either within their own private houses, or in the said or particular chapels. Liberty shall also be granted to them to bury in the Dominican republic, in the manner, they may freely establish and maintain, their subjects who may die in the territories of the said republic. In like manner, the citizens of the Dominican republic shall enjoy, within all the dominions of Her Britannic Majesty, a perfect and entire liberty of conscience, and shall be allowed to exercise their religion publicly or privately, within their own dwelling houses, or in the chapels and places of worship appointed for that purpose.
Art. 9. Slavery being perpetually abolished in the Dominican republic, and having been already declared by her an act of piracy punishable with the pain of death, the Dominican republic engages to permit any British vessel of war, which may be furnished with special instructions under the treaties between Great Britain and foreign powers, and with the formalities as are provided for in such cases by the said treaties relative to the prevention of the infamous slave trade, to visit any vessels sailing under the Dominican flag, which may, upon reasonable grounds, be suspected of being engaged in this vile trade in slaves; it being understood that the distances and places between which the right of visit shall be exercised as restricted as they are in the treaties with other powers, for Cuba and Porto Rico, shall likewise refer to the same distance of twenty leagues from the coasts of the Dominican republic; and if, by the result of the visit, it shall appear to the officer in command of such British vessel of war that the suspicions of the commander are well grounded, the vessel shall be sent, without delay, to the port of Santo Domingo, in the Dominican republic, and shall be delivered up to the local authorities, to be proceeded against according to the laws of the republic.
It is understood that the present article shall not be extended to other cases, which might occasion a vexatious and unnecessary visit to the Dominican vessels in their voyages and commercial enterprises; but that, with the aid of the Dominican authorities, authorized to expect protection and assistance; and, if the case should arise, which, however, is not to be supposed, that the Dominican republic should receive a conviction of having suffered a vexatious molestation, it rests with her to withdraw it, after having given a year's previous notice thereof.
Art. 10. In order that the two contracting parties may have the opportunity of hereafter treating and agreeing upon such other arrangements as may tend still further to the improvement of their mutual interests, and to the promotion of the commerce of their respective subjects and citizens, it is agreed that the present treaty shall remain in force for the term of ten years from the date of the exchange of the ratifications, and either of the contracting parties shall have the right of giving to the other party notice of its intention to terminate at the expiration of the said ten years the stipulations of the present treaty; and the present treaty shall cease to be binding after ten years, and all notice that might be given and amity shall remain obligatory to both nations.
Art. 11. The present treaty shall be ratified, and the ratifications shall be exchanged at Santo Domingo, within the space of eight months, or sooner, if possible, counted from the date of this treaty, or sooner, if shall be possible.
In witness whereof, the respective plenipotentiaries have signed the same, and affixed thereto the seals of their arms.
Done at Santo Domingo, the sixth day of March, in the year of our Lord eighteen hundred and fifty.
(L. S.) ROBERT H. SCHOMBURGK.
(L. S.) JOSE MARIA MEDRANO.

ADDITIONAL ARTICLES.
As the circumstances of the Dominican with the Haytien nation might oblige the Dominican republic to modify the third article, it is hereby especially understood and agreed between the two contracting parties, that the Dominican republic shall have perfect liberty of making during the space of ten years such changes as she may think fit in her duties, notwithstanding the stipulation of article 3 aforesaid; but the subjects of her Britannic Majesty shall not be restrained or affected by any monopoly, contract or exclusive privilege of purchase or sale; and as her disposition is constant to afford and protect commerce, it should enter in her views to adopt any measures of limited or except in the case that the existing laws should continue.
The present additional article shall have the same force and validity as if it were inserted, word for word, in the treaty signed this day. It shall be ratified at the same time. And in consequence of the exception in article 3, it is to be understood that the sanction or disapprobation of the treaty is naturally reserved to Her Britannic Majesty.
In testimony whereof the undersigned have, in virtue of their full powers, signed and sealed the present article.
Done at Santo Domingo, the sixth day of March, in the year of our Lord eighteen hundred and fifty.
(L. S.) ROBERT H. SCHOMBURGK.
(L. S.) JOSE MARIA MEDRANO.
Ratified in the city of St. Domingo, September 27, 1850. BUENAVENTURA BAEZ.
DR. JOSE MARIA CAMINERO.

records.headline: News from Haiti to October 15 states that hostilities have actually commenced between the Haitians and Dominicans
records.summary_en: News from Haiti to October 15 states that hostilities have actually commenced between the Haitians and Dominicans, with about 500 Dominican troops driving back Soulouque's vanguard at the Pass of Bonica, and a Haitian brig of war with 200 men captured off Scott's Bay by two Dominican schooners and carried into Macao Roadstead. It adds that the Emperor marched on the 11th from Petit Goave, at the head of his staff and 400 guards, to take the field in person, and that the hostilities had disastrously affected the island's trade, with no coffee to be had and cutting of logwood and mahogany restricted.
records.summary_es: Noticias de Haití hasta el 15 de octubre afirman que las hostilidades han comenzado realmente entre haitianos y dominicanos, con unos 500 soldados dominicanos rechazando la vanguardia de Soulouque en el Paso de Bonica y un bergantín de guerra haitiano con 200 hombres capturado frente a Scott's Bay por dos goletas dominicanas y llevado a la rada de Macao. Añade que el emperador marchó el día 11 desde Petit-Goâve, al frente de su estado mayor y 400 guardias, para tomar el campo en persona, y que las hostilidades habían afectado desastrosamente el comercio de la isla, sin café disponible y con el corte de palo de tinte y caoba restringido.

records.headline: Late from St. Domingo—Peace Declared Between the Haytiens and Dominicans.
records.summary_en: According to an account from St. Domingo City received via the brig *George Otis* and reported from Boston on November 30, 1850, a treaty of peace between the Haytiens and Dominicans had been concluded through the intervention of the English and Americans, following some brief fighting that caused no serious loss. An English man-of-war was in port at the time of the treaty. The newspaper also reported on a separate railway collision near Batavia involving an emigrant train and an express train, which resulted in fatalities and injuries.
records.summary_es: Según despachos de la ciudad de Santo Domingo recibidos por el bergantín *George Otis* y difundidos desde Boston el 30 de noviembre de 1850, se formalizó un armisticio entre haitianos y dominicanos merced a la mediación de ingleses y estadounidenses, tras escaramuzas menores que no arrojaron pérdidas de consideración. Un navío de guerra británico se encontraba fondeado en la rada al ajustarse el convenio. La gaceta daba cuenta por separado de un siniestro ferroviario cerca de Batavia entre un tren de emigrantes y un convoy expreso, saldado con víctimas mortales y heridos.

records.full_text: Accounts from St. Domingo City, to the 2d instant, received by the brig George Otis, represent that, through the intervention of the English and American agents, a treaty of peace between the Dominicans and Haytiens had been concluded. Previous to this there had been some brisk fighting between the contending parties, but no serious loss had been sustained by either party. There was, at the time of the treaty, an English man-of-war in port.

records.summary_en: The *Polynesian* reported that the Dominican Republic was preparing to repel an expected invasion by Hayti under Faustin, with Santa Ana placed in chief command of the army. Additionally, a treaty with England acknowledging Dominican independence was celebrated at a public dinner attended by the British Consul—who stated England would not interfere in the contest—while no American consul or shipmasters were present. Under this new treaty, British vessels are allowed to enter Dominican ports at a fifty percent lower tonnage duty than American vessels.

records.full_text:
The Commissioners on Mexican Claims have this morning completed their awards. They amount to forty thousand dollars less than the sum appropriated to meet them, of one million and a quarter of dollars.

Major Donelson publishes a letter in the Union this morning, three columns and a half long, to the editor of the Union, upon assuming the editorial control of that journal. The Major endeavors to make the compromise a tower of patriotism above the ordinary spirit of party; but says that 'if the ultra Democratic party of this nation can be brought together in no other way than by an abandonment of the Union, or a compromise with the enemies of the compromise, we can never consent to buy peace on such terms.' He thinks the Democratic party, nevertheless, will unite on a constitutional basis, and elect the next President.

The intelligence brought by the last arrival from England, relative to the movement of British naval force, is considered to have a direct bearing upon the movements of Southern adventurers. It is supposed that the British vessels which have been dispatched may first meet the West India fleet somewhere near the shores of St. Domingo, for the purpose of obtaining redress, instant and immediate, from the Emperor of the black republic; while the adventurers from the Southern States may effect a landing on Dominica, and unite with those forces to assault the black republic in the flank. It is very true that our government at Washington can't declare war, or commence hostilities, without an act of Congress, but it can connive at the movement of a body of armed men, who may choose to emigrate to Dominica.

The intelligence brought by a letter from Mr. Riddle, United States Commissioner to the World's Fair, relative to the space allotted to the United States, is believed to be very onerous and expensive. The custom house commission on each package amounted to nearly $2, besides which, all the duties, tares, draperies, &c., for the display of goods, have to be provided by each nation, and those of other countries are very brilliant. He has had to employ a number of clerks to make out a descriptive catalog. Among these, he says, he is behind hand, owing to the late hour at which goods arrived.

The charge against Collector Lewis, of Philadelphia, after a full investigation by the President and Secretary of the Treasury, has been dismissed.

The Hon. John M. Clayton arrived here yesterday.

records.summary_en: The *Wilmington Journal* reported on April 25, 1851, that because St. Domingo (the Dominican Republic) was unrecognized by the United States, it was regarded as a piratical government rather than a nation requiring an act of Congress for military action. The newspaper suggested that U.S. vessels fitted out at Norfolk and New York could join other American ships to demand redress from the "emperor" of Hayti or demolish his regime. Additionally, it noted rumors that expeditions from the Southern States purportedly bound for Cuba were likely intended to land on the Dominican part of the island to assist the Dominicans and revolutionize the social and political condition of the blacks.
records.summary_es: El *Wilmington Journal* comunicó el 25 de abril de 1851 que, por carecer de reconocimiento oficial por parte de Estados Unidos, Santo Domingo (la República Dominicana) era conceptuado más bien como un gobierno pirático que como una nación formal que demandase una ley del Congreso para emprender acciones militares. La hoja apuntaba que buques de guerra estadounidenses alistados en Norfolk y Nueva York podrían concurrir con otras unidades navales para exigir satisfacciones al «emperador» de Haití o derribar su régimen. Recogía además comentarios de que expediciones armadas procedentes de los estados del Sur, supuestamente destinadas a Cuba, tendrían por objeto desembarcar en la parte dominicana para auxiliar a los naturales y trastocar el ordenamiento político y social de las poblaciones negras.

records.summary_en: Captain Hollins of the schooner Mary Chilton, from Port-au-Prince, reports that the Chamber of Deputies had been in session to consider the American government's proposition relative to acknowledging the independence of the Dominicans. It was generally believed the day the Chilton sailed that the Chamber had rejected the proposition and had also rejected a claim for the detention of the American brig Leander and the imprisonment of her captain, that the Haitians were daily expecting the American squadron, and that five conspirators against the Empire had been shot.
records.summary_es: El capitán Hollins, de la goleta Mary Chilton, procedente de Puerto Príncipe, informa que la Cámara de Diputados había estado en sesión para considerar la propuesta del Gobierno estadounidense relativa a reconocer la independencia de los dominicanos. Se creía en general el día en que la Chilton zarpó que la Cámara había rechazado la propuesta y también una reclamación por la detención del bergantín estadounidense Leander y el encarcelamiento de su capitán, que los haitianos esperaban a diario la escuadra estadounidense y que cinco conspiradores contra el Imperio habían sido fusilados.

ONE DAY LATER FROM HAYTI.—A letter from Porte-au-Prince, dated April 10, published in the New York Journal of Commerce, says that the Haytien Congress have not yet made a decision on the offer of mediation between the Haytiens and Dominicans, by the three commercial powers. This is one day later than the report that the offered mediation had been rejected. A Boston dispatch of the 1st inst. has the following:
The schooner October, from Porte-au-Prince, with advices to April 13, arrived here to-day. It is currently reported at St. Domingo that the Chambers had refused to comply with the demands of the American Commissioner, or to make peace. Emperor Soulouque was preparing to march on St. Domingo with all his forces. He had dismissed his Cabinet, and replaced them with men who were in favor of war.
The steamboat General Taylor arrived at Port-au-Prince on the 10th April, and was offered for sale.

records.full_text:
THE INTERNATIONAL MAGAZINE FOR JUNE. Price 25 cents.
This number is one of the best and most attractive yet issued. It contains a great variety of interesting and valuable matter, among which we notice a very interesting and well-written account of the mission of Mr. Robert M. Walsh to Hayti, as Special Agent of the United States. Mr. Walsh's instructions were to act in concert with the agents of France and Great Britain in an endeavor to induce the Emperor Soulouque to recognize the independence of the Dominican Republic. The writer gives a very graphic description of the character and court of the sable monarch, and of the progress and results of the mission. He represents Mr. Walsh as having acted with great energy and decision, and at various places in Hayti, as threatening to blockade and bombard Port-au-Prince in case Soulouque should still refuse to recognize the eastern part of the island as separate and independent. Armed coercion was apparently as familiar to him as his own title of "Special Agent," and his dreams by night and his talk by day seem to have been mainly of seventy-fours, frigates, paixhans, bomb-shells, rockets and thirty-two pounders. An inexorable and most unmitigated "interventionist" was Mr. Walsh, and if his advice had been followed, the "Napoleon of the West" would have been taught a lesson which he would not soon have forgotten. The Magazine contains also a great variety of other interesting matter, including several original stories and poems, and a large number of well-executed wood-cuts.

records.summary_en: In a historical sketch using the paper's period language, the writer traces Santo Domingo from Spanish rule to independence moves, saying Boyer entered and occupied Dominica, which his successors kept until 1843, when Santana led a revolt, drove out the Haitians and established a free government. For this site's framing, Boyer's entry is reported as the paper presented it; historically the period was an invasion and occupation of the Dominican Republic, not a merger of the two countries.
records.summary_es: En un bosquejo histórico que usa el lenguaje de época del periódico, el autor traza Santo Domingo desde el dominio español hasta los movimientos de independencia, diciendo que Boyer entró y ocupó Dominica, que sus sucesores mantuvieron hasta 1843, cuando Santana lideró una revuelta, expulsó a los haitianos y estableció un gobierno libre. Para el marco de este sitio, la entrada de Boyer se reporta como la presentó el periódico; históricamente el período fue una invasión y ocupación de la República Dominicana, no una fusión de los dos países.

records.headline: The idea and the wish to dissolve the com pulsory union
records.summary_en: The newspaper reported that after the expulsion of Boyer in 1843 and the accession of Gen. Riviere, the Dominicans seized an opportunity while the garrison was reduced to capture the remaining troops, proclaim a provisional independent government in early January 1844, and issue a revolutionary manifesto on January 16, 1844. It described the Dominican population as consisting of pure whites—who were the intellectually predominant and ruling class—and mixed races of various colors, all of whom were constitutionally declared equal citizens before the law. Additionally, the excerpt noted that Santana, the Dominican liberator and first President, resigned in 1848 and was succeeded by Jimenez, who was described as a traitor.
records.summary_es: El periódico relató que tras el derrocamiento de Boyer en 1843 y la exaltación del general Rivière, los dominicanos aprovecharon la mengua de la guarnición para reducir a las tropas restantes, proclamar un gobierno provisional independiente a principios de enero de 1844 y promulgar una manifestación revolucionaria el 16 de enero de 1844. Describía a la población dominicana integrada por blancos puros —que constituían la clase intelectualmente rectora y gobernante— y razas mixtas de diversos matices, proclamados todos constitucionalmente ciudadanos iguales ante la ley. Añadía el extracto que Santana, libertador dominicano y primer presidente, renunció en 1848 y fue sucedido por Jimenes, a quien se tildaba de traidor.

them home, and then proclaimed a provisional inde

1844, and preliminary to the publication of the

Dominicans as a race. The population is composed
of the pure whites, and the mixed races of all shades
of color bearing about tho same relative proportion

the intellectually predominant, and consequently
the ruling class. All, by the constitution, are, with
out distinction of color, citizens and equal before the
law.

records.headline: The paper recounts that Soulouque never recognized the Dominican Republic, kept up a state of war and constantly
records.summary_en: The paper recounts that Soulouque never recognized the Dominican Republic, kept up a state of war and constantly threatened new expeditions, until the representatives of France, England and the United States intervened. It says he refused to make peace or agree to a ten-year truce but promised to suspend the war virtually and proclaimed that Dominicans could come in and trade with assurance of kind treatment, though a Haitian officer who crossed the frontier under a flag of truce to carry the proclamation was driven back with a few killed and wounded.
records.summary_es: El periódico relata que Soulouque nunca reconoció la República Dominicana, mantuvo un estado de guerra y amenazó constantemente con nuevas expediciones, hasta que intervinieron los representantes de Francia, Inglaterra y los Estados Unidos. Dice que se negó a hacer la paz o a aceptar una tregua de diez años, pero prometió suspender la guerra en la práctica y proclamó que los dominicanos podían venir a comerciar con garantía de buen trato, aunque un oficial haitiano que cruzó la frontera con bandera de tregua para llevar la proclamación fue rechazado con algunos muertos y heridos.

records.headline: The Turks Island Gazette reports that President Baez, after some months in retirement with his family at Azua
records.summary_en: The Turks Island Gazette reports that President Baez, after some months in retirement with his family at Azua, returned to Santo Domingo on Saturday the 6th and entered the city under a salute of guns, escorted by his life guards and four hundred dragoons to the National Palace. The same report describes General Santana, old and in poor health, making his slow way to Santiago, where the military guard turned out to salute him, on his way to assume command of the Dominican army assembled on the frontier, as Soulouque had joined his army at Port au Prince with the avowed purpose of invading Dominican territory.
records.summary_es: La Turks Island Gazette informa que el presidente Báez, después de algunos meses de retiro con su familia en Azua, regresó a Santo Domingo el sábado 6 y entró en la ciudad bajo una salva de cañonazos, escoltado por su guardia personal y cuatrocientos dragones hasta el Palacio Nacional. El mismo informe describe al general Santana, viejo y de salud quebrada, haciendo su lento camino hacia Santiago, donde la guardia militar salió a saludarlo, en ruta a asumir el mando del ejército dominicano reunido en la frontera, pues Soulouque se había unido a su ejército en Puerto Príncipe con el propósito declarado de invadir el territorio dominicano.
records.passage: President Baez, after spending some months in retirement with his family at Azua, returned to St. Domingo, on Saturday, the 6th inst. and entered the city under a salute of [illegible] guns. The elite of the Dominican army, newly accoutred and uniformed, received His Excellency, who was escorted by his life guards and four hundred dragoons from Azua, Bani, and San Cristobal; the body guard were in full dress, and wore their splendid new brass helmets, ornamented with horse tails; the cavalcade rode to the National Palace, through streets ornamented with flags, and followed by the troops. The triumphal entry into Rome of Scipio Africanus was less ostentatious than President Baez's appearance in the city of St. Domingo, on the morning of the 6th inst. and we may be allowed to remind our readers that Scipio subsequently lost his popularity with the Roman people when he claimed for himself and the Senators a station at public festivals which the laws of the republic did [illegible] either. También dice que está autorizado a contradecir un informe de que se había disparado contra un buque estadounidense desde el fuerte de Cabo Haitiano.

records.headline: How They Do It.
records.summary_en: The newspaper reported that after being left to themselves by Colombia and Spain, the Dominicans were invaded and subjugated by Haytian President Boyer under the pretext of aid. Under Haytian rule, local institutions and the University of Santo Tomas de Aquinas were destroyed, public edifices were dismantled, and property was confiscated due to constitutional laws forbidding white property ownership. Consequently, many Dominicans fled the country while the rest remained stripped of their means to leave.
records.summary_es: El diario relató que, tras quedar desamparados por Colombia y España, los dominicanos fueron invadidos y sojuzgados por el mandatario haitiano Boyer so pretexto de auxilio. Bajo la dominación haitiana, las instituciones vernáculas y la Universidad de Santo Tomás de Aquino fueron desmanteladas, los edificios públicos arruinados y los bienes confiscados en virtud de preceptos constitucionales que vedaban a los blancos el derecho de propiedad. En consecuencia, numerosos dominicanos huyeron de la patria, en tanto los restantes quedaron desprovistos de recursos para emigrar.

records.full_text: HOW THEY DO IT.—Some time in 1849, Mr. King, of Georgia, then a member of the House of Representatives, made a speech on the subject of the recognition of the independence of Hayti, in which he gave a brief history of the manner in which the Dominicans were brought under the yoke of the Haytians. In 1821, the Spanish part of the island of St. Domingo declared its independence of Spain, and sent commissioners to ask admission as one of the States of that republic. The Colombians were then too much engaged with their own affairs to undertake the defence of the Dominicans. Spain, engaged in the vain effort of reclaiming her other more populous and valuable colonies, left the Dominicans to themselves. Boyer, then president of Hayti, called out his whole military force, and passing the frontier, under pretence of aiding the Dominicans, took possession of the country, and annexed it to Hayti.

records.summary_en: The paper argues that unless a new system replaces the present mode of dealing with such questions, Soulouque will succeed in his project of subduing the Dominicans, a project it says is in reality warmly sustained by England. It argues that under Mr. Fillmore the United States lost what Mr. Calhoun's system had gained — holding Soulouque in check and upholding the Dominicans without direct intervention or protectorate — and has been trapped into a coalition with France and England in which it will exercise but nominal influence in Haitian affairs.

records.summary_en: The *New York Herald* reported that the Dominican Republic comprises about two-thirds of the island of Hayti and occupies a position of significant commercial importance, though its ability to meet the annual interest on a £760,000 loan was doubted. The article noted that the Dominican population is estimated at 200,000 of Spanish origin (including whites, blacks, and a mixed race), contrasting it with Hayti proper, which was under the despotic rule of Emperor Soulouque, possessed a population of 700,000 all-black citizens, and barred white persons from holding property. Furthermore, the excerpt stated that the entire island had been united under the Haytien government from 1821 until 1844, when Dominica separated due to Haytien violations of annexation terms and a refusal to permit white immigration.

At the same time, it is impossible to comprehend the purpose for which it can be required. The depreciated paper circulation might be bought up for £30,000, and the idea of a State with only 200,000 inhabitants, and scarcely yet sure of its independence, or secure from the domestic intrigues peculiar to all races of Spanish origin, taking upon itself a debt of £760,000 simply to promote enterprise and immigration, is preposterous. records.headline: The paper says the Republic of San Domingo, in the eastern portion of the island, has long excited the jealousy of Soulouque

records.summary_en: The *New York Herald* reported that France allegedly intended to take control of the Dominican Republic to subsequently conquer the western part under the black regime and restore French dominion over the island. According to the excerpt, these secret machinations—initially pursued under Louis Philippe and later renewed under Louis Napoleon—found a warm supporter in Dominican President Buenaventura Baez, who was educated in France and held French notions.

A juicio del extracto, semejantes maquinaciones secretas —fraguadas inicialmente bajo Luis Felipe y reactivadas luego con Luis Napoleón— hallaron un decidido valedor en el presidente dominicano Buenaventura Báez, instruido en Francia e imbuido de ideas francesas.

records.full_text:
THE FRENCH MOVEMENT IN ST. DOMINGO.

American, French, and Spanish Views of the Question.

THE NEW CASUS BELLI.

[From the New York Herald of April 21, 1852.]
OUR PORT-AU-PLAT CORRESPONDENCE.
PORT-AU-PLAT, Dominican Republic, February, 1852.
I have on former occasions addressed a word to you, to draw the attention of the public of the republic, respecting what it pleases our present administration to throw dust into the eyes of the United States citizens. I mean the false information which the President officially stated in his message, that the differences between the Dominican republic and the Haytian empire were arranged, while such a desirable event is as far off as ever—thanks to the intrigue of public agents.

I may as well advise; for if you will refer to the Revue des Deux Mondes, for May, 1851, its pages corporate more than a sentiment, since Mr. M. Barrot, a member of the Assembly, contains an article on the empire of Hayti and the Dominican republic, which, it is confidently reported, has the French Consul in Port au Prince for author. Now, for its author, and is so filled up with misstatements that it is impossible that the reviewer in Paris could assemble a print contained therein to insert similar stuff it is clumsily attempted, in these pages, to make it appear that the Dominican republic desires a French protectorate over St. Domingo, is the most ardent desire of the Dominican population, who would see with pleasure their President, Senor Baez, (who, to his shame be it said is more Frenchman than Dominican,) and a small clique of French partisans, surrender the republic, although the inhabitants utterly despise Johnny Crapaud with as deep a hatred as ever did their Haytian neighbors.

I am now resident here for some years, during which time I have studied the character of the Haytians, and remarkably; and I must confess that the steady exercise of French diplomatic agents in Hayti, for some years past, inspires me with a suspicion that those agents have only had one aim—namely, to get hold under some plausible appearance of the Dominican republic and to conquer afterwards the western part, under the black ribbon, with comparative facility, thereby restoring the 'Queen of the Antilles' to the dominion of France; or, if you will, since the Dictator has restored 'the eagles' of Napoleon to the French army, to the claws of the rapacious bird, which, although it may resemble ours in form, has no relationship with it in character.

The supposition of an intended protectorate in St. Domingo is further strengthened by the arrival of the Prince de Joinville and the Duke d'Aumale in Hayti, during the presidency of General Guerrier. The children of Louis Philippe, the late King of the French, came to Hayti under the pretext of paying the Montalais their legacy, which was left by the late King of Hayti to the widow of Prince de Joinville's brother, the late Prince of Joinville, and to her sister-in-law, the Duchess of Orleans; but the real object of their visit was to prepare the way for the French fleet to come and occupy Cuba and Porto Rico to her sister, bidding the young princes a very cool adieu, and telling them they had better turn back, as they would find nothing there to do, and to render it in time the stronghold of these seas, and to conquer the rest of Hayti.

The Emperor's downfall and the revolution interrupted the intrigue, but scarcely had Louis Napoleon reached the presidency than the old schemes of Louis Philippe's agent were recommendations, and found a warm supporter in a French agent, named Mr. Raybaud, who was sent to the Dominican republic, clever, educated and French in heart, although a Dominican citizen.

The Revue des Deux Mondes tells us that this patriotic citizen had proposed to Mr. M. Barrot, the French Consul in Port au Prince—'You have only to give us your support, or a company of 2,000 men, to convince France of our sincere desire to place ourselves under her protectorate.' But Mr. Raybaud, although a Dominican citizen, was so far from having the modesty to refuse the proposal, that he had even the face to ask for more—namely, that 5,000 French troops should be sent to occupy the republic of Dominica.

So far from having the modesty, or to make statements from the executive of the Dominican republic, will be still more surprised if they continue to deny them for a short distance. They will find that Mr. Senor Baez, the President of Dominica, actually sent Mr. Raybaud to induce the acceptance of the young republic, foot and arm, of the French flag, and to place it under the protectorate of France; and that, at this moment, Mr. Raybaud (Mr. Green)—sent to St. Domingo with full powers from President Baez, to treat on this subject; so that, as long as there is a spark of hope that France will accept my proposals, I will wait with resignation.'

The author of these precious state papers from St. Domingo sent to Paris, where he went to further the object of his mission to produce the annexation of St. Domingo to the French empire, was Mr. Raybaud, although it is well known that another agent, whose name was kept secret, while the English cabinet employed only intrigue, which altogether failed.

The objects of Mr. Green's mission are well-known to the public of Dominica, although it was stated by the president's partisans that he was merely sent to Paris to purchase arms, &c. But Mr. Raybaud (Green), whose real name was known, selected young Green, who by the situation he had formerly held in Mexico, seemed to be a proper person for the mission to Paris; and his brother, who is now in his cabinet, although he never affirmed his connection with it.

I need not tell you how Mr. Green succeeded in his cabinet at Aranjuez. I never heard of any; but I can tell you what he did in Paris, and also what Mr. Baez's Carminero, then Minister of Foreign Affairs of the Dominican republic, did in London. Mr. Carminero was offered him the protectorate, promising that the British flag should be hoisted in St. Domingo; but Mr. Carminero refused it in the name of his government, and that the same Mr. Carminero, as soon as he found that Mr. Green was sent to London, sent the British Cabinet a diplomatic note, in which he declined to accept any such proposals.

The intention of Mr. Raybaud was not to produce an aggrandizement, but desired merely the prosperity of Dominica, and to avoid the trouble of getting a new prince to govern the republic. He added however, should France reject the offer, that if the Dominican republic can flag, it would be the sign to him to strike the British flag. Now, is it not surprising that after such facts, the city of a person who fabricates falsehoods in his message to Congress, in the manner of Mr. Fillmore, could assert such fables?

To show how far he abuses the Ministers of France and England, he says, 'We have offered to the United States to place ourselves under her protection, but no answer was given.' Now, no such proposal was ever made by Mr. Baez to the United States. He also says, 'We have offered to the Dominican flag to be hoisted in St. Domingo.' Now, this is another falsehood of Mr. Fillmore. Mr. Fillmore says, 'We have offered the Dominican flag to be hoisted in St. Domingo.' He says, 'We are forced by the French to consent.' This is another falsehood of Mr. Fillmore. Now, this is another falsehood of Mr. Fillmore, who says, 'We are forced by the French to consent.' Our lethargy, he says, 'has prevented us from accepting the offer, or the financial obstacles that might be given as an excuse to us for not having accepted it.' Now, no such excuse can be made, for no offer was ever made to us. We have not even the trouble to carry it there—it is all a invention of Mr. Fillmore; and we are sure that, if such a proposal had been made to the Dominican republic, the New World the future entrepot of the two hemispheres would not have been rejected. But Mr. Fillmore, it is openly, may be objected to us: 'Good God! because it is a secret.' If it is a secret, how does Mr. Fillmore and his friends know of it? because it such a legitimate and honorable mission that it must be kept secret. Yes, because others already dispute themselves publicly for the Dominican republic; and Mr. Fillmore, who has done so far for the eight years has answered to the gut vice of the cabinet of Paris.

Answer to Mr. Green: But if Mr. Green might succeed under such circumstances, the diplomatic tendency of the British cabinet, although it may seem so, is entirely different; how different with the Dictator, Louis Napoleon at the head of the French army, and the article of the Revue des Deux Mondes, written by Mr. Raybaud, is still more surprising. If we look at the article in the Revue des Deux Mondes, written by Mr. Raybaud, we find that the writer, after describing the state of Hayti, says that the French flag, hoisted in Dominica, would be a strong inducement for France to accept the proposal; and he adds that the French government ought to accept it, because it would give France the key of the Gulf of Mexico, and enable her to conquer Hayti, and to regain the control of the Queen of the Antilles. Now, it is well known that Mr. Raybaud was the principal agent of Louis Philippe in Hayti, and that he directed all the intrigue which led to the overthrow of General Guerrier; that he was the person who persuaded Prince de Joinville and the Duke d'Aumale to visit Hayti, and that he accompanied them when they returned to France. This is the man who has now been sent by Mr. Baez to Paris on the mission of annexation. On his arrival, he was received by Louis Napoleon, and received the cross of the Legion of Honor, and the rank of colonel. The article of the Revue des Deux Mondes, which was written by him, shows that he still continues to entertain the same views; and he has now been sent to Paris to finish what he commenced in Hayti.

[From Le Phare de New York Dec. 11, 1851.]
FRANCE AT ST. DOMINGO.
It is on the faith of a simple private letter that we take upon us to announce, the day before yesterday, the taking place possession by a French naval force of the Dominican republic difficulties of its own to contend with, to be able to offer a certain and efficacious support; England and the United States, known for their annexationist humor were, besides separated from the Dominican population by the profound distance of manners, religion, traditions and languages to permit the idea of applying to them until after having exhausted all other resources.
Dominica, therefore turned towards France, whose origin, religion and language are the same as hers, or at least in that part of the ancient colony of St. Domingo. The central position of St. Domingo, the extent of its coast, the magnetic sympathies...

The negotiations were long and difficult. The cabinet of the Tuileries hesitated to assume the responsibility which was offered to it, and the news of the expedition might have been prevented to it, that excess of timidity which formed the base of French diplomacy under the republic, until the 2d of December, 1843, a treaty was signed upon the following bases:—
First. France should send an effective support to the Dominican republic to protect it against Haiti, until peace should be firmly established.
Second. The Dominican republic should yield to France the peninsula of Samana, to found a permanent establishment there.
It was added that the Dominican republic, under these conditions should be the direct personification of the protectorate; that the governor of the island should be named by France and he should be invested with full powers to this effect.

This treaty, accepted by M. Ferdinand Barrot, was modified by M. de Trobriand, who, finding it contained an engagement which it had assumed, had causing the modified treaty to be signed by Mr. Baez and the Rear Admiral de Mogen, Commander of the West India squadron.
By this new arrangement, which is an amendment, France officially proclaimed the independence of St. Domingo and promised it her moral protection, reserving to the French government to install at Samana the effective force necessary for its defense; while the Dominican republic requests her prayers, nor even the threat of throwing herself into the arms of the United States. It was, besides, a question of a protectorate, an eclipse to a measure which might involve some diplomatic complications, but simply an intervention of humanity, which French diplomacy, with its usual dexterity, did not fail to reveal. The revolution of February, which overthrew the Orleans dynasty, came to produce an absolute change in this state of things, forcing the republic to seek an offset, and finding it in the peninsula of Samana, which her former government had found the means of possessing, and to which the present government appears attached.
We understand that the French government has gone so far as to establish a post in St. Domingo, that the island has fallen into the hands of France, and if the news of the 2d of December had been known, it would have changed the situation of affairs. “By some means, publicity has been given to the correspondence between the State Department and Mr. Robert M. Walsh, its agent in the negotiation for the pacification of Hayti. In the various papers which constitute this correspondence, the motives and purposes of the Administration in proffering its good offices in behalf of the Dominican republic are frankly and clearly set forth.

“In 1821 the Spanish portion of the Island of St. Domingo voluntarily subjected itself to the government of Hayti, then presided over by Boyer. On the expulsion of Boyer, and on account of the wrongs and grievances which they had endured, with a repetition of which they were menaced, the Dominicans threw off the subjection of negro government and established an independent republic. To this step the Spanish inhabitants of St. Domingo were driven by the necessity of self-preservation. Not only were their political rights and their liberty invaded and trampled upon by the black barbarians of Hayti, but the doom of indiscriminate slaughter and extermination was incessantly held before them in the threats of the Macaya and Dessalines.

“By the most imperious necessity, then, were the Dominicans impelled to set up an independent government. Nevertheless, their act of separation was regarded as a revolt by the negroes of Hayti, who prepared to reduce the rebel whites to subjection by the strong arm of force. All the efforts of the Haytien government were unequal, how ever, to the reconquest of Dominico. The Spaniards defended themselves with valor and energy, and, despite the disparity of numbers, successfully repelled the invasions of their foes. They achieved and established their independence. France formally recognised the republic of Dominica. England and the United States recognised it by their acts. Still Soulouque refused to acknowledge the independence of the Dominicans, and persisted in his efforts to reduce them to subjection. In this juncture, under the apprehension of a very formidable attack by Soulouque, the Dominican government solicited the mediation of the United States,

records.full_text:
HAYTI AND ST. DOMINGO.

The official paper of France (the Moniteur) lately contained an article from which we translate the following paragraphs:

“The Emperor Faustin I, immediately upon his accession to power, manifested his hostile views against the people of the eastern part of the island of Hayti, who, after the fall of the President Boyer, in 1844, had proclaimed their independence and established the Dominican Republic.

“The first essay of the Haitien Emperor, however, was not fortunate; defeated at the battle of the Ocoa, in 1849, his armies were entirely broken up, and he was obliged to retire, followed by the Dominicans, who would have carried their successes much further had it not been for the friendly mediation of the Powers which intervened in the conflict.

“On this occasion France was naturally called upon to act the first part. In 1843, in fact, before the division of the island had taken place, and when the eastern part was yet under the Haytien yoke, the inhabitants of the province of St. Domingo had, of their own accord, invoked the protection of the King of the French, and offered, on this condition, to deliver up to him the peninsula and bay of Samana.

“This treaty, accepted by M. Ferdinand Barrot, was ratified at Paris early in 1844. Soon after France fulfilled the first engagement it had assumed, by causing the Dominican movement to be supported by Vice Admiral de Moges, commander of the West India squadron. Strong in this support, the Dominicans were enabled to maintain their separation, and on the 27th February, 1844, hoisted the national flag.

“When, however, the French Government came to be called upon to carry out the conditions of the treaty of 1843, the Chamber of Deputies was not favorably inclined to it; they found that it would be dangerous to accept a military post in the proximity of a colony which had so cruelly escaped from us, and in the possession of which an attempt might be made to establish ourselves; moreover, and above all, the Chamber did not like to take up a position which seemed to engage us to assume in future the permanent protectorate of the Dominican Republic.

“These considerations prevailed: the treaty of 1843 was abandoned; the peninsula of Samana was not occupied; but France, nevertheless, remained the declared protectress of the new State, and it was in this capacity that she afterwards offered her mediation to put an end to the contest between the Haitiens and the Dominicans.”

The readers of the Intelligencer will not have forgotten that this was the project which was defeated by the unremitted vigilance and resolute conduct of the lamented Commodore Knox. The scheme is far from being abandoned, as the public may soon have occasion to perceive. England has already secured an island (the island of Alta Vela) in the same quarter, but having an eye to an establishment on that very point of Samana.

records.headline: Our National Reputation.
records.summary_en: The *West-Jersey pioneer* reported on December 18, 1852, that recurring American expeditions against Cuba and the Rio Grande caused neighboring regions—including St. Domingo, which barred its doors against foreigners—to view American commercial enterprises with extreme suspicion as disguised filibuster incursions. The newspaper lamented that these actions damaged the reputation of the United States, causing foreign nations to regard the American government as a piratical force rather than an honorable republic.
records.summary_es: El *West-Jersey pioneer* expuso el 18 de diciembre de 1852 que las recurrentes intentonas expedicionarias estadounidenses contra Cuba y el río Bravo suscitaron que los territorios colindantes —incluido Santo Domingo, que cerró sus accesos a los forasteros— contemplasen los tratos mercantiles norteamericanos con hondo recelo, teniéndolos por desembarcos filibusteros solapados. El periódico deploraba que tales desafueros menoscabaran el crédito de Estados Unidos, incitando a las potencias extranjeras a considerar al gobierno estadounidense como una potencia corsaria antes que como una república honorable.

records.full_text: From the Saturday Gazette. OUR NATIONAL REPUTATION. The United States is rapidly becoming the terror of the world. We are a nation of filibusters and colonizers of weaker nations, whose territories lie within range of our commerce or speculation. New Grenada is alarmed at the infusion of our population into her territories, and last, of all, the little republic of St. Domingo has been in a panic about a report, received by way of Turks Island, to the effect that an American steamer had put into Puerto Plata, but had fled on sight of an English steamer, and that this solitary steamer was bound to land a force that would take possession of the Dominican Republic and straightway annex it to the dominions of Uncle Sam. However absurd such a report might be made, it is wild to suppose that the government of the United States would sanction it, or shoulder the responsibility of it. It would rather have declared the whole affair illegal and outrageous, and done every thing to give up the lawless invaders to the justice of the injured government. That such would have been the result, we have an assurance in the policy laid down by our government, in various administrations, when similar troubles have been menacing us with Canada, Cuba and Mexico. But neither the declared policy nor the actual practice of a government can give confidence to foreign powers, so long as the shameless spirit of encroachment, annexation and revolution exists as it does among so large a portion of the American people. The lawlessness of a class inspires more faith than the promises of a President, and the reputation of the nation suffers for the shamelessness of a faction. Thus it is that every commercial enterprise that is set on foot in an American port is at once looked upon as a Fillibuster expedition in disguise. Cuba shakes in her shores at the sight of an American steamer; St. Domingo bars her doors on all foreigners, lest a stray American invader may come in and upset her government, and we shall next hear that Soulouque, the supreme, the Emperor of Hayti, drawing a cordon across his land frontier and fortifying his ports, to prevent his Imperial domains from being carried off bodily to be annexed to the great American Republic. While we can laugh at the folly of these foreign fears, we cannot help lamenting that the name of the United States should have fallen into such an odium as to justify, in the slightest degree, such absurd alarms. But, thanks to the oft-repeated and shameless enterprises upon cuba and the Rio Grande, the government of the republic fought for by the fathers, and identified in all honor by Washington and those around him, has now come to be looked on as a species of piratical craft cruising in all seas, and ready to plunder and capture all foreign property. It is beginning to be a sort of national Rob Roy, whose policy is '—the simple plan, That they shall take who have the power, And they shall keep who can.' Right-minded citizens, who respect national honesty and deem acts of national wrong as shameful as pocket-picking, should set their faces against all movements that may tend to strengthen the opprobrium into which we have fallen among foreign governments. The mere fact of our being a nation of unexampled prosperity, and rapidly growing in wealth and power, should not satisfy us, so long as we are looked upon abroad as a lawless people, with a government incapable of checking the growing popular frenzy for annexation. There is something more than mere power and wealth to be attained by a nation—and that is the reputation as well as the fact of national integrity.

records.headline: The editorial calls it preposterous for The Union to talk of the United States assuming a protectorate over the Dominican
records.summary_en: The editorial calls it preposterous for The Union to talk of the United States assuming a protectorate over the Dominican Republic, or over any of the republics south of the United States, and says the true American policy is to keep clear of all protectorates. It argues that the Dominicans themselves would refuse and repudiate such protection, having instead solicited France for eight years, so that an American protectorate would have to be enforced at the cannon's mouth while France's would be welcomed.
records.summary_es: El editorial califica de absurdo que The Union hable de que los Estados Unidos asuman un protectorado sobre la República Dominicana, o sobre cualquiera de las repúblicas al sur de los Estados Unidos, y sostiene que la verdadera política estadounidense es mantenerse alejada de todo protectorado. Argumenta que los propios dominicanos rechazarían y repudiarían tal protección, pues en cambio la han solicitado a Francia durante ocho años, de modo que un protectorado estadounidense tendría que imponerse a cañonazos, mientras que el de Francia sería bien recibido.

records.summary_en: In a comparison of the two peoples, the paper argues that the Haitians had a considerable and increasing foreign commerce and cultivated the soil, while it claims the Dominicans had little or no commerce and practiced mainly the primitive herding of cattle. The excerpt is an opinion piece weighing which people, in the paper's terms, deserved to be called civilized in the quarrel between Haiti and the Dominican Republic.
records.summary_es: En una comparación de los dos pueblos, el periódico sostiene que los haitianos tenían un comercio exterior considerable y creciente y cultivaban la tierra, mientras afirma que los dominicanos tenían poco o ningún comercio y practicaban principalmente la primitiva cría de ganado. El extracto es un artículo de opinión que sopesa qué pueblo, en los términos del periódico, merecía ser llamado civilizado en la disputa entre Haití y la República Dominicana.

records.headline: AMERICAN AND ORIGINAL. THE KNICKERBOCKER MAGAZINE. Edited by Louis Gaylord Clark.
records.summary_en: The *Daily National Intelligencer* reported that a mission by the Creole Minister of Foreign Affairs failed to persuade the Haitian Emperor Soulouque to sign a peace treaty or a ten-year truce with St. Domingo. Soulouque argued that the island was naturally one and indivisible, viewing the Dominicans as rebels who had no right to secede, and therefore peremptorily declined the propositions through his Senate. However, the Emperor's Minister of Foreign Affairs subsequently volunteered a positive assurance that hostilities against the Dominicans would not be renewed.
records.summary_es: El *Daily National Intelligencer* refirió que la legación encabezada por el canciller de origen criollo no logró inducir al emperador haitiano Soulouque a pactar un tratado de paz ni una tregua decenal con Santo Domingo. Soulouque adujo que la isla era indivisible por naturaleza, conceptuando a los dominicanos como facciosos sin potestad para segregarse, por cuya causa desestimó rotundamente las proposiciones ante su Senado. Con todo, el ministro de Negocios Extranjeros imperial brindó ulteriormente seguridades formales de que no se reanudarían las hostilidades contra los dominicanos.

records.full_text:
The December number, for January, 1853, will be the first of the forty-first volume of the Knickerbocker Magazine.
Since the price of subscription has been reduced from five to three dollars a year, the circulation of the Knickerbocker has been increased nearly four to one. In many places ten are sold where there was but one before, and through the year it has been steadily increasing. It is now offered as cheap as any of the Magazines, all things considered. Instead of making new and prodigious promises, we submit a few extracts from notices of late numbers, which we might extend to a number of pages.
Those familiar with the Editor's monthly "gossip" with his readers have, doubtless, with ourselves, admired the taste and judgment displayed in the selection of articles that adorn its pages. It is a sufficient guarantee that no contribution is admitted to its pages that is not in every way worthy of his perusal. When storms and wild tempests are abroad, and the "stormy spirit of the storm" is out, and all is drear and desolate without, ask for no more agreeable companion than the KNICKERBOCKER. Its contents impart valuable information, its sallies of genuine wit are a sovereign specific for all the "ills that flesh is heir to," and it never fails to drive away the "blue devils" of the horrors, and time passes merrily on.—[Courier, Burlington, Vermont.]
[National Intelligencer, Washington.]
'The December number of the Knickerbocker is a capital one. It contains a very interesting article on "The Creole Minister of Foreign Affairs," which gives a graphic account of the mission of the late Mr. Walsh to the Court of the Emperor of Hayti. Mr. Walsh was sent by the United States Government to negotiate a treaty of peace between the Emperor and the Government of St. Domingo. He had several interviews with the Creole Minister of Foreign Affairs, but failed to accomplish the object of the mission. Neither persuasion nor argument could induce the Emperor to make a definite treaty of peace, or a truce of ten years, with the Government of St. Domingo, which he regarded as a rebel whose subjection was necessary to the maintenance of his own authority. He argued that nature had designed the whole island to be under one Government, that the constitution of Hayti so declared it, and that he was bound to maintain the integrity of his empire. The article is well written, and contains much interesting information.'
'The Knickerbocker has been and will be a fact of its own: it is a sort of "institution." We never yet took up a new number of its pages, filled with articles not printed from English authors, but we felt a sort of "home-feeling" in its company and welcome.'—New York Christian Inquirer.
'The Fudge Papers, by Ik. Marvel, author of the "Reveries of a Bachelor," "Dream Life," &c., the "Sequel to St. Leger, or the Threads of Life," by Richard B. Kimball, Esq., and "Meister Karl's Sketch Book," by Charles G. Leland, Esq., will be continued, uninterrupted, unless by the absence or illness of the authors.'—[Courier, Natchez, Miss.]
Rev. F. W. Shelton, author of 'Letters from Up the River,' &c., will be a regular contributor.
Fitz-Greene Halleck has engaged to furnish poetical contributions from time to time.
The present number, which will be found to be one of the best ever issued, is for sale by all the Booksellers. Price three dollars per year, or twenty-five cents per number.

records.headline: The paper prints instructions for mediating agents: they are to pass Dominican objections to Haiti's Minister of Foreign Affairs
records.summary_en: The paper prints instructions for mediating agents: they are to pass Dominican objections to Haiti's Minister of Foreign Affairs, require an answer, and, if it is not given in reasonable time or is unsatisfactory, require the Emperor to conclude a permanent peace with the Dominican Government on a jointly prescribed basis or consent to a truce of not less than ten years. It says Great Britain and France instructed their agents to menace Soulouque with hostility if he refused, but he persisted in his designs against Dominica and would in no manner acknowledge its independence, so the utmost the mediating powers could effect was prolongation of an existing truce.
records.summary_es: El periódico publica instrucciones para los agentes mediadores: deben pasar las objeciones dominicanas al ministro de Relaciones Exteriores de Haití, exigir una respuesta y, si no se da en un tiempo razonable o no es satisfactoria, exigir al emperador que concluya una paz permanente con el Gobierno dominicano sobre una base prescrita conjuntamente o que consienta una tregua de no menos de diez años. Dice que Gran Bretaña y Francia instruyeron a sus agentes a amenazar a Soulouque con hostilidad si se negaba, pero él persistió en sus designios contra Dominica y no quiso reconocer de ningún modo su independencia, por lo que lo máximo que las potencias mediadoras pudieron lograr fue la prolongación de una tregua existente.

records.summary_en: The newspaper reports that the U.S. government employed special agents, including Mr. Green (employed by Mr. Clayton) and Mr. M. Walsh (employed by Mr. Webster under the current Administration), as emissaries to St. Domingo. It notes that the Senate requested copies of Mr. Walsh's official correspondence, which was communicated on August 27 and subsequently published in the *New York Evening Post* on the 13th. The publication criticizes these missions as a discreditable violation of the administration's professions of non-intervention in the affairs of a people whose independence has not been recognized.
records.summary_es: El rotativo consigna que el gobierno de Estados Unidos comisionó agentes confidenciales, entre ellos al Sr. Green (nombrado por el Sr. Clayton) y al Sr. Walsh (designado por el Sr. Webster bajo la actual administración), en calidad de emisarios ante Santo Domingo. Señala que el Senado demandó copias de la correspondencia oficial de Walsh, remitidas el 27 de agosto y divulgadas el día 13 en el *New York Evening Post*. La publicación censura estas misiones calificándolas de infracción censurable al principio de no injerencia proclamado por el ejecutivo respecto a un pueblo cuya independencia no había sido convalidada.

records.summary_en: The newspaper criticizes United States policy toward Hayti, attributing it to slavery-dominated diplomacy and the failure to recognize Hayti's independence. It reports that, following domestic interference and joint bullying with foreign governments, the French have taken possession of Samana as a naval station under the pretext of intervening for Dominica. The publication warns that this acquisition will allow France to monitor American commerce and facilitate hostile actions against the United States in the event of war.
records.summary_es: El periódico desaprueba la directriz diplomática de Estados Unidos hacia Haití, imputándola a la servidumbre de intereses proesclavistas y al desconocimiento de su independencia. Afirma que, tras presiones conjuntas con gabinetes europeos e injerencias intestinas, los franceses tomaron posesión de Samaná a guisa de apostadero naval con la excusa de proteger a la República Dominicana. La publicación previene que dicho enclave consentirá a Francia vigilar las rutas mercantiles norteamericanas y propiciar acometidas bélicas contra Estados Unidos en coyunturas de guerra.

But we have not yet reached the final result of our indefensible conduct towards Hayti. As we have already said, had we recognised her independence, and exchanged with her the usual international courtesies, we should have enjoyed the largest portion of her valuable trade, and obtained an influence over her, beneficial to her internal interests, and protective against foreign aggression. In obedience to a blind and bigoted sectional Interest, we have pursued an opposite policy, and now retribution is about to overtake us. We have interfered impertinently in her domestic affairs, we have united with foreign Governments in bullying her—and now, one of these Governments, if the latest intelligence be correct, has taken possession of a most important station on the island, on pretence of making its intervention for Dominica more effective, but in reality with a view to secure a most important naval station, close upon our shores. Samana has been taken possession of by the French, by whom, it is stated, it is to be held as a naval station. And its positien is such, that it will enable France to keep an eye upon our commerce, and, in the event of war, facilitate hostile movements against our shores. And this is the result of negro-phobia—of Slavery domination—of pro-slavery diplomacy—of the base policy which we have pursued towards that important island.

records.summary_en: The *Wilmington Journal* reported on December 24, 1852, that the Dominican Republic had long sought French protection and offered annexation, a step the current French Emperor was taking to secure a strategic point for monitoring American movements regarding Cuba under existing treaties. The newspaper contrasted the history of the former Spanish portion—which achieved independence without a servile insurrection and retained a white and mixed population superior in society and education—with the former French portion (Hayti), where a violent slave uprising had occurred.
records.summary_es: El *Wilmington Journal* comunicó el 24 de diciembre de 1852 que la República Dominicana procuró largamente el patronato de Francia y propuso su anexión, resolución que el actual soberano galo aprovechaba para guarecer un apostadero estratégico desde el cual observar las maniobras norteamericanas respecto a Cuba al amparo de las convenciones vigentes. El diario contrastaba los antecedentes de la antigua sección española —que conquistó su autonomía sin insurrecciones de esclavos y preservó un vecindario blanco y mestizo más encumbrado en cultura y letras— con la antigua colonia francesa (Haití), teatro de un sangriento levantamiento servil.

records.summary_en: The paper defends the Fillmore administration's mediation, arguing that the Monroe declaration was aimed at European colonization and aggressive intervention, not at France and Great Britain cooperating with the United States to pacify Haiti. It says the Dominicans besought the mediating powers to protect them, and that the powers interfered only to shield a feeble community from destruction.

Dice que los dominicanos suplicaron a las potencias mediadoras que los protegieran, y que las potencias intervinieron solo para escudar a una comunidad débil de la destrucción.

records.summary_en: The *Pawtucket Gazette and Chronicle* reported that Haitian Emperor Soulouque rejected Dominican independence, insisting the island was indivisible, though he offered assurances that hostilities would not resume. The ongoing truce was attributed in part to the depletion of the Haitian treasury following Soulouque’s lavish coronation ceremonies. An observer, Mr. Walsh, concluded that Dominican independence could ultimately only be maintained by force of arms against Haiti.
records.summary_es: La *Pawtucket Gazette and Chronicle* notificó que el emperador haitiano Soulouque desconoció la emancipación dominicana persistiendo en la indivisibilidad insular, si bien dispensó promesas de que las acciones de guerra no se reiniciarían. La subsistencia del armisticio obedecía en grado sumo a la ruina del erario haitiano provocada por los suntuosos fastos de coronación del monarca. Un observador, el comisionado Walsh, dedujo que la independencia dominicana sólo podría asegurarse a la postre por la vía de las armas contra Haití.

records.summary_en: Based on the provided excerpt, the newspaper reported on a discussion regarding whether the United States had the right to protect and intervene on behalf of the Dominican Republic against the extermination policy of Emperor Soulouque of Hayti. The excerpt noted that the Administration had already conceded and acted upon the principle that the Dominican Republic was entitled to such U.S. protection and interference. Additionally, the text briefly mentioned subsequent remarks concerning U.S. policy regarding Nicaragua, the Clayton and Bulwer treaty, and the growing national interest in Cuba.
records.summary_es: A estar del extracto suministrado, el periódico dio noticia de los debates sobre la facultad de Estados Unidos para tutelar e intervenir a favor de la República Dominicana frente a la conducta implacable del emperador Soulouque de Haití. La pieza hacía constar que el gobierno estadounidense ya había admitido y aplicado la doctrina de que los dominicanos eran acreedores a dicha tutela e interposición de Estados Unidos. El suelto aludía sucintamente por último a consideraciones sobre las miras de Washington hacia Nicaragua, el tratado Clayton-Bulwer y el manifiesto interés patrio por Cuba.

The newspaper also noted that Mr. Brooke withdrew a resolution regarding the suspension of official relations with Nicaragua's minister for later introduction in Executive session. Additionally, the Senate considered Mr. Cass's joint resolutions reaffirming the Monroe Doctrine and applying it to Cuba.

La gaceta registró asimismo que el Sr. Brooke retiró una moción tendiente a interrumpir los lazos diplomáticos con el ministro de Nicaragua a fin de someterla en sesión secreta. El Senado atendió además las resoluciones conjuntas del senador Cass que revalidaban la Doctrina Monroe aplicándola a Cuba.

records.summary_en: The *New-York Daily Tribune* reported on January 19, 1853, that a treaty with France involved aiding individuals to dismember Haytian territory and establish a new government through a revolutionary conspiracy. The article compared this French action to supporting South Carolina in seceding from the Federal Union and suggested that the Emperor of Hayti would be justified in considering the French debt cancelled if France does not disclaim the acts. The report also states that no peace treaty has been signed between the Dominican Republic and the Haytian Empire, raising expectations that hostilities would resume following the expiration of the armistice. records.headline: From Our Paris Correspondent.
records.summary_en: The *Daily National Intelligencer* reported on foreign newspaper discussions regarding rumored French acquisitions, specifically the alleged occupation of the Samana peninsula by French forces and a possible French protectorate over the Dominican Republic. French sources, such as *La Patrie* and the *Journal des Débats*, dismissed reports of a territorial seizure, attributing the presence of the French frigate *la Sibylle* to a routine cruise following an epidemic in Martinique. Additionally, the *Journal des Débats* recalled that a decade prior, the Dominican Republic had offered a protectorate to Louis Philippe to protect against western neighbors, which was interrupted by the 1848 revolution.
records.summary_es: El *Daily National Intelligencer* resumió el debate en diarios del exterior respecto a supuestas anexiones francesas, singularmente la alegada ocupación de la península de Samaná por destacamentos galos y un previsible protectorado sobre la República Dominicana. Fuentes de prensa francesas como *La Patrie* y el *Journal des Débats* descartaron una usurpación de tierras, explicando que la navegación de la fragata gala *la Sibylle* obedecía a un crucero ordinario tras una epidemia sufrida en Martinica. El *Journal des Débats* rememoró además que diez años atrás la República Dominicana brindó el protectorado a Luis Felipe para guarecerse de sus convecinos occidentales, proyecto truncado por la revolución de 1848.
