All the news from France seems to-day to confirm the story of the imperial programme announced in the Moniteur on the 1st of January. Indeed, the French have the few words uttered by the Emperor himself at the Tuileries on the 1st January, in reply to felicitations of the Diplomatic Corps, at the head of the few members of the diplomatic corps whom the official sheet represents as having been present to present themselves, had repaired to the palace to offer to the Emperor the compliments of the season. He said:
"I trust, with the Divine protection, to be enabled to maintain the prosperity of France, and assure the peace of Europe."
Then we have a little note in the official Moniteur, which was no sooner inserted in the official sheet than it formed part of NAPOLEON III. to the odious treaties of 1815, which it was the ambition of his life to undo, as ruinous and degrading to France. This curious note was elicited by the evident sensation produced in the political circles (if there can be said to be political circles now in France) by the appearance of a pamphlet entitled Limites de la France, the object of which was to indicate the tendency of the new Government to total conquest, or at least the absorption of all nations and fractions of nations west of the Alps and the Rhine. This publication was so identified in style and arguments with those which preceded and pamphlets which occur instantly to every one's mind as issuing from the highest source, as preceded the advent of the empire, that, of course, the bare announcement of the title caused all ears to prick up and all eyes to open wide. The author of Limites de la France published, it was asked, if it were not approved of? It would have been so easy to prevent it—to refuse the Government imprint. Sensation becoming so deep, the pamphlet in question was really intended to indicate the line of policy intended to sound public opinion upon the subject. The Government, soliciting this impression, and innocent of preparing, seeing that its silence was being interpreted in a manner dangerous, deemed it best—as Government is bound to do under such circumstances—instantly did, what it had formerly done in relation to the pamphlet which preceded the Empire, and which was used under its cover for the preparation of the empire; and what it did, not with regard to a compromising document upon Swiss affairs, published by a member of the Government, came out and repudiated all connection with the document, in the Moniteur of yesterday, the 5th of January, in the French, following and satisfactory terms:
"There have appeared recently several works, one among others under a title which seems calculated to excite—they seem to be intended to flatter tendencies which are supposed to exist in the French nation. The Moniteur repels all connection with the authors of these works, of which the spirit is as far removed from the intentions of the Emperor as from his loudly-declared policy."
After this, it is to be hoped that the most suspicious and incredulous as to the origin and intent of Limites de la France will submit his error, and abandon his apprehensions. To be sure, the Empire has come, as predicted by the pamphleteers of two and three years ago, and the said pamphleteers are now high in imperial favor. But that I don't pretend to be any thing more than a remarkable coincidence, which if I were a French writer it would be very indiscreet to remark upon. To be sure, the document on Swiss affairs, of which the existence was so positively denied, was afterwards published, in totidem verbis. That was certainly unlucky; but it does not authorize the suspicion, and still less the plain charge, that the disclaimer above quoted from the Moniteur is not irreproachably sincere and correct.
Extraordinary movement in the high functionary world has taken place in France upon the occasion of the new year. A decree of the 31st December nominated thirty-three new Senators. This body may now consist of 150 members, besides the ex-officio members, i. e. the French princes, the cardinals, marshals, and admirals of France. Six seats, original creation, by the decree of 1852, still remain, therefore, yet unfilled, in order to complete the Senate, forty-four nominations to make. These will doubtlessly be held back, only to be used to reward possible future exigencies. I must mention some of the names of the new Senators. The MARQUIS DE DAMPIN, the MARQUIS DE LAROCHEJAQUELIN, and the DUKE DE MOUCHY. These are three Legitimists, who have rallied to the Empire. In the Senate, M. DUPIN (ainé) has been replaced by Henry V. upon whom they wished to impose their own peculiar views as to the political course he should pursue. Legitimism has lost almost from history one of its most illustrious names, which he inherited, coming with all the luster that approved devotion to a principle, loyal fidelity to the King, and chivalric heroism could cast upon it, of which he never had any thing to bestow upon a cause, but which he has to-day honored by the connection with it in his person of the Senatorial dignity under an imperial Bonaparte. We have also M. DE HEECKEREN, late Baron DE ANTHES. This is the person who went to England to arrange Sir HUDSON LOWE after the death of Napoleon I, and who went to Russia, who was so grossly and publicly insulted the keeper of the Emperor. Beside these three, we have in the Senate three names of note: then M. FIALIN DE PERSIGNY, the devoted Minister of Louis Napoleon on 2d December, 1851; CLARY; SANTOUR DE LA TRESSONIER; MARSHAL VAILLANT; LUGUI; LUCIEN BONAPARTE, cousin of the Emperor Napoleon III, and son of Lucien Bonaparte; the DUKE DE BASSANO, and TASSCHER DE LA PAGERIE, cousin of the Empress.
The military enterprise of Count G. DE RAOUSSET-BOULBON in Northern Mexico, has, as might be expected, excite here a marked interest. The Paris papers give a large share in their columns to the latest news from the scene of operations. The Assemblée Nationale publishes the following letter from the French adventurer, written, it would seem, when just upon the eve of starting upon his expedition. If it has not yet appeared in print in the United States, it will be read with interest:
"I have for a year devoted my whole life, all my resources, all my exertions to the realization of a colossal enterprise, one of the boldest which has been witnessed for a long time. I have fully succeeded in my combinations, and I am now about to put my projects into execution. I start with two hundred men, adventurous, resolute, and full of faith. I shall find reinforcements in the country. I have foot soldiers, horsemen, and cannon, and I am about to put my project into execution..."
The Moniteur, among its foreign items, has merely stated the fact of the conquest of Count RAOUSSET-BOULBON—but the semi-official comments, in a tone, however, which would indicate a thorough consciousness of the danger of the ground they were treading on, and of the immenseness of collision with the United States, if this Government should give the slightest intimation of an intention to profit by the victory of the French band of adventurers in Northern Mexico, for the establishment of "a nascent colony" or by asserting the protectorate of an independent State upon the North American continent or on the borders of the United States. But I apprehend no such result. Whatever may be his personal instincts, by those of a victorious, NAPOLEON III. will seek other vent for his lust of enlarged dominion. He meditates other conquests; for the success of which he desires, IF NOT WINS THE AID, AT LEAST THE NEUTRALITY OF THE UNITED STATES. He is conscious, moreover, of many reasons not to provoke us by assuming a sovereignty or a protectorate in defiance with the policy loudly proclaimed by the United States for the last thirty years, and which no European State has dared to contest for the space of even one year. The Count, would-be imitator of Cortez, must therefore, in spite of himself, remain a buccaneer with the products of his enterprise, unless the Mexicans should succeed in repelling him, or unless we should nip his "nascent" glories in the bud by purchase from Santa Anna, and Santa Anna should not succeed to become a citizen of our Republic, or seek his ancient leader, Santa Anna, to the conquest of yet another province from Mexico. The Constitutionnel, I say, in putting allusions to the same subject, before summing up her article, as follows: "This column, which left California to seek its fortune in Mexico, is acting, be it well understood, on its own account, on its own risk and responsibility. It is a romantic episode, but one of an exclusively private character, to which, as between State and State, no importance attaches except as a matter of curiosity. It is strictly for the satisfaction of that word which we borrow from the Courrier des Etats Unis all the new details with which here column is filled..."
This Journal, I remember, has found phrases much less academic than "romantic episode," "column of adventurous spirit," "enterprising spirit," when it attempted to stigmatize the very similar, and certainly equally excuseable, invasions of American citizens into neighboring countries by citizens of our own "enterprising" population. Far be it from me to justify or even to palliate those invasions; but I dislike to see France engaging in these culpable adventures. The French journals have found no terms too severe by which to stigmatize them. I only insist that equal justice be rendered to all, and that an act be not qualified as enterprising, admirable, romantic, chivalrous, or heroic, when it happens to be French or American origin.
The occupation of Samana, in the Dominican Republic, by a portion of the French fleet in the West Indies, has been matter of lively interest here during the last week. What appeared in the official Journal, but—we well understand—La Patrie, a more or less semi-official sheet, thus explains the fact, which it seems has been sadly exaggerated and misinterpreted in the United States. It would certainly add something to the value of this explanation if it had appeared in the official journal; but we well understand how the official would seem not too anxious to show that this Government has avoided interference with the well-known American policy touching European acquisitions of territory or influence on our side of the Atlantic and Pacific oceans. La Patrie would have hardly ventured the following explanation of the Samana affairs if it were not true:
"English and American papers speak of an occupation by the French forces of the peninsula Samana. This news is like all those of the same sort (a very profound invention of the same sort), destitute of all foundation. A mark that the French semi-official) which many foreign sheets, and among them those of the United States, have given to the corvette La Silphide, which had remained in the West Indies, had no other purpose than a change of air. It proceeded upon a cruise in the seas of the Dominican Republic to give a passage to the French Consul, who had previously requested to report upon the news given to him in that country."
The Journal des Débats, alluding to the same report, had previously rated as quite unworthy of credit the supposition that the French Government had seized upon, with intention to appropriate, the eastern portion of the Island or St. Domingo; but regarded as at any rate less improbable than the news that Louis III. had accepted the protectorate of the Dominican Republic. And it calls to mind, in this connection, the fact that ten years ago the Republic offered the protectorate to Louis Philippe, in order to secure it from hostile invasion by its neighbors of the West end. Before Louis Philippe had positively accepted or refused the protectorate, a revolution broke out in Paris and led to negotiations. They were afterwards renewed, and the proposition was finally rejected by France under the Republic. It was apprehended that NAPOLEON III, so solicitous to increase the influence, and especially the maritime force of France in the West Indies, had reviewed and reversed the decision of the statesmen of the Republic. But I feel sure that NAPOLEON III. will commit no such folly; that he has too lively a sense of the "reproach of humiliation and effacement," which he says rests upon France, to seek glory for her at St. Domingo, when opportunities near home, of more facile execution, of better promise; opportunities in which he would be better supported by the strong national instincts, by the fierce, inextinguishable antipathies of his subjects, than he would be were he to throw down his glove to the young giant of America. Selfish, doubtless, and unjust those instincts and evoke those antipathies, and it will require the supreme efforts of all Europe to stay the deluge which may be made to pour upon it from France. A war with the United States would not stir up in France and array for action those terrible elements which would constitute the force of NAPOLEON III, and make him almost invincible if he sagaciously chooses the moment and the occasion for foreign war. He will therefore accept no protectorate of the petty West Indian Republic, and ratify no conquests of roving French adventurers, more brigands than soldiers, that would inevitably bring him

records.summary_en: A Paris correspondent examines a French press article arguing that France had missed chances to extend its influence in America. The article says the peninsula of Samana and the whole Dominican Republic were offered to the French government in exchange for its flag and protection, and the correspondent suspects Napoleon III is now seriously considering a larger French role in America.
records.summary_es: Un corresponsal en París examina un artículo de la prensa francesa que sostiene que Francia había perdido oportunidades de extender su influencia en América. El artículo dice que la península de Samaná y toda la República Dominicana fueron ofrecidas al gobierno francés a cambio de su bandera y su protección, y el corresponsal sospecha que Napoleón III está considerando ahora seriamente un papel francés mayor en América.

records.summary_en: A vessel claimed as a prize by the Dominican government was declared piracy under republic laws, resulting in prison sentences of two years for the captain, mate, and pilot, and one year for the rest of the crew. Court proceedings revealed a questionable letter involving Senor Jose Maria Pando, the Spanish commercial agent at Curacao, regarding instructions and financial advances for the ship via a merchant in Porto Plata. Additionally, the Dominican Republic celebrated the February 15 inauguration of General Santana as president.
records.summary_es: Una embarcación apresada como presa de guerra por el gobierno dominicano fue condenada por piratería bajo el ordenamiento legal patrio, dictándose penas de dos años de prisión para el capitán, contramaestre y práctico, y un año para los restantes tripulantes. Las audiencias sacaron a luz una sospechosa misiva que comprometía a don José María Pando, agente comercial español en Curazao, tocante a instrucciones y adelantos de caudales girados al navío a través de un comerciante de Puerto Plata. Por su parte, la República Dominicana conmemoró con regocijo la asunción de mando del general Santana como mandatario el 15 de febrero.
records.passage: declared piracy by the laws of the republic. records.full_text:
We have received files of El Progreso, published in Saint Domingo, extending up to the 1st of May. It seems that the Dominicans are making preparations for war, as it is feared that Soulouque might meditate an invasion of their territory. El Progreso says:—

Last week a vessel of war left our port for Azua, loaded with troops; and to-day another goes to the same destination, taking provisions for the army. The Dominican President had already left for that town, where he is organizing a powerful army, capable of supplying the northern frontiers with whatever may be necessary to repel an invasion. Up to the present, no hostile activity on the part of Hayti has been observed; but it is known that Soulouque has assembled a considerable force in the Canton of Maissade, and that a single caprice of the Emperor of Hayti, is sufficient to draw us into an unexpected conflict. Up to the present, the Dominicans have accepted the mediation of the three powers; but we want peace, not a truce, and if Hayti will not make peace, we feel confident that above all the conduct of the Liberator is guided by wisdom and prudence.

The most conclusive argument against force is force itself. We have, besides, an army in the field; and we should not, therefore, be surprised if our liberty is protected by our troops. In the mean time, a Spanish vessel of war, the Cortes, and an English vessel of war, the Cormorant, are in the Canton of Guayubin, as has been reported, to protect their respective subjects; but we are assured that, on the contrary, the intervention of the Spanish vessel, through its captain, has brought about a reconciliation between the two parties.

The Spanish brig of war, Veloz, under the command of Don Carlos Valcarcel, had arrived at Saint Domingo on the 26th of April, bringing on board the envoy of the President of the republic in the name of Her Catholic Majesty. On coming into port, the Veloz saluted the Dominican flag with twenty-one guns, which were returned by the fort. The Spanish captain and officers were received at the house of the President of the Republic with the highest honors, and were entertained at a banquet given in their honor.

On Sunday, the 17th of April, the ratification of the treaty of peace, navigation and commerce between France and the Dominican Republic was celebrated in Saint Domingo with great pomp. The day was announced by the firing of cannon and the ringing of the cathedral bells. Three high masses were celebrated in the cathedral, after each of which off went a broadside from the French vessel of war, Iphigenie, which was lying in port; after which the French flag was hoisted on the cathedral, and the French consul was received at the portal by the President of the Republic. In the evening a grand ball was given by the President, at which all the authorities, civil and military, were present. The festivities were concluded on the 18th, when the treaty was solemnly ratified with a salvo of twenty-one guns.

records.summary_en: The Tribune reprints an editorial urging U.S. treaties of recognition and alliance and generous encouragement for Dominica, then rebuts it point by point, disputing its racial claims. The rebuttal says the Dominicans are not whites, that a considerable proportion are pure Africans and the great majority of mixed blood, that President Baez was of mixed descent, and that no distinction of color was made in the distribution of office, honors or social position.
records.summary_es: El Tribune reproduce un editorial que insta a tratados estadounidenses de reconocimiento y alianza y a un generoso estímulo para Dominica, y luego lo refuta punto por punto, disputando sus afirmaciones raciales. La refutación dice que los dominicanos no son blancos, que una proporción considerable son africanos puros y la gran mayoría de sangre mezclada, que el presidente Báez era de ascendencia mezclada, y que no se hacía distinción de color en la distribución de cargos, honores o posición social.

records.headline: The editorial argues the United States should assume its proper attitude in Dominica, warning of British designs
records.summary_en: The editorial argues the United States should assume its proper attitude in Dominica, warning of British designs through Haiti and of the influence Dominica could exert in a crisis in Cuba. It presents Dominican friendship and independence, backed by the United States, as a way to check British views on Cuba and carry reprisals into British West India possessions if provoked.

records.headline: The paper gives a dramatic, racially framed period account of an attack on a Dominican village by a party led by one of Soulouque's captains
records.summary_en: The paper gives a dramatic, racially framed period account of an attack on a Dominican village by a party led by one of Soulouque's captains after Santana raised the flag of Dominican independence, and of local horsemen rallying residents to a hand-to-hand fight. It says the account ended with a truce said to be consolidating into peace.

Dice que el relato terminaba con una tregua que se consolidaba en paz.

records.summary_en: According to the *New-York daily tribune* on April 21, 1854, martial law was declared in Santiago following a conspiracy, with five ringleaders before the court and over forty persons under arrest. Meanwhile, the revision of the Dominican Constitution was completed, featuring an increased number of representatives and senators, the creation of a vice president, and changes reducing the naturalization time periods required for foreigners to become eligible as representatives and senators. Additionally, while the standard presidential and vice-presidential term was set at four years, actual President General Santana was granted two terms in office, allowing him to hold the chair until February 1861.
records.summary_es: Con arreglo al *New-York daily tribune* del 21 de abril de 1854, se declaró el estado de sitio en Santiago a raíz de una conspiración, encausándose ante los jueces a cinco cabecillas y permaneciendo más de cuarenta sujetos en prisión. Entre tanto, concluyó la reforma de la Constitución dominicana, elevándose la representación en el cuerpo legislativo con mayor número de diputados y senadores, estableciéndose la magistratura de vicepresidente y abreviándose los plazos de avecindamiento para que los forasteros optasen a ser elegidos representantes y senadores. Asimismo, fijándose en cuatro años el mandato ordinario del presidente y vicepresidente, al actual mandatario, general Santana, se le concedieron dos períodos sucesivos, autorizándosele a regir la presidencia hasta febrero de 1861.

records.full_text:
TO THE EDITOR OF THE NEW YORK HERALD.

The Evening Post, in an article so maliciously and contemptibly false that it could not possibly be written by a gentleman, and to which no gentleman would condescend a written answer, accuses me of playing a very secondary part in what he calls the "St. Domingo intrigue." My whole course in the matter of a Dominican treaty, from the first moment of her revolution to and since annexation, will answer for me; nor did I ever speak or think of influencing any man's party or acting on any man's dictation.

By one accident, has happened one truth: I do feel a deep sympathy for the brave Dominicans, and I shall not be driven by the tricks of any anti-American clique, or partisan who prostitute their cause until the Dominican republic obtains its deserved and honored place in the family of free American States. I protest against the insolence of the Post in abandoning my principles whenever the popular tide sets against them, or fleeing my colors from newspaper warfare.

I could not descend to reply to the Post—for my way—but it is my duty as an American citizen to throw light on the subject of the Dominican treaty.

I charge the New York Evening Post with working—at standard prices—for His Imperial Majesty Faustin I., Emperor of Hayti, for the destruction of the white population of that island.

I charge it—in its capacity of organ and co-laborer of the imperial government of Faustin I.—with habitually garbling and suppressing the news from St. Domingo, for the purpose of keeping people from turning their attention and sympathy to that brave struggle of the Dominicans for liberty and self-government. It has aimed to sustain Hayti in its anti-American system for the exclusion of whites, and as such, has denied the right to carry into their territory an army of invasion for the purpose of destroying her sovereignty.

I charge it with asserting disgraceful ignorance or wilful falsehood, in asserting that the Dominican is not an independent state, and that there is not a negro in the Dominican territory, while the fact is that the number of pure black Haytien inhabitants in this small American State is smaller than of any other.

I charge it with attempting to deceive and mislead the American people by fabricating, under the form of Post editorials, the fabulous bulletins of Soulouque, written by his own tools; of glossing over the invasion of the Dominican republic in 1849; and of glossing over, and indirectly justifying, the burning of whole villages, and the indiscriminate slaughter of women, children, and even domestic animals, on his savage march. Faustin and the Post say he marched an army into the Spanish portion of the island, "with the intention of restoring the integrity of the republic." They suppress the history of Soulouque's humiliating defeat at Las Carracas, by a small force of Dominicans, and his retreat—or rather his covered retreat by stating that, "in consequence of the mutual distress of the troops, and the impossibility of getting food for his horses, he was obliged to return;" but "gave notice that he intended to renew hostilities the following year—1850"

The Post says, Mr. Pierce ought not to send Mr. Fillmore "to prevent Soulouque's executing his purpose of subduing Hispaniola to his government and territory," and is as indignant as his friend Faustin can be at Mr. Fillmore's threat to check these wholesale butcheries. It regrets that "this absurd pretension directly led to a second attempt by Soulouque with more respect than it deserved—for he did not make it until the Dominicans refused to give any pledges for the future;" and then this false organ of Hayti adds, "the President could not put it hard in so publishing the affair as to make it appear that the threats of the United States had any effect, for the simple reason that these things are taken from its own open and glorified in-structions to the French commander." This was a significant visit of one of the concern to Hayti! and the author of the article above quoted was sent to learn what reward for past service, or what pay for future exertion, was then arranged with Faustin.

Finally, I charge the Post with wilfully misrepresenting the Dominican government and people, in order to discourage the American government and people, in order to prevent a treaty between them... and turn it, if possible, into Haytien channels, to carry out their plan of Haytien policy, which is already enjoying the best of the St. Domingo trade, through secret pay with the Haytien government. This young, enlightened and pro-gressive people, with a debt of not a dollar in their treasury, has ably sustained its domestic government for ten years, and is as free to form alliance and make treaties with other nations as any nation on earth, and far more worthy of American sympathy.

I finally charge the Post with subterfuge in in-sinuating that the President is attempting by these in-trigues to frighten weaker children than itself—if it refers to the Dominican people as symptoms of new slave States and future annexations. I have had no interest, directly or indirectly, in the Dominican treaty, nothing to hide, deny or conceal in my plans, princi-ples or conduct.

Whatever I have done in the matter of Dominican independence, has been because I thought it right, necessary and beneficial to both countries; and while life lasts, my whole influence, so far as it extends, shall be used to preserve the white race from Haytien supremacy.

WILLIAM L. CAZNEAU.

records.headline: The paper reports, citing the New York Post, a revived scheme attributed to Mr. Calhoun
records.summary_en: The paper reports, citing the New York Post, a revived scheme attributed to Mr. Calhoun to get the Dominican Government under American control, with a view to annexing the whole island and putting down Soulouque's empire in Haiti. It says Mrs. Cazneau has been appointed special commissioner to inquire into its feasibility, while her husband is ostensibly the commissioner.
records.summary_es: El periódico informa, citando al New York Post, de un plan revivido atribuido al Sr. Calhoun para poner al Gobierno dominicano bajo control estadounidense, con miras a anexar toda la isla y derribar el imperio de Soulouque en Haití. Dice que la Sra. Cazneau ha sido nombrada comisionada especial para investigar su viabilidad, mientras su esposo es nominalmente el comisionado.

records.headline: The editorial recounts Boyer's occupation of the Dominican part of the island, the Dominicans' achievement of independence
records.summary_en: The editorial recounts Boyer's occupation of the Dominican part of the island, the Dominicans' achievement of independence, and repeated Haitian attempts at reconquest repulsed until 1849, when Santana routed Soulouque's army and a truce for twelve months was concluded. It says Soulouque had recently been making formidable preparations for another invasion of Dominica and invokes the sympathies of the country on behalf of the Dominicans.
records.summary_es: El editorial relata la ocupación por Boyer de la parte dominicana de la isla, la consecución de la independencia por los dominicanos y los repetidos intentos haitianos de reconquista rechazados hasta 1849, cuando Santana derrotó al ejército de Soulouque y se concluyó una tregua de doce meses. Dice que Soulouque había estado haciendo recientemente formidables preparativos para otra invasión de Dominica e invoca las simpatías del país en favor de los dominicanos.

records.summary_en: A correspondent signing FELIX reports from the Dominican side that Santana reviewed five thousand men who are daily expected on their march for the Haitian frontier, and that the whole army of the republic will reach nearly thirty thousand. The correspondent says the government remains in charge of Santana's principal minister while Santana heads his troops to meet Soulouque, and that the French Consul General from Port-au-Prince is there to await the result.

records.chapter_es: Una república en busca de reconocimiento
records.full_text:
It would hardly seem possible to deny, in a formal manner, the ridiculous stories put in circulation by the New York Evening Post respecting Gen. Cazneau's mission last winter to St. Domingo. His honorable career as a public officer, his high standing in Texas as head of the State Department, attest his character and capacity in a sufficient manner; but the letter we give below is the most complete refutation that could be given to the unmerited attacks of the Evening Post. It tells its own story, and we think our New York contemporary will find it no easy matter to extricate itself from its false position—never so satisfactorily as Gen. Cazneau does his with the Dominican and the Dominican republic.

To the Editor of the Union:
The Evening Post persists in grossly misrepresenting the Dominican people, and even goes so far in its spirit of Haytien partisanship as to deny that I desire the white or mixed race to be dominant. It branded that article as "so malicious and false that it could not possibly be written by a gentleman;" and if that is what the editor of the Post calls an admission of the truth, he is welcome to all the benefit of it. I ask no authority for its assertions, and I most emphatically deny, so far as I am concerned, all knowledge, past or present, of any "conspiracy" or "design," on my part for the acquisition of Domingo.

I do know, however, that the people of the Dominican republic, are anxious for the recognition of their independence, and of public justice. It has a right to expect this from our government; and its recognition as an act of justice and public faith. It has a right to expect this from our government; and its recognition and application as will secure that promising young State from the aggressions of Hayti.

It is the duty of the United States government to carefully promote our commerce with all the Republics on this continent.

Our ships are in a position to do their carrying-trade, and we should encourage and facilitate them in every way for the requirements of their people. It is our interest to cherish the peace of the world, and expand our commerce with all the American States, for their wealth and strength contribute to our own. It is our duty to maintain our peace with all European powers, in opposition to the present and future pretensions of European discussion. This is the principle of the American Monroe doctrine. The recognition of Dominica has long been urged upon my friends the propriety of giving it our warmest support. Generals Cass, Douglas, Houston, Rusk, and many other distinguished members of both houses of Congress, have advocated it with success, and their authority should be as good authority with an enlightened people as that of the Evening Post.

"We infer," says the Post, coming at last to the real question, "that it is the intention of the Dominican party to claim that Dominicans and Hayti are two different races; and that it is the interest of the whites for which they contend."

This is precisely the issue; they are different races: Dominicans are white and mixed, the Haytiens are black; and I repeat, and, a white government. I repeat, Mr. Editor, what I said, that, "since the late peace congress, or the convention, that has just adjourned, who has no sympathy with the color of his line. Hayti is an intolerant, irresponsible, stubborn negro despotism, without a language, though their tongue assimilates to the French.

They are governed throughout by men of pure African race. In their wars, they are as merciless as savages; and it has been, on more than one occasion, their declared intention to wholly annihilate the white and mixed race on this island. The Post is extremely unfortunate in taking into its service "rights of Hayti," which the Post's editorials maintain in terms remarkably like the official bulletins of Soulouque.

The Dominican people, on the contrary, are brave, orderly, and peaceful. Their long conflict, "sustained by their own courage," is proved by the manner in which they have successfully maintained their independence since the expulsion of the Haytien government in 1844. They have been victorious in every battle with the Haytiens; and always against great odds. In the battle of Las Carreras, Faustin had five hundred men, (and three pieces of artillery,) killed; yet the Dominicans had the character and courage to cut off his retreat, taking several pieces of artillery. His retreat across the frontier was characterized by Haytien cruelties, by the sacrifice of blood and ashes, by the destruction of property and the cruel slaughter of women and children.

Haytien atrocities cause among the colored Dominicans that horror which I take to be common to their race, to torture and murder the whites in the interior districts. They were used until the Dominicans were compelled to make slaves of them—in the style of the Post planters, which they "succeeded in doing;" but the Dominican blacks were not ignorant enough to believe those white men were their enemies; and, if the Post's editorial does not cause distress, and should fail to shake them, American slavery would be more tolerable than the Haytien, which alarms and excites the blacks into insurrection, while it defends the "rights of Hayti," to make a general destruction of the white race.

The editor of the Post may keep his eyes on the white race of the world, but he cannot see that a white-black war in Dominica would not destroy the line of white people, as it does in some of our southern States—but it is surprising that he, on the contrary, insists that we are doing nothing to promote peace and harmony between the white and black populations.

I not only "pretend to believe," but positively assert, that there are African fringe in that brave soldier and patriot statesman, President Santana. Look at the president of Hayti, Faustin, and at President Santana, educated in Louisiana, and Senior Baez, a quadroon—and compare the former monster in the South upon that accomplished gentleman as a "full-blooded white man." The American consul, or commercial agent, at Santo Domingo may inform the Post whether he considers his father-in-law, the dignified Don Domingo de la Roca, a white man. He is the minister said to be now in charge of the government, while Santana heads the army. Baez was a quadroon, but he owed his short-lived elevation to European intrigues, which are always at work in the Antilles to elevate the African, and harass and subdue the white race. He attempted, with their aid, to fraternize with Hayti, and was banished from the country in consequence.

The editor of the Post probably met some of the Baez party last winter, in the select circles of the negro nobility, during his stay of about six months ago. This is very natural, considering some of his extraordinary information in regard to Santo Domingo; for example—"that there are not two hundred whites, all told, sailors and diplomats included," in the republic of Santo Domingo.

The editor of the Post informs his readers that he knew nothing about me six months ago. This is very natural, considering the difference in our tastes and associations; but there is no occasion for the rancorous violence he exhibits because I prefer the free, permanent and intelligent white society of Dominica to the attractions of his Haytien circle. He may don a coat of mail, if he choose, and present a breastwork to Hayti; but I did not thereupon write home slanderous attacks upon the character of a citizen who was doing no wrong to his family. Men do not engage in work like this. My own character is above the reach of those mischievous misrepresentations which are calculated to lead to the wholesale murder of the white race in the island of Santo Domingo.
WM. L. CAZNEAU.

Additionally, the article states that Haitian emissaries attempted to incite colored Dominicans last winter to murder whites in the interior districts by falsely claiming Americans were coming to enslave them.

records.full_text:
It was hardly worth the trouble to deny, in a formal manner, the ridiculous stories put in circulation by the New York Evening Post respecting Gen. Cazneau's business last winter in St. Domingo. His honorable career as a [illegible] of their people. It is our interest to cherish the power, production, and general welfare of all these American States, and build up a strength to contribute to our own. It is so much strength added to the American force, in opposition to the present and future pretensions of European dictation. This is the principle of the American system, or it has none. In accordance with that principle, I have been urging upon my friends the propriety of giving to the Dominican republic the encouragement of a friendly recognition, as long and as earnestly as I have opposed it in the service of the black Emperor Faustin Soulouque.

The only plan I have ever heard of, or advocated, in connection with Gen. Cazneau, or any successor of his in office, was to strengthen the country relation with all the Spanish American States, and to establish them where they did not exist, as in the case of Dominica. It was only on this principle of American policy, that the recognition of Dominica was discussed with Senators Rusk, Douglas, Mason, Slidell, and many other distinguished members of the Senate, prior to Gen. Cazneau's connection with them; and those gentlemen should be as little suspected of a scheme of "filibustering" as the allies of Faustin.

We infer, says the Post, coming at last to the real question, "that it is the intention of the Post's editorial friends to show that Dominica and Hayti are under the control of different races, and that it is the interest of the whites for which they show such an anxiety."

This is precisely the issue; they are different races. Dominica is governed by civilized white manners, with a democratic constitution, and, obedient to the laws of nations. There is not, to name one man, either in the cabinet, Congress, or the Dominican forces, that has a drop of African blood in his veins. Hayti is an ignorant, barbarous, stubborn negro despotism, without a legal code, and obedient to no laws, unanalogous to the French.

They are governed throughout by men of negro blood and negro ideas. In their wars, they are as merciless enemies to quadroons as to whites, for they audaciously proclaim their intention to wholly annihilate the white and mixed race on the island. This creed of extermination is the leading point in those "rights of Hayti," which the Post's editorials maintain in terms so remarkably like the official bulletins of Soulouque.

The Dominican people, on the contrary, are from Spanish stock, and their character is not "without character and courage," as the Post says. As a matter of history, having sustained themselves since the establishment of their republic, they have been victorious in every battle with the Haytians. Under Santana, as well as under Santana's predecessors—at the battle of Las Carreras, Faustin had five times their force, and yet victory was with the Dominicans. Have the Dominicans had the "character and courage" to put him to flight, with the loss of thousands of his troops? He escaped, and the frontier was characteristic of Haytian warfare, and marked by blood and ashes, by the destruction of property and the cruel slaughter of women and children.

Haytian emissaries came among the colored population in Dominica, and tried to set the country on fire, to incite them to rise and murder the whites in the interior districts. They asserted that the Americans were coming to make slaves of them—in the style of the Post's phraseology about "the extension of slavery;" but the Dominican blacks were not ignorant enough to believe these monstrous absurdities. Their prudence does not excuse, and should put to shame an American journal in continually presenting the case in a shape to alarm and excite the blacks into insurrection, while it defends the "rights of Hayti" to make a general destruction of the white race.

records.summary_en: In an editorial argument using the paper's period racial language, the writer recounts Dominican independence, repeated Haitian attempts at reconquest repulsed through 1849, and a truce after Soulouque's rout by Santana. It argues the United States should protect the Dominican Republic and says France was intriguing for its conquest.

Sostiene que Estados Unidos debería proteger la República Dominicana y dice que Francia intrigaba para conquistarla.

records.summary_en: The *Liberator* reported that the Boston Post defended the United States government's disposition to recognize the independence of Dominica while ignoring the absence of any proposed recognition for Hayti and Liberia, despite stronger commercial and historical reasons to do so. The article argued that Dominica is of little commercial importance and would be politically united with Hayti—from which it rebelled due to religious differences—were it not for outside intrigues. records.full_text:
From the Boston Commonwealth.
THE SLAVE POWER AND ST. DOMINGO.

Filibustering Manifest Destiny has proclaimed that the Slave Power must have ‘our Southern islands,’ and that the negroes of Cuba, Hayti, &c., must be doomed to perpetual slavery, and ‘kept at work under white republican masters.’ When this language was used in the Democratic Review, Hayti was named particularly, and it expressed no more than the Slave Power actually means and is now planning to accomplish. The purpose is to get possession of Hayti by means of filibusterism cunningly introduced into Dominica. One insidious attempt has been made upon Dominica, but failed. Duff Green was concerned in that affair, and his son was the agent employed in Dominica by our government. The conspirators sought to make an arrangement with the Dominican authorities, which should secure filibusters the privilege of ‘colonizing’ on that part of the island, with a separate and independent military organization of their own. Ostensibly, they were to be cutters of mahogony and dye woods, but really a filibustering army designed for the subjugation of the island when strong enough in numbers. But the Dominicans were suspicious, and the negotiation fell through.

Recently, Mrs. Cazneau, the ‘Cora Montgomery’ of some of the newspapers, and Gen. Cazneau, her husband, have been sent to Dominica to negotiate, plot, and intrigue, in behalf of this scheme of the Slave Power; and ‘Cora,’ it is said, has far more genius for the business than the General. It is reported that they have made some progress, that our Government will make a formal treaty with Dominica, and recognize its independence as a nation, and that the matter will soon be in shape to come before Congress. Of course, all this will not be done without such provisions in the treaty as will give our Slave Power that foothold in the island which it seeks. The whole purpose, on the part of our Government, is a filibustering invasion of both Dominica and Hayti. It means nothing else. It is seeking to execute that decree which says the African race in that island must be reduced to slavery, and ‘kept at work under white republican masters.’ If what is reported is true, (and it is fully credited by those likely to be best informed on the subject,) this is one of the next forms in which the slavery question is to be presented to the country, and the people should take it to their thoughts and feelings. The following statement in regard to this Cazneau treaty shows what is on foot:—

‘As far as could be collected from the first proceedings, the treaty is to have for one of its various ostensible objects, to stipulate for certain rights in the ports of the Republic, and especially in the spacious and secure bay of Samana, for the armed vessels of the United States, in case of war, and in time of peace, for the establishment of a kind of colonization, black or white, of individuals from the United States, in some part of the Dominican Republic.’

The Boston Post has already begun its defence of this villany, in a characteristic parrgraph of three or four lines, full of hypocritical wonder that anti-slavery men should put forth hostile criticism on the disposition of our government to recognize the independence of Dominica. Of course, that paper will never intimate to its readers, that, if this disposition of our Government were honest—if it is not, in fact, full of plotting piracy—it would also propose a recognition of the independence of Hayti and Liberia. There are more and stronger reasons for recognizing either of these gevernments than can be invented for this negotiation with Dominica. We have a large commerce with Hayti, and Liberia has grown up under American influences. Dominica is of little or no importance commercially, and would now be politically united with Hayti, if it had not rebelled and withdrawn, because that government proclaimed free toleration of all religious sects. The Dominicans have the religious training and bigotry of Spanish Catholics. They occupy what was the Spanish portion of the island, and the Haytiens that part which was held by the French. But they are all of African descent, and would constitute but one people, if not interfered with by the rascally intrigues of outsiders.

Our Slave Power has decided that it will injure the peculiar institution to allow the Dominicans and Haytiens, whose parents were slaves, to realize a prosperous and happy fortune. It will not do to let the world see them work out for themselves such a fortune; and, moreover, the slaveholders hope to prepare that island for annexation to the Union as a slave State. ‘Our Southern islands,’ they say; and how much that signifies!

President Santana and the Cibao region strongly rejected diplomatic advice to adopt the Haitian flag, threatening instead to invite American forces to assist in conquering Haiti. records.full_text:
Correspondence of the N. Y. Tribune.
Santiago, (Island of Hayti,) Sept. 14, 1854.
The Island of Hayti is divided nominally between two independent powers, the Dominican Republic at the east, which is under white preponderance, and the west, which is exclusively under the black. There is, however, a third district that differs in its moral elements almost from either. The rich district of the gold-teeming Cibao, and the fertile plain of the Vega is considered a part of the Dominican Republic, but its population are a distinct race and sympathize not entirely in accordance with those of the capital and extreme east of the Republic.

The Cibao district is not of Indian, as Eastern Hayti is white with a dash of African, and more than any other part of the island it cherishes an uncompromising hatred of the Haytians. In every quarter the inhabitants have stories of Haytian acts of cruelty to tell their children, and every family has its own tale of horrors about the Haytian invasions. They look upon even a peaceful presence and free intercourse with Hayti, lest it might lead, as it did once before, to a union of the whole island under a colored government. They openly declare themselves in favor of annexation to the United States, and have never ceased to demand white immigration. This district once memorialized the United States Government on the subject of receiving it into the Union, or making it a separate and neutral State, with ports entirely and forever open to our commerce, on condition of being protected from the all-destroying inroads of the Haytians. This memorial was buried, like Sir John Moore, in silence and darkness, without a word from the American press, but it awakened France and England to insist upon a peace between the belligerent parties.

Eastern Hayti has a large colored population, and the fusion of the races, with the final supremacy of the blacks, is fast approaching there; Santana, the Liberator, Generals Alfau and Contreras, are Dominican whites, and their death or another dash of their stamp could be out of the way; but Central Hayti would never consent.

The British Consul has more than once advised the Dominicans to strike the white cross and raise the Haytian tri-color, but President Santana was enraged at the counsel, and the Cibao said if it was attempted they would form a new State and call on the Americans to come with letters of marque and conquer Hayti on their own account.

You can understand, therefore, that the Island of Hayti is divided in two governments and three parties, and that each party textually demands its share of the territory, but the Haytians have two-thirds of the entire population—or 650,000 out of 800,000 inhabitants.

Eastern Hayti is so much under European influence that it can never be annexable under European policy, which is declared here without reserve, of uniting with Hayti, but for the central district, whose standard of political independence is high.

The geographical position of these districts is much against their independence, for they are between the two Haytis of Hayti on one side and European Hayti on the other, and it is only by a union with the United States would be reliable protection to the island, for the protection of an American State would unite its sections in a common sentiment, and settle it firmly in its place among the republic of nations. America ought to wish to see this island or any part of it annexed to the United States. It would be an immense field for our enterprising citizens, who would then have the monopoly of her trade, and entirely clothe this people with our manufactures.

A Commissioner from the United States is at St. Domingo City at this moment, negotiating a Treaty which will give our citizens the right to buy land and work mines, and all the rights and privileges of American citizens. This is the same as giving a new State to American enterprise, and we must hope that Gen. Cazneau will succeed in spite of all opposition from abroad; but Hayti is of all classes and colors, and in particular it opens a fine field for American enterprise, being of mixed blood. The laws and the constitution make no distinctions of colors, and the customs of society prefer the white race all to whom the white blood visibly preponderates.

If southern American protection would pass, for I have not met any one whose education and position would place him in the highest society if he were white, who would think of southern Americans keeping down the blacks here quite as positively as they are in the South.

Let the friends of the colored race try out the problem of its capacities on this friendly soil and under a favorable climate. There is nothing here, not even the prejudices of society to hinder their efforts. Land is cheap, fertile, the laws liberal, society kind, and the country very near to you. Send school books and teachers, and encourage the honest and industrious of the colored race of the Union to come here and show the world what they are worth. There will be order and safety so long as American results will be tangible facts, and we want some real solid facts to thicken all the froth of philanthropy with which the United States are simmering.
AMERICUS.

records.full_text:
VIRGINIA REINS.—The New York Tribune is a monomaniac on the Southern question. Not a paper comes from that office which does not bear its "testimony" against the "curse" of slavery. Greeley evidently thinks that the salvation of his soul depends upon blazing away at slavery in every number of his paper. He cannot eat, drink, or sleep, without slavery, emancipated negroes, blood, chains and lashes, before his eyes. Lately he is talking about Virginia ruins, and thus sesquipedally he discourseth:
'The ruins of Jamestown but typify the ruins of the whole State,' &c. This is the substance of the sneering article recorded. For example: Norfolk is a small village; Richmond, if not a ruin, is a place of very small importance, and has no human flesh. The fields of Virginia, too, are ruined, and the people, and tobacco-chewers, smoking, spitting have contributed to wear them out and drive the chivalry to other lands. The people, too, are intellectually ruined.'
In this elegant manner, the New York Express, thus handsomely raps the demented philosopher over the knuckles:
'The New York Tribune is mistaken! Norfolk is in a high state of prosperity. Richmond is as prosperous as any city in the Northern States.—There are some things in Virginia, however, of a higher science displayed on them, than any where in New York, negro-traders, tobacco juice, equal in our State. The people have an amount of brain and power we feel else, they would never have given us that class of statesmen who are living in the Northern States more than two-thirds of them (Everett and Fillmore) equal to Rives and Hunter. Bayly, a member from Accomac even, has more practical and actual power, from mind and experience, than any Northern State in the House of Representatives. The people of Virginia have their vices and their faults, but the breed of its mighty men is in some degree run out; but the State only needs manufacturing to become a great and ancient power. The vice of its system is, that it is not commercial and agricultural. The undistinguishing slanders upon the people of our own countrymen are simply disgusting.'
The New York Tribune may find a more inviting field for its philanthropy in the history of Hayti. The bravest of them provoked their savage masters to kill them at once, but some others were known to drag out their miserable lives under the whip like ill-treated slaves on the country patches of ten negroes. No negro was responsible by negro law, for the murder or maltreatment of even a mulatto, much less of a white person. The cruelties which the mixed bloods suffered in attempting to hide and protect some white families of San Christoval, are too horrible to be related. If the Tribune wants a field for its philanthropy, let it look to Hayti, and not to Virginia.

records.summary_en: The *New-York Daily Tribune* reported on Dominican resistance to Haitian control, noting that memories of severe mistreatment and violence during past Haitian rule deterred locals from favoring Haitian dominance. Despite rumors circulated that Americans intended to enslave the population, both white and mixed-race residents remained fearful of a Haitian return. The correspondent urged the United States to counter British diplomatic influence by officially recognizing the Dominican Republic.
records.summary_es: El *New-York Daily Tribune* dio cuenta de la irreductible resistencia dominicana a la hegemonía haitiana, observando que la memoria de atropellos y rigores padecidos durante el régimen anterior apartaba a los naturales de cualquier simpatía hacia el dominio haitiano. Pese a las patrañas propaladas de que los norteamericanos proyectaban esclavizar a la población, tanto los moradores blancos como los de color temían sobremanera la restauración del yugo haitiano. El corresponsal encarecía a Estados Unidos a contrarrestar la injerencia diplomática británica mediante el reconocimiento oficial de la República Dominicana.

This our Plenipotentiaries will not agree to, and so there is a 'hitch' at present, which Santana is urged to remove by a coup d'état, like Louis Napoleon's; but he has not yet screwed his courage up to that point. El despacho mencionaba además la arribada y residencia del comisionado Cazneau [nombrado Oatneau] y su consorte en Santo Domingo.

records.full_text:
THE UNITED STATES AND ST. DOMINGO.—MR. CAZNEAU AND THE TREATY—FRENCH INTERFERENCE—NEW SCHEME OF COLONIZATION—ALLIANCE BETWEEN NAPOLEON AND SOULOUQUE, &c., &c.

[From the National Democrate.]
Great events are about to come forth in this island in behalf of the children of Africa, and may God turn the result of the events alluded to in the United States to befriend our cause.

Louis Napoleon, the Emperor of France, of he highest rank among the sovereigns of the world, will not leave the whole island of Hayti under the just and vigorous sceptre of Faustin the First.

The Dominicans pretend to be a white population, and although there may be some who can show a clear skin, look at the characters, and try to find out their progenitors. If a man is so white that no one can perceive that he has African blood in his veins, then he may pass; but not else.

The Dominicans have, they say, made propositions to the French and English nations, and for the sale of St. Domingo to France, and Samana to England; but they cannot touch them; but these great European powers will never allow a single square inch of Hayti to be given up to the United States.

These powers have given full authority to their agent in St. Domingo to arrange for the return of the Dominican Republic—to the dominion of the empire. They will be allowed to retain the houses they really live in, but all the rest of the property will be restored to its original owners. The unoccupied land will be taken by the Dominican government, to be given to those who, for the offered terms, which our Emperor intends to make, shall come from France to populate the country.

This warm climate suits the African race, and there are no people under the sun so much indebted to us as those who have no house or home. To these the Emperor Faustin will give lands, and the great influence of their friends in the United States will help them to a noble existence.

It is said that the French Emperor will remit one million of francs from the French indemnity, which is to be employed in assisting ten thousand men of color to come to us from France. They will, by their intelligence, maintain the peace of the Haytian Empire, which is finally the only source of security to France for her indemnity, and that of Hayti itself.

There are at least fifty thousand small farms at St. Domingo, which could be divided among ten thousand families of color; but the Dominicans are not disposed to give them up. All will be offered to settlers of African blood from the United States, who wish to come to Hayti.

Our brethren in the United States may be certain of success. There is so much land in Hayti that thousands of smart settlers could come out to us from America, and clear up the country, and make it flourish.

Mr. Bigelow's letters about our Emperor are terribly exaggerated. He came here with his head full of ridiculous notions, directly from the United States, to write a book for the Emperor Faustin, and here his letters are coming out, of which he ought to be ashamed; for he has written what he can hardly read, and must have lately improved in his intellect if he can write so well. Mr. Bigelow should not set him up for the lawful lord of the whole island, when we are under the French rule. Faustin has the weakness of his race for fine clothes, and should not carry it to excess, though—which is the dominant language here—than is taught him by rote for scholastic occasions.

If this is the way our friends talk of us in France, we are not surprised that our enemies in America should speak ill of us; but as for Faustin, we can only say, if he does not know how to govern this island, we at least do not keep Bigelow's faith with us, it will all be ours again.
QUAROU.

THE FRENCH ACCOUNT.
We are in the reception of details of the famous mission of Mr. Cazneau at Santo Domingo, and of the negotiations carried on by this diplomatic pair, and of the present state of the Haytian question, which we hope will have the double merit of edifying and of interesting our readers. The correspondent to whom we are indebted for them might have added many others even more piquant. "A great deal might have been said," he writes us, "about Mr. Cazneau personally, the position which he has assumed since his arrival, and especially that of his eccentric half; their establishment in a sort of negro hut, covered with thatch, and other means of seeking popularity, not less singular, contrived by her; but I have endeavored to abstain from everything of a personal nature."

We therefore give the history of this conjugal mission, stripped of all accessories:—

Port au Prince, Domingo, Dec. 1, 1854.
The treaty concluded between the United States and the Dominican Republic, signed on the 7th of August, was printed and laid before the public on the 1st of November. It created here the greatest emotion. It was generally believed that Mr. Cazneau had failed in his mission as to Samana, threatened to return to Washington, and that Mr. Cazneau had taken his threat, he became resigned, and for the present, at least, gave up the Samana project, provided that he obtained a ceded tract. This article would have secured to the United States, under the name of a public naval depot, a tract of land on the Bay of Samana, for the purpose of a naval station, and given the United States jurisdiction over American citizens who should settle upon this tract.

This article of the treaty, which has been for so long a time so frequently mentioned by the attraction of the public, which Mr. Cazneau has so long tried to conceal, and which has spent all Mr. Cazneau's journey across a country not less famous for its iron than its copper, was the only point between this point and New York, the only one put forward to excite the vanity of the Americans, to awaken the attention of the English and French governments, and to make the latter believe that if the treaty was ratified, the independence of Santo Domingo from Hayti, Samana, as its position, threatens not only Hayti, but Cuba and the Spanish islands.

The Cazneau treaty, as signed, stipulates that the powers who shall have signed it within eighteen months, come immediately to secure that of his government, the second for six months, and the third for an indefinite period of delay. But Mr. Cazneau, who lacks a little of that energy of which he speaks, was afraid to send the treaty, such as it was signed, with the French modification to the United States Congress, for fear that it would be rejected, and he chose rather to consider the French text as having been accepted, as last, for the sake of getting his treaty passed. The treaty was signed on the 11th of November; but as it was first agreed upon, before the French modification was added, it aroused the fears of the English and French consuls of Santo Domingo, who dispatched a vessel of war to Port au Prince, and sent the English minister of the foreign affairs belonging to the French naval station of the Antilles, M. Raybaud. He arrived on the 15th at Santo Domingo, on board of a French brig of war, called the Le Yeketallow, and by his parasite, Angulo Guridi, a native of Santo Domingo, presented to the Dominican government the form of a protest, to the French and English consuls, against the treaty signed between the Dominican government and Mr. Cazneau, and threatening them with the arrival of the whole force of the French and English naval forces. To this message, marked by a humor quite in character with M. Raybaud, the Dominican ministers as brief as they were determined.

This energetic language was little favorable to the plans of M. Raybaud, and he was obliged to have recourse to intimidation to the people who were convinced that the treaty was signed, and he excited a strong movement of party on the soil of the offer, provided they submitted to Hayti. The French consul had even offered to pay the Dominicans, because of the color of nineteen-twentieths of the population, a sum of money which could scarcely be honorable to the country without real advantage, and they had declared that they would never unite with the United States because of their local laws and of their institution of slavery. He urged that if the treaty was signed, the white portion of the population exposed, whatever be their fortune and personal merit, to be expelled from the island. The threat of a treaty to the Dominican Congress cooled of wonderfully, and they refused to give their sanction to the modification in the hope of seeing this counter-movement subside. In this state of things, M. Raybaud, seeing the success which he desired, he sailed on the 23d of November a second time for Port au Prince, to get a temporary postponement. The government answered four days after, by a refusal to give a delay, saying that they would wait for no further negotiations, but that as soon as Mr. Cazneau should withdraw the treaty, it it was not ratified, they would invade Santo Domingo. They forbade this presentation at that time. Mr. Cazneau sent a copy of his treaty to Washington, but he has, as a man of color, as are also three out of his four ministers, signed the treaty, and if it is not ratified in eighteen months he would break off all correspondence. He has sent by a vessel belonging to his government, the steamer Metropolis, to his government for instructions. This is where matters stand now. St. Domingo has, and has completely, escaped from the clutches of the French consul; but more particularly of M. Maxime Raybaud, who has for four years used all his influence, that it should be attached to St. Domingo, on his way to Paris, where he was sent by Faustin; and from where M. Raybaud crossed to St. Domingo, with the idea of making it a Haytian province, or at least that he might quietly in the way of a truce, for a long period, between the two countries, which would finally result in a total submission. The establishment of a French naval station at Samana, at which the Haytian government would seem to be with and good cause, singularly alarmed.

The French consul, however, was mistaken as to the devotion of the Dominican Congress, which will give its sanction to the treaty, and Mr. Cazneau will sign within two days the between the readinigs. It is generally supposed that Mr. Cazneau will stay long enough to be able to dispose of such persuasive means, if necessary, as to make the Dominican Congress accede to his details; still it is impossible to discover any advantage to this position, except for the greater or less success of certain parties.

records.full_text:
Our St. Domingo Correspondence.
ST. DOMINGO, Nov. 24, 1854.
Antics of European Diplomacy on the Island—The European Consuls think St. Domingo is Sebastopol—Uncle Sam has his Laugh at them.

The mail packet from St. Thomas brought to St. Domingo on Sunday, 19th inst., news of the fall of Sebastopol. Fresh French and English forces, and great was the joy and loud the shouting thereat.

Mr. Maxime Raybaud, the French Charge d'Affaires at the Haytien court, came here to forbid any treaty whatever with the United States; for, he says "England and France will not permit." This is a simple falsehood, based a good deal like European encroachments on the independence of an American power; but of course it will appear all right to the Haytiens and the Spanish junkers of the Dominican States.

Monsieur Raybaud has lorded it largely over both the white and black governments on this island for some time past, threatening one with the other when he desired to bring it down. He feeds it, now using the seventy millions of francs claimed by his government from Hayti as a screw; now, when he professes a condescending friendship to the Dominicans, to put the Haytiens in the way of conquering this fine territory, in the hope that, after a while, both will be able to pay their debts to France. The Dominicans would rather make a free gift of their country to the United States.

These European Consuls will chafe mightily at seeing all their fine plans frustrated by this treaty with the United States.

But to return to the Sebastopol news: These French and English diplomats in their imagination forgot that Sebastopol was only one extreme corner of the Russian empire, and that it would take a hundred such victories to break down Nicholas, with his six-million subjects, and they carried themselves as if Russia was entirely at their feet.

At their command, the Comandante of St. Domingo was directed to raise the French and English flags to the highest place of honor, higher than a national flag. By some mistake, the officer raised the American flag higher, and had hardly got it hoisted, when in came a messenger in haste from Monsieur Raybaud, ordering down the American flag. The officer attempted to obey, but the obstinate flag took firm hold of the rope by the upper outside corner, and spread out in full size—refusing to come down—there to the confusion... for twenty minutes, our stars half covering the French and English flags, to the supreme anger of Monsieur Raybaud and the British Consul, Mr. Schomburgk, and the secret satisfaction of the Dominicans, who were delighted with this emblem of arrogance. They were compelled to lower all the flags before the stars and stripes could be taken off. Sebastopol was forgotten, and the flags had to be hoisted and saluted the following day.

Then they wrote such a brag story... these diplomatic gentlemen ... that, having disposed of Russia, "Our governments would now turn their attention to the United States."

Sunday was a great Dominican gala day. Some two thousand troops, in full uniform, received their banners and attended divine service. Monsieur Raybaud, taking advantage of the occasion, got a French priest to sing a Te Deum, and preach a sermon, explaining to the troops the glorious Christian victory; for, according to the Padre and this diplomat, the Turks must be super-excellent Christians. Oh, "what a great day for Santo Domingo!"

But the mail packet of the 6th comes in and says that all the news from Europe is false, that Sebastopol was not taken, and that the story of the glorious victory was a great hoax. The Consuls go about with long faces and a very downcast air.

You will know all about the fate of Sebastopol before us; but if it is not taken when this reach you, you may go to bed in peace, for Monsieur Raybaud does not intend taking the United States until Sebastopol is used up.
AN AMERICAN.

St. Domingo, Nov. 25, 1854.
Invasion of the Rights of an American Citizen by the Haytien Consul—Threats of Violence—Expression of American Sympathies—The Feeling of the Dominicans with the United States.

If the Dominicans have a party, and even a press, in the United States, they may seek to deny the facts I relate; but the person legally vested with the character of representative of France and Hayti at this capital, has forced the Dominican government to destroy the liberty of the press, and also prevented the treaty with the United States.

Allow me here to state some facts which will prove I am correct.

I saw in the NEW YORK HERALD of February last, an article containing a very exact description of the festivities of the sixth anniversary of the republic, French republic, with the context, and, on its site; point, Houston and Brasseur, my paper, El Orden. M. Raybaud made very haughty complaints that this was a disrespect to his imperial master, and that the article must be written by an American, because my paper was printed in the government printing office.

President Santana therefore withdrew the privilege, and stopped the Orden. I was ruined; but, feeling the injustice, submitted without murmur.

Again, in October last, I, with two of my Dominican friends, got up a paper called El Oasis, the prospectus of which, as we had not as yet the machinery necessary, we had permission to use the government type and press. No sooner had it appeared, than M. Raybaud again complained, with extreme reserve, in order that this French dictator should not be offended, President Santana again took away our freedom of speech—proposing to continue our editorial observations carefully and exclusively to Dominican affairs.

The treaty with the United States was at this time known to be on the carpet. It excited the enthusiasm of all patriotic Dominicans, but there were also the most violent and absurd slanders put in circulation respecting the object of the mission of General Cazneau—no less than the American government. No one pretends to doubt these vile slanders were prepared at the European Consulates, and were exciting panic among the Haytiens in the country.

The editors of the Fenix, in the simple desire to have the truth understood by the Dominican people, republished the articles from the NEW YORK HERALD, as being printed at the moment for the use of Congress. M. Raybaud came from Hayti to stop the treaty, and he pretended to find in those articles that the Dominican editor was an American paper, and must be stopped.

I happened to see the proofs as they first came from the type, and when he found the trespass... he inserted the word "Santo Domingo," with the headline "Santo Domingo and the United States," he republished the article without any comments, in order that these offensive truths could see the light. I enclose an exact copy of it to the editor of the NEW YORK HERALD, in order that the Americans may know in what manner French agents in Santo Domingo pretend to master American interests and the liberty of the press in St. Domingo.

The article was as follows:
"Our readers will find below the treaty of friendship, alliance and trade, concluded between the United States and the Dominican republic, which we have no doubt will be read with interest by every one of our citizens, not only for the interest it must inspire in the minds of all who sincerely desire a prosperous future for our country, but even more for its effect on the destiny of that interesting island. To those who are spectating this new tie of friendship which is to enlarge our commerce and increase the power and dignity of our country, it will be gratifying to know that it was produced in the atmosphere of suppositions, conjectures and fears which the allies were so anxious to spread over the zenith and scatter the clouds that float in space. No one knew the terms of the treaty until its final signature and general. The only difference is the article regarding Santo Domingo, which is now considered as mutual and general and unquestionable interest. Besides, the terms of this stipulation are equally high on both sides, and it will end by a treaty with the United States.

"The Haytiens, who are alike the enemies of the United States and the Dominican republic, have displayed and are displaying extraordinary alarm at the mission of General Cazneau, the American Plenipotentiary near this government. This is natural—a true treaty between the two republics would not agree with their hopes to make the passive attitude of the United States applicable to all the Spanish country around the gulf... No one can foresee the end of this drama; but there is no reasonable why one American State should not be the friend of another, they try to turn to tricks and falsehoods to prevent the realization of this friendship.

"The press of Hayti, directed by Frenchmen, spreads a fear that General Cazneau came here to exact some concessions in favor of the United States, and to ask a precedence. We can only laugh at these fables and fantasies. What can Hayti do to Santo Domingo? The Haytien press is a St. Domingo Columbia. We will not insult the United States so much as to believe that it would compromise its dignity by taking part in these petty internationalities. We believe, besides, that the Dominican republic, however weak, is strong enough to maintain itself now; for though small in power and population, God, the protector of justice, will save us from the Haytiens, and even in climate—our lack of strength and numbers.

"The editor of the Fenix has republished this article as an ultimatum messis, which we give to these false reports, that those who believe that the United States intends to compromise the independence or sovereignty of the Dominican republic, may see their error. Santo Domingo, if she was not independent, would choose of making this island what nature intended it should be—an asylum for European despotism; and if we believed there was in Samana the seeds of danger to Santo Domingo, we would be the first to oppose the mission of Commodore Perry, of the United States navy, who obtained that point. Is there a Dominican, we would ask, who does not see that foam with consternation and in a state of desperation, all those whose interests are opposed to the prosperity of our country? They see in the progress of the State most dreaded by Hayti. But we say to all these alarms, the treaty with the United States is concluded, and there is nothing in it incompatible with our national independence and sovereignty—so we may smile at all these Haytien reports.

"The treaty is now given to the public light, and we leave it to the judgment of our citizens, whether it is not one of the best steps which the government could have taken, and one which we have conceived for advancing the condition of the country, and one which will bring us fruit.

"It is no slight satisfaction to us, after having been President of the republic, to have effected this convention—and it is a still greater satisfaction when we think, and the great majority of the country is of the same opinion, that it will destroy forever the pretensions of the Cbao, who have thus declared themselves the enemies of our prosperity. So long live the friendship of the American Union a powerful support to our independence, and long live President Santana!

"This article, Mr. Editor, and this alone, was sufficient to cause the arrest of Mr. Guridi, and threatened, at the same time, the hopes of your friend and servant,
ANGULO GU RIDI.
