records.full_text:
Seizure of the Sch. Chas. Hill at St. Domingo.

The case of the Sch. Chas. Hill, which was seized at San Domingo, by the San Dominican government, may seem to many of little importance compared with the great question that agitates the public: but small acts of injustice between governments often lead to the most fatal results, and we wish now, in the commencement, to give a fair statement of the whole affair.

The sch. Chas. Hill, of this port, according to the statement of the Captain, as represented in papers by the owners, and the protest by the Commercial Agent of the United States, Mr. Jonathan Elliott at Porto Rico, on the evening of the 5th of March, off the port of St. Domingo. Nothing of importance occurred until about 5 o'clock, A. M., of the 7th, it being quite dark at the time, when the schooner C. Hill, running down for St. Domingo on the starboard tack on board, heading N. W. and the wind N. E., was collided with by an unknown vessel, standing by the wind with the larboard tack on board. This unknown vessel proved to be a Dominican government vessel, bound from San Domingo for St. Thomas. In attempting to go to the windward of the Charles Hill she struck her, the latter went through her main sail about half way from the gaff down to the boom, and cut her larboard leech rope, and the topping lift not giving way, caused the vessel to come along side and do some damage to her rail. Capt. Smith hailed the commander of the Chas. Hill, ordered his mate to lower the larboard boat, while the Dominican officer of the other vessel came on board the schooner and let go the halliards of her foresail and jib, which injured their sails, and then took the vessel in tow, no person having been injured nor list been lost alone. The vessel reached St. Domingo... Capt. Smith, of the C. Hill, immediately continued his voyage to San Domingo, fitting for sea as best he could, and presuming no great injury was done to the vessel in collision.

First—The collision took place on the high seas some twelve miles from San Domingo, as appears from the chart and distance run, and also from the fact that he did not take a pilot on board until 10 o'clock, and did not arrive at San Domingo until 11 1-2, the distance of twelve miles from that point making his making more than 12 miles into port. On his arrival at St. Domingo, the Dominican government demanded the enormous sum of $3,200 as restitution for injuries to their vessel, and imprisoned Capt. Smith before their courts to answer the charges made against him. Capt. Smith denied the jurisdiction of the Dominican government, as neither government nor individuals can be held liable for collision on the high seas... with the advice of our Commercial Agent, Jonathan Elliott. Capt. Smith moreover demanded an investigation to present to the Dominican government, an international question and not one to be tried by a local court. The San Dominican court refused to abide by the arbitration of the commanders of a French and English man-of-war then in port. This the San Dominican government refused doing, and proceeded to provide counsel for Capt. Smith, who was then inside of prison, and after hearing the evidence of their own men, without the testimony of any of the crew of the sch. Hill, condemned the schooner, and fined her heavily. Meanwhile the vessel not being coppered, was greatly eaten by the worms in the harbor, and Capt. Smith was advised to deliver the vessel up to the Dominican government, under a protest. This he did, and returned secretly to our country, as he was himself detained under false charges by the San Dominican government.

We have but three points to make after this short statement of the affair, which has been endorsed as correct by our Commercial Agent, Mr. Elliott, and which is corroborated by the good character for veracity Capt. Smith bears. In the first place, the collision took place on the high seas more than 12 miles from land, and by an acknowledged maritime law no country has a right of jurisdiction more than three miles from land. The San Dominican government had, therefore, no right to try the Chas. Hill 12 miles at sea. In the second place the Dominican government could not try a case in which the vessel broke loose, there is every justice and reason demand that governments no more than individuals are not to suffer for collisions at the same time. The question for restitution was a pure international question of international law, and ought to was to be decided by arbitration or agreement.—Thirdly and finally, if the collision had not taken place on the high seas, and the Dominican government had rightful jurisdiction in all actions arising, except by law Dominican government could not, and by maritime law vessels on the starboard tack are not accountable for collisions with vessels on the larboard tack.

We leave the conclusions to be drawn from so simple a statement and text of the affair, and we trust that our government will not hesitate to defend its citizens against the aggressions of other powers.

A correspondent of the New York Herald writes from St. Domingo, May 10, regarding this matter of the affair:

"It has now been some seven weeks since the American schooner Charles Hill, Captain Smith, while on her passage to this port, was run into on a dark night came in collision with the Dominican packet Charles, belonging to President Baez. The American schooner came in here, and when ready for sea was seized, it is said, and the captain brought before a court. He was sentenced to pay the sum of $3,200 for damages, besides costs of court, amounting to several hundreds more.

Now, every one knows that the captain was right, as he was on the starboard tack, with the wind on his port side, the other had his larboard tack aboard and from the wind; besides the collision took place at sea, before he crossed the bows of the American. This any Master of a vessel knows. This sentence was rendered without a trial, and not being able to pay was sentenced to close confinement. The captain, Capt. Smith, has abandoned his vessel to the Dominican government, and has made his escape to the United States... It is a pity government like this. It is too bad. I hope our government will interfere."

In the Gaceta Oficial of Santo Domingo of May 1st, we find the official correspondence regarding the case, published under the head of "official:"

Commercial Agency of the United States of America.
San Domingo, April 20, 1857.
To the Minister of Foreign Affairs:
Sir—You will find herewith the protest of Mr. Abner Smith, Captain of the American schooner Charles Hill, against the Dominican authorities, on account of their taking possession of his vessel as a legal and unjust detention. I am, sir, &c.
JONATHAN ELLIOTT.

To the Commercial Agent of the United States of America:
Minister of Foreign Affairs,
San Domingo, April 20, 1857.
Mr. Agent—My government has been informed that Mr. Abner Smith, Captain of the American schooner Charles Hill, after having fulfilled the duties of your functions, entrusted an interim to Mr. Jonathan Elliott, Commercial Agent of the U. S., notified my government thereof in an official manner, and that the said Mr. Elliott, when Capt. Smith arrived, accompanied by the protest of Capt. Smith, I have to state that Mr. Elliott is not a Commercial Agent, proceedings to which it may give rise.
Seeing that Mr. Elliott is not a Commercial Agent, I only availed of himself of the means of conciliation which offered themselves, and that a friendly arrangement as speedy as it would have been peaceable, but being rejected by Mr. Elliott, my government has to submit the matter to the common tribunals, to be decided according to the laws of the country.
I also believe that it would have been more meet of Mr. Elliott to await, as it was his duty, who had charge of the matter, the illegal proceedings taken against Capt. Smith, than to express, before being impartially examined the might be redress for damages to the packet. Accept &c.
FELIX M. DELMONTE,
Minister of Foreign Affairs.
SAN DOMINGO, March 16, 1857.

The Dominican Minister of Foreign Affairs to the American Consul.
SAN DOMINGO, March 27, 1857.
Sir—I have received receipt of your official note of this day, in which, after mentioning that Capt. Smith will not avail himself of the court of appeal which the laws permit him to do, you ask to be informed whether the confiscation of the vessel will be prevented before the execution of the sentence of the tribunal of commerce.
I assure you that the government has no other intention than to leave the court to act without any interest of the laws having the facility, or distribution of justice in this case. The party who believes himself injured by the sentence of the tribunal may appeal to the tribunal above to answer the question asked by your note, which I cannot answer. Accept, &c., I am, &c., FELIX M. DELMONTE,
Minister of Foreign Affairs.

The Commercial Agent to the Minister of Foreign Affairs.
Commercial Agency United States, Restauration, etc.
SAN DOMINGO, April 21, 1857.
Sir—It was I ought to say, to my great regret that Mr. Abner Smith, captain of the American schooner Charles Hill, of Portsmouth, N. H., was sentenced on the 18th to two years imprisonment in the jail of this city, and to pay the damages done to the Dominican packet, and to pay the cost of court.
The accusation against the captain for having run into the San Dominican packet "19th of March" is irrational.
Capt. Smith has already been in jail for a week, his vessel line six weeks, and as it has not been coppered far from six weeks, and if it remains here long will be a large outlay to repair it.
The Commercial Agent, commercial agent of the United States, I ask in the name and on the behalf of our government, that the vessel Charles Hill, with all her cargo, now in possession of the Dominican republic, to be paid or secured before the 23d inst., and further to allow the captain, vessel and its crew to depart hence on that date.
Accept the assurances of the high consideration with which I have the honor to be your ob't serv't,
JONATHAN ELLIOTT.
To the honorable Minister, &c.

The Minister's Reply.
DOMINICAN REPUBLIC,
MINISTRY OF FOREIGN AFFAIRS,
SAN DOMINGO, April 21, 1857.
The undersigned Minister of Foreign Affairs has the honor to reply to your note of 21st inst., Mr. Agent, stating that Mr. Abner Smith, captain of the American schooner Charles Hill, has been sentenced to two years imprisonment by the tribunal of commerce of this city, which through wish-recklessness, negligence, or malice, he collided with the Dominican packet 19th of March, as also to pay the costs and damages, and the detention of the vessel until it is paid:
The undersigned is surprised at your note, after the explanation I had the honor to give you in my note of the 20th inst., relative to this affair.
Neither the fact itself nor the consequent detention—the one is a violation of maritime law, and the knowing a theory fatal to all nations, ie. That the captain is not accountable for his acts, neither can nor carry responsibility for the losses occasioned; nor the Dominican government prevent the execution of the sentence until the laws take their course.
If the captain or the agent does not even admit of an appeal, and the 2d contains the 1st, because in the court of appeal the sentence may be revoked, or the damages diminished, the Dominican government having no jurisdiction in the western world to decide upon this case, it belonging to the tribunals, and if it the fact had taken place on the coasts of the Dominican republic, the tribunals could not judge for the first time since the event, and the aggrieved party must apply to the courts for justice, and if the assertion that justice is in this republic and in no other, can it be stated that there is a denial of justice when the question to the tribunals has done no wrong to any one.
The Dominican government cannot admit that by the right of appeal—to resort to the tribunals—because by doing so it would violate the laws, and the act of the government which invited him several times to use his right of appeal, or to give security to carry the case to court, and no to the means which unitly—and no government would do so—unless a fatal precedent being permitted, it would be impossible for any nation to govern, or to protect the rights of its citizens.
If such a question had occurred between an American and an English vessel, the American government would not have allowed the English government to demand the delivery of the vessel, under a demand of internal way. In way, because the one party had not exhausted all the legal means, nor was it considered as abuse of power or the other a denial of justice.
The Dominican government, on the contrary, when demand is not founded on reason. The government can do no more than leave the tribunals to carry out justice, and to trust the intelligence and rectitude to decide the question according to law; and hopes that the Commercial Agent of the United States will see the justice of its method and just proceedings in the present affair.
SAN DOMINGO, APRIL 21, 1857.
FELIX M. DELMONTE.

From the London Anti-Slavery Reporter.

The following remarks on Hayti are so pertinent, and contain so much information, which is not extensively circulated as our own columns.—They are from the pen of Mr. F. W. Chesson.

"Hayti is a country unfortunately but little known in England, and is generally associated with treatment not calculated to inspire much affection and respect. But while a retrospect of Haytian history may, to a great extent, justify this idea of the country, so far as the past is concerned, it by no means follows that this idea is applicable to the present state of affairs. On the contrary, we have great pleasure in stating that under the firm and enlightened rule of the Emperor Faustin, as well as from a widespread education, Hayti has entered upon an era of peace and prosperity, during which she has developed her resources, and which cannot fail to be of lasting benefit, and to constitute the chief glory and strength of a nation.

"Few Englishmen (so far as our knowledge extends) know much either about the geographical position of Hayti, or the character and condition of her people; and yet the communication between England and Hayti is very frequent, and they are engaged in a large and lucrative trade with us, to the extent of which her custom-house entries are able to testify. Hayti is second to no country in the world in the quality of her soil and the excellence of her produce. Her coffee, cocoa, sugar, indigo, and mahogany are world-famed; and we believe that in the matter of cotton particularly, there is a glorious probability of Hayti playing a very prominent part in removing the necessity for the almost exclusive use of slave-grown cotton which is now painfully imposed upon us.

"But Hayti possesses other claims upon our attention besides those which are yielded from the richness of her soil and the value of her natural products. In the artistic standard of her work, particularly in those which, like cabinet making, require skill, taste, and ingenuity, Hayti is second to no nation on earth. The following extract from an article on Haytian Industry, from the pen of a distinguished Haytian, M. Durvelas Durval, will afford our readers some idea of the progress in this respect which his country has already made:

"'At the exhibition, these products were made: formerly some coarse cotton stuffs, known by the name of 'manganes,' baggings, saddle-cloths, saddles, ropes of the palm tree, and baskets, and large wicker-work baskets; now cloths of fine cotton and gold thread of different shades, and the making of artificial flowers and fruits in wax, which occupy the delicate hands of our young city girls, tanning, although not of the most perfect kind, shoemaking, harness-making, hatmaking, goldsmithing and clockmaking, all afford products worthy of notice, and employ many excellent workmen. The tailor's art, practised by Haytians as well as foreign workmen, follows the European fashions.—But the business in which the improvement is most striking is cabinet-making. It is to some skilful German workmen we owe the formation of those brave and intelligent Haytian operatives, whose number is increasing every year; in our shops, and also under their own direction, after the European manner and in a highly finished style.

"'There is, indeed, no department of mechanics, agriculture, or art, for that matter, which the people of Hayti have not afforded a proof of their ability to keep pace with European civilization.

"'A Haytian friend of ours tells an amusing story of a French bishop who was appointed to a diocese in Hayti, and who went out to the country with the idea that he was going to labor among a people as barbarous as the negro tribes of Western Africa. What was his astonishment, on landing at Jacmel, to find himself surrounded by all the evidences of an advanced civilization, and welcomed by a society whose good breeding and polished manners rivalled the social habits of Paris or London! But the bishop would have felt little surprise at what he saw and heard if he had been acquainted with the history, throughout the country, of an admirable system of education, founded by Emperor Christophe, that so far back as 1815, King Christophe introduced the Lancasterian system into his dominions, under the supervision of a number of enlightened English teachers, whom he invited over for that purpose. The country is divided into sixty-five parishes, in each of which a public school is maintained by the State; while in Port-au-Prince, Cape Haytian, and Cayes, there are high schools, academies, colleges, schools of medicine, and other superior educational establishments, provided for by the liberality of the community. In the colleges the English language is taught; the value of this requirement being universally appreciated, especially by those who intend to engage in commercial pursuits. All the teachers are natives of the country, and many of them are men of high respectable ability and attainments. The Emperor himself gives the highest encouragement to the education of his people, and no man is more fully conscious of the fact, that education is the most powerful and effective means of increasing the happiness and promoting the best and most permanent interests of a nation, and securing the stability of the empire. Hence His Majesty takes such a warm, paternal interest in the principal schools, and endeavors, from time to time, to increase their efficiency and usefulness.

"'Of the literature of Hayti we will, at present, say little, although much might be written thereupon. Mr. Alphonse de Saint-Remy, and M. Madieu, by name, have acquired some celebrity—the former by his biographical works, and the latter by his poems. But we have now before us several newspapers published in Hayti, containing original articles—copies of which we have had the pleasure to receive—written with great ability and spirit, and instinct with a high tone of moral feeling.

"'American journalists have grossly calumniated Hayti, but never were the primary cause of her social and political degradation. The writers of America naturally regard her with an unfriendly eye, because Hayti is a practical protest against the system of negro Slavery, and a convincing evidence of the capacity of the African race. And while we are gratified to observe that the French government and nation are disposed to view Hayti with a friendly eye, yet we cannot but deplore the subtle efforts which have been made to incite feelings of hostility between the two nations, and which efforts were excited by the successful efforts she made to cast off her galling yoke.

"'As a consequence of the state of public opinion in America we find the pro-slavery press making insidious attempts to obtain such a footing in the hitherto ill-governed and disorganized Dominican Republic, as will enable them the more effectually to attack the independence of Hayti, through what is logically her weakest and most powerful section of the island. But we are glad to be able to state that General Santana, the President of the Dominican Republic, who, there is grave reason to believe, had availed himself of his elevated position to promote the intrigues of American agents, has been removed from office amid general expressions of satisfaction. His successor is M. Baez, a patriotic statesman, whom he banished on his elevation to power, and whose Presidentship says the Journal des Debats, 'was inaugurated by public rejoicings.' 'The people,' continues the same journal, 'repaired in a body to the residence of the Archbishop, the ex-President, General Reglamota, the Consuls of Spain, England, and France, where speeches were delivered in celebration of this joyous event.'

"'We earnestly wish that the Journal des Debats exhibited as intelligent an acquaintance with the State of Hayti as it does with that of St. Domingo; for the truth is the very reverse of what it states, and it has so misinterpreted the condition of the former country that the Baron Damien, the Haytian Minister at Paris, felt himself called upon to address a dignified reply to the statements of the French journalist. In his reply he uses language to the following purport:

"'"I beg you and the whole world to believe me when I declare that the Emperor of Hayti has no desire to see St. Domingo subject to him. She is a State duly organized, that requires no suggestion, but quietly and unremittingly exerting herself to take the rank which belongs to her among other nations of the world... Her government... Her sovereign... and every foreigner who visits our country is astonished at the progress... that the chief to whom it has confided its destinies is a ruler of extraordinary wisdom, and fully competent to fulfill his mission; that he has no desire to disturb the internal peace and prosperity of the country, and that he has nothing more at heart than to protect the rights and interests of all who are interested in the future of the Haytian nation. Under these circumstances, it is the conviction of our dignity as a nation, and with a sense of the duty which devolves upon us, we shall, with the blessing of the Almighty, keep strictly within our own border, maintaining a position which will constitute the best justification for our independence, and win the respect of every friend of humanity.'

"It is a pleasure for us to turn from the Journal des Debats, to a late issue of the organ of the French press, Le Courrier de Havre. In an article on Hayti, this journal remarks that Hayti is putting forth efforts to raise herself to an equality with other civilized nations, both as regards the richness of her soil and her geographical position, and the desire she has to secure a strong and stable government. The following extract from this article cannot fail to be interesting:

"'"The two allied nations, especially France and England, should keep up a good understanding with that empire and its government, and to respect its independence. They ought to consider Hayti as a free, sovereign, and independent State... with which European ideas are penetrating into... Hayti has been made a subject of mockery... which has been laughed at because people did not understand the true state of things. The inhabitants to constitute themselves into a nation... Imagine the feuds, the jealousies, and probably even the wars, which would arise if England were divided into two separate principalities, each maintaining a different form of government, and each maintaining a different system of legislation... But if Hayti made an attempt at imitation, it is ridiculous to laugh at. Ought the attempt at imitation to be treated with laughter? Is the effort to raise herself to a level with European civilization to be answered by the contact with civilization? To prosecute such a course would be as unjust as it is contrary to humanity. The slanderers of Hayti did not give her time to move; they have judged her prematurely, and without reason; they did not see that it would have been honorable in them to encourage these generous efforts instead of insanely abusing a people composed of men, former slaves, who became independent by their valor, and were left to themselves to create a nationality. The man, who better than all his predecessors, understood the future of his country, who he felt in himself the force and energy necessary to overwhelm anarchy, and to found a strong and stable government, is the Emperor Faustin I. In spite of reverses, he has been able to establish... without caring for obstacles, which he overcame with admirable firmness, laying the foundation of the groundwork upon which he is raising a monumental edifice which is to assure the destiny of his people.'

"We cannot but deplore as a calamity the continued disunion subsisting between Hayti and St. Domingo. The fact simply is, that the island ought not to be ruled by two distinct governments. Imagine the feuds, the jealousies, and probably even the wars, which would arise if England were divided into two separate principalities, each maintaining a different form of government, and each maintaining a different system of legislation. The state of the actual affair of affairs in the island of St. Domingo is the greater pity; because, a direct misfortune, it is that the isolation of the Dominican Republic, from its weakness and instability, has enabled foreign intrigue to aim successful blows at the independence of the whole country. The Haytian government may have erred in its mode of expression, but, in the case of Hayti, it becomes a distinct right, and we cannot but deplore, and shall not think that negro capacity for self-government will have been fairly tried, so long as the two States under one government would form a far more efficient guarantee of the political independence of the entire nation, and of the tri-color flag, than all the treaties and all the foreign engagements into which France and England might enter to protect them, or any fleet which they might make in the Gulf of Mexico or the Caribbean Sea.

"Postscript.—Since the foregoing was written, a suspension of hostilities between Hayti and St. Domingo has been agreed to."

records.headline: The Revolution in St. Domingo.
records.summary_en: A private letter published in the *Turks Island Standard* reports that a revolution has broken out in the Dominican Republic. According to the excerpt, the primary cause of the uprising was an attempt by the government to depreciate the paper currency or alter the rate of exchange by twenty percent, alongside grievances regarding the central government's appropriation of provincial resources. Additionally, the revolutionists' manifesto—modeled after the American Declaration of Independence—complains of oppressive administrations, despotism, violations of personal liberty, arbitrary arrests, and the suppression of the press.
records.summary_es: Una misiva particular divulgada en el *Turks Island Standard* expone el estallido de un alzamiento revolucionario en la República Dominicana. Según el relato, el detonante principal consistió en la pretensión oficial de devaluar el papel moneda o alterar en un veinte por ciento el tipo de cambio, aunada a los agravios por la incautación de recursos provinciales por el poder central. Se añade que el manifiesto de los sublevados —inspirado en el Acta de Independencia de Estados Unidos— denunciaba administraciones vejatorias, tiranía, conculcación de la libertad individual, prisiones arbitrarias y clausura de la imprenta.

records.headline: The Revolution in St. Domingo.
records.summary_en: A vessel arriving in New York from Turk's Island reported that the revolution in St. Domingo was rapidly nearing its close, with the entire Republic—except for the city of St. Domingo—declaring for the new Government. An army of 8,000 revolutionists was encamped before the city walls, expecting the inhabitants to declare in their favor, while President Baez had retired to the fortress and Soulouque was reportedly assembling a force on the northern frontiers. The movement had thus far been accomplished without bloodshed or arrests, and a July 8 proclamation by the people of Cibao at Santiago detailed grievances against previous governments regarding personal liberty, the press, and national freedom.
records.summary_es: Un buque fondeado en Nueva York procedente de las islas Turcas participó que la revolución en Santo Domingo tocaba rápidamente a su término, habiéndose pronunciado toda la república —a excepción de la capital— en favor del nuevo régimen. Un ejército sitiador de 8.000 revolucionarios acampaba ante las murallas de la plaza aguardando que el vecindario se declarase de su parte, mientras el presidente Báez se acogió a la fortaleza y Soulouque concentraba tropas en la frontera septentrional. El alzamiento se consumó hasta entonces sin efusión de sangre ni prisiones, detallando una proclama del 8 de julio rubricada por los cibaeños en Santiago las vejaciones de gobiernos precedentes sobre las garantías ciudadanas, la imprenta y la soberanía patria.

The first of the series appeared in the Intelligencer of Thursday last; the second is given to-day.

THE REVOLUTION IN ST. DOMINGO.

A vessel arrived at New York from Turk’s Island brings some interesting details of the progress of the revolution in St. Domingo. The advices from Port-au-Platte are to the 17th ultimo. The revolution is said to be drawing rapidly to a close. With the exception of the city of St. Domingo, the whole of the Republic has declared in favor of the new order of things. Baez was still in the capital, but it was thought he could not hold out much longer. The revolutionary party have established a provisional government at Santiago, of which Gen. Jose Desiderio Valverde is President. The new government has issued a decree for the election of a convention to frame a new constitution. The revolutionists have also issued a decree opening all the ports of the Republic to the commerce of all nations. The revolutionary army is said to be well organized and well equipped. The people are said to be enthusiastic in favor of the revolution.

records.full_text: We have received files of the St. Christopher Gazette to the 28th ult., containing interesting details of the revolution now in progress in the Dominican republic of St. Domingo, to remove President Baez and restore Santana. The Baez party, being hard pressed, had formed an alliance with the Emperor Soulouque, who had despatched assistance to his ally. The Royal Standard of the 22d inst. says: By the sloop Seaflower, from Port Platta, we have advices from that place to the 17th instant. From a correspondent we learn that the revolution is gaining ground, and that the Baez party are losing their influence. The revolutionary party have possession of the whole of the Cibao, and have established a Provisional Government at Santiago, of which General Jose Desiderio Valverde is President. The city of St. Domingo is closely besieged by the revolutionary party, and it is expected that it will soon be in their possession. The Baez party have called in the assistance of the Haytiens, and it is said that Soulouque has sent them 1,500 men. This has caused much indignation among the Dominicans, and many of the Baez party have, in consequence, joined the revolutionists.

records.full_text:
News from Saint Domingo.
THE LIBERTY PARTY ORGANIZING A CONSTITUTION—
ELECTIONS ORDERED—SIEGE OF SAN DOMINGO CITY
—TWO WAR VESSELS AND A LARGE MORTAR WANTED
—BAEZ’S FRIENDS FALLING OFF—THE AMERICAN
SCHOONER CHARLES HILL.

The schooner City Belle, Captain Pendleton, arrived at this port yesterday from Port au Plata, with news dated at that place on 29th of October.

The authors of the revolution of the liberty party in the Dominican republic are fast organizing a new government very different from that of Senor Baez.

The election for the deputies of the nation was to take place on the 10th of November, and the members were to meet at the town of Moca on the 1st of December.

General Santana and several other valiant Generals were besieging the city of St. Domingo with a force of 8,000 men. The besiegers are very moderate in their fire against the city, as it was momentarily expected that Baez would be forced to capitulate. An expedition of 2,000 men strong were marching against Samana, the only place holding for Baez.

Business in Port au Plata and Santiago continued quite safe and easy, although all the military in the province of Cibao were under arms.

The Cibao government wish to purchase two small clipper schooners of 150 to 180 tons, to blockade the port of St. Domingo; vessels that are staunch and strong, that will be able to carry a twenty-four pounder upon a pivot, besides small guns of smaller calibre. There being no vessels in port suitable, any American speculator might find a good offer from the government, if quickly attended to, in Port au Plata.

News had reached Port au Plata that many of the first families had lately left the city of St. Domingo, besides natives that Baez has sent away.

The people and foreign residents were very much astonished that the American government did not send a vessel of war to St. Domingo, to demand satisfaction in the case of the American schooner Charles Hill, which was seized by Baez (valued at $10,000), and as yet not claimed by the American government. The American Consul at St. Domingo had sent all the documents relative to this affair in May last to Washington.

Fighting men, friends to the republic, would be well received. Arms and ammunition were in good demand, and they were in want of an 18-inch mortar, for which the highest rates would be paid.

records.summary_en: Baez and his party are reported to be hard-pressed by Santana, leading to official steps to procure peace through the mediation of English, French, and Spanish consuls. Santana has rejected their initial terms and insists that Baez submit a written proposition for the capitulation of San Domingo. Meanwhile, Santana's forces have occupied the peninsula of Samana, and the war-brig *Nineteenth of March*, carrying munitions, provisions, and documents implicating Baez in the misuse of public funds, has surrendered to the Provisional Government.
records.summary_es: Se comunicaba que Báez y su bando se hallaban cercados por Santana, entablándose trámites oficiales para alcanzar un avenimiento mediante la interposición de los cónsules de Inglaterra, Francia y España. Santana desechó las condiciones preliminares y exigió que Báez presentase una propuesta formal y por escrito para la capitulación de Santo Domingo. En el ínterin, las tropas de Santana ocuparon la península de Samaná, y el bergantín artillado *19 de Marzo*, con cargamento de pertrechos, bastimentos y pliegos que comprometían a Báez en la malversación de fondos públicos, se rindió al Gobierno Provisional.

records.full_text:
Interesting from Santo Domingo.

THE BAEZ PARTY REDUCED TO THE LAST STRAITS—POSITION OF HIS FORCES AT SAN DOMINGO CITY AND SAMANA—WANT OF PROVISIONS—GENERAL PALMANAT AT POINT DE SAMANA—NAVAL NEWS—GERMAN IMMIGRANTS DYING OF HUNGER, ETC.

By the schooner Brenton, from Puerto Plata, we have received files of the Gaceta Oficial of the Dominican republic, from Santiago de los Caballeros, and the following correspondence:

OUR DOMINICAN CORRESPONDENCE.
ST. DOMINGO, Jan. 19, 1858.
Return of the Exiled Correspondent—Position of the Besieging Armies—Surrender of the Baez Steamers—Hopes of Recognition by Foreign Governments—War Vessels Arrived—Naval News, &c.

It is a long time since I had the pleasure to address you, but it has been owing to the political affairs of this country, in consequence of which I have been to exile, residing in Curacoa and Turks' Islands. But now that I am back again, you will receive my letters as regularly as before.

Enclosed you will find a file of the Official Gazette, by which you will perceive that Baez is strictly confined to the city of St. Domingo, and Baez's general at Samana, Gen. Suero, in the city of Samana, by the forces of a large army, besieging said city, where foreign provisions are very scarce, and none at all of the domestic. Produce, also, is very scarce, and the provisions brought by a very few traders, are very small, and sold at exorbitant prices.

According to that account, which confirms the reports brought by the different assemblies of all the communes of the republic, Baez has sent his commissioners to all the towns and villages twelve miles from this city, in order to make a new levy, which has produced a very poor result. Baez's position is very critical. The people are very tired of him, and there is every reason to expect that the new political state of things will soon commence, as Baez suffers the penalty of death for political faults being forever abolished, the right of trial by jury established, harmonizing the democratic principles with the strength of the government. The constitution is favorable to foreigners; not only to those belonging to friendly nations, but to all nations and states of the world that enter into Santo Domingo.

We entertain the hope that as soon as the new authorities take the helm of state we shall see a large number of nations which have representatives in this country take part in it, and we shall see trade again flourishing and concord with international respect, not forgetting that the soil of Santo Domingo is full of resources to be developed by enterprise; and that the whole population of this country, having lost all hope of Baez, expects the new government to expect from every civilized nation that their new rulers will be recognized by the different powers. We have already seen two small sailing vessels of our own fitting for war at Samana, and now there is on the stock at the shipyard of this place three small ones that Baez has on the waters of Samana.

Trade here is getting somewhat better, although money is scarce, and business goes straight and lively, the tobacco crop having been a very large one this year.

[Translated for the New York Herald from La Gaceta Oficial of Santiago de los Caballeros, Jan. 17.]

The facts which the Generals commanding the besieging armies of St. Domingo and Samana, with all their details, have officially communicated to the government, as well as the letters written by private persons from the first of these two places, both to us and to other persons, fully confirm our prediction, that within a very short time we should see the complete downfall of Baez. Such is the inference naturally drawn from the relation made by Gen. Baez at the head of the army besieging the city of St. Domingo, as well as that of Gen. Suero, who commands the troops at Samana, of the loss experienced by them over the troops of Palmanat. No other reason than that he has in advance imposed silence with regard to the siege of Samana could have induced Baez to repeat the repeated defeats our valiant troops caused to him, and it is for this reason that he tries to sustain himself by force of that place is inevitable. It is for this reason that he in advance imposed silence with regard to the war which Generals Puello and Mella are carrying on against the troops of Baez, and prints only reports of the defeats of the enemy, as if a body of troops, residing on that point, has in advance put a curb on Baez's power to corrupt, and monopolized the bad news he is receiving from Samana.

Be this as it may, our predictions receive every day new confirmation relative to the speedy termination of the existence of Baez, whose forces are diminishing every day. As our readers will learn from the communication addressed by Gen. Bide, under date of the 7th inst., to the provisional government, the spirit of revolt against Baez, which is everywhere, and more particularly among the inhabitants of the communes of the south, both on the coast and in the interior, is going on increasing. When Santana left that place it was with no other view than to go to the different communes of St. Domingo, such as San Cristobal, Los Banos and Pajarito, who, unfortunately for them, since the war began, had given their assistance to the faction of Baez, and the troops of the race, who, although small in number, have done great hurt to the provinces. We must, in consequence of this move, expect Baez to invite the population of St. Domingo to surrender within two or three days. It is impossible, besides, the great majority of the population, that Baez has gathered inside the two localities above mentioned, are composed of very poor people, who can produce no bread (nor produce what they did not find) and any others on their small farms which they leave to take up arms; they cannot even eat a little cocoa nut, what kind of food can they get out of them? We do not see how Baez can sustain himself in those two places, both to us and to other persons.

To the above must be added those military persons who, in consequence of their not having received their pay, and idea that our flotilla might cut off their retreat. Poor wretches, they say, 'Baez promises them to-day and to-morrow to pay for their experience, and takes them on board his vessels, and what sort of treatment does he give them?'—they ask—'he leaves them to die of hunger!'

It is known, besides, that the Baez ships sent by Baez to Samana he has not had any news, although they left St. Domingo since the 1st inst. He expects the Baez ship, the Baxe, every moment, but she does not appear. Thus Baez has at present no slip left at his disposal, since those three carry on trade, create no end of trouble, named El Liberador, la Australia and El Cirus, 19 de Julio, having been given up or taken by the forces of the Dominican government, as well as the flotilla of Baez, and the government by Her Commander, and la Merced having been run on shore by a merchant vessel; and as to the former left that place that he was not even able to speak.

According to that account, which confirms the reports, the soldiers who form the battalion under the command of General Palmanat, which has arrived at Samana, have experienced a series of bad treatment and hardships, as is confirmed by the commander of Puerto Plata in his despatch of the 13th instant to the government, in which he states that the former left that place that he was not even able to speak; and to these must be added that the remaining of the peninsula find themselves in a very very bad situation as far as food is concerned, being reduced to eat cocoa nuts and palmae, as stated by the same individual.

What must be added to all these facts is, a sincere sympathy, adds of that his companions act like him, and have fled to St. Domingo and to Samana, for wickedness and crimes, and have made their submission. Only two days ago two or three of them had asked from us their pardon, which we granted them, on condition to the contract on the stipulation of which they had left their work; and to these must be added that their intention, and kept even for some days in the neighborhood of St. Domingo, is to make their submission, as it is intended to send them to the provisional government, to be released by the government, if they have not committed crimes. Why have they not accepted the benevolent offer of Gen. Santana? Because they know, as it is said in the contract, that they would be punished; and those who were under those unfortunate persons had been taken by Gen. Santana with military measures to prevent them from perishing by hunger.

records.summary_en: According to *The New York Herald* on March 4, 1858, French immigrants in Samaná and St. Domingo suffered from severe provisions shortages, resulting in deaths from sickness and famine. The report notes that General Santana had offered to have them provided with land to work in the fields, but questions why the offer was not accepted and criticizes the French Consul for failing to prevent their starvation. Additionally, the newspaper reported on personal intelligence, noting the presence of Judge Bourdier, commissioner to the Sandwich Islands, and Admiral Forrest in town.
records.summary_es: A juicio de *The New York Herald* del 4 de marzo de 1858, los colonos franceses avecindados en Samaná y Santo Domingo padecieron una crítica falta de mantenimientos, produciéndose víctimas por enfermedad e inanición. La crónica hacía constar que el general Santana se brindó a adjudicarles terrenos de labor, preguntándose por qué no se acogieron a tal providencia y censurando al cónsul galo por no conjurar la hambruna de sus connacionales. El diario consignaba por añadidura notas de sociedad dando cuenta de la estancia en la ciudad del juez Bourdier, comisionado en las islas Sandwich, y del almirante Forrest.

records.full_text:
By the schooner Brentea, from Puerto Plata, we have received files of the Gaceta Oficial of the Dominican republic to the 31st January, and a letter from our correspondent at St. Jago de los Caballeros, the provisional seat of government.

OUR DOMINICAN CORRESPONDENCE.
ST. JAGO DE LOS CABALLEROS, }
Jan. 19, 1858. }
Return of the Exiled Correspondent—Position of the Contending Parties—Sufferings of the Baez Partisans—Hopes of Recognition by Foreign Governments—War Vessels Fitting Out—Lack of Provisions—&c.

It is a long time since I had the pleasure to address you, but it has been owing to the political affairs of this country, in consequence of which I have been in exile, residing in Curaçoa and Turks' Islands. But now that I am in freedom again, you will receive my letters as regularly as before.

Enclosed you will find a file of the Official Gazette, by which you will perceive that Baez is confined to the city of St. Domingo, and that the provisional government, heading it in the form of a large army, besieging said city, where foreign provisions are very scarce, and none at all of the domestic. Cattle, equal to $4 to $5 per head produce, &c. are very few, and these destroyed almost daily, three by three and five by five, and sometimes in larger numbers.

The government, as shown by its decree, has appointed by the different conventions of all the communes of the republic, to meet on the 1st of February, at Moca, a town about twelve miles from this city, in order to make a new constitution, reform many of the old laws, and reorganize the republic on a firm and stable basis; and there is every reason to expect that the new political code will be fully adequate to prevent the repetition of the penalty of death for political faults being forever banished; taking a step forward in civilization, and harmonizing the democratic principles with the strength of the executive power, and granting broader security to foreigners; not only to those belonging to friendly nations, but to all, without exception, who may choose to come to the republic.

We entertain the hope that as soon as the new authorities take the helm of the state, foreign nations—such as those which have representatives in this country—will recognize it as a government, which, as it is strictly conformable to the national will, ought not to be delayed. Up to the present, trade has been at a total stand-still, and the entire population of the country are waiting for the extraordinary production of coffee and cocoa to commence, which will give life to business again. We have two small sailing vessels of our own fitting for war at Puerto Plata, and two others at St. Jago, besides three or four small ones that Baez has on the waters of Samana.

According to that account, which confirms us in our opinion that trade has already commenced again at Puerto Plata, and business goes straight and lively, the tobacco crop coming into a very large figure.

[Translated for the NEW YORK HERALD from the Gaceta Oficial, January 31.]

The facts which the Generals commanding the besieging army of the South, as well as those of the North, have officially communicated to the government as to the situation of the forces of the enemy inside the first of these two places, both as to us and other persons, give, week to week, the same idea as to their complete state of distress, and their utter inability to move. Such is the inference naturally drawn from the relation made by an individual who left Samana on the 7th inst., who states that at that date Baez had only sixty men in that peninsula, under the command of General Juan Esteban Francis, who had replaced the expelled Captain Baldomero Victorino.

According to that account, Baez prohibited that the condition which Samana at present is in be spoken of, or the number of his troops there; and brave Generals at the head of the army besieging that place, for the purpose of removing all suspicion on the part of the enemy, had permitted some thirty persons to be taken up by them over the troops of Palmerino. No other reason can be assigned for the extraordinary prohibition. In consequence of the official communications, in which General Juan Esteban Francis speaks of Samana, Baez repeated the default regarding various troops he had in Samana, and by force the fall of that place is inevitable. It is for this reason that he has taken the resolution to enter into a naval war which Generals Puelio and Mella are carrying on with some success in those seas, who have captured two small vessels and burnt two others in Samana, since on that point, Baez having in advance put a curb on the trade of the coasts and monopolized the bad news he is receiving from Samana.

But this is not the only reason which confirms us in our conviction relative to the speedy termination of the blockade of Samana, which was established by General Francis. As our readers will learn from the communication addressed by Gen. Bide, under date of the 7th inst., to the provisional government, the population of that peninsula, which is at present, and more particularly among the inhabitants who have taken up arms for the cause of the city, is going on increasing. When the Arriano left that bay, there were 100 head of cattle, a number not sufficient to provide the entire population of St. Domingo with meat, which is also wanted by the inhabitants of San Carlos and Pajarito, who, unfortunately for them, since the 21st of July, have taken the side of Baez; to say nothing of the troops, and the garrison of the race, who, although small in number, have been made one of the provisions. The stock of taro, planted by the force of Baez, has lasted for about two weeks; but will the poor be able to buy this crop at a cost of 24$ the quintal? This is impossible. Besides, the great majority of the population who inhabit the localities above mentioned, are composed of very poor people, who can find no work at present (since they can find not any) and others on their small farms which do not yield at this season of the year, or on small cocoa nuts, what kind of food can they get out of them? We do not see that there can be any other resource for them than to suffer the consequences of their temerity and folly.

To the above must be added three hundred military persons, who, in consequence of their not having provisions, came to the conclusion that their situation was not good, and left the peninsula on the 7th inst. under the command of Gen. Bide. Thus Baez has at present no sloop left at his disposal, since he can no longer use the three vessels he named the Liberador, the Australia and El Cirus, 19 of January, to carry provisions and troops to Samana, as, by the government, he is restricted from sending any more to the peninsula. This result is further confirmed by the directed balls of the besieging army before Pajarito.

As regards Samana, the capture of General Francis by the besiegers under the command of General Palmero, is confirmed, who, after having taken up his position at the point of the peninsula, has been reinforced by the governor of Puerto Plata in his dispatch of the 23d inst., in which he states that he had seen a foreigner left that place that he was not even able to speak; and there is no doubt but that the population of that peninsula find themselves in a very bad situation as far as provisions are concerned, a chicken bringing gold for five pesos, as is stated by the same individual.

This latter, with whose misfortunes we sincerely sympathize, adds that of his companions immigrants like himself, eight died in St. Domingo and six in Samana, one of sickness and the others by famine. The unfortunates, in September last, left Hamburg for Santo Domingo, with the intention of establishing themselves as agriculturalists, and have ended their career in the manner above mentioned. We hope that the government will take the necessary measures to prevent them from perishing by hunger.

The St. Jago government stated it would seek foreign aid before yielding to Baez, whose fleet's movements were favored by English and French consuls, leaving the United States as the sole government to depend upon. Additionally, the American schooner *Wing of the Wind* successfully ran the blockade with a cargo from New York on the 27th, while the U.S. Consul at St. Domingo, Mr. Elliott, remained imprisoned in his house for fear of his life without the presence of U.S. warships.

records.full_text:
The steamship Moses Taylor, has arrived from California, with one million eight hundred thousand dollars in specie.
The Moses Taylor left at Aspinwal, the U. S. steamer Colorado, which arrived on the 17th from San Domingo.
The Powhatan was at Hong Kong. It is rumored that the Chinese intend to destroy all the European dwellings on the Hong Kong river.
The Emperor of Russia has invited the French Ambassador to accompany him on a tour through the Southern Provinces.
The Colorado brought intelligence that President Baez, of the Dominican Republic, had capitulated to Santa Anna, and was to leave San Domingo on the 12th for Curacoa. The most of his adherents left the day previous.
Santa Anna had given Commodore McIntosh the strongest assurances of the protection of American citizens and desired him to express to his government his wish to maintain the most amicable relations. It is said that the Commodore succeeded in obtaining from President Baez all the documents for which he was sent.
The Colorado was to sail on the 21st for Havana.
The U. S. steamer Saranac and the Vandalia, were lying at Panama.
The Decatur sailed on the 13th, and the Merrimack on the 19th.
The excitement in California in relation to the Frazier river gold mines continues. Three thousand persons have already left San Francisco for that region.
The California mines are yielding largely and accounts from every section are highly favorable. The agricultural prospects were never brighter, and a full harvest is confidently anticipated.
The California papers contain more than the usual amount of murders, assassinations, casualties, etc.
The advices from Oregon are to the 24th of May, they announce a general Indian outbreak there. Col. Stevens' command on Snake river was attacked on the 16th of May and forced to retreat with the loss of fifty privates, three officers, two howitzers, baggage wagons, and nearly all the animals.
Three companies of dragoons and one of infantry were engaged with one thousand five hundred Indians. The names of the officers killed are Capt. Winder and Lieut. Gaxen, the name of the third is not given.
A fire in Nevada on the 23d of May, destroyed nearly all the business portion of the city.
The town of San Andreas, Calveras county was entirely destroyed by fire on the 2d of June.
The U. S. surveying steamer, Shubrick, arrived from Philadelphia, via Panama, at San Francisco, May 27th.

records.headline: The editorial looks back on the eleven-month civil war just ended in the Republic of San Domingo, describing it as largely
records.summary_en: The editorial looks back on the eleven-month civil war just ended in the Republic of San Domingo, describing it as largely a geographical contest between the northern and southern sections, led by the rival cities of Santiago and San Domingo under Pedro Santana. It sketches the two cities and the republic's history: independence declared in 1821, twenty-two years united with Haiti under Boyer, the proclamation of the Dominican Republic in 1844, Haitian invasions beaten back by Santana, who received the title of Liberator, and the dissatisfaction that followed under President Jimenez.
records.summary_es: El editorial repasa la guerra civil de once meses que acaba de terminar en la República de Santo Domingo, describiéndola como en gran parte una contienda geográfica entre las secciones norte y sur, encabezada por las ciudades rivales de Santiago y Santo Domingo bajo Pedro Santana. Esboza las dos ciudades y la historia de la república: la independencia declarada en 1821, veintidós años unida a Haití bajo Boyer, la proclamación de la República Dominicana en 1844, las invasiones haitianas rechazadas por Santana, quien recibió el título de Libertador, y el descontento que siguió bajo el presidente Jiménez.

Historically, the territory acknowledged Spanish authority until declaring independence as the Republic of Spanish Haiti in 1821, though the inhabitants soon united with the western Haitian Republic under President Boyer. Following the fall of Boyer twenty-one years later, the people of San Domingo seized the opportunity to regain their independence.

Tras el derrocamiento de Boyer veintiún años después, el pueblo dominicano aprovechó la coyuntura para reconquistar su libertad política.

records.summary_en: The *New-York daily tribune* reported that Baez has been overthrown and Santana has taken power in the Republic of Dominica. While Southern journals view this as a triumph of the white over the black race and urge the U.S. government to formally recognize the Dominican Republic, the newspaper supports recognition regardless of racial distinctions. However, the publication questions whether the U.S. government and its Washington court circle would tolerate diplomats or future presidents of darker complexions in a country where the vast majority of the population is of African lineage.
records.summary_es: El *New-York daily tribune* notificó que Báez fue derribado y Santana asumió el timón de la República Dominicana. Con todo, la hoja se pregunta si el gabinete estadounidense y las tertulias de Washington consentirían a diplomáticos o futuros mandatarios de tez morena oriundos de una nación cuya gran mayoría desciende de linaje africano.

records.summary_en: The *Wilmington Journal* reviewed the history of Hispaniola, explaining the division between the western French colony of Haiti and the eastern Spanish colony of Santo Domingo. It recounted that Santo Domingo declared independence in 1821, was subjugated by Haiti, and subsequently expelled Haitian forces in 1844 to establish a republic under General Santana. Dice que Santana rechazó la presidencia salvo como general en jefe, por lo que el cargo fue conferido a su amigo íntimo y colaborador, a quien se atribuye haber organizado el país y liberarlo de la carga de la guerra.

records.headline: A political history of the republic traces the rivalry of Baez and Santana, beginning with Baez, twice called to the presidency
records.summary_en: A political history of the republic traces the rivalry of Baez and Santana, beginning with Baez, twice called to the presidency, as Santana's intimate friend and able co-operator in securing independence after Soulouque, the Emperor of Haiti, twice invaded and was beaten back. It recounts an embassy to Port au Prince that found Soulouque would accept nothing but the complete subjugation of Dominica and produced only an exchange of prisoners, the fight over ratifying a treaty with the United States, Santana's election and the friendship turning to bitter hostility, and Baez being sworn in again amid the demands of the naturalization party.
records.summary_es: Una historia política de la república recorre la rivalidad de Baez y Santana, comenzando con Baez, llamado dos veces a la presidencia, como amigo íntimo y capaz colaborador de Santana en asegurar la independencia después de que Soulouque, el emperador de Haití, invadiera dos veces y fuera rechazado. Relata una embajada a Port au Prince que descubrió que Soulouque no aceptaría nada más que la completa subyugación de Dominica y que solo produjo un intercambio de prisioneros, la lucha por la ratificación de un tratado con los Estados Unidos, la elección de Santana y cómo la amistad se convirtió en hostilidad amarga, y la nueva juramentación de Baez en medio de las exigencias del partido de la naturalización.

records.summary_en: Forty-five Dominican officers and civilians signed a manifesto from Baní on October 27, 1858, expressing indignation over a memoir by Senor Maximo Reybaud that proposed sacrificing their nationality to Hayti. The signatories declared that patriotism among Dominicans remains strong, asserting their readiness to defend the freedom and independence won in 1844 rather than submit again to Hayti.
records.summary_es: Cuarenta y cinco jefes militares y próceres civiles dominicanos estamparon su firma en un manifiesto fechado en Baní el 27 de octubre de 1858, exteriorizando su viva indignación ante una memoria de Maxime Raybaud que proponía el sacrificio de la nacionalidad patria en provecho de Haití. Los signatarios proclamaban que el sentimiento patrio permanecía inalterable entre los dominicanos, jurando hallarse resueltos a empuñar las armas para defender la libertad e independencia conquistadas en 1844 antes que someterse de nuevo a la servidumbre haitiana.

records.headline: The paper gives an account of Geffrard's revolution: Geffrard, joined by the military and town people, marched to a palace of Soulouque
records.summary_en: The paper gives an account of Geffrard's revolution: Geffrard, joined by the military and town people, marched to a palace of Soulouque, a deputation proclaimed the republic of Haiti with Geffrard as provisional head, and on Thursday, December 23, the republic was publicly proclaimed in the grand square and Geffrard named provisional President, which office he accepted. It says the fortified town of St. Marc was taken without opposition, the insurrection was spreading north and south, and decrees had been issued reviving the constitution of 1816, calling a legislature, releasing all political prisoners, increasing soldiers' rations, ordering the destruction of the Fort of Gonaives, and depriving Soulouque of all power.
records.summary_es: El periódico ofrece un relato de la revolución de Geffrard: Geffrard, acompañado por los militares y la gente de la ciudad, marchó a un palacio de Soulouque; una diputación proclamó la República de Haití con Geffrard como jefe provisional, y el jueves 23 de diciembre la república fue proclamada públicamente en la gran plaza y Geffrard fue nombrado presidente provisional, cargo que aceptó. Dice que la ciudad fortificada de Saint-Marc fue tomada sin oposición, que la insurrección se extendía al norte y al sur, y que se habían emitido decretos que restablecían la constitución de 1816, convocaban una legislatura, liberaban a todos los prisioneros políticos, aumentaban las raciones de los soldados, ordenaban la destrucción del Fuerte de Gonaïves y privaban a Soulouque de todo poder.

records.headline: The paper gives a biographical account of Soulouque, saying he was elected President of Haiti almost by accident
records.summary_en: The paper gives a biographical account of Soulouque, saying he was elected President of Haiti almost by accident when contending candidates were about even, was declared Emperor in August 1849 after two years as President, and instituted orders of nobility with princes, dukes, marquises and knights. It says he never acknowledged the independence of the Dominican Republic, always avowing it was a portion of his empire, and undertook to reduce it to subjection, advancing with an army of five thousand men to the frontiers of Dominica, where the Dominicans under Santana met him.
records.summary_es: El periódico ofrece un relato biográfico de Soulouque, diciendo que fue elegido presidente de Haití casi por accidente cuando los candidatos contendientes estaban casi empatados, fue declarado emperador en agosto de 1849 tras dos años como presidente e instituyó órdenes de nobleza con príncipes, duques, marqueses y caballeros. Higgins, from Gonaives Jan. 1st, reports that a revolution broke out in Hayti, Dec. 22d, between the Haytien Government and a party of Republicans headed by General Goffard, one of the Haytien Generals. [Translated from La Presse of January 8, for the NEW YORK HERALD.]

They dream of possessing Cuba, and are endeavoring to establish themselves on the island of Hayti, and the Dominican government has up to the present time favored their pretensions. records.full_text:
To the Editor of the Anti-Slavery Reporter.'

SIR,—The island of St. Domingo, once united under the firm administration of Boyer for a period of twenty-two years, is now divided into two parts; the East, or Spanish part, forming the Dominican Republic, and the West, or French part, being constituted into the empire of Soulouque. It is not, at present, my intention to enter into the history of the civil war in the eastern province which led to the separation, nor is it necessary to show to any one who has studied the recent history of the country, that this separation has occasioned much present weakness and past ruin to both, and surrounded both with perils of incalculable magnitude. The existence of two independent states on so small an island, necessarily influenced by mutual jealousies and hatreds, and each looking to foreign aid for protection against a foreign power and a revolted province, could not fail to invite foreign aggression and intrigue. The great representatives of England, France, Spain, and the United States, have, in turn, taken advantage of the weakness of the local governments to play the game of their respective countries, but the aggressions of the latter power appear to have been influenced by the most evil motives, and to have a direct tendency to encourage new attacks on the liberty and independence of the island. These intrigues doubtless form a part of a systematic plan of American encroaching policy, holding propaganda, which aims to extend the ‘blessings of the peculiar institution’ over Hayti, Central America, and Cuba. The first-fruits of American diplomacy in the Dominican Republic were gathered in 1854, when, by dint of intrigues with Santana, the President, and, as it is asserted, heavy bribes to the petty representatives of the Dominican Republic, the United States’ Commissioner, General Cazneau, obtained the cession of Navaza, in the splendid peninsula bay of Samana, together with other privileges to which I need not more particularly allude, further than to say that they included a right to establish factories on land and to construct railways to the interior, and, in short, to work mines. This object of this treaty was, doubtless, to allure large numbers of American adventurers into the country, who, dazzled by the certainty of immediate profit and the prospect of far more substantial rewards, would form a powerful nucleus. Fortunately, this plot was not carried out, owing, in a great measure, to the exertions of the French and English Consuls, who, by showing to the Dominican Congress the danger of making such important concessions to the United States, prevented its ratification. The agent of General Santana, however, still refused to encourage American interests, and shortly afterwards the invasion of Dominican territory in 1855 by the Emperor Soulouque, whose fears were not unnaturally excited by the prospect of an American occupation of St. Domingo. This war turned out to be disastrous to Santana, however, which took place in 1856, when he was compelled to resign the presidential office amid the execrations of his countrymen. In his flight through the streets of San Domingo, *A bas le tyran! A bas les Americains!* rang from every lip. Baez, the former President, was compelled to leave the country; but he returned after a short absence, and by decree of the Senate succeeded in capturing the city of San Domingo, and restoring himself to power.

It is not difficult to discover what political advantages the possession of territorial rights in the Dominican Republic, together with the important bay of Samana, would have conferred upon the Americans; nor is it more difficult to see that, had it come to pass, they would have been able to prevent that union of the two sections of the island which alone can give a fair chance of success to the great experiment of negro self-government, and thereby prove the falseness of those theories of the natural and inherent inferiority of the African race, which form the sole justification for American slavery. This would have given them a pretext, of which they would not have been slow to avail themselves, to interfere by force in the domestic affairs of the whole island; and if no worse result happened, they would, at least, have placed the Haytian Government and Dominican President in a position of abject dependence upon the United States; while the bay of Samana might have formed a point from which to carry on filibustering operations against Cuba, and even our West India possessions; thus giving a new lease of life to slavery, if not a new field of action. No doubt all these considerations were well weighed by the Cabinet of Washington in instructions to their commissioners, and by Santana and his confederates bought with American gold, and to whose standard every enemy of his country seemed by destiny to rally. Happily, however, the temporary overthrow of Santana put an end to these projects, or at least suspended their execution; but their revival is not unlikely, now that Santana, by the defeat of Baez, has been restored to power. General Cazneau, it is true, has retired from the scene, but his party still continues in the ascendant at Washington, and Mr. Buchanan, like his predecessor, is its creature and instrument, rather than its director.

That a change of Presidents in the United States has produced no change of policy is but too evident from the proceeding of Mr. Buchanan in regard to the island of Navaza. This island, which forms a part of the Dominican territory, is small and uninhabited, situated between the south-western extremity of Hayti and the island of Jamaica, and is about thirty miles from Cape Tiburon. That the island belongs to Hayti is proved by incontrovertible historical evidence. A French authority, Moreau de St. Mery, is agreed on this point. Herrera says, in his ‘Descripcion de las Occidentales,’ chap. vi. p. 7, Madrid, 1730:—‘The harbors, &c., and the isles belonging to the coast of that island (Hispaniola) are found several small isles that are annexed to her, and that may still be very useful to her. The most considerable are the Saona besides Navaza and Mona, the first being ten leagues from Cape Tiburon towards Jamaica.’ Several months ago the Haytian Government learnt that this island, which contains extensive deposits of guano, had been invaded by a party of American adventurers, who had established themselves there for the purpose of digging and exporting the guano, without making any attempt to obtain the permission of the authorities at Port-au-Prince. The Haytian Government immediately forwarded a statement of the facts of the case to the Cabinet at Washington, soliciting their intervention as a medium of communication with the American adventurers occupying Navaza, because, up to the present time, no diplomatic relations had been established between the two countries. They also dispatched two Commissioners to Navaza to report upon the actual state of affairs in the island. The Commissioners, on their return, reported that they discovered on the northern side of the island three distinct establishments for the exportation of guano. This establishment consisted of about fifty persons, together with a wharf, boats, and houses, and two four-pounders. The whole party was under the management of Mr. John L. Frazier, who acted as agent for the officers of an association at Baltimore which had entered into a treaty with the leaders of the pirate party in the Caribbean Sea, for the exportation of guano from such of them as might be found to contain that valuable manure. It is scarcely necessary to say that no such treaty had ever been made with the Haytian Government, and that Mr. Frazier’s statement was an invention of his own.

As might be expected, the remonstrances of the Haytian Government have failed to produce any effect upon the American Cabinet. The protest sent through the American commercial agent was answered by Mr. Cass to the effect that the President had ordered the appearance, at Port au Prince, of two American men-of-war. The American commodore notified to the Haytian Government that he had not come to vindicate the sovereign rights of Hayti, but to raise the flag of the United States, and protect the intruders at Navaza, who, he alleged, had a clear right by virtue of an Act of Congress passed on the 18th of August, 1856, which authorized the President to protect American citizens who may discover guano on any island not within the lawful jurisdiction of any other Government. The Haytian commodore, not being empowered to discuss the question,—for in all likelihood, the very size of his vessel formed the principal reason why he was susceptible of too easy a proof—sailed off without making any reply. The Haytian Government have addressed a new protest to Washington, and there, for the present, the matter rests. It will be remembered that this is not the first case of a similar difficulty that arose between the United States and Peru, when the island of Lobos was invaded by a party of American citizens. Then the Cabinet at Washington was compelled, after a brief show of bluster, to respect the rights of Peru. Why, then, should America treat Peru with respect, and refuse to render equal justice towards Hayti? The reason would certainly appear to be, either that she cares no longer to recognize the rights of weak nations, or that, in the particular case of Hayti, she has ulterior designs to accomplish. It is certainly more than probable that this aggression, like most others of a similar character, has for its ultimate object, not the mere possession of guano, which, according to report, is of such an inferior quality, that it was impossible to find a market, and the vessel in which it was loaded was compelled to take it back again, thereby involving the speculators in a serious loss. But although America may not be able to turn the guano of Navaza to profitable account, she may, nevertheless, retain possession of the island for more important purposes. What could be easier than for her to erect on the island a small fort, and garrison it with soldiers? or to use it as a coaling station for American steamers? But whether the act of 1856 be made by America or not, the principle involved in the question remains precisely the same: If an American is allowed to retain possession of Navaza without protest, what is to prevent him from seizing on the numerous other islands which dot the Haytian coast, and, under similar pretexts, erect a fort upon such of them as he may please to occupy?

Clearly it is the duty of England to interpose her powerful influence, and to exert all the influence she can exert, to protect the rights of a feeble ally. St. Domingo may have fallen, and Hayti may have fallen, under the hand of Lord Malmesbury; but as this is necessarily a matter of truth and importance to humanity, we cannot but hope that the influence of Lord Brougham and of other distinguished friends of the negro in both Houses of Parliament, will be exercised to accomplish this most desirable object.

With your permission, in a future communication I shall call attention to another and a later phase which American designs against St. Domingo have assumed.

I am, Sir, your obedient servant,
F. W. CHESSON.

records.summary_en: The paper says its latest intelligence from Haiti leaves scarcely room for doubt that Soulouque has been compelled to abdicate and is probably on his way to a foreign land for safety. It gives a biographical sketch: about sixty-eight years of age, born a slave on Mr. Vallet's property and freed by him, entered the army under General Dessalines at the French evacuation, rose to colonel by the fall of President Boyer, and was admitted into the secrets of the political conspiracies that followed from 1843 to 1847.
records.summary_es: El periódico dice que su información más reciente de Haití apenas deja lugar a dudas de que Soulouque se ha visto obligado a abdicar y probablemente está en camino a una tierra extranjera en busca de seguridad. Ofrece un esbozo biográfico: unos sesenta y ocho años de edad, nacido esclavo en la propiedad del Sr. Vallet y liberado por él, entró en el ejército bajo el general Dessalines en la evacuación francesa, ascendió a coronel para la caída del presidente Boyer y fue admitido en los secretos de las conspiraciones políticas que siguieron de 1843 a 1847.

Our latest intelligence from Hayti leaves
scarcely room for a doubt that his Royal High
ness, Faustin Soulouque, the black Republican

records.summary_en: A Kingston letter praises President Geffrard as a patriotic lover of liberty and says Soulouque was a tyrant feared and secretly despised, with Haitians in the city intending a thanksgiving. The paper's account of the revolution says discontent grew after a financial crisis brought about by the broker Reimbaud's flight carrying off a million dollars and plunging the island into commercial ruin, with Soulouque freely charged with having aided his escape, and that cruelty, avarice and love of personal aggrandisement had made him extremely unpopular.

records.summary_en: The account describes Geffrard's revolution in Haiti: after a church ceremony and speeches promising thorough reform, he established himself at St. Marc, towns across the north acknowledged him, and the two armies faced each other without an engagement. It says Soulouque's army gradually lost confidence in him, and he abdicated and fled, leaving the popular party in bloodless possession of the country.
records.summary_es: El relato describe la revolución de Geffrard en Haití: tras una ceremonia en la iglesia y discursos que prometían una reforma profunda, se estableció en Saint-Marc, las ciudades del norte lo reconocieron y los dos ejércitos se enfrentaron sin llegar a combatir. Dice que el ejército de Soulouque perdió gradualmente la confianza en él, y que abdicó y huyó, dejando al partido popular en posesión incruenta del país.
