records.full_text: HOSTILITIES BETWEEN DENMARK AND DOMINICA.—New York, April 6.—Letters from St. Domingo of the 15th of March announce hostilities between Dominica and Denmark. A Danish Envoy, who recently arrived in a war vessel, peremptorily demanded $150,000 as indemnity for the seizure of two Danish vessels by President Baez during the recent revolution in Dominica. President Santana offered to refer the matter to arbitrators, but the Danish functionary declined, giving the Dominicans only twenty-four hours to comply with his demands, with the understanding that a refusal would be followed by a blockade of the port.

records.headline: The schooner Independence arrived from Santo Domingo bringing word that the government would take up Baez's paper
records.summary_en: The schooner Independence arrived from Santo Domingo bringing word that the government would take up Baez's paper money, while paper issued elsewhere would not be included in the redemption, a move expected to cause excitement and loss. The paper also prints President Santana's decree granting a French and English company, for forty years, the right to explore and work mines and state forests in the republic.
records.summary_es: La goleta Independence llegó desde Santo Domingo con la noticia de que el gobierno recogería el papel moneda de Báez, mientras que el papel emitido en otros lugares no sería incluido en la redención, una medida que se esperaba causara agitación y pérdidas. El periódico también publica el decreto del presidente Santana que concede a una compañía francesa e inglesa, por cuarenta años, el derecho de explorar y explotar minas y bosques del Estado en la república.

records.summary_en: According to the *New-York daily tribune* of August 1, 1859, the Dominicans (described as Spanish negroes and mulattoes) seceded from the government of Boyer's successor. While their manifesto listed the new constitution's establishment of religious toleration as the chief grievance, the real reason for secession was reportedly that Boyer treated them unequally by sending Haytians to rule them and spending their tax proceeds in Western cities rather than their own division. Additionally, they were rejoicing at the success of President Geffrard, anticipating that a treaty of peace and commerce would soon be made.
records.summary_es: Según el *New-York daily tribune* del 1 de agosto de 1859, los dominicanos (descritos como negros y mulatos españoles) se separaron del gobierno del sucesor de Boyer. Aunque su manifiesto señalaba el establecimiento de la tolerancia religiosa en la nueva constitución como el principal agravio, se afirmaba que la verdadera razón de la secesión era que Boyer los trataba desigualmente enviando a haitianos a gobernarlos y gastando la recaudación de sus impuestos en las ciudades occidentales en lugar de en su propio departamento. Además, se regocijaban por el éxito del presidente Geffrard, anticipando que pronto se concertaría un tratado de paz y comercio.

records.full_text:
AT GONAIVES.

My last letter, I believe, descriptive of the country, left me, knapsack on back, tired and indisposed to walk, at a distance of several leagues from this ancient town. The hour was sunset—a season here of truly celestial splendor; for the clouds and scenery at this time, as elsewhere at the same hour in the tropics, are indescribably and inconceivably beautiful. Neither the poet's pen, in my opinion, nor the brush of the divinest painter, could do the vaguest justice to a sunset in the tropics: and far from me be that too common profanity which attempts, with flippant phrase, to attempt what Genius could never fully achieve.

We walked on, traversing a wide sandy plain nearly all of it uncultivated, and occasionally showing symptoms of the violence of earthquakes, and along through sections of well-tended gardens to the house of a friend—a gentleman whose knowledge of the country and whose familiarity with their history—for his actions, I find, are extensively written—may be of service to the student and philanthropist; to his topics of the characteristics of the historical Haytians he added:

Toussaint L'Ouverture, he said, was a great man—for a slave—a great man for the Times: he was the first to conceive the idea of Independence, but he feared the power of France; he had not the energy, being then an old man, to achieve it by force of arms, he sought to secure it by a treaty. The Constitution he drew up was a marvel: Franklin was as great a politician as Toussaint was for war; perhaps was naturally not inferior to Napoleon. The other Haytian generals had not the clear ideas of liberty that they so often dedicated the general of Napoleon. If Hayti had possessed a larger field of action, they would have equalled the best generals in Europe. Christophe was a brave soldier, but a cruel tyrant—Toussaint was not cruel. Toussaint he was my peer of Peter the Great—only a savage instead of a Christian ruler. Petion he regarded as the greatest man that Hayti had produced; he was the greatest in peace. I neglected to put down what he said of Boyer.

He had read Franklin's Hayti—the work of an intelligent traveler, but full of errors. Franklin said that extreme old age was very unusual here. He branded it rather briefly as a lie. He offered to conduct me to a Congo woman, of the ripe age of one hundred and twenty; and stated that not long ago Gen. Apollon—one of Toussaint's generals—died, in his one hundred and thirtieth year. (Of this Franklin, I afterward heard, that he was accused while in Hayti of a very grave crime. What it was, however, I could not discover. His book is sufficient to make any Haytian hate him.)

A RELIC OF SLAVERY.

I spoke of the slave-necked women that we had seen at the streams.

He said that in the days of Slavery the female slaves were prohibited by law from wearing shoes and dresses; they were only allowed to have a petticoat and chemise. Hence, the habit of exposing the upper part of the body had originated; and it still continued in the rural districts when they washed in the streams. Travelers seldom passed; the natives thought nothing of it.

It is only just to add here (so that chicken-limbed modesty may not say that this proves the natural inferiority and degradation of the negro), that the habit of exposing the upper part of the body is characteristic of all the Central American, Mexican and South American communities.

On the other hand, after reading the above note to an English missionary, he said that in his opinion the immorality of the people and the indecent exposure of the person in the interior, proceeded from a lack of an innate sense of modesty and decency—not from the habits of slave life or the laws of the Colonists. "I have often traveled," he said, "from Cape Haytian to this place, and yet, in all my trips, I have seen only one woman who exhibited, when seen in her washing path, any sense of modesty. She had only a cloth around her loins, as usual, and when she saw me she tried to conceal herself. Often, when crossing rivers and seeing them in that state, I have turned my eyes away out of shame for them; but they never exhibited any delicacy about it—they would continue to stare at me without a particle of shame."

I agree with both of these opinions. Doubtless the slave code, and their life as slaves, did not tend to civilize them—but it must also be remembered that previous to their being slaves they were savages. Savages have no scruples about the exposure of their persons: the negro women, there, fore, never knew, and were never taught, the requirements of civilization in that respect. Yet, while they seemed to be without shame, to my English friend, and it would be unjust to believe that they were shameless in the sense of willfully immodest. They deem it, doubtless—their actions proved it—no more immodest to expose their bodies, from the loins upward, than our belles—when the fashion says so—consider it indecent to have arms and necks uncovered. I doubt whether they are no less conscious of any wrong in doing so.

DISPROPORTION OF THE SEXES.

My molestous friend did not think that the disproportion of the sexes was considerable in the Republic, although it might appear to be so, because the women visited the cities only. It was apparent in the cities rather than real, because so many men were all ordinary laborers.

THE CATHOLIC PRIESTS.

It was true, he said, that the Catholic clergy in Hayti were immoral—so true—that they lived in concubinage openly, and even legally recognized their illegitimate offspring. It was true, also, that polygamy prevailed among the lower class, but a sentiment, he said, was daily extending in favor of legalized marriages. There are no Protestant missionaries in the interior, he said, although they are not only tolerated, but protected in the cities, and preaching everywhere in the Republic.

AFRICAN RITES.

We spoke of the traces of African worship that still linger in the mountains of Hayti. He said that these Pagan rites were sometimes performed at funerals in the interior, but secretly, and by natives of Africa chiefly, of whom there is still a considerable number living. Dessalines whipped every one detected in practicing these rites. Petion and Boyer passed laws against them, and their rural police strictly enforced the penalties prescribed for them. The French Célestine were never bigots in religion; hence, in ever green, they never showed bigotry or hatred toward other creeds and races; were of all nations the most tolerant; and they succeeded, in the Eastern division of the island, in ingrafting this sentiment into the creed of their bondmen. You see how the better nature of Christianity will show itself even in Romanism "in the abstract and principle," but in their life they encourage it and give it every protection.

WHITE LAW.

I think I have already mentioned that in Hayti there is no white race; the color of a white man is black; there, the testimony of a black man against a white is good, while the testimony of a white against a black is void! There, a slave state, being himself a black—or, rather, a free negro—possesses no rights; there, the Constitution—which is the law—says: "henceforward no white shall ever set his foot in this island in the capacity of a master or proprietor." Here, in our Southern States, a marriage between a black and a white is illegal; so antagonistical are the races, that, if a native woman at old marry a foreign white, she would instantly lose her nationality and be regarded in future as a foreigner; also: "To one who has never lived where the prejudices of color, to use a common phrase, are 'on the boot,' where the whites are the subjects and the blacks are masters—where the capacity of the negro for self government and self sustenance is no more a problem than the similar capacity of the Saxon race, where the color of the skin is neither the index of nobility nor the measure of intellect, it is difficult to conceive how exceedingly ludicrous these Pagan Black Laws of America appear. Our Slave Code, and its appendices in the Northern States are worse than the Haytian White Laws, for they were the offspring of an indubitable necessity, and were provoked by fourteen years of slaughter and two centuries of the foulest oppression. But what has the negro ever done to us, that, except to labor untiringly for our pecuniary interest, as contrasted with his own, that we should manifest such fear and hatred of him as the Slave Code of the South displays in every page?"

THE MASONIC ORDER IN HAYTI.

The Masonic Order in Hayti is very popular, numerous and influential. In 1851, Mr. D. informed us, there were thirty-nine lodges, thirty-four chapters, and three Areopagiti, in the Empire. He did not know the number of brothers. It must be very great; for one sees the symbols of the fratemity wherever he goes. "S. M. Faustin the first," I noted on the Report, held the honorable office of Grand Protector, Emperor, Pope, Grand Protector of the Masons, leading officer in the heathen Vandoux Order—important positions for a man born a slave, not long ago an overseer, and now, in his old age, an imperial exile! Let us live in hope. If we could not well mount higher than he—the Emperor of an Empire which he called into existence—surely, also, we could not well wish for an humbler starting point.

COMMERCE OF HAYTI.

He furnished me with a published statement, which, as he has made the subject his special study, is certainly deserving of consideration:

In the last days of French slavery and under the severest forms of slavery, St. Domingo furnished annually to the mother country not less than 150,000,000 pounds of frane (upward of $20,000,000 American) in the amount of producers which it produced for exportation, and its ports contained a considerable number of foreign ships. At present 400 vessels have been counted at once in the harbor of Cape Haytien, and 90 at that of Port-de-Paix, one of the most contracted. But, when these terrible catastrophes which were introductory to the liberty and independence of the Island, took place, plantations have been destroyed by fire, the fields laid waste, and the population disorganized and transformed into soldiers, it is obvious, then, that the same result can no longer be obtained. Afterward, the intestine wars, waged for the purpose of humbling or of maintaining the pride of chiefs, dispute among themselves the supreme power, completed the ruin of this once beautiful territory, reducing every day its population; for there, where on the field of battle and by emigration to other countries, a modern population had lived, for there, where former ly stretched out, as far as the eye could reach, vast plantations of sugar-cane, with their white plumes; where stood those superb sugar-houses, whose smoke ascended into the air in lofty cone-like columns, and where the measured song of a thousand male and female laborers, under the whip of the overseer, filled the air day and night with harsh accents, now extend thick forests, where the eye of the traveler sees only ruins and rubbish, a chapless mixture of walls, ponds and aqueducts, utensils broken to pieces, and aqueducts on beautiful arches, speaking witnesses everywhere of the opulence of colonial times.

"During the ten years of the peace of the adminis-tration of Toussaint, the revenue of Hayti was $4,000,000. In 1842, it had dropped to $2,000,000, and now it does not exceed $1,000,000. The weight of the indemnity—$12,000,000 to be paid to France by Boyer's imbecility—has already been paid, he says, four times over, in the shape of a bonus. In 1820, the statel that installed was regularly paid every year, but Boyer pocketed the money.

"The Haytian dollar has fluctuated during residence in Hayti, from 174 to 154 to the Spanish dollar. It is gradually appreciating. January and February last year, one gentleman informed me, the value of the gourde was equal to 67 cents net.

"Coffee," said a merchant, "is the real currency of the country. For example: During the month of November, December, January and February—it sells at $100 to $108 (Haytian dollars per cwt.); with the interior of the country in June, July and August, at from $160 to $180; by December, January and February, the exchanger will receive 16 Haytian for one Spanish dollar; during June, July and August it will run from eighteen to twenty. Thus, therefore, in consequence of these fluctuations, an exporter may lose by the coffee but gain upon the currency.

Here is an average of the value of the gourds or dollars for a number of years past; never hitherto, nor any similar statement, published. There are about 300 commercial days in the year, Sundays and fest days bearing no quotations, although the principal days for the retail trade:

At the average rate of last year, the paper money of Hayti, 3 single gourde or dollar bills, is worth somewhere between $5,000 and $5,500 (American currency) per acre! Some of them are nearly 7x9 inches in size! They are nearly all in two-dollar bills—that is, worth 12 American cents. A few hundred dollars' worth of this money I fear would break down a first-rate mule.

JAMES REDPATH.

Much of this letter has been revised, since it was written with special reference to recent events, and with information which I gathered at Port-au-Prince during a second visit which I gathered subsequent to my visit to that city.

records.chapter_es: Una república en busca de reconocimiento
records.full_text:
INTERESTING FROM ST. DOMINGO.

Our St. Domingo Correspondence.
ST. DOMINGO, Dec. 13, 1859.
A French and English Squadron Before the City—Peremptory Demands—The Depreciated Paper Currency—Requisition for Its Redemption at Extravagant Rates—History of Its Issue—Venality of European Consuls—Their Efforts to Crush the Liberal Government—Probable Ultimate Designs of the Present Demonstration, &c.

We have now four European ships of war on parade before this city. They have come to St. Domingo on a mission so strange and scandalous that it almost staggers belief. There are two French vessels, one English and one Spanish steamer engaged in bullying this government into sanctioning a stupendous swindling operation, but the moneyed profits of the speculation will remain to the exclusive benefit of two or three British officials.

To begin at the beginning, and make a clear statement, we must go back to 1857-8, when—thanks to European intervention—Baez became the despotic ruler of the Dominican republic. Baez has the warm support of a large portion of the negroes, who wish to unite with Hayti on the basis of holding the white race in absolute subjection to the black; but when left to themselves, this party is much the weaker, and can only keep the control while European vessels of war are on hand to sustain them in the possession of the capital and other seaports.

Baez, with his staff of ministers and officers, being thus backed, were disposed to shear as large a fleece as the closest cutting could collect from the backs of the poor Dominicans while he had them in hand. They had many ways of fleecing the people, but the one in which they operated the most extensively was in the issue of paper money. During the whole of his administration, Baez kept the government press hotly at work manufacturing paper dollars, until the whole country was swamped with it. Millions of it was employed by Baez and his agents in buying up property of every kind on speculation? Among other friends and partners in these operations, some members of the British consular corps became deeply interested in the Baez money, or as the people here call it, “Mangolino papeletes.”

There are limits to everything, and the issue of forty or fifty millions of “papeletes” banished specie circulation to such a degree that not even a copper coin was visible in trade—necessarily the Baez paper went down to nothing. The poor people who had received it for their rice, sugar and tobacco; for their corn, cattle, wax, honey, yams, cocoanuts, &c., were dismayed to see their little all melting away into bits of waste paper. They had sold the fruits of their labor for this “government currency,” because it was the only circulating medium of the country, and there was no help.

While Baez yet held the supreme power in St. Domingo, his “Mangolino papeletes” sunk down to the rate of two thousand to the dollar under his own eyes; yet he went on printing it off by millions, and sent it into the interior to buy up produce for shipment to Europe on his own account.

At last the whole country rose against the Baez government and his iniquitous nest of money-makers. The whole concern, except the foreign consuls, were forced to leave the Dominican territory, but not without the “spoils,” for the European consuls used their official position to cover their own and their partners’ ill-gotten wealth. The French Consul, who governs the other consuls here just as his master—Napoleon—governs their masters at home, abetted and sustained Baez and all his corruptions in their most offensive forms, although no one accuses him of any personal interest in the papelete speculation.

This may be perhaps explained by considering this support the reward of Baez’s disposition to carry out the Anglo-French plan of annexing this republic to Hayti.

When General Santana succeeded to the Presidency this proposition of accepting the negro rule of Hayti, was pressed upon the Dominican Cabinet with such disrespectful urgency that the Executive sent Mr. Raybaud his passports. This gentleman was the late Charge d’Affairs of France at the court of Soulouque, but is now the special annexation agent of France, England and Hayti. While Santana was battling with the European scheme of Haytien supremacy, the Consular speculators in Baez’s paper were pressing him to recognise the “Mangolino papeletes” as government currency. This Santana had no right to do, for, by an act of Congress, provision had already been made to call in and cancel this paper at a fixed price. This was at the highest rate at which it was circulating before Baez went out of power—that is, at 2,000 papeletes to the dollar. But this liberal law did not satisfy the demands of the European Consuls, and they officially informed the government that they would be “treated as null and void.” None of them pretend that a rag of the millions of it they have on hand cost either of them more than the government offers to allow and it is known that they have bought nine-tenths of it at 3,500 and 4,000 “papeletes” to the dollar. Yet, in the face of these admitted facts, they have brought a fleet to “insist” upon this poor and friendless government allowing them twenty times as much as they paid for their 18,000,000 mangolino papeletes.

After an official correspondence full of dictatorial arrogance on the part of the French, English, and Spanish Consuls, these gentlemen informed the Dominican government that they would close their consulates and leave the country in a body if their demands were not acceded to at once. They were answered that the Dominican executive had not the right or power to annul an act of Congress, and they were reminded that the act was in itself most just and liberal, as it provided for the acceptance of the Mangolino papaletes at a much better rate than its makers had left it in circulation; the government therefore could do no more in the premises.

On this the Consuls of France, Spain and England struck their flags with a great deal of parade, and left the country. The Dominican government despatched agents to Paris, London and Madrid, with full statements of the case, but all those courts have united in the plan of suppressing—that is, of crushing out the Dominican republic—and refused to entertain the question.

This republic has not an ally on this continent, and the European Powers take advantage of its friendless, unsupported position to oppress it outrageously. Revenons a nos moutons. The French, English, and Spanish squadron now pointing its guns on our city, has brought back our consular masters with a list of new demands, amounting in fact to an unconditional surrender of the independence of the Dominican republic.

Some of these demands are secret, but there is scarcely room for a doubt that it is a repetition of the old alternative—negro rule or ruin. Be certain that American commerce, American enterprise and American citizens must be forbidden the Dominican territory, or the Dominican republic must be “suppressed,” and the white race driven out if it does not yield submission to Hayti.

This is the sum and substance of the old quadruple alliance of France, England, Spain and Hayti, and it will not be changed until this republic is recognized by the United States, or the negroes of Hayti are put in full possession of the whole island.

It is the cue of the consuls to let the Dominicans understand that the Anglo-French alliance no longer consider it an independent nationality. Spain and Hayti are but passive tails to this kite, although they are counted in as equal Powers in the quadruple alliance. Since Faustin has dropped out of the square, his imperial brother, Napoleon, and his august sisters, Victoria and Isabella, may only stand for a triangle, though it is very far from a right angled triangle. The square of the French base is a good deal more than equal to the square of the British and Spanish sides which Napoleon subtends, and, what is more than Euclid knew how to reduce to geometry, extends at his pleasure without increasing their power. Before they landed the consuls sent a note to the Dominican Executive ordering that a salute of twenty-one guns should be given within twenty-four hours to each of their flags. The Dominican Cabinet felt and said that such an order would only be issued to a dependent, or in chastisement of some wrong inflicted, and outside of the “Mangolino Papelete question” no offence had been alleged. The consuls only replied by commanding the salutes to be given within six hours.

The Dominican government complied, though under protest that it yielded to force, for they could not expose the city to the horrors of a bombardment for a form. After this preliminary the French consul carried his British colleague to the palace, that he might repeat after him, and endorse in the name of the English government, the recent orders of the Emperor Napoleon. What these are no one knows positively, but enough has leaked out to justify the belief that they relate to Hayti, and contain a death blow to this republic.

After this was attended to, the British consul had his turn, and was let loose on his Papelete business. John Bull is not to be balked of his pennies, and the allied squadron is here to see everything settled to their mind.

John Bull’s fight for the opium smugglers was a noble and honest war by the side of this bullying a weak republic into bankruptcy in support of a fraudulent paper issue; and the Anglo-French exploits in doctoring “sick Turkeys” to death and robbing bits of “broken China,” become in comparison fair business transactions.

POSTSCRIPT.
DECEMBER 14.
The government has surrendered to the consuls at discretion. It agrees to redeem all the Mangolino papelites at 500 to the Spanish dollar, and pledges the custom house and all other resources for principal and interest. The eighteen or twenty millions of it stored at the British consulate was bought at 2,500, 3,000 and 4,000 to the dollar. To buy 18,000,000 papelites at an average of 3,500 to the dollar and sell them off at 500 is a very good spec for a couple of these consular worthies; but that is the way John Bull uses his navy to take care of his children.

records.summary_en: The *New York Herald* reported from San Domingo on February 22, 1860, that the city was celebrating George Washington's birthday, with the American flag displayed alongside the Dominican white cross on government and private balconies, including those of Minister of the Interior Don Domingo de la Rocha and Senate President Don Manuel Delmonte. The correspondent noted a favorable change toward Americans compared to past mistreatment by Haytians who wanted to drive whites from the island, alongside prospects for closer commercial relations and an increase in American vessels.
records.summary_es: El *New York Herald* informó desde Santo Domingo el 22 de febrero de 1860 que la ciudad celebraba el natalicio de George Washington, exhibiéndose la bandera estadounidense junto a la cruz blanca dominicana en balcones gubernamentales y privados, incluidos los del ministro del Interior, don Domingo de la Rocha, y del presidente del Senado, don Manuel Delmonte. El corresponsal señaló un cambio favorable hacia los estadounidenses en comparación con los maltratos pasados de los haitianos que pretendían expulsar a los blancos de la isla, junto con perspectivas de relaciones comerciales más estrechas y un aumento de buques estadounidenses.

News from St. Domingo.
REVIVAL OF COMMERCE—IMPORTANT DECREE—EDUCATION—IMMIGRATION—CURRENCY.

Files of St. Domingo papers have been received in Havana to May 17. We translate the following from the Diario de la Marina of the 14th inst.:—

Judging from the tone of the press the country is visibly recovering the low condition it has been in, consequent upon the frequent upheavings it has suffered from, and the government, as well as private individuals, were busy with administrative and other reforms relative to commerce and agriculture. Amongst the measures adopted by the former is the annexed decree, which we publish entire for the benefit of our commercial readers:—

The Senate, at the instance of the Executive power, considering that the advancement of commerce is one of the most important causes of national wealth, and being desirous of attracting to to the ports of the republic, by immunities and privileges of every kind, the flags of all commercial and friendly nations, to increase our revenue and develope the elements of prosperity which our privileged soil possesses, has resolved, in the name of the nation, to issue the following

DECREE.

Article 1. From and after the day of the publication of this decree, the vessels of those friendly nations with which the republic has not had treaties will be placed on a similar footing with respect to the payment of import, export, tonnage, or lighthouse dues, and everything else relating to the commerce of the most favored nations.

Art. 2. The vessels of those nations which, after the lapse of a year from the publication of this decree, shall not have granted to the vessels of this republic equal advantages shall be deprived of the benefits of this measure.

Art. 3. This decree repeals every other act that may be contrary to it, and shall be transmitted to the executive power for constitutional purposes.

Given at the National Palace of the Senate, on the 8th day of May of the year 1860, and the 17th of the Country.

On the following day it was signed by Vice President Alfan, in the absence of President Santanna, and by the Minister of Commerce and Finance.

We see, besides, that they are not unmindful of other useful branches. The subject of public instruction is prominently spoken of, thanks to the spirit of progress which animates the government. In addition to the opening of various free schools, we read in the Gazette that the High Directing Junta of Education was occupied with praiseworthy interest in drawing up the project of a law on the restoration of the old University, to be submitted to the Senate, and it was hoped that that body would sanction it before the close of the present session.

records.summary_en: The Dominican Senate requested the President to demand explanations and immediate reparation from Venezuela regarding the shooting of several Dominicans, warning that recourse would otherwise be taken. The President replied that no expostulations or reprisals were warranted because the individuals had abandoned their nationality and entered the enemy's ranks, noting further that letters from Venezuela asserted those men had actually been killed in battle rather than executed. Additionally, the press advocated for establishing a bank to suppress paper money, and the value of the gold ounce was fixed at 4,000 national dollars.
records.summary_es: El Senado dominicano solicitó al presidente que exigiera explicaciones y reparación inmediata a Venezuela con respecto al fusilamiento de varios dominicanos, advirtiendo que de lo contrario se recurriría a otras medidas. El presidente respondió que no se justificaban protestas ni represalias dado que tales individuos habían renunciado a su nacionalidad y se habían sumado a las filas enemigas, señalando además que cartas procedentes de Venezuela aseguraban que esos hombres en realidad habían muerto en combate y no fusilados. Por otra parte, la prensa abogó por la fundación de un banco para retirar el papel moneda, y el valor de la onza de oro se fijó en 4.000 pesos nacionales.

The question of immigration from the Canaries, of those who were forced to fly from Venezuela on account of the revolution in that republic, was occupying the attention not only of the press but of the government of St. Domingo. Vessels had been provided for bringing them over, and those who had arrived from Laguayra, to the number of seventy-six, had been provided with excellent lands. This humane conduct of the Dominican government had produced an unfavorable feeling in Venezuela, where the periodicals cry down Dominican nationality, as we gather from an energetic article on this subject, published in the Dominican Semi-Monthly Review.

The shooting of several Dominicans in Venezuela was also engaging the attention of the government. The Senate addressed a letter to the President, in which the Executive was requested, in view of the compromise of national honor, to demand explanations from the goverment of Venezuela, and if immediate reparation for those outrages "to the nation, the rights of persons, and the very laws of humanity," was not made, recourse would be had, as a last resource, to the right of reprisal, and the Venezuelans residing in St. Domingo would be treated in like manner. His Excellency replied, reminding the Senate that they were not treating of a general measure of the Venezuelan government against every Dominican, but of a chastisment inflicted on individuals who had abandoned their nationality and had entered the enemy's ranks, on which account there could be neither expostulations nor reprisals. This reply had called forth a vote of thanks from the resident Venezuelans; and, moreover, it appears that letters received from Venezuela assert that the Dominicans in question were not executed, but had been killed in battle, with the exception of one who was assassinated by a party of marauders.

Finally, the press warmly advocates the establishment of a bank as the best means for suppressing the paper money in circulation, which occasions serious inconvenience to the government and citizens. To regulate the operations of the public administration, the value of the gold ounce is fixed at 4,000 national dollars each.

records.headline: A travel narrative describes approaching Santo Domingo by sea and entering Puerto Plata, whose harbor the writer
records.summary_en: A travel narrative describes approaching Santo Domingo by sea and entering Puerto Plata, whose harbor the writer calls a poor one surrounded by sublime scenery. It recounts the coming of the pilot and the custom-house officers, some white and some colored, along with Mr. Collins, an American gentleman to whom the writer was addressed.
records.summary_es: Un relato de viaje describe la aproximación a Santo Domingo por mar y la entrada a Puerto Plata, cuyo puerto el escritor califica de malo rodeado de un paisaje sublime. Relata la llegada del piloto y de los oficiales de aduana, algunos blancos y otros de color, junto con el Sr. Collins, un caballero estadounidense a quien el escritor venía recomendado.

records.full_text:
To the Militiamen of the State of Arkansas.
Executive Office,
Little Rock, Ark.,
Sept. 22, 1860.

I have caused to be published, the foregoing laws of his State and of the United States, on the Subject of the militia, for the information, observance and government.

The constitution of our State declares "that the military shall be kept in strict subordination to the civil power." The constitution of the United States declares "that a well regulated militia is necessary to the security of a free State."

I appeal to you to remember that it is the duty of every good citizen to yield to his country such services as the law requires of him. You cannot perform those duties without a knowledge of them, nor can officers without being thoroughly organized. "To keep the military in strict subordination, and a well regulated militia," to be such security as is meant in the constitution declares to be necessary.

I point you to the State of Arkansas: I point you to the laws of the United States, and appeal to you to prompt, zealous and active duty. In doing so, I would remind you that those who continue to hold office, and who shall be elected or appointed to perform, as far as possible, the duties of their respective offices, as well as those who are different on the subject of organizing the militia, are mistaken. We do not know how soon the strong arm of the military may be needed. Then, if we have any State pride, let us be prepared, and let us work together, and have the returns made as required by law. By the laws of this State and of the United States, each officer is required to furnish his own arms and equipments. The State has a quantity of arms, such as muskets, pistols and carbines on deposit, at the U. S. arsenal, at Little Rock.

The State of Arkansas is entitled to receive, under the acts of Congress, seven hundred and ninety-four muskets, at an aggregate valuation of thirteen dollars for each musket. If armed with artillery, or cavalry accoutrements, the State is entitled to but three hundred and forty-seven muskets. Let arms be applied, the number of them will be according to their value and cost. There has no law of this State authorized the Governor to receive this or any other company of militia with arms. In 1856, the quota was 1,172 muskets. The General Assembly has not yet passed any law to distribute these arms to the militia. But the whole amount of arms due from the United States to the State of Arkansas, would be sufficient to arm all the militiamen in the State. In 1856, the quota was 1,494 muskets now due from the United States, or an aggregate valuation of $21,169. It is therefore manifest that the militia, to be armed and equipped, must first be fully armed by the State, nor by the United States, until the volunteer companies are called into actual service of the United States. The expense of arming all the volunteer companies of the State, or of the United States and of this State require that each company shall be furnished with such arms and equipments as the law prescribes; and the volunteer companies authorized by law in every county in the State should be organized and thoroughly organized and disciplined, and bearing the state flag or national banner as soon as possible. The only mode, as I conceive, for the volunteer companies, there is one mode by which the State or county could procure them and have them placed under the control of the proper authorities of the State, for the use of the State, when in use by the volunteer companies.—That is, for the county court to levy a tax, or by voluntary subscription, to raise money to buy arms and equipments to arm all the volunteer companies in the county; or a portion of these companies may be organized in each county in the State, as a company of cavalry, or infantry, one of light infantry or riflemen, or a company of artillery. This company shall be wholly independent of the militia regiments, except at battalion and regimental parades.

Were the whole of the volunteer companies in the State, organized and armed as they should be, each composed of fifty men, including officers, making the amount in the aggregate to twenty-two hundred men, well disciplined, equipped, and at all times ready for service, in addition to the volunteer companies, we should now have six-two regiments, and which will soon be organized.

Under the provisions of chapter 112, provides that volunteer companies "shall elect their own officers," and the place to be ordered by the colonel of the regiment, and the certificate of election commissions shall issue.

The law in section 20 of chapter 113, that "out of the militia enrolled, there shall be formed for each battalion, at least one company of light infantry, or one of riflemen, and that to each division there shall be at least one company of artillery, and one troop of horse." These volunteer companies are to be formed as part of the regiments of the regular militia.

Under section 22, a volunteer company shall consist of not less than thirty-four nor more than one hundred non-commissioned officers and privates. Section 23, each company may have not less than three commission officers—a captain, first lieutenant, and second lieutenant.

A battalion cannot consist of less than three companies.

No regiment shall consist of more than two battalions. All volunteer companies in a regiment are designated by the letters of the alphabet.

Volunteer companies are designated by proper terms indicating the character of troops—infantry, riflemen, or cavalry. Each volunteer company is entitled to three officers, and the colonel of the regiment of the regular militia is entitled to but two—a colonel and lieutenant colonel.

It devolves upon each colonel commandant to organize his regiment, but he is also to have formed within the bounds of his regiment these volunteer companies, independent of his regiment, as well as the required quotas, and the number of militiamen will not exceed forty or fifty men to a company, in the bounds of any regiment than necessary to form three volunteer companies, containing one hundred non-commissioned officers and privates each. If there are an excess of the militiamen, all the volunteer companies are formed, and there should still be a surplus, the colonel would have to apply to the brigadier general of the brigade to divide the regiment and make a new regiment out of part of it.

The law in section 20 of chapter 113, prescribes that "it shall be the duty of the colonels, at all times, to keep the vacancies of all officers in their regiments filled."

Every officer will promptly comply with the important and solemn duty so positively and clearly enjoined upon him by the laws of his State, and he will feel himself in conscience and law bound to obey as long as he holds the office of colonel commandant of a regiment, the militia of our State will be organized, and will be kept continually organized.

Let every officer remember that the chief honor derived from holding an office, is that which an honest and intelligent community will ever accord to an officer who promptly, faithfully and efficiently performs his duties. To know "what these duties are," he must read the law. He must study to understand the laws and the duties required of him, and he will then be prepared to act, and if he have pride and energy of character, he will promptly and efficiently discharge the public trust reposed in him.

I have prepared and had published with the militia laws, a register of the divisions, brigades, regiments and companies, with the names of the major generals, brigadier generals, colonels, and lieutenant colonels. If these officers will go to work in earnest, as they ought to do, under the law, they will acquire credit and distinction for themselves, and put the militia to be such to the security of the State as the constitution declares to be necessary.

While the constitution declares to be necessary to the security of a free State; and while I urge the militia by preparing and organizing under the law, to avert coming danger;

It is for no purpose for trouble or danger, which can certainly be brought upon our borders, that I would move you to less and indifferent the security of the people of Arkansas and their property. The dangers which threaten the political status of the people of Arkansas are of such a character that no patriot, however he may hope, will be willing, calmly to encounter them. He will be willing, nay, anxious to exert his influence in favor of raising money in the county where he resides, to buy arms to arm and equip the volunteer companies of his county. He will take hold of this matter and petition the General Assembly, at its coming session, to pass such a law as I have suggested, to enable every county may be enabled to have its volunteer companies fully armed and equipped, so that they would afford ample protection to the people of the county, in their persons and property. Is there any reason to doubt that the British government, or her abolition emissaries, or the non-slaveholding States, or the unconstitutional acts of our government shall have placed her armed forces or her political mercenary agents stationed in our midst, or in our neighborhood, in every county in our State, and near every slaveholder's house, and that things ready at the appointed time, to incite and encourage slave insurrection? The open and notorious acts of the British government, the long continued, deep-laid and settled secret policy of the British government to destroy the supremacy and equality of the United States. That it is her object to break up and destroy our government, and establish her own power and supremacy over the whole of the British possessions on this continent, and then establish her own power in America.

In 1850, the British, French and United States governments entered into a truce, for ten years, between the Empire of Hayti and the Dominican Republic. That truce has expired. The British government has entered into a treaty with the Dominican Republic, by which the Dominican Republic gives its adhesion to the said truce under the guaranties of the same powers: 1st. Not to alienate, lease, hypothecate, or cede gratuitously, either temporarily or permanently, any portion of the Dominican territory, particularly in the Bay of Samana, to any government whatever. 2d. Not to contract any engagement with any foreign State; not to accept any subsidy from a foreign company; not to hypothecate much of the revenues of the Dominican Republic to any foreign State; 3d. Not to accept any protectorate, nor to submit to any foreign intervention, or any other act contrary to her independence.

The political status of the slaveholding States is now such that no reflecting man, who was fully aware that the British government was acting in concert with the abolitionists of the non-slaveholding States, in a policy that disturbed the domestic tranquility of the United States, but must admit that there is an "irrepressible conflict" between the free States and the slave States. Is it not a fact known to all men, that British gold have been and will be spent in multiplying abolition emissaries in the United States to stir up and intensify this "irrepressible conflict" between the free States and slave States. That the policy of the British government has been to use all her efforts to overthrow our government, (by using her abolition emissaries and domestic emissaries,) that the mischiefs and outrages of the non-slaveholding States would seem to have been prompted by the British government for the purpose of destroying the States. It is my opinion that the British government has been at the bottom of all of the mischiefs and outrages perpetrated against the slave States, and that the identity of one federal government, and of the domestic policies of the United States to hold the British government in check, and preserve the domestic tranquility of the United States. It is my opinion that the British government has determined that, as long as the federal government exists, that she henceforth has no domestic tranquility in the United States, and that British gold has been and will be used to hire unprincipled abolitionists in the free States, and send them into the slave States, with a view to excite or encourage that the people of the South will become weary of the Union, and the north, and the aggressions and outrages perpetrated upon the slave States, and those hired abolition British emissaries, prompts the people, in 1860, to elect, and it is voted that civil war will be produced, the Union dissolved, the non-slaveholding States left with domestic evils and deeds of plunder, robbery, arson and murder, and under prevailing.

I believe that such a conspiracy exists against our federal government, and that, if successful, it will be carried into execution, as above indicated, and the names of the secret agents and emissaries of the British government, distributed throughout the United States, to stir up abolitionism, were detected and made public, the patriotic people of the United States, when he announced with astonishment; and having that disclosed, every honest author and instigator of the mischief, all anti-slavery men in both free and slave States would at once be dismayed.

It would then be seen that abolitionism would become formally and more firmly united with the British government, and that the patriotic citizens of the whole Union would unite, as one man, against those agents and emissaries, would be so completely unmasked and declared against the British government for her interference of months.

In conclusion, in making these statements, I my duty to the people of the State of Arkansas to urge them to organize, and arm, and equip themselves, and thoroughly prepare themselves, for any emergency, to be ready to protect themselves and our State against all foes, and to be satisfied that our government intends shall not be violated, and that the "irrepressible conflict" is indeed "irrepressible" and terrible.

Every county in the State of Arkansas should have at least one or two volunteer companies, well armed with arms; and that every citizen who has a gun, should keep it in repair and unmolested, and that volunteer companies should be ready at all times to defend the State.

Let these important matters not be lightly considered, but promptly and maturely considered. We must look as far as human foresight can reach, and prepare to guard against evil before it is too late to prevent it.

Then as wise men and prudent, as men who feel a deep interest in the welfare of the militiamen of the State of Arkansas, let us put our shoulders to the wheel, and emergency which shall call for their strong arms in defense of our rights and our country.

HENRY M. RECTOR, Governor of the State of Arkansas, and Commander in chief of the militia thereof.

records.summary_en: The paper argues that Alto Vela is a guano island and a dependency of Haiti, and that a Baltimore guano company squatted upon it in spite of protest, defended in the Senate on the ground that present occupation did not necessarily involve permanent possession. It says the government of Haiti was compelled to submit when a ship of war was sent to protect the guano diggers, but President Geffrard, watching his opportunity, has broken up the settlement of squatter-sovereigns upon Alto Vela.

Dice que el Gobierno de Haití se vio obligado a ceder cuando se envió un buque de guerra para proteger a los excavadores de guano, pero el presidente Geffrard, esperando su oportunidad, ha desmantelado el asentamiento de ocupantes soberanos en Alto Vela.

records.summary_en: The *New-York daily tribune* reported that following the hoisting of the Spanish flag on the 16th—which caused consternation among local inhabitants—the fully armed Spanish frigate *Blanca* was dispatched from Havana on the 22nd with regular troops to assist the Spanish protectorate or annexation. Additional naval and military forces, along with approximately 5,000 regular troops on the *Petronila* and *Derenguela* and about 10,000 more from Spain, were reported to be following. Meanwhile, business on the island remained depressed, and passengers traveling on the *Quaker City* included ex-President Miramon of Mexico and Major Patterson, a bearer of dispatches from St. Domingo to Spain.
records.summary_es: El *New-York daily tribune* informó que, tras el izamiento de la bandera española el día 16 —lo que causó consternación entre los habitantes locales—, la fragata española totalmente artillada *Blanca* fue despachada desde La Habana el día 22 con tropas regulares para apoyar el protectorado o anexión española. Se reportó que fuerzas navales y militares adicionales, junto con aproximadamente 5.000 soldados regulares a bordo de la *Petronila* y la *Derenguela* y unos 10.000 más procedentes de España, les seguirían en breve. Entretanto, el comercio en la isla continuaba deprimido, y entre los pasajeros que viajaban en el *Quaker City* figuraban el expresidente Miramón de México y el mayor Patterson, portador de pliegos oficiales desde Santo Domingo hacia España.

records.chapter_en: Annexation to Spain and the Restoration War
records.chapter_es: La anexión a España y la Guerra de la Restauración
records.full_text:
The Spanish steam frigate Blanca, with a full complement of troops, and the steam sloop Isabel, left our anchorage in our harbor Saturday evening last for St. Domingo, having in view a mission of an aggressive policy and to defeat any opposition that might be made by the government or people of the Dominican Republic to the proposed annexation of Spain. Many thousands of people were upon the wharf to cheer this enterprise for the restoration of the banner of the old and haughty Spanish power upon their ancient domain, where were impressed almost the first footsteps of the pioneers of Spanish civilization. In the wake of the ships above mentioned the steam frigate Berenguela and Petronila, also heavily armed and with many hundred men drawn from the army, to compel respect for Spanish power and to enforce obedience, it is said that five or six thousand soldiers are to be sent to St. Domingo to be distributed as may be signified by the Spanish government, by a quiet introduction of the people, ostensibly as the home and field for their services by grants of lands which were to be given to them, but in reality to be distributed at government where they pretend to seek homes and prosperity.
Every demonstration tending to territorial acquisition on the part of Spain in St. Domingo, from the reports of those who have recently returned from the city of St. Domingo, to defeat the policy of the United States—the Monroe doctrine—is being carried out with every good faith with the Dominican republic, through their agents here. It is said that the terms of annexation and support, after the same had been thoroughly discussed and agreed upon by the high contracting parties—the one to surrender and the other to receive—have been made to include the following:—To recognize the Spanish officers of high rank in the army and navy, and to continue them in their respective positions, as heretofore, for the purpose of future action to construct a case against the republic of Hayti to be followed by annexation.
Through the facts, views and deductions of your correspondent have been subsequently fully verified and confirmed, and the arrangements, although not officially made public, are known to be the current news. Effectual steps have been taken to check or prevent the slightest opposition on the part of the people to this change of jurisdiction. These demonstrations of a Power you have so often and so justly characterized as a "dying" country by their own assertions are of great importance at this time, as they are to share the island of Hayti between an upstart and a throne. The Dominican republic, it is said, is to be the share of Spain, and the republic of Hayti is to share the fate of her sister republic under the wake of Spanish policy, by previous understanding with the French government.
England is not, under this view of advantage for Spain, to be an idle spectator, but she is under the influence of her yarns, when a free people pass under the yoke of a power where the most cruel and unmitigated power, where slavery and slave traffic are to be found in their most hideous forms. She will not, she cannot, interfere with the policy of Spain, because her England is, still, with folded arms, and says nothing against the policy of Spain, because she is the principal consumer of the world, for none of which can be substituted for the southern products of your heritage. How will it be with the growing prosperity and power of the people of the United States? Spain sees her opportunity, and she will not only take St. Domingo, but her designs to annex Mexico she only held in restraint until she saw your internal difficulties, and then her subsequent movements would flow towards the shores of Mexico.
The political disturbances in the United States showed that the time was ripe for the aggrandizement of Spain, and hence the prompt action she has taken of it. But what will be the result hereafter? Are not all the people, in or out of the Union, interested in the cause of liberty—in political and social rights? and is there not some power to check the aggressive policy of Spain and compel the respect of foreign Powers?
The future is soon to show us these things. Who is to control? The colored race will cry aloud if Spain controls the island of Hayti, for they know that their freedom will not be likely to receive any recognition from Spanish power.
The United States war steamer Mohawk, Lieutenant Commanding T. A. Craven, arrived here on the 20th inst. from Key West.
The health of the eminent merchant, Mr. Drake, is said to be somewhat improved.
The suicides of the coolies continue to be of frequent occurrence, and it is said that no less than seven or eight have occurred within the last few days.
The steamship Panama, from New York, arrived here on the 21st inst.
General Miramon, ex-President of Mexico, and family, left here on the 22d inst. in the Spanish mail steamer for Cadiz, via New York.
The news of the political sentiments and action of the new President of the United States of America has been received here with much interest, and the dark dreams of fanatical raids upon our peaceful domain have passed with the shadows of the night. Circumstances have occurred in the last few years to leave a very deep and many painful shadows following in the trail of more than one of your expeditions, and they were not likely to wind up a good many more on the same string; yet there is now room to hope for the better and we will take it. The business circle among those interested in the sugar market is not as active as it has been for some time, and the prices have not been as well sustained as they were at our last advice. The sugar market at the close of the week is very dull, and the prices are as follows for sugar:—No. 12, 4 1/2 rs.; No. 11, 4 1/4 rs.; No. 10, 4 rs.; No. 9, 3 3/4 rs.
Molasses in net tierces demand at 1 3/4 a 2 reals per keg of 5 1/2 gallons. Exchange on London, 14 1/2 a 15 per cent premium; on New York, 2 1/2 a 3 per cent discount. The shipments of sugars and molasses to a considerable extent have been made to the United States during the last few weeks. Freights—Demand on declining, but will probably be better as the season advances.

records.summary_en: Following years of division and subsequent unification under Boyer, the Dominican population rose in insurrection against Haytian ascendancy and chose Pedro Santana as president. After Santana's term expired in 1849, Jimenes was elected Chief Magistrate while Santana was banished due to suspicions of intriguing with Madrid; however, Jimenes soon conspired with Hayti's Emperor Soulouque to unite the island, prompting the Dominicans to recall Santana from exile and invest him with dictatorial power.
records.summary_es: Tras años de división y la subsiguiente unificación bajo Boyer, la población dominicana se alzó en insurrección contra el predominio haitiano y eligió a Pedro Santana como presidente. Al concluir el mandato de Santana en 1849, Jimenes fue elegido primer mandatario mientras que Santana fue desterrado por sospechas de intrigas con Madrid; sin embargo, Jimenes pronto conspiró con el emperador Soulouque de Haití para unificar la isla, lo que impulsó a los dominicanos a llamar a Santana del exilio e investirlo de poderes dictatoriales.

records.passage: FROM HAYTI — APPEAL TO THE PEOPLE. By the arrival of the brig Echo at New York we are placed in possession of Hayti files to March 9th. The Dominicans have issued the following proclamation against the Spanish invasion. APPEAL TO THE NATION. Dominicans! The country is in danger, and there is but one way to save it — by revolution. — Santana, since his last elevation to power, has sold the Republic. The price of the Yankees did not suit him. To-day he has adjudged it to Spain, and is preparing to crush the Dominican people under the colonial yoke for the vile price of a few puerile dignities, and of the gold which will be distributed to him and five or six principal accomplices. To-morrow the Tartars will enjoy in quiet the riches gained by this criminal bargain, and will welcome us with an ironical smile on hearing the clank of our chains. To-morrow shame will settle on our hearthstones, and the stigma of ignominy will soil our brows. To-morrow, our wives will fly from our arms, our mothers will refuse their caresses, and our children their smiles — a degenerate people merit them not. To-morrow we shall be able to leave to our families neither country, glory, honor, prosperity, nor even the repose of the domestic hearth. To-morrow — to express it once for all — we shall have changed the noble aegis of the Cross for the livery of slavery. What, then, shall be the way of restoration? "Revolution. A revolution, holy, noble, just, grand, because it has for its object the preservation of a nationality created

records.summary_en: The newspaper reported that the Dominican Republic, covering an area of 1,000 square miles with a population of 136,000, declared its complete independence from the French portion, though Spain had never formally admitted its independence after forty years out of its possession. According to Mr. James Redpath, officially connected with the Republic of Hayti, the Dominican Republic has been divided between two alternating parties represented by Santana and Baez, whose policies indicate re-union and independence. Redpath explained that after Santana failed to repay a million-dollar loan borrowed from Spain and offered a mortgage on the custom-houses, a small band of eighty Spaniards arrived in St. Domingo last summer to work as custom collectors and mechanics, which fueled the opposition's revolutionary claims that Santana was selling the country.
records.summary_es: El periódico informó que la República Dominicana, con una superficie de 1.000 millas cuadradas y una población de 136.000 habitantes, declaró su completa independencia de la porción francesa, aunque España nunca había reconocido formalmente su independencia tras cuarenta años fuera de su dominio. Según el Sr. James Redpath, vinculado oficialmente a la República de Haití, la República Dominicana ha estado dividida entre dos facciones alternantes representadas por Santana y Báez, cuyas directrices apuntaban respectivamente a la anexión y a la independencia. Redpath explicó que, tras no poder Santana amortizar un empréstito de un millón de dólares solicitado a España y ofrecer en garantía las aduanas, un reducido contingente de ochenta españoles llegó a Santo Domingo el verano anterior para ejercer como recaudadores aduaneros y artesanos, lo que avivó las denuncias revolucionarias de la oposición de que Santana vendía la patria.

records.summary_en: Following the 1844 secession of the Dominican Republic, two alternating political parties led by Santana and Baez emerged, representing reunion and independence policies respectively. Santana repeatedly and unsuccessfully sought to place the republic under the control of Spain, France, or Venezuela, and also failed in his efforts to induce white emigration from the United States.

records.headline: The transfer was to be effected by a coup it main
records.summary_en: According to *The New York herald* on April 19, 1861, three members of the Dominican cabinet orchestrated a transfer of power to Spain through a coup, supported by secret agents landed from the war steamer *Don John de Austria* and Spanish vessels arriving from Cuba and Porto Rico with paid emigrants, arms, and soldiers. When local authorities questioned these arrivals, they were officially told that the soldiers came to help repel Haytian invasions and the emigrants to till the ground, explanations that the people eventually came to believe after several months passed without further movements.
records.summary_es: Según *The New York Herald* del 19 de abril de 1861, tres miembros del gabinete dominicano orquestaron la entrega del poder a España mediante un golpe de Estado, secundados por agentes secretos desembarcados del vapor de guerra *Don John de Austria* y por navíos españoles procedentes de Cuba y Puerto Rico con inmigrantes pagados, armas y tropas. Cuando las autoridades locales inquirieron sobre estos desembarcos, se les contestó oficialmente que la tropa llegaba para ayudar a rechazar invasiones haitianas y los colonos para labrar la tierra, explicaciones que la población terminó por creer al cabo de varios meses sin que se registraran nuevos movimientos.

records.summary_en: Based on the provided newspaper excerpt, forty-three notable persons from Cibao were arrested and sent under escort to St. Domingo, while Padre Moya hoisted the Spanish flag in Vega despite public opposition and subsequently escaped the pursuing populace. The nation is described as indignant over being sold and betrayed through annexation, with unarmed citizens struggling in Moca following disarmament, a movement resulting in seven persons being shot in Azua, and reinforcements requested from Porto Rico. Consequently, Spain finds herself engaged in an unforeseen labyrinth of trouble stemming from the annexation.

records.headline: The latest true intelligence from Hayti is that the Dominican Generals
records.summary_en: A report from Cadiz dated the 6th states that exiled Dominican generals—including Cabral, Sanchez, Valentine, and Baez—joined disaffected populations to lead a serious insurrection against the Spanish occupation, raising the Dominican flag in La motta, Ney be, Cerca, and San Juan. The insurgents declared that if they could not remain independent, they would prefer incorporation with the Haytien Republic, while the Haytien Government maintained an attitude of observation with only a few prudent frontier troops stationed near the border.

Los insurrectos manifestaron que, de no poder preservar la independencia, preferirían la unión con la República de Haití, en tanto que el gobierno haitiano guardaba una postura de observación destacando únicamente escasas y prudentes tropas de frontera en las inmediaciones del límite limítrofe.

records.headline: The republic was virtually dead, and the island was openly presented
records.summary_en: According to a January 13 dispatch reported by *The New York Herald* correspondent in San Domingo, the Dominican Republic was virtually dead and openly presented to the world as a Spanish province ruled by General Santana as the commissioned Captain-General for Queen Isabella. Spain promised numerous reforms as part of its policy of absorption—including declaring Samana a free port, inviting universal emigration, reducing tariffs on foreign-imported goods, proclaiming full religious toleration, and abolishing slavery—while it was also thought Queen Isabella would invite President Lincoln to send surplus negroes and contrabands to San Domingo. Additionally, the city's streets were enlivened with foreign carriages, buggies, drays, and new toilets, and the new United States Consul had not held any official intercourse with the government.
records.summary_es: Según un despacho del 13 de enero remitido por el corresponsal de *The New York Herald* en Santo Domingo, la República Dominicana había prácticamente dejado de existir, mostrándose abiertamente al mundo como provincia española gobernada por el general Santana como capitán general comisionado de la reina Isabel. España prometía múltiples reformas como parte de su política de absorción —incluida la declaración de Samaná como puerto libre, la invitación a la inmigración general, la rebaja de aranceles a las importaciones foráneas, la proclamación de una entera libertad de cultos y la abolición formal de la esclavitud—, al tiempo que se suponía que la reina Isabel cursaría una invitación al presidente Lincoln para asentar en Santo Domingo a los libertos negros rescatados de la Confederación («contrabands»). Asimismo, las calles de la capital se veían animadas con carruajes, calesas y carretas foráneas y novedades en el vestir, mientras que el nuevo cónsul de los Estados Unidos se abstenía de mantener trato oficial alguno con las autoridades.

records.summary_en: According to the *New York Herald* on February 25, 1862, Spanish forces in the Dominican Republic maintained social distance from natives while leasing land, driving up rents and creating a strong market for duty-free wooden houses from Baltimore and ship bread. The newspaper also reported that local copper ore contained gold, Samana coal beds showed promise for miners, and suggestions were made to relocate four million American "contrabands" to the island to develop its wealth. El diario también señaló que el mineral de cobre local contenía oro, que los yacimientos de carbón de Samaná resultaban prometedores para los mineros y que se sugería asentar en la isla a cuatro millones de «contrabands» (libertos) estadounidenses para explotar sus riquezas. Por otra parte, correspondencia desde Trujillo, Honduras, con fecha del 5 de febrero, dio cuenta de que una reciente revolución culminó con el asesinato del presidente Guardiola tras una conspiración autorizada por el coronel Agurcia.

records.full_text: Our correspondent in St. Domingo City writes, under date of the 31st of January, that the Spaniards still held apart from intimate social intercourse with the native Dominicans. They had rented or leased lots of land on which to erect aristocratic mansions for their families. House rents had advanced considerably. In the meantime wooden houses, ready fitted for construction, found a good market—a lot just landed, from Baltimore, commanding profitable prices. A government decree admits such material free of duty. Ship bread is also ordered for free entry into the ports. Copper ore taken from mines near St. Domingo City was found to be strongly impregnated with gold. The coal beds of Samana promised a rich return to experienced miners. Napoleon had not yet appointed a French Consul in the city, or committed himself in any recognition of the new rule of Spain. The American “contrabands” left on Mr. Lincoln’s hands after the war can be taken, it is said, to the extent of four millions, on the island. They would be set to work, and really develope the wealth of the country. There was no American vessel in port.

records.headline: A correspondent writing from St. Domingo City
records.summary_en: A correspondent writing from St. Domingo City on May 17 reports that Spain is making its mark under the new rule, silencing the remaining malcontents and welcoming foreign capital and labour. A railroad from Santiago to Angelina on the Yuna has been decided upon, giving the Vega Real valley an outlet to the Bay of Samana, an American company has proposed navigating the Yuna, and a new tariff cutting duties from thirty to twenty per cent is expected to take effect in July.
records.summary_es: Un corresponsal que escribe desde la ciudad de Santo Domingo el 17 de mayo informa que España está dejando su huella bajo el nuevo régimen, silenciando a los descontentos que quedan y dando la bienvenida al capital y la mano de obra extranjeros. Se ha decidido construir un ferrocarril de Santiago a Angelina, sobre el Yuna, que dará salida al valle de la Vega Real hacia la bahía de Samaná, una compañía americana ha propuesto navegar el Yuna, y se espera que en julio entre en vigor un nuevo arancel que reduce los derechos del treinta al veinte por ciento.

records.summary_en: According to the *New-York daily tribune*, the Dominican Republic was unexpectedly annexed to Spain on March 12, 1861, through the treason of President Santana without consulting the public, and the annexation was formally accepted by the Queen of Spain on May 20, 1861. While resident Spaniards and their descendants favored the change, citizens of African or mixed descent opposed it and desired to retain a republican form of government. Cuban papers report that the national party subsequently made an attempt to regain their independence.
records.summary_es: Según el *New-York daily tribune*, la República Dominicana fue anexionada inesperadamente a España el 12 de marzo de 1861 debido a la traición del presidente Santana sin consultar a la ciudadanía, y dicha anexión fue aceptada formalmente por la reina de España el 20 de mayo de 1861. Aunque los españoles residentes y sus descendientes favorecieron el cambio, los ciudadanos de ascendencia africana o mestiza se opusieron y desearon conservar la forma de gobierno republicana. Los diarios cubanos señalan que el partido nacionalista intentó posteriormente recuperar la independencia.

Recent reports indicated that Spanish troops suffered heavy losses, including a division of 2,000 men that was forced to capitulate after Santiago was burned, while another division of 1,600 men was repulsed. Additionally, the town of San Carlos near Santo Domingo city was reportedly burned by the rebels.

records.summary_en: According to the *Chicago Daily Tribune* of October 10, 1863, the Dominican people are fiercely rebelling against Spanish rule following President Santana's annexation of the country to Spain. The newspaper reports that Spanish forces have suffered significant defeats—including a routed division of 3,000 men with over 1,000 casualties and the capitulation and retreat from Santiago—amid a conflict marked by mutual atrocities and the burning of towns such as San Carlos. Additionally, while the Dominicans reportedly receive sympathy and support from neighboring islands and the Unitedest States, the article questions their capacity for self-government due to past deficiencies in vigor and cohesion.
records.summary_es: Según el *Chicago Daily Tribune* del 10 de octubre de 1863, el pueblo dominicano se subleva con ferocidad contra el dominio español tras la anexión del país a España efectuada por el presidente Santana. El periódico consigna que las tropas españolas han sufrido considerables reveses —entre ellos una división dispersada de 3.000 hombres con más de 1.000 bajas, así como la capitulación y evacuación de Santiago— en el curso de una contienda signada por atrocidades recíprocas y el incendio de poblaciones como San Carlos. Además, si bien se señala que los dominicanos reciben la simpatía y el respaldo de islas vecinas y de los Estados Unidos, el artículo pone en duda su capacidad de autogobierno debido a su pasada falta de vigor y cohesión.

records.summary_en: According to *The Lancaster gazette* on November 5, 1863, fighting and fires in the Dominican Republic resulted in the destruction of the Government House, the Roman Catholic Church, and the American and British Consuls' residences, the latter of whom arrived at Grand Turk. Reports indicated that the entire south side of the island was in actual rebellion with 40,000 Dominicans in the neighborhood, and that Spanish soldiers pillaged the town before 600 Spaniards sortied from the fort and drove the Dominicans away with the aid of the fort's guns. The resulting fires destroyed numerous stores and properties belonging to foreign merchants, with losses in Santiago and Port-au-Platte expected to reach several millions of dollars.
records.summary_es: Según *The Lancaster Gazette* del 5 de noviembre de 1863, los combates e incendios en la República Dominicana ocasionaron la destrucción de la Casa de Gobierno, la iglesia católica y las residencias de los cónsules británico y estadounidense, habiendo llegado este último a Gran Turca. Los informes indicaban que toda la vertiente sur del territorio se hallaba en rebelión abierta con unos 40.000 dominicanos en las proximidades, y que la soldadesca española saqueó la población antes de que 600 peninsulares salieran de la fortaleza y rechazaran a los dominicanos con el auxilio de los cañones del fuerte. Los incendios resultantes destruyeron numerosos comercios y propiedades de comerciantes extranjeros, previéndose pérdidas millonarias en Santiago y Puerto Plata.

What, then, can be the cause of the wonderful change which has come over St. Domingo? records.summary_en: The *Wilmington Journal* reported that Dominicans took up arms against Spanish troops in San Domingo, claiming that President Pedro Santana's invitation of the Spaniards was an unauthorized and treacherous surrender of their rights. An issued manifesto from Santiago declared the country's independence, denounced Santana's power to deliver the country to Spain, and appealed against the injustices and oppression of Spanish representatives. Additionally, the newspaper reported that General Trim, the Spanish commander, sought permission from Hayti to cross 6,000 troops over its territory to act against the Dominicans, but was refused.

Un manifiesto promulgado en Santiago proclamó la independencia patria, negó a Santana toda facultad para entregar el país a España y clamó contra los desafueros y la opresión de las autoridades peninsulares. Asimismo, el rotativo refirió que el general Prim [Trim en el texto], comandante español, solicitó autorización a Haití para cruzar con 6.000 soldados por su territorio a fin de combatir a los dominicanos, petición que le fue denegada.

records.summary_en: Based on the provided excerpt, Spanish forces attempting to capture St. Christabal were harassed by Dominican guerrillas and driven back in confusion at the river Jaina with a loss of 200 casualties. The Dominicans also captured supplies, rifles, ammunition, a field piece, and a cannon at Santa Anna's supply depot, and defeated the Spaniards in a battle at Purata Plata on December 20th. Consequently, the Spaniards are reportedly confined only to the ground they stand upon, prompting a resume in *The Standard* to suggest that Spain should withdraw from the contest.
records.summary_es: A juzgar por el extracto, tropas españolas que intentaban tomar San Cristóbal fueron hostigadas por guerrilleros dominicanos y rechazadas en desbandada en el río Haina con un saldo de 200 bajas. Asimismo, los dominicanos se apoderaron de provisiones, fusiles, municiones, una pieza de campaña y un cañón en el parque de suministros de Santana, y vencieron a los españoles en un combate librado en Puerto Plata el 20 de diciembre. En consecuencia, se afirmaba que los peninsulares apenas dominaban el suelo que pisaban, lo que motivó a un balance en *The Standard* a insinuar que España debía retirarse de la contienda.
