records.summary_en: According to the newspaper, a leader deceived the Dominican people by inviting in Spanish forces under the guise of assistance and instruction, subsequently collecting their arms, declaring the Republic extinct, and proclaiming the Queen of Spain as ruler. After being oppressed by Spanish officials and failing twice in armed resistance, the Dominicans achieved victory on their third attempt, restoring their free constitution while retreating Spanish forces burned towns in vengeance. The report notes that the Spanish navy subsequently maintained a strict blockade of most of the seaboard with six thousand Spanish soldiers.
records.summary_es: Según el periódico, un caudillo engañó al pueblo dominicano llamando a las fuerzas españolas con el pretexto de ayuda e instrucción militar, para luego confiscarles el armamento, declarar extinguida la República y proclamar soberana a la reina de España. Tras padecer la opresión de los funcionarios coloniales y sucumbir en dos tentativas armadas, los dominicanos alcanzaron la victoria en su tercer alzamiento, restableciendo su constitución libre mientras las tropas españolas en retirada quemaban poblados por venganza. El informe agrega que la escuadra española impuso subsiguientemente un riguroso bloqueo sobre la mayor parte del litoral apoyada por seis mil soldados peninsulares.

records.full_text:
ENGLAND’S RECOGNITION OF THE DOMINICANS.
[From the Madrid Epoca, Dec. 18.]
In consequence of the effect produced upon the public mind by this announcement, Sir John Crampton, the English Ambassador at this Court, felt bound to request explanations from his government upon a matter in which he was without official instructions. Earl Russell lost no time in replying, and his despatch reached the English representatives yesterday evening, at the same time that the First Secretary of State received the despatches from our Minister Plenipotentiary in London, previously announced by telegraph to the Spanish Cabinet. These despatches contained ample details of all that had occurred. On account of certain questions arising from events that have taken place in consequence of the blockade of the Dominican coasts by the Spanish squadron, the English government considered it necessary to take the opinion of the legal advisers of the crown, following its practice in all matters of this kind. Their opinion was favorable in a certain manner to the recognition of the Dominicans as belligerents—Spain being bound, according to their view, by the maritime law laid down in the treaty of Paris, to maintain a real and effective blockade of all the points of the island where she undertook to prevent the entry of supplies destined for the rebels. Earl Russell communicated this opinion to our representative in London, who in his turn considered it urgently necessary to acquaint the Spanish government with the same. Hence the origin of a news which, having come to the knowledge of the telegraphic agents of various periodicals in this city, was transmitted by them with the urgency which its importance dictated, although the want of the details above mentioned caused some exaggeration in their communications. The reply of Earl Russell to the English Ambassador could not be expressed in more satisfactory terms. The English Minister confirmed the explanations given by Senor Comyn, and, wishing to afford a proof of the friendly attitude of England in questions so greatly affecting the prestige of our country, he authorized the English Ambassador to acquaint the Spanish Cabinet with his determination to indefinitely postpone any act which might be considered hostile, or as tending to exercise any sort of influence in the settlement of our internal affairs. We, who cannot be accused of being ardent admirers of the English policy, have satisfaction in declaring that its conduct in the present circumstances has been worthy of a great Power, and therefore merits our most sincere eulogies.

records.summary_en: According to *The New York Herald* on April 30, 1865, European monarchies were described as quaking with fear over the growing strength of the United States and its potential impact on Spanish possessions like Cuba and Porto Rico. The article specifically cited a fearful argument presented by the "Conqueror of Africa," which claimed the United States planned to send thousands of freed colored people to St. Domingo to form a negro nationality and army to ultimately attack and destroy Cuba. The newspaper dismissed this theory as a "raving of an imagination entirely possessed by fear," asserting that no dilatory measures would be needed if the United States truly intended to conquer European possessions.

Gándara and the Dominicans had not agreed on a final evacuation treaty. The Dominican government rejected a drafted treaty because Gándara's preferred language made the agreement appear to be a Spanish concession rather than a surrender, and Gándara subsequently refused to receive new commissioners unless they confirmed the objectionable treaty. records.chapter_es: La lucha por la anexión estadounidense
records.full_text:
The Revolution in Hayti—President Jeffrard preparing to Escape—Suffering among the Negroes on the Island of Jamaica—An outbreak Feared—San Domingo Affairs.

NEW YORK, Sept. 1.—The Herald's Kingston, Jamaica, correspondent says, that the headway which the revolutionists are making in Hayti, has been deemed by President Jeffrard sufficiently alarming to induce him to make preparations for escape from his country. A mail steamer has therefore been chartered at Kingston to proceed to Port au Prince and there remain till the time arrives for him to seek safety in flight or till the danger of such an event has passed.

Owing to the severe drought of the present summer in the Island of Jamaica, the heavy taxes and other causes, the negro laborers there have been reduced to the most abject poverty and great suffering, and thousands of them are on the verge of starvation. They blame the governor and his officers as the cause of their afflictions, and so strong and bitter is their feeling against the local government that an outbreak on their part is feared in the western part of the Island, in consequence of which two gunboats have been dispatched to that locality.

The Herald's Santiago correspondent says, notwithstanding the havoc and destruction of the Spaniards during their invasion of San Domingo, the crops are now coming forward which promise ample subsistence for the inhabitants, and that the sacrifices which the war has compelled the people to endure have made them more united and determined to maintain their independence. The latter statement is hardly borne out by reports which we have already published of threatened hostilities between two native chiefs, Gen'ls Penisutal and Cotral. It is said that the Spaniards stole and destroyed large quantities of fine wools, principally the property of American merchants, which had been stored at different places, and now Gen. Gandana, the Spanish commander, having withdrawn his troops from the interior, has blockaded the principal forts of the Republic because the Dominican Government will not submit to his haughty and unreasonable demands in the peace treaty, thus preventing the exportation of large stocks of tobacco belonging to Americans as well as Europeans. To offset this blockade the Dominicans have determined to commission privateers to prey on Spanish commerce and an agent authorized to issue letters of marque has already left for the United States and Europe.

records.headline: News from St. Domingo
records.summary_en: News from St. Domingo to September 9 describes Dominicans celebrating the second anniversary of their liberation from Spain, after eighteen months of fighting forced Spain to evacuate the island. General Pimentel, elected provisional president in March, became unpopular for harsh and unlawful acts, and after citizens in the capital repudiated him he resigned, while General J. M. Cabral was commissioned as Protector of the republic to summon a National Convention.

El general Pimentel, elegido presidente provisional en marzo, se volvió impopular por actos duros e ilegales, y después de que los ciudadanos de la capital lo repudiaron, renunció, mientras el general J. M. Cabral fue nombrado Protector de la república para convocar una Convención Nacional.

records.summary_en: The *Daily National Intelligencer* reported on November 13, 1865, that Don Pedro Valverde, a member of the "Yankee party," supports opening Dominican gold mines, mahogany forests, and pearl fisheries to immigrants under a liberal colonization law, and proposes establishing free and neutral ports jointly with President Geffrard of Hayti. In contrast, the newspaper noted that General Cabral has intimate relations with European consuls while the United States is unrepresented, and suggested that Cabral might pursue a close union with Hayti that could threaten the white race in the eastern part of the island. Additionally, the article stated that if Valverde is elected, the Dominican Republic would respond to Spanish demands for the repayment of conquest costs with a counter-demand.
records.summary_es: El *Daily National Intelligencer* dio cuenta el 13 de noviembre de 1865 de que don Pedro Valverde, miembro del «partido pro-yanqui», promovía abrir las minas auríferas dominicanas, los bosques de caoba y los placeres de perlas a colonos extranjeros al amparo de una liberal ley de inmigración, proponiendo asimismo la habilitación de puertos francos y neutrales en concierto con el presidente Geffrard de Haití. Por el contrario, el rotativo señalaba que el general Cabral cultivaba estrechos nexos con los cónsules europeos mientras los Estados Unidos carecían de legación oficial, insinuando que Cabral podría propiciar una federación estrecha con Haití susceptible de comprometer a la población blanca de la parte oriental. El reporte concluía que, de resultar elegido Valverde, la República Dominicana ripostaría a las exigencias españolas de indemnización bélica con una enérgica contrademanda.

records.summary_en: An armed man abruptly entered a session of the Dominican Congress to announce the impending arrival of revolutionary forces and proclaim General Baez as president, causing the ministers to flee in terror. Following this confusion, General Pedro Guillermo was appointed dictator until Baez could arrive, and an election on December 14th unanimously named Buenaventura Baez President of the Dominican Republic. Meanwhile, Cabral accepted a military position under the new government, which Guillermo practically headed.
records.summary_es: Un individuo armado irrumpió súbitamente en una sesión del Congreso dominicano para anunciar la inminente llegada de huestes revolucionarias y proclamar presidente al general Báez, haciendo que los ministros huyeran despavoridos. En medio del desconcierto subsiguiente, el general Pedro Guillermo fue investido como mandatario provisorio hasta la llegada de Báez, y en los comicios del 14 de diciembre se proclamó unánimemente a Buenaventura Báez presidente de la República Dominicana. Entretanto, Cabral aceptó un cargo militar bajo el nuevo régimen, que de facto encabezaba Guillermo.

records.summary_en: An armed man carrying a cutlass interrupted a session of the Supreme Congress to announce the arrival of General Baez and demand peace from General Cabral. In the ensuing confusion, ministers sought refuge with foreign consuls, while Cabral stated he would consent to Baez's rule if demanded by the public. Ultimately, General Pedro Guillermo was appointed dictator until an election on December 14 by the Constitutional Assembly unanimously appointed Buenaventura Baez President of the Dominican Republic, with Cabral accepting a military position under Guillermo's government.
records.summary_es: Un sujeto armado con machete interrumpió una sesión del Congreso Supremo anunciando la llegada del general Báez y exigiendo la sumisión pacífica al general Cabral. En el tumulto consecuente, los ministros buscaron asilo ante los cónsules foráneos, mientras Cabral manifestó que acataría la jefatura de Báez si el pueblo así lo reclamaba. Finalmente, el general Pedro Guillermo asumió el mando dictatorial transitorio hasta que una asamblea constitucional, el 14 de diciembre, eligió por unanimidad a Buenaventura Báez presidente de la República Dominicana, aceptando Cabral un cargo militar subordinado a Guillermo.

records.summary_en: A mysterious armed man suddenly entered a congressional session and declared himself an emissary of General Baez, causing the ministers to flee in terror while General Cabral agreed to the popular will. The intruder was revealed to be General Pedro Guillermo, who had himself appointed dictator until an election on December 14 unanimously made Baez President of the Dominican Republic. Consequently, Cabral accepted a military position under the new government, of which Guillermo became the practical head.
records.summary_es: Un enigmático hombre armado irrumpió sorpresivamente en el recinto del Congreso proclamándose emisario del general Báez, lo que provocó la huida aterrorizada del gabinete ministerial mientras el general Cabral se plegaba a la voluntad popular. El intruso resultó ser el general Pedro Guillermo, quien se hizo ungir dictador provisional hasta que en las votaciones del 14 de diciembre se designó por unanimidad a Báez presidente de la República Dominicana. A consecuencia de ello, Cabral aceptó una comandancia militar en la nueva administración, cuyo timón efectivo retenía Guillermo.

records.summary_en: According to *The Evening Telegraph* of January 30, 1866, Mr. Baez attained the presidency through a coup d'état aided by General Cabral's relinquishment of power and Pedro Guillermo's armed force. The article reports that the majority of the nation opposes Baez's administration due to his service as a Spanish Field Marshal during the independence struggle, and notes that his regime is currently jailing and persecuting suspected opponents of a thwarted uprising at Puerto Plata.

records.summary_en: The *New York Herald* reported on February 5, 1866, that Secretary Seward stated the United States would receive a minister from the Dominican Republic and conduct negotiations in accordance with the law of nations and friendly relations. The newspaper noted that the U.S. government had recognized the independence of Dominica and that the President nominated General Cazenau, who was engaged as a merchant there, as Minister to that republic. Additionally, the excerpt briefly reported on a fire that broke out in a closet of a building on Chatham Street between 12 and 1 o'clock on Sunday morning.
records.summary_es: *The New York Herald* publicó el 5 de febrero de 1866 que el secretario Seward declaró que los Estados Unidos recibirían a un ministro de la República Dominicana y entablarían negociaciones con arreglo al derecho de gentes y a las relaciones amistosas entre naciones. El diario consignó que el gobierno de Washington reconoció la independencia de Santo Domingo y que el presidente propuso al general Cazneau, quien residía allí como comerciante, como ministro plenipotenciario ante esa república. Asimismo, el texto hizo una breve mención sobre un siniestro ocurrido en el armario de una edificación de Chatham Street entre las doce y la una de la madrugada del domingo.

records.summary_en: In an exchange printed by the paper, a Dominican speaker pleads for recognition by the United States, calling the enjoyment of American favor essential to Dominica's stability and peace and hoping that the proclamation of general liberty in the United States had removed the obstacles to recognition. Secretary Seward replies by recounting how the United States established itself as a republic on the principle of the equality of men while African slavery still existed under state laws.

El secretario Seward responde relatando cómo Estados Unidos se estableció como república sobre el principio de la igualdad de los hombres mientras la esclavitud africana aún existía bajo las leyes estatales.

records.summary_en: Based on the provided excerpt, President Baez provided a concise view of the contest and struggle on the island of St. Domingo, while Secretary Seward outlined U.S. progress following the rebellion that crushed the pro-slavery power. Seward explained that the abolition of slavery removed barriers to recognizing Liberia and Hayti and enabled the United States to extend fellowship to the republic of Dominica, which had been fighting monarchical influences.

records.summary_en: According to the *New-York Tribune* on October 4, 1867, the peoples of Hayti and the Dominican Republic recognized that union was necessary to maintain their independence and prosperity, following past experience and Spanish intervention. A treaty—awaiting only the ratification of the Dominican Congress—had its preliminaries signed six days after the arrival of six delegates sent by President Balnave, amidst great enthusiasm from the government and people. The treaty's articles provided for the suppression of frontier brigandage and the extradition of political refugees, a commitment by both parties to preserve the inviolability of their respective territories (ruling out any United States purchase of the Bay of Samaná), and the settlement of claims arising from injuries sustained during the 1844 separation.
records.summary_es: Según el *New-York Tribune* del 4 de octubre de 1867, los pueblos de Haití y de la República Dominicana reconocieron la imperiosa necesidad de la unión para preservar su independencia y prosperidad tras las lecciones del pasado y la intervención española. Se firmaron las bases de un tratado —pendiente solo de la ratificación del Congreso dominicano— a los seis días del arribo de seis delegados comisionados por el presidente Salnave, en medio del fervor popular y oficial. Los artículos del convenio pactaban la represión del bandolerismo fronterizo y la extradición de asilados políticos, el solemne compromiso de ambas partes de salvaguardar la inviolabilidad de sus territorios respectivos (descartando cualquier adquisición estadounidense de la bahía de Samaná) y la indemnización de reclamaciones por perjuicios sufridos durante la separación de 1844.

records.headline: Among its articles is one providing for the suppression of brigandage
records.summary_en: A newly signed treaty between Haiti and St. Domingo includes articles providing for the suppression of frontier brigandage, the extradition of political refugees, the preservation of territorial integrity, and the settlement of claims dating from the 1844 separation. Because the treaty pledges that no portion of either territory will be alienated, the newspaper notes there is no longer any hope of the United States acquiring the bay of Samana by purchase. The agreement, initiated by Salnave's government and welcomed by the Dominican people, aims to heal 23 years of strife and is already benefiting the region through peace and resource development.
records.summary_es: Un reciente tratado suscrito entre Haití y Santo Domingo comprende estipulaciones tendientes a la represión de correrías y bandoleros fronterizos, la extradición de reos políticos, la preservación de la integridad territorial y el arreglo de reclamaciones pendientes desde la separación de 1844. Dado que el convenio consagra que ninguna fracción de ambos territorios podrá ser enajenada, el periódico hace notar que se desvanecen las aspiraciones de los Estados Unidos de adquirir por compra la bahía de Samaná. El acuerdo, promovido por la administración de Salnave y recibido con beneplácito por el pueblo dominicano, procura restañar veintitrés años de querellas y rinde ya provechosos frutos de paz y desarrollo en la región.

records.full_text: Another article of the treaty pledges the contracting parties to preserve inviolate the integrity of their respective territories. No portion of either Hayti or St. Domingo is on any account to be alienated. This being so, there is now no hope of the United States becoming the owner by purchase of the bay of Sanana. Cabral was, we are aware, willing to part with it, but the Dominicans would not allow him to do so; and so long as the treaty between the two republics remains in force it is clearly impossible that our government can acquire a foot of land in any part of the island, for it provides that both republics shall unite to repel any attempt on the part of any foreign Power to take possession of a single foot of territory in any part of the island. And the Dominicans and Haytiens, however bitterly they may hate each other, will readily unite to prevent a foreign Power from obtaining a lodgement on the soil of St. Domingo.

St. Domingo.

General Cabral, at all events, has ordered the Minister lately sent to Port au Prince to exchange the ratifications of the treaty to suspend all relations with Salnave's government, and leave the Haytien territory without delay. For this purpose he despatched a schooner to Jacmel with the necessary instructions to the Minister.

The Dominican government is actively raising troops, not only in the capital, but in Seybo, Azua, Bani and the northern provinces, the common belief of the Dominicans being that Salnave is on the eve of his downfall.

HAVANA, Nov. 17—We have the announcement that St. Domingo City has been destroyed, probably by an earthquake. I have telegraphed for details, which I shall forward at once.

The news of the insurrection in Hayti is confirmed. On the 12th of October the scene in the legislative chambers was very violent, and the language used was of the most threatening character. It all arose from a motion made to relieve Montes, who is in a Cape Haytien dungeon. The members all spoke in his defence. It is said Prince Salnave became so audacious as to secretly incite a rabble of women and boys to attack the House of Assembly. This they did with loud vivas for Salnave and cries of “Down with the Assembly,” hurling at the same time bricks, bottles, sticks, &c. The dwellings of many were vigorously stoned. The American consul was fired at, but escaped unhurt. A unanimous protest of the diplomatic corps has been presented against any further repetition of such scenes, and demanding of the government to see to it that the like does not again occur. At last accounts the city of Port au Prince was quieting. The treaty with the United States is as yet in suspense.

Additionally, a dispatch from Havana stated that the treaty with St. Domingo had been annulled, the Haytian Minister had returned, revolutionary movements were rife with Dominican forces on the Haytian frontier, and an intended issue of $600,000 in bonds was unpopular.

ST. DOMINGO.

SPECIAL TELEGRAM TO THE HERALD.

Terrific Hurricane—Destruction of Property on Land and Afloat.

HAVANA, Nov. 18, 1867.

A terrible hurricane blew over the island on the 30th of October. It desolated the capital and destroyed two hundred lives. The hurricane lasted four hours and destroyed nearly all the shipping in harbor. No American vessels are reported. Comercio street, St. Domingo city, is in ruins. There was no news from the interior.

records.summary_en: The *New-York Tribune* reported on an extraordinary audience where the French Charge d'Affairs presented President Salnave with a friendly letter from Emperor Napoleon regarding a previous assassination attempt, which was met with Salnave's expressions of sympathy for France. The newspaper also noted that President Salnave received an autograph letter from Peruvian President Col. Prado assuring amicable relations, and reported that the Cacos Insurrection had been entirely suppressed, leaving the country quiet.

El diario añadió que Salnave recibió una carta autógrafa del presidente de Perú, el coronel Prado, asegurando fraternales relaciones, y consignó la extinción total de la insurrección de los cacos, recobrando el país entera calma.

LATE FROM HAYTI.

The Dominican Government had recalled its Minister to Hayti, in consequence of an insurrectionary outbreak in the district of Cibao, in Santo Domingo, wnich the Dominican authorities believed had been instigated by the Haytians. The Haytian Government, in delivering his passports to the Minister, Gen. Valvende, had addressed a note to him, assuring him of the sincere desire of the Haytians for peace, and that whatever aid had been given the Dominican insurgents had been given by the Haytian rebels. Gen. Cabral, however, had notified the Haytian Government that relations between the two countries were suspended, and President Salnave had issued a proclamation reciting the facts of the dispute, and declaring that if the Dominicans made war, the Haytians were ready.

From St. Domingo.

HAVANA, Dec. 6.—Evening.—Señor Pujol is not at all reserved as to the commission which he bears. It is to close negotiations in relation to Samana. He will leave here to-morrow by the steamer Morro Castle for New York.

General Cabral's position is thought to be desperate, through the influence of the clergy, and the fact that the Dominican troops have not been paid. Baez will probably be President within a few weeks.

records.summary_en: News from San Domingo reports that Señor Pujol will leave for New York by the steamer Moro Castle to close negotiations in relation to Samaná, and that part of President Cabral's cabinet has resigned, with Valverde, Curiel and Perdomo appointed to fill the vacancies. FROM HAVANA.

Late from St. Domingo—Baez Probably President.

HAVANA, Dec. 6.—Evening.—Senor Pujol is not at all reserved as to the commission which he bears. It is to close negotiations in relation to Samana. He will leave here to-morrow by the steamer Moro Castle for New York.

Gen. Cabral's position is thought to be desperate through the influence of the clergy and the fact that the Dominican troops have not been paid. Baez will probably be President within a few weeks.

SANTO DOMINGO.

SPECIAL TELEGRAM TO THE HERALD.

Baezist Policy—Samana to be a Free Port—An Alliance with Hayti.

HAVANA, April 27, 1868.

The steamer Pajaro del Oceano, Captain Ochoa, has arrived here with advices from St. Domingo to the 20th inst.

Although General Baez had taken the usual oath as President of the republic, Congress was endeavoring so to amend the Constitution during its present session as to confirm the leading points of General Baez' policy. These were the following:— To make Samaná a free port of entry and a general foreign mail station. To arrange the mail and trade service at Samaná so that it should form a neutral station and become the centre of the Caribbean telegraphic cable service.

A brother of General Baez and General Caminero had gone to Hayti to negotiate for a permanent alliance between both republics. According to the proposed terms of the new alliance all disputed territory shall contribute *provisionally* a line of division. But such neutral provinces shall be bound to complete the geological and mineralogical survey of their respective limits. The general survey of the respective republics thus completed shall specify the situation and value of the gold and silver mines and of the debts secured by guaranties of such mines.

The general banker, Jesurun, and Colonel Fabens have been charged with the negotiation of a loan to be secured by the revenues from customs of the Dominican republic.

ST. DOMINGO.

Carlos and Valentin Baez have lately been in Hayti on a confidential mission, offering, it is said, a treaty of great and self-evident advantages to both republics. It proposes to establish a liberal and uniform tariff, place all the frontier ports under a common system of regulations, and open a free and unreserved transit of merchandise from one to the other.

This would open a large and valuable trade across the frontier to both parties, and do away with the ruinous smuggling that has heretofore enriched a few border chiefs at the expense of both treasuries.

ST. DOMINGO.

The Reactionary Forces at Work Against Baez—His Brother Held by the Haytien Cacos—Interesting Review of the Situation—Dominican Speculators on Their Way to the United States.

ST. DOMINGO, May 20, 1868.

Several Dominican generals recently made the island of St. Thomas a rendezvous. Among them were Cabral, Luperon, Embert, Adon, Pina, Ricardo, Fernandez and Pimentel. They concerted a plan of operations against Baez. The result was that ex-President Cabral sailed for Jacmel May 15 on board the English steamer. He is to take command of the revolutionists along the southern frontier—in San Juan, Neyba, Las Matas, Cercado, Barahona, &c. The chieftains Timoteo and Andres Ogando, Sico Moreno, Damian Castillo and Mariano Rodriguez sent a young man named Abelard Dubreuil through Haytien territory to meet General Cabral. Baez and his partisans, as well as Cazneau, represent that this movement in the south is in favor of President Salnave. This is like what such would report to carry out their own schemes.

General Luperon went to Turks Island so as to operate against the north of this republic—the provinces of Cibao—whither the people call him as their leader. He will there meet Generals Polanco, Alvarez and many others who await his arrival to pronounce against General Baez.

General Pimentel is to go from Curaçao in company with General Castillo, Linares, Valverde and others to operate against Seybo and St. Domingo provinces, in which neighborhood they are to meet the brave General Manzueta, whom Baez has been unable to put down, either with threats or promises or by the imprisonment of his family. He kept in the vicinity of Llamasá, a district in St. Domingo province, and never ceased fighting the Baezists.

General Baez does not know how to get his government into working order, as the employes resign almost immediately after appointment. They all regard Baez's government as illegal and transitory, and no one is willing to compromise himself therewith. This is the reason why Señor F. M. Delmonte has not accepted the portfolio that Baez has tendered him, although he has been urged and besought to accept it.

By letters from St. Thomas we have learned that the Cacos hold Carlos Baez a prisoner. He was on his way to Salnave's government for the purpose of selling that portion of Dominican territory bounded on the south by the Rio Yaqui. This sale was the condition by which Baez agreed with Salnave's Minister, Delorme, for the aid which the latter would give in overthrowing Cabral. The western portion of the island, the Haytien side, has no savannas nor pasture lands to raise cattle. From the Rio Pedernales, whence the dividing line goes, according to the Aranjuez treaty of 1777, to the Rio Yaqui there are magnificent bays, which the Haytiens have always coveted without ever having taken the measures to secure so valuable a portion of our island. To fulfil this part of his engagements Baez has had to mutilate our constitution by dropping the article which points out the limits of the republic as well as the clause which creates the office of Vice President. Baez wants absolute power, and as the constitution of 1865 is very liberal and controlled the President's action while it abolished the death penalty in political cases, he has substituted the constitution of 1854, which makes him master and lord over the Dominicans and imposes capital punishment for political offences. This same substitution he attempted in 1865, when he came to power, but before he could carry it out he was overthrown and had to take refuge in the French Consulate.

Baez has also presented to Congress a bill of his expenses during the revolution that has just brought him to power, but out of decorum they have not made public the amount. The following is the only allusion to it made in the reply of Congress to the President's message:—"As to the detailed accounts of the revolutionary outlays which have been presented by the worthy General Buenaventura Baez, they are entirely approved, as well as the agreement entered into with Señores J. A. Jesurun & Zoons of the neighboring island of Curaçao, which amounts to $37,145 80, which is approved in all its tenor and conditions."

So many documents and mortgages will be secured by Baez in the names of Jesurun, Fabens and Cazneau that, even if the peninsula of Samana were sold for ten times its value, the proceeds could not liquidate all the claims that he will have on the treasury of the republic. In connection with this trio of speculators it is very positively asserted here that Jesurun and Fabens are authorized by Baez to raise a loan of $200,000 in the United States, on account of Samana. This money is needed to improve Baez's situation, at least until such time as the bay and peninsula of Samana can be disposed of for good. I do not think these rumors can be well founded, as Jesurun and Fabens left here on April 20 and Baez was inaugurated only on May 2. The Boletin Oficial of that date attacked such a project, and brought severe charges against ex-President Cabral for having sought to alienate Samana. What is certain, however, is, that whatever engagements those gentlemen make in the United States are null and of no validity, as they are not authorized by government legally constituted. Baez has been proclaimed by a faction who overthrew Cabral without electing Baez in a constitutional manner through popular suffrage, as the constitution then in force required. The latter has seated himself in the Presidential chair in spite of the will of the majority, and has imprisoned, exiled and persecuted the most distinguished citizens of the republic.

ST. DOMINGO.

Precarious State of the New Government—The Reaction Organized—Expected Invasion from Venezuela—Health of the Island, &c.

ST. THOMAS, July 14, 1868.

The news from St. Domingo confirms the impression that the government of General Baez is by no means secure. While it is ostensibly master of the country, there is an under-current of deep dissatisfaction, which must soon burst forth into open rebellion.

The leaders of the movement in the south are anxiously waiting to see the north and east take up arms. A simultaneous movement in all sections was the plan agreed upon at St. Thomas, so that the strongest force could be directed against Azua and thence on to St. Domingo City.

General Cabral was expected to land on the southern coast with a well-equipped expedition from Venezuela. Should he succeed in effecting a landing, there is little doubt that the whole south would rally to his support. The health of the island, however, is good.

THE NEWS.

EUROPEAN.

The steamship City of Baltimore, from Liverpool via Queenstown, arrived at this port yesterday.

The public mind in England was very much occupied with the approaching general election.

Accounts from the manufacturing districts of England and Scotland were unfavorable.

The London money market was easy and the stock market steady.

DOMESTIC.

The steamship Morro Castle, from Havana, brings later advices from Hayti and St. Domingo.

Salnave was still holding Port-au-Prince, which was being besieged by the revolutionary forces.

Salnave is directing the defence in person. He has received the American Minister with every mark of kindness. Baez was offering the bay and peninsula of Samana as security for a loan of $1,000,000 from the United States.

EXPECTED ATTACK ON PORT-AU-PRINCE.

ADVVICES FROM HAYTI.

Salnave Still Defending the Capital—The American Minister—The Cacos Approaching.

Advices from Port-au-Prince to the 10th ult. report that the revolutionary forces under Salnave's opponents were closing around the city.

The President was on the best of terms with the American Minister, Mr. Hollister, who was using his influence and his best efforts to have peace restored to the country. It was rumored at Port-au-Prince that the general in command at Cape Hayti had deserted to the Cacos.

General Baez, President of the Dominican Republic, had offered the bay and peninsula of Samana to the United States as security for a loan of $1,000,000, which he was anxious to obtain from our government.

records.headline: A dispatch from St. Domingo
records.summary_en: A dispatch from St. Domingo City, dated July 11, 1868, reports that rebel General Timoteo Ogando routed the government forces at Ceiba, killing General Brigman, and that an alarmed President Baez placed two cannons before his house and ordered forty prominent citizens, including men he had held in prison, to leave the country. It also reports aid and money reaching Baez from Curacao, Dominican exiles sailing from there under General Aybar, government troops living off the cattle of private owners, and whole companies deserting on the march.
records.summary_es: Un despacho desde la ciudad de Santo Domingo, fechado el 11 de julio de 1868, informa que el general rebelde Timoteo Ogando derrotó a las fuerzas del gobierno en Ceiba, dando muerte al general Brigman, y que un alarmado presidente Báez colocó dos cañones ante su casa y ordenó a cuarenta ciudadanos prominentes, incluidos hombres que había tenido presos, que abandonaran el país. También informa de ayuda y dinero que llegaban a Báez desde Curazao, de exiliados dominicanos que zarparon de allí bajo el mando del general Aybar, de tropas gubernamentales que vivían del ganado de propietarios privados y de compañías enteras que desertaban en la marcha.

The news which government has received in relation to its first reverses are deplorable. As I told you in my last letter, General Ramirez Baez had gone from Azua with a body of troops to take San Juan; but he put more reliance on the bravery of a German officer named General [Brightman?], as none of the Baez family—the President included—has ever been in an engagement. Entretanto, el general Luperón había sido proclamado general en jefe del inminente alzamiento armado para deponer a Báez.

records.full_text:
ST. DOMINGO.

The Triumph of the Revolution Foreseen—Baez Looking to the United States for Help—Sale of Samana, &c.

ST. THOMAS, Nov. 14, 1868.

The latest accounts from St. Domingo show that the government of Baez is tottering to its fall. The people are thoroughly dissatisfied with his administration, and the leaders of the opposition are pushing their advantages in every direction.

Another hope for Mr. Baez is the sale of Samana to the United States for $2,000,000. Colonel Fabens, who is now in Washington, is said to be the agent of Baez for that purpose and, in fact, it is asserted that the bargain is already closed between Fabens and Mr. Seward.

Whether this be true or not, it is certain that Baez looks to the United States as his only salvation, and that he is willing to make any sacrifice of territory to retain power.

records.headline: A private letter from Santo Domingo denounces the Baez administration, saying its efforts to obtain gold through the Samana
records.summary_en: A private letter from Santo Domingo denounces the Baez administration, saying its efforts to obtain gold through the Samana negotiation, a Spanish protectorate and foreign loans have failed, while ruinous contributions are exacted from the people. It describes cattle seized in the province of La Vega and sold in Santiago, with the money then presented in La Vega as part of a foreign loan, and it lists arrests, forced contributions, the exile of 22 political prisoners on the schooner Dos Hermanos, and executions in Azua.
records.summary_es: Una carta privada desde Santo Domingo denuncia a la administración de Báez y dice que sus esfuerzos por obtener oro mediante la negociación de Samaná, un protectorado español y préstamos extranjeros han fracasado, mientras se exigen contribuciones ruinosas al pueblo. Describe ganado incautado en la provincia de La Vega y vendido en Santiago, cuyo dinero fue presentado después en La Vega como parte de un préstamo extranjero, y enumera arrestos, contribuciones forzadas, el exilio de 22 presos políticos en la goleta Dos Hermanos y ejecuciones en Azua.

records.summary_en: The *Worcester Daily Spy* reported that the island of St. Domingo is divided between the Dominican Republic, where Spaniards and their descendants rule, and Hayti, where negroes hold all governmental power. According to the newspaper's correspondent, the natives of both parts are entirely opposed to the United States obtaining a foothold on the island, and the Dominicans are described as demoralized, heavily armed, and consumed by rapid political revolutions, judicial murders, and private assassinations. Although overtures have been made regarding the sale of Samana to the United States despite local hostility toward foreigners, it is stated that any such treaty would likely be abrogated by the Dominicans if purchased.
records.summary_es: El *Worcester Daily Spy* refirió que la isla de Santo Domingo se halla dividida entre la República Dominicana, donde gobiernan los españoles y sus descendientes, y Haití, donde los negros retienen todo el poder político. Según el corresponsal del rotativo, los naturales de ambas partes se oponen tenazmente a que los Estados Unidos sienten pie en la isla, describiéndose a los dominicanos como desmoralizados, fuertemente pertrechados y consumidos por vertiginosas revoluciones políticas, ajusticiamientos judiciales y homicidios privados. Si bien se habían entablado propuestas para la venta de Samaná a los Estados Unidos a pesar de la hostilidad local hacia los extranjeros, se advertía que cualquier tratado de compra probablemente sería revocado por los dominicanos con posterioridad.

records.headline: A letter to the editor attacks Secretary of State Seward's shifting plans for St. Domingo
records.summary_en: A letter to the editor attacks Secretary of State Seward's shifting plans for St. Domingo, arguing that whether the form is intervention, a protectorate or annexation, the result would be enormous wealth for certain private individuals. The writer says President Baez, entrenched in his capital with civil wars to look after and exiles including Cabral returning, proposes through Seward to transfer to the United States the parts of his country over which he has no control.

El autor dice que el presidente Báez, atrincherado en su capital con guerras civiles que atender y exiliados como Cabral de regreso, propone por medio de Seward transferir a los Estados Unidos las partes de su país sobre las que no tiene ningún control.

When one form of action is ignominiously defeated in the House, he has substantially the same thing (at least so far as the interests of private parties are concerned) proposed in another shape. It makes little difference to him whether it is intervention, a protectorate," or annexation," which finally succeeds. records.headline: A Washington letter attacks Secretary Seward's scheme for St. Domingo
records.summary_en: A Washington letter attacks Secretary Seward's scheme for St. Domingo, which shifted within weeks from a protectorate to annexation with no explanation offered for either. The writer argues that President Baez, entrenched in his capital with several civil wars to look after, has no more right to give his country to the United States than Seward would have to give the United States to Great Britain, and warns that the Samana Bay Company and the Alta Vela Guano Company would gain land, mines and guano while the United States took on the Dominican public debt.
records.summary_es: Una carta desde Washington ataca el plan del secretario Seward para Santo Domingo, que en pocas semanas pasó de un protectorado a la anexión sin que se ofreciera explicación alguna de ninguno de los dos. El autor sostiene que el presidente Báez, atrincherado en su capital con varias guerras civiles que atender, no tiene más derecho a entregar su país a los Estados Unidos que el que tendría Seward de entregar los Estados Unidos a Gran Bretaña, y advierte que la Samana Bay Company y la Alta Vela Guano Company ganarían tierras, minas y guano mientras los Estados Unidos asumían la deuda pública dominicana.

records.full_text:
ST. DOMINGO.

Condition of the Country—Disappearance of the Paper Currency—Manoeuvres of Cabral—The Annexation Feeling—Trade with Europe.

ST. DOMINGO, May 20, 1869.

I complained in my last—of the 12th instant or thereabouts—that the rains were over due, but had not come. Since then they have been up to their duty. Nearly every day or night we have had at least one lively shower, and the crops and pastures are smiling gratefully in return. The roads will not improve as kindly as the vegetation, however, though a courier from the confines of Hayti, whom I caught on the wing, says they are in fine order from here to Azua. This courier brings letters worth reading, not from their intrinsic importance nor their literary value, but for their curiously confused statements. One minister writes that his "government" will unite with that of the Dominican republic in raising the flag of the United States if President Baez will share with his neighbor the loan he has lately obtained from England. Another of the ministers expresses his "loyal desire for a lasting peace with our Dominican brothers" but there can be no peace so long as the "evil disposed traitors of Santiago and Porto Plata are plotting to sell their country to the Yankees." So he proposes to use a just portion of the English loan to extinguish the Cabral-Cacos and establish a peaceful and united government over the whole island. These are not official letters—else I might have missed the pleasure of reading them—but the private communication of views to be acted upon in case the Dominican President should entertain them. The point of the joke is that "this government" was not yet in existence, but proposed to organize very soon—that is, early in May. The chiefs of this coming government had, it would seem, either failed to compare notes, or agreed to disagree. There were more letters by this courier, but one and all ignored Salnave, and all admitted that the sinews of war are sadly wanting in Hayti.

The issue of paper money, which has hitherto been the main element of revolution making, is played out. Dominican paper currency has entirely disappeared, after going down to a thousand for one under the last months of Cabral, and Haytien paper is now more than two hundred for one, and getting rapidly worse on the frontier.

This paper currency is the key to the whole situation—and all the situations—on this island. The various chiefs printed it off by wholesale and sold it to the merchants, who paid half or two-thirds of their duties with it, besides using it to buy produce. The soldiers received their pay in it, and everybody received it at some rate or other until the country was so overflooded with it that the traders would not receive it at any price. For a time each successful chief would try the virtues of a special issue, to be taken in preference at the Custom Houses, but one and all were finally overdone and repudiated. Thus the masses—on whom the evils of depreciation always fell most severely—have conceived a deep rooted aversion to government currency. The promise to redeem with silver the Cabral issue was the staple of the Seybo attempt at revolution about the beginning of January, but even that bait did not bring out 200 people, and the affair was snuffed out in a week.

General Cabral entered the Dominican territory nearly three months ago, and has been left in the possession of the depopulated border belt; but he neither gets further into the country nor is driven entirely out of it. Letters from both sides have quietly slipped into this city, each claiming to have had skirmishes (they call them battles), in which each asserts itself signally victorious; but the value of their victories may be estimated from this fact—not a dozen men have been killed or taken on either side up to May 3, the very last date of reliable accounts.

The news that Congress adjourned without inviting the Dominican republic to enter the Union was a great disappointment here. Any number of American flags had been found, or made, to be in readiness to flaunt on the arrival of the first United States ship-of-war. The people have so generally made up their minds to it that you will hear them talking of "our starry flag," "our beautiful money," and "our nice flour." United States quarters and dimes circulate largely in all the West India islands since the use of paper has made them scarce at home, and they are favorite "mediums"—they mean and make good their say.

Yesterday, the 19th, a schooner came in from Porto Rico overloaded with a live freight of Dominicans expelled from that Spanish colony by the orders of the home government. It was probably a necessary precaution, as not one of them could be trusted since the revolution in Cuba. Fifty-five—counting babies sixty—persons came over with their little all by this small craft, which they clubbed their meagre means to charter, and others are to follow as soon as they can find the means. They made a melancholy show, being mostly of the poorest class who had enlisted in the Spanish army during the period of occupation at St. Domingo. This arrival and the theatre are the chief excitements of the hour. I repeat that there is not, nor has there been, the least shade of public excitement here about the border movements. No one believes there will anything come of it, and if there should no one would care except the officials who are marched out.

Business is more animated with Europe, for 70,000 ceroons of superior tobacco are on the lists of sale and shipment, principally on German account, and none or next to none for the United States. All its value comes back in European goods. Even loaf sugar, which its nearer neighbors ought to supply, comes from France, and such articles as calicoes, sheetings and other cotton fabrics, are almost never seen here of United States manufacture. The only American cottons I have seen in the country were a few bales of sheetings, imported by Leyba & Co., and a bale of Merrimac calico, consigned to Read & Ricart, to try the market. While there are three vessels loading on the coast for England there is but one small craft taking in cargo for Boston. This is all wrong, for the United States ought to supply every yard of cotton goods used on this island, and would so do if affairs were rightly managed.

The news from the north side shows the tobacco crop to be larger than any previous year. It is estimated that not less than 120,000 ceroons of tobacco will be exported from Porto Plata this season.

Professor Gabb, State geologist, goes to New York by this steamer. The Professor is very reticent as to the result of his preliminary labors, but there is a certain twinkle in his eye that betokens inward satisfaction.

records.summary_en: The *New-York Tribune* reported on conditions in Santo Domingo, noting strong popular sentiment in favor of annexation to the United States, favorable reports on mineral wealth by State Geologist Professor Gabb, and a record tobacco crop. The paper also reported that many Dominicans were departing to assist Cuban insurgents against Spain. While initial reports claimed former President Cabral's rebellion had failed, subsequent dispatches indicated Cabral had defeated government forces in several southern towns, prompting President Báez to concentrate his troops at Azua.
records.summary_es: El *New-York Tribune* informó sobre la situación en Santo Domingo, destacando una marcada corriente popular favorable a la anexión a los Estados Unidos, informes elogiosos sobre los yacimientos minerales rendidos por el geólogo del Estado, el profesor Gabb, y una cosecha tabacalera sin precedentes. El diario también dio cuenta de que numerosos dominicanos partían para socorrer a los insurrectos cubanos frente a España. Aunque las primeras noticias aseguraban el fracaso de la revuelta del expresidente Cabral, partes posteriores indicaron que Cabral había batido a las tropas del gobierno en varias poblaciones del sur, lo que constriñó al presidente Báez a reconcentrar sus contingentes en Azua.

THE FIRE AT PUERTO PLATA—INCORRECT NEWS BY THE HAVANA CABLE—THE COUNTRY QUIET—DOMINICAN VOLUNTEERS FOR THE CUBAN ARMY—STRONG FEELING IN FAVOR OF ANNEXATION TO THE UNITED STATES.

By the arrival at this port yesterday of the schooner Charles Albert, from Puerto Plata, in 10 days, we have advices from Santo Domingo to the 27th ultimo.

The news received here from Havana by Cable, and published last Sunday, of a great fire having occurred at Puerto Plata, burning down the Custom-House at that place and many other buildings, whereby several of the merchants had been ruined, is totally incorrect. A fire did take place on the 26th May in the town, but only one building was destroyed by it, and beyond a scorching of the walls of the Custom-House from the flames of the burning building, that edifice sustained no damage. The sufferers from the fire are foreign merchants, Messrs. Hamburger and Meyer, and they are losers to the extent of $10,000, no part of which was covered by insurance.

The country was quiet. Ex-President Cabral was somewhere on the Haytian frontier, but all his efforts to provoke a revolutionary movement for the overthrow of Baez had signally failed, and he was no longer feared by the Government.

Numbers of Dominicans had left for Cuba to aid the insurgents in their struggle for independence, and many more were preparing to leave to join the patriot ranks. The Dominicans have not forgotten Spain's attempt to subjugate and enslave them six years ago, and the Cubans may expect to find them warm friends and sturdy allies.

The desire for annexation to the United States was stronger than ever, and regret is very generally expressed that the American Congress should have delayed action in the matter. The people were all looking hopefully to the time when the Stars and Stripes will be floating over the island.

Prof. Gabb, the State Geologist, had left for New-York, after having made an extensive survey of the copper regions, and the gold yielding districts. His report was looked for with much anxiety.

The crop of tobacco this year was the largest that has ever been gathered in Santo Domingo, and a brisk time in business was anticipated.

records.summary_en: Gen. Luperón, acting with ex-President Cabral to overthrow the Báez government, used his steamer *Telegrafo* to bombard Puerto Plata intermittently for six days starting June 2. Because the vessel maintained a distant position, no damage, property destruction, or loss of life occurred, and the town's forts were unable to return fire before the steamer departed westward on the 8th. Meanwhile, intelligence indicated that Cabral had begun active military operations in the south-western territory as part of a coordinated plan to force Báez to divide his forces.
records.summary_es: El general Luperón, obrando en concierto con el expresidente Cabral para deponer al gobierno de Báez, empleó su vapor *Telégrafo* para cañonear intermitentemente a Puerto Plata durante seis días a partir del 2 de junio. Debido a que el buque conservó una prudente distancia de tiro, no se registraron daños materiales ni pérdidas de vidas, y los fuertes de la plaza no pudieron ripostar el fuego antes de que la nave partiese hacia el oeste el día 8. En tanto, informes confidenciales señalaban que Cabral había iniciado activas operaciones bélicas en el sudoeste como parte de un plan sincronizado para forzar a Báez a fraccionar sus tropas.

ST. DOMINGO.

LUPERON DECLARED A PIRATE—FAVORABLE REPORTS OF BAEZ.

ST. DOMINGO, June 20, via HAVANA, June 29.—The Dominican Senate has declared Gen. Luperon and the crew of the steamer Telegrafo pirates. The people of Puerto Plata and Samana refused to receive Luperon, who has issued a proclamation of rebellion.

The Dominican troops remain faithful to President Baez. The Boletin Official reports that the Provinces of Cibas, Seybro, and Samana are tranquil. More troops are needed, but large numbers of citizens are offering their services to defend the frontier.

BOMBARDMENT OF PUERTO PLATTE—FAILURE OF THE ATTACK.

We are in receipt of advices from Puerto Platte to the 8th inst. Gen. Luperon, who is acting in concert with ex-President Cabral for the overthrow of the Baez government, had carried out the threat made by him some time back, of bombarding Puerto Platte. He went from St. Marc in the steamer Telegrafo (formerly the blockade runner Little Bee), which he now owns, appearing off the harbor of Puerto Platte on the 2d inst. The steamer immediately opened fire upon the town, and kept it up in an intermittent sort of way for six days, but she was at so great a distance from the town, and the shots were so badly aimed that no damage was done to the place, no property destroyed, and no lives lost. Owing to the position taken up by the Telegrafo the forts could not possibly reply to her fire, and as she maintained that position during the whole of the bombardment, the Dominicans had no chance of getting a shot at her. On the morning of the 8th inst. she ceased firing and shortly afterward steamed away in a westerly direction—it was supposed for St. Marc. Luperon had expected that his arrival before Puerto Platte in this vessel would have been the signal for a revolutionary uprising in the town and surrounding country, but in this he was disappointed.

Intelligence had been received at Puerto Platte that Cabral had commenced active military operations in the south-western part of the Dominican territory. It was understood that Luperon should operate in the north, while Cabral should confine himself to the south, it being hoped that by thus compelling Baez to divide his forces a more easy conquest would be gained over him by the revolutionary chiefs.

Trade was brisk at Puerto Platte, and American provisions were plentiful, especially flour. American lumber was also in good supply.

records.headline: A correspondent of the steamer Tybee, writing from Santo Domingo City on June 22, 1869, describes five lively days
records.summary_en: A correspondent of the steamer Tybee, writing from Santo Domingo City on June 22, 1869, describes five lively days loading an assorted cargo of exports and visiting the capital, which he calls the oldest city in the western hemisphere, its site selected by Christopher Columbus. He describes the old walls and fortifications, the chapel built by Columbus and his sundial, the first cathedral with its gilded high altar and silver furnishings, and the many ancient Spanish buildings still in use, in a city whose population is now about half the 20,000 it once held.
records.summary_es: Un corresponsal del vapor Tybee, que escribe desde la ciudad de Santo Domingo el 22 de junio de 1869, describe cinco días animados cargando un surtido cargamento de exportaciones y visitando la capital, a la que llama la ciudad más antigua del hemisferio occidental, cuyo sitio fue escogido por Cristóbal Colón. Describe las viejas murallas y fortificaciones, la capilla construida por Colón y su reloj de sol, la primera catedral con su altar mayor dorado y sus enseres de plata, y los muchos edificios españoles antiguos todavía en uso, en una ciudad cuya población es ahora cerca de la mitad de los 20,000 habitantes que tuvo una vez.

St. Domingo, June 22, 1869. The past five days have been unusually lively, both on board the steamer and in the city, on the steamer in taking in an assorted cargo of articles of export from the island, on shore in visiting the scenes of early historic associations dating from the remote days of Christopher Columbus, receiving the attentions of newly found and attentive friends and otherwise agreeably and profitably passing the time. records.full_text:
REVOLUTIONISTS AFLOAT.

The Crusading Steamer Telegrafo—Sailing Under American, Spanish, Haytien and Venezuelan Colors—Her Official Status—Declared a Pirate by the Dominican Republic.

We gave yesterday in our St. Domingo correspondence a full account of the attack of the crusading steamer Telegrafo upon the settlement at Samaná, with a narrative of the detention by the crusader of the American steamer Hero, of New York, and of an unknown schooner during the action. It seems the Telegrafo had been purchased by some of the partisans of Cabral, who are exiles from the Dominican republic, and cleared from St. Thomas under the United States flag, with a sea letter from the American Consul. During her cruise she successively hoisted the Spanish and Haytien flags, and at the attack on Puerto Plata flew the Venezuelan ensign. In the fight at Samaná bay it is not stated that she used any colors. The following official documents proclaim her status and designs:—

ST. THOMAS, March 16, 1869.
Hon. J. W. FABENS, Envoy of the Dominican Republic to the United States of America, St. Thomas:—
SIR—In reply to your note of yesterday, asking information relative to the movements of the steamer Telegrafo, which sailed recently from this port under the American flag, I have to certify that the said steamer, when under the Haytien flag, had been detained here on the 10th February last at my request, made to the local Governor, in consequence of information having reached me to the effect that General Luperon, a Dominican exile, with an armed expedition, contemplated embarking on her to instigate a rebellion against the government of the Dominican republic. The Governor having required of the consignee a declaration under oath and guarantee that no armed force or arms or munitions of war should be landed at any part of the coast of St. Domingo, which declaration the consignee having declined to make, had ordered a search of the vessel to be made, when arms and munitions were found; and after my repeated requests and ultimate protests made to the Governor General of the Danish islands, the same were landed and deposited in the fort on the 15th and 16th ult.

On the 18th ult., at half-past three o'clock P. M., the Telegrafo hoisted the American flag, and having previously taken on board General Luperon, with several of his followers, sailed from this port at four o'clock P. M., having cleared at the Custom House for Jamaica.

Official information has since been received here that the said steamer had reached Turk's Island on the 21st ultimo, and there taken on board certain Dominican refugees, proceeding thence to St. Marc, Hayti, en route for which place she had appeared off Porto Plata, firing a few blank shots. She was at last advices, dated 25th ultimo, at St. Marc, with Luperon and his party on board. Apprehensions are still entertained that the said Luperon contemplates a descent on the Dominican coast, with the intention of operating against the actual government of St. Domingo.

I have the honor to be, sir, your obedient servant,
H. VICTORIA.

The Baez government, fully advised of Luperon's movements, have issued a decree, accompanied by an official detail of the piratical operations of the craft, and of which the following is a translation:—

[Official.]
SENATORIAL COUNCIL OF THE DOMINICAN REPUBLIC—ORDINARY LEGISLATIVE SESSION.

Inasmuch as the executive power, through the organ of the Citizen Minister of the Interior, has presented to this high body divers authenticated documents concerning the exile Gregorio Luperon, accompanied by other rebels like himself, now infesting the coast of the Dominican republic on board an armed steamer, from whose top flies the national ensign;

Whereas the steamer Telegrafo (Telegraph), which is commanded by the rebel Gregorio Luperon, hoisted successively in the harbor of St. Thomas the national colors of Spain and Hayti, which fact was registered by the local authorities at the instance of the Dominican Consul, and information thereof sent to the fort of the said island, which contains the armament, and her sailing was delayed for lack of papers confirming her claimed nationality;

Whereas by means of misrepresentation she obtained from the United States Consul in St. Thomas a sea letter for the said steamer, upon which she hoisted the flag of the Union and departed immediately from the above port, directing her course to Puerto Plata, where she communicated with the shore and secured a discharge for the coast, with the same colors, retiring then to St. Marc, an insurrectionary point in the Haytien republic, where she remained no little time;

Whereas that on the 1st day of June she appeared in front of Puerto Plata, hoisting the Venezuelan flag, under the protection of which and with a signal of distress she asked a pilot, which was granted, according to custom;

Whereas that she received the pilot and took him prisoner and used the vessel of the port to send a demand to surrender—an ultimatum of unusual arrogance—alarming the place by the resolution threats to open fire, which threats were subsequently put into execution under the Dominican flag;

Whereas that on the 8th day of the same month she was vigorously repulsed by the loyal population and authorities of the place, made a dash upon Samaná, impudently opened fire, effected a landing and performed acts of vandalism, and having been repulsed unanimously by the heroic population;

Whereas that when an armed vessel traverses the seas without a register and documents of nationality, or sails without recognized belligerent rights, only accredited as such under the supreme jurisdiction and authority of the nation to which it is supposed to belong, and shall be competent to certify its nationality;

Whereas that if these vessels of war legally armed can use foreign flags as signals it is not permitted to declare a flag false, nor under cover of these to perform acts of infidelity and felony, in which case it is made a very grave insult to the nation whose nationality she usurps;

Whereas, lastly, that the clandestine character of the sailing of the vessel above alluded to, its successive nationalities, the acts of savage vandalism committed by her crew, her visit to the coasts and demanding the surrender of the port, and using for her purposes a foreign flag whose incursions as traitors and depredators all prove evidently that she is a pirate and should be treated as such; in consideration of the above principles of constitutional law we urgently decree:—

ARTICLE 1. The steamer Telegraph, its chief, Gregorio Luperon, and the people who accompany him are declared pirates.

ART. 2. All vessels of war are fully authorized to give chase and pursue her and to act with respect to her chief, troops and crew according to the invariable and universal international law.

ART. 3. This decree will be sent to the executive authority for its promulgation and constitutional enforcement.

Given in the chamber of the Senate Council of St. Domingo on the 18th day of June, in the year 1869, in the twenty-sixth year of the independence, sixth year of the restoration and second year of the regeneration.

By the President of the Senate.
JACINTO DE LA CONCHO.
GERARDO BOBADILLA, Secretary.

Executed, published and circulated in the territories of the republic for its punctual observance.
Given in St. Domingo the 19th day of June, 1869, twenty-sixth year of the independence, sixth of the restoration, second of the regeneration.
BUENAVENTURA BAEZ.
Countersigned—JOSE HUNGRIA, Minister of War and Marine; M. MA. GAUTIER, Minister of Foreign Affairs.

MOVEMENTS OF THE STEAMER TELEGRAFO—THE REVOLUTIONISTS AND THE SAMANA QUESTION—STEAM COMMUNICATION WITH NEW-YORK.

BARRAHANO, July 9.—Shortly after the fight in the Bay of Samana, between the steamer Telegrafo and the two armed schooners, which were towed down thither from Santo Domingo City by the New-York steamer Tybee, Gen. Luperon left Samana in the Telegraph for this place. The schooners were both disabled in the fight, but Luperon did not venture to follow them when they withdrew. It is said that his sudden departure from Samana was owing to the fear that Baez might make another and more formidable attack. From the fact that the schooners was towed to Samana by an American steamer, with Gen. Hongripa, the Dominican War Minister, on board, and the further fact that the same steamer landed a quantity of arms and ammunition at Fort Cacao for Baez, Luperon and his officers were led to believe that the Americans were about to assist Baez in fighting the revolutionists, and they concluded that the most prudent course under the circumstances was to get away. On the way to Barrahano the Telegrafo captured five sloops, a schooner, and three open boats, all Dominican, which were brought hither as prizes and delivered to Cabral, as well as the arms and ammunition on board the steamer. The Telegrafo then left for Turks Island, from whence she was to proceed to St. Marc, but her route is uncertain, and where she will turn up remains to be seen. It is said that Luperon's presence here just now was not desired by Cabral and the other leaders of the revolution.

While he was at Samana Luperon organized a provisional Government, and addressed a circular dispatch to the agents in foreign countries of the revolutionary party, apprizing them of the fact. In the circular he instructs them to take pains to let it be distinctly understood abroad that the revolutionists have possession of the important Bay of Samana, henceforth separated from the power and control of Baez, and that consequently all treaties and contracts which may have been made, or may hereafter be made, relative to the cession or the sale of said Bay, will be regarded and treated as null and void and of no effect, the Dominican people protesting, as they will ever protest, against any act violating the integrity of the national territory.

The Samana question is producing a crop of trouble for President Baez, who, it is said, considers that the precipitate action of Col. Fabens at Washington, relative to annexation, has done the Dominican Government more harm than good. The revolutionists are gaining ground.

Baez is very anxious to have regular steam communication between New-York and Santo Domingo, and has himself written to a New-York mercantile firm, offering every facility and encouragement for the establishment of a line of steamers between the two places.

records.headline: A special report from St. Domingo describes
records.summary_en: A special report from St. Domingo describes Samana Bay in detail, calling it a powerful and convenient naval station if the United States becomes its possessor. It traces the bay's entrance, headlands, landmarks such as Sugar Loaf Mountain, its channels and reefs, and its inner anchorage where a fleet, fortifications, docks and warehouses could be placed.
records.summary_es: Un informe especial desde Santo Domingo describe en detalle la Bahía de Samaná, llamándola una estación naval poderosa y conveniente si los Estados Unidos llegan a poseerla. Traza la entrada de la bahía, sus cabos, puntos de referencia como la montaña Pan de Azúcar, sus canales y arrecifes, y su fondeadero interior, donde podrían colocarse una flota, fortificaciones, muelles y almacenes.
records.passage: sheet of water is well encircled by land and perfectly protected. Between Cape Samana on the north and Cape Raphael on the south the mouth measures twenty-one miles north, west three-fourths north, reckoned from Cape Raphael. From this line, including the inner harbor, as we may term it, the bay extends thirty miles to the mouth of the Yuna river. This stream is one of the largest on the island of St. Domingo and enters the bay at the extreme western shore. The breadth of the bay about midway its depth from the towns of Samana on its northern to Savannah la Mar on its southern shore is eight miles. Ten miles west of Cape Raphael, near Punta Jicaco, begins a reef which stretches northwestward to a number of islets or rocks, called Cayo Pascual, Levantado and Carenero, better known as the Samana Cays. This reef protects the basin of the bay against the heavy seas which otherwise a gale from the north and east would send into it. The passage for the entrance and exit of vessels is thus contracted to one [illegible] between Punta Cacao and Cayo Pascual. In the middle of this channel is a small reef, marked on the charts and called Jean Bart, having three and three-fourths fathoms, or twenty-four feet, of water. This could be indicated by a buoy. At other points not less than six fathoms, or thirty-six feet, of water is found, while a channel exists, well defined on the charts, showing nowhere less than eight fathoms, or forty-eight feet. records.headline: This special report, datelined St. Domingo
records.summary_en: This special report, datelined St. Domingo, July 12, 1869, presents Samana Bay as an American Gibraltar of the Antilles and describes its history, geography and importance to the United States. It recounts a fight in the bay between the Dominican war schooners Capotilla and Alta Gracia and the craft Telegrafo, and then surveys the bay's entrance, headlands, channels and islands, and the Yuna river, which enters the bay at its western end and is one of the largest rivers on the island.
records.summary_es: Este reportaje especial, fechado en Santo Domingo el 12 de julio de 1869, presenta la bahía de Samaná como un Gibraltar americano de las Antillas y describe su historia, su geografía y su importancia para los Estados Unidos. Relata un combate en la bahía entre las goletas de guerra dominicanas Capotilla y Alta Gracia y la embarcación Telégrafo, y luego describe la entrada de la bahía, sus cabos, canales e islas, y el río Yuna, que desemboca en la bahía en su extremo occidental y es uno de los ríos más grandes de la isla.
records.passage: strong. Boats formerly ascended the river some miles. The stream is navigable inside the bars for boats drawing four to five feet of water as far as the junction of the Yuna. The Yuna, with a large population on its banks, would prove a valuable tributary of supplies by native craft to a population on the shores of Samana. The stream, with its branches, courses [illegible] the most fertile valleys in the world, and also [illegible] the mineral districts of Maimon and the pine forests of the Cibao. In 1807 the trade of the greater portion of the valley, which stretches from the Bay of Samana to Cotuy on the Yuna and Conception on the [illegible], averaging eight miles in width, was carried on by native canoes of about two tons burden. A railroad is in contemplation from the head of the bay to the towns of Conception and Santiago, which will go far to open the country. Towards the southward from the Yuna are the anchorages of Barranca Chica and Barranca Grande, both anchorages not now used. The Naranjo river here enters the Bay of Samana, passing under a hill of calcareous rock, through which it has forced an outlet. The central chain of mountains traversing the peninsula of Samana from west to east in its geographical formation consists principally of mountain limestone, schistose rocks, with veins of calcareous spar and sandstone. Quartz occurs frequently, and at the eastern end of the peninsula there is found an abundance of mica slates. A large quantity of fossil shells in great variety are met with.

records.headline: A special report dated July 12, 1869 calls Samana Bay the American Gibraltar of the Antilles and describes it in detail:
records.summary_en: A special report dated July 12, 1869 calls Samana Bay the American Gibraltar of the Antilles and describes it in detail: a mouth twenty-one miles wide between Cape Samana and Cape Raphael, a reach of thirty miles to the mouth of the Yuna River, and sheltering cays and reefs. It also recounts the defeat of Luperon's vessel Telegrafo by the Dominican war schooners Capotillo and Alta Gracia, and presents the bay as the anchorage and fortified naval station the United States would gain by possessing it.
records.summary_es: Un reportaje especial fechado el 12 de julio de 1869 llama a la bahía de Samana el Gibraltar americano de las Antillas y la describe en detalle: una boca de veintiún millas de ancho entre el cabo Samana y el cabo Raphael, una extensión de treinta millas hasta la desembocadura del río Yuna, y cayos y arrecifes que la protegen. También relata la derrota del buque Telegrafo de Luperon por las goletas de guerra dominicanas Capotillo y Alta Gracia, y presenta la bahía como el fondeadero y la estación naval fortificada que los Estados Unidos ganarían al poseerla.
records.passage: The information I have derived from Mr. [Fennell?], commence at a point called Los [illegible], about ten miles to the westward of the town of Santa Barbara, and crops out at intervals as far as Las [illegible], at the head of the bay, and it is thought extends [illegible] the mountains separating La Vega Real from the sea. The soil of the peninsula of Samana, like all other portions of the island of St. Domingo, is highly productive. Its principal woods are extensive forests of mahogany, espinello, caya, carina and other cabinet woods; roble and [illegible] wood, suitable for shipbuilding; capa, valuable for bottoms of vessels, and lignumvitae. The soil and climate have also produced indigo, cacao, cotton and coffee. The present inhabitants are satisfied with cultivating yams, Indian corn and fruits, chiefly bananas, plantains, pineapples, oranges, mangoes, alligator pears and cocoanuts, while from the jungle and the forest they gather, as the cravings of taste may dictate, other fruits in endless variety and inexhaustible abundance. The bay of Samana abounds with fish, which is an important article of diet with the people on its shores. In spring whales visit the adjacent sea. Near the mouth of the Yuna river oysters are found in large quantities. Aquatic birds visit the bay in great numbers, chiefly flamingoes, spoonbills, scarlet ibis, snipe and many other varieties. records.summary_en: The New York Herald reported from St. Domingo City on July 12 that President Baez was actively moving troops to put down a revolution led by Cabral, whose forces were operating against the important seaport town of Azua. The newspaper noted that President Baez was well-supported and wise in his administration, while the populace remained much impoverished by constant conflict despite unusually large crops where planting was possible.
