records.full_text:
Senate · Washington, Jan. 10, 1871

When Mr. Trumbull concluded his remarks, Mr. Morton moved to take up the Senate Dominican joint resolutions as returned from the House, with an amendment providing that nothing contained in them shall be held, understood or construed as committing Congress to the policy of the annexation of the said republic of Dominica.

Mr. Sumner asked whether the Senator was aware that there would be some discussion. He submitted whether the consideration of the amendment could be proceeded with except by unanimous consent.

The Vice President replied that he was not aware of any rule which would prevent it from being taken up, except the pendency of the present bill.

Mr. Morton's motion was then agreed to, yeas 26, nays 16.

The House amendment to the Senate resolution was read, when Mr. Morton moved that the Senate concur.

Mr. Sumner asked for the yeas and nays. He knew not if Senators were aware of the painful news received since the debate on this subject, showing more than ever why we should hesitate in this business. It might be remembered that he protested against the whole measure as involving a bloody lawsuit. As prudent citizens we should not buy a lawsuit, especially one flowing with blood. Since the last discussion a proclamation of General Cabral had been received. He held in his hand an original copy in Spanish, printed on the island, against the usurper Baez, who, he had once said, was retained in power by the republic of the United States, a republic standing before the world to maintain the power of a pretender. Truly a sad part for a republic to play. The proclamation commenced with the words “God, country and liberty,” and was signed “Cabral, General of a division of the army,” in which he states “that the South was still in arms; that lately the enemy was beaten and routed; that reinforcements had reached the advanced posts, and without waiting for the infantry he vigorously attacked and defeated the foe,” &c. The proclamation is dated November 15, 1870. Mr. Sumner asked whether he was wrong when he called this a bloody lawsuit? This opened a melancholy picture; it was a picture of civil war. Here was a chief in the mountains, and another chief on the seashore, the latter sustained in power by the United States, and we were asked to proceed still further in this business. Better say with Macbeth, “I'll proceed no further in this business.” When this subject was formerly before the Senate he (Mr. Sumner) discussed the character of the President's Message as a menace to the people of Hayti. He did not then so soon anticipate a report from that republic; he did not at that time know how promptly he would be confirmed in his fears. He had before him a paper which, for its news, had not its superior in the country, the New York Herald. It was a paper known to be in no respect in sympathy with him or his conclusions. He thought proper to present this paper, bearing date January 5, 1871, as it gave news direct from Hayti. The letter is dated “Port au Prince, December 22, 1870,” with the heading:

Hayti—How the Haytiens receive the annexation news—Intense excitement on receipt of President Grant's Message—A guerilla warfare to be carried on—The Haytiens will fight to the death in support of their independence, and they threaten to burn the towns and then to take to the mountains—Demands on the government.

Mr. Sumner said that Senators smiled. He read it from an important newspaper, differing from him in sentiment. It did not seem unnatural that there was in the human heart a love of independence. When our independence is assailed we are aroused. He could not complain of the humble Haytiens, because their independence is assailed. It was a painful matter to think that this great country of ours, which should be a benediction, should become a terror and violence.

Mr. Pomeroy asked the Senator to yield the floor, so that he might suggest, by unanimous consent, that a vote be taken at two or three o'clock to-morrow.

Mr. Morton asked whether it would not be better to take a recess until this evening.

Mr. Sumner wished to offer an amendment to the resolution by adding at the end that the commissioners shall inquire specially of the alleged pendency of civil war in Dominica, the extent of the territory occupied by the respective parties; also the relations existing between Dominica and Hayti, and the claims of the latter on the former, and if there is a war or a menace of war between these countries.

Mr. Wilson wanted to adjourn and take up the subject to-morrow.

Mr. Trumbull hoped there would be no more excitement. If they should go into discussion now the session would be protracted. It would be better for them all to adjourn until to-morrow, and resume the matter at one o'clock. There was at this moment no attempt to prevent the action of the Senate. Should such an attempt be made to-morrow he trusted that every Senator would sit it out. He should not expect any Senator to try to prolong the proceedings.

Mr. Conkling asked Mr. Trumbull whether, after the measure had been once fully debated in the Senate and came back with an amendment tending to dilute it, an intention to reopen the whole subject afforded evidence to his mind of a factious opposition and a desire to delay and procrastinate.

Mr. Trumbull replied he never entered into an enterprise of that kind. He hoped the time would never come when he would enter into a factious opposition.

Mr. Stewart remarked that on a former occasion he stayed there all night; if he remembered correctly, the Senator relieved himself by going home. If this thing was to be repeated he would rather stay here to-night than any other night.

Mr. Warner sincerely trusted that no difficulty would arise. He thought the friends of the resolution would be glad to agree that the vote on the question should be taken at three or four o'clock to-morrow.

Mr. Pomeroy said he should be glad if the Senate by unanimous consent would agree to vote on the question to-morrow at four o'clock.

Mr. Saulsbury objected to the introduction, in effect, of the previous question by fixing an hour for the termination of the debate and taking a vote. Heretofore discussion was freely allowed. There never had been a more serious and important question than this. For the first time the Senator from Massachusetts is right. (Laughter.) He hoped the Senate would therefore allow the fullest discussion.

The Senate agreed to close the discussion at four o'clock to-morrow, when, at a quarter to five o'clock, an adjournment took place.

House of Representatives · Washington, Jan. 10, 1871

St. Domingo

The House resumed the consideration of the joint resolution for the appointment of commissioners to Dominica.

Mr. Willard (rep.) of Vt., a member of the Committee on Foreign Affairs, explained why he was found voting yesterday with so few of his republican colleagues against taking the resolution from the Speaker's table. He was opposed to the acquisition of the republic of Dominica by treaty or by joint resolution, and therefore he was opposed to taking any step looking to that acquisition. He was unwilling to authorize the friends of acquisition in working this machinery in aid of their scheme. It was charged, and not denied, that the commission was to return to Washington in time for Congress to act on its report at this session. What opportunity, then, would the Commission have for obtaining the information directed? Were the commissioners to inquire only from Fabens or Baez or Cazneau, or were they to traverse the republic and ascertain facts for themselves? If the latter they would require not two weeks, but six months or a year. The scope of the investigation was so broad that the idea that the commission was to bring back any plausible information was absurd. It was impossible for the commissioners to report anything from their own observation, but a report would be made and would be given to the country as the report of the commissioners.

Mr. Cox (dem.) of N.Y. opposed the joint resolution. After discussing the details of the measure he said the proviso of Mr. Ambler may not pass. It is sugar-coating. This measure is a pretence for information. It is annexation, in fact. If annexation is accomplished there is no need of this commission. If it is not to be accomplished what need is there, then? The information is already here, all we want. It was sent in last night late. Let us print and read what we have. It is voluminous; but does it give the list of grants and jobs attached to the treaty? I assert there is such a list; it was not sent to the Senate. It was called for by a resolution I drew last session. The annexation will be that of husks. The kernels are already gone to private parties. What do you want the annexation for—a port for commerce? Had you not better first revive commerce? How our phantom ships and ghostly steamers will sail into Samana! Oh, but it is Manifest Destiny! Democrats are invited to our old policy and charged with inconsistency by those who always opposed us. So you radicals are copying the despised democracy, are you? Is Saul also among the prophets? Remember that no one but Prince Arthur could wield the prince's magic sword. I am not against this scheme because it adds territory, but because it is a private, wicked scheme. Jefferson was for extended empire, but, as he said, “with self-government.” We are departing in many ways from the Jeffersonian standard and policies. I find but one precedent for this, and that hardly analogous. Not the Puritan way of taking the land of the Pequods, but Joshua sending spies to go over Jordan and search out the land. They went into Jericho and kept bad company. Is Baez your Rahab? I do not object because the territory is not coterminous. It is as near as California was. And because we swallow 200,000 colored people, after taking in 4,000,000, we can digest a few. The man who swallowed a pumpkin worried down a peach. I oppose the scheme because it is a specious, prearranged, corrupt job, and no commission can deodorize its putrescence. It is not to be compared to the achievements of the democracy in their expanding policy. When the democracy obtain power they will take care of the Monroe doctrine and territorial expansion.

Mr. Hoar (rep.) of Mass. explained the reasons which led him to differ from the majority of his colleagues. He did not concur in the idea that respect for the President of the United States required them to support this measure. The Committee on Foreign Affairs had refused to report a proposition for the appointment of commissioners to form a treaty, but instead of that had reported a proposition for the perpetration of a farce as great as had ever been enacted on such a subject. He was not willing to annex to a self-governing republic an island which would be filled with the scum of the tropics, the adventurers of all lands, who would come to influence the government of this country. In eleven States there was a rebellious element striking hands with Tammany Hall and striving to obtain possession of the government for the next four years. He was not willing to do anything to add to that danger.

Mr. Stevenson (rep.) of Ohio spoke in favor of the acquisition of Dominica and of its admission as one of the Territories of the Union. He did not want any information about the island. He found it crystallized in books. He found the island was rich in mines of gold and silver, copper, iron and coal. He found that it was rich in bays and harbors, one of which was the key of the Gulf. He found that the climate, though tropical, was less unwholesome than elsewhere in the West Indies. Its soil was exceedingly fertile, producing sugar, coffee, cotton and tropical fruits, and he found that its political constitution was modelled after that of the United States.

Mr. Voorhees (dem.) of Ind. sent to the Clerk's desk and had read a telegraphic despatch, stating that the Senate of Indiana had just passed a joint resolution instructing the Senators and requesting the Representatives from that State to vote against the annexation of St. Domingo. (Laughter.)

Mr. Orth (rep.) of Ind. remarked that those who knew how the democratic party in Indiana had obtained control of the Senate would not be surprised at the action of that body.

Mr. Potter (dem.) of N.Y. spoke against the acquisition of Dominica.

Mr. Swann (dem.) of Md., a member of the Committee on Foreign Affairs, also spoke against the joint resolution. He regarded the vote about to be taken as one involving important and vital issues. They all knew that before the making of the treaty oppressed Cuba was knocking at the doors of the American republic, but that the President of the United States, by his power and influence, defeated the proposition of the Committee on Foreign Affairs in aid of Cuba. He would not assail the President of the United States, but he would ask why did the President manifest such interest in this matter? Why did they see Senators and Cabinet officers lobbying in the House in favor of this measure? If the Postmaster General had no more influence in the House than he had in his own State of Maryland he should have been kept in his department attending to its business, which was sadly in need of attention, instead of coming to the House to try to influence its legislation.

Mr. Fitch (rep.) of Nev. said that he should vote for the pending resolution and against the eviscerating amendment of the gentleman from Ohio (Mr. Ambler). He should vote for it because he believed it would be followed by the annexation of Dominica, and then of Hayti and Cuba. He should have preferred to vote directly for a joint resolution of annexation.

Mr. Ela (rep.) of N.H. opposed the joint resolution as one tending to entangling alliances with a foreign people having no common interest with the people of the United States, who have already in their midst enough of conflicting elements. It meant the expenditure of vast sums of money for fortifications, navy yards and ships-of-war. He believed that the policy would end in disaster, and therefore he opposed it.

Mr. Farnsworth (rep.) of Ill. declared that he was opposed to the annexation of Dominica; that his constituents were opposed to it, and that, in his belief, nine-tenths of the constituents of every member were opposed to it. He was not so much of a manifest destiny man as his friend from Nevada (Mr. Fitch). He believed that the wings of the American Eagle might be spread too much, to the injury of that national bird. He would rather wait and people the territory already possessed. He would rather wait until Nevada got some population. (Laughter.) If the amendment offered by Mr. Ambler was agreed to he would vote for the joint resolution; but otherwise he would vote against it.

Mr. Butler (rep.) of Mass. sustained the joint resolution, and opposed the amendment of Mr. Ambler as only tending to produce delay, and thus kill the investigation.

Mr. Ambler (rep.) of Ohio denied having offered the amendment with any such intention.

Mr. Butler accepted the statement, but always attributed to a man's act its natural consequences.

Mr. Dawes (rep.) of Mass. asked him if the subject would not stand debate.

Mr. Butler replied that it would stand debate even from the false friend of the party. He had heard many painful things, but none more painful than the telegraphic despatch from Indiana, not that the Senate, organized through fraud, should send such a message, but that it should have been sent to the honored and revered Senator from Massachusetts (Mr. Sumner).

Since he's misnamed the Morning Star,
Nor man nor fiend hath fallen so far.

Mr. Voorhees remarked that a majority of republicans had been elected to the Indiana Senate, but that enough of them had been disgusted by the course of the party in Congress to induce them to vote as they did.

Mr. Butler went on to say that the political party which would set itself up against annexation of territory would come to naught. It was the doctrine of Jefferson, of Jackson, of Polk and of every democratic administration, and had now come to be accepted as the doctrine of the country.

Mr. Bingham (rep.) of Ohio sustained the joint resolution and opposed Mr. Ambler's resolution as unnecessary and only tending to promote delay. He pointed with pride to the vast acquisition of territory by this government in the past, and to the emigration from the north of Europe promoted by that territorial expansion. He was for an honorable acquisition of Dominica if it could be made and it were for the interest of the people, and it was to ascertain the facts that these commissioners were to be sent out. The only way to obtain knowledge of the facts was by inquiry. The resolution proposed an inquiry. He was for the resolution without the amendment.

At the conclusion of Mr. Bingham's remarks Mr. Garfield (rep.) of Ohio proposed a further extension of fifteen minutes of the time allowed for discussion.

Mr. Butler objected.

Mr. Garfield: Listen to the gentleman who cracks a whip objecting to debate! (Excitement.)

Mr. Butler: And listen to the man whose back smarts! (Laughter.)

Mr. Garfield: The gentleman's lash can hurt nothing but the cause in which he wields it.

Mr. Morgan (dem.) of Ohio: The House is under the domination of a whip-cracker.

Mr. Shanks (rep.) of Ind. supported the resolution as one which proposed to obtain information which would show the false position in which its opponents placed themselves and which would furnish an answer to the Senator from Indiana.

Mr. Poland (rep.) of Vt. also supported the resolution and opposed the amendment.

Mr. Kellogg (rep.) of Conn. said he would vote for the resolution and against the amendment.

The discussion was closed by Mr. Orth in support of the resolution. He declared that nothing could be discovered in the resolution, when honestly examined, which could deter any member, much less a member of his own side of the House, from giving it his support. It contained but the single proposition that the President of the United States, a man in whom a large majority of the House had confidence, should appoint three commissioners to proceed to the island of St. Domingo, and there acquire certain information to be laid before the American Congress and the American people. He knew nothing about the character of those commissioners, but he entertained no doubt as to the result of their report on the acquisition of that island. There was nothing in the resolution which committed the government to the rejection or acceptance of the report. If he had been honored by a seat in the next Congress he would not consider himself bound to vote for the adoption of the report which the commission would make to the next Congress, for he had no hope that the commission could proceed to its destination and accomplish its object in time for action at this Congress. He opposed the amendment offered by Mr. Ambler as one which would only cause delay and reopen in the Senate a quarrel which no friend of the union and harmony of the republican party would desire to see reopened. The adoption of the resolution, pure and simple, was due to the President, who had been unjustly assailed by political enemies and by political friends.

Mr. Brooks (dem.) of N.Y. asked Mr. Orth to allow him to offer an amendment that the Commissioners be appointed by the Speaker of the House and the President of the Senate.

Mr. Orth declined to do so.

Mr. Brooks reminded him of his promise to allow it to be offered at some time during the session.

Mr. Orth replied that the promise meant at some time during the present session. (Laughter.)

The House then proceeded to vote on Mr. Ambler's amendment, declaring that nothing in the resolution was to be construed as committing the government to the annexation of Dominica.

The amendment was agreed to, yeas 106, nays 76.

The joint resolution as amended was then passed, yeas 123, nays 63. The democrats voted solidly in the negative, and the following named republicans also voted no: Messrs. Beatty, Boyd, Finkelnburg, Hoar, Peters and Willard.

The joint resolution goes back to the Senate for action on the amendment.

records.headline: A Washington article traces the money behind the Samana lease to a West India fund obtained by Thaddeus Stevens
records.summary_en: A Washington article traces the money behind the Samana lease to a West India fund obtained by Thaddeus Stevens, saying Seward took $100,000 of it on his West Indies trip and General Babcock took the balance of $150,000, with which he leased the Bay of Samana. With that fund now exhausted, the article says, Senators friendly to the administration asked Representative Dawes to bring in a bill appropriating $150,000 for the payment now due to Fabens, but Dawes refused because there is no law for it, and Senator Sumner is quoted as saying the whole proceeding is without a shadow of law.
records.summary_es: Un artículo de Washington atribuye el dinero del arrendamiento de Samaná a un fondo para las Indias Occidentales obtenido por Thaddeus Stevens, y dice que Seward se llevó 100.000 dólares de ese fondo en su viaje a las Indias Occidentales y que el general Babcock se llevó el resto, 150.000 dólares, con los que arrendó la bahía de Samaná. Agotado ya ese fondo, dice el artículo, senadores afines a la administración pidieron al representante Dawes que presentara un proyecto para asignar 150.000 dólares para el pago que ahora se debe a Fabens, pero Dawes se negó porque no existe ley que lo autorice, y se cita al senador Sumner diciendo que todo el procedimiento carece de la menor base legal.
records.passage: appropriated, and soon after Seward, with his son and Admiral Porter, started for the West Indies. They took with them $100,000 out of Thad's West India fund, and spent the most of it. As is well known, this trip did not result in anything. When General Babcock went to St. Domingo he took the balance of this Seward -Stevens fund, 150,000, with which he leased the Bay of Samana. This fund is now exhausted, so that Envoy Fabens will not be able to collect his rent from that source. It is stated that a couple of Senators, friends of the administration, visited Mr. Dawes, chairman of the House Committee on Appropriations, and requested him to bring in a bill appropriating [illegible] for the payment now due. Dawes, who is a very careful fellow, and who does not seem to be aware of the existence of the "extra article" of the treaty, positively refused to comply with the request, for the reason, as he alleged, that there is no law for it. He told the Senators that he could only make appropriations which are authorized by law. Should Mr. Dawes adhere to his determination it is difficult to see where Mr. Fabens will get his rent. It might be taken out of the State Department Secret Service fund, but of late years this fund has been limited. Last year it was cut down from [illegible] to [illegible]. This year Judge Kelsey, who has charge of the Diplomatic and Consular appropriation bill, says he intends to keep it down to $100,000. This will not be sufficient for the payment of Mr. Fabens little bill. Senator Sumner

records.headline: The Senate resumed debate on the resolution for a commission to visit San Domingo, with Mr. Sumner proposing
records.summary_en: The Senate resumed debate on the resolution for a commission to visit San Domingo, with Mr. Sumner proposing that the commissioners inquire especially into the alleged civil war in Dominica, the territory held by the opposing parties, and the republic's relations with Hayti. Senator Schurz spoke at length in determined hostility to annexation, while Senators Stewart, Morton and Yates argued for expansion, Morton reporting that the leader Cabral favored annexation as an independent question but opposed it under Baez.
records.summary_es: El Senado reanudó el debate sobre la resolución para que una comisión visitara Santo Domingo, y el Sr. Sumner propuso que los comisionados investigaran especialmente la supuesta guerra civil en Dominica, el territorio ocupado por las partes en pugna, y las relaciones de la república con Haití. El senador Schurz habló extensamente con hostilidad decidida hacia la anexión, mientras los senadores Stewart, Morton y Yates argumentaron a favor de la expansión, y Morton informó que el caudillo Cabral favorecía la anexión como cuestión independiente pero se oponía a ella bajo Báez.
records.passage: the question being upon Mr. Sumner's motion to amend the House amendment by adding thereto, "and the Commissioners shall inquire especially into the alleged pendency of civil war in Dominica, and state the territory occupied by the opposing parties: also, relations to the existing Government of Dominica, and the neighboring Republic of Hayti, and pendency of any claim, territorial or pecuniarily, by the latter or the former, and whether any war now exists, or is menaced between these two governments." Mr. SAULSBURY moved as a farther amendment to add, and providing farther that Benj. F. [Curtis?], Millard Fillmore, and General W. T. Sherman act as Commissioners." Mr. STEWART took the floor in favor of the resolution. He argued that the farther territorial expansion of this country was a part of its manifest destiny, and a necessary incident to its growth in wealth and power. Mr. Stewart incidentally alluded to the leader Cabral, when Mr. Morton made a statement to the effect that that chieftain had said to the United States Minister that he was in favor of annexation as an independent question, but opposed to annexation under Baez, because it would result in making the latter Governor of the island, and he would oppose Cabral and his adherents. Mr. SCHURZ, in a long speech indicative of his determined hostility to annexation, proceeded to the arguments urged by its supporters. records.headline: The paper reports Senate debate on the Dominican annexation inquiry, in which amendments by Senator Sumner
records.summary_en: The paper reports Senate debate on the Dominican annexation inquiry, in which amendments by Senator Sumner, including withdrawing U.S. naval forces from Dominican territory before the commission began its investigation, were rejected. Other rejected amendments concerned whether a Dominican government was authorized to treat for annexation and whether the Dominican constitution forbade ceding territory.

Otras enmiendas rechazadas trataban de si un gobierno dominicano estaba autorizado a negociar la anexión y de si la constitución dominicana prohibía ceder territorio.

Mr. Morton of Indiana, interrupted to assert his belief in such a personage, as Cabral had sought an interview with the United States representatives at Hayti, and had expressed himself in favor of annexation. records.summary_en: The paper reports that Senator Sumner's amendments to the Dominican annexation inquiry were rejected, including proposals to withdraw U.S. naval aid, to inquire whether any Dominican government could authorize annexation, and to inquire into imprisonment or exile for hostility to annexation. records.full_text:
Misrule and oppressive taxation brought about the revolution of 1863, the restoration of the republic in 1865, and of Baez as President, but no cessation of the intrigues of Cabral, who, though much inferior in intelligence to Baez, who was educated in Paris, has many partisans in the interior, the principal strength of Baez being at the capital and the large seaports.

San Domingo is one of the richest in natural resources of the West India Islands, though thus far little has been done to develop them, notwithstanding the unusual mildness of its tropical climate and its many fine harbors. The soil is generally fertile in the highest degree, the soil of the mountain slopes being almost as fertile as that of the plains and valleys. The south part of the island is intersected and watered by many rivers, which not only increase the natural productiveness of the soil, but afford a means of communication with the interior districts.

records.headline: A correspondent who travelled extensively through the island reports that in Santiago, Puerto Plata, La Vega
records.summary_en: A correspondent who travelled extensively through the island reports that in Santiago, Puerto Plata, La Vega, Macoris and Moca the universal sentiment was in favour of annexation, with people heartily tired of war and the better class of merchants and property holders enthusiastically endorsing President Baez and his policy. He reports that the election at Azua resulted in an unprecedented majority in favour of annexation, and denies the charge that grants had been given to those sent to negotiate the treaty. A further dispatch adds that news of the appointment of a United States commission was generally favourably received at St. Domingo.
records.summary_es: Un corresponsal que viajó extensamente por la isla informa que en Santiago, Puerto Plata, La Vega, Macorís y Moca el sentimiento universal era favorable a la anexión, con un pueblo muy cansado de la guerra y la clase alta de comerciantes y propietarios apoyando con entusiasmo al presidente Báez y su política. Informa que la elección en Azua dio una mayoría sin precedentes a favor de la anexión, y niega la acusación de que se hubieran dado concesiones a los enviados a negociar el tratado. Otro despacho añade que la noticia del nombramiento de una comisión de los Estados Unidos fue recibida en general favorablemente en Santo Domingo.
records.passage: lar inquiries as to the sentiments of all classes on the subject. In the towns of Santiago, Puerta Plata, La Vega. Macoris and Moca the universal sentiment expressed was in favor of the measure. The people are heartily sick and tired of war, and look to annexation as the sound way to put a stop to such petty factions as that now held by Cabral. All the better class of merchants and property holders are enthusiastic in their endorsement of President Baez and his policy, and esteem him as a statesman and a patriot. The election at Azua resulted in an UNPRECEDENTED MAJORITY IN FAVOR OF ANNEXATION. and their voice was re-echoed all over the island. As to the charge that the [illegible] here to negotiate the treaty were interested in plantations, and that grants had been given them, it is like the balance of the Senator's statements? simply untrue. Your correspondent has had access to the records in the Department of the Interior, and knows that no grant ever has been given or offered to further this or any similar movement. He has, further, in the official handwriting of Minister Delmont, a specific denial of the charges made. This fact will be shown conclusively to the new Commission coming on its arrival. It is to be hoped in the future those opposing the proposed annexation will deal in facts, and not risk their reputations, as the Hon. Senator from Massachusetts has done, by making assertions unbecoming and unmanly.

records.full_text:
I have not ascertained satisfactorily what is the situation here, but I will briefly state my belief on the subject.

President Baez, as a statesman and patriot, sincerely desires the annexation of Dominica to America. Delay in accomplishing this is attended by financial trouble, anxiety and risk of insurrection. There is a very rich and large extent of valley country on the western frontier of Dominica, watered by the affluents of the Artibonite, containing some small towns, bearing Spanish names, but of which the Dominicans have not had the complete possession. It is here that Cabral operates with a small predatory party, which President Baez believes is procured and supported by Hayti. Cabral is now at San Juan, say forty miles east of the boundary line between Dominica and Hayti, according to the treaty between Spain and France, with his followers, variable in numbers, but always small, whence he makes raids and retreats as occasion requires. His last operation, noised about as a movement to defeat annexation, was very insignificant and amounted to a few persons killed, wounded and captured by his followers. At Azua and at the posts on several roads leading westward from it the Dominicans have some 1,000 or 1,500 troops. These seem to be in position for defence against incursion from without or insurrection from within. They appear to form the main organization of troops, though there are some troops here and in other places. Though the ordinary expenses of the military, which is the chief administration, are estimated at about $7,000 monthly, the revenue is so small and the paper money of the country is of so little value that the employés of the government have been a long time unpaid, and measures are now proposed looking to treating the paper money like our Continental currency and the French assignats, and providing for receiving some real money for duties wherewith to carry on the government.

records.headline: The editorial argues that Dominican annexation, if accomplished at all, should be accomplished honorably, and that it
records.summary_en: The editorial argues that Dominican annexation, if accomplished at all, should be accomplished honorably, and that it cannot be while the U.S. fleet lies in the waters of Santo Domingo after threats conveyed to the president of the Haitian republic by the American minister and admiral. It calls the recall of the ships the first necessity of the situation and says an admiral who threatened to open fire on the Haitian chief should be called before a court of inquiry, as that was an act of war Congress had not declared.

Califica la retirada de los buques de primera necesidad de la situación y dice que un almirante que amenazó con abrir fuego contra el jefe haitiano debería ser llamado ante un tribunal de investigación, pues aquello fue un acto de guerra que el Congreso no había declarado.

records.headline: Commander John Irwin reports how, at President Baez's request, he sent Lieutenant Commander McCook and the Nantasket
records.summary_en: Commander John Irwin reports how, at President Baez's request, he sent Lieutenant Commander McCook and the Nantasket to Azua, where partisans of Cabral, accompanied by Haitians, were causing trouble, and then to Puerto Plata when Baez warned that Luperon's partisans, aided by men from Turks Island, intended to seize that place. Añade que Báez informó después que Cabral avanzaba sobre Azua con una fuerza de haitianos y dominicanos, con el respaldo del gobierno haitiano, y le pidió llevar despachos a St. Thomas para el gobierno estadounidense.

records.summary_en: An editorial (from Harper's Weekly) against annexation under naval guns: with American warships lying before the Dominican and Haitian capitals to sustain Báez and coerce Haiti, the country cannot know whether Dominicans freely wish annexation, and the fleet should be recalled.

Public opinion in this country may finally acquiesce in Dominican annexation if the Dominicans themselves wish it. But while our ships are lying before their capital we cannot know whether they wish it or not. The Secretary of State admits that the influence of the ships was to keep the peace. Then if they had not been there, the peace might have been broken, and the Baez Government overthrown, and annexation defeated. If the United States mean to coerce the Dominicans, let the ships remain. But if we intend that their action shall be entirely free, let the Secretary of the Navy order the ships away. It expects the commission's report to give a favorable summing up of the island's material resources and a strong commendation of Samana as a naval station.
records.summary_es: Una carta describe la ruta prevista de los comisionados de anexión por Azua y el lado norte de la isla, probablemente con paradas en Puerto Príncipe y Puerto Plata, y enumera las cuestiones consideradas más importantes, incluida si una guerra con Haití seguiría pronto a la anexión y si el tesoro estadounidense podría soportar la asignación requerida. Espera que el informe de la comisión haga un balance favorable de los recursos materiales de la isla y una firme recomendación de Samaná como estación naval.

records.headline: A Herald dispatch from Samana reports local claims that there is no sickness there worth speaking about, while
records.summary_en: A Herald dispatch from Samana reports local claims that there is no sickness there worth speaking about, while cautioning that the people have every motive to make a favorable impression on the Commission. The writer finds the climate agreeable and the breezes on the bay balmy, the soil rich and the vegetation luxuriant with palms and coconut groves, but notes that little is raised for market except a few oranges and coconuts, and that improving the country is above all a question of labor.
records.summary_es: Un despacho del Herald desde Samaná recoge las afirmaciones locales de que allí no hay enfermedades de las que valga la pena hablar, advirtiendo a la vez que la gente tiene todos los motivos para causar una impresión favorable a la Comisión. El autor encuentra el clima agradable y las brisas de la bahía templadas, el suelo rico y la vegetación exuberante con palmeras y cocotales, pero señala que poco se cultiva para el mercado salvo unas cuantas naranjas y cocos, y que mejorar el país es ante todo una cuestión de mano de obra.
records.passage: here worth speaking about, one man, an industrious and enterprising white citizen of the United States, who has settled and acquired property here, declared this country the healthiest in the world, while in the room adjoining the one in which we sat and where he made the remark his only child was lying sick with fever. Then, the people say this is the hottest season of the year, though the sun is fifteen or sixteen degrees the other side of the equator, and in June it is right over head. This is called the dry season, although it rains every day and often many times a day. we may imagine what floods come down in the wet season. These heavy and almost constant rains may, however, modify the temperature and make the season of the summer solstice cooler than it would be otherwise. Looking, then, at the motive the people of Samana have for making a favorable impression upon the Commission and those accompanying it, and the natural enthusiasm of nearly all in this expedition over a country so luxuriant and a climate so much in contrast with that they had just left, it is not surprising that everything is viewed in couleur de rose. records.summary_en: The dispatch reports that the officials at Samana pray for annexation, and explains that Colonel Abreu, whom the commissioners had honoured as the chief man there, is only the special agent and military commander of the Dominican government, while the governor of this section is General Acosta. The commission, with its geologists, botanists, naturalists and correspondents, has been sending parties out to explore the country bordering the bay and up to the mouths of the Yuna River, and going ashore daily to talk with the people and examine their plantations.
records.summary_es: El despacho informa que los funcionarios de Samaná ruegan por la anexión, y explica que el coronel Abreu, a quien los comisionados habían honrado como el hombre principal del lugar, es solo el agente especial y comandante militar del gobierno dominicano, mientras que el gobernador de esta sección es el general Acosta. La comisión, con sus geólogos, botánicos, naturalistas y corresponsales, ha estado enviando grupos a explorar el país que bordea la bahía y hasta las bocas del río Yuna, y desembarcando a diario para hablar con la gente y examinar sus plantaciones.

records.headline: A Herald correspondent reports arriving at St. Domingo City
records.summary_en: A Herald correspondent reports arriving at St. Domingo City on February 3 after a thirty-five hours' passage from Samana, and describes the so-called harbor as a poor roadstead the Tennessee could not leave, where vessels roll heavily even in a light land breeze. In the morning the ship fired a salute of twenty-one guns, which the Dominican fort returned, and the correspondent describes St. Domingo as a quaint, ancient and dilapidated town of seven or eight thousand inhabitants, the oldest place built by Europeans in America.
records.summary_es: Un corresponsal del Herald informa de su llegada a la ciudad de Santo Domingo el 3 de febrero tras una travesía de treinta y cinco horas desde Samaná, y describe el llamado puerto como una mala rada que la Tennessee no podía abandonar, donde los buques se balancean pesadamente aun con una ligera brisa de tierra. Por la mañana el buque disparó una salva de veintiún cañonazos, que el fuerte dominicano devolvió, y el corresponsal describe Santo Domingo como una ciudad pintoresca, antigua y derruida de siete u ocho mil habitantes, el lugar más antiguo construido por europeos en América.

records.headline: The Tennessee arrived at Santo Domingo from Samana, a few hours after the Nantasket, and the United States commissioners
records.summary_en: The Tennessee arrived at Santo Domingo from Samana, a few hours after the Nantasket, and the United States commissioners came ashore. The dispatch recounts how President Baez's offer of an unoccupied palace for the commissioners was declined by their secretaries, who instead rented a smaller house belonging to Baez and then had to ask him for cots and other necessities, while the correspondents accepted the palace. That day the commission paid a formal visit to Baez, presenting President Grant's autograph letter, and Baez replied that he desired a closer union of the two republics and offered every facility for inquiry, including hearing opponents of annexation.
records.summary_es: El Tennessee llegó a Santo Domingo desde Samaná, pocas horas después del Nantasket, y los comisionados de los Estados Unidos bajaron a tierra. El despacho cuenta cómo el ofrecimiento del presidente Báez de un palacio desocupado para los comisionados fue rechazado por los secretarios de estos, que en su lugar alquilaron una casa más pequeña perteneciente a Báez y luego tuvieron que pedirle catres y otros artículos necesarios, mientras que los corresponsales sí aceptaron el palacio. Ese día la comisión hizo una visita formal a Báez, presentándole la carta autógrafa del presidente Grant, y Báez respondió que deseaba una unión más estrecha de las dos repúblicas y ofreció todas las facilidades para la investigación, incluida la de escuchar a los opositores de la anexión.

M., having been preceded a few hours by the Nantasket. The Commissioners sent for the American Consul, Dr. Ames, to come on board, and this morning they all came ashore. A MISUNDERSTANDING. An unpleasant incident has occurred, which shows either great ignorance and mismanagement on the part of those who conduct matters for the Commissioners or else great cowardice on their part. The messengers who came across country from Samana, after presenting their despatches to President Baez, received from him an offer of an unoccupied palace for the accommodation of the Commissioners and suite. This offer was not to include provisioning them, but simply to afford them proper accommodations. As it was extended through courtesy, and as quarters for such a large party were difficult to be obtained, the offer was accepted on behalf of the Commissioners. When the latter arrived, however, their private secretaries in their wisdom deemed that public opinion in the United States would frown upon such an undemocratic proceeding, and vetoed the whole arrangement. Wise philosophers! They declined the kind offer and hired, for a small price, a smaller house, which, however, belongs to President Baez as his private property; and then, not being able otherwise to procure cots and many other necessary articles, they were compelled finally to ask President Baez to furnish them. records.headline: A Santo Domingo dispatch says President Baez emphatically denies reports that he intended to leave the country, and that because of reported
records.summary_en: A Santo Domingo dispatch says President Baez emphatically denies reports that he intended to leave the country, and that because of reported troubles at Azua the United States steamer Nantasket would probably sail for that port. The commission had a long interview with Baez and his cabinet, and Baez offered guides, interpreters and, if needed, a guard, and agreed to grant safe conduct to the city even to Cabral or any of his partisans whom the commission wished to consult.

La comisión tuvo una larga entrevista con Báez y su gabinete, y Báez ofreció guías, intérpretes y, si fuera necesario, una guardia, y aceptó conceder salvoconducto hasta la ciudad incluso a Cabral o a cualquiera de sus partidarios a quienes la comisión deseara consultar.

The manner in which information is to be obtained from all parts of the island was particularly debated, and certain arrangements made by which the enemies of Baez and the annexation scheme may be reached, The Commission having asked the President's aid in the matter, the latter said he would cheerfully furnish guides, interpreters, and, if thought necessary, would supply a guard to protect the Commission or their agents through the island, He also consented to grant safe conduct to this city to all persons whom the Commission desired to consult. During the stay of the commission at Samana Bay the Tribune correspondent wrote as follows: Samana is a poor little dirty place enough, for all its romantic and picturesque appearance. It is built in a random haphazard sort of way along half-a-mile of curving shore at the foot of a ridge of high wooded hills, and what with its rambling lanes and grotesque huts, I think it is one of the most absurd places I ever saw. There are [illegible] or [illegible] buildings, all told, consisting for the most part of a light framework of scantlings brought from the States, and clapboarded with bamboos split in half and pressed flat by piling stones upon them while wet. records.headline: A Tribune correspondent describes the San Domingo expedition's voyage to Samana Bay: charming weather for two days
records.summary_en: A Tribune correspondent describes the San Domingo expedition's voyage to Samana Bay: charming weather for two days, then stormy seas from the latitude of Hatteras onward, until land was sighted on the morning of January 24. Rounding Cape Cabron and entering the bay, the party saw the roofs of Santa Barbara de Samana, palm tops, green hills and small farm patches, and dropped anchor in the outer harbor at two o'clock that afternoon.
records.summary_es: Un corresponsal del Tribune describe el viaje de la expedición a Santo Domingo hasta la bahía de Samaná: tiempo encantador durante dos días y luego mares tormentosos desde la latitud de Hatteras en adelante, hasta que se avistó tierra en la mañana del 24 de enero. Al doblar el Cabo Cabrón y entrar en la bahía, el grupo vio los techos de Santa Bárbara de Samaná, las copas de las palmas, las colinas verdes y pequeños pedazos de tierra cultivada, y echó el ancla en el puerto exterior a las dos de esa tarde.
records.passage: A [letter?] in the New York Tribune giving an account of the San Domingo expedition, in addition to what we published yesterday: THE [illegible] [illegible] THE ARRIVAL AT SAMANA BAY THE BAY AND ITS SURROUNDINGS. Writing in the Bay of Samana, on January 27, the Tribune correspondent says: We had charming weather for the first two days out cold, indeed, but bright and clear, with fresh and favoring winds, and every prospect of a pleasant voyage. But toward evening of the second day, in the rough latitude of Hatteras, our troubles began, and from that time until we neared our destination we experienced abundant discomfort and many stormy seas, though without any specially severe test of the seagoing qualities of the frigate. Using generally both steam and sails, we have made a moderately quick passage; but the behavior of the vessel under steam is far from satisfactory, and the machinery is found to be full of serious defects. As a sailer, however, the ship is pronounced faultless. We had been out of sight of land six days and a half, when on the morning of the 24th we heard from the look-out in the maintop the welcome cry of "Land ho!" and the passengers rushed upon deck. records.headline: A correspondent describes his ship's arrival at Samana, sighting land on the morning of the 24th, tracing the mountain
records.summary_en: A correspondent describes his ship's arrival at Samana, sighting land on the morning of the 24th, tracing the mountain range westward from Cape Cabron, and entering the bay past hills, palm groves and small settlements to Santa Barbara de Samana. The ship anchored in the outer harbor about two miles from the village, where the American flag floated over the property leased by the United States and the steamer Nantasket lay, and the commissioners landed to visit the local authorities.
records.summary_es: Un corresponsal describe la llegada de su barco a Samaná, el avistamiento de tierra en la mañana del 24, el seguimiento de la cordillera hacia el oeste desde el cabo Cabrón, y la entrada a la bahía pasando colinas, palmerales y pequeños poblados hasta Santa Bárbara de Samaná. El barco ancló en el puerto exterior, a unas dos millas del pueblo, donde la bandera americana ondeaba sobre la propiedad arrendada por los Estados Unidos y se encontraba el vapor Nantasket, y los comisionados desembarcaron para visitar a las autoridades locales.

Thick clouds hung heavily over a dark line about two points off our starboard bow, hardly discernible at first; but as we came nearer we gradually traced the outline of the mountain range which stretched westward to the mainland from Cape Cabron at the extremity of the peninsula of Samana. Behind this mountain barrier and opening to the east lies the bay to which we were bound. The morning was the hottest we had yet felt. A burning sun blistered the deck. The brass work of the frigate glowed like fire, and the waters glittered like burnished metal under the blazing heavens. There was hardly a breath of air, and as we steamed through the calm sea the sails hung useless from the yards. Long before noon the whole country around the mouth of the bay was distinctly visible in outline. There were the hills rising abruptly close to the shore, the palisade-like rocks almost surrounding the peninsula, the irregular and picturesque profile of the range stretching back as far as the eye could reach. We could discover no table-land; we saw no beach; and at first there was no sign of life except in the waters, from which a flying fish darted now and then; nor was there much appearance of vegetation. It was not until we had rounded Cape Cabron and entered the mouth of the bay that the dingy aspect of the landscape changed, and we realized something of that tropical luxuriance and freshness upon which travellers have loved to dilate. records.headline: The correspondent describes sailing into Samana Bay on the 24th, rounding Cape Cabron to find Santa Barbara de
records.summary_en: The correspondent describes sailing into Samana Bay on the 24th, rounding Cape Cabron to find Santa Barbara de Samana coming into view, and anchoring in the outer harbour near the United States steamer Nantasket, with the American flag flying over the property leased by the United States. Ashore the next day, the party inspected the town's few public buildings, its Catholic church, a Methodist church being built, and schools whose pupils include descendants of the coloured colony sent here from Philadelphia, whose textbooks are all in English.
records.summary_es: El corresponsal describe la entrada en la bahía de Samaná el día 24, doblando el cabo Cabrón hasta ver aparecer Santa Bárbara de Samaná, y el fondeo en el puerto exterior cerca del vapor americano Nantasket, con la bandera americana ondeando sobre la propiedad arrendada por los Estados Unidos. Al día siguiente en tierra, el grupo inspeccionó los pocos edificios públicos del pueblo, su iglesia católica, una iglesia metodista en construcción, y escuelas cuyos alumnos incluyen descendientes de la colonia de color enviada aquí desde Filadelfia, cuyos libros de texto están todos en inglés.
records.passage: It was not until we had rounded Cape Cabron and entered the mouth of the bay that the dingy aspect of the landscape changed, and we realized something of that tropical luxuriance and freshness upon which travellers have loved to dilate. In the distance, we soon descried, peeping above the horizon, the roofs of Santa Barbara de Samana, and little by little the whole scene broke upon us in its delicious beauty. One by one appeared the spreading tops of the palms. The brown hue of the hills changed to the most brilliant shades of green, their sides showed here and there a little patch of farm-land shut in by waving forest, and over all the country was a mantle of that soft, beautiful verdure which we never see at home except after the showers of early summer. We could appreciate now the rapture with which Columbus (and we were sailing so they say in the very track of the discoverer) painted the beauties of this island paradise. Close to the shore, in a little gully through which a stream of water ran singing to the sea, stood a hut, with round thatched roof and a single window looking out upon the ocean. Waving palms shaded it in front and rear; blooming hills sheltered it from the winds, and close by was a huge ragged rock against which the lazy surf beat perpetual music. This perfect picture was succeeded by views of larger houses, with patches of cleared land and groves of cocoonuts and bananas. records.headline: A correspondent at Samana describes landing with the commissioners and inspecting the town's public buildings
records.summary_en: A correspondent at Samana describes landing with the commissioners and inspecting the town's public buildings, including its Catholic church, a Methodist church being built, and its schools, where the textbooks are all in English and published in Philadelphia. He also describes the barefoot, half-clad troops guarding the jail, their varied knives, swords and muskets, and a village where more than half of the eighty houses are in some way devoted to trade.
records.summary_es: Un corresponsal en Samaná describe el desembarco con los comisionados y la inspección de los edificios públicos del pueblo, incluidos su iglesia católica, una iglesia metodista en construcción y sus escuelas, donde los libros de texto están todos en inglés y publicados en Filadelfia. También describe a las tropas descalzas y semivestidas que guardan la cárcel, con sus variados cuchillos, espadas y mosquetes, y un pueblo donde más de la mitad de las ochenta casas se dedican de algún modo al comercio.
records.passage: some time was passed in pleasant conversation over the news from home and from the fleet. Later in the day the commissioners landed for a visit to the local authorities, and these latter distinguished officials hastened to return the compliment. It was not until the morning of the 25th that the rest of the party went ashore. SCENES AT SAMANA. After giving the description of the town, already published by us, the correspondent continues: We pushed our way through the lazy, grinning, good-natured crowd, and made an inspection of the public buildings of Samana. It did not take us long, for there are none at all except two churches and a calaboose and, perhaps, I should add a couple of school houses. The Catholic church is a rude structure, much larger than the inhabitants seem to require, and full of the oddest images dressed in quaint, not to say grotesque, habiliments. We tried to converse with the priest, but he spoke none of the three languages at the command of our party, so we gave it up. We afterwards learned that he was an Italian. A Methodist church is building under the auspices of the English Mission Society, and the British flag is displayed on the unfinished edifice as well as on the residence of the minister. The Rev. Joseph James is a colored man of ordinary intelligence, and has a congregation including about three hundred communicants, mostly descendants of the colored colony sent here from Philadelphia in [illegible]. records.headline: A dispatch from Samana reports that small parties of the scientific corps will be sent into the country in various directions
records.summary_en: A dispatch from Samana reports that small parties of the scientific corps will be sent into the country in various directions, and that those who examined the place as a naval station agreed the harbor where the coaling station stands should be obtained by the United States Government by lease or purchase. It says the commission hopes to start home soon after March 1, with no case of illness in the party.
records.summary_es: Un despacho de Samaná informa que pequeños grupos del cuerpo científico serán enviados al interior en varias direcciones, y que quienes examinaron el lugar como estación naval coincidieron en que el puerto donde está la estación carbonera debería ser obtenido por el Gobierno de los Estados Unidos mediante arrendamiento o compra. Dice que la comisión espera partir de regreso poco después del 1 de marzo, sin ningún caso de enfermedad en el grupo.
records.passage: that point in all directions. A second and less formal meeting was arranged to take place at Back's house, [EXPLANATIONS?]. Small parties of the scientific corps will be sent into the country from here in various directions. VALUE AS A NAVAL STATION. What was seen of the people around Samana was of little consequence compared with the investigation into the value of the place as a naval station. All seemed to agree that if the present condition of the finances would justify it, that the harbor where the coaling station is should be obtained by our government, by lease or purchase. SCENERY AND [illegible]. The magnificence of the foliage, beauty and grandeur of the mountains and [illegible] of the country cannot be overrated. There is, however, neither energy nor thrift. STARTING FOR HOME. The commission hopes to start home soon after the first of March. HEALTH OF THE PARTY. There has been no case of illness in the party, and the season is healthy everywhere in the island, so far as heard from. All United States officers upon the island are well.

[FROM OUR SPECIAL CORRESPONDENT] On Board THE TENNESSEE, Samana Bay, Jan. 30.—Samana is, without doubt, the most fortunate starting point for any exploring expedition. One cannot help accumulating a fund of enthusiasm which may help him endure possible future hardships and disappointments. He who has glowing views of annexation feels them confirmed, while the anti-annexationist is content to have his pet arguments overthrown by such a pleasant refutation. Far out at sea the rough outline of the yellowish mountains disappoints and prepares one for a rocky, barren coast but, as you approach, the somber mountains gradually disappear, and ranges of low hills, covered with the densest vegetation, come in sight. A week before we had been in New York, with cold and sleet and leafless trees; now we were warm with linen clothes, and the hills before us were covered with a mass of trees and vines, green beyond all description, a clear, fresh color, such as the woods with us have in Spring after a shower. The vegetation extended down to the very surf which dashed its spray over the graceful cocoa palm. Higher up were dense groves of cecropia and palmas reales—the former a slender, branchless tree with a tuft of large white leaves, the latter with a curiously swelled out trunk and thin wavy leaves. records.headline: The commissioners made an excursion to the plantation of Mrs. Dichmain
records.summary_en: The commissioners made an excursion to the plantation of Mrs. Dichmain, about two miles from Samana, where they drank fresh coconut milk and saw a primitive sugar mill turned by two bulls, with the juice boiled nearby into coarse brown sugar. Mrs. Dichmain, who has lived 42 years in Santo Domingo and has 15 children and 50 grandchildren, farms 100 acres producing bananas, pineapples, sugar, coffee and chocolate, and she told the visitors she was most decidedly in favor of annexation, longing intensely for quiet and order.
records.summary_es: Los comisionados hicieron una excursión a la plantación de la señora Dichmain, a unas dos millas de Samaná, donde bebieron leche fresca de coco y vieron un primitivo molino de azúcar movido por dos bueyes, con el jugo hervido cerca de allí hasta convertirlo en azúcar moreno grueso. La señora Dichmain, que lleva 42 años viviendo en Santo Domingo y tiene 15 hijos y 50 nietos, cultiva 100 acres que producen plátanos, piñas, azúcar, café y chocolate, y dijo a los visitantes que estaba decididamente a favor de la anexión, pues anhelaba intensamente la tranquilidad y el orden.

records.headline: The Herald's correspondent reports that the evidence taken at Samana, and his own dealings with the people, show a majority
records.summary_en: The Herald's correspondent reports that the evidence taken at Samana, and his own dealings with the people, show a majority in favor of annexation to the United States, which they expect would bring peace and security to a productive country left desolate by constant revolutions. He identifies the opposition as the Cabralists, who largely object only out of hostility to Baez, foreign merchants fearing the loss of their monopoly, and a limited anti-American feeling, while the Catholic clergy decline to express any opinion and some intelligent Dominicans fear their race would be swamped by a superior one.
records.summary_es: El corresponsal del Herald informa que las declaraciones recogidas en Samaná, y su propio trato con la gente, muestran una mayoría a favor de la anexión a los Estados Unidos, de la que esperan que traiga paz y seguridad a un país productivo dejado desolado por las constantes revoluciones. Identifica a la oposición como los cabralistas, que en gran parte objetan solo por hostilidad hacia Báez, los comerciantes extranjeros que temen perder su monopolio y un limitado sentimiento antiestadounidense, mientras que el clero católico se niega a expresar opinión alguna y algunos dominicanos ilustrados temen que su raza quede ahogada por una superior.

records.headline: A correspondent quartered in St. Domingo City describes
records.summary_en: A correspondent quartered in St. Domingo City describes the so-called Palace, the former palace of the Spanish Captain Generals, where several of the visiting party are lodged, and a superstition that no president can reside there and leave it alive, which has kept President Baez and other presidents from living there. He also describes the city as a fortified place of about five thousand people, with walls, a ditch and guarded gates, narrow streets and mostly one-story houses.
records.summary_es: Un corresponsal alojado en la ciudad de Santo Domingo describe el llamado Palacio, antiguo palacio de los Capitanes Generales españoles, donde se hospedan varios de los visitantes, y una superstición según la cual ningún presidente puede residir allí y salir con vida, lo que ha impedido que el presidente Báez y otros presidentes vivan en él. También describe la ciudad como una plaza fortificada de unos cinco mil habitantes, con murallas, un foso y puertas custodiadas, calles estrechas y casas en su mayoría de un piso.
records.passage: religion and religious orders the Spaniards brought with them. THE THEATRE. One of the largest convent churches is the theatre now, though, as might be supposed, it is little used. No European or American stars are likely to come here, nor even fourth-rate actors. THE PALACE. The best building, perhaps, in St. Domingo, is the so-called Palace, where several of our party are quartered. It was the viceregal Palace of the Spanish Captain Generals. It is not so old as some of the other buildings, and until a recent period was kept in order. It has the luxury of glass windows, which no other building I have seen has, and the floors are of coarse marble laid in squares. There was no furniture in it, and those of the Tennessee party who took quarters there had to provide themselves with stretchers to sleep on and such other things as they needed. This palace was offered by the government to the Commissioners for their accommodation while here; but the offer was declined, because it was thought such regal style would sound badly at home and because the Commissioners did not wish to accept any favor from the government.

records.headline: A section of the commissioners' report describes life on the Samana peninsula, where the only schools the party
records.summary_en: A section of the commissioners' report describes life on the Samana peninsula, where the only schools the party could hear of included a small private school of not more than 20 pupils, started by the late Rev. Dr. Judd and now kept by his son at a dollar a month in tuition. It notes that the Methodists, whose meeting house was burned by the Spanish troops in 1863, are building a new one to hold 500 persons, that settlers of American descent are regarded as the foremost men in the settlement, and that farming is done on small plots of three to five acres with heavy hoes, picks and machetes rather than ploughs.
records.summary_es: Una sección del informe de los comisionados describe la vida en la península de Samaná, donde las únicas escuelas de las que el grupo pudo tener noticia incluían una pequeña escuela privada de no más de 20 alumnos, fundada por el difunto reverendo Dr. Judd y ahora a cargo de su hijo, con una matrícula de un dólar al mes. Señala que los metodistas, cuya casa de reunión fue quemada por las tropas españolas en 1863, están construyendo una nueva con capacidad para 500 personas, que los pobladores de ascendencia estadounidense son considerados los hombres más destacados del asentamiento y que la agricultura se hace en pequeñas parcelas de tres a cinco acres con azadas pesadas, picos y machetes en vez de arados.

We could hear of no other school on the peninsula, and were assured that there is no other church. The former minister here was Rev Mr Vanderhorst, whose son, Peter R., a trader, is the most intelligent man I have met in Samana. His patronymic will be recognized by the old Knickerbocker aristocracy. He and Mr James affirm that "those of American descent are the foremost men in the settlement, always have to go ahead, and are depended on for efficient action." They state that there is no interference between the churches, and that though the priest might grumble, no Catholic is molested for attending their church, the meeting house of the Methodists was burned by the Spanish troops in 1863, and they are building a new one to hold 500 persons, on the hill at the west end of the village, overlooking the extensive flat still farther west, where hundreds, some say thousands of their persecutors lie buried, smitten by the merciless pestilence.

records.summary_en: A dispatch from Santo Domingo City dated February 11 reports that the United States commission had met, exchanged views, and decided to make its full field of inquiry wider than first expected, naming the middle of April for its arrival in Washington. Expeditions were out across the island: Professors Blake and Crane on their way to Puerto Plata, Professor Ward exploring, parties gone to Azua and to examine the copper region, and others making botanical and medical researches, while the second payment for Samana had not been made, leaving Baez embarrassed and nearly all his officers without pay.

records.headline: The Sun argues that Mr. Baez
records.summary_en: The Sun argues that Mr. Baez does not seem to understand that the annexation treaty has been rejected by the Senate and the alternative treaty for leasing Samana Bay has lapsed, so the United States is not bound to pay him a second year's rent. It calls Samana a poor and unhealthy harbor where coal costs eighty-five dollars a ton, against twelve dollars at St. Thomas, and contrasts the $150,000 rent Baez asks with the $5,000 a year the United States pays for a coaling wharf at St. Thomas.
records.summary_es: The Sun argumenta que el Sr. Báez no parece comprender que el tratado de anexión ha sido rechazado por el Senado y que el tratado alternativo para arrendar la bahía de Samaná ha caducado, por lo que los Estados Unidos no están obligados a pagarle un segundo año de renta. Califica a Samaná como un puerto malo e insalubre donde el carbón cuesta ochenta y cinco dólares la tonelada, frente a doce dólares en St. Thomas, y contrasta los $150,000 de renta que pide Báez con los $5,000 al año que los Estados Unidos pagan por un muelle carbonero en St. Thomas.
records.passage: be impossible to get another hundred and fifty thousand dollars out of the Treasury without a vote of both House of Congress. Mr. Baez does not seem to understand that the treaty of annexation has been rejected by the Senate of the United States, and that the alternative treaty for the lease of Samana Bay has not been acted upon by that body, and has accordingly lapsed. The United States are not bound to pay him any second year's rent. It is true that the President of the United States has promised to pay it but Congress has not approved the promise and has not voted the money, and from present appearances it is not probable that it ever will vote it. records.headline: The editorial reports that the steamer Tennessee, after much talk of her loss, has reached the Bay of Samana safely
records.summary_en: The editorial reports that the steamer Tennessee, after much talk of her loss, has reached the Bay of Samana safely, and that some of her passengers, including members of the San Domingo Commission, crossed the island to the city of Santo Domingo on the south coast. Quoting a Republican writer's account of the country and its people, the editorial argues against President Grant's annexation of St. Domingo and warns that he and his friends will likely find the Dominicans a burden before many months are over.
records.summary_es: El editorial informa que el vapor Tennessee, tras mucho hablarse de su pérdida, ha llegado sano y salvo a la bahía de Samaná, y que algunos de sus pasajeros, incluidos miembros de la Comisión de Santo Domingo, cruzaron la isla hasta la ciudad de Santo Domingo, en la costa sur. Citando el relato de un escritor republicano sobre el país y su gente, el editorial argumenta contra la anexión de Santo Domingo por el presidente Grant y advierte que él y sus amigos probablemente encontrarán a los dominicanos una carga antes de que pasen muchos meses.
records.passage: of Africans with that of Europeans the product of which is a human mass of as much laziness, idleness and essential worthlessness as can be found on any part of the globe, scarcely excepting barbarous Africa and the morally effete islands of the Pacific. Were ancient Hispaniola even a blessing to us, modern Dominicans would be a curse, as Gen. Grant and his friends will probably find before they are many months older. As to its inhabitants, we have the high Republican authority of Mr. Fulton for this: "The majority of the people of the country are of pure African descent. Of this there cannot be the slightest doubt, and we could trace but little evidence of what is called a mixture of races among the country people, though the population of Santo Domingo is mixed and motley. Among the elderly men and women especially there is a grace of carriage and a dignity of manner that is peculiarly attractive, and reminds one of the high-toned Spanish character. They are cleanly but very slightly appareled. The men wear a white mantle when out at night or to protect them from the rain, and assume quite a picturesque aspect. They all carry swords at their side, and I saw some boys not over fifteen years of age with the inevitable sword. Thus with the annexation of St. Domingo comes "the inevitable darkie" in all his grandeur, to beautify and harmonize our Model Republic. To the practical advantages of the Southern, Gen. records.headline: Herald correspondence from Samana reports that the United States Commission, with its geologists, botanists
records.summary_en: Herald correspondence from Samana reports that the United States Commission, with its geologists, botanists, naturalists and press correspondents, has been at work since arriving, sending parties out to explore the country bordering the bay up to the mouth of the Yuna river and into the interior. The commissioners go ashore daily to talk with the villagers and examine their small cleared plantations, while the correspondent cautions that newcomers, dazzled by the warm climate and lush growth, are viewing everything in rose color, though the soil is rich, vegetation grows rapidly, and palms, oranges and coconuts abound.
records.summary_es: Una correspondencia del Herald desde Samaná informa que la Comisión de los Estados Unidos, con sus geólogos, botánicos, naturalistas y corresponsales de prensa, ha estado trabajando desde su llegada, enviando grupos a explorar el territorio que bordea la bahía hasta la desembocadura del río Yuna y hacia el interior. Los comisionados desembarcan a diario para hablar con los aldeanos y examinar sus pequeñas plantaciones despejadas, mientras el corresponsal advierte que los recién llegados, deslumbrados por el clima cálido y la vegetación exuberante, lo ven todo de color de rosa, aunque el suelo es rico, la vegetación crece con rapidez y abundan las palmas, las naranjas y los cocos.

Several parties have been sent out from the Commission to explore the country bordering the bay, up to the mouths of the [Yuna?] river and in the interior. Every day the Commissioners and others have been ashore to talk with the people of the village and to examine the so-called plantations, which are merely little cleared spots, imperfectly cultivated, and ascertain what are the natural products of the soil. The sudden transition from cold and dreary winter at home to this warm climate and luxuriant verdure has made them very enthusiastic. It is amusing to hear them as they return to the ship exclaim in glowing language about the beauty and richness of the island. records.headline: A correspondent in Samana finds the climate most agreeable and the bay breezes balmy, but the land mostly dense wood
records.summary_en: A correspondent in Samana finds the climate most agreeable and the bay breezes balmy, but the land mostly dense wood with only a few poorly cultivated acres, though the rich soil could grow sugar cane, coffee, cocoa and oranges abundantly if labor could be found. He describes an interview in which President Baez pressed the country's boundless resources and the people's wish for annexation, and he questions the enormous land grant to Fabens, said to cover a tenth of the whole republic, which Baez defended but was also said to regret.
records.summary_es: Un corresponsal en Samana encuentra el clima muy agradable y las brisas de la bahía templadas y refrescantes, pero el territorio es en su mayor parte bosque denso con solo unos pocos acres mal cultivados, aunque el suelo rico podría producir caña de azúcar, café, cacao y naranjas en abundancia si se encontrara mano de obra. Describe una entrevista en la que el presidente Baez insistió en los recursos ilimitados del país y en el deseo de anexión del pueblo, y cuestiona la enorme concesión de tierras a Fabens, que según se dice abarca una décima parte de toda la república, la cual Baez defendió pero también, según se dijo, lamentó haber hecho.

records.headline: A dispatch from Santo Domingo dated January 23, 1871, describes sailing into Samana Bay and anchoring about two
records.summary_en: A dispatch from Santo Domingo dated January 23, 1871, describes sailing into Samana Bay and anchoring about two miles from Santa Barbara, the only town on the peninsula. It describes the town's roughly one hundred small bamboo and palm houses, its roughly three hundred inhabitants, many of them descendants of a colony of Black Americans sent there more than forty-five years earlier, and its small trade in tobacco, hides and woods.
records.summary_es: Un despacho de Santo Domingo fechado el 23 de enero de 1871 describe la entrada navegando a la Bahía de Samaná y el fondeo a unas dos millas de Santa Bárbara, el único pueblo de la península. Describe las cerca de cien casas pequeñas de bambú y palma del pueblo, sus cerca de trescientos habitantes, muchos de ellos descendientes de una colonia de negros americanos enviada allí más de cuarenta y cinco años antes, y su pequeño comercio de tabaco, cueros y maderas.
records.passage: At 11 o'clock in the morning we were only seven miles from the entrance of the harbor, and as we slowly sailed between Cape Samana and Cape Raphael, entering the magnificent gulf, we thought we [could?] understand the feelings of Columbus when he beheld the same beautiful green hills, and kissed the earth with transport. At 1:45 o'clock (exactly seven days after leaving New York) we anchored in Samana Bay, about two miles from the town of Santa Barbara, commonly called on American maps Samana. By-the-way, we had found a very great diversity in the topographical charts of this island, and the only correct guide is probably the map prepared at the instance of President Baez [illegible]. The town lies upon Samana Bay, a little harbor about three miles in depth on the southeastern portion of the peninsula which bears its name, and the [Gulf?] has the same dimension. SANTA BARBARA. The only town upon the peninsula is Santa Barbara, opposite which we are anchored. It nestles at the foot of the hills on the beach, and would be called a village in America, and a very wretched one, too.
