records.headline: Writing from San Domingo on February 15, 1871, the correspondent describes the capital on the western bank of the river
records.summary_en: Writing from San Domingo on February 15, 1871, the correspondent describes the capital on the western bank of the river Ozama, a walled city 375 years old that is now utterly indefensible against modern artillery by land or sea. He walks through its ruins, above all the great Franciscan religious house covering several acres, where a tall orange tree laden with fruit grows in the very centre of the roofless church, bees swarm in the crevices of its walls, and animals are stabled by its altars.
records.summary_es: Escribiendo desde Santo Domingo el 15 de febrero de 1871, el corresponsal describe la capital en la orilla occidental del río Ozama, una ciudad amurallada de 375 años que hoy es totalmente indefendible contra la artillería moderna por tierra o por mar. Recorre sus ruinas, sobre todo la gran casa religiosa de los franciscanos, que cubre varios acres, donde un alto naranjo cargado de fruta crece en el centro mismo de la iglesia sin techo, las abejas bullen en las grietas de sus muros, y hay animales estabulados junto a sus altares.
records.passage: Is very massive, lead to the country, the chief of which is the Puerto del Conde, just outside this gate is a cemetery. Past this runs the old Spanish highway along the southern coast to Azua, once a fine road, but now akin to everything else in this blasted and ruined land, if any one doubts the "great first cause," —the all-prevailing law that controls the universe, let him come and look at Dominica. If the cry of Cacique and Carib rises to heaven for plundered kingdoms, and slaughtered households; —if the land is red with the blood of her children;—so, too, it is full of the bones of her oppressors, and in less than four centuries their monuments have crumbled and their mightiest works have perished. This city is full of ruins, and no small part of its limited area is occupied by them. The most impressive are those of the great religious house of the Franciscans, located on the highest ground within the walls, and covering several acres, with the wreck of buildings and desolated gardens. Ascending a steep street over antiquated pavements which grandee and Caballero have trodden before you, you pass under a massive portal, and stand in a growth of shrubbery and trees, so thick that the eyes can hardly penetrate it. An orange tree 80 feet high, laden with fruit stands in the very center. records.headline: A correspondent writing from Santo Domingo describes the city as orderly and its people as honest in their dealings
records.summary_en: A correspondent writing from Santo Domingo describes the city as orderly and its people as honest in their dealings, estimating the population at no more than about 8,000 and saying he has seen no intoxicated Dominican or brawl since arriving. He then turns to the United States commission, which in two weeks had conferred with the government, received deputations, questioned officials and examined records, while members set out to investigate Azua, Puerto Plata, Santiago de los Caballeros and other districts.
records.summary_es: Un corresponsal que escribe desde Santo Domingo describe la ciudad como ordenada y a su gente como honesta en sus tratos, estima la población en no más de unos 8.000 habitantes y dice que no ha visto a ningún dominicano ebrio ni ninguna riña desde su llegada. Luego pasa a la comisión de los Estados Unidos, que en dos semanas había conferenciado con el gobierno, recibido delegaciones, interrogado a funcionarios y examinado registros, mientras sus miembros salían a investigar Azua, Puerto Plata, Santiago de los Caballeros y otros distritos.
records.passage: what they mean to take, they appear to be honest and as faithful to trusts as their laziness will permit. The order of the city is perfect, and voluntarily so. We have not yet seen an intoxicated Dominican, and no brawl has occurred since we came here I should say that the population does not exceed 8000, though as high as 10,000 is claimed. But I have traversed nearly every street, and looked into all the odd places, and I cannot find 6000. In the northern and western sections are many huts made of narrow slabs overlapping each other and nailed to posts set in the ground. These have thatched roofs and earthen floors, and contain the densest population but they are very neat; and in order and cleanliness put to shame the tenements of the similar class in our Massachusetts towns. The health of the community appears to be reasonably good, and the same rules hold here that should be observed at Samana. To become acclimated kindly, and to live comfortably, "take care of yourself." records.headline: In the closing of a published letter on San Domingo, the writer argues the case for annexation on the ground that a united
records.summary_en: In the closing of a published letter on San Domingo, the writer argues the case for annexation on the ground that a united United States, with its commerce growing, would have in Samana an ever-ready harbor and safe retreat. He adds that a government stands on fear or on affection, and that it would be unwise to display only enough force to irritate but not enough to overawe.
records.summary_es: En el cierre de una carta publicada sobre Santo Domingo, el autor defiende la anexión con el argumento de que unos Estados Unidos unidos, con su comercio en crecimiento, tendrían en Samana un puerto siempre listo y un refugio seguro. Añade que un gobierno se sostiene sobre el temor o sobre el afecto, y que sería imprudente mostrar solo la fuerza suficiente para irritar pero no la bastante para imponer respeto.
records.passage: more and demand of them no less than we, in the ardor of our honest purpose, have done, and hope yet to do for our country's weal. This, I think, is the main argument—or at least a sufficient one; and with our country united, except in that division by party that makes the equipoise graceful with our commerce growing and its ocean [illegible] around Samana offering an ever-ready harbor and safe retreat, the future must develop future wants or dangers ere we could form for it future wishes or safeguards. Besides, a government can stand upon but one of two foundations—fear or affection. They are usually blended, but one or the other must largely predominate. Force characterizes the one, kindness the other, and it would seem unwise to display an amount of force sufficient only to irritate, but too small and marked to overawe. Pennsylvania has great cause for congratulation upon the position her Governor has taken on this subject. His message has the ring of the true metal, and he had struck in peace, as he did in war, so often, in the right place at the right time, a telling blow and with that true political sagacity that marks the statesman, is in the advance of, but not beyond, the true sentiment of the hour. Having periled his life in the subjugation of organized treason, and having enrolled his name high on the list of his country's bravest defenders, it is to him and his compeers that the nation now looks for such counsel as marks at once the soldier in magnanimity and the statesman in wisdom. And such he gives.

records.headline: A report of the United States Commission finds the people of Samana enthusiastic and unanimous for annexation
records.summary_en: A report of the United States Commission finds the people of Samana enthusiastic and unanimous for annexation, though their opinion should not be taken for that of a majority of the islanders, since all the trade, protection and support of the settlement come from the United States. In a sample conversation, a resident says annexation means getting into the States and having law, that it gives protection for themselves and their property and prevents the wars that have destroyed their crops a dozen times, and that many will not stay if the annexation scheme is defeated.
records.summary_es: Un informe de la Comisión de los Estados Unidos encuentra que el pueblo de Samana está entusiasta y unánime a favor de la anexión, aunque su opinión no debe tomarse por la de la mayoría de los isleños, ya que todo el comercio, la protección y el apoyo del asentamiento provienen de los Estados Unidos. En una conversación de ejemplo, un residente dice que la anexión significa entrar en los Estados y tener ley, que da protección para ellos y su propiedad y evita las guerras que han destruido sus cosechas una docena de veces, y que muchos no se quedarán si el plan de anexión es derrotado.

records.headline: An exploring party of the commission travelled from Samana up the Yuna River and overland to St. Domingo
records.summary_en: An exploring party of the commission travelled from Samana up the Yuna River and overland to St. Domingo, finding at Punta Gorda only lignite coal, worthless for fuel, and a river navigable by small boats for forty-two miles through an extremely fertile plain. The party passed through San Francisco de Macoris, a town of about 8,000 people making cigars and raising stock, and through La Vega, Cotuy and the mountain ranges beyond, and reports that the people along the route favoured annexation with great unanimity.
records.summary_es: Un grupo explorador de la comisión viajó desde Samaná remontando el río Yuna y por tierra hasta Santo Domingo, y encontró en Punta Gorda solo carbón de lignito, sin valor como combustible, y un río navegable por embarcaciones pequeñas durante cuarenta y dos millas a través de una llanura sumamente fértil. El grupo pasó por San Francisco de Macorís, un pueblo de unos 8.000 habitantes que fabrica cigarros y cría ganado, y por La Vega, Cotuí y las cordilleras más allá, e informa que la gente a lo largo de la ruta favorecía la anexión con gran unanimidad.

records.summary_en: With the commission at Port-au-Prince: Commissioner Howe sends a liberated Haitian prisoner to invite Cabral to a meeting; the commissioners - Wade and Howe now both for annexation, White still opposed - prepare a favorable report while waiting for White's overland journey from Santo Domingo City.

records.passage: desired to converse with him on the great subject of annexation. Many rumors were prevalent as to the chances of the messenger ever reaching Cabral's lines, doubts being expressed that Baez would permit him to actually go through. Yesterday, however, the 6th inst., information was received on board the Tennessee that a messenger had made his appearance at the Haytien lines, bearing a despatch from Cabral, and a courier had immediately been sent from this place for instruction as to whether the letter should be received. The Commissioners were informed by the Haytien authorities that, as they desired to preserve the strictest neutrality between the contending forces in the Dominican portion of the island, they would only allow the messenger to come through their territory at the request of the Commission, and then to be received on the vessel. Dr. Howe immediately made preparations for accepting the messenger and endeavoring to see Cabral if possible, but Mr. Wade considered that the proper course was to treat him as an outlaw and a cutthroat, and not to have any dealings with him. The Doctor, however, went ashore, where he remained until nine o'clock in the evening. The result has not yet been made known. THE VIEWS OF THE COMMISSIONERS. Without doubt Ben Wade is strongly in favor of annexation, having become convinced of the strong and unanimous desire on the part of the people for it. records.summary_en: According to the *Worcester daily spy* on March 17, 1871, U.S. commissioners Messrs. Wade and Howe met with the president of the Haitian republic and his cabinet. Mr. Wade stated that the commissioners were charged with making inquiries regarding the Dominican republic with a view toward more intimate relations, though the meeting itself had no reference to annexation. records.full_text: PORT AU PRINCE, March 7.—The commission reached here the second of March, from Azua. All are in excellent health. They will wait here for Commissioner White, who is expected here by the 10th, bringing with him two scientific expeditions, under Professors Blake and Ward, that crossed before him. The Tennessee will then start immediately for home, touching at Santiago de Cuba and Key West for coal. The questions of debt and disputed boundary are the most important since the last dispatches. The Haytiens are bitterly opposed to annexation. The commissioners, however, were received civilly. Cabral's strength consists almost wholly of Haytien support. The information that the Tennessee had been reported missing first reached the party here. The statement of Gen. Banks that she was unseaworthy was received with great indignation, and denounced as heartlessly cruel. She is one of the strongest and best ships in the navy, with a select company of efficient officers, who expect now, unless delayed by the Nantasket, to reach home by the 25th of March, or, at the farthest, the 1st of April. A delay of one week from this cause is possible, and if the ship is not heard from for two weeks it should not cause anxiety. Mail from the commission leaves for New York to-day by the steamer Port au Prince.

records.headline: A letter from Azua dated February 25, 1871, describes excursions by the visiting overland party to mineral springs
records.summary_en: A letter from Azua dated February 25, 1871, describes excursions by the visiting overland party to mineral springs about eighteen miles away, including a hot sulphur spring, and to a petroleum district a few miles from Azua. At the oil wells they found a derrick and dilapidated machinery, two bored wells and visible oil, and were told former American Consul Arthur Folsom had invested about $10,000 there and secured a hundred barrels of good lubricating oil.
records.summary_es: Una carta de Azua fechada el 25 de febrero de 1871 describe excursiones del grupo visitante a unos manantiales minerales situados a unas dieciocho millas, incluido un manantial caliente de azufre, y a un distrito petrolero a pocas millas de Azua. En los pozos de petróleo encontraron una torre y maquinaria deteriorada, dos pozos perforados y petróleo visible, y les dijeron que el ex cónsul americano Arthur Folsom había invertido allí unos 10.000 dólares y obtenido cien barriles de buen aceite lubricante.
records.passage: an unlimited amount of rock salt; indeed the story is that it is a mountain of salt. We have been unable to visit it on account of the very unsettled condition of the country. A PETROLEUM EXCURSION. On Sunday morning last we secured horses, provisions and a guide and started for a visit to a petroleum district distant a few miles from Azua. For a short distance we followed a main road, which was in pretty good condition; but soon leaving this we struck into a narrow wood path winding around through the dense chaparral, swaying our bodies and bending our heads to avoid the low branches, most of which were provided with sharp thorns. The morning was well advanced when we started and the sun was quite hot, but we have become somewhat accustomed to the heat and do not mind it as we did at first. Soon we came to a beautiful spring, carefully protected from animals by an enclosure of woven branches. The water was not very cold, but was good, and its appearance had a refreshing effect upon us. Near this spring we found several large mango trees, where we left our pack mule and servant, with directions to prepare our repast by the time we should return from the oil wells. A short distance further on we came to the petroleum, and found that considerable labor had been expended here in order to make use of the oil. A derrick was still standing and machinery was lying about in a dilapidated condition. Two wells had been bored, and a considerable supply of oil obtained, large quantities of which were visible. records.headline: In a letter to Benjamin F. Wade
records.summary_en: In a letter to Benjamin F. Wade at Azua, Captain William G. Temple begs him to withhold his consent to a proposed expedition and to ask President Baez to forbid the passage of the party through his lines. However remote the chances of their capture may seem, Temple argues, the chances of deriving any benefit from their journey are more remote still, and he adds that there are other points of view he does not care to commit to writing.

About ten days ago, our telegraphic dispatches gave an incoherent account of riots and murders in Meridian, Mississippi. The statement was in substance that a large fire had occurred there some days before, that a negro was on trial in the city court, charged with being the incendiary, and that while the trial was in progress, a negro shot the presiding judge, Bramlette, upon which a riot ensued, eight or ten negroes were shot, Mr. Sturges, the mayor of the city, a native of Connecticut, left the place at midnight by order of the mob, with a promise never to return, and the series of crimes was wound up by the burning of the house of another negro and the African church. This story, while it left no doubt that the town had been the scene of riot and outrage, in which the negroes and their friends were the principal sufferers, gave a very obscure account of the origin of the disturbances, with the implication that the colored people were responsible for them. records.headline: The excerpt prints a Haitian protest against U.S. annexation of the Dominican portion of the island
records.summary_en: The excerpt prints a Haitian protest against U.S. annexation of the Dominican portion of the island, deploring the United States' course of territorial conquest entered on the strength of Baez's plebiscite. The protest proclaims that the Haitian people desire to live in peace and amity and develop commercial relations with the United States, and hopes the annexation will be rejected by the U.S. Senate or Congress.

La protesta proclama que el pueblo haitiano desea vivir en paz y amistad y desarrollar relaciones comerciales con Estados Unidos, y espera que la anexión sea rechazada por el Senado o el Congreso de Estados Unidos.

records.headline: A correspondent of the Boston Advertiser who accompanied the commissioners writes that its last days at the capital
records.summary_en: A correspondent of the Boston Advertiser who accompanied the commissioners writes that its last days at the capital were spent ascertaining the full extent of San Domingo's debt and the concessions made to private individuals, and that although the authorities insisted a million and a half dollars would discharge the entire public debt, a list of pending claims prepared after persistent effort made the debt much larger. He reports that under the terms Baez was willing to offer, the public lands not already disposed of were to be held to settle the claims, and that Baez had staged the show of support for annexation, with societies coming at his request and men who declared for the project in public giving strong reasons against it in private.
records.summary_es: Un corresponsal del Boston Advertiser que acompañó a los comisionados escribe que sus últimos días en la capital se dedicaron a averiguar la magnitud completa de la deuda de Santo Domingo y las concesiones hechas a particulares, y que aunque las autoridades insistían en que un millón y medio de dólares saldaría toda la deuda pública, una lista de reclamaciones pendientes preparada tras un esfuerzo persistente hizo la deuda mucho mayor. Informa que, según los términos que Báez estaba dispuesto a ofrecer, las tierras públicas aún no enajenadas quedarían afectas al pago de las reclamaciones, y que Báez había montado la demostración de apoyo a la anexión, con sociedades que acudían a petición suya y hombres que en público se declaraban por el proyecto y en privado daban fuertes razones en contra.

He says: "The Tennessee, with two of the Commissioners, Mr. Wade and Dr. Howe, arrived here from Azua on the 3d instant. Here they will await the arrival of Mr. White, who came across by land from San Domingo to Puerto Plata. The work of the Commission was really finished before it came to Hayti, as it had been decided, since ascertaining the temper of the people and government there, not to ask any direct questions in regard to their claims against or relations to San Domingo. The investigation has probably been as thorough as was possible in so short a time, though much of this brief period has been consumed by over a dozen changes in plans, each necessarily involving delay. The harmony which marked the first week of the work at the capital was unfortunately almost entirely destroyed toward the close of the stay there; and this, of course, detracted much from the efficiency of the inquiry and the value of the results. records.summary_en: In a letter from Azua, W. G. Temple asks Commissioner B. F. Wade to withhold consent to a proposed expedition and to ask President Baez to forbid the gentlemen's passage through his lines. The correspondence adds that a new plan had been devised since arriving at Azua: Dr. Howe questioned prisoners and deserters from Cabral's force and, with Baez's consent, sent one prisoner back to the mountains with a letter to the revolutionary chieftain requesting a conference on Haitian territory, the messenger to receive three Spanish doubloons on his return.

records.headline: Senator Sumner argued, in the paper's account, that Baez was maintained in power by the U.S. Navy
records.summary_en: Senator Sumner argued, in the paper's account, that Baez was maintained in power by the U.S. Navy to enable him to carry out the sale of his country, and that the neighboring republic of Haiti was violently menaced in breach of public law. Sumner contended that the promise to employ the war powers without the authority of Congress was void, since the Constitution gives Congress the power to declare war.

Sumner afirmó que la promesa de emplear los poderes de guerra sin la autoridad del Congreso era nula, ya que la Constitución otorga al Congreso el poder de declarar la guerra.

records.headline: A Senate speech charges that Baez was sustained in power by the United States Navy while the annexation voting
records.summary_en: A Senate speech charges that Baez was sustained in power by the United States Navy while the annexation voting proceeded, citing a dispatch of March 19, 1870 placing the Severn at Santo Domingo, the Swatara sent to Samana, the Nantasket to Puerto Plata and the Yantic in the river, and an official's sworn testimony that the navy's acts were protecting Baez from the citizens of St. Domingo. It also tells how the American citizen Davis Hatch was arrested on a trumped-up charge and, even after his formal pardon, kept in prison at the instance of Cazneau and with Fabens's connivance to prevent his opposition to the treaty, as a Dominican minister's note admitted his imprisonment was only to prevent his hostile action in New York.
records.summary_es: Un discurso en el Senado acusa que Baez fue sostenido en el poder por la Marina de los Estados Unidos mientras se realizaba la votación sobre la anexión, citando un despacho del 19 de marzo de 1870 que situaba al Severn en Santo Domingo, al Swatara enviado a Samana, al Nantasket a Puerto Plata y al Yantic en el río, y el testimonio jurado de un funcionario de que los actos de la Marina protegían a Baez de los ciudadanos de Santo Domingo. También relata cómo el ciudadano americano Davis Hatch fue arrestado con un cargo inventado y, aun después de su perdón formal, mantenido en prisión a instancias de Cazneau y con la complicidad de Fabens para impedir su oposición al tratado, pues una nota de un ministro dominicano admitió que su encarcelamiento era solo para impedir su acción hostil en Nueva York.

records.headline: The article reprints a letter from Captain Temple of the Tennessee, written at Azua Bay on February 11, 1871
records.summary_en: The article reprints a letter from Captain Temple of the Tennessee, written at Azua Bay on February 11, 1871, warning Commissioner Wade that members of the Santo Domingo expedition who were about to travel overland toward Port-au-Prince would be placing themselves in the position of spies. Temple argues that because President Grant has ordered the American navy to protect the Baez government against any demonstration by Haiti or Cabral, Cabral would be justified in treating the travelers as spies liable to a drum-head court martial, and he asks Wade to refuse his consent to the trip and to ask President Baez to forbid their passage through his lines.

records.headline: In a Senate speech, Mr. Sumner recounts
records.summary_en: In a Senate speech, Mr. Sumner recounts how Cabral became president by a direct vote of the people, how the exiled Baez came to Washington seeking money and arms and got no encouragement, and how Cabral, pressed by financial difficulties, offered a lease of the Bay of Samana. He says Baez then denounced the sale of his country, organized a hostile force with the help of Salnave of Haiti, forced Cabral's capitulation on February 8, 1868, and was named dictator by an appointed convention, after which treaties were signed to sell the country for $1,500,000 and lease Samana Bay for $150,000 a year, with the United States Navy used to keep Baez in power.
records.summary_es: En un discurso en el Senado, el señor Sumner relata cómo Cabral llegó a la presidencia por voto directo del pueblo, cómo el exiliado Baez fue a Washington en busca de dinero y armas y no recibió apoyo, y cómo Cabral, presionado por dificultades financieras, ofreció el arrendamiento de la bahía de Samana. Dice que Baez denunció entonces la venta de su país, organizó una fuerza hostil con ayuda de Salnave de Haití, forzó la capitulación de Cabral el 8 de febrero de 1868 y fue nombrado dictador por una convención designada, tras lo cual se firmaron tratados para vender el país por $1,500,000 y arrendar la bahía de Samana por $150,000 al año, con la Marina de los Estados Unidos empleada para mantener a Baez en el poder.

records.headline: This account of Dominican history relates that after Baez was overthrown, General Jose Maria Cabral became lawful president
records.summary_en: This account of Dominican history relates that after Baez was overthrown, General Jose Maria Cabral became lawful president by the direct vote of the people in September 1866, the first time a question had been submitted to a direct vote in the country's history, and that peace ensued. It says Cabral, embarrassed by financial difficulties, turned to the United States offering a lease of the bay of Samana, while the exiled Baez denounced the sale of his country, organised a hostile force with the help of Salnave of Hayti, and compelled Cabral's capitulation on February 8, 1868, after which a convention named Baez Grand Citizen with unlimited powers and his enemies were exiled or executed.
records.summary_es: Este relato de la historia dominicana cuenta que, tras la caída de Báez, el general José María Cabral llegó a ser presidente legítimo por el voto directo del pueblo en septiembre de 1866, la primera vez que una cuestión se sometía al voto directo en la historia del país, y que sobrevino la paz. Dice que Cabral, agobiado por dificultades financieras, se dirigió a los Estados Unidos ofreciendo el arrendamiento de la bahía de Samaná, mientras Báez, desde el exilio, denunciaba la venta de su patria, organizaba una fuerza hostil con la ayuda de Salnave, de Haití, y obligaba a Cabral a capitular el 8 de febrero de 1868, tras lo cual una convención nombró a Báez Gran Ciudadano con poderes ilimitados y sus enemigos fueron exiliados o ejecutados.
records.passage: also manifesto of Cabral, assigning at still greater length reasons for the overthrow of Baez, and holding him up as the enemy of peace and union; also a manifesto by the Triumvirate, constituting the Provisional Government, declaring his infractions of the Constitution; also a manifesto from the General in command of the City of Santo Domingo, where, after denouncing the misdeeds of one man, it says, "this man, this monster, this speculator, this tyrant is Buenaventura Baez." Soon after the disappearance of Baez, his rival became lawful President by the direct vote of the people, according to the requirement of the Constitution. Different numbers of the official journal now before me contain the election returns in September, 1866, where the name of Gen. José Maria Cabral appears at the head of the poll. This is memorable as the first time in the history of Dominica when a question was submitted to the direct vote of the people. By that direct vote Cabral became President, and peace ensued. records.summary_en: The paper reports Senator Sumner argued President Grant usurped power by using U.S. naval power for Dominican annexation after the Senate rejected the treaty, while Senator Morton defended the accused and said the Haitian minister disavowed any desire to interfere while assisting Cabral to attack Dominica. Morton said the government merely notified Haiti it would not allow war on Dominica while negotiations were pending.
records.summary_es: El periódico informa que el senador Sumner argumentó que el presidente Grant usurpó el poder al usar el poder naval estadounidense para la anexión dominicana después de que el Senado rechazó el tratado, mientras el senador Morton defendió a los acusados y dijo que el ministro haitiano negó cualquier deseo de interferir mientras ayudaba a Cabral a atacar Dominica. Morton dijo que el gobierno simplemente notificó a Haití que no permitiría la guerra contra Dominica mientras las negociaciones estaban pendientes.

records.headline: Senator Morton's reply to Sumner: the commission could not negotiate, Haiti itself assured Minister Bassett it would not interfere
records.summary_en: Senator Morton's reply to Sumner: the commission could not negotiate, Haiti itself assured Minister Bassett it would not interfere with the Dominicans' free will, and the United States merely warned Haiti - which had given Cabral passage and war vessels - not to make war during the negotiations.
records.summary_es: La respuesta del senador Morton a Sumner: la comisión no podía negociar, Haití mismo aseguró al ministro Bassett que no interferiría con la libre voluntad de los dominicanos, y Estados Unidos solo advirtió a Haití - que había dado a Cabral paso y buques de guerra - que no hiciera la guerra durante las negociaciones.
records.passage: Mr. Morton then had read by the Secretary a dispatch to United States Minister Bassett, from the Haytien Secretary of Foreign Affairs, assuring him that Hayti had no disposition or desire to interfere with the free will of the Dominicans. As a further reply to Mr. Sumner, he reminded the Senator, as evidence, that the Administration had not proposed to take any immediate action upon annexation; that Commission had no authority to negotiate a treaty, and that no one went with them who could take a single step in that direction. The Haytien Government, in violation of the law of nations, had given free passage across its territory to Cabral, and had furnished him with war vessels to attack Dominica, and the United States had merely notified Hayti that while our negotiations were pending with Dominica we would not allow him to make war on the island. This the United States had an undoubted right to do, because our Government had information of organizations on foot in Hayti to defeat annexation. No one need tell him (Morton) that the Senator from Massachusetts was a friend of liberty or the colored man when he so industriously spent his time in an effort to put the Democratic party in power, for to destroy the President is to destroy the great party of which he is the head (applause), and we know the terrible effect upon the liberties of this country if the Democratic party comes into power.

records.headline: Senate debate on Senator Sumner's San Domingo resolutions continued, with Senator Howe speaking at length in reply
records.summary_en: Senate debate on Senator Sumner's San Domingo resolutions continued, with Senator Howe speaking at length in reply to Sumner and defending the action of the President, and Senator Frelinghuysen questioning why the discussion had been precipitated in advance of the commission's report. The excerpt also carries Sumner's closing appeal for a peaceful effort to reconcile Haiti and Dominica and establish tranquility throughout the island.
records.summary_es: El debate en el Senado sobre las resoluciones de San Domingo del senador Sumner continuó, con el senador Howe hablando extensamente en respuesta a Sumner y defendiendo la actuación del presidente, y el senador Frelinghuysen cuestionando por qué el debate se había precipitado antes del informe de la comisión. records.passage: Annexation Means War with Hayti. Another Washington correspondent telegraphs that it seems to be the general opinion of the Commissioners that annexation cannot take place without involving the United States in a war with Hayti. Baez admitted to the Commissioners that one thousand square miles of territory belonging to the Dominican republic, and lying contiguous to Hayti, are under control of Cabral and his followers. It is stated that Baez did not make any effort to allow the Commissioners to meet Cabral, but on the contrary assured them that he could not afford them any protection if they visited the part of the island that Cabral controlled. All speak in the highest terms of the island, its climate and productions, but appear to entertain a very poor opinion of the people, who are described as indolent, superstitious and exceedingly undesirable in their present condition as an addition to the population of the United States. records.full_text:
Hayti and Santo Domingo.

Chronological Epitome.

1795—By the treaty of Basle, the Spanish portion of Santo Domingo is ceded to France.

1798—Hedouville lands at French Cape, and sends Toussaint L'Ouverture, an emancipated slave, to France. On the 8th of May, the English leave the island, and civil war between Toussaint L'Ouverture and Rigaud.

1801—Toussaint L'Ouverture takes the Spanish portion of the island, and assumes the title of Governor General for life.

1802—The French squadron, under Leclerc, arrives at Port au Prince in February; takes the Cape and burns the town, Dessalines opposing. A truce concluded May 1st.

1803—In April, L'Ouverture dies in France, having been taken prisoner during the truce. The French are driven into Cape Haytien, where, November 30th, they surrendered to English commanders.

1804—1st of January, Hayti is declared independent, and Dessalines made Governor General for life. October 8th he is crowned Emperor, with the title of James I. (Jacques 1er.)

1805—A proclamation of Dessalines, of April 28th, orders the massacre of all French residents, and the order is at once put in force. Those spared are subsequently assembled on the Place d'Armes to receive certificates of protection, and the little remnant of survivors are then shot.

1806—Dessalines is executed as a tyrant October 17th, at Pont Rouge. The east part of the island repossessed by Spain.

records.headline: A Herald letter from aboard the frigate Tennessee, off Port-au-Prince on March 1871, describes the Santo Domingo Commission's return
records.summary_en: A Herald letter from aboard the frigate Tennessee, off Port-au-Prince on March 1871, describes the Santo Domingo Commission's return journey, with the steamer Nantasket arriving from Puerto Plata bringing Professor White and the parties who had rendezvoused there after traversing the country. The commissioners are shown quarreling over the journey home: Ben Wade wants to make the most direct course home now that their business is done and their report almost completed, while Dr. Howe and Professor White outvote him, to the general dissatisfaction of everyone on board, and the letter doubts the three will even settle on a joint report.
records.summary_es: Una carta del Herald desde a bordo de la fragata Tennessee, frente a Puerto Príncipe en marzo de 1871, describe el viaje de regreso de la Comisión de Santo Domingo, con la llegada del vapor Nantasket desde Puerto Plata trayendo al profesor White y a los grupos que se habían reunido allí tras recorrer el país. Los comisionados aparecen discutiendo sobre el regreso: Ben Wade quiere tomar el rumbo más directo a casa ahora que su trabajo está hecho y su informe casi terminado, mientras el doctor Howe y el profesor White lo superan en votos, para disgusto general de todos a bordo, y la carta duda que los tres lleguen siquiera a acordar un informe conjunto.
records.passage: Correspondence With Cabral. UNITED STATES FRIGATE Tennessee, Off Port au Prince, Hayti, March [illegible], 1871. [illegible] delay—Incomprehensible delay! Kept at anchor in this delectable harbor, where filth and stench, both in the streets and in the miserable government, alike breed rottenness and disease. At three o'clock yesterday the steamer Nautasket steamed into this harbor, having left Puerto Plata the morning before. Professor White determined not to await the arrival of the Tybee, which might not reach there for several days, so, collecting together all the scattered parties who had been traversing the country and who rendezvoused at Puerto Plata, they sped around to join the Tennessee. Her arrival caused the greatest delight among our party, who had become heartily tired of this unsocial and unsightly town; and as we have only been waiting for her to come we looked forward to our quickly leaving for home with certainty. The Haytiens, who have looked with great suspicion upon the Tennessee, deeming her object to be hostile to their petty government, are now no doubt doubly alarmed at the presence in their harbor of another American man-of-war. records.headline: In a letter from his headquarters dated March 5, 1871, General Jose Maria Cabral tells the United States
records.summary_en: In a letter from his headquarters dated March 5, 1871, General Jose Maria Cabral tells the United States Commissioners, Wade, White and Howe, that he has no power to enter into any negotiations on the annexation of his country, that he has protested against it and that his people have been protesting with arms in their hands for more than a year. He invites the Commissioners to visit the people and his headquarters, but White and Howe reply that a visit is not convenient for the present, while Mr. Wade declines to sign the reply; the correspondent adds that Cabral in fact holds only a small strip of mountainous land along the Neyba River.
records.summary_es: En una carta desde su cuartel general fechada el 5 de marzo de 1871, el general José María Cabral dice a los comisionados de los Estados Unidos, Wade, White y Howe, que no tiene poder para entrar en ninguna negociación sobre la anexión de su país, que ha protestado contra ella y que su pueblo lleva más de un año protestando con las armas en la mano. Invita a los comisionados a visitar al pueblo y su cuartel general, pero White y Howe responden que la visita no es conveniente por el momento, mientras el señor Wade se niega a firmar la respuesta; el corresponsal añade que Cabral en realidad solo ocupa una pequeña franja de tierra montañosa a lo largo del río Neyba.
records.passage: GENERAL HEADQUARTERS, [illegible], March [illegible], 1871. To Señors Benjamin B. Wade, Andrew D. White and Samuel G. Howe, members of the Commission of the United States: GENTLEMEN: I have read the contents of your communication, dated on the 21st of the past month, with an additional note dated on the 28th of the same month in Azua, and have duly countered them. But not having any power to enter into any class of negotiations, or to treat in any way as to the annexation of my country, and having protested in the month of March past in behalf of the people and the army which I have the honor to govern, it appears to me altogether useless to be interviewed as to the subject which you propose to me. If you have instructions from your government to study the opinions and desires of the Dominican people upon these particulars, according to the expressions in your communications, the best way in which you can fulfil your instructions is to pass through and visit the people, and in this way you will be able to assure yourselves better of that which I have already said in my communication of the 28th of February. And it will appear that we have not alone protested in uniting against the annexation, but that it will be shown to be a fact that for more than a year we have been protesting against annexation with arms in our hands. records.full_text:
ST. DOMINGO REPORT.

The report of the Santo Domingo commissioners was read in the Cabinet meeting to-day, and will probably be submitted to Congress on Monday. It will be accompanied by a brief message from the President, in which, it is reported, he will inform Congress that while their official report is merely confined to answering the inquiries proposed by Congress, he has, nevertheless, been informed by them that they are in favor of the immediate annexation of Santo Domingo. It remains to be seen whether the President thus proposes to travel outside of the official record. If so, his only excuse will be the opinion expressed to him by the commissioners that Baez's condition is such that the annexation question must necessarily be disposed of at the earliest practicable moment. Several Republican Senators favor disposing of the question by passing a resolution now declaring Congress opposed to annexation, and thus obviate the negotiation and subsequent discussion of a new treaty. A Republican Senator has prepared such a resolution, and is only awaiting events before offering it.

records.headline: The Santo Domingo report is not yet finished, but the commissioners are understood to be in full accord and their report
records.summary_en: The Santo Domingo report is not yet finished, but the commissioners are understood to be in full accord and their report as favorable to annexation as Wade's first draft, with the documentary evidence - enough for a large book - being readied for the printer.
records.summary_es: El informe de Santo Domingo aún no está terminado, pero se entiende que los comisionados están en pleno acuerdo y que su informe será tan favorable a la anexión como el primer borrador de Wade, con la evidencia documental - suficiente para un libro voluminoso - preparándose para la imprenta.
records.passage: THE SANTO DOMINGO REPORT NOT READY YET — NO DISAGREEMENT AMONG THE COMMISSIONERS — SPECULATIONS CONCERNING THE PRESIDENT'S INTENTIONS — THE NEW-YORK APPOINTMENTS. [BY TELEGRAPH TO THE TRIBUNE.] WASHINGTON, Monday, April 3, 1871. The Santo Domingo report is not yet finished, but those who have been most familiar with the views of the Commissioners believe that there is not the slightest variation in the general views of the members, and that the report, when finally finished and signed, will be as favorable to annexation as the first report prepared by Mr. Wade. The report which will be presented to the President will be more full in details, will embrace more subjects, and give more space to discussion of the subjects laid down in the resolutions of Congress than the report which was first considered. It seemed doubtful yesterday that the Commissioners were in full accord, but the intimate friends of all the Commissioners say that there will be no disagreement, and that the report will be mainly straightforward and emphatic, and not meaningless recital of what was seen and heard by Commissioners in making their investigation. One of the Commissioners says that any one who reads the report cannot be in doubt as to the opinions and views of the members. The report is now [finishing?], and a meeting of Commissioners to-morrow will determine the whole subject. A sufficient number of clerks are now engaged in arranging the documentary evidence and testimony of witnesses, which the investigation elicited, and all the documents and testimony, enough to make a large book, will be ready for the printer by time the report shall be handed in.

During the conversation, Mr. Sumner asked Fabens if he thought that annexation would stop with Santo Domingo. "Oh, no!" replied the Dominican Envoy, "you must have Hayti too." And is that all, continued the Senator. Fabens thought that we could not stop with Hayti, but must, in the nature of things, finally absorb Porto Rico, Jamaica, Cuba, the Windward Islands, and, indeed, all of the West Indies. Mr. Sumner then called the attention of Fabens to the fact that the treaty involved not only the question of the annexation of the little republic of Santo Domingo, but an entirely new foreign policy for the United States. He professed his friendship for the people of the island, and his willingness to aid them by every means in his power; but while he doubted that Santo Domingo would in the end gain by annexation, he was sure that the United States would lose. Mr. Sumner believes that the West India Islands are destined to be the home of the black race. In proof of this he points to the fact that in almost every instance the blacks have increased there much more rapidly than the whites, so that in some of the islands the white population is not more than 25 per cent of the whole, while in many others it is less than 50 per cent. records.headline: The Commission reports that it examined the originals of the annexation treaty and the Samana lease in the archives of the Dominican Government
records.summary_en: The Commission reports that it examined the originals of the annexation treaty and the Samana lease in the archives of the Dominican Government in Santo Domingo City, in the presence of the President and his Cabinet on February 18, 1871, and found no particle of evidence of any secret clause or concession favoring any United States official. President Baez told the commissioners his government was willing to stand by the 1869 treaty, but asked whether the Samana rent for the nearly two years of delay might fairly be paid without deduction, and he agreed to modify the treaty to devote one-fifth of the public lands to common schools if the United States would add land for colleges of agriculture, mining and engineering.
records.summary_es: La Comisión informa que examinó los originales del tratado de anexión y del arrendamiento de Samaná en los archivos del Gobierno dominicano en la ciudad de Santo Domingo, en presencia del Presidente y su Gabinete el 18 de febrero de 1871, y no encontró ni la menor evidencia de cláusula secreta o concesión alguna en favor de ningún funcionario de los Estados Unidos. El presidente Báez dijo a los comisionados que su gobierno estaba dispuesto a mantener el tratado de 1869, pero preguntó si no sería justo que la renta de Samaná por los casi dos años de demora se pagara sin deducción, y aceptó modificar el tratado para dedicar una quinta parte de las tierras públicas a escuelas comunes si los Estados Unidos añadían tierras para colegios de agricultura, minería e ingeniería.

Los comisionados concluyeron que la independencia dominicana nunca había sido una realidad y que la incorporación como Estado de la Unión constituía la única vía para afianzar sus libertades e independencia, aun cuando se abstuvieron de formular una recomendación explícita sobre dicho camino.

records.full_text:
FINANCIAL.

The Commissioners made a thorough and careful examination of the debt of San Domingo, and find the sum total of all debts and outstanding claims against the Republic to be $1,565,831. The receipts of the government for 1870 were $772,684, of which $728,605 was from customs and $35,466 from taxes. The Commissioners lay great stress on their efforts to get the exact state of the debt of the Dominican Republic, and believe their conclusions substantially correct. San Domingo is not believed to be liable for any of the indemnity exacted by France from Hayti, and the Commission is assured that no obligation or negotiations have been entered into with any country except the United States.

The extent of undisputed Dominican territory is 22,512 square miles. The portion which formerly involved a dispute with Hayti being 1000 square miles. The Commissioners present a full statement of all the grants and concessions of public lands and franchise, and declare that after the most searching and complete investigation they were unable to find any grant or concession in any form or manner to any U. S. official, either in connection with the negotiation or preparation of the treaty.

records.full_text:
...sequent treaties, all of which refer to it as the undisputed boundary. It is doubly important in the history of the island. It marks the separation of different languages, different national traditions and characteristics, different modes of dividing and surveying the soil, different peoples. In 1821 the people of what is now the Dominican Republic threw off the Spanish yoke and proclaimed a republic. At this time the boundary was not disputed, and the republic included all the Spanish part of the island, or, in other words, was along the line of 1777.

In 1822 the Haytien President Boyer acquired possession of the whole island, and it remained under one government until the revolution of 1844 resulted in the expulsion of the Haytien rulers and the re-establishment of the independence of the Dominican Republic throughout the Dominican or Spanish speaking portion of the island, except a few interior valleys on the Dominican side of the line, in some of which there has been an almost constant struggle. Since that time the Haytien and Dominican forces alternately held all the disputed territory. Of this disputed territory the Haytiens have held practically constant possession of the towns of San Rafael, San Miguel, and Las Caobas.

The Banica valley east of these, with Banica as its principal town, and the Nezba valley to the south, have been alternately overrun by both governments. The attention of the Commission has been drawn to a map issued by private parties in our own country, claiming to be based on a Haytien report made on this subject in President Geffrard's time. The boundary given by this map from a point just east of Monte Cristi, on the north shore of the island, in a nearly north and south line to a point on the south shore nearly opposite the island of Alta Vela.

Whether the Commission be right or wrong in judging that any infringement on Dominican territory has been based on usurpation, and is therefore null, the claim to any such line as that above indicated must seem preposterous to any one conversant with Dominican or Haytien affairs. The town of Monte Cristi, which by that map is placed under Haytien control, was at a recent visit by a member of the commission found to be inhabited by a Spanish-speaking people, with Dominican authorities, and no one seemed to be at all aware that it had been claimed since 1844 by any other government than Dominica.

As to the Banica valley and the other valleys thus claimed, the people are Dominicans, and from all that could be learned have never considered themselves otherwise. The Commission also made inquiries regarding the foundation of the Haytien claims outside of 1775, both of intelligent persons living in Hayti and of the Haytien ex-President Geffrard, now an exile in Jamaica, but from neither source could they obtain any direct presumptive evidence for the Haytien claim.

Sumner calls Baez not only a usurper but a perjurer, because the Dominican Constitution of 1866 declares that neither the whole nor any part of the territory can ever be alienated, and he says the American David Hatch was arrested and held in prison, at Cazneau's instance, to prevent his hostile action in New York against the annexation treaty.

Sumner llama a Báez no solo usurpador sino también perjuro, porque la Constitución dominicana de 1866 declara que ni la totalidad ni parte alguna del territorio pueden enajenarse jamás, y afirma que el americano David Hatch fue arrestado y mantenido en prisión, a instancias de Cazneau, para impedir su acción hostil en Nueva York contra el tratado de anexión.

records.headline: The excerpt denounces the annexation scheme as forcibly maintaining a usurper in power in Santo Domingo so that he
records.summary_en: The excerpt denounces the annexation scheme as forcibly maintaining a usurper in power in Santo Domingo so that he might sell his country, and as a blow at the republic of Haiti, done by prerogative alone without the authority of an act of Congress. It also condemns the president's intervention in the Senate, through appeals to senators and the appointing power, to secure consummation of the scheme.
records.summary_es: El extracto denuncia el plan de anexión como el mantenimiento forzoso de un usurpador en el poder en Santo Domingo para que pudiera vender su país, y como un golpe contra la república de Haití, realizado solo por prerrogativa sin la autoridad de una ley del Congreso. También condena la intervención del presidente en el Senado, mediante apelaciones a los senadores y el poder de nombramiento, para asegurar la consumación del plan.

records.headline: The Commissioners' report describes St. Domingo's forests
records.summary_en: The Commissioners' report describes St. Domingo's forests as its most striking feature, with palms near the coast and mahogany, satinwood, Dominican oak, pitch pine, lignum vitae, logwood and other valuable woods inland. It says wide forests in the interior remain untouched for lack of roads, that large mahogany logs are left to decay by the roadside within thirty miles of the principal northern seaport, and that no sawmill was found in the country.
records.summary_es: El informe de los Comisionados describe los bosques de Santo Domingo como su rasgo más llamativo, con palmas cerca de la costa y caoba, palo satín, roble dominicano, pino resinoso, guayacán, campeche y otras maderas valiosas en el interior. Dice que amplios bosques del interior permanecen intactos por falta de caminos, que grandes troncos de caoba se dejan pudrir junto a los caminos a menos de treinta millas del principal puerto del norte, y que no se encontró ningún aserradero en el país.

The testimony of the head of a thrifty New England family, who had resided in the neighborhood of Samana Bay nearly two years, was to the effect that there was as little difficulty in keeping a house clear from troublesome insects, as in our Northern States. products [illegible] The most striking characteristic of St. Domingo, at first sight, is the wonderful luxuriance of its forests. In many parts, and especially in the neighborhood of the Bay of Samana, although there are abrupt ridges, perpendicular cliffs and bold headlands, no bare rocks can be seen, being hidden by a mass of strong vegetation. But on close observation another and not less striking characteristic is revealed: an astonishing variety in forest products. The cause of this variety is to be found, doubtless, in the great difference in elevation of the surface exposure and character of the soil. Near the coast various species of palm are abundant, and very valuable in constructing such houses as have been generally found best suited to the climate. On the mountain slopes, at different heights, grow in abundance both the choicest cabinet woods, as mahogany, satinwood, &c., and a great variety of timber especially valuable in housebuilding. The roble, or Dominican oak, and a hard pitch pine were found in abundance in various parts of the country. In the more dry districts flourish several valuable woods, the best known of which, perhaps, is the lignum vitae, of which the quantity is very great. records.full_text:
The following statement of receipts for 1870 is here presented, in order to give, as far as possible, a complete view of the financial condition of the Dominican Republic: Resume of the income of the Government for 1870: First, Customs receipts, tonnage, $2,730,660; entrance fees, $147,995; light houses, $67,901; anchorage, $196,995; pilotage, $142,827; lighterage, $21,800; interpreter, $646 26; signal men, $59,410; quarantine, $48,016; wharfage, $679,888; recargo municipal, $110,586; recargo for steamer, $588,614; water, $24,100; impost dues, $691,393 64; export dues, $71,419 20; coast fees, $7,511 11.

The Commissioners believe that the statement of the public debt given above includes all the indebtedness or obligations for which the Dominican Republic is in any degree liable, as well as that which it considers valid and binding, as that which it regards as unfounded or overstated by the claimants. Throughout the inquiry it was urged upon the Dominican authorities that every claim known to exist, of whatever character, should be exhibited to the Commission, whose object was not to determine the precise amount that was justly due and binding, but to get at the bottom and find the utmost limit of their obligations, and setting forth everything for which the Government could under any circumstances be made liable. The above account contains much that the Dominican Government believes to be partially or wholly groundless, and some which upon the inspection will appear questionable. Among the pending claims is one of President Baez for the destruction of property. It is alleged by the claimant that the Spanish Government recognized this claim as valid, and ordered an examination to fix the amount, but the Commission can in not understand how this claim could be valid against the Dominican Government.

A question has been raised in our country whether the Government and people of the Dominican Republic, having once been under the rule of Haytiens, might not be liable for a portion of the indemnity exacted for France from Hayti, for the estates of French families which had been confiscated by the Haytiens during the revolution of 1791. The Commission made inquiries on the subject of the Dominican Government, and also in Hayti, and they could not learn that the Haytien Government had ever made this claim upon the Dominican Republic, and they think that if made it would be wholly without foundation.

The Commissioners were informed by the Dominican authorities that the present administration of the Government has not had diplomatic representation or made treaties or engagements with any other government except the United States. An enumeration of the treaties made during the previous history of the Republic of France, Great Britain, and other powers, will be found in Ex. Doc. 17, Forty-first Congress, second session. They are mostly treaties of navigation and commerce, and contain no unusual provision requiring notice here.

The extent of undisputed Dominican territory is 22,212 square miles, the portion of which has been formerly involved in dispute with Hayti being about 1,000 square miles.

records.summary_en: In a Senate speech against annexing San Domingo, Mr. Morrill argues that the Bay of Samana would be a source of weakness rather than a defensive point, and that the Dominican people would prove a serious political, moral and financial encumbrance. records.headline: Senator Morrill, speaking on President Grant's Santo Domingo policy, treats the commissioners' report with open
records.summary_en: Senator Morrill, speaking on President Grant's Santo Domingo policy, treats the commissioners' report with open skepticism, saying they praised the soil for producing bananas and pine-apples and were despondent about finding coal at Samana, where there is only a poor show of lignite. Their report, he argues, will be found neither more exhaustive nor more trustworthy than the works of impartial travelers who spent far more time on the island, and will be chiefly valuable for vindicating the personal integrity of the President and of the officer charged with negotiating the defeated treaty.
records.summary_es: El senador Morrill, hablando sobre la política del presidente Grant hacia Santo Domingo, trata el informe de los comisionados con abierto escepticismo, diciendo que alabaron el suelo por producir bananas y piñas y que se mostraron desalentados por encontrar carbón en Samaná, donde solo hay una pobre muestra de lignito. Su informe, sostiene, no resultará ni más exhaustivo ni más digno de confianza que las obras de viajeros imparciales que pasaron mucho más tiempo en la isla, y será valioso sobre todo para vindicar la integridad personal del Presidente y la del oficial encargado de negociar el tratado derrotado.

records.summary_en: The commission's report on the Dominican constitution and the condition of the country: Báez respected by the majority, the insurrections of Cabral and Luperón kept alive by Haitian help, and finances so straitened by civil commotion that the government cannot meet its expenses.

From all that the Commissioners could ascertain, President Baez has the respect of the great majority of the Dominican people for his administrative abilities, and the strong attachment of many leading men, who regard him as the only statesman among them who can hold them together against domestic factions and foreign foes. In 1848, after five years of anarchy, consequent on the expulsion of the Haytien power, Gen. Baez was regularly elected President of the republic. It appears that he was chosen as the man who, by his education, fortune and public services, would be most likely to secure general confidence and heal the wounds inflicted by the civil and foreign wars. In one of the delegations of leading citizens who tendered to him the chief magistracy, was Gen. Cabral. There is creditable testimony to the fact that, under him, despite the difficulties that have beset him, the republic has enjoyed as much liberty as any of his predecessors dared to allow, and more tranquility than they knew how to give. Nor do the Commissioners find that there is any opponent of the present administration of that republic who has now, or who ever has had, any claim to the chief magistracy by a title superior to that of the present incumbent. Whatever technical defects there might have been in his original title to the office, it was confirmed by a national convention and ratified by the assent and support of the people. records.passage: every function of Government, with General Baez as Chief Magistrate, in full and peaceable possession of all part in the Republic, except on the Haytien border, which is disturbed by insurrectionary leaders, aided by Haytiens and political intriguers. These are incited to be active at this time by fear of annexation to the United States. From all the Commissioners could ascertain, President Baez has the respect of a great majority of the Dominican people for his administrative ability, and strong attachment to many leading men who regard him as the only statesman among them who can hold the nation against domestic factions and foreign foes. The Commissioners do not find that there is any opponent to the present administration of the Republic, who has now or who ever had any claim to the chief magistracy by a title superior to the present incumbent. Whatever technical defects there might have been in his original title to the office, it was confirmed by national convention, and ratified by the assent and support of the people. The frequency of civil commotion during a long period, and consequent insecurity of property, have paralyzed industry and discouraged accumulation, and so impoverished the country that for the last two years the financial resources of the Government have been inadequate to pay expenses. The insurrections which still exist are led by Cabral and Luperon. The former of these is universally conceded to be the more important, but neither has a distinct flag or a regularly organized army. They said President Báez had the respect of a great majority of Dominicans, recounting his 1848 election after the expulsion of Haitian power and the liberty and tranquility under him.

records.full_text:
UNANIMOUS FOR ANNEXATION.
The Dominicans repeat their wish to be annexed on the terms of the treaty of 1869, asking, in addition payment for rent for Samana bay during the two years the negotiations were pending. They are also willing to appropriate one-fifth of the public funds for schools, providing the United States will appropriate $300,000 for the establishment of an agricultural and scientific college. In relation to Dominican independence, the Commissioners say that there is but one chance for that republic ever to retain its independence; to become, after a period of probation, one of a union of states, the freedom and substantial dependence of each being guaranteed by the strength of all. It is under the resolution of Congress, to recommend that such a course be adopted or abstained from. They simply state as their belief, founded upon the observations they could make, and all the facts they could learn, that this is the only way in which Dominican independence can be secured, that if it should be judged best not to adopt that course, even the present shadow of independence will be taken away. The Dominican territory is one of the purest and richest on the earth. Unless some such means as are above mentioned are resorted to, it will lie exhausted and helpless until some nation shall seize and hold it in colonial subjection.

records.full_text:
THE GRANTS TO AMERICANS.
The Commissioners were not unmindful of various rumors which had been circulated on divers occasions, that concessions or grants of land were made to officials of the Government of the United States when the treaty of annexation was negotiated in 1869. No pains were spared to ascertain the exact truth of this statement. In addition to the examination of all grants from the government of the republic, the Commission further carried their researches to all municipal grants by the town of Samana, where rumor had located the supposed grants. The officers of the municipality and the records were carefully examined. Inquiries were also made of the authorities of the city of San Domingo. After this investigation the Commissioners can declare, without hesitation, that there is no particle of evidence for these charges.

records.headline: The commissioners' report describes the island's navigable rivers and its three great bays, Samana, Azua and Manzanillo
records.summary_en: The commissioners' report describes the island's navigable rivers and its three great bays, Samana, Azua and Manzanillo, and calls Samana a powerful military and naval station whose future under United States authority would be of national importance. It then sets out the Dominican government's finances, giving a total of $1,565,831 in debt and claims, together with the government's income for 1869, and states the commissioners' belief that the statement includes every obligation for which the republic could be held liable, while noting that some claims appear questionable.
records.summary_es: El informe de los comisionados describe los ríos navegables de la isla y sus tres grandes bahías, Samaná, Azua y Manzanillo, y califica a Samaná como una poderosa estación militar y naval cuyo futuro bajo la autoridad de los Estados Unidos sería de importancia nacional. A continuación expone las finanzas del gobierno dominicano, con un total de $1,565,831 en deudas y reclamaciones, junto con los ingresos del gobierno en 1869, y declara la convicción de los comisionados de que el estado incluye toda obligación por la que la república pudiera ser responsable, señalando a la vez que algunas reclamaciones parecen cuestionables.

From all that the Commissioners could ascertain, President Baez has the respect of the great majority of the Dominican people for his administration and abilities, and the strong attachment of many leading men, who regard him as the only statesman among them who can hold the nation against domestic factions and foreign foes. In the year [illegible], after five years of anarchy, consequently upon the expulsion of Haytien power, General Baez was regularly elected President of the Republic. It appears that he was chosen as the man who, by his education, fortune and public services, would be most likely to secure the general confidence and heal wounds inflicted by civil and foreign wars. In one of the delegations of leading citizens who tendered to him the chief magistracy, was General Cabral. records.full_text:
A BULLY AMONG REPUBLICS.
Our reputation among sister republics in America the Senator did not consider wholly unblemished, and it was not likely to grow brighter from Santo Domingo complications. Our experience with Mexico when Texas became a part of this Union; the Greytown affair in 1852; the career of Walker, the fillibuster; our difficulty with Paraguy for ten years or more; our attitude toward Cuba; the trouble with Peru in 1860; a recent unpleasantness with Brazil in regard to the passage of the gunboat Wasp, up the Paraguy to relieve Minister Washburn, were recited to show that there was no special love for this government among those nations. The annexation of Santo Domingo, whether of spontaneous origin or nursed by the military, naval and financial power of the United States, cannot fail to excite the jealousy and fear of all the American republics.

records.headline: An editorial attacks the report of the Commissioners appointed by Grant to investigate whether it was politic to annex
records.summary_en: An editorial attacks the report of the Commissioners appointed by Grant to investigate whether it was politic to annex San Domingo to the United States, calling it a document prepared to please Baez and full of falsehoods, and noting that Grant, after laying it before Congress, backed down and refused to press its consideration. The paper also publishes two letters from General Cabral inviting the Commissioners to visit his headquarters and the country held by his forces and ask the people whether they favored annexation, an invitation the editorial says the Commissioners were very careful not to accept.
records.summary_es: Un editorial ataca el informe de los comisionados nombrados por Grant para investigar si era conveniente anexar Santo Domingo a los Estados Unidos, calificándolo de documento preparado para complacer a Báez y lleno de falsedades, y señalando que Grant, después de presentarlo al Congreso, dio marcha atrás y se negó a impulsar su consideración. El periódico publica también dos cartas del general Cabral invitando a los comisionados a visitar su cuartel general y el territorio ocupado por sus fuerzas y a preguntar al pueblo si favorecía la anexión, una invitación que el editorial dice que los comisionados tuvieron mucho cuidado de no aceptar.

It described the island as the gateway to the Caribbean Sea and noted that its sparse population is industrious, free of caste, and anxious to join their fortunes with the United States. Additionally, the excerpt detailed England's strategic military positions and island holdings around Cuba, the Gulf of Mexico, and the Caribbean Sea.

Describió a la isla como la llave de acceso al mar Caribe y ponderó a su escasa población como laboriosa, exenta de prejuicios de casta y ansiosa por enlazar su destino al de los Estados Unidos. El texto desgranó además las posiciones militares estratégicas y las posesiones insulares que Inglaterra mantenía en torno a Cuba, el golfo de México y el mar Caribe.

records.full_text: San Domingo is admitted to be an island of great fertility. That part of it known as the State of San Domingo contains an area of 20,000 square miles, or 12,800,000 acres. Much of this is now covered with the most valuable timbers known to commerce, at an elevation above the diseases incident to a tropical climate, and is capable of producing, when cleared of its native forest, one thousand five hundred pounds of coffee per acre. The valleys and lowlands are of great productiveness, the sugar-cane requiring resetting only once in twenty years, and producing to the acre, with much less labor, nearly double that of the best sugar lands of Louisiana.

records.headline: Letters of General Luperon from Capotillo in early 1871 report him organizing a small force for a campaign in the Cibao
records.summary_en: Letters of General Luperon from Capotillo in early 1871 report him organizing a small force for a campaign in the Cibao, with anti-annexation propaganda very active around Guayabin and Monte Cristi and word that the American flag has been raised at Monte Cristi. He writes that Cabral could send him no men from the south, that he will make his sortie with only forty or fifty officers, and he urgently asks for at least fifty thousand chassepot cartridges; a Santo Domingo letter adds that Luperon was later defeated and his secretary, General Manuel Rodriguez Objio, captured and shot.

Escribe que Cabral no pudo enviarle hombres desde el sur, que hará su salida con solo cuarenta o cincuenta oficiales, y pide con urgencia al menos cincuenta mil cartuchos para fusiles chassepot; una carta de Santo Domingo añade que Luperon fue derrotado después y que su secretario, el general Manuel Rodriguez Objio, fue capturado y fusilado.

records.passage: HONORS TO PRESIDENT BAEZ. Baez started out upon the journey, from which he has just returned, accompanied only by Gautier, Delmonto, Curiel, and a colonel of cavalry. He went unarmed — a thing said to be before unknown in his history. A few days ago, the Commandante Macoris became intoxicated, abused his office and his people, was removed, and undertook to rebel against his successor. He was captured and put in prison. This was said to be a new revolution, and was reported to Gen. Camenero as such. The General, with 60 men, went to Macoris, but the man had been captured before he reached there, and was lodged in the old castle in this city. Gen. Camenero has just told me that the only foundation for the story was, that a mob was raised to punish the man for abusing his wife. The German war steamer Gazelle, Capt. Avent, was here some 10 days ago, and remained several days. Thirty-five of the officers came up into the city, and had a jolly time. The captain gave a dinner on board of his ship to foreign representatives, and prominent merchants of the place. He gave a toast to the Dominican Government — the Governor being present — and remarked that he hoped they would be able to sustain themselves, and the principles they had avowed before the world. He had hoped to set forth his views more fully to the Government, but as the President was absent he would reserve further remarks till the return. He was going to Hayti, and would return in a few days, when he hoped to see the President, and more fully make known the object of his visit. T

records.full_text:
THE CASE OF THE STEAMER TELEGRAFO.
HER UNJUST SEIZURE FOR PIRACY—A MEASURE INSTIGATED BY THE UNITED STATES GOVERNMENT TO PROMOTE THE ANNEXATION SCHEME.
To the Editor of The Tribune.
SIR: The connection of the steamer Telegrafo with the wicked and cruel attempt of a few speculators to get possession of the Dominican part of San Domingo is familiar to all who have taken an interest in the subject. The English Court of Chancery having now confirmed the decision of the Admiralty Court of Tortola, given in May, 1870, this case becomes one of great interest to us by the action of our Government in seizing her on the alleged ground of her being a pirate; and this case acquires additional interest in the fact that the high Courts of the British Empire have decided a claim against a British subject, and in favor of a citizen of the United States, Mr. George A. Philips, (of the firm of George A. Philips & Co. of St. Thomas,) formerly of Collins of New-York, to whom a jury of merchants awarded £18,000 indemnity for the seizure and illegal sale of the Telegrafo, of which he was the owner. The history of this remarkable case is as follows:

The Telegrafo was chartered in St. Thomas, in May 1869 by Dominican exiles. The vessel was to carry the American flag, and was to be employed against the usurper Baez in the waters of the Dominican Republic. She proceeded to the British Island of Inagua, where she was put under the British flag, armed and fitted as a vessel of war. Thence she proceeded to Santo Domingo.

HAYTI.
—
Another of our Consuls in Trouble.
NEW YORK, April 13.—Haytien advices report the arrest and imprisonment of the American Consul at Port au Prince, because of his having given protection to Gen. Batellia, insurrectionary leader who escaped the custody of the guard and sought refuge in the Consul's office while on his way to be imprisoned. The Consul has conferred with Minister Bassett on the subject, who, it is understood, will apply to the Haytien government for redress.

Threat of War with San Domingo.
PORT AU PRINCE, April 13.—The invasion from Monte Christo consisted of 200 men. Eight Haytiens, five Dominicans, and one Frenchman were captured and executed. It is reliably reported that the Haytien Government will probably declare war against Baez, who is charged with an attempt to overthrow President Saget.

records.full_text:
And yet, again: Here at Santo Domingo City other popular ideas, propagated by Congressional speeches, are found to have no basis save in the distempered imaginations of political leaders.

How often have our people been assured that our Executive was guilty of maintaining a fleet in these waters, at vast expense, without necessity, and "solely to maintain a usurper in power!"

How confidently, how earnestly, how frequently have our orators asserted that the Baez administration was kept in power mainly by our naval forces, and that it could not stand a day after their withdrawal!

How have our orators thundered against this abuse of national power, this degrading service of our navy; and how have weak-kneed Republicans shaken their heads in disapproval of the supposed error and wrong! But what is the truth about it? We must have a squadron in the West Indies. The Dominican ports are capacious and convenient, and thither our ships frequently resort. But at this time there is not one of our war vessels in Dominican waters! The last one, the "Nantasket," sailed away some time ago, to return no one knows exactly when. But yet President Baez has not fallen nor fled! He sits more firm in the saddle than ever, and his administration has the confidence and the almost unanimous support of the people!

History will show, what all in these regions admit, that the moral effect of the presence of our fleet in Dominican and Haytian waters has been blessed indeed, because it has helped greatly to deter fillibusters, and to maintain peace and order.

records.summary_en: The *New York Herald* reported that the President utilized three warships and a presidential aide—operating outside constitutional and legal authority—to negotiate two treaties and keep a usurper in power in Dominica. According to the excerpt, these official actions involving intervention in Dominica and threats against Hayti constituted an unconstitutional seizure of the government's war powers and a disregard for the equality of nations.
