records.chapter_es: La lucha por la anexión estadounidense
records.full_text:
On his return to Washington the young man who had assumed to be "Aid-de-Camp of His Excellency General Ulysses S. Grant," and had bound the President to become a lobbyist for a wretched usurpation, instead of being disavowed and reprimanded, was sent back to the usurper with instructions to negotiate two treaties—one for the annexation of the half island of Dominica, and the other for the lease of the Bay of Samana. By the constitution of the United States ambassadors and other public ministers are appointed by the President, by and with the advice and consent of the Senate; but our aid-de-camp had no such commission. Presidential prerogative empowered him. Nor was naval force wanting. With three war ships at his disposal, he entered upon negotiation with Baez and obtained the two treaties. Naturally force was needed to keep the usurper in power while he sold his country, and naturally such a mission required a Presidential aid-de-camp unknown to constitution or law rather than a civilian duly appointed according to law.

On other occasions it has been my solemn duty to expose the outrages which attended this dark business, where at each step we are brought face to face with Presidential pretensions—first in the seizure of the war powers of the Government, as if he were a Caesar; forcibly intervening in Dominica and menacing war upon Hayti, all of which is proved by the official reports of the State Department and Navy Department, being nothing less than war by kingly prerogative in defiance of that distinctive principle of republican government first embodied in our Constitution, which places the war powers under the safeguard of the legislative branch, making any attempt by the President to declare war an undoubted usurpation.

records.full_text:
THE DOMINICAN TREATY.
Let us examine the evidence, and, first of all, take up the charges and evidence against him. The Santo Domingo Treaty, unlike going to Long Branch, smoking a cigar, or riding in a palace-car, was a piece of public business, and is, therefore, a topic not forbidden or unworthy. His guilt and his innocence in this respect can all be briefly stated.

The Monroe doctrine is one of the traditions of our country, and of both political parties. The Monroe doctrine means opposition to acquisitions on this continent by European powers. When President Grant came in no such question was pending, but such a question soon arose. An agent from the Dominican Republic presented himself to the President, saying that the people of Dominica, few in numbers, but rich in one of the most fertile isles of any sea, lying close to our shores, desired to come under the American flag; and that, failing this, that they would look to a European alliance. The President made no reply, and afterward a second agent appeared, repeating these statements, with glowing accounts of the fertility and resources of the Island of Santo Domingo.

Gen. McClellan, Admiral Porter, Commissioner Fabens and others had previously examined and reported upon the island, and had strongly stated its advantages as a coaling station, a naval station, a military key to the Gulf of Mexico, and as an area prolific in coffee, sugar cane, rice, dye-stuffs, mahogany, and other valuable woods, and in other products of the tropics, besides coal, copper, gold and salt.

records.full_text: Soon after his accession to power, he gave his mind, not to the great problems the solution of which the people so anxiously looked for, but to a project of his own—the acquisition of Santo Domingo. A subject of such importance as the incorporation with our political system of a tropical country with an utterly heterogeneous people, called for the most careful and earnest consideration. It is believed that the Secretary of State did not favor the scheme, and the State Department, whose office it is to conduct all the diplomatic affairs of the Government, was unceremoniously set aside. The President commenced a personal negotiation with Baez, the ruler of Santo Domingo, which he intrusted to one of his young aides de camp, whose zeal he had reason to believe equal to his own. The extraordinary character of this proceeding did not trouble him. He wanted to have the thing done; and to do it, an aide de camp was better than a Secretary of State. The aide de camp made a sort of a personal treaty between the two potentates, in which the President was pledged to propose to the favor of Congress for the scheme of the lobby at once. This disgraceful engagement would have revolted the sensibilities of any President having the dignity of his high office and the honor of the nation at heart.

The publication defended U.S. actions regarding San Domingo—asserting it was under U.S. protection and duty-bound to prevent outside pressure—while accusing the Haytien government of aiding opponents of the legal executive of San Domingo, including Cabral, with men-of-war, arms, and mountaineer forces. records.full_text:
Sajet, I say, showed at once his desire to continue the usual Haytien policy of bullying San Domingo. Fabre Geffrard and Salnave were the only Haytien executives who had not sought to embroil or invade the feebler republic. Four times the Haytiens have swept over the Dominican territory. Only once have their troops entered it on a mission of friendship and good faith, and that was when Salnave’s army, under General Alexandre Tate, (the accomplished soldier and diplomat, who for a brief space represented Hayti here,) aided the Dominicans, in 1864, to recover their independence from Spain. Mr. Sumner knows he cannot plead ignorance—that the claims of Hayti upon the territory of Dominica have always been a leading cause of the want of progress and prosperity therein. Hayti has been the bully! Hayti has alway been the hawk sailing in the air and ready to swoop upon Dominica, which it has always insisted was

ITS LAWFUL PREY.

Hayti has 800,000, San Domingo less than 200,000, inhabitants. Hayti is nearly all black, made up of slaves from over sixty African tribes, whose descendants have nobly, and savagely, too, fought and won their personal freedom and national independence. But, though they may be honored in this, there’s nothing in their history for sixty years past to go in ecstacies over. When Mr. Sumner says we bullied them, San Domingo was, in diplomatic usage, under our protection. We had the right, and it was our duty, to prevent outside pressure. The Haytien government was doing all it dared do to create this pressure. Its men-of-war were loaned to Luperon and others to make war on Baez—not a usurper, but the legal executive of San Domingo.

records.summary_en: The newspaper reported that Hayti repeatedly sought to subjugate Santo Domingo, whose government eventually appealed to the United States for protection amidst an imminent crisis. In response, the U.S. administration notified Haytian authorities that, pending a decision by Congress on the preliminary annexation treaty, any foreign invasion of Dominican territory would be considered an unfriendly act toward the United States. The author defended this action as a necessary duty in the interest of peace and humanity rather than a violation of international law.
records.summary_es: El diario consignó que Haití procuró en reiteradas ocasiones sojuzgar a Santo Domingo, cuyo gobierno acabó solicitando la protección de los Estados Unidos ante una crisis inminente. Como réplica, la administración de Washington notificó a las autoridades haitianas que, mientras el Congreso deliberase sobre las bases del tratado de anexión, toda invasión foránea al territorio dominicano se consideraría un acto hostil hacia los Estados Unidos. El autor justificó dicho proceder como una obligación ineludible en aras de la paz y de la humanidad, y no como una transgresión del derecho internacional.

records.full_text:
1. The alleged outrage upon Hayti occurred as follows: No sooner was it known that a negotiation for annexation was pending than preparations were made by the Haytian authorities to invade their feeble neighbor, instigated to this course by the diplomatic representatives of certain European Powers, who were jealous of American supremacy. Hayti, which comprises less than one-third of the island, (10,000 square miles,) has repeatedly sought to subjugate the whole (32,000 square miles.) She feared that Santo Domingo would forever escape from her clutches. The population of Hayti (500,000) is four-fold that of Santo Domingo, (125,000,) and is governed by a military despotism under the forms of a republic. Hayti was possessed of an armed steamer. The seaports of Santo Domingo, protected by only two small schooners, were liable to bombardment. The crisis was imminent, and the Government of Santo Domingo appealed to our Government for protection against a danger growing out of this very negotiation.

What did the Administration do? Just this: in the interest of peace and humanity it notified the Haytian authorities that a preliminary treaty of annexation had been negotiated, and that, until Congress should have expressed its decision, an invasion of the Dominican territory by any foreign Power would be regarded as an act unfriendly to the United States.

records.full_text: We were at one time inclined to think the action of the Administration in sending ships into the waters of San Domingo was, at least, questionable. Mr. Schurz says that to re-elect the President after such conduct is to condone the most flagrant and perilous violation of the Constitution, and to invite despotism. That is an extravagance at which a man can only smile. For never was anything more frank and fair than the position of the President upon the whole subject. Indeed, nothing has commended him to the confidence of the country more than his entire candor upon this question. For the satisfactory truth about the ships is told by Mr. Blackwell. The Dominican republic, helpless and hopeless under the perpetual aggressions of Hayti, proposed annexation to the United States upon condition of our assumption of its debt, which was about a million and a half of dollars. The President, who was not at first inclined to the project, at last sent a confidential and honorable agent to ascertain the precise facts. Satisfied with the inquiry, a treaty was prepared and submitted to the Senate. But as soon as Hayti knew that a negotiation was pending, she prepared to invade her neighbor, undoubtedly instigated by European influence.

1. The alleged outrage upon Hayti occurred as follows: No sooner was it known that a negotiation for annexation was pending than preparations were made by the Haytian authorities to invade their feeble neighbor, instigated to this course by the deplomatic representatives of certain European Powers, who were jealous of American suprmacy. Hayti, which comprises less than one-third of the island (10,000 square miles,) has repeatdly sought to subjugate the whole (32,000 square miles.) She feared that Santo Domingo would forever escape from her clutches. The population of Hayti (500 000) is four fold that of Santo Domingo (125,000,) and is governed by a military despotism under the forms of a republic. Hayti was possessed of an armed steamer. The seaports of Santo Domingo, protected by only two small schooners, were liable too bombardment. The crisis was iminent, and the Government of Santo Domingo appealed to our Government for protection against a danger growing out of this very negotiation. Congress was not in session at the time.

What did the Administration do? Just this: In the interest of peace and humanity it notified the Haytian authorities that a preliminary treaty of annexation had been negotiated, and that, until Congress should have expressed its decision, an invasion of the Dominican territory by any foreign Power would be regarded as an act unfriendly to the United States.

SAMANA OURS.

The Money Sent to Baez by New York Merchants—Trade With Santo Domingo Secured.

From the New York World, Dec. 7.
It is now three and a half years since President Grant took up the subject of the annexation of Santo Domingo. The main idea urged in favor of the plan was that it was indispensible to the prosperity of American commerce for the United States to have in their possession a substantial territory in the West Indies. In June, 1869, the President appointed an agent to obtain information about the Dominican Republic, and General Babcock was finally sent out there. In September, 1869, he negotiated a preliminary treaty, which was approved by President Grant, and in November a regular treaty with President Baez was concluded. The matter was debated in Congress, a commission was sent to the island in January, 1871, and finally in April of that year President Grant relinquished the plan.

But it has since been taken up by prominent business men of this country, who were persuaded that it would be profitable to them to secure what the Government had rejected. Some of them had visited Santo Domingo, and the result is that the steamer Tybee has just taken out, with other valuable cargo, the money required by the Baez Government for a certain specified amount of territory, including the Bay of Samana and for which Congress refused an appropriation. It is reported in business circles that one gain that will accrue to the new company will be in the shape of the port dues.

The following coloquy with Mr. C. K. Garrison gives all the particulars upon the matter that are now obtainable:

Mr. Garrison, when found at his office at the Bowling Green, was at first unwilling to communicate what he knew upon this important subject, but finding that the main facts were already known to his visitor became more communicative.

When asked, "Is it really true, that the Tybee has gone out with important lading connected with the new enterprise of the mercantile association that proposes tofollow up the Santo Domingo project?" he replied in substance, "Yes, a number of us, merchants and others, have concluded that we will accept the bargain that the government has refused. This is apart from all political considerations; is a mere matter of business."

"What shape has your action taken?"

"We have raised the money demanded and sent it out in the Tybee, and will thus gain control of the Port of Samana, the finest in the West Indies, and capable of holding the navies of the world."

"You will have special rights and privileges, I suppose—be a sort of western 'East India Company?'"

"Well, we are paying out a great deal of money, and of course we are not giving it for nothing, but expect ample returns."

"Will not this first outlay need to be followed by other large expenditures for warehouses, etc.?"

"We don't know much about what will come after. We shall move cautiously, and be governed by circumstances."

"Are only New York capitalists in the enterprise?"

"No; there are capitalists of Boston, Philadelphia and other towns in the movement."

"It appears to be a legitimate transaction. I suppose that many of you have long had mercantile dealings with those regions?"

"Yes; I, for one, have been running steamers to those islands, as far down as Brazil. I have no connection with the administration, and it is a matter of business with us all."

"This is certainly a good way to settle a vexed question, and prevent further political controversy on the subject. But what is the condition of the island? Is there much industrial activity there?"

"There is a large export trade of coffee and other tropical products; but the point of the greatest importance will be the possession by Americans of such a fine port in the West Indies?

records.chapter_es: La lucha por la anexión estadounidense
records.full_text:
The annexation of the eastern portion of Santo Domingo, known as Dominica, and formerly a colony of Spain, was very actively discussed by the public and Congress. The following are the facts of the early negotiations and treaties: Two treaties between the governments of the United States and Dominica were signed. The first was known as the Samana treaty. By this Dominica cedes the entire domain of the district described therein, which includes the Peninsula and Bay of Samana, for a term of fifty years, reserving the free navigation, for an annual rental of $15,000 gold. Four months are stipulated for ratification, during which the United States protects Dominica from foreign intervention. One year's rent was paid down, and possession duly taken.

The second, known as the annexation treaty, provides for a renunciation of sovereignty in favor of the United States, and that the Dominican Republic be incorporated on the footing of a territory, eligible to admission into the Union in the discretion of Congress. Dominica cedes her property, as specified in a schedule, but reserves all other property not scheduled; delivery not to be made nor consideration paid until Congress shall have appropriated the money. This is $1,500,000 in gold; and is in consideration of property only. Its disposition is provided for—Dominica is to apply it to her debts. But the application is to be made by a commission which the United States is to respect and protect, to be appointed by those who at the signing of the treaty constituted the present actual Dominican Government. For all debt, liquidated and unliquidated, in excess of such sum, public bonds of Dominica shall stand as security; likewise all the public lands and other property reserved from cession. After the execution of the treaty no grants or concessions of lands, or of rights in lands, were to be made, or any debt contracted. Franchises other than those are not prohibited. It is also agreed that the United States is in no event liable for Dominican debts or obligations. The cession was not to be valid unless ratified by a vote of the people.

Both treaties were signed at the city of Santo Domingo November 29, 1869, on behalf respectively of President Grant and President Baez. In execution of anticipatory instructions, an adequate naval force under the direction of a representative of the army immediately carried into effect the protection clauses. This protection has never been remitted. Hayti, either as a foreign nation or as the government de jure of the whole island, as they claim, ostensibly remonstrated.

In March, 1870, the result was received of an election held in Dominica during a fortnight, beginning under a decree of President Baez and his Senate, dated February 16, 1870. The returns indicated a general approval of the treaty. About eighty days, however, had intervened before an election was found "possible." In appropriate localities an official registry was opened, in which citizens were invited to inscribe their suffrages. On the first day of opening the polls a citizen recorded himself in the negative. He was seized on the spot and sent out of the city by the military guard, present in strong force. Several, afterwards expelled from the country by President Baez, found refuge from violence in the house of the Italian consul. President Baez, in presence of the commercial agent of the United States, threatened influential citizens with banishment if they opposed the treaty, and frequently expressed the like intolerance.

The unanimity thus obtained was so suspicious as to require negative votes by invitation. The Dominican President habitually declared the dependence of his authority upon that of the United States in force, and said that the death or expulsion of himself and his cabinet could be averted only by this annexation.

The public property of Dominica in the main was to be left to her, with the corresponding burden of her own debts and liabilities, necessarily, without prejudice to third parties. Encumbrances then became matter of essential consequence. Beyond the fact that they were large, only the most obscure and meagre data were before the United States government concerning them previous to the report of the commissioners. A person named Fabens, resident in Dominica, made, as agent of the United States, a report placing the aggregate at $600,000. With some additions since it has been reckoned at some millions. It was reported that mortgages of enormous scope, grants of public lands—of which a single one to Fabens absorbed one-fifth—perpetual navigation and commercial franchises and other monopolies, mining right, banking privileges, right to valuable woods, guano, &c., land grants and charters for railroads, for immigration societies, &c., existed; and thus there was excited the belief that by way of grant or lien all the appropriable resources of the country have fallen under private control.

Subsequent to the signing of the treaty grants and concessions of every description were solicited of the Dominican government, against zealous remonstrances of their regular United States diplomatic agent, made without encouragement from Washington. The President, on sending the report of the commissioners to Congress, accompanied it with a message, in which he took strong ground for annexation, but, as is well known, without success.

records.full_text:
SANTO DOMINGO.

ANNEXATION IN A COMMERCIAL PHASE.

VIEWS OF DR. SAMUEL G. HOWE.
What He Thinks of Santo Domingo—His Opinions Concerning the Haytians—Annexation Popular in Santo Domingo—The Great Commercial Enterprise.
To the Editor of The Tribune.
SIR: The likings and preferences of different men for different parts of the earth are sometimes accounted for, sometimes not. A mountaineer loves his home with an exceeding love, because it is finite and comprehensible to his senses; the mountain is to him a thing apart from earth; it stands out against the sky; he can compass its foot, and can take in at a glance from its green and flowery base to its cold and snowy crown. The isles of the sea, you may love them as things having definite existence and form, and space and outline; you may sail around them; you may traverse them from shore to shore, and from the high points see all their contour. Not so with a vast continent; you cannot comprehend it; cannot make it a mental unit; while thinking of one part, you lose the thought of the rest.

Most men love the islands of the West Indies for their gorgeous tropical beauty, the like of which has not been seen; his eyes have not seen the earth's glory of the Lord. I love them for their delicious climate; their soft winds coming fresh from the sea every morning, and after fanning the mountains going out again at night as cool land breezes. I love them for their clear and ever-flowing brooks; their ever flowers; their ever crystal seas. They are the Eden of the earth, which the choicest races of men in the fullness of time shall possess and regard as paradise.

Especially do I love Hayti, the mountainous, the queen of the Antilles, whose natural beauties and advantages distinguish her even among the beautiful grouped around. I take deep interest in the condition and fate of the two peoples who to-day divide her territory between them. The western end, the seat of the negro republic, is a land of rare beauty, marvelous fertility, varied production, notwithstanding the dreadful insalubrity of its seaboard; well fitted for the black man to try the experiment of self-government, and maintain the independence so gallantly won by his ancestors. It is sadly true that during the half century of that independence very little progress has been made toward civilization, even in the seaport towns, and that barbarous superstition and pagan sacrifices prevail in the interior among negroes as uncivilized as those of central Africa. Well did Frederick Douglass exclaim after a short sojourn at Port-au-Prince: "Alas! is this all that my fellow-men of color can accomplish?"

It may be, perhaps, that the black races cannot originate a new and high civilization of their own; but they can certainly imitate and carry on a civilization originated by others. But there is much in the history of Hayti to account for its present wretched condition; and there are men among Haytians who would honor any people. The French slave system was more horrid and debasing than the Spanish, which prevailed at the eastern end; and during its domination in Hayti the slaves became brutalized. Their long, bloody war for freedom was full of horrible atrocities on either side that further brutalized them. Then, after gaining their independence, they adopted the fatal policy of national isolation. They drove away most of the whites, and have continued to keep them out; they deny to them ownership of land and the right of full citizenship. Thus they have attempted to found and conduct a republic upon the narrow basis of race. Their friends abroad have sustained them in this foolish policy, and the end is the establishment of a conservative and odious aristocracy in the State, which sustains itself by a reign of terror.

But in spite of all this, we must give the black man all the aid and comfort we can, and say heartily: Vive la Republique d'Haiti, quand meme! I believe that the best way to help the Haytian is to set in his immediate neighborhood, over the mountain border, the flag of our Union, and carry thither our political and social institutions, our arts and our agriculture, that he may see them, imitate them, and profit by them. I know of no better way than to profit by the one which is now open, and obtain the right to say peace shall be kept in these regions, and they shall be opened to the peaceful spread of our commerce and our institutions.

It is for this end that I have labored, and shall labor, for the annexation of the eastern (Spanish) end of the island, now occupied by the Republic of Santo Domingo. This country is far more favored in felicitous geographical position, and salubrity of climate; is well adapted for the residence of white men, and for varied agricultural and industrial pursuits. It lies to windward, and the trade winds, drawing through the valleys between the two mountain ranges which traverse it from east to west, deposit their moisture, which is condensed on these mountains, keeping everything green to their very summits, and trickling down in constant rills and brooks. But by the time the trade winds reach the cross range which, running from north to south, separates the two republics, they have become dry and hot, and bring neither moisture nor coolness to the western end; hence proceed mainly the salubrity of the former and the insalubrity of the latter region.

Santo Domingo has been still more favored than Hayti in respect to its civil and political conditions. Its inhabitants were a mixed race of Spanish, Indian, and blacks, who live together on terms of equality; they fought side by side in the wars for driving out the Haytians and other invaders, and have a common and strong feeling of nationality. The Spaniards, during their long domination, maintained a mild form of slavery over the blacks; but with their usual liberality they accorded to the inhabitants considerable municipal rights and privileges. Hence, instead of the barbarism and the heathen practices which prevail in the interior of Hayti, we find throughout that of Santo Domingo a gentle and peaceful people, living in villages and observing the customs of civilized life. We find regular civil institutions, with civil magistrates chosen by the people; we find property pretty equally divided, and regular registries of titles, births, deaths, and the like. We find in almost every village well-bred and well-mannered men, speaking Spanish and French, and showing considerable intelligence. We find everywhere a tolerant and democratic spirit. There is not a general desire for education and improvement; but there are men who comprehend the situation of their country, and the ways and means by which to elevate it. These men give the tone to public opinion. They believe that annexation to the United States will be the greatest blessing to their country.

With the exception of here and there an enthusiast, who cries Viva la Republica, these men despair of the persistent independence of their own isle. They know that their black neighbors of Hayti never will forego the purpose, so often manifested by bloody invasions, of subjugating and dominating the whole island. This knowledge keeps them in constant dread, and paralyzes all attempts at self-improvement. To ward off these invasions the government maintains an army which keeps all the young men from work, and fits them for plunderers of the peasantry. The Government is too feeble to repel foreign invasions, and hence the apprehensions of their island being again seized upon by Spain, or some other foreign power.

These and other causes have made many Dominicans look to some foreign power which would not accord them, as Spain did, "the protection which vultures give to lambs, covering and devouring them," but aid upon equal terms of reciprocity. Since our victory over Slavery, the desire for annexation to our country has become unanimous and intense among the Dominican people. I have seen proofs enough of this fact. I saw it plainly on my official visit as Commissioner two years ago; I saw them more plainly still during a more protracted residence among the Dominicans last winter. Their best men unceasingly use their influence toward bringing about a measure to which they look as their surest guarantee of freedom, safety and prosperity.

I am more and more convinced of the truth contained in the first Presidential message upon the subject of annexation to the United States: would be a furtherance of the Monroe doctrine; that it is a national protection, asserting our just and controlling influence over the great commercial traffic soon to flow from east to west by way of the Isthmus of Darien; build up our merchant marine, furnish new markets for the products of our farms, shops and manufactories; make slavery insupportable in Cuba and Porto Rico at once, and ultimately in Brazil; and settle the unhappy condition of Cuba and its exterminating conflict; and therefore I have labored in season and out of season to bring about annexation in some shape.

It will rather thwart the one proposed by him, and therefore it is hoped that it will escape the vehement invectives and abuse heaped upon that. It is not a political measure, and cannot excite well-founded political opposition. There may be some who will oppose it in the supposed interest of the dominant party in Hayti, which continually aims at possession of the whole island, and means by force if it can.

It is a great commercial enterprise, undertaken by men of wealth and energy; and whether it yields them the rich returns they look for or not, it will open the vast resources of Santo Domingo, and establish between it and this country relations advantageous to both.
Yours, &c.,
SAMUEL G. HOWE.
Boston, Jan. 1, 1873.

records.summary_en: A despatch announces the completion of a treaty between the Samana Bay Company and the Republic of St. Domingo under President Baez, ceding the peninsula of Samana with the waters of the bay, its islands and reefs. Under the treaty the company may acquire and sell property, carry on any kind of business, issue bonds, establish banks, collect port dues and taxes in its possessions, keep its own police and other forces, and sail vessels under its own flag, with the stated object of building up a free state and a great centre of trade at Samana Bay.
records.summary_es: Un despacho anuncia la conclusión de un tratado entre la Compañía de la Bahía de Samaná y la República de Santo Domingo bajo el presidente Báez, que cede la península de Samaná con las aguas de la bahía, sus islas y arrecifes. Según el tratado, la compañía puede adquirir y vender propiedades, ejercer cualquier clase de negocio, emitir bonos, establecer bancos, cobrar derechos portuarios e impuestos en sus posesiones, mantener su propia policía y otras fuerzas, y hacer navegar barcos bajo su propia bandera, con el propósito declarado de construir un estado libre y un gran centro de comercio en la bahía de Samaná.

records.summary_en: According to *The New York Herald* on January 17, 1873, a business or stock-jobbing scheme involving St. Domingo gained thousands of dollars in free advertising through press coverage. The newspaper stated that while American enterprise abroad is acceptable provided the government is not dragged into defending land grants, the President must define the administration's position to prevent annexation or complications. Finally, the article expressed strong opposition to annexing St. Domingo, describing it as a distant tropical island with little trade and a sparse population, while asserting that the United States already has sufficient territory.
records.summary_es: Según *The New York Herald* del 17 de enero de 1873, un tinglado especulativo de bolsa centrado en Santo Domingo cosechó miles de dólares en publicidad gratuita mediante la cobertura periodística. El diario opinó que, si bien la iniciativa privada estadounidense en el exterior es lícita con tal de que no comprometa al gobierno en la defensa de mercedes de tierras, el presidente debe deslindar la postura oficial para precaver anexiones o conflictos. Finalmente, el artículo expresó una enérgica repulsa a incorporar a Santo Domingo, caracterizándola como una remota isla tropical de precario comercio y escaso vecindario, concluyendo que los Estados Unidos gozan ya de suficiente extensión territorial.

We do not think the President would act in such a surreptitious manner. We believe he honestly thinks that the possession of the territory of St. Domingo, or the Samana portion of it, by an American company, would be a benefit to the trade of the country. records.headline: The Samana Bay Company persistently refused to give the press a copy of its treaty with the Dominican government
records.summary_en: The Samana Bay Company persistently refused to give the press a copy of its treaty with the Dominican government, even as its officers freely praised the resources and prospects of their acquired possession. The Herald prints the treaty's full text and reports that the commissioners, after weeks of daily sessions with President Baez in the Executive Palace, obtained concessions more favorable than they had hoped for, and that the Dominican Senate accepted the treaty after about a week of debate, stipulating only that it be submitted to the people for ratification.

El Herald publica el texto completo del tratado e informa que los comisionados, tras semanas de sesiones diarias con el presidente Báez en el Palacio Ejecutivo, obtuvieron concesiones más favorables de lo que habían esperado, y que el Senado dominicano aceptó el tratado tras aproximadamente una semana de debate, estipulando solo que fuera sometido al pueblo para su ratificación.

records.summary_en: The *New York Herald* reported on the terms of a convention involving territories under the joint protection of the Dominican Republic and the United States, as well as the Samaná Bay Company. According to Articles 11 through 13, the convention requires ratification by the Dominican nation and Senate, specifies conditions for nullification—such as war or *force majeure* following an annual rent payment—and outlines the Dominican Republic's jurisdiction and its agreement to provide the company with necessary documents and security.

The company is entitled to emit bonds for railroad, canal, telegraph and highroad constructions, with the faculty of guaranteeing payment there-against, and further, shall have the right to hypothecate the bonds emitted for the purpose of raising funds to carry on the work, and shall further have the right to emit further stock for the completion of said work.

Neither:—Emigrants who shall purchase land of the company or the agents of said company, or merchants who shall be engaged in commercial pursuits between Samana and other points of the Dominican Republic shall be compelled to pay higher imposts than Dominican citizens. It is also further understood that no taxes shall be levied by the Dominican government upon works of public utility, or the banking establishments—and, in a word, the company shall be treated as the most favored of Dominican citizens.

The company shall have the privilege of authorizing the formation of other companies, and has the right of ceding land to them upon such terms and stipulations as may be considered most advantageous, and, by so doing, carry out the aims and objects for which the company was organized.

The aforesaid smaller companies shall have their names designated by the said Samana Bay Company, and shall be under the superintendence and inspection of the said company, which shall have the privilege of holding shares in the said smaller companies.

The privileges and concessions accorded to this company shall be without prejudice to privileges and concessions accorded to any other person or persons by the Dominican government, for, up to the present time, no such privileges or concessions have been granted similar to those now conceded to the Samana Bay Company, which is now empowered, for the space of thirty days, to accept or refuse said treaty.

ART. 10.—These concessions, rights, privileges and immunities shall take effect on the first day of January, in the year eighteen hundred and seventy-three, and will continue in force and will remain in force for ninety-nine years from the said date (with the exception of a certain time that is to be conceded to the company for the purpose of taking possession, on the condition that the said company, its successors or representatives, pay or cause to be paid, to the Dominican government the sum of $150,000, in American gold, in advance, to the Dominican government. The said sum to be charged in advance to the company on the 1st day of January of each year, and the payment thereagainst to be made in the capital city of St. Domingo on the same, or at any place that may be designated by the Dominican government.

The first of these annual advance payments shall be made on the 1st of January, in the year 1873, unless it has been made before. The company and its territories shall remain under the united protection of the Dominican Republic and the United States of America, and the company and its agents, when they deem it necessary, shall ask the protection and intervention of either of these nations or of both.

ART. 11.—For the purposes of ratifying this convention a vote will be taken on the subject by the Dominican nation and the Dominican Senate. The non-payment of the annual rent alluded to in article 10 or the breaking out of war or other circumstances of force majeure will cause the said convention to be considered null and void after thirty days' notice has been given by the Dominican government.

records.full_text:
The Herald says: "It is absurd to speak of a vast trade with St. Domingo. One little steamer making monthly trips does the principal trade with the United States. There is hardly any other. The Company speaks of a prospective trade amounting to hundreds of millions. This is ridiculous. San Domingo has scarcely any production in itself. However rich the soil may be, there is not the labor, nor do we think it can be carried there to make the soil productive. Then it is an error to say that the island has a commanding position for trade with the Antilles and South America. It lies on the outer verge of the whole group, and is not properly in the track of commerce."

The Company, however, say they will make Samana virtually a free port, and gradually absorb all the trade of the West Indies. Governor Fabens has posted the Company's flag at Samana, and the steamship Tybee, at Pier No. 4, North River, floats the same emblem from her fore. It is a combination of the Dominican and United States flags. From edge to edge across its centre, lengthwise and crosswise, is a broad white band, dividing the flag into four other parts. In the upper left-hand corner is the union jack, a blue field and white stars. The upper right-hand corner is red, the lower right blue, and the lower left-hand corner red. The negotiations with Baez for the purchase of Samana extended through two weeks. Audiences were given daily in the Executive Palace, the hours being from 8:30 a. m. to 4:30 p. m., with an intermission for dinner. The negotiations were conducted in Spanish, and during their progress the Commissioners had no relations of intimacy with the members of the Government, living on board the ship, and not seeing the Dominicans except in business hours. When the negotiations were completed, and the treaty ratified, the President gave a grand ball in honor of the Commissioners, who returned the compliment by a dinner on the Tybee.

Several times the negotiations were nearly broken off. On one occasion the Commissioners retired to their steamer, got up steam, blew their whistle, and were nearly off, and then they were recalled. Whether the Dominicans were frightened by the steam whistle is not known, but the negotiations were resumed, and finally the President and his Ministers ratified the contract. It was then referred to the Senate, which comprises nine members. The Senate discussed the Convention several days, during which the members of the Government were invited before that body to explain the various provisions of the treaty. The result of these deliberations was the ratification by the Senate. That branch of the Government agreed with the Executive, that a treaty, which was such an innovation on the laws of the country, and which granted such unusual and extraordinary powers to a private company, should not be finally and wholly carried into effect without its ratification by the people at the polls. This has doubtless been accomplished before the present date. Perhaps nine-tenths of the population, altogether about 240,000, are uneducated and ignorant. The voters of this class are expected to have no opinion but to vote as their superiors direct. The educated and wealthier classes favor the scheme and therefore the Company have no doubt that the Convention will be overwhelmingly ratified at the polls.

records.summary_en: The secretary of the Samana Bay Company says the company was to protect itself from outside interference but counted upon the sympathy and aid of foreign governments, and that it would first declare Samana Bay a free port to the whole world. A Washington dispatch adds that congressmen considered the Samana Bay scheme impracticable, and that the Haitian minister thought the American purchasers would find they had made a bad speculation, the bay being fit for nothing but a naval station.

Un despacho de Washington añade que los congresistas consideraban el plan de la bahía de Samaná impracticable, y que el ministro haitiano pensaba que los compradores estadounidenses descubrirían que habían hecho una mala especulación, pues la bahía no servía para nada más que para una estación naval.

Additionally, the Associated Press reported from New York that the Company is expected to seek United States Government protection, lease a naval station in the bay, and agitate for annexation utilizing powerful lobby interests.

Further Details of the Sale to the American Company—Creation of a Sovereign Power—Speculations and Surmises Regarding the Future Action of the New Nation.
Special Despatch to The Chicago Tribune.
NEW YORK, Jan. 18.—The full text of the Samana purchase convention confirms the fact that the Company has obtained absolute sovereignty over the peninsula, with its inhabitants and private interests. The sovereignty conceded to the Company is greater than that of the State of New York, or any other State in the Union, for it includes the right to levy and collect custom duties, and to do many other things which can only be done by a sovereign nation. Baez not only sells them these extraordinary privileges, but he sells them the flag of the Republic of St. Domingo to use as they may see proper. Besides all this, the Company can build railroads and telegraphs in any part of the island, obtaining grants as extraordinary as those accorded to the Union Pacific and other railroads when Congress was giving away the public domain. Every league of railroad constructed by the Company brings its square league of land, and every three leagues of telegraph, a square league grant. The Company promised Baez to use all their influence with Congress to bring Dominican products into the ports of the United States, free of duty, which would be a singular discrimination against other tropical countries.

A most extraordinary feature of the treaty is that it frees the men composing the Company from the operation of our Register and Navigation laws. Under the acts of Congress, American merchants cannot buy ships abroad. This Company, though composed mostly of Americans, can buy ships where it can buy them cheapest, for it has bought a flag under which to run them.

The Herald says on this head: "A few judicious alliances with American railway monopolies would make the Company as powerful in the United States as in St. Domingo, and in the end it might rule us as effectually as our tan-colored brethren in the West Indies."

[To the Associated Press.]
NEW YORK, Jan. 18.—A great deal of speculation is rife in this city as to the Samana Bay Company seeking aid from the United States Government in furthering its objects. It is thought that the Company will endeavor first to obtain the formal protection of our Government, and, if possible, to lease it a naval station in the bay, and, further, to agitate the idea of annexation. Already it is stated that powerful lobby interests are to be created with these ends in view, and that Congress will be asked soon to pass exceptional tariff laws applying to the trade from San Domingo.

records.headline: A message from the commissioners at Puerto Plata announces the ratification by the Dominican Senate of the convention
records.summary_en: A message from the commissioners at Puerto Plata announces the ratification by the Dominican Senate of the convention leasing the Bay of Samana to a company, on terms similar to those once offered to the United States administration. In addition, the company is allowed to build railroads, construct canals and telegraphs in return for land grants, and for its privileges, which could let it monopolize the commerce and port duties of the island, it will pay the Dominican Government $150,000 in gold annually.
records.summary_es: Un mensaje de los comisionados en Puerto Plata anuncia la ratificación por el Senado dominicano del convenio que arrienda la bahía de Samaná a una compañía, en términos similares a los ofrecidos en su día a la administración de los Estados Unidos. Además, la compañía podrá construir ferrocarriles, canales y telégrafos a cambio de concesiones de tierras, y por sus privilegios, que podrían permitirle monopolizar el comercio y los derechos portuarios de la isla, pagará al Gobierno dominicano 150.000 dólares en oro al año.

records.headline: A letter recounts the San Domingo loan affair: a commission of five was sent to examine the securities offered for repayment
records.summary_en: A letter recounts the San Domingo loan affair: a commission of five was sent to examine the securities offered for repayment, which consisted of the country's revenues, a guano deposit said to exist on the island of Alta Vela, and gold mines. Henry Lawson returned to London persuaded the securities were worthless, yet a very large sum had already been sent to Baez, and the loan, after damaging newspaper articles, was withdrawn and voted a swindle; the account then follows the promoter Hartmont on to New York and the Samana Bay scheme.
records.summary_es: Una carta relata el asunto del préstamo de Santo Domingo: se envió una comisión de cinco personas a examinar las garantías ofrecidas para el pago, que consistían en las rentas del país, un depósito de guano que se decía existía en la isla de Alta Vela, y minas de oro. Henry Lawson regresó a Londres convencido de que las garantías no valían nada, pero ya se había enviado una suma muy grande a Báez, y el préstamo, tras artículos dañinos en los periódicos, fue retirado y considerado una estafa; el relato sigue luego al promotor Hartmont hasta Nueva York y el proyecto de la bahía de Samaná.

records.summary_en: According to the Burlington weekly free press on January 31, 1873, U.S. Commissioners reported that a convention regarding a contract in the Dominican Republic was submitted to a public vote to prevent future administrative interference, with voting underway on the 9th inst. The Commissioners expressed confidence that the popular vote would be nearly or quite unanimous for ratification, making the convention part of the Republic's fundamental law. Additionally, they noted receiving good wishes from leading foreign merchants and European consular representatives, along with assurances that the free port and city of Samana could quickly attract a large population from various West Indian islands.
records.summary_es: Según el *Burlington Weekly Free Press* del 31 de enero de 1873, los comisionados de los Estados Unidos informaron que la convención relativa a un contrato en la República Dominicana se sometió a plebiscito popular para conjurar futuras injerencias de gobiernos venideros, habiéndose iniciado la votación el día 9 del corriente. Los delegados manifestaron su certidumbre de que el sufragio popular respaldaría casi unánimemente la ratificación, elevando la convención a rango de ley fundamental de la república. Añadieron haber recibido parabienes de los principales mercaderes foráneos y agentes consulares europeos, junto con el augurio de que la ciudad y puerto franco de Samaná atraerían prontamente una copiosa corriente inmigratoria proveniente de diversas islas antillanas.

records.headline: Dr. Samuel G. Howe writes
records.summary_en: Dr. Samuel G. Howe writes that he and Benjamin F. Wade, as United States Commissioners to Santo Domingo, favored political annexation, and that after annexation was rejected he worked for a commercial company to lease the peninsula and bay of Samana for ninety-nine years. He describes negotiating the terms with President Baez and his cabinet, consulting the Dominican Senate of Seven, and organizing the company, with the first year's rent of $150,000 to be paid in advance.

records.summary_en: A correspondent describes the Dominican part of the island as the center of a tobacco trade finding a market in Hamburg, of rich cocoa plantations, and of gold and iron mining in the neighboring mountains, around towns including Cotui, La Vega and Santiago. The account then contrasts that region with the western division, Haiti, which it portrays in disparaging terms as bankrupt and decaying despite a favorable climate and soil.

El relato contrasta luego esa región con la división occidental, Haití, a la que retrata en términos denigrantes como arruinada y en decadencia pese a un clima y un suelo favorables.

records.headline: A proclamation issued at headquarters on January 10, 1873, and signed by Dominican leaders including Gregorio Luperon
records.summary_en: A proclamation issued at headquarters on January 10, 1873, and signed by Dominican leaders including Gregorio Luperon and Jose Maria Cabral, calls on Dominicans in this hour of sorrow to come as brethren and array themselves under the banner of liberty. It declares that the land must be rid now and forever of traitors and of the burning disgrace that has fallen upon it, and gives the rallying cry of liberty and independence, and down with Baez, their perpetual enemy.
records.summary_es: Una proclama emitida en el cuartel general el 10 de enero de 1873, y firmada por líderes dominicanos, entre ellos Gregorio Luperón y José María Cabral, llama a los dominicanos en esta hora de dolor a acudir como hermanos y formarse bajo la bandera de la libertad. Declara que la patria debe librarse ahora y para siempre de los traidores y de la ardiente vergüenza que ha caído sobre ella, y da como grito de unión libertad e independencia, y abajo Báez, su enemigo perpetuo.

records.headline: A dispatch from New York confirms that the revolutionary chiefs in San Domingo have allied against Baez, in a pronunciamiento
records.summary_en: A dispatch from New York confirms that the revolutionary chiefs in San Domingo have allied against Baez, in a pronunciamiento by Luperon, Cabral and twelve other leaders issued a few days after the sale of the Samana Peninsula. The proclamation protests the sale of Samana to an American company that will transfer its powers to the United States Government, denies that the Dominican Senate has power to grant such a commission to a foreign nation, and concludes with an appeal to all Dominicans to rally and wage a vigorous war against Baez.
records.summary_es: Un despacho de Nueva York confirma que los jefes revolucionarios de Santo Domingo se han aliado contra Báez, en un pronunciamiento de Luperón, Cabral y otros doce líderes emitido pocos días después de la venta de la península de Samaná. La proclama protesta por la venta de Samaná a una compañía americana que transferirá sus poderes al Gobierno de los Estados Unidos, niega que el Senado dominicano tenga facultad para otorgar semejante comisión a una nación extranjera, y concluye con un llamado a todos los dominicanos a unirse y hacer una guerra vigorosa contra Báez.

records.headline: A correspondent's letter from Santa Barbara, Samana Bay, dated February 13, 1873, describes arriving aboard the Tybee
records.summary_en: A correspondent's letter from Santa Barbara, Samana Bay, dated February 13, 1873, describes arriving aboard the Tybee at sunrise and being welcomed by Colonel Joseph Warren Fabens, presented as governor of the peninsula, and by Mr. Price, the consul. The pioneer emigrants of the Samana Bay Company settlement are aboard inspecting the discharge of the vessel's freight and looking over the village of Santa Barbara, with its eighty-four houses, as the place where their future settlement and homes are to be made.
records.summary_es: La carta de un corresponsal desde Santa Bárbara, bahía de Samaná, fechada el 13 de febrero de 1873, describe la llegada a bordo del Tybee al amanecer y la bienvenida del coronel Joseph Warren Fabens, presentado como gobernador de la península, y del señor Price, el cónsul. Los emigrantes pioneros del asentamiento de la Compañía de la Bahía de Samaná están a bordo inspeccionando la descarga del cargamento del buque y observando el pueblo de Santa Bárbara, con sus ochenta y cuatro casas, como el lugar donde se harán su futuro asentamiento y sus hogares.
records.passage: plants and trees familiar to the readers of tropical botany. Presently there came on deck Colonel Joseph Warren Fabens, who owns a handsome slice of this territory. I looked for some display of emotion in his address of welcome, for was he not Governor of the Peninsula, and were we not the pioneer colony destined to make Samana the talk and the envy of the world! He was happy to see us, and so was Mr. Price, the Consul, whose residence on the high jutting promontory made every [pilgrim?] [illegible] expand with the anticipation of having some such elevated station for life. Fabens set about the work of inspecting the discharge of the vessel's freight, and the voice of Albert, the mate, might have been heard through the early morning echoing among the hills, keeping the dusky stevedores to their duty. One of the native canoes rowed by a darky, whose Philadelphia parents allowed him to get hopelessly involved in the Spanish dialect, took two of us to Santa Barbara, and through the various streets, lanes, alleys and nondescript squares of that singular village of eighty-four houses we wandered in the early forenoon. In the meantime, of course, there was great commotion among the emigrants on board. All eyes were riveted on the scene of the future settlement. To be Sure, there were no ready-made plantations to the eye, but there was a general concurrence that all the material was right there in front of us out of which to carve happy homes and fortunes. There was a general anxiety to see the carpenters from Harlem at work, to see that hotel erected

records.headline: An editorial presents a first look at the 'dreamland' in St. Domingo
records.summary_en: An editorial presents a first look at the 'dreamland' in St. Domingo that speculators of the Samana Bay Company have fenced in with treaties, leases and powers, describing Santa Barbara as a delightful spot, the bay as first-class anchorage, and the soil as fertile. It notes that the $150,000 paid to Baez smoothed away much of the first difficulty and that Baez's ministers reported 22,000 votes cast for the treaty, while questioning what would happen when the people saw how little of the company's money reached beyond Baez's coffers.
records.summary_es: Un editorial presenta una primera mirada al 'país de ensueño' en Santo Domingo que los especuladores de la Samana Bay Company han cercado con tratados, arrendamientos y poderes, describiendo Santa Bárbara como un lugar encantador, la bahía como un fondeadero de primera clase, y el suelo como fértil. Señala que los 150.000 dólares pagados a Báez allanaron gran parte de la primera dificultad y que los ministros de Báez informaron de 22.000 votos a favor del tratado, mientras se pregunta qué pasará cuando la gente vea lo poco del dinero de la compañía que llega más allá de las arcas de Báez.

records.headline: The paper reports that a Dominican governor forcibly removed three men who had sought refuge under the British flag
records.summary_en: The paper reports that a Dominican governor forcibly removed three men who had sought refuge under the British flag at the home of the British consul, an act the community feared could draw a response from an expected British warship. It also recounts an earlier mountain revolt against President Báez, linked in the report to opposition to a territorial surrender to a company, which the governor quickly crushed.
records.summary_es: El periódico informa que un gobernador dominicano sacó por la fuerza a tres hombres que habían buscado refugio bajo la bandera británica en la casa del cónsul británico, un acto que, según se temía en la comunidad, podría provocar una respuesta de un buque de guerra británico esperado. También relata una revuelta anterior en las montañas contra el presidente Báez, vinculada en el informe a la oposición a una cesión territorial a una compañía, que el gobernador aplastó rápidamente.

records.headline: A Puerto Plata report prints a letter from the British vice-consul stating that General Juan Nuezl, former governor of the city
records.summary_en: A Puerto Plata report prints a letter from the British vice-consul stating that General Juan Nuezl, former governor of the city, and his sons Martin and Claudia had claimed the protection of the British flag at his home. When the authorities ruled that the consul's private house was not his consulate, the mayor surrounded the house, entered it by force after three summonses, and took the three Nuezis prisoner to the fort in irons; one son said his father opposed the Samana lease and had determined to oppose it by physical force.
records.summary_es: Un informe de Puerto Plata publica una carta del vicecónsul británico que declara que el general Juan Nuezl, antiguo gobernador de la ciudad, y sus hijos Martín y Claudia habían reclamado la protección de la bandera británica en su casa. Cuando las autoridades resolvieron que la casa particular del cónsul no era su consulado, el alcalde rodeó la casa, entró en ella por la fuerza tras tres requerimientos, y llevó a los tres Nuezl prisioneros al fuerte con grilletes; un hijo dijo que su padre se oponía al arrendamiento de Samaná y había decidido oponerse a él por la fuerza física.

Shortly after writing the letter just quoted, Mr. Hamburger called on Governor Gonzales, and said to him it would be a politic stroke for him to make if he would state publicly that he had been aware the day before that Nunez and his sons were coming to seek an asylum at the British Consul's, to which Gonzales replied that he could not tell the public a lie, for if he had been aware of any such thing he should certainly have taken measures to apprehend them. records.headline: A Herald correspondent interviews an imprisoned former governor who says he took up arms because he wanted liberty of expression
records.summary_en: A Herald correspondent interviews an imprisoned former governor who says he took up arms because he wanted liberty of expression in the vote concerning the sale of Samana. He insists the people were dragooned into voting for the Baez measure and would have voted against it if the pressure had been taken off, that none of the money paid by the Americans would benefit the country but would go into the pockets of Baez and his associates, and that the government has done nothing for the people toward Monte Cristo who have had no rain in two years.
records.summary_es: Un corresponsal del Herald entrevista a un exgobernador encarcelado que dice que tomó las armas porque quería libertad de expresión en la votación sobre la venta de Samaná. Insiste en que la gente fue obligada a votar por la medida de Báez y habría votado en contra si se le hubiera quitado la presión, que nada del dinero pagado por los estadounidenses beneficiaría al país sino que iría a los bolsillos de Báez y sus asociados, y que el gobierno no ha hecho nada por la gente de hacia Monte Cristi que lleva dos años sin lluvia.
records.passage: English, without being perfect, was at least plain. I entered into conversation with the old man. I inquired what was the motive of his going into [illegible] acts of hostility to the government, and he answered that he was anxious to have liberty of expression in the vote concerning the Samana sale. Had he succeeded in capturing Puerto Plata the sense of the people would have been freely given on the question of renting Samana Bay to the Americans. They would not have been dragooned to vote for the Baez measure, and if the pressure had been taken off a majority would have been found against it. Every man who voted did so in dread of the consequences of recording himself in opposition to the government wishes. Only one or two had the temerity to say "no," but they were mere lads and their conduct was overlooked, he was OPPOSED TO THE BAEZ ADMINISTRATION because he believed it was composed of a set of thieves, and Baez was the biggest thief of the lot. records.headline: An editorial reports that at Puerto Plata a civil and military force under the Dominican Minister of Finance forcibly
records.summary_en: An editorial reports that at Puerto Plata a civil and military force under the Dominican Minister of Finance forcibly entered the residence of the British Vice Consul, Mr. Hamburger, and seized three citizens, enemies of Baez and opponents of the Samana sale, who were thrown into a dungeon, and that Baez approved the arrests and ordered the prisoners brought to Santo Domingo City. It warns that a British man-of-war is expected to demand satisfaction, and that Baez must not imagine the United States will protect him, since the Americans who paid $150,000 down for a year's rent of Samana Bay represent only themselves and their purchase implies no American protectorate.
records.summary_es: Un editorial informa que en Puerto Plata una fuerza civil y militar bajo el ministro de Finanzas dominicano entró por la fuerza en la residencia del vicecónsul británico, el señor Hamburger, y apresó a tres ciudadanos, enemigos de Baez y opositores a la venta de Samana, que fueron arrojados a un calabozo, y que Baez aprobó los arrestos y ordenó llevar a los prisioneros a la ciudad de Santo Domingo. Advierte que se espera un buque de guerra británico para exigir satisfacción, y que Baez no debe imaginar que los Estados Unidos lo protegerán, pues los americanos que pagaron $150,000 por un año de renta de la bahía de Samana solo se representan a sí mismos y su compra no implica ningún protectorado americano.

records.headline: Writing from Santiago de los Caballeros on March 4, the correspondent describes his eight-day journey across St. Domingo
records.summary_en: Writing from Santiago de los Caballeros on March 4, the correspondent describes his eight-day journey across St. Domingo from Samana, three days of it in a canoe slowly ascending the Yuna River from Santa Barbara to Almacen. On the way the party spent a night in hammocks at Bebedero and joined a marriage feast at a house near Santa Capuza, with music, dancing, tiny cups of coffee and revolver shots fired in honour of the event, before entering the small mouth of the Yuna at midday.
records.summary_es: Escribiendo desde Santiago de los Caballeros el 4 de marzo, el corresponsal describe su viaje de ocho días a través de Santo Domingo desde Samaná, tres de ellos en una canoa que remontaba lentamente el río Yuna desde Santa Bárbara hasta Almacén. En el camino el grupo pasó una noche en hamacas en Bebedero y se unió a una fiesta de boda en una casa cerca de Santa Capuza, con música, baile, tacitas de café y disparos de revólver en honor del acontecimiento, antes de entrar al mediodía por la boca pequeña del Yuna.
records.passage: retired to a palm grove, near the house, and fired off half a dozen rounds of ammunition in honor of the event, a proceeding which tickled the rejoicing household Immensely. It was midday When we entered the Boca [Chica?] or small mouth of the Yuna, the river on which the Samana Bay Company expect to put a steamer one of these days to drain the trade of the La Vega country. There is a bar at this mouth and a bar at the other, a short distance off the Boca Grande or large mouth, and the depth of water over each is about two feet and a half. The shores at the entrance, covered with vegetation, are exceedingly low, not more than a few inches above the water, disappearing altogether when the river is full. Here the festive alligator may be found and the mud he loves, for his pallet is spread over endless acres. A few hundred feet within the mouth of the river the depth is three feet, which is retained throughout all the tortuous windings of this stream to the village of Almasin, thirty-three miles' sailing distance, or seventeen as the bird flies.

Never were such unpromising subjects examined by the statesman's eye as are the rival nations who hate each other in Hayti. Placed side by side on an island smaller than Ireland, they dislike each other as heartily as a Montague disliked a Capulet. People who know nothing of their idiosyncrasies wonder why they cannot join hands and be happy. They have been joined by the sword, but it all depended on who had hold of the hilt to say how long they should remain so. They have been colonies and independent States. They have had burlesque kings and opera bouffe emperors, as well as military dictators and regular republican presidents. They have in the end insisted that, whoever was at their head, he should not be a stranger, and, much as we deplore their backwardness in the arts and sciences of civilization, we are constrained to admire something that looks so much like rugged patriotism.

records.headline: It is a pity both races cannot live on better terms
records.summary_en: According to the *New York Herald* on April 22, 1873, international animosity and border warfare between Hayti and the Dominican Republic had depopulated the border region, reducing towns like Dajabon to near-desolation. While Hayti's President Saget unsuccessfully sought a treaty of amity and commerce through the British consul general, Dominican leader Baez allegedly maintained hostilities to frighten Dominicans into supporting annexation to the United States. Additionally, the article contrasted the two nations' populations, noting that Hayti had a larger population and smaller territory with a seven-eighths black demographic, whereas the Dominican Republic was three-quarters Creole, with Creoles serving as the ruling and aristocratic element in both republics.
records.summary_es: Según *The New York Herald* del 22 de abril de 1873, las querellas internacionales y las guerras de frontera entre Haití y la República Dominicana habían despoblado la comarca limítrofe, sumiendo en la ruina y el abandono a villas como Dajabón. En tanto el presidente haitiano Saget gestionó infructuosamente un convenio de concordia y comercio con la mediación del cónsul general británico, se aseguraba que el gobernante dominicano Báez sostenía los enconos armados para intimidar a sus conciudadanos y forzarlos a cobijarse bajo la anexión a los Estados Unidos. El artículo contrastó asimismo la composición demográfica de ambos estados, refiriendo que Haití contaba con una población más densa en un territorio menor constituida en sus siete octavas partes por negros, en tanto que la República Dominicana era en sus tres cuartas partes criolla, integrando los criollos el estamento dirigente y aristocrático en ambas repúblicas.

The sentiment of fear on the part of the Dominicans is not inspired by the superior prowess of the Haytians. On the contrary the former are the better soldiers, and the latter know it so well that in a contest of equal numbers they invariably decline coming to close quarters, so great is their

TERROR OF THE MACHETE,
in the use of which no people excel the Dominicans. I saw a two-minute fight at Monte Cristi between a couple of Dominicans armed with machetes, and in that brief time the ground was littered with fingers and ears and pieces of skin and clothing from various parts of the body. In portions of the island it is rare for a native to have his full complement of fingers. To a Dominican the machete is everything. To cut his toe nails or cut down a palm tree he brings this weapon alone into requisition. In battle he throws away his gun if the enemy happen to be handy and sails in with his trusty machete. The article argued that acquiring the island solely for a naval station is an extravagant burden and that annexation would only benefit New England manufactures if foreign commerce from Germany, France, and England were excluded.

records.headline: An editorial notes that St. Domingo's difficulties
records.summary_en: An editorial notes that St. Domingo's difficulties are many and that Cabral, the revolutionary leader interviewed by a Herald correspondent, holds very decided views on them. The epithets he applies to President Baez are strong and numerous, his opinion of the future of the Samana Bay Company is not encouraging to the trusting shareholder, and while he is not himself opposed to the introduction of American hard cash, he is presented as waiting on the mountain ledges to swoop down on Baez.

records.summary_en: Buenaventura Baez writes to President Grant appealing for the Dominican people, saying the agreement with the Samana Bay Company has been followed by silence and indifference and that they cannot alone support the consequences of combined hatred against them. He solicits the establishment of an efficient United States protectorate to preserve them from unwarranted attacks aimed at their very existence.

Solicita el establecimiento de un protectorado eficaz de los Estados Unidos que los preserve de ataques injustificados dirigidos contra su propia existencia.

It not being possible for the Dominican people to continue to support alone and unaided the horrible consequence of a combined hatred, which manifests itself in disguised attacks and machinations, they appeal to the great Republic of the United States through your Excellency, soliciting the establishment of an efficient Protectorate which may preserve them from unwarranted attacks aimed at their very existence. The Dominican people believe that this will not be distasteful, even to the opponents of the plan of annexation, It would be an act of munificence and generosity whereby the Republic of the United States would risk nothing, since It would simply cover with its aegis an inoffensive and friendly people, whom Providence designed to be its natural ally, and all the sons of this people would greet with joy the day when their powerful sister should stretch out [her?] hand to save them from the dangers which encompass them, which dangers would instantly disappear in view of such a diplomatic act, If your Excellency, seeing that the fate of a people with pretensions is at stake, shall feel, as [I?] hope will be the case, a sympathetic impulse to do them justice, and shall make an effort to secure for them the protection of the Republic of the United States, you will have the immense satisfaction of having saved the future of a people of the world discovered by Columbus, without having assured any responsibility,

records.summary_en: The *New-York Tribune* reported that Mr. Báez proposed that President Grant establish a U.S. protectorate over Santo Domingo to guard against attacks and influences from Hayti, having exhausted other resources after the failure of annexation and the Samana Bay enterprise. Báez also forwarded a disavowed treaty between Hayti and Santo Domingo containing a clause against alienating territory to foreign powers, attempting to provoke national jealousy regarding European machinations. President Grant laid the communication before Congress without making any recommendations, and the scheme was deemed unlikely to receive favor from the National Legislature.
records.summary_es: El *New-York Tribune* informó que el Sr. Báez propuso al presidente Grant erigir un protectorado estadounidense sobre Santo Domingo para repeler las agresiones e influencias procedentes de Haití, habiendo agotado todos sus recursos tras frustrarse la anexión y la empresa de la Samaná Bay Company. Báez remitió asimismo un desautorizado convenio entre Haití y Santo Domingo provisto de una cláusula prohibitiva de toda cesión territorial a potencias foráneas, en una tentativa de azuzar los celos geopolíticos frente a maquinaciones europeas. El presidente Grant dio traslado de dicha comunicación al Congreso sin formular recomendación alguna, juzgándose improbable que el parlamento dispensase una acogida favorable al proyecto.

Additionally, the company owns the Samana peninsula in fee simple and seeks to acquire possession of La Vega Real.

An officer of the Samana Bay Company was questioned yesterday by a reporter of THE TRIBUNE relative to the effect the revolution in Santo Domingo would have on its possessions at Samana Bay. He stated that he did not think it would have any injurious effects. C. S. Pussalaigue, the accredited agent of the revolutionary party, who recently came to this city, has called on the officers of the Company and assured them that there is no feeling of hostility felt toward the Samana Bay Company; on the contrary, they were going to aid by all legitimate means the development of the country. The Company have been backward in promoting immigration, although thousands had applied for passage; this was because the possessions of the Company were not yet in a condition to invite immigration. The Company own the peninsula of Samana in fee simple, but they are anxious to acquire [illegible] of La Vega Real, a beautiful valley about 12 miles in width by 75 in length, extending from the head of Samana Bay to Santiago. In consequence of the delay in learning that President Baez and the Santo Domingo Legislature had agreed to the terms proposed by the Commissioners who were sent down by the Samana Bay Company, the Company were not [illegible] in taking possession of their territory before March. records.summary_en: After the insurgent commander obtained a four-day armistice and President Baez had made his arrangements for leaving the country, Baez sent the Senate a message on January 2, 1874 laying down the presidency, recalling that he had been called in 1868 when paper money had brought bankruptcy and public credit had vanished. That same afternoon Baez left Santo Domingo for St. Thomas on the French war vessel Kersaint, declaring he was in no sense an exile, having left voluntarily, and that he was tired of office and wished to rest and consult physicians about his eyes.

Samuels, had returned to the North in order that they might lay the matter before their directors, and subsequently before the Government. Dr. Howe, with his wife, Mrs. Julia Ward Howe, would remain at Samana, acting as Acting Governor, to protect the interests of the Company. When the Commissioners left Santo Domingo the Government had dispatched a force to take possession of the Company’s property, and as the Tybee was getting under way the Dominican steamer was also on her way to Samana. Although these events caused a great deal of discussion in Santo Domingo, he did not deem it probable that any popular tumult would occur. Gov. Fabens further said that while he could not say precisely what action the Company would take, he thought it very probable that they would call upon the United States Government for protection of its citizens, and demand that the matter be referred to arbitration. The Company had leased the Island of Levantados in Samana Bay to the United States, as a coaling station, on such terms as the United States deemed proper and equitable.
Paul N. Spofford, another of the directors, said that he did not care to connect himself with the expression of any views as yet. The Samana Bay Company would have a meeting this week and discuss the situation. He understood that the abrogation of the treaty was largely due to British influence, backed by the promised support of the British Government, the loan and full equipment of a vessel of war and the loan of an amount amounting to several millions of dollars to the Dominican Government to be repaid when convenient, without interest. He did not believe, however, that the failure of the Hartmont (English) loan, which had been the cause of some diplomatic and other correspondence between the Dominican Government, was responsible for the abrogation of the treaty.
Another director said that the Dominican Government had some time since granted concessions to the Company, and another to the Samana Surveying Company. The Samana Bay Company had not absorbed the last-mentioned Companies, and any defaults of either of the last-mentioned Company would not vitiate its grants.
