The United States mail steamship Tybee, Captain Delanoy, from St. Domingo 30th ult. at this port reports the following important intelligence:—
Soon after leaving Samana Bay the Tybee fell in with the Dominican man-of-war Capotillo, bound in.

BRITISH DIPLOMACY AND TREATY MAKING.
Mr. St. John, British Consul General at Port au Prince, had been on a tour of observation to Samana Bay in Her Majesty's ship Woodlark, where he spent several days in informing himself as to the great natural advantages of the position, and had afterwards visited St. Domingo with propositions from the Haytian government for a treaty between the two republics. Among the conditions of the proposed treaty, it is said, were the cession to Hayti of the disputed territory on the frontier and the annulment of the Samana Bay Convention, made with citizens of the United States. These conditions being admitted by the Dominican government, Hayti (or England) was to loan a considerable sum to St. Domingo, payable at convenience and without interest.
The discussion of this measure was causing great excitement throughout the island.

CONSTITUTIONAL DIFFICULTIES.
The President elect, Ignacio M. Gonzalez, who styles himself "General of the National Armies and Supreme Chief of the Republic," had not yet been installed in office, as the Convention called for the purpose of framing a new constitution was still unable to agree upon the articles thereof.

THE SAMANA BAY COMPANY IN A DIFFICULTY.
The Special Commission of the Samana Bay Company, composed of Dr. Samuel G. Howe, of Boston; Captain Samuels, of Dreadnaught celebrity, and Governor Fabens, of Samana, have not succeeded in obtaining an amicable settlement of the question pending between the government and the Company, including outstanding and overdue accounts against the government, and the provisional government has declared the Samana bay Convention null and void.

AN APPEAL TO WASHINGTON.
The Commissioners have protested against this summary act as arbitrary and illegal, and, on being instigated by British-Haytian influence, demanded an arbitration upon the matters in dispute according to the terms of the Convention. The company will, in the meantime, call upon the United States government for protection against any violent proceedings on the part of the Dominican authorities.
The inhabitants of Samana, most of whom are Americans or of American descent, were at first greatly incensed against the Gonzalez government on receipt of the news of the annulment of the lease, and declared their determination to resist any attempt at enforcing it. The Commissioners explained to them that such a course would retard and perhaps defeat a just and equitable settlement of the question, and enjoined upon them to deport themselves in a peaceable manner, to pay their taxes, and, if necessary, to pay them under protest.
The paper money of the Gonzalez government was being issued in large quantities, and was already at a discount of 50 per cent. Business was entirely suspended, and the prospect for trade was very poor.
ex-President Baez is making efforts to get back to power, and intends establishing a paper in St. Thomas to advocate his cause.

WHAT GOVERNOR FABENS SAYS.
Governor Fabens—ex-President Baez is a warm friend of the United States, and is desirous to promote the annexation of St. Domingo to this country. Baez is the representative of American ideas and Gonzales is not, the latter being strongly imbued with Haytian-English proclivities. Now, with reference to what you ask about Baez and the news from St. Domingo, I cannot tell you, for I have, as you know, just landed from my trip.
REPORTER—Governor, do you find the Americans in your troubles, seeing that there is no established government in St. Domingo?
GOVERNOR FABENS—Well (musingly) I think the United States government ought to step in and aid, in answer to our appeal, and we rely upon it to protect our interests against any over-acts of the Dominican authorities.

The Proclamation Annulling the Contract.
IGNACIO MARIA GONZALEZ, General of the National Armies, &c.:—
Whereas, in conformity with article 10 of the contract for the lease of the peninsula and bay of Samana and its islets, made in the city of St. Domingo, on the 28th of December, 1872, between the Minister of the Interior and Police and Foreign Relations, Citizens Manuel Maria Gautier and Messrs. Samuel Samuels, T. Scott Stewart and Burton S. Harrison, Commissioners of the Company styled "The Samana Bay Company," and by decree dated 19th February, 1873, of the Dominican Executive is called the "Samana Bay Company of St. Domingo," it was stipulated and decreed that the amount of rent fixed at $150,000 annually should be paid each year in advance on the 1st day of January;
Whereas, according to article 11 of the aforesaid contract, the non-payment of the annual rent at the time fixed upon, and, in case of war or other circumstance of force majeure, finally proven one month after that date at furthest, incurs the rescinding of the Convention, it being so expressly stipulated;
Whereas, when the provisional government, under date of 2d of December, 1873, ordered the withholding of the annual payment due on the 1st January of the present year, because, in virtue of the proclamation of the 25th of November previous, it had ignored the authority of General Baez, it did so solely with the object of avoiding future difficulties with the company if it should pay the late administration;
Whereas, in the official notice that it gave to the company, on the above mentioned date of 2d December, the Provisional government assured the company that it would respect the Samana Bay Company convention so far as it should be in the interest of the country and the conditions that were being fulfilled;
Whereas the company, through its Vice President, Mr. Paul Spofford, under date of 13th January of the present year, advises the Minister of Foreign Relations that the annual payment has been withheld, thus conforming to the order of the said Minister, while at the same time he states that he is awaiting official communications upon the subject;
Whereas, in virtue of the advice to which the preceding paragraph refers, the Treasury Department, by resolution of the government and by order of the Secretary of the Treasury, drew in favor of several merchants of the capital and the Minister of Foreign Affairs and Finance drafts for the sum of $147,224.14, on account of the rent due since the 1st of last January, the said drafts being presented for acceptance, and the company, in the meantime, told the government that they would not be accepted;
Whereas at the time the government drew against the company it gave it official notice of its establishment in this capital, and through the Minister of Foreign Affairs and Finance granted the company a prolongation, responding to the annual rental due, the reasons which until then it might have had for withholding the payment;
Whereas the non-payment of the amount said in advance is a sufficient cause for declaring the convention rescinded, as stipulated in the eleventh clause of the same, there being no cause on the part of the company for its inability to withhold the payment at the time mentioned;
Whereas the propositions that, verbally and in writing, have been made to the government on the 21st, 23d and 24th of the present month by the Commissioners, Samuel Samuels and Samuel G. Howe, in the name of the company, tending to modify the contract, grant extensions for the payment of the rent and to reduce the amount of said rent, are not and cannot be accepted by the government, since they would impose upon the nation a responsibility from which it could not release itself;
Whereas the Dominican government, in virtue of the communication of the 10th of January, signed by the Vice President of the company, and of the perfect right that it has as a depositor to the rent due, ought to consider said rent paid, and as such it was accepted by the government when it drew against the company, which reason it drew a portion for the amount of $147,224, and the drafts having been presented for non-acceptance, costs and damages are due, apart from the liquidation of the respective accounts of reclamation;
Whereas the company called the "Samana Bay Company of St. Domingo" has enjoyed the advantages of the lease of said bay, peninsula and keys for the time elapsed since the last payment, it is not allowed, up until the date of this decree, making use of the benefits which said lease may have produced;
Whereas, according to the terms of the mentioned eleventh clause of the convention, the right is reserved to the Dominican government of declaring null or rescinding the contract whenever the company fails to make the payment of the rent;
Whereas the government, after having taken into account the opinion of the Council of the Secretaries of State and the Council of the Government, has decreed and does hereby decree:—
ARTICLE 1.—The convention made in this city, under date of 28th of December, 1872, between the Dominican government and the company entitled the "Samana Bay Company of St. Domingo," for the lease of the peninsula and bay of Samana and of the islands and quays in those waters, is and is hereby declared from this date, in virtue of the non-fulfillment of its conditions in all its parts and null and of no value nor effect.
ART. 2. The Peninsula and Bay of Samana and the islands and keys of its waters will again from this date, as before the celebration of the Convention of the 28th of December, 1872, be ruled by the Dominican laws and authorities in the same form and manner as the provinces and districts of the Republic and islands adjacent to its territory.
ART. 3. The company will make good the amount of the account of damages incurred through the bills protested through its fault, and what concessions to the portion of the rent due since the first of January up to the date of this decree for the time that it has had the control of the said bay, peninsula and keys, until the same date.
ART. 4. The respective departments charged with the direction of the different branches of public administration will name the authorities that are to be installed in the peninsula and bay of Samana, and will take the necessary measures for the fulfillment of this decree.
Given in the National Palace of St. Domingo, the 25th of March, 1874, the 31st year of the Independence and the 11th of the Restoration.
(Signed) IGNACIO MARIA GONZALEZ.
Countersigned:—
The Minister of the Interior and Police, (Signed) P. G. ESPAILLAT.
The Minister of Foreign Relations, (Signed) J. DE LA C. ALFAU.
The Minister of Justice and Public Instruction, (Signed) T. C. DE CASTRO.
The Minister of Finance and Commerce, (Signed) J. M. COHEN.
The Minister of War and Marine, (Signed) M. M. CASTILLO.

THE DECREE AGAINST THE COMPANY.
The Samana Bay Company to all intents and purposes is dead. The investigation of the committee sent out from Washington on board the United States war vessel to report on the projected annexation of St. Domingo confirmed the idea. The people of this country may therefore congratulate themselves that the loss inflicted upon the community at large has not been larger than it is. It remains but to show below how the insolvent company has received its quietus, at the hands of the President elect of St. Domingo, Ignacio Gonzalez.
INTERVIEW WITH GOVERNOR FABENS.
Two members of the Samana Bay Commission returned to this city yesterday by the Tybee, and upon Governor Fabens, at Messrs. Spofford’s office, the following description of his visit was received.
Mr. Fabens was very courteous, but evidently very much chagrined at the unhappy fate of the enterprise. The following dialogue ensued:—
REPORTER—It is reported down town that the Samana Bay Company is dead; is that so?
GOVERNOR FABENS (hesitating)—Well, I hardly think we can say that; we have hopes of yet coming to an amicable arrangement with the Dominican government. I do not think the company can be called defunct; it is merely suffering under temporary embarrassment. When we receive proper recognition from the Dominican government we will pay over the $150,000 in gold due last 1st January. In addition to this we have claims upon that country for provisions furnished to the government, and, in addition to that, we have to receive payment for the regular performance of the mail service, &c. Our claims in the aggregate amount to about $50,000.
HIS INTERVIEW WITH THE PRESIDENT ELECT.
I had a long interview with Gonzalez, who I consider to be the head of the revolutionary party, and not the legitimate representative of the Dominican people. He has not taken the oath of office, and I therefore cannot consider him at present as the accepted Chief Magistrate. The proclamation of Gonzalez must therefore be taken for what it is worth. A new constitution, I may here remark, is being framed at St. Domingo City.
Dr. Howe has written a long letter to President Grant on the subject, while the United States Consul has also made a full report to Secretary of State Mr. Hamilton Fish, touching the occurrence.
WHERE THE SHOE PINCHES.
The publication of the decree of Gonzalez has a most prejudicial effect upon our company, for it prevents our placing on the commercial centres a loan for the company which we have had in contemplation. “Yes, sir,” said Mr. Fabens, with animation, “I think we have been very unfairly dealt with.”

In response, the commissioners protested the act as arbitrary and illegal, demanded arbitration, and announced plans to request protection from the United States Government. Meanwhile, the island was experiencing great excitement over potential loans from Hayti or England, and the installation of President-elect González was delayed because a convention framing a new constitution had not yet agreed on all its articles.

records.full_text:
The Samana Bay Company have succeeded as ill as President Grant in their efforts at the annexation of Santo Domingo. They have failed, however, from contrary reasons to those which caused the defeat of the Babcock treaty. An unusual conscientiousness induced the Senate to reject that instrument, and a far from unusual lack of conscience has instigated Señor Gonzales to abrogate his predecessor's concession to the American Company. An attempt will be made by the projectors to involve the Government in their quarrel, and this attempt will be met according to the logical habit of a portion of the press by efforts to defeat this scheme through abuse of the enterprise and those interested in it. We see no necessity for siding with either party in this matter. When the enterprise was set on foot, we rendered full justice to the motives and purposes of the capitalists who were endeavoring in this way to open up a new highway of commerce. But while we saw nothing objectionable in their scheme and hoped for its success, we could not refrain from the prediction that sooner or later the exigencies of Dominican politics would give rise to trouble which would call for the intervention of the United States, and that this would be refused, no matter under what pretext it was asked. The gentlemen who went into this business were not born yesterday. They knew what risks they were taking. They knew the character of those ex-officio brigands who make their living out of revolutions in that island. It was the business of the buyers to look carefully at their bargain, and not to look to the Government to avenge them in case they were cheated. They have no more right to ask the Government to defend them against the scoundrels who are trying to rob them.
It is not worth while to complicate the question by bringing in the supposed influence of the British Government in inducing Gonzales to take his recent course. It was an old maxim of art that a god should not be brought out of the flies, unless the matter on the stage were important enough to call for his assistance. In this case the cruise of the Woodlark is not a necessary explanation of Gonzales's action. We need not look any further than the dictator's cabinet for a motive. No one suspects Señor Baez of any very lofty motives in making the original concession. When he and Captain-General Gonzales arranged the recent farcical revolution by which he gave up the Government to him, there is no question that the annual rental of Samana Bay was the principal resource the new rulers looked to for furnishing their empty treasury. But it is stated that Gonzales did on arriving at his capital warn the Company not to pay their rent to anybody else, and to assure them of his friendly regard. While they were waiting for official information of his inauguration, which did not come, and were naturally hesitating about paying $150,000 to a usurper who might be driven out to-morrow, he took their silence for a refusal or for a notice, and they allowed his drafts to be protested. After this, nothing he could do ought to surprise them. In common with statesmen of his class, if he has no money, he has no quantity of any dignity. He needed no further incentive, from Consul-General St. John, the British Government, or anybody else, to resent the prudent suspicions of the Yankees, and to answer them by an act as public and as thorough as possible.
The cause of the Company's failure was inherent in this enterprise from the beginning. They had no right to expect honest and fair dealing from the Dominican Government, and it was not reasonable to hope for any permanency in the occupants of power at Santo Domingo. Their scheme was in most respects an admirable one, but it has been mismanaged from the start. It could only have succeeded by making a sufficient force of Americans on the place against the greedy and treacherous "statesmen" who made the grant. This was the only course to adopt if the enterprise was a genuine one. If it was merely intended for a piece of stock jobbing, it might as well die now as later, and in either case it has no just claim that we can see to come upon the United States for protection or indemnification.

records.summary_en: The *Knoxville Weekly Chronicle* reported that the Dominican provisional government declared the Samana Bay convention null and void after a special commission failed to reach an amicable settlement. In response, the commissioners protested the act as arbitrary and illegal, demanded arbitration, and announced plans to call upon the United States Government for protection against violent proceedings by Dominican authorities. Meanwhile, the island experienced excitement over a proposed loan from Hayti or England, and the installation of President-elect Gousale? remained delayed due to a constitutional convention's inability to agree on a new constitution.
records.summary_es: El *Knoxville Weekly Chronicle* informó que el gobierno provisional dominicano declaró nula y sin valor la convención de la bahía de Samaná luego de que una comisión especial no lograra llegar a un acuerdo amistoso. En respuesta, los comisionados protestaron por considerar la medida arbitraria e ilegal, demandaron arbitraje y anunciaron planes para recurrir al Gobierno de los Estados Unidos en busca de protección contra las actuaciones violentas de las autoridades dominicanas. Entretanto, la isla experimentaba agitación a causa de un propuesto empréstito de Haití o Inglaterra, y la toma de posesión del presidente electo González continuaba demorada por la incapacidad de una convención constituyente para acordar una nueva constitución.

THE PROCLAMATION ANNULLING THE CONTRACT.
Ignacio Maria Gonzalez, General of the National Armies:
WHEREAS, In conformity with Article 10 of the contract for the lease of the Peninsula and Bay of Samana and its keys, made in this city on the 28th December, 1872, between the Government of the Republic represented by the then Minister of the Interior and Police and Foreign Relations, Citizen Manuel Maria Gautier, and Messrs. Samuel Samuels, T. Scott Stewart, and Burton N. Harrison, Commissioners of the Company which was called and by decree dated 19th February, 1873, of the Dominican Executive is called the “Samana Bay Company of St. Domingo,” it was stipulated and decreed that the amount of rent fixed at $150,000 annually should be paid each year in advance on the 1st day of January.
WHEREAS, According to Art. 11 of the aforesaid contract, the non-payment of the annual rent at time fixed upon, and, in case of war or other circumstance of fuerza mayor, legally proved one month after that date at furthest incurs the rescinding of the Convention, it being so expressly stipulated.
WHEREAS, When the Provisional Government, under date of 7th December, 1873, ordered the withholding of the annual payment due on the 1st January of the present year, because in virtue of the proclamation of the 23d of November previous, it had ignored the authority of Gen. Baez, it did so solely with the object of avoiding future difficulties with the Company if it should pay the late administration.
WHEREAS, In the official notice that it gave to the Company, on the above mentioned date of the 7th December, the Provisional Government signified to the Company that it would respect the Samana Bay Company Convention in the form stipulated by the late Government and under the conditions laid down therein.
WHEREAS, The Company, through its Vice-President, Mr. Paul Spofford, under date of 10th January of the present year, advises the Minister of Foreign Relations that the annual payment has been delayed, thus conforming to the order of the said Minister, while at the same time he states that he is awaiting official communications upon the subject.
WHEREAS, In virtue of the advices to which the preceding paragraph refers the Treasury Department, by resolution of the Government and by order of the Secretary of the Treasury, drew in favor of several merchants of this and other places in the Republic and abroad for the sum of $11,084 upon the Company and on account of the rent due since the 1st of last January, the bills having been protested for non-acceptance, notwithstanding the assurances that the Government had that they would be accepted.

records.headline: A court report describes an application for a receiver for the Samana Bay Company, which was incorporated in 1873 by a special
records.summary_en: A court report describes an application for a receiver for the Samana Bay Company, which was incorporated in 1873 by a special act of the Dominican government, with all its stockholders citizens of the United States and its headquarters in New York, to promote mining, agriculture and railways. Creditor William Rowland argued that General Gonzales's decree had dissolved the company, while director Paul Spofford, himself a creditor for $50,000, argued that Gonzales's act was not the act of the republic; Judge Donohue reserved his decision.
records.summary_es: Un informe judicial describe una solicitud de un síndico para la Samana Bay Company, que fue incorporada en 1873 por un acto especial del gobierno dominicano, con todos sus accionistas ciudadanos de los Estados Unidos y su sede en Nueva York, para promover la minería, la agricultura y los ferrocarriles. El acreedor William Rowland argumentó que el decreto del general Gonzáles había disuelto la compañía, mientras que el director Paul Spofford, él mismo acreedor por 50.000 dólares, argumentó que el acto de Gonzáles no era un acto de la república; el juez Donohue reservó su decisión.

Mr. Warren claimed that bankers or brokers could not be taxed on stock sold for themselves, but only on stock sold by them on commission. Judge Woodruff yesterday rendered a decision in favor of the defendant. This was a test case, and twenty-eight other suits of a similar character go along with it. NEGOTIATIONS FOR A TREATY OF COMMERCE BETWEEN SANTO DOMINGO AND HAYTI—A SHAMEFUL SCENE DURING A FUNERAL SERVICE.

records.headline: Affairs in Santo Domingo.
records.summary_en: The *New-York Tribune* reported on April 5, 1875, that a treaty of peace, amity, extradition, and reciprocity between the two republics on the island had been ratified and exchanged, demonstrating an *entente cordiale*. Additionally, the newspaper stated that the Dominican Government was being pressed by about 2,000 citizens—victims of Báez's actions while under the protection of U.S. warships—to present a claim against the United States Government for £3,000,000 in losses and injuries. This prospective claim, drawing its foundation from Senator Sumner's March 27, 1871 speech, argues that Báez was maintained in power by U.S. troops and attempted to dispose of the country and the lease of Samaná.
records.summary_es: El *New-York Tribune* informó el 5 de abril de 1875 que se había ratificado y canjeado un tratado de paz, amistad, extradición y reciprocidad entre las dos repúblicas de la isla, evidenciando una *entente cordiale*. Asimismo, el periódico indicó que el Gobierno dominicano sufría presiones de cerca de 2.000 ciudadanos —víctimas de las acciones de Báez mientras este se hallaba bajo la protección de buques de guerra estadounidenses— para que presentara una reclamación contra el Gobierno de los Estados Unidos por 3.000.000 de dólares en daños y perjuicios. Dicha reclamación proyectada, fundamentada en el discurso pronunciado por el senador Sumner el 27 de marzo de 1871, argumentaba que Báez fue sostenido en el poder por tropas estadounidenses e intentó disponer del país y del arrendamiento de Samaná.

records.full_text:
AFFAIRS IN SANTO DOMINGO.
THE PRESIDENT IN FAVOR OF FREE SPEECH—
AMICAL RELATIONS WITH HAYTI—CLAIMS FOR
INDEMNITY AGAINST THE UNITED STATES.

SANTO DOMINGO, March 22.—The yacht Tarolinta of the New-York Yacht Club arrived here on the 19th inst. from Porto Rico, having on board Mr. Kent, her owner, and a party of friends who have been making a tour of the islands. Yesterday they called on President Gonzales, who returned the visit in the afternoon, accompanied by two of the ministers and other dignitaries. The President in a speech on the yacht said he was determined to try the experiment of free speech, a free press, and as much liberty as existed in the United States, even though he should perish in the attempt. No one had been exiled but Baez and a few of his family, and they were at liberty to return here now if they wished. The Tarolinta left here this morning for Kingston, Jamaica, from which place she will proceed to Havana, and thence home.

President Gonzales, accompanied by three of his ministers, his staff and some friends, returned a few days since from the province of Azua, where he had a conference with President Domingue of Hayti. The meeting was near the boundary line, and, by preconcert, took place on February 27, the anniversary of the separation of the two Republics in 1844, which is another proof of the entente cordiale now existing between the two Governments and people of the island. The treaty of peace, amity, extradition, reciprocity of trade guarantees to each other that neither any part nor the whole of the territory of either shall be alienated, has been ratified and exchanged.

It is stated that this Government is now being hard pressed by about 2,000 of its citizens, victims of Baez’s action, while under the immediate protection of the United States ships of war, to prepare and present a claim on the United States Government for losses and injuries to the Government and people arising therefrom. The foundation of this claim has been taken from the speech of Senator Sumner, of March 27, 1871, on violations of international law and usurpations of war powers. The Government intends, it is said, to present a claim for $5,000,000, but has not yet decided how or by whom they will present it, having no diplomatic representative in Washington. The argument which it is said the Dominican Government will submit in support of this claim recites the facts in connection with Baez’s accession to power, his attempt to dispose of the country, and the lease of Samana; declares that he was maintained in power by the United States troops, and was compelled to fly when they ceased to support him, and that, while occupying the Presidency, protected by United States ships, he plundered the Treasury of a large portion of its revenue, and ill-treated the citizens; alludes to many other facts in regard to the relations between the United States and Santo Domingo which have occupied attention during several years, and asserts that the acts of the United States Government were in violation of international law, and that it is responsible for the losses and injuries occasioned by the protection of Baez.

records.summary_en: According to the *Clarksville Weekly Chronicle*, a British House of Commons committee investigated the negotiation of foreign loans in England, hearing testimony from Mr. Edward Hertzberg Hartmont regarding a Dominican loan nominally valued at $3,788,500. Hartmont testified that he received only $1,800,415 in cash—of which the San Domingo government received merely $230,000—with the remainder spent on arms in Berlin and disbursed in Washington, where Hartmont was sent to work for annexation. The newspaper questions whether the unaccounted-for funds were paid to General Grant's military favorites, such as Babcock, who became suddenly prosperous and invested in real estate, and suggests that the next Congress should investigate the matter.

records.full_text:
SAN DOMINGO.
The Facts About the Annexation Job Coming to Light—Disgraceful Revelations Before a House of Commons Committee.
New York Sun.
The boldest and by odds the most infamous scheme of pillage organized under the first administration of Grant was that for the annexation of San Domingo. It was in its very inception lawless and cruel and base beyond any-thing in the history of the Western world, since Cortez and Pizarro. Baez had usurped the Presidency of San Domingo without a decent pretext of an election; and finding that his barbarous murders, confiscations and treasons would be borne no longer, he deliberately determined to sell the country and divide the price with his accomplices. These were the camp followers and personal intimates of the two Presidents, Grant and Baez.
Grant's dependents, Babcock, Porter, Ingalls, and the rest, were to have spoils so rich and tempting that Grant actually stipulated in terms to lobby the scheme through Congress. But Baez in the meantime was in evil ease. He frankly declared that he had no popular strength in the country he had proposed to sell, and that he could not hold out long enough to consummate the sale without extraordinary aid of money, and a fleet from the United States. Thereupon Grant ran his hand into the Treasury and seized certain unappropriated moneys for the use of Baez, and sent them down by Babcock, with a fleet large enough to keep this savage wretch in power until the temper of the American Congress could be tried.
We recur to this shameful history now only to ask how much of the proceeds of the British loan which Baez about that time put upon the London market was used at Washington? The House of Commons has appointed a committee to ascertain and report the methods by which foreign loans are negotiated in England. One of the witnesses on the 15th of April last was Mr. Edward Hertzberg Hartmont, who negotiated in 1869 a Dominican loan for the nominal amount of $3,788,500. He confessed that he received in cash only $1,860,445. Of this the Government of San Domingo received only $250,000, and the remainder was expended in England and the United States.
Hartmont was sent to Washington to work for annexation, where he testifies a large amount of the money was expended. Who got it? For his loan of $3,788,500, Harmont received in cash $1,860,445. The difference between $1,860,445 and $250,000 is rather startling. “A part” of it, Mr. Hartmont swears, was sent to “Berlin for arms;” but the rest was disbursed in Washington.
It was a great sum. To whom was it paid? About that time several of Gen. Grant's military favorites became suddenly prosperous, and invested their money in the real estate pool which throve so fabulously under the two bosses, Shepard and Grant. One of these was Babcock. Is it possible that Hartmont could have paid him any part of this vast sum yet unaccounted for? If not, to whom? The next Congress might profitably follow the example of the House of Commons and inquire.

records.full_text:
General Brutus Brice was a man of great repute and intelligence. He was a son of a distinguished general under the Emperor Soulouque, bearing the same name. The subject of this sketch was born at Miragoane, in Hayti. At an usually early age he graduated as bachelor of arts in the National College of Port-au-Prince. Shortly afterward he became one of President Geffrard's private secretaries. In the year 1860 he became one of President Salnave's aids-de-camp with the honorary rank of lieutenant colonel. Shortly afterward he was elected deputy to the Legislature, representing Port-au-Prince, and became one of the most prominent leaders of the opposition against Salnave. In 1868 he commanded the revolutionary forces at Jeremie, and withstood a siege of a year's duration, the town being bombarded by the Haytian fleet. After the revolutionary forces became victorious he was elected to the position of commandant-in-chief, and with that grade effected a landing at Port-au-Prince at the head of the troops and captured the capital city of Port-au-Prince in December, 1869. In consideration of his brilliant services he was elected Speaker of the Legislature. The next position he held was that of envoy extraordinary and minister plenipotentiary to the courts of the Tuileries and St. James in the years 1871 and 1872.
In the year 1873, after his return to Hayti, he was sent on a special mission to the court of Berlin with reference to the outrage committed by Commandant Basch, who had threatened to bombard Port-au-Prince with the Prussian corvettes Augusta and Gazelle, and in addition to this had seized two Haytian gunboats, for the reason that Hayti had not paid her debts to some German citizens of Hayti. His mission to Berlin on this subject was a successful one, and Commandant Basch was censured for hasty and unwarrantable conduct. Shortly after his return he was again elected deputy for Port-au-Prince. About this time he obtained a concession from the government for the construction of a railroad from Port-au-Prince to the Dominican frontier. He also erected a large manufactory in the neighborhood of the capital for the extract of dyes from logwood, to compete with the three great similar establishments in the United States. Since the advent of President Domingue to power, the General retired to private life, and has been known as an avowed enemy of Domingue, although he took an active part in the election and held a prominent position in the army.
SKETCH OF GENERAL PIERRE.
General Montplaisir Pierre, of the Republic of Hayti, who committed suicide on May 3, at Port-au-Prince, in Hayti, after being captured in a revolutionary uprising on that date by the government troops, was a native of Anse-a-Veaux, in the south side of Hayti. He was formerly minister of war under President Nessage Saget, and was an old soldier. Upon the occasion of the recent presidential election in Hayti he ran against President Domingue, the present chief magistrate, and was largely defeated. He has been Speaker of the Assembly and was a man of literary tastes and had traveled considerably in this country and Europe. During the presidential terms of Salnave and Geffrard he held important offices.—New York Herald.

records.summary_en: A traveler arriving from Port-au-Platte on August 24 reported that recent telegrams from Havana concerning a revolution in Santo Domingo were entirely false. According to the source, the rumor was fabricated and circulated by a banished individual named Barrera upon his arrival in Porto Rico. Furthermore, the traveler stated that no general disaffection existed and the government was fully capable of handling any conspirators.

records.summary_en: A professed agent of the Government of Santo Domingo made overtures to the President regarding the annexation of the island to the United States, though the President initially suspected the agents might be adventurers. To ascertain the real feelings of the people, the President dispatched a confidential agent who found an enthusiastic desire for annexation, leading to a treaty that was subsequently submitted to the Senate for ratification.

Con el fin de constatar el auténtico sentir de la población, el presidente despachó a un enviado confidencial, quien constató un ferviente deseo de anexión, lo que dio origen a un tratado sometido posteriormente al Senado para su ratificación.

records.full_text:
THE SANTO DOMINGO QUESTION.
After a lapse of six years since the President submitted to the Senate a treaty for the annexation of Santo Domingo to the United States, we venture to refer again to the subject for the purpose of reaching other matters. In justification of the President, however, it might be stated that the question of acquiring insular possession never occurred to him until the matter was forced upon him by circumstances. Soon after his first inauguration he was waited upon by a professed agent of the Government of Santo Domingo, who explained very vividly the topography, climate, products, &c., of that part of the island under the Dominican Government, the number and character of its population, the desire of the people and authorities to become a part of the United States, and that he was authorized and directed to make overtures to our Government for the purpose of bringing about annexation. The President listened to all that was said without venturing a remark that could in any way be interpreted as an indication favorable to the proposition. In fact, his whole judgment at the time was against the proposition. But later a second agent appeared, making substantially the same statements as the first, and was listened to and treated in a like manner. The President seemed to feel no assurance that these parties were not adventurers, anxious to make something for themselves out of the transfer. In view, however, of the close proximity of the island to our shores and of the oft-repeated Monroe doctrine on our part, he believed it his duty to ascertain the real feelings of the people and Government of Santo Domingo in relation to the question of annexation. For this purpose he dispatched a confidential agent who visited nearly every portion of the island, held free intercourse with both officials and non-officials, and found that it was the enthusiastic desire of all to become a part of “the Great Republic.” Under these circumstances a treaty was entered into and submitted to the Senate for ratification. records.summary_en: Based on the provided excerpt, the newspaper reported that the President viewed the acquisition of Santo Domingo as politically and financially vital because the island could produce vast amounts of sugar, coffee, and tropical goods without relying on slave labor, unlike current imports that supported slavery abroad. Furthermore, the President believed that annexating Santo Domingo would have honorably resolved the ongoing Cuban revolution and its associated issues regarding slavery, U.S. commercial interests, and international obligations.

Sostenía además el presidente que la anexión de Santo Domingo habría zanjado con honor la contienda revolucionaria cubana y sus repercusiones respecto a la esclavitud, los intereses comerciales estadounidenses y las obligaciones internacionales.

The sugar and coffee we consume are largely the products of slave labor, and we are made to pay an export duty which to a very great extent if not wholly supports the institution of slavery. The island of Santo Domingo is capable of producing much more of these products and kindred tropical products than all that are now imported into our country. The United States having abolished slavery at so great a cost of blood and treasure, the President did not see why we should continue to be the supporters of the institution in other countries. Then, the year before, a revolution had commenced in the island of Cuba for independence and separation from Spain, with the abolition of slavery in that island, if the revolution succeeded. The contiguity of the island to the United States, and the present commercial relations by which under revenue laws now in operation in Cuba we are almost excluded from tendering anything in payment of commercial debts but sterling exchange, give our country an absorbing interest in the contest which could scarcely be restrained from going beyond anything that could be justified with due regard to international obligations. The annexation of Santo Domingo, the President believed, would have settled the Cuban question in a manner highly honorable to the United States, to humanity and to the elevation of races and nations. records.headline: A correspondent writing from Puerto Plata on February 23 traces the revolution to President Gonzales's treaty with Spain binding
records.summary_en: A correspondent writing from Puerto Plata on February 23 traces the revolution to President Gonzales's treaty with Spain binding Santo Domingo to return Cuban refugees accused of incendiarism, and to a governor's decree that Cuban exiles embarking more than three on a vessel would be seized and delivered to Spanish war vessels. He describes street fighting on January 23 and 24 around the government house and General Luperon's residence, Governor Ortea's demand to capture Luperon dead or alive, and troops deserting and fraternizing with the Cubans as families fled the city.
records.summary_es: Un corresponsal que escribe desde Puerto Plata el 23 de febrero atribuye la revolución al tratado del presidente Gonzales con España, que obligaba a Santo Domingo a devolver a los refugiados cubanos acusados de incendios, y a un decreto del gobernador según el cual los exiliados cubanos que embarcaran más de tres en un buque serían apresados y entregados a buques de guerra españoles. Describe los tiroteos callejeros del 23 y 24 de enero alrededor de la casa de gobierno y la residencia del general Luperon, la exigencia del gobernador Ortea de capturar a Luperon vivo o muerto, y cómo las tropas desertaban y fraternizaban con los cubanos mientras las familias huían de la ciudad.

records.full_text:
AN INSULT TO BE RESENTED
WHERE THE UNITED STATES WILL DEMAND REPARATION.
Our Flag Dishonored by a Power that Probably has not yet Employed the Son-in-Law of the Secretary of State as Counsel.
SAN DOMINGO, June 29.—The Stars and Stripes have been insulted by the Government of this country in the roadstead of this capital. The Baezist General, Villanueva, has, since the election of Espallart to the Presidency of this republic, been endeavoring, on the Haytian frontier, in the neighborhood of Cape Hayti, to foment a revolution against the existing Government of this republic, and several skirmishes have occurred on the border line in the northwestern part of the territory, resulting in the killing of fifty or sixty Dominicans. For a purpose which has not hitherto transpired—Gen. Villanueva says, for the purpose of settling some private business affairs in this capital—he took passage in the steamer Tybee from this place. He touched at Puerto Plata and Samana, but did not land. On his arrival here, the Government, knowing of his presence on board, demanded his surrender.
Capt. Kuhl declined to deliver the General, and claimed the protection of his flag. An interview followed in the United States Consulate between the Consul and the emissaries of this Government, and the Consul protested against the forcible removal of Gen. Villanueva from the deck of the Tybee. At length a file of soldiers was sent on board, and as Villanueva refused to move from the chair on which he was sitting on the quarter deck, he was tied to it with ropes and handed over the ship's side. Capt. Kuhl spread the Stars and Stripes on the deck so that the men who were carrying Gen. Villanueva had to step over the flag.
It is currently reported that a United States man-of-war has been sent for to exact reparation.

From official advices received at the State Department to-day in relation to the reported insult to the American flag at San Domingo, it appears that ex-Minister of War Villenueva, formerly of Dominica, a fugitive from justice, took refuge on board the steamer Tybee, lying at San Domingo. The authorities there demanded his surrender, but the Captain of the Tybee refused to comply with the demand. When they went aboard and took him off no insult was offered to the American flag, the United States Consul or the Captain of the Tybee, and there was no violation of the international law or treaty stipulation. The Tybee carries Dominican mails under a subsidy from the Dominican government.
The President has signed the bill extending for ten days from to-day the late provision act.

In response, President Espaillat declared the entire republic in a state of siege and sent troops to the area, where insurgents surrounded Puerto Plata and prevented the steamer *Tobcc* from landing its cargo.

En respuesta, el presidente Espaillat declaró a toda la república en estado de sitio y despachó tropas a la comarca, donde los insurgentes cercaron Puerto Plata e impidieron que el vapor *Tybee* desembarcara su carga.

A DOUBLE-HEADED INSURRECTION IN SAN DOMINGO
HAVANA, August 12.—Advices from San Domingo of July 18th report that an insurrection has broken out in the Ciboa provinces, formerly the northern part of the Dominican republic. The insurgents may be said to be divided into two parties. Those east of Puerto Plata are fighting on account of their envy of or dislike for Cubans, who have emigrated in large numbers to that quarter of the island. This feeling of hostility has been intensified by the murder of a native, recently committed in Puerto Plata, by one of the Cuban emigrants. The other party appears to seek revolution for its own sake, calling now for the restoration of Baez and now for Gonzales, without knowing who they prefer or what they want.
President Espaillat has promptly taken vigorous measures to quell the insurrection. The whole republic has been declared in a state of siege, and troops have been dispatched from the capital to the scene of insurrection. At last accounts Puerto Plata was surrounded by insurgents, who had made several ineffectual attempts to enter the town.
The steamer Tybee had touched at Puerto Plata from New York, but was unable to land her cargo on account of fighting there, and left for San Domingo city.

SANTO DOMINGO.
Signs of Progress—Wonderful Resources of the Island.
The following is from the London Times: Holders of the Santo Domingo loan, who remember that Colonel Mendes, the diplomatic representative of Santo Domingo, expressed before the Foreign Loans Committee the willingness of his government to refund to those entitled the sum of £38,000, which the government had received out of the total proceeds of the loan, will read with interest Major Stuart’s hopeful report upon the resources of the Dominican Government. The report appears among the commercial papers recently issued by the Foreign Office. Major Stuart is Minister Resident at Hayti and Charge d’Affaires to the Dominican Republic. The imports in 1875 were £171,159 in value, the exports £97,936 at the port of Santo Domingo alone. The direct imports from Great Britain amounted to only £3,581, but British manufactures (cotton, hardware, crockery) to the value of £72,000 were imported through St. Thomas and Curacoa. This country is thus the leading state in the trade, the United States coming next with £48,000, while France, the next European state to ourselves, in this branch of commerce only sends goods to the value of £13,731. records.full_text:
SUMNER AND GRANT.
Maj. Poore's Story of their Disagreement.
Washington, Oct. 26.—Maj. Ben. Perley Poore, who was Senator Sumner’s guest at the time of his estrangement from President Grant, has explained the cause of the trouble. He says the removal of Jas. M. Ashley, ex-Congressman from Ohio, from the governorship of Montana, and the appointment of Col. Potts, which had just happened, was the subject of a table conversation, and a letter from Ashley protesting against the change had been read, when the President was announced. He was received and shown Ashley’s letter, and became immediately excited, denouncing Ashley as a worthless mischief-maker. The next topic discussed was the San Domingo treaty. Sumner dwelt especially upon the expenditure by Gen. Babcock on San Domingo of a large sum taken from a secret service fund, for promoting intercourse with the West India Islands, which Seward had prevailed on Thad. Stevens to have inserted in an appropriation bill during the war, and the President impressed Sumner with the idea that he feared an attack in Congress for that expenditure. Poore adds his opinion that Sumner thought that the President had come to enlist his services in defending this expenditure by Gen. Babcock, but the President meant the treaty for the acquisition of the Dominican Republic. The President and the Senator misunderstood each other. After a while the President promised to send Gen. Babcock to call on the Senator the next day with copies of the papers, and left. As Sumner escorted him to the door, he told him that he was a Republican, and a supporter of the Republican administration, and that he should sustain the administration in this case if he possibly could, after he had examined the papers. He meant to sustain the expenditure of $100,000 in cash and $50,000 in a light battery and muskets purchased at New York, but the President meant the treaty.
Maj. Poore's statement thus removes a grave historical doubt, and seems to set at rest the stories recently published of the cause of the difficulty between Grant and Sumner.

According to Major Poore's statement, Sumner believed the President wanted him to defend the expenditure, while the President actually meant the acquisition treaty.

Conforme a las declaraciones del mayor Poore, Sumner creyó que el gobernante deseaba que defendiera el desembolso pecuniario, cuando el mandatario aludía en realidad al tratado de anexión.

records.full_text:
CAUSE OF THE TROUBLE BETWEEN GRANT AND SUMNER.

CHICAGO, October 26.—A Tribune Washington special says: Major Ben. Perley Poore, who was Senator Sumner’s guest at the time of his estrangement from President Grant, has explained the cause of the trouble. He says the removal of James M. Ashley, ex-congressman from Ohio, from the governorship of Montana, and the appointment of Colonel Potts, which had just happened, was the subject of table conversation, and a letter from Ashley, protesting against the change, had been read when the President was announced. He was received, shown Ashley’s letter and became immediately excited, denouncing Ashley as a mischief-maker. The next topic discussed was the San Domingo treaty. Sumner dwelt especially upon the expenditure by General Babcock on San Domingo, of the large sum taken from the secret service fund for promoting intercourse with the West India islands, which Seward had prevailed on Thad. Stevens to have inserted in the appropriation bill during the war, and the President impressed Sumner with the idea that he feared an attack in congress for that expenditure. Poore adds: “My opinion is that Sumner thought that the President had come to enlist his services in defending this expenditure by General Babcock, but the President meant the treaty for the acquisition of the Dominican republic. The President and the senator misunderstood each other. After a while the President promised to send General Babcock to call on the senator next day with copies of the paper and left. As Sumner escorted him to the door he told him that he was a Republican, a supporter of the Republican administration, and that he should sustain the administration in this case, if he possibly could, after he had examined the papers. He meant to sustain the expenditure of $100,000 in cash ($50,000 in a light battery and muskets purchased at New York), but the President meant the treaty.” Major Poore’s statement thus removes a grave historical doubt, and seems to set at rest the stories recently published of the cause of the difficulty between Grant and Sumner.

records.summary_en: Following remarks by Wendell Phillips regarding General Grant's statements on the St. Domingo treaty, a *New York Herald* representative interviewed ex-Secretary of State Fish in Boston. Fish stated that Senate records show multiple drafts of treaties remained in the hands of the Foreign Affairs Committee under Senator Sumner for months—and in some cases over two years—whereas the entire batch was disposed of within four months after Sumner's retirement.
records.summary_es: A raíz de las manifestaciones de Wendell Phillips sobre las declaraciones del general Grant acerca del tratado de Santo Domingo, un reportero de *The New York Herald* entrevistó en Boston al exsecretario de Estado Fish. Este afirmó que las actas del Senado prueban que numerosos proyectos de tratados permanecieron estancados en manos del Comité de Relaciones Exteriores bajo la presidencia del senador Sumner durante meses —y en ciertos casos más de dos años—, en tanto que la totalidad de ellos se despachó a los cuatro meses de su salida.
records.passage: Wendell Phillips upon the statement of General Grant, when in Edinburg, to a New York Herald correspondent, regarding the course of Senator Sumner on the St. Domingo treaty and of the administration in the removal of Mr. Motley from the position of Minister to the Court of St. James, a representative of the Herald waited on Mr. Fish, who was in attendance upon the Episcopal Convention in Boston, to learn his version of the matters. When informed of the tenor of Mr. Phillips' remarks the distinguished ex-Secretary of State said that with regard to the alleged negligence of the late Mr. Sumner while Chairman of the Foreign Affairs Committee, it was a fact that was susceptible of proof from the Senate records, that drafts of treaties from eight to eleven in number, remained in the hands of the committee for several months; some of them, as near as Mr. Fish could remember, for more than two years. Mr. F. did not impute this delay of public business to negligence on the part of Mr. Sumner. The fact, however, remained that business was delayed, together with another fact, that after Mr. Sumner's retirement the entire batch of treaties was disposed of in less than four months.
records.full_text:
GRANT AND SUMNER.
Ex-Secretary Fish in Defence of His Late Chief.
ANOTHER VERSION OF THE AFFAIR.
BOSTON, Oct. 19, 1877.
In view of the recent severe strictures by Wendell Phillips upon the statement of General Grant, when in Edinburg, to a New York Herald correspondent, regarding the course of Senator Sumner on the St. Domingo treaty and of the administration in the removal of Mr. Motley from the position of Minister to the Court of St. James, a representative of the Herald waited on Mr. Fish, who was in attendance upon the Episcopal Convention in Boston, to learn his version of the matters. When informed of the tenor of Mr. Phillips’ remarks the distinguished ex-Secretary of State said that with regard to the alleged negligence of the late Mr. Sumner while Chairman of the Foreign Affairs Committee, it was a fact that was susceptible of proof from the Senate records, that drafts of treaties from eight to eleven in number, remained in the hands of the committee for several months; some of them, as near as Mr. Fish could remember, for more than two years. Mr. F. did not impute this delay of public business to negligence on the part of Mr. Sumner. The fact, however, remained that business was delayed, together with another fact, that after Mr. Sumner’s retiracy the entire batch of treaties was disposed of in less than four months.

According to Mr. Fish, Sumner supported the treaty until J. M. Ashley of Ohio was not nominated as a commissioner to St. Domingo, after which Sumner opposed it. REMOVAL OF MR. SUMNER.
The reasons for the removal of Mr. Sumner from the chairmanship of the Foreign Affairs Committee were then spoken of. The statement that Mr. Grant placed the St. Domingo treaty into Mr. Sumner’s hands, as related by Mr. Phillips, Mr. Fish characterized as ridiculously untrue. The President never had the treaty papers in his possession. They were in the hands of the Secretary of State. The facts were these: The President in conversation with Mr. Sumner laid before that gentleman the features of the treaty. This information was imparted orally; no written or printed document was read to the Senator. Mr. Sumner made no opposition to any of its features. Indeed, so warmly did he express his approval of it that a gentleman present at the interview, who prior to that time had placed himself in opposition to the measure, was made friendly to it solely be the arguments used by Mr. Sumner. Mr. Fish said that Mr. Sumner continued to favor the treaty until the selection of a commissioner to St. Domingo came up for settlement, and when he found that J. M. Ashley, of Ohio, was not to be the nominee he then all at once lost interest in the treaty, until finally he placed himself in direct opposition to it.

GRANT—SUMNER.
Maj. Ben Perley Poore Rises to an Explanation.
[Washington Cor. Chicago Tribune.]
Maj. Ben Perley Poore has at last given to the world an authentic statement of the causes of the estrangement between Sumner and President Grant. This explanation has been called out by the recent statements of Gen. Grant, Wendell Phillips, ex-Secretary Fish, and John W. Forney. Maj. Poore was the guest of Sumner at the time of the estrangement, and heard all of the conversation between President Grant and Sumner. Maj. Poore’s story, in substance, is this: The removal of James M. Ashley, ex-Congressman from Ohio, from the Governorship of Montana, and the appointment in his place of Col. Potts, which had just happened, was the topic of table conversation. A letter just received from Ashley, protesting against the change, had been read at table, when the servant announced that the President was at the door. He was received, and in the course of the conversation the letter from Ashley was handed to the President. The latter became immediately excited, and denounced Ashley as a mischief-maker and a worthless fellow.
The next topic discussed was the San Domingo treaty. Sumner, Maj. Poore says, dwelt especially upon the expenditure by Gen. Babcock on San Domingo of a large sum taken from a secret-service fund for promoting intercourse with the West India islands, which Seward had prevailed on Thad Stevens to have inserted in an appropriation bill during the war, and the President impressed Sumner with the idea that he feared an attack in Congress for that expenditure. Poore adds the opinion that Sumner thought that the President had come to enlist his services in defending this expenditure by Gen. Babcock, but the President meant the treaty for the acquisition of the Dominican republic. The President and the Senator misunderstood each other. After a while the President promised to send Gen. Babcock to call on the Senator the next day, with copies of the papers, and left. As Mr. Sumner escorted him to the door he told him that he was a Republican, a supporter of the Republican administration, and that he should sustain the administration in this case if he possibly could, after he had examined the papers. He meant, sustain the expenditure of $100,000 in cash, $50,000 in a light battery and muskets, purchased at New York, but the President meant the treaty.
Maj. Poore’s statement thus removes a grave historical doubt, and seems to set at rest the stories recently published of the cause of the difficulty between Grant and Sumner.

records.full_text:
HAYTI AND ST. DOMINGO.
PROGRESS OF THE DOMINICAN INSURGENTS—DRIVING BACK THE GOVERNMENT TROOPS—HAYTI QUIET.
HAVANA, Nov. 23, 1877.
The English mail steamer from St. Thomas, November 17, brings the following advices:—
The latest St. Domingo date is November 9. The accounts of the political situation are confused. The revolutionists in the southeastern province of Seibo were driving back the government troops at every encounter. The insurgents were daily approaching the city of St. Domingo, and great consternation prevailed. The city prisons were crowded with political prisoners. The revolt in Seibo is attributed to the following:—Baez declared Romana a port of entry with the sole object of exporting cattle. Baez is said to have entered into a private contract with a Cuban firm for the supply of cattle. The people of Seibo, considering the scheme the speculation of a ring and damaging to the people’s interests, revolted.
The situation in the other provinces was unchanged. Victory was favoring the government troops and the revolutionists alternately.
HAYTIAN INTELLIGENCE.
The Haytian news is to November 11. Peace prevailed. Coffee was quoted at $12 per quintal.
The mercantile communities of Caracas and Laguayra had sent $7,000 and the Venezuelan government $4,000 in aid of the sufferers by the hurricane at Curacoa.
The prospects of the sugar crop in all the West Indies are splendid.

The families of many of them had been compelled to take refuge on the shipping in the harbor. It would seem that at such a place as this, if anywhere, the pretence or occasional visits of a man-of-war would have some effect to secure the lives and property of alien residents against needless perils and destruction, yet we are informed that no vessel of the American navy has made her appearance at Puerto Plata since the last outbreak began, now more than three months ago. Under these circumstances, even Mr. Douglass, the consul, has found the country too uncomfortable to remain in it any longer, and has come away, leaving behind him as vice consul a native of San Domingo, who is a relative of the minister of war under President Baez. CONGRESSIONAL DOINGS.
records.full_text:
St. Louis Journal.

One of the objects for which the United States maintain a costly naval establishment in time of peace is presumably to protect American commercial interests in foreign countries. Intelligence from the West Indies indicates that the administration at Washington has lost sight of this object in one important instance at least. On the northern shore of Hayti or San Domingo is the town of Puerto Plata, one of the chief seaports of the Dominican republic. It has a population of about three thousand inhabitants, and carries on a considerable trade with the United States. Formerly our government was represented there by a consular agent but more recently the trade with the United States has been regarded as important enough to justify the establishment of a full consulate, and a son of Frederick Douglas was appointed the first American consul.

This action certainly indicates that there are American interests of some consequence in Puerto Plata. The commercial and political importance of the town has made it a prominent point of attack and defense during the revolutionary contest, which has now prevailed in San Domingo for many months. For sixty days preceding the date of our latest dispatches the conflict in the outlying districts had been almost incessant, and scarcely a day passed without more or less musketry firing among the warehouses and dwellings of the foreign merchants. The families of many of them had been compelled to take refuge on the shipping in the harbor, It would seem that at such a place as this, if anywhere, the presence or occasional visits of a man-of-war would have some effect to secure the lives and property of alien residents against needless perils and destruction; yet we are informed that no vessel of the American navy has made her appearance at Puerto Plata since the last outbreak began, now more than three months ago.

Under these circumstances, even Mr. Douglass, the consul, has found the country too uncomfortable to remain in it any longer, and has come away, leaving behind him as vice consul a native of San Domingo, who is a relative of the minister of war under President Baez. It is anything but pleasing to the American residents of Puerto Plata to find themselves represented by a man who must needs be influenced in its acts by his adherence to one of the two parties now at war for the possession of San Domingo; and the fear is expressed that even if an American man-of-war should come into the harbor, this vice consul would try to convince the commander that she was not needed.

THE WEST INDIES.

THE STEAMSHIP OCTAVIA PUT UP AT AUCTION--EARTHQUAKE AT ST. THOMAS--LOOKING FOR THE BODY OF COLUMBUS--GOOD COFFEE CROP IN HAYTI.
HAVANA, Jan. 23, 1878.
The British mail steamer, from St. Thomas January 17, has arrived, and brings the following advices:--

THE STEAMER OCTAVIA.
ST. THOMAS, Jan. 17, 1878.
The British steamer Octavia, of Cuban notoriety, now lying at Puerto Rico, was put up at public auction here to-day. The highest bid was only $3,000 and she was withdrawn from sale.

SHOCK OF EARTHQUAKE.
A slight shock of earthquake was experienced here this morning.

CONTINUANCE OF THE DOMINICAN REVOLUTION--LOOKING FOR THE BODY OF COLUMBUS.
ST. DOMINGO, Jan. 17, 1878.
Political affairs continue complicated. Neither the government troops nor the revolutionists are advancing.

SEARCH FOR THE BODY OF COLUMBUS.
On the 26th ult. the Spanish steamer Alcantara arrived here from Havana, bringing a commission appointed by the Spanish government to examine a box supposed to contain the remains of Christopher Columbus. The examination was permitted after many formalities had been gone through with. The box was removed from the place of its deposit, the seals broken and the inscription closely examined. The bones were scrupulously inspected and photographs taken of the remains. Several physicians were present.

And yet the dispatch asserts that "an uneasy feeling exists." If such a feeling really has a local habitation, it probably exists in the bosom of Señor Buenaventura Baez, who is now for the sixth time in exile, and who is sometimes restless during his periods of expatriation. One dark night in February last this chieftain climbed into the Dominican Navy, which was formerly a pilot boat in this harbor, and sailed out into the "ever-tepid crystal seas." But he didn't go to stay; he never does. It is thirty years since he first began to be president, but his eye is not dimmed nor his natural force abated, and he is liable to survive alternate election and exile for many years to come. A ruler who was willing to trade off his country to the Samana Bay Company for $150,000 can hardly be considered a national deliverer of the highest type, but, after all, he seems to be about the crowning product of Dominican civilization, and the sooner he returns, drives Luperon back to the Haytian marches, sends Gonzales across the mountains to Puerta Plata, with a flea in his ear, and borrows enough money on a cargo of bananas to set the wheels of government in motion, the better it will be for our sister Republic.

Additionally, the newspaper stated that the separate project of annexing Canada could never be accomplished without an earnest petition from Canadians and specific governmental guarantees.

records.passage: matter of such minute consideration, that there is no need of trying to exhibit the moral or political principle of the transaction except under a microscope. The price we had to pay for it is big enough to see without common spectacles. If the authors of the project for annexing St. Domingo had been able to show that the Dominicans were largely in favor of it, they would have been able to make a much better show in Congress and among the people of the United States. The other project so often broached, of annexing Canada to the Union, a most undesirable thing, as we have always thought, can never be accomplished except on the earnest petition of the Canadians, and then only with guarantees that the Federal government shall not be bound by the restrictions of the old treaty between Great Britain and France, which maintains a wealthy and powerful hierarchy inside of a political authority, and leads to the chief disorders that are continually occurring in the Dominion.
records.full_text: Annexation of foreign territory to another nation ought never to take place except by a common agreement between the annexer and the annexed. The annexations to the United States have not been conducted on such principles, unfortunately for our principles. The monarchs of Spain and France sold us their possessions at the South without consulting their inhabitants, because they wanted to get rid of them, as they cost them more than they were worth. The people of Texas generally did desire annexation, but it would not have been accomplished when it was but for the determination of the Democratic party to procure more territory in which to extend slavery and create larger representation in the senate and house for the slave holding aristocracy. A bloody war had to be fought to secure this end, which might, at a later period, have been secured without war and with the deliberate and formal consent of Mexico as well as that of the people of Texas. When Alaska was annexed, there were no people to consult worth speaking of, and the advantage or disadvantage to the United States or the Alaskans is a matter of such minute consideration, that there is no need of trying to exhibit the moral or political principle of the transaction except under a microscope. The price we had to pay for it is big enough to see without common spectacles. If the authors of the project for annexing St. Domingo had been able to show that the Dominicans were largely in favor of it, they would have been able to make a much better show in congress and among the people of the United States. The other project so often broached, of annexing Canada to the Union--a most undesirable thing, as we have always thought--can never be accomplished except on the earnest petition of the Canadians, and then only with guarantees that the Federal government shall not be bound by the restrictions of the old treaty between Great Britain and France, which maintains a wealthy and powerful hierarchy inside of a political authority, and leads to the chief disorders that are continually occurring in the Dominion.

Two Dominican Conspirators Shot.

NEW YORK, Jan. 18.--A rumor prevailed throughout the city today to the effect that two well known Spanish subjects had been forcibly taken from a steamer in San Domingo, and cruelly put to death, and it created no little excitement among our Spanish and Cuban population. Senor H. Bellini, Dominican Consul in this city, when spoken to on the subject, said that General Valentine Perez and Manuel Cammino, both of whom were Dominicans and not Spanish subjects, had taken passage from Mayaguez, Porto Rico, for Porto Platte, San Domingo, on the Spanish steamer Manuel, after having combined with General Baez, ex-President of the San Domingo Republic, in a revolutionary movement for the overthrow of the existing government. Governor Lithgood, of Porto Platte, learned of the conspiracy, and when the vessel touched there demanded the men of her captain. They were delivered under protest, both claiming to be Spanish citizens, and were taken to the office of the Minister of War, when the form of trial was gone through, lasting about two hours. They were found guilty of conspiracy to overthrow the government and sentenced to be shot, and four hours after they left the vessel their bodies were riddled with bullets. They appealed for respite, but their judges were inexorable. General Perez was at one time Governor of Azua, San Domingo.

Quiet in San Domingo--The Recent Rebellion in Hayti.
SAN DOMINGO, June 29.--Perfect tranquility prevails. The report that Congress authorized the conclusion of a treaty of commerce with the United States was inexact. Congress only directed the executive to propose to the United States free exchange of two specified products--sugar and tobacco--against any two products of the United States.

The government finally drove the rebels out of the city, three men being killed and wounded, and a large number of arrests made. Gen. Business is paralyzed and the harbor crowded with vessels waiting for cargoes, and produce comes in slowly owing to heavy rains.

records.full_text:
A Letter from the Dominican Consul.

TO THE EDITOR OF THE SUN--Sir: For some time the press of this city has been giving reports respecting the trouble between Spain and San Domingo, and yesterday the Evening Telegram gave some private information received in this city, which sets forth that "should Spain bombard, as she threatens to do, the capital of San Domingo," the Dominican Government will issue letters of marque for vessels to prey on Spanish shipping.

I am not aware that Spain has made any direct threat to the Dominican Government, nor have I learned that any Spanish squadron is expected at San Domingo; but, regarding the letters of marque, the Dominican republic having no marine forces, its Constitution authorizes the Executive to issue letters of marque in case of war with any other nation.

I have not begun to buy arms and ammunition, as is reported; since the election and inauguration of Gen Cesáres Guillermo as President, his Government has been regularly buying arms and ammunition merely to equip the army.

The cause of the dispute between the two nations has been more or less misrepresented. The facts are simply these: About six months ago, on the arrival of the regular Spanish mail steamer at Porto Plata, correspondence was landed stating that there were on board two Dominican Generals, members of the Baez party, who, according to the correspondence, were going upon the Dominican frontier to start a revolution against the existing Government. The authorities of Porto Plata interviewed the Spanish Consul, asking him to give the necessary orders for the surrender of the said Generals, which the Captain did, following the instructions of his Consul, protesting at the same time against him and not against the Dominican Government. It is as well to say here that, in making his Custom House entry at Porto Plata, the Captain did not mention either in the bill of health or in the passenger list, the presence on board of the two Generals. As everybody knows, these were court martialed and shot.

My Government has done nothing against Spain, nor has it been the habit of the Dominican republic to disregard the law of nations. In all the international questions it has had, it always has behaved with moderation and dignity. In this present trouble with Spain (which my Government has in no way occasioned), President Guillermo and his Cabinet will sustain themselves at the height of their dignity.

The Dominican republic has been misrepresented, and, on account of our political commotions in this country and in Europe, it is generally believed the foreign residents there and their properties are not respected. Now, this is a great injustice; never has a foreigner suffered any inconvenience, or his property either, by any Government or revolutions; these are purely political. The country is now enjoying perfect tranquillity and foreigners are every day flowing into the republic, and with the franchises that the Government has given in favor of all agricultural establishments, large sugar, coffee and other plantations are rising up. The Government has asked of Congress authority to propose to the United States a treaty of reciprocity, and the Dominican press has been for some time, and is yet, discussing and elucidating that question. The Dominican republic has no doubt entered into an era of happiness and peace.

I hope you will have the kindness to insert this letter in your valuable paper and oblige
Your obedient servant, H. BILLINI,
Dominican Consul.
NEW YORK, Aug. 8.
