records.summary_en: A speaker at an event, identifying as a fifty-year-old Democrat, publicly praised Mr. Astwood and expressed a desire for him to remain in his position as United States Consul at San Domingo. The speaker also asserted that the colored race can demonstrate the capability to occupy any position held by a white man, and that existing prejudices among white people can be easily overcome.
records.summary_es: Un orador, que se proclamó demócrata de cincuenta años, encomió públicamente al Sr. Astwood e hizo votos por su confirmación en el cargo de cónsul de los Estados Unidos en Santo Domingo. Proclamó además que la raza negra reúne sobrada capacidad para desempeñar cualquier dignidad detentada por el hombre blanco y que las prevenciones raciales de estos últimos se pueden disipar con facilidad.
records.passage: am, when I became acquainted with this gentleman on my left (Mr. Astwood) it gave me very great pleasure to write to the President, although he was a Republican, he was the right man in the right place, and that it would be a personal favor to me if he continued him in the position of United States Consul at San Domingo. (Applause.) A longer and better acquaintance with him has assured me that he is still the right man in the right place, and though I am a Democrat of the Democrats, fifty years old and [illegible] a Democrat, I have not changed my opinion in regard to Mr. Astwood, and I am ready and shall always be ready to stand by him, as I have done from the first instance. (Voices: "Hear, hear.") Now I suppose it might be excusable in me on an occasion of this kind to say exactly what I feel, and I think that I can say with a better grace, because I belong to that party which is supposed to be opposed to the advancement of the colored race in this country, that I think that there is but one thing for the colored race to show, and that is that they are capable to occupy any of the positions in this country which a white man can occupy. And I believe that in a short time those prejudices which have [illegible] many, and we must confess they exist amongst the white people, can be easily overcome, if they could only see, as we have seen to-night, the magnificent ability which has been shown in this entertainment. Certainly where can you find among white people greater eloquence than has been manifested by Mr. [illegible], my friend opposite? (Applause.) [illegible] here among
records.full_text:
Mr. Langston spoke as follows:
Gentlemen: I understand that the object of this occasion is to honor my friend who sits opposite to me, whom I have known a long time; whom I have known very intimately. I have known him in Louisiana, I have known him in the walks of political life in this country, I have known him in the ways of religion, as a pulpit orator, as the pastor of a flourishing church; I have known him as I have seen him, as I have been with him in his work as United States Consul at San Domingo; I have eaten in his house, I have slept in his house; I have seen him in his office, I have seen him with Presidents, I have seen him with diplomats, I have seen him with Consular officers, I have seen him in war, and I have seen him in peace. I have seen him defending American citizens and I have seen him caring for them after they have been abused; I have known of his winding up their cases with honor to himself and with credit to his Government, maintaining in dignity the authority and the power of his Government, and those great chiefs who stood over him.

records.summary_en: The author of the article states that San Domingo is the finest island in the Antilles and the only republic in the island group—aside from Hayti—that maintains its sovereignty free from European dictation. Despite being portrayed in American journals as a revolutionary and barbarous country, the author argues that its political revolutions are less destructive to life and property than United States labor strikes. Furthermore, the writer notes that the island possesses a vast territory with a population under four00,000, and aims to correct misrepresentations regarding the commerce between the two countries.
records.summary_es: El articulista califica a Santo Domingo como la isla más rica de las Antillas y la única república insular —fuera de Haití— que preserva su soberanía exenta de tutela europea. Frente a la estampa que la prensa estadounidense divulga como comarca bárbara y sediciosa, arguye el autor que sus revueltas políticas ocasionan menos estragos a la vida y la propiedad que las huelgas obreras de los Estados Unidos. Subraya por añadidura que la isla encierra un vasto suelo patrio con una población inferior a los cuatrocientos mil habitantes, teniendo por propósito su escrito rectificar los falsos juicios esparcidos sobre el comercio entre ambos países.

My friends, I cannot find words to express to you my thanks for this very high compliment paid to me, in my official capacity, by you gentlemen, and the honor you do me in bringing me on an occasion like this in relations with the honorable gentlemen that surround this board, and inviting me to speak upon a subject so important as the commercial relations between San Domingo and the United States. records.summary_en: According to *The New York Freeman* on May 14, 1887, a speaker at a meeting credited President Heureux of the Dominican Republic, Minister of Foreign Nations M. M. Guetieu, and the Minister of Public Improvements for offering inducements to United States capitalists to develop the Dominican Republic's resources. The speaker asserted that erroneous reports had been circulated by designing individuals to discredit the country and maintain a monopoly, to the detriment of commercial relations between San Domingo and the United States.
records.summary_es: Según *The New York Freeman* del 14 de mayo de 1887, un orador ensalzó al mandatario Heureaux de la República Dominicana, al ministro de Relaciones Exteriores M. M. Gautier y al ministro de Fomento por brindar garantías a los capitalistas estadounidenses para la explotación de las riquezas dominicanas. Aseveró el tribuno que individuos malintencionados propagaban especies falsas para desprestigiar a la nación y perpetuar un monopolio comercial, con grave quebranto de las relaciones mercantiles entre Santo Domingo y los Estados Unidos.
records.passage: ness will be increased from a few millions to scores of millions. I trust, gentlemen, that this meeting here to-night will be the means of the beginning of an investigation which will go far in determining and developing all of these great enterprises now contemplated by our people, and in which a great many here present are positively interested. If I have done anything, gentlemen, to merit the high honor conferred upon me by you in tendering me this compliment to-night, it has been by the humble efforts which I have put forth in behalf of my country and people, in developing that happy condition of affairs, both commercial and otherwise, existing to-day between the people of the United States and San Domingo. records.full_text: The many American enterprises now undertaken by our people, if carried into effect in good faith, cannot fail to build up a large business within a very few years. The San Domingo Central Railroad, whose President and Vice-President sit at this board, starting in at the point of Barahona, crossing the Great Salt Mountains twenty-one miles from the terminus, passing through the District of Neiba with its immense mahogany forests and other valuable woods, thence through the fertile region known as the St. John's Valley, crossing the mountain range over to Sabanata, going through the fertile district of Guyabin with its immense pine, log-wood and other forests, would be an immense outlet to the commodities of this country, to say nothing of the hundreds of thousands of acres of land that would be thrown open to emigrants from this and other countries for the production of tropical fruits, cotton, etc., in great abundance. The fruit industry to be established at Samana Bay by the Bay State Fruit Company of Boston, of which Willis M. Snow is president, and the other Northern ports of the Island, will be a great factor in connection with its commerce, to say nothing of the immense tract of land contracted for by a Boston syndicate upon the Romana Camayasa and Chabon Rivers, in the District of Seybo, represented by Hiram Newcomb and Edgar R. Champlin, where a Winter resort will be established upon the most picturesque and fertile region known in the New World. Negotiations are also being effected with capitalists of the United States for bettering the financial condition of the country which if successfully carried out will at once establish the commercial destiny of San Domingo, and in the course of a very few years the business will be increased from a few millions to scores of millions.

Involving Treaty Relations With Two Countries.
WASHINGTON, Dec. 14.—An important case, involving the treaty relations of the United States with Hawaii and San Domingo, was argued to-day in the United States supreme court. The case stands on the docket as No. 1,012, High Kelly, plaintiff in error, against Edward L. Hedden, collector, in error to the United States circuit court for the southern district of New York. The question presented is the alleged exemption from duty, under the existing tariff, of products of the Dominican republic which are identical in kind with products of the Sandwich islands admitted free of duty under the special act of congress, approved Aug. 15, 1876. About twenty years ago the United States entered into a treaty with the Dominican republic by the terms of which each country agreed not to charge higher import duties on the products of the other than were imposed upon like products from any other country. The importers, who are the plaintiffs in error in this and another similar case, claim exemption from duty for certain sugars and other products imported by them from San Domingo, upon the ground that the articles were of such a character that had they been imported from Hawaii they would have been admitted free of duty under the treaty between the United States and Hawaii and the act of Aug. 15, 1876, enforcing that treaty. The importers assert that if their contention is not sustained, the Dominican republic will be released from its treaty obligations by virtue of the failure of the United States to keep its engagements, and that San Domingo may then practically exclude United States manufacturers from her ports by exemptions and discriminating duties in favor of the European countries, which are seeking the trade of the island.
The United States government on the other hand maintains that the treaty with the Hawaiian islands was not a mere reciprocity treaty, but was in substance a commercial contract by virtue of which Hawaii pays a valuable consideration for the admission of certain merchandise to the ports of the United States. The importations from that country are not free, but the nation whence the articles came has made a special bargain by which the nation, and not the importer, pays the duties. It is furthermore contended by the United States that more than eleven years have passed since the promulgation of the Hawaiian treaty and that although the products of San Domingo have during all that time been charged with the duties now complained of, the Dominican government has never alleged a violation of her treaty rights, nor does it appear that any of her citizens either in this case or heretofore has complained of wrong.

Always Prevail Over Its Treaties.
Associated Press dispatches to the HERALD:
WASHINGTON, January 9.—Decision was rendered to-day in the case of James F. Whitney and others against William A. Robertson, formerly Collector of the Port of New York. The question raised was the scope and force of certain provisions contained in the treaties concluded between the United States and the Republic of San Domingo and the Kingdom of Hawaii, respectively. The plaintiffs who appeared are New York merchants who imported in 1882 from San Domingo a large quantity of molasses and sugars similar in kind to those imported from the Sandwich Islands. The Collector exacted duties on these San Domingo sugars amounting to $22,000, plaintiffs paying the same under protest. They then brought suit against the government to recover the amount exacted, on the ground that by virtue of article 9 of the treaty between the United States and San Domingo, the United States was debarred from imposing a higher duty, or any other duty, upon the products of San Domingo than is imposed upon similar products of other countries with which the United States might have commercial relations. Sugars similar to those in controversy were imported free of duty from the Sandwich Islands under the treaty provisions; therefore, it is contended, they should be admitted free from San Domingo.
THE COURT HOLDS
First, that the ninth article of the treaty between the United States and San Domingo is merely a pledge of the contracting parties that there should be no discriminating legislation against imported articles of either country. It was never designed to prevent special concessions like those granted Hawaii, and the clearest language is necessary to justify the conclusion that the United States Government intended to preclude itself from such engagements with other countries, which might become of highest importance to our interests.
Second: The act of Congress under which the duties in this case were collected, authorized their exaction. It was of general application, making no exception in the favor of the goods of any country, and passed after the treaty with the Dominican Republic, and if there is any conflict between laws and treaties the former must prevail. The country disatisfied with the action of the legislature must address its complaints to the executive head of the government, and take measures which it deems essential to protect its own interests. When the law is clear its validity cannot be assailed before courts for want of conformity with treaty stipulations.
The judgment of the United States Circuit Court in favor of the collection, is therefore affirmed.
A SIMILAR DECISION
Was rendered in the case of Hugh Kelly vs. Edward L. Hedden. Had these decisions been adverse to the Government, the United States would have had to pay out many millions of dollars as refunds for duties exacted, as the above suits were test cases. Justice Field wrote the above detailed decision.

PROTESTS COME FROM HAYTI.
AMERICAN TRADERS IN THE INSURGENT NORTH WANT A CRUISER.
Hippolyte and Jimenes in the Presidential Ticket in the North—The Saginaw's Arms Going to Jimenes—Dutch Gold Greatly Soothe the Dominicans.
The steamship George W. Clyde of the Clyde line got here yesterday with news from the Haytian and Dominican republics. She left Santo Domingo city on Oct. 24, and touched at Samana, Porto Plata, Cape Haytien, Port de Paix, and Turk's Island. Two American merchants doing business at Gonaives and Cape Haytien have forwarded protests to this Government against the Haytian blockade on account of its effect on their business, and ask that a United States cruiser be sent to protect the interests of American citizens in the North of Hayti. The whole North is said to have risen in its might and demanded that Légitime withdraw from the Presidential candidacy and leave the island. The merchants say that there is now no Government of Hayti, and that, therefore, there can be no blockade. If Légitime will withdraw the North will then be ready for a real election. Meantime all business is neglected in the North, for everybody joined the army when the blockade was announced. The enthusiasm is so great that even old men and boys have joined the ranks. This army is only waiting for arms and ammunition to advance on Port-au-Prince and avenge what it terms the assassination of Seïde Thilemaque.
In regard to the arms shipped in the Saginaw, it is said that the Dominican Government may find itself in serious trouble if it allow these munitions of war to be smuggled across the Haytian frontier in the interest of the North. The Dominican Government has no war ships, and both Monte Criste and Santo Domingo could be bombarded by Légitime's little navy.
Another interesting bit of news brought by the George W. Clyde is to the effect that Juan F. Jimenes of the firm of Jimenes & Haustedt of this city is a candidate for the Vice-Presidency in the North, F. Hippolyte being at the head of the ticket. The cabalistic address
P.
Monte Criste
J.
on the Saginaw's consignment of arms is now understood to mean that the goods are intended for Gen. Papillon and Mr. Jimenes.
The relations between the Haytian and Dominican Governments are reported to be far from cordial. A Dominican merchant in this city said yesterday that there was little intercourse between the two countries. Légitime is thought to be backed up by French capital furnished by merchants interested in the Haytian trade. The Dominican republic is itself on the verge of the election of a new President. These elections have usually been followed by insurrections, the party defeated at the polls not caring to give up so easily. This election, however, bids fair to be a peaceable one. The present President is Ulysses Herreux, and the opposition candidate is Gen. Luperon. On the 22d of October Gen. Luperon cabled from Porto Rico to Santo Domingo that he should not run against Herreux. This news was received with great joy throughout the Dominican republic, and at the Dominican ports where the George W. Clyde put in bonfires illumined the hills far and near. Herreux is said to have arranged a loan of $4,000,000 with Holland, and before the Clyde left, £30,000 of Dutch gold had arrived at San Domingo. The Dominican republic has been in a very bad way, financially, and this money is greatly needed. Hence the bonfires, and hence Gen. Luperon's decision not to run against a man who can borrow money like that. The Royal Standard, an English paper published at Turk's Island, bearing the date of Nov. 3, says a United States war vessel had just left Cuba to investigate the seizure of the Haytian republic by one of Légitime's vessels.

records.full_text:
1,000 MORE RIFLES FOR HAYTI.
The George W. Clyde Takes Them to a Little Port on the Dominican Frontier.
According to Minister Stephen Preston, the Dominican port of Monte Cristi has about 1,000 inhabitants. If this estimate is true as to numbers, and that part of the cargo of the two last Clyde steamers that cleared for Dominican ports that were shipped for Monte Cristi can be taken as any index of the character of the town's inhabitants, they must love guns and drums. Not contented with the munitions of war, amounting to some $80,000, shipped them by the Saginaw, which sailed from this port on Nov. 5, some one at Monte Cristi is now awaiting another shipment of similar goods that are included in the cargo of the George W. Clyde, another of the Clyde line steamers that sailed yesterday.
Most of the partial manifest filed by the agents of the George W. Clyde at the Custom House yesterday is peaceful. But sandwiched in between a shipment of confectionery consigned to San Domingo and four cases of corsets for the same port was a consignment of goods for Monte Cristi which included these articles:
One thousand rifles, 25,000 cartridges, 12 cases of belts, and 3 cases of scabbards.
This consignment will bring the total value of munitions of war sent to Monte Cristi to about $100,000. Mr. L. Julia, the Dominican Consul in this city, maintains that these goods are shipped for the use of the Dominican Government, but members of the Haytian Legation say that in that case they would be sent to San Domingo City and not to the little port of Monte Cristi, in the northwestern corner of San Domingo, and near the Haytian frontier. Besides, the goods were purchased by Jimenes, Haustedt & Co., who also appeared as the purchasers of the munitions of war which the insurgent General, Papillon, sailed with in the Saginaw. Mr. Jimenes's connection with the insurgents now holding out in Hayti against Légitime's Government has already been described in THE SUN of Nov. 10. This time a junior partner of the firm of Jimenes, Haustedt & Co. by the name of Oscar Hurtlinger is the shipper of the goods. He is said to be a relative of Mr. Julia, the Dominican Consul.
Among the passengers on the George W. Clyde were Tertullien Guilbaud of Port à Paix, who has been at the Hotel Griffon, and R. A. Deetjen of Cape Haytien, who has been at the Union Square Hotel. Both are said to be in sympathy with the insurgent element.
Mr. Bassett, the Haytian Consul, went in the afternoon to the Custom House, together with Secretary of Legation Charles Preston, and represented the state of affairs to Assistant Collector McClelland, as Collector Magone was in Washington. Finding that the George W. Clyde had cleared for Dominican ports only, Mr. McClelland decided that he had no power to detain her. Consul Bassett then went to the law office of the Marquis de Chambrun and made an affidavit, which was deposited at the Custom House as a formal protest. His affidavit stated that, to the best of the Consul's belief, the munitions of war on the Clyde steamer were intended for the use of insurgents against his Government. He considers it probable that if the Haytian gunboat Dessalines can overhaul the George W. Clyde it will do so, and seize the arms on board of her and let the vessel with the rest of her cargo continue on her voyage.
Mr. J. S. Cameron of the Clyde Company said yesterday that they had heard from the Saginaw at San Domingo. He added that the George W. Clyde has cleared for exactly the same ports as the Saginaw, and that that was all there was to her voyage. As to the Haytian Republic, Mr. Cameron said that he had seen the despatch to the effect that the prize court at Port-au-Prince had confiscated the steamer and fined the owners $50,000 for violating the blockade and actively participating in the rebellion now existing in Hayti. Mr. Cameron thought the owners of the vessel were now in an excellent position, for even if the charges were proven, which he considered doubtful, he did not think it likely that this Government would allow the decision, on the ground that the prize court itself was illegal in not having been properly constituted by recognized authorities.
Mr. Lockwood, a buyer of logwood in Hayti, who returned on the George W. Clyde, brings a report of the Haytian Republic's movements which tallies with that of the Haytian representatives, only he says the steamer took larger bodies of men and greater quantities of supplies from one insurgent port to another than had been related.
Dr. Juan E. de Contreras received a personal letter yesterday which stated that St. Marc had already surrendered to Légitime.

REBELS DEFEAT GOVERNMENT TROOPS.
CASES OF RIFLES SHIPPED FOR HAYTI — THE STORY OF A MERCHANT ABOUT THE INSURRECTION.
Consul-General Bassett said yesterday that private advices had been received in this city, dated Port au Prince, November 12, which said that the port of St. Marc, which had been held by the insurgents, had been surrendered by them to the Haytien Government; but up to last night he had received no official communication to corroborate the information. The Clyde Line steamer George W. Clyde was cleared at the Custom House yesterday for Monte Christi, a small Dominican port near Cape Haytien. Her manifest showed that she had among her cargo 500 cases of rifles and ammunition on board. Consul Preston said that these goods were for the insurgents in Hayti and that among the passengers on the steamer were two rebel agents. He waited on the Customs authorities requesting them to stop the sailing of the ship, but as the vessel had cleared for a port outside of the Haytien Republic, they were powerless to act in the matter, and the vessel was expected to go to sea last night. William P. Clyde, one of her owners, yesterday acknowledged that the arms were on board the ship, but added that as the goods were consigned to a Dominican port his firm had no concern with their ultimate destination after they were landed from the steamer. Referring to the question of the alleged rebel agents being on board, he said that they sold tickets to any passenger applying and paying for them, without making inquiries as to their religion, politics or private affairs.
E. Lockwood, a merchant of New-Haven, Conn., who arrived here from Hayti on the George W. Clyde on November 10, said yesterday that he was on board the steamer Haytien Republic at Port de Paix when Captain Compton took on board 300 armed insurgents who were landed at Gonaives on October 18, where they encountered the Government troops. A battle ensued which lasted for some hours and resulted in a victory for the rebels. The general in command of the Government troops fled to the woods, where he was taken prisoner by the rebels and severely beaten. He subsequently swore allegiance to the rebels and is now fighting on their side.
Mr. Lockwood said that he had heard that Captain Compton had previously carried 500 armed men from Cape Haytien to Gonaives, and he told the captain when he boarded the ship that the Government troops were looking out to capture his vessel. The captain said that he had nothing to do with the men, as they were ordinary passengers and he was in no way responsible for their acts.
Notice has been given to the Haytien Government that the case of the Haytien Republic will be appealed to the higher Haytien courts, as the owners consider the confiscation of their vessel illegal. They say, furthermore, that the court was illegally constituted.

At half-past 6 last night Rear Admiral Luce was snugly ensconced in the cabin of the Richmond, although his flag flew on the Galena.
"Orders have been received from Washington," he said, "for the Galena and Yantic to set sail for Port-au-Prince to-morrow. I won't undertake to state the exact hour at which the vessels will sail, for if it should be fifteen minutes out of the way you newspaper men would pitch into the United States navy. It is quite certain that we won't go before 7 o'clock, and very likely not before 10. We thought we could get the Richmond ready to accompany the Galena, and so my flag was transferred to her. When we found that that was impossible the flag went back to the Galena, and I shall sail on that ship. The difficulty about the Richmond has been to get her decks properly calked. Our calkers have gone and got permanent jobs in New York. The Richmond can get her coal and ammunition on board in four or five days, and will then be ready for sea. She will follow on to Port-au-Prince, and if I am still there she will take me on board. Otherwise she will go on to St. Thomas, where we shall be waiting for her. Do I expect to bombard Port-au-Prince? Why, of course not. You surely wouldn't have us act so cruelly toward a weaker sister republic. The fact is I don't believe there will be any necessity for a bombardment, because I feel certain the Haytian Government will promptly release the Haytian Republic."
Some newspaper had printed an alarming report that the Galena was full of holes. Admiral Luce laughed as he encountered this weather-worn naval chestnut.
"Port holes," he chuckled. "You can depend upon it that the Galena is quite seaworthy or your uncle would not sail on her. Capt. Cooper, formerly of the Haytian navy and commander of the Dessalines, made me a brief call this morning and said that the Dessalines was a fine gunboat in good condition. Mr. Morse, one of the Boston agents of the Haytian Republic, will go with us by special permit to look after the interests of that steamer. There is plenty of coal stored on an island in the harbor of Port-au-Prince, the owner of which will be very glad to sell all the coal he can to the owners of the Haytian Republic, which can then be taken home by a crew sent out for the purpose. We take along a deck load of coal because we don't want to pay Port-au-Prince prices. Besides, yellow fever can be brought aboard ship with a load of coal. I take along no sealed instructions of any nature. That used to be the custom in the days of Paul Jones, but the last case that I know of personally was in 1853. Then the Captain of a ship might be ordered to proceed to a certain latitude and longitude before he could learn what his destination was to be."
The Yantic lay last night at the ordnance dock ready to sail at a moment's notice. On Monday night her Captain was surprised to get an order to take aboard the ship's powder. This was an unusual night's order, but all the lights were put out, and the powder was taken aboard in the dark.
Every one at the Haytian Consulate seemed to be in a good humor yesterday. Minister Preston laughed when he was asked whether there was any likelihood of the Galena's goat Billy striking terror into the hearts of the Haytian soldiers.
"I don't think there would be much chance of that," said the Minister. "Goats are one of the chief products of Hayti. We eat them in Hayti as you do mutton here, and the flavor very much resembles that of Welsh mutton. Besides, goat's milk is very highly esteemed in Hayti, and commands a high price."
Speaking of the reported revolution in San Domingo, a representative of the legation said: "We hear, unofficially, that affairs in San Domingo are in a rather serious condition. It appears that Gen. Luperon, one of the candidates for the Presidency of the Dominican Republic, published a manifesto about Nov. 1, withdrawing in favor of President Heraux, provided the election should be a fair one and express the will of the people. It seems that the election that followed was not satisfactory to Luperon or his adherents, and was followed by riots and a general uprising. The news now comes that the Dominican insurgents have seized all the arms they could get their hands on, and it is said that the arms brought by Papillon to Monte Cristi for the use of Hippolyte's followers were also taken by the Dominicans. If this proves to be true, it will be a great blow to the North."
Mr. J. S. Cameron of Clyde & Co. said:
"That is all nonsense. Gen. Luperon and M. Heraux are great personal friends, and Gen. Luperon was glad to withdraw in Heraux's favor. The fact is that after the election a lot of Gen. Luperon's friends got drunk at Porto Plata and captured the Captain of the port. Then they went to Luperon's house, and bade him lead them against Heraux and capture the city of Santo Domingo. Gen. Luperon came out, and told his misguided friends to go home and sleep it off. They kept up their demonstration until some of them were arrested and taken to Santo Domingo city to be tried. That is all there was in that alleged insurrection."

records.full_text:
The Haytian Difficulty.
For some months past there has been going on in Hayti a quarrel between two rival faction, each claiming the right to govern the republic. Outside of the merchants and ship owners who do business in West Indian and Haytian waters and who have been rendered anxious as to the safety of their vessels and property now in Haytian ports or bound for that region, the rebellion attracted little attention in this country until the seizure and confiscation of the Haytian Republic, a Boston steamer, for alleged running the blockade at the port of St. Marc on the west coast of the island, occurred. Aside from the affront to the national dignity, hostile action of this sort is a serious matter to Americans interested in shipping and mercantile transactions with ports under the Haytian government's control. Last May figures submitted to Congress showed that the population of Hayti was 800,000, its imports amounted to $4,121,162, and its exports to $6,271,475, according to the official statistics for 1886. Since that time our trade with the country has doubtless increased as the result of the passage of the act of May 24, which invited closer commercial relations between South American West Indian States and the United States.
The present trouble between the Haytian and United States governments was begun on November 5, when the Haytian consul at New York waited upon the collector of the port and requested that official to send a revenue cutter down the bay and detain the steamship Saginaw, which sailed for Dominican ports with, as the consul alleged, a cargo of arms and ammunition for the insurgents, consigned to Haytian ports. A cutter was despatched as requested, but the vessel had gone too long and was out at sea long before the cutter got down to Sandy Hook and the chase was fruitless. A few days prior to this the Haytian Republic, the steamer above referred to, had sailed for Port au Prince. The vessel is now seized and held by the Haytian government as a prize, it being claimed by the government that she carried contraband of war and had aided the insurgents, not only by supplying them with munitions of war, but by the transportation of rebel troops from Cape Haytian to Gonaives, where, it is alleged by the Haytian government, they were landed, and the same day met and defeated the government troops, after a short and decisive battle, lasting about four hours. The story of the seizure of the steamer and of the gallant conduct of her commander in refusing to lower the American flag and deliver the steamer over to the Haytians has already been published.
The owners of the Saginaw deny that their steamer carried any supplies for the insurgents and say that the ship was not consigned to Haytian ports at all, but to ports under the Dominican government where she landed her cargo, and claim that their connection and responsibility therewith entirely ceased when the goods were over the ship's side, the ultimate destination of the goods being none of their business. One of the agents of the Haytian Republic, speaking of the allegation made by the Haytian authorities that the steamer had been engaged in the transportation of rebel troops, said:
Our vessels, in the regular course of their voyages, call at several ports where they both receive and discharge cargo, and take on board or land such passengers as may be desirous of travelling by our line, the same as is done by any line of steamships in the world. We do not make it our business to inquire of such persons from whence they come, where they are going, or what is their object in travelling. In the case of the alleged rebel carried by our vessel, it was not within Captain Compton's province to inquire of these alleged rebels their business. They paid their passage in the usual way and as far as reports received by us show, behaved themselves in such a manner on our vessel as to give rise to no suspicions on the part of the ship's officers that there was any illegality or wrong-doing connected with the object of their voyage.
With reference to the alleged blockade, for violating which the Haytian authorities seized and condemned the steamer, it is claimed that it was invalid by reason of the absence of due notice to neutral powers, and because of its manifest inadequacy. Furthermore, it was, and is, nothing more than a paper blockade of the northern ports of the little republic by a provisional government which holds the southern half of the country, and asserts that the government that controls the northern half is insurrectionary in character. The appearance of our fleet in Haytian waters will doubtless result in the release of the seized steamer unless it has already been burned. If such is found to be the case the fullest compensation will be demanded and the demand will be enforced. As the Haytian government has only two small gunboats available our ships of war are not likely to have a very hard task. The officers and sailors are more likely to rejoice at the prospect before them, for the weather down there is said to be delightful at this season of the year.

A Haytian merchant stated that these men signed articles at the British Consulate to serve on any Atlas line vessel, potentially bringing them under the English flag.

records.full_text:
Among the passengers on the Saginaw was Dr. Nemour Auguste of Cape Haytien. The Doctor is said to be on his way to Washington, where he will try to persuade President Cleveland to recognize him as the representative of Hippolyte, the anti-Légitimist leader. M. Auguste denies this statement as a matter of course, and says, as all Haytian insurgents do who arrive, that he is on his way to Paris. Other passengers were Joseph and J. E. Hernandez, H. T. Jones, and Thomas Good, but they only confirmed the reports already given. The Saginaw also brought Capt. M. H. Greeno of the English brig M. E. Brady, from Windsor, N. S. With the Captain came his wife, First Mate J. P. Vaughn, and six sailors. The brig left Annapolis on Oct. 13 and was struck by a gale on Oct. 28, and stranded on a Dominican reef shortly after. Capt. Greeno sold his cargo of lumber to a Dominican merchant and made his way to Porto Plata with his wife and crew.
The Captain, his wife, and the crew reached the shore in the brig's boats, losing all but their personal effects. On the morning of the 30th they went on board the wreck and brought some sails ashore, with which they erected temporary tents. On the same day fifty armed Haytians came to the beach and demanded all the shipwrecked crew possessed, threatening to kill them unless everything was given up. A sailor from the brig, who talked Spanish, conciliated the natives somewhat, and they finally gave the crew till the next morning to surrender. Meanwhile, under cover of the night, Capt. Greeno sent a boat's crew to a brig anchored up the coast a few miles, to ask her Captain to assist them. The latter responded promptly by arming his crew, and sending them with sufficient arms to equip the castaway crew, so when the Haytians came back in the morning the tables were turned, and they were told that their opponents were Englishmen and Americans and all well armed. "If you make any attempt to molest us," said the brig's Captain, "we will kill every one of you." The Haytians scattered in a hurry. "I never saw people so scared," said the Captain. Capt. Greeno and his wife made their way to a fishing village, she remaining there until their effects could be transferred to the village. From there they were finally taken in a brig to Santo Domingo city.
The report that the Haytian Republic sailed yesterday for New York in charge of the crew which was sent out for the purpose in the Atlas steamer Alene that sailed for Jamaica on Dec. 8, could not be verified yesterday. Mr. Forwood of Pim & Forwood, the agents of the Atlas line, said yesterday:
"The report came from Charles W. Brooke of 111 Broadway, and no one was more astonished at reading it than myself. Mr. Brooke is not our counsel and I never saw him in my life. Mr. E. P. Wheeler handles most of our law business. It is true that men did go down on the Alene other than the crew, but I do not know that they were intended for the Haytian Republic. They may have been intended to help man the Belize for all I know. They did not pay any passage money, and I cannot say who paid it for them. Several of the men will work as boiler makers for us at Kingston."
A Haytian merchant said yesterday: "The men sent down on the Alene signed their articles at the British Consulate, and agreed to serve on any vessel of the Atlas line. This would bring them under the English flag, and if they are put aboard the Haytian Republic that vessel might fly the flag of Great Britain, and even if she had not left the harbor of Port-au-Prince when the Galena and Yantic arrived, those vessels would not be likely to interfere with her under the circumstances. It is, in fact, a clever coup on the part of the Haytian Government."
Minister Preston, Gen. Contreras, and Lord & Austin knew nothing of any such crew being sent to man the Haytian Republic. Just before sailing in the Galena Mr. Morse, the agent of the Boston owners of the steamer, said that no crew had been sent down, nor would any be sent until after his arrival. If the crew is intended for the Haytian Republic it will be interesting to know what Capt. Compton has to say on the subject.

records.headline: Captain Greeno's story: wrecked in the brig Martha J. Brady
records.summary_en: Captain Greeno's story: wrecked in the brig Martha J. Brady on the southeast coast of San Domingo at San Luis Petit Trou, his party was threatened by some fifty armed Dominicans who demanded their property by morning, and was saved by reinforcements from a brig anchored offshore.

records.passage: CAPTAIN GREENO'S STORY. A Timely Rescue When Threatened by Dominican Desperadoes. [illegible] According to the story told by Captain W. [illegible] Greeno, who formerly commanded the Nova Scotian brig Martha J. Brady, and who with his wife, mate, and six seamen arrived on the steamer Saginaw yesterday, the protection of American men-of-war is needed somewhere else than in Hayti. Captain Greeno left Annapolis, Nova Scotia, in the Martha J. Brady, bound for the West Indies. On the night of October 28th the brig was blown ashore on the southeast coast of San Domingo at a place called San Luis Petit Trou. The vessel had struck a reef and lay in a very dangerous position, so Captain Greeno got his wife and crew into the boat and succeeded in getting ashore. They had only the clothes on their backs and a few articles and shipstores they could lay their hands on. Next morning, after passing a night exposed to the elements, Captain Greeno saw that it would be possible to reach the stranded brig and obtain from it the [illegible] of the crew, the sails, and other property. A boat went over to her and succeeded in getting a quantity of useful things. On its return and while the Captain was engaged in putting up a tent to shield the party somewhat from the rays of the tropical sun, a band of ferocious-looking Dominicans, armed to the teeth, descended on the camp. NEW YORK, December 19. — At the Produce Exchange a vote was taken by the members in relation to closing the Exchange Monday before Christmas and was lost by 401 in favor to 444 against. A two-thirds vote was necessary for closing. The Coffee Exchange will adjourn from the close of business Saturday, December 22d, to Wednesday morning, December 25th, and from Saturday, December 20th, to January 2d. The Cotton Exchange has had an adverse ballot on the question, but the members have petitioned their Board of Managers to act under the "emergency" clause in the by-laws, which permits them to close the building independent of the ballot. records.full_text:
Official Notification of the Bombardment.
[By telegraph to the Dispatch.]
WASHINGTON, December 19.—The State Department has been informed by the United States Consul at Cape Haytien that the Haytien steamer Toussaint L'Ouverture "appeared before that city on December the 3d and bombarded it for two hours. The consular corps immediately protested against this action. Upon the receipt of this protest a vessel was granted thirty-six hours for the foreigners to leave. This time had not elapsed when the dispatch was written December 5th."
The Consul also informs the department that two steamers, seven barks, and nineteen schooners have entered that port in a month's time from November 2d to December 1st. The State Department is also informed that the incipient rebellion was promptly suppressed by the existing authorities of San Domingo at Puerto Plata, in the early part of November and by the authorities of Venezuela at Barcelona, Venezuela, in the latter part of November.

records.full_text:
SAN DOMINGO TO TAKE A HAND.
It Is Reported that President Heraux Will Send a Gunboat to Port-au-Prince.
According to reports received from San Domingo, Hayti's troubles did not come to an end when she surrendered the Haytian Republic at the muzzle of Admiral Luce's guns. This time Légitime has not trodden on the toes of a power like the United States and Germany, but has aroused the ire of Florville Heraux, President of the republic of San Domingo, which occupies about two-thirds of the island of Hayti, although it has but about one-third as large a population as the black republic. Last month THE SUN described how Heraux had managed to effect a loan of some $4,000,000 from Holland. The first installment of this loan arrived in Dutch gold at Santo Domingo City about the middle of October, and the news that the loan had been effected caused great rejoicing throughout the Dominican republic. This occurred before the recent reëlection of Heraux to the Presidency, and the rival candidate, Gen. Luperon, cabled from Porto Rico to Santo Domingo on Oct. 22 that he would not run against Heraux. He wasn't going to set himself up against a man who could borrow money like that.
According to advices received from Porto Plata it now appears that a part of this money was used to purchase a war vessel by Heraux. It is further said that Heraux is about to send his new ship to Port-au-Prince to demand an apology from Légitime for the rudeness of his representative who came to Santo Domingo City on the Grande Rivière, which vessel is still in pawn at that harbor, her commander not having money enough to buy coal to get away.
Merchants here say it would be just like Heraux to make such a demand upon the Haytian Government. The Dominican President is said to be a man absolutely incapable of fear and a regular fire-eater. Whether Légitime will bow down before his black brother from the other end of the island remains to be seen. Heraux's new vessel is said to be about 400 tons burden, or less than half the size of the Dessalines, not to mention the Toussaint l'Ouverture and the Belize, which vessels jointly ought to be able to make things merry for the Dominican cruiser.
The Ozama, which sails on Saturday for Dominican ports, will take arms and ammunition to Porto Plata, and it is believed that this time the Dominicans will use the guns themselves instead of allowing them to be smuggled across the frontier to the insurgents in the north of Hayti. Much indignation is expressed here owing to the action of the commander of the French cruiser Bisson. It is claimed that this vessel has hung around the ports of Gonaives and Mole St. Nicholas continually, doing more blockading on her own hook than all the Haytian gunboats put together.
Mr. F. Carvalho, the nephew of Hippolyte, the insurgent General, who has been at the Stevens House, complains that he has been overrun with people trying to sell gunboats, steamers, ferryboats, and even rowboats. Others have beset him with offers to supply big guns, small arms, and clubs at the lowest market rates. Mr. Carvalho says he is not here to make such purchases, and adds that Dr. Auguste took the $100,000 subscribed by Hippolyte's friends to Paris with him.

records.full_text:
MORE FIREARMS FOR HAYTI.
A QUEER STORY OF A PRIZE CREW.
MINISTER PRESTON AND OTHERS WILL NOT COMMIT THEMSELVES.
There were taken to Pier No. 15, North River, yesterday fifty cases of rifles, which were marked "G., Cape Hayti." These rifles, together with nine Gatling guns, are to be shipped on the Clyde steamer Ozama to-morrow, which is to go to Monte Cristo and other places in the West Indies. As it is doubtful that a clearance will be given to the vessel for Cape Haytien, she will probably stop first at Monte Cristo and get a consular certificate there for Cape Haytien, as was done in the case of the Saginaw. It is also reported that General Carvalho, a nephew of General Hyppolite, who came north "on a visit" recently, and who has been staying at the Stevens House, will return as a passenger on the Ozama. He declared yesterday that he had not purchased the Gatling guns and rifles. They were invoiced by Schuyler, Hartley & Graham, who refused to disclose the name of the purchaser.
This disposes of the rumor published yesterday that the Ozama was to land these arms at Puerto Plata, presumably for the Dominicans, who anticipated war with Hayti through the aggressiveness of President Heraux, of Santo Domingo. At the Haytian Consulate there was much anxiety for news from Hayti, and the report that the steamer Prinz Mauritz did not sail from Jacmel until Sunday, and would probably not arrive here before Saturday, seemed disturbing.

records.summary_en: *The Sun* reported on the surrender of the seized American steamship *Haytien Republic* to Admiral Luce following a firm United States naval demonstration. Haitian President Légitime ordered the vessel repaired and returned to its original mooring under formal protest, asserting the ship had aided domestic rebels. The correspondent noted that the assertive American naval posture exerted a salutary moral effect in Port-au-Prince.

records.full_text:
WE SCARED HAYTI NOBLY.
A War of Etiquette, Too, In Which Admiral Luce Came Out Strong.
ON BOARD THE UNITED STATES STEAMSHIP GALENA, OFF PORT-AU-PRINCE, Dec. 21.—
The United States steamships Galena and Yantic, which left New York Dec. 12, steamed into the harbor of Port-au-Prince Dec. 20, at 9 A. M., with shotted guns, torpedo booms, ships cleared for action, and crews standing at quarters, to demand of the alleged Haytian Government the instant release of the steamer Haytian Republic. On their arrival in the outer harbor Rear Admiral S. B. Luce transferred his flag to the Yantic, which has a draught of but fourteen feet. The Yantic was then run slowly into the inner harbor to within 100 feet of the docks where the Haytien Republic was at anchor. Anchor was dropped, and a stern line was at once attached to the Haytien Republic, the guns of the Yantic being trained on the city. The Galena remained in the outer harbor with a broadside and pivot guns trained on the Haytian man-of-war Dessalines, and prepared to fire at the first hostile demonstration. The Dessalines' crew also stood at their guns until the result of the interview of Lieut. Griffin with Gen. Légitime was made known.
Lieut. Griffin went ashore shortly after 9 o'clock with communications from the State Department and Admiral Luce demanding the release within four hours of the detained steamer and the withdrawal of her guard. Admiral Luce's message was to this effect, only more polite:
"I want the Haytien Republic. You will turn her over to me by 1 P. M. to-day or I will send men on board and tow her out. Resistance by force will necessitate my using force and shelling your town in return."
While this was doing we could see ammunition put on board the Dessalines and other gunboats, and could see them load their guns. The reply to the Admiral's message was to this purport:
"We will give her up if the United States Government demands her, but we do it under formal protest, and reserve our right to bring our claims against your Government to arbitration. She was aiding and abetting revolutionists."
A point in etiquette international was raised in that Admiral Luce had not saluted on entering the harbor. His reply was that the Galena had saluted the Haytian flag in this harbor within six months, and it was not our habit to do it more frequently. Admiral Luce made the point that the commander of the Dessalines, a Commodore, had failed to call on him, Luce. The reply made in person by the Commodore, in a very dignified and courteous manner, was that it was so unusual for foreign men-of-war to go so far in as the Yantic had done, and to do it with men at quarters, that he, the Commodore, thought possibly our visit was not friendly in its motive.
This exchange of lessons in politeness was followed by the surrender of the Haytien Republic some hours before the time set by Admiral Luce. Gen. Légitime commanded one of his gunboats to tow the Haytien Republic to the position in the harbor occupied when captured, and to have such slight damage as had been done to her repaired by his mechanics. Night fell before her cable could be severed, as had been planned.

records.full_text:
The steamer George W. Clyde, Captain Holmes, arrived from Quarantine early yesterday morning, bringing the latest news from Hayti and San Domingo. An interesting story of her adventures and experiences was gathered from her passengers, among whom were Thomas Clyde, the Rev. Mr. Moran, Charles Elliott, of Norfolk, Va.; Mr. Munoz, ex-Purser Nells, of the Clyde, and C. Kroncke y Rebatet, of Vera Cruz. The voyage southward was unusually severe. A cyclone struck the vessel, which dashed the seas about furiously and tossed the steamer about as though she were feather-ballasted. The waves rolled over the deck, carrying with them the starboard rail; the skylights were broken and the staterooms and saloon were flooded with water several feet deep. The gale lasted several days, and it is believed that the Samana went down during the raging storm. She weathered the tempest, however, and arrived at San Domingo City on December 8, steaming thence for Samana, where she arrived on December 15. She touched at Puerto Plata December 17, and reached Monte Cristi on December 18, where she loaded a cargo of logwood.
Shortly after anchoring at Monte Cristi two men-of-war were sighted, which upon nearer approach proved to be the Haytian gunboats Toussaint l'Ouverture and Manzel, owned by the Riviere Steamship Company, which gets a subsidy of $100,000 for their use. These were keeping strict watch of the coast, and were determined to see what the Clyde was about. To accomplish this, two smaller boats left the Toussaint, well manned with sailors and officers, who carried arms. They rowed up near the Clyde and encircled her first from one side and then from the other. During this performance, which surprised the crew of the American steamer, the heavy gun of the Toussaint was pointed in a menacing manner toward her. However, the rowboats returned to the man-of-war. On the evening of December 20 the Clyde, owing to a severe storm which had come up, shifted her position from Manzanillo Bay to President's Bay, which is the dividing line between Hayti and San Domingo. This brought the men-of-war nearer.
Here the roar of cannon and the unmistakable noise of battle coming from the coast of Hayti were distinctly heard on that day. Captain Holmes had occasion to visit a small steamer lying near the coast, thinking that she had orders for him. To do this, he was forced to pass near the Toussaint, from which boats were again sent to intercept the captain's passage. The drum was sounded calling the marines, who stood in fighting array with pointed guns as the officer passed. He was cut off from his course several times by the boats from the men-of-war, but finally reached his destination and returned without further molestation.
On the morning of December 22 a small schooner, the Aurora, flying the Dominican flag, under Captain Wilson, came from Turk's Island, and attempted to go to Cape Haytien. She was intercepted, however, by the Manzel, whose men seized her and took the captain and crew aboard and placed them in irons. They then took the crew of a little wrecked brig which was lying in Dominican waters, and forced them to man the captured Aurora. They were retained at this work only twenty-four hours and then dismissed, and it was from them that the story of the captain, whose wife was also on board, was learned. On the following day, the 23d, the two men-of-war hove anchor and steamed away with the Aurora in tow. They were afterward seen through glasses bearing off toward Cape Haytien, where it is supposed they were waiting to see if the Clyde attempted to run the blockade. But before going they seized several sailing-boats which attempted to land near Manzanillo Bay. They were carrying on a genuine system of piracy in the interest of Legitime, the Haytians having declared, too, that they would sink any vessel belonging to the Clyde line. It is supposed that the seizure of the brig Aurora will even create trouble between San Domingo and Hayti.
At present, however, contrary to other reports, one of the passengers, a merchant, who came directly from the island, where he received large orders, says that perfect harmony exists between the two. The people of San Domingo are well satisfied with their President, General Heraux, their crops are unusually good, and prosperous times are anticipated. "During my visit," continued the merchant, "the General made no reference to Hayti. The report that he did not receive the deputation sent from Hayti to protest against the landing of arms in San Domingo for the north of Hayti is false. On the contrary, they were received with all honor, and were perfectly satisfied with their success. A reception and fireworks were given in their honor. The vessel El Pacificador, which the Dominican Government recently purchased from England, is to be used as a dispatch-boat along the coast, and not for warlike purposes."
FIGHTING BATTLES WITH CHAMPAGNE
Another passenger, now at the Hotel America, who spent several weeks in San Domingo City before embarking on the Clyde, tells a somewhat different tale. He said: "In the Hotel Philipo, where I was staying, in San Domingo City, was the delegate from the north of Hayti who had been sent to get the privilege of landing arms in the Dominican territory and transmitting them thence to the region which is faithful to Hyppolite. Although he would not speak of the result of his mission, it was the general opinion that his constant good humor and haughty boast that Hyppolite would gain supreme control of Southern Hayti before the end of December were indicative of its success. A few days after his arrival a man-of-war, painted white, whose name I do not remember, appeared in the harbor and landed a delegation from Port-au-Prince, which had come to protest against unrestricted transmission of arms and other articles to the north of Hayti on the part of San Domingo. It so happened that they entered our hotel one day while we were at dinner and seated themselves at an neighboring table. Here they ordered beer and began to drink. The Ambassador from the North became excited over their presence and determined to outdo them. He ordered champagne for all who were in the room, and a general demonstration in favor of Hyppolite was made, during which a Frenchman made a toast to the General. The Ambassador from Legitime soon departed in downcast spirits. During the remainder of their sojourn their spirits did not rise, and it was the supposition that their mission was in vain. While in San Domingo, I heard that 15,000 rifles and 600 kegs of powder had been landed there for Hyppolite and his followers. Indeed, from what I learned, the sympathies of the people of San Domingo are entirely with the North, though probably not strongly enough to lead them to take up arms in their behalf. I met a man who had been on board the Haytien Republic when she was seized. He was taken to Port-au-Prince, where he was imprisoned. He escaped from that city, and reached San Domingo City in safety. He then met a schooner going north, and returned to Cape Haytien, whence he originally came. He was unable to tell much of the state of affairs in Hyppolite's country, and I failed to get from him anything of importance, further than that the insurgent leader has a large and thoroughly equipped army and plenty of funds, and is bound to win. He spoke of the devotion of Hyppolite's soldiers, who, he said, fought with the desperation of madmen, and said that nothing could stay their progress when once fairly started. He said that a letter had been received from a reliable merchant at St. Marc, stating that the Northern troops had possession of nearly all the territory to the north of St. Marc, among them being Verrettes, La Chapelle, Marchand and Dessalines. Rosa was the last of the officers under General Seide Thelemaque who surrendered to General Legitime after September 28, and he is now fighting for him. The letter announces further that the bombardment of Montrouis and St. Marc is expected at any time."
Minister Preston, who is still at the Westminster Hotel, will leave for Boston to-morrow, and cannot, therefore, be in Washington for the President's New Year's reception. "I received a letter from the commodore of the fleet," said the Minister, "in which it is stated that when the Dessalines was off Cape Haytien, on the 3d or 4th inst., Fort Picolet opened fire on her. The battering-guns of the vessel soon silenced the guns of the fort, and she steamed past. When opposite St. Joseph's Battery, which is some distance further inland, she was again shot at, but succeeded in approaching the old French Battery, which is near the Custom House. In returning the fire from this point, a shell dropped near the house of the American Consul, who is said to be responsible for some of the dispatches which have been published. The commander, however, had no orders to bombard Cape Haytien, and simply answered the fire."
C. F. Cavallo, who was reported to have left the city on Saturday by the steamer Ozama, was seen in the streets yesterday. It is said that he left the Ozama at Quarantine. Upon inquiry, it was found that his name was still on the lists at the Hotel Griffou. The reasons for changing his plans could not be learned.
A HAYTIAN PAPER'S ACCOUNT OF IT.
The following is a translation of an extract from "La Verite," of December 22, a paper published at Port-au-Prince:
On Tuesday morning the population of this city were surprised to see an American naval vessel enter the inner harbor. She entered without having a pilot on board or making communication with the land; nor did she fire the usual salute. She immediately steamed alongside of the Haytien Republic and put a garrison of men on board. At the same time another United States naval vessel lay in the outer harbor. This conduct of the Americans surpasses all possible attempts at explanation. They are acting under the doctrine of "might makes right." It is a sad thing that a friendly nation should offer to us an outrageous insult, especially that of the United States; still, we have confidence that a similar humiliation will not be visited upon us again.

records.full_text:
[SPECIAL TELEGRAM TO THE DISPATCH.]
NEW YORK, January 2.—A week ago last Saturday, Dr. Auguste sailed from this port for Paris. It was common report at the time, credited generally by merchants having business with Hayti, that he had gone there on a mission from Hippolyte, the leader of the revolutionary forces of the North of Hayti. The belief was strengthened by the knowledge that the French authorities in Hayti were astride the fence. In the South they were openly for Legitime. In the North they sided with Hippolyte.
It was reported yesterday that a cable had been received from Paris by a merchant of this city stating that Dr. Auguste had had an interview with President Carnot, of the French republic. Dr. Auguste asked that Hippolyte be recognized. President Carnot replied evasively. The cabled statements that France stands with Legitime through thick and thin, and that the American squadron would not have taken the Haytien Republic away without a fight had a French man-of-war been on the spot, are scouted by Haytian merchants in this city. France stands, they say, exactly as the United States stands.
The statements in an afternoon paper that Legitime was imprisoning Americans and had declared that he would shoot every foreigner who interfered with Haytian politics if he had to shoot 500, is not believed genuine by merchants in this city having relations with Hayti.
The purchase of the British tramp steamer Red Rose by the Dominion Government as a national man-of-war has been widely heralded as an indication of approaching war between San Domingo and Hayti, the result, it has been stated, of Haytian seizures of Dominican vessels in Dominican waters. Consul Julia, of San Domingo, talked last night, for the first time of the new Dominican navy. The Holland loan of $4,000,000, he said, was made long before any difficulty arose between North and South Hayti, and was made solely for the purpose of reorganizing the army and procuring a navy for ordinary purposes of national self-defense. The Dominican navy was to consist of four vessels, and an agent is now in Europe negotiating for their purchase. The first of them, and the only one so far purchased, was the Red Rose. She is now due in San Domingo. She will be called El Presidente.

George Bowman told a reporter he had sold her to the Haitian Consul of New York and that she was bound for Samana, in Santo Domingo, to be used as a gunboat under the Dominican flag, while Captain Terry laughed off suggestions of guns aboard or blockade-running; the crew, a motley crowd who were not seamen, had been hired only to take the vessel down and return as passengers.

Her register was changed from the Novelty to the Mercedes in the Custom House here yesterday. she also cleared for Samana. TOOK GAS THROUGH A TUBE. SUICIDE OF THE PRESIDENT OF AN IRON FOUNDRY COMPANY IN ARLINGTON, N. J. Samuel Beckett, of the firm of Beckett McDowell, manufacturing machinists, No. 120 Liberty-st., and president of an iron foundry and machine company at Arlington, N. J., was found dead in his bed yesterday morning, at his house in Grand-st., in Arlington. Death had been caused by suffocation from gas. Mr. Beckett retired on Thursday night, and slept alone in a room adjoining one occupied by his wife and children. Nothing was heard of him during the night, At 7 a m. his wife went to the room and found it filled with gas. A rubber tube was found connected with the gas jet near the bed, and the jet was turned on full head. It was apparent that he had inhaled the gas by inserting the tube in his mouth. Dr. Exton, a local physician, was called in, and pronounced the man dead. He granted a certificate of burial. Mr. Beckett had been depressed in mind by business reverses. About eighteen months ago cellonite factory in Arlington blew up, and badly damaged surrounding property, including the works of the iron company. The cost of repairs drained the company's resources. The specialty of the company is mining

records.full_text:
MYSTERY ON THE MERCEDES.
CONSUL JULIEN SAYS SHE IS HIS.
MINISTER PRESTON CONTRADICTS HIM—IS SHE INTENDED FOR HYPPOLITE?
From information obtained yesterday from Minister Preston and the detectives employed by him it is fairly certain that the Mercedes is intended for the Hyppolite Navy. The money for her purchase was furnished by Jimines, Haustedt & Co., No. 5 South William-st.; she was purchased in the name of Carlos Julien, the Dominican Consul, and sailed from here under the Dominican flag. Mr. Jimines ran for Vice-President on the ticket with General Hyppolite recently; Oscar Hurtlinger, a member of the firm of Jimines, Haustedt & Co., is a nephew of Consul Julien, and another of the firm is his brother-in-law.
The first act of the firm of Jimines, Haustedt & Co. was to send a large consignment of arms and ammunition to Hyppolite; they also sent a large consignment on the steamer Saginaw through the favor of Consul Julien. President Herraux, of Santo Domingo, had got President Legitime's consent to land some arms and ammunition at Monte Christi, upon the representation that they were for Santo Domingo, and he so informed Consul Julien, and they were to be sent on the steamer Saginaw. Instead of the Santo Domingo consignment going, it is alleged that Jimines, Haustedt & Co. sent down a similar quantity for Hyppolite and Herraux's purchase did not go.
Minister Preston's detectives and General Contreras were in Boston when the Mercedes (then the Novelty) sailed from there on Thursday for New-York, and they had considerable information about her. When they traced her to this port on Friday it was too late to take any action to prevent her sailing, and they deferred appealing to Collector Magone until yesterday morning. But the boat sailed long before daylight, passing outside of Sandy Hook at 3:40. Her manifest at the Custom House shows that she had no freight, and carried 200 tons of coal and "no passengers." However, Mr. Hurtlinger sailed upon her, and under ordinary circumstances would have been a passenger. It was the impression that as soon as she got outside she would pull down the Dominican flag and hoist the Haytian colors, and would be intercepted by some vessel which would transfer guns to her. It is believed by Mr. Preston's detectives that she had some guns in her coal bunkers intended for the Madrid, which vessel is now being transformed into an armor-belted cruiser in the Erie Basin.
Carlos Julien, the Dominican consul, met a Tribune reporter with a happy smile yesterday, and was perfectly willing to unbosom himself regarding his part in the story of the mysterious Mercedes, otherwise known as the Novelty, now that she was under way for Samana. In fact, he seemed proud of it. He said that he was the owner of the Mercedes, and that he had bought her from a Boston firm about two weeks ago, but merely for a private speculation. He paid, he declared, $60,000 for her, and expects to make money by selling her. "You see," continued the consul, "they need vessels in the South, and they are willing to pay for them. I know that the Haytian Government is in great need of proper boats. I know that General Hyppolite needs them, and I know that General Legitime needs them, and whoever is the highest bidder shall have the Mercedes. That may be, for all I know, my own government. I sailed her under the Dominican flag in order to make the sale easier. I know nothing about the make-up of the crew. Should the speculation be profitable, however, I may repeat the operation, and send other vessels South. The Mercedes carried no arms of any kind, her cargo consisting of two hundred tons of coal."
Minister Preston contradicted Mr. Julien's statements. "That vessel," said he, "was bought with Haytian money. We have known this for two weeks. She will be used as a pirate and privateer in the Northern navy. Mr. Julien has no money to buy her with."
The superintendent of the Merritt Wrecking Company was indignant over the report that the Mercedes had taken guns on board while lying at Stapleton. He denounced it as utterly untrue, saying that she had taken no cargo on board, and that no lighter had been alongside of her when she was lying at the Merritt dock.

records.full_text:
HIPPOLYTE'S VICTORY.
The News Confirmed by the Captain of a Blockade Runner.
LEGITIME THREE TIMES BEATEN.
Sixteen Prisoners Captured in the Engagement at Montrouis.
GEN. PIQUANT'S INGLORIOUS ESCAPE.
A Navy for Hippolyte Almost at His Hand, About as Good as New.
[SPECIAL TELEGRAM TO THE DISPATCH.]
NEW YORK, January 26.—The steamer Wensleydale, Captain Coull, arrived here from Port-de-Paix this evening. She took provisions shipped by Hugo Kainor & Co. to that "blockaded" Hatian port and sold out at a big profit. She brought logwood back for the Green Point Dye Works.
Captain Coull says he entered Port-de-Paix on the evening of the 8th, with all the lights burning and the Legitimist gunboat Belize in sight. When she whistled the Belize made off and disappeared. The town was hungry. The garrison was small and half clothed. The soldiers were armed chiefly with old-fashioned horse-pistols, and the artillery consisted of old cannon four or five feet long.
There were two passengers on the Wensleydale—B. DePendry, a French-Canadian schoolmaster, who is on his way home after teaching two years in Port-de-Paix, and Frederick Elie, who described himself as a merchant on business, but is believed to have come straight from Hippolyte, at Cape Haytien.
LATE NEWS CONFIRMED.
Mr. DePendry confirmed the late news that Hippolyte had beaten Legitime's forces in three successive engagements. They were at Las Cahobas, Mirobalais, and Achaies. In the Montrouis engagement, which was reported here from Port-au-Prince as a victory for the Legitimists, he says the Northern forces badly whipped General Piquant, and took as many as 16 prisoners. General Piquant fled, closely pursued, and made for the coast, where the Toussant l'Ouverture was lying. In such close quarters did he find himself that he didn't dare to wait for the Toussant's boat to get to him, but jumped into the ocean and swam to meet the boat, while his pursuers popped their pistols at him from the shore.
Two weeks ago the Toussant L'Ouverture attacked Cape Haytien again, and fired shells for a whole day. Fort Piccolet replied. Only one shell reached the town. Mr. DePendry said that Hippolyte was putting off an aggressive campaign until his new navy was ready for action. The plan then was to march the entire Northern army straight for Port-au-Prince, while the gunboats worked around to the harbor.
A NAVY ON THE SPOT.
Hippolyte will not have to wait for the arrival of the Madrid. He has a navy on the spot. Mr. DePendry says that a courier arrived at Cape Haytien recently, overland from Hippolyte's agent in San Domingo, with the news that President Hereaux has sold his new gunboat, El Presidente, to Hippolyte. The gunboat was the Red Rose, and was purchased recently in France by Hereaux. The news also came that the Mercedes had reached Samana and had been promptly sold to Hippolyte. This is the boat recently purchased on speculation by the Dominican Consul in this city.
Mr. DePendry said that the armament had been brought by the Ozama from New York, and was being put aboard the boats in Dominican waters. One of them was fitting up in Monte Cristi. The guns will be handled by American gunners. Ten of them, he said, arrived by the Ozama, with the guns. It will be remembered that the Ozama took nine Gatling guns and a long heavy box that was supposed to be a piece of heavier ordnance.
Minister Preston said a cable message had informed him that there had been a fire in Port-au-Prince. Two or three private houses were burned, the result of an oil explosion. If the fire was so small, it seems rather peculiar that Legitime should cable the news at $1 35 a word.

records.full_text:
SHE WASN'T SUNK.
A Clyde Steamer Returns from a Haytien Cruise.
NEW YORK, Feb. 9.—[Special Telegram to THE BEE.]—There is considerable stir among the merchants of the Haytien trade over the arrival of the Clyde steamship Ozama, which a Haytien gun boat was expected to send to the bottom, if found in Haytien waters. But the Ozama had not only been in Haytien waters, but she remained two days at Cape Haytien and took a full cargo of coffee. She had on board General Segundo Imbert, vice president of the republic of San Domingo. General Imbert did not leave San Domingo of his own accord. General Henriux, president of the republic, mildly suggested that his presence was not desired and placed $2,000 at his disposal, requesting him to make immediate arrangements for his departure. The vice president, so the story goes, took the hint and secured passage on the Ozama when she touched at Monte Cristo. When the steamer left General Henriux went on board a Dominican gunboat lying in the harbor and accompanied the Ozama some distance out to sea. The Haytien gunboat is said to have been watching the Ozama, but she made no hostile movement. The Ozama continued her way to Cape Haytien, where she arrived January 30. The American steel cruiser Atlanta, which had arrived that morning, was lying off Port Picolet and the Clyde steamer entered the port with colors flying.
Major Colwel, commander of the Ozama, said: "There was not the slightest pretense of a blockade and no Haytien gunboats were in sight. The Atlanta, on rounding to off the port, fired a salute of twenty-one guns and the fort responded with her thirty-two pounder. General Hippolyte, I was told, went on board the Atlanta and was received with the same honors tendered Legitime on his visit to Rear Admiral Luce on board the Galena at Port-au-Prince."
A dispatch was received at Cape Haytien from St. Marc January 31 which announced that a body of Legitime's troops, under General Belize, attempted to land from three gunboats at that place. The invaders were repulsed by the soldiers under General Montploint. Later reports, still unconfirmed at the time of the Ozama sailing, were that 700 of Legitime's troops landing at Saline had been captured by Montploint's men. This probably relates to the battle reported on Wednesday last. One of the Ozama's passengers from Turk's Island said General Alexis Nord has succeeded in reaching Cape Haytien and had assumed command of Hippolyte's forces. General Nord went from Fortune Island in a schooner which touched at Turk's Island and then proceeded to Monte Cristo, where Nord landed and found his way to the Cape.

Who Owns the Madrid?
NEW YORK, Feb. 16.—Consul Julia, of San Domingo, applied to the deputy collector of port for clearance papers for the steamer Madrid, which is supposed to have been purchased for Hippolyte. He presented two certificates, one showing that he represented the owner of the vessel and the other certifying that she was owned by the Dominican government. Minister Preston, of Hayti, appeared in the collector's office at this time and begged the deputy collector not to clear the vessel. He said the vessel was intended for Hippolyte, and it would be a violation of law to allow her to clear. The deputy collector declined to clear the Madrid until he had looked into the matter, and asked both gentlemen to call again. Collector Magone will probably give his decision at that time.
