records.headline: President of the Dominican Republic Has Retired.
records.summary_en: The *Indianapolis Journal* reported that the Dominican capital surrendered to General Horacio Vásquez on May 2 following two days of severe combat outside the city. President Jimenes took refuge in the French consulate, while other officials sought asylum in the American and French legations as rebel troops occupied the capital without public demonstrations. The report added that Puerto Plata, the final stronghold loyal to Jimenes, had also capitulated, leaving Vásquez in full control of the country.
records.summary_es: El *Indianapolis Journal* informó que la capital dominicana se rindió al general Horacio Vásquez el 2 de mayo tras dos días de encarnizados combates en las afueras de la urbe. El presidente Jimenes se refugió en el consulado francés, mientras otros funcionarios solicitaron asilo en las legaciones estadounidense y francesa cuando las tropas rebeldes ocuparon la capital sin manifestaciones públicas. El informe agregó que Puerto Plata, el último bastión leal a Jimenes, también había capitulado, dejando a Vásquez con el control absoluto del país.

records.full_text:
PRESIDENT OF THE DOMINICAN REPUBLIC HAS RETIRED.

Horacio Vasquez, Leader of the Successful Revolutionary Movement, Now at Head of the Government.

SURRENDER OF PUERTO PLATA

LAST CITY THAT WAS HELD BY THE EX-PRESIDENT'S TROOPS.

New Government Probably Will Be Promptly Recognized by the United States—The Looting of a Town.

WASHINGTON, May 7.—Cable advices received here state that President Jimenez, of the Dominican Republic, has signed a relinquishment of his claims to the presidency and on his part Horacio Vasquez, the late Vice President, has granted amnesty to the adherents of the late government and assumed the presidential office.

Senor Don Foo Leonte Vasquez, the charge of the Dominican Republic, has received cable advices from home announcing the success of the revolution. It is probable that he will now become a resident minister here. Naturally the charge is desirous that the United States shall recognize at once the new government. This is a matter, however, that is by custom left to the United States minister resident, but it is not doubted that Mr. Powell will, as he has heretofore done, soon put himself in communication with the de facto government.

Puerta Plaza, the last place held by the Jimenez adherents, has capitulated.

Advices from San Domingo, under date of May 2, say the Dominican capital capitulated to-day to the revolutionary forces commanded by Gen. Horatio Vasquez, the Vice President of the republic. President Jimenez sought refuge in the French consulate and many government officers obtained shelter in the French and United States legations. The revolutionary troops entered the capital quietly. There was no enthusiasm shown by the population here at the entry of the victorious army. The approach of the revolutionists to the capital was announced after two days of heavy fighting between the government troops and the forces of General Vasquez, during which many were killed or wounded on both sides. When it became known here that General Vasquez threatened to attack Santo Domingo, the United States minister, J. S. Powell, as dean of the diplomatic corps, requested the Dominican government to inform him regarding the arrangements made to protect the lives and property of foreigners here, adding that in case no precautions were taken he would consider it his duty to take measures to provide for their safety as the situation demanded. The reply was satisfactory.

SACKING OF BARAHONA.

Sailors Describe the Capture of the Town by Revolutionists.

NEW YORK, May 7.—Members of the British brigantine Alice, Captain Inness, which has just arrived from the West Indies, report that while the brigantine lay about eighty-five yards from the shore at Barahona, on the southwest coast of San Domingo, a force of revolutionists entered the town and began discharging rifles. Inhabitants of the port ran shrieking from their homes along the beach. “The revolutionists first sacked the principal saloon in the town,” said one of the crew. “They broke all the windows, drank all the liquor in bottles and then smashed the bar. They rolled barrels of rum out into the street, and what they could not drink they turned into the gutters. Next they attacked the jail and took out all the prisoners they wanted. The freed convicts joined the insurrectionists. In the attack eleven guards and one prisoner were killed. Two civilians were killed in the woods, which thickly skirt the town at the base of the mountain. The women and children who fled along the beach sought the protection of Captain Inness, who brought off as many as the gig would hold. A sloop brought off the rest of the refugees. The refugees, 100 in number, remained about three days. Meantime about 100 government soldiers appeared and were driven to retreat by the revolutionists, who then disappeared.”

records.summary_en: The *Age-Herald* detailed the formal capitulation terms accepted by President Jimenes, which guaranteed the security of state officials, the protection of private property, and the immediate liberation of political prisoners. Insurgent troops took possession of government buildings in Santo Domingo under terms monitored by the foreign diplomatic corps, while the cruiser *Cincinnati* was en route to the island. records.summary_en: A San Juan report quotes a letter received by a native of Santo Domingo living there saying the situation in the Dominican Republic is decidedly critical and the new government in momentary danger of being overthrown. records.passage: VASQUEZ ADMINISTRATION EXPECTED TO TUMBLE SOON. San Juan, P. R.. June 28--A native of San Domingo, living here, is in receipt of a letter, the writer of which says the situation in the Dominican Republic is decidedly critical. The new government, according to this correspondent, is in momentary danger of being overthrown. President Vasquez, it is reported, is mentally affected and half the time does not know what he is doing. The writer of the letter adds that the finances of the republic are in a deplorable condition, that the government employees receive only half pay, that the people have lost all confidence in the administration and that numbers of them are leaving the country. The present regime, he declares, cannot last longer than October. In response, Commander Mason of the cruiser *Cincinnati* departed Cape Haitien to investigate the disturbances and protect American interests at the Dominican port. The dispatch also noted that Haitian government forces had successfully reclaimed Gonaives following the flight of Haitian rebel leader General Firmin.

El despacho señaló además que las fuerzas del gobierno haitiano habían recuperado con éxito Gonaïves tras la huida del líder rebelde haitiano, el general Firmin.

Dice que una cañonera gubernamental disparó tres tiros la noche anterior sin causar daños, que la ciudad estaba fortificada y decidida a resistir, y que se desembarcaron marines para proteger el consulado.

records.summary_en: The *Essex County Herald* emphasized the strategic importance of Samana Bay as the naval key to the Caribbean, recalling President Grant's earlier annexation efforts. It reported that an unexpected revolution had seized the capital of Santo Domingo during the president's absence, complicating recent American diplomatic agreements compensating a U.S. steamship company. With the Dominican president on the run and the foreign minister sheltering in the American consulate, the paper suggested U.S. marine landings or intervention might follow.

Con el presidente dominicano en fuga y el ministro de Relaciones Exteriores refugiado en el consulado estadounidense, el periódico sugirió que podrían producirse desembarcos de la infantería de marina de EE. UU. o una intervención militar.

records.headline: This article argues that Samana Bay, on the eastern coast of Santo Domingo, is one of the great maritime positions of the Antilles
records.summary_en: This article argues that Samana Bay, on the eastern coast of Santo Domingo, is one of the great maritime positions of the Antilles, a harbour from which operations could be conducted by any kind of war vessel and in which a blockaded fleet might lie in safety. It praises the island's fertility, rivalling Cuba's, and its possible products of tobacco, coffee, indigo, sugar, cocoa, fruits and vegetables, noting that millions of acres lie wild for lack of cultivators and transport, and recalls the era of comparative peace under President Heureaux, who was assassinated on July 26, 1899.
records.summary_es: Este artículo sostiene que la bahía de Samaná, en la costa oriental de Santo Domingo, es una de las grandes posiciones marítimas de las Antillas, un puerto desde el cual podrían realizarse operaciones con cualquier clase de buque de guerra y en el que una flota bloqueada podría permanecer a salvo. Elogia la fertilidad de la isla, que rivaliza con la de Cuba, y sus posibles productos de tabaco, café, añil, azúcar, cacao, frutas y vegetales, señalando que millones de acres permanecen incultos por falta de cultivadores y de transporte, y recuerda la era de paz comparativa bajo el presidente Heureaux, asesinado el 26 de julio de 1899.

records.summary_en: The *New-York Tribune* reported that the entire northern region of the Dominican Republic had joined an armed insurrection against President Alejandro Wos y Gil. The insurgents published a manifesto at Puerto Plata detailing grievances against the administration, including the imprisonment of dissidents, widespread financial waste, and default on national debt obligations. The document also fiercely denounced new fiscal burdens on cocoa, port fee concessions granted to the Hamburg-American Line, and an unconstitutional proposal to neutralize Dominican harbors during wartime.
records.summary_es: El *New-York Tribune* informó que toda la región norte de la República Dominicana se había sumado a una insurrección armada contra el presidente Alejandro Wos y Gil. El documento también repudiaba enérgicamente las nuevas cargas fiscales sobre el cacao, las exenciones de derechos portuarios otorgadas a la Hamburg-American Line y una propuesta inconstitucional para neutralizar los puertos dominicanos durante conflictos bélicos.

Dominican exiles in New York received reports that insurgent forces had proclaimed General Juan Isidro Jimenes president of the republic. Jimenes had previously resigned as Dominican fiscal agent to organize the armed movement to reclaim the presidency from which he had been ousted.

Exiliados dominicanos en Nueva York recibieron informes de que las fuerzas insurgentes habían proclamado presidente de la república al general Juan Isidro Jimenes. Jimenes había renunciado previamente a su cargo de agente fiscal dominicano con el propósito de organizar el movimiento armado para recuperar la presidencia de la cual había sido desalojado.

In Dominican waters, insurgents fired unsuccessfully on the American steamer *New York* at Samana, while Minister Powell rejected rebel appeals for diplomatic recognition. In response to American diplomatic pressure, the Dominican government named Foreign Minister Galván and Judge Gray as arbitrators to resolve the San Domingo Improvement Company claim.

En aguas dominicanas, insurgentes dispararon infructuosamente contra el vapor estadounidense *New York* en Samaná, al tiempo que el ministro Powell desestimaba las peticiones rebeldes de reconocimiento diplomático. En respuesta a la presión diplomática estadounidense, el gobierno dominicano designó al ministro de Relaciones Exteriores Galván y al juez Gray como árbitros para resolver la reclamación de la San Domingo Improvement Company.

records.summary_en: There was a heavy artillery duel between government troops and the insurgents at Santo Domingo City on the night of November 17, and the United States cruiser Baltimore landed a force of marines for the protection of American interests. Minister Powell's despatches to the State Department call the situation desperate: the city is constantly under fire, shells are falling in it, it is surrounded on three sides, an assault is momentarily expected, and it is believed the Dominican government cannot much longer hold out against the revolutionists.

Los despachos del ministro Powell al Departamento de Estado califican la situación de desesperada: la ciudad está constantemente bajo fuego, caen proyectiles en ella, está rodeada por tres lados, se espera un asalto de un momento a otro y se cree que el gobierno dominicano no podrá resistir mucho más contra los revolucionarios.

records.summary_en: In an interview, deposed President Alejandro Wos y Gil says the future of the Dominican Republic hinges on recognition of the protocol signed by the Vásquez government with Minister Powell, which demands arbitration of differences between Santo Domingo and the United States. He says President Roosevelt agreed he could accept no other arbitrator than his appointee, Señor Galván, now in Washington, and when asked if he was urging a United States protectorate, he put a finger to his lips and waved his hand, indicating the rumor about Galván's mission was true.
records.summary_es: En una entrevista, el depuesto presidente Alejandro Wos y Gil dice que el futuro de la República Dominicana depende del reconocimiento del protocolo firmado por el gobierno de Vásquez con el ministro Powell, que exige el arbitraje de las diferencias entre Santo Domingo y los Estados Unidos. Afirma que el presidente Roosevelt acordó que no podría aceptar otro árbitro que su designado, el señor Galván, ahora en Washington, y al ser preguntado si procuraba un protectorado estadounidense, se llevó un dedo a los labios y agitó la mano, dando a entender que el rumor sobre la misión de Galván era cierto.

I had the chair through peace; I do not want It through war, which is demoralizing to the country. "The future state of the Dominican republic hinges upon the recognition of the protocol signed by the Vasquez government with Minister Powell. I never wanted the protocol ratified unless the Dominican Congress accepted It; my acceptance of it was forced when the revolution came. This protocol demands the arbitration of certain differences between Santo Domingo and the United States. In accordance with President Roosevelt's agreement with me, personally signed by the President and received In Santo Domingo, Mr. Roosevelt cannot accept any other arbitrator than mine. Signor Galvan, who was appointed by my government and is now in Washington. I do not care to say more now.” Gen. Wos-y-Gil will remain here two months. records.headline: Plot against Powell: a letter from an official of the present Dominican government discloses a Woss y Gil party
records.summary_en: Plot against Powell: a letter from an official of the present Dominican government discloses a Woss y Gil party scheme to assassinate Minister Powell in a staged street fight - and President Jiménez by plain assassination, two attempts on him having already failed; the Powell plot was abandoned, but he is carefully guarded.
records.summary_es: Complot contra Powell: una carta de un funcionario del actual gobierno dominicano revela un plan del partido de Woss y Gil para asesinar al ministro Powell en una pelea callejera fingida - y al presidente Jiménez por asesinato directo, con dos atentados ya fallidos contra él; el complot contra Powell fue abandonado, pero se le custodia con cuidado.
records.passage: PLOT AGAINST POWELL. Wos y Gil Party Plans to Assassinate U. S. Minister. New York, Dec. 15. An alleged plot to assassinate William F. Powell, United States minister to Hayti and charge d'affaires at Port-au-Prince, Santo Domingo, has been disclosed in a communication from an official of the present Dominican government to a fellow countryman in this city, who formerly was an official under Wos y Gil, the recently deposed president of the republic. The letter states that the plot had been so arranged that ex-President Jiminez, under whose leadership Wos y Gil was overthrown, was to have been killed at about the same time. The plot to assassinate Minister Powell, it was asserted, was conceived because of his opposition to plans of certain officials. The plan as reported was to let two or three men get into a fight on a street along which Mr. Powell was passing. It was arranged that in the melee other plotters should engage, and it would be an easy matter to kill the American "by accident." With regard to Jiminez, the writer asserts that he was to be the victim of plain assassination and that already two unsuccessful attacks have been made upon his person. With the gunboat *Newport* remaining as the only foreign warship in port, concerns grew over the safety of foreign residents. Meanwhile, insurgent leader Juan Isidro Jimenes scored a decisive victory at Moca against 500 government troops under General Ramón Cáceres, who was wounded, clearing the path for an advance on Santo Domingo.

Government forces successfully retook Baní and San Cristóbal and repelled a major assault on Santo Domingo following an engagement at Haina. Denver, Jan. 20 — Judge Moses Hallett in the United States District Court today, after consideration of the Sherman Parker habeas corpus suit against the military authorities of Colorado, announced that his court is without jurisdiction in the matter. Parker is the union miner of Cripple Creek who was held in the military bull pen without warrant. Chicago, Jan. 21. — As the result of a storm train service on the South Side elevated road was paralyzed for nearly two hours during the day, endangering life and discommoding hundreds of passengers. Rain soaking the wood superstructure of the road caused the moisture to communicate to a defective third rail support near a network of switches. The electric current deserted the car motors and flowed through the ironwork of the structure to the ground. The entire structure for a considerable distance was electrified and menaced the safety of horses and men below, until the current was shut off at the powerhouse. Trains on the road were crowded. Passengers on the stalled trains, after waiting for some time for signs of life in the motors, took surface lines and reached their work downtown after long delay.

records.summary_en: The *San Francisco Call* reported that pressure was mounting in Washington for President Roosevelt to establish an American protectorate over the Dominican Republic to end persistent revolutionary instability. While Secretary of State Hay opposed such an intervention, President Roosevelt was considering steps to protect American commercial investments, though final decisions awaited ratification of the Panama Canal treaty. The report highlighted that six American, German, and French warships were guarding foreign interests, with European governments receptive to American measures restoring order.
records.summary_es: El *San Francisco Call* informó que crecía la presión en Washington para que el presidente Roosevelt estableciera un protectorado estadounidense sobre la República Dominicana a fin de terminar con la constante inestabilidad revolucionaria. Aunque el secretario de Estado Hay se oponía a dicha intervención, el presidente Roosevelt consideraba medidas para proteger las inversiones comerciales estadounidenses, si bien las decisiones definitivas aguardaban la ratificación del tratado del Canal de Panamá. El informe subrayó que seis buques de guerra estadounidenses, alemanes y franceses custodiaban los intereses extranjeros, mostrándose los gobiernos europeos receptivos ante medidas estadounidenses que restablecieran el orden.

records.summary_es: Un despacho desde Monte Cristi fechado el 6 de febrero informa que el vapor New-York de la línea Clyde llegó esa mañana seguido por el cañonero dominicano Presidente, y que cuando las lanchas salieron a traer a tierra municiones que formaban parte de su carga, el cañonero disparó contra ellas y los revolucionarios en la costa respondieron con cañones y fusiles Mauser. El New-York partió hacia Puerto Plata, el cañonero fue alcanzado dos veces por balas de cañón y por muchas balas de fusil durante media hora de tiroteo, y el fracaso en desembarcar las municiones se califica como un golpe serio para el general Jiminez, cuyo ataque a Santiago de los Caballeros estaba fijado para el domingo.
records.passage: the cruisers Montgomery and Detroit, now at Culebra, have been ordered from there to Porto Plata. The Clyde Liner New-York Fails to Land Cargo at Monte Christi. Monte Christi, Santo Domingo, Feb. 6. — The Clyde Line steamship New-York, which sailed from New-York on January 30, arrived here this morning. It was followed by the Dominican gunboat Presidente. Lighters were sent alongside the New-York, to bring ashore some ammunition, which formed part of her cargo. When the lighters had nearly reached the steamship the gunboat fired on them, and the revolutionists on shore replied with cannon and Mausers. Being in danger, the New-York thereupon left Monte Christi for Porto Plata. The firing continued for half an hour, after which the gunboat sailed for Porto Plata. She was hit twice by round shot, and apparently by many bullets, for she stopped and lowered boats, evidently to plug the holes made in her hull. The failure to land the ammunition is a serious blow to General Jiménez, for whom it was intended, and may cause him to lose the ground he had already gained. An attack on Santiago de los Caballeros had been fixed for Sunday.

records.summary_en: A United States naval report tells of the commander going aboard the Newark to interview General Morales after a charge that Morales had violated asylum granted by the American consular agent at Samana to two men; Morales replied the men were taken not from the consulate but from a farm outside the town belonging to the agent, and the commander warned him to respect the American flag and consulate. The report also covers Morales's decree closing Monte Cristi and Macoris, the firing on the Clyde liner New-York's lighters at Monte Cristi and the agreement to deposit her cargo at Puerto Plata, and the insurgents holding La Vega and the southeastern peninsula while Santo Domingo City is closely invested by about 1,200 men.
records.summary_es: Un informe naval de los Estados Unidos relata que el comandante subió a bordo del Newark para entrevistar al general Morales tras la acusación de que Morales había violado el asilo concedido por el agente consular americano en Samana a dos hombres; Morales respondió que los hombres no fueron tomados del consulado sino de una finca fuera de la ciudad perteneciente al agente, y el comandante le advirtió que respetara la bandera y el consulado americanos. El informe también cubre el decreto de Morales que cerró Monte Cristi y Macoris, los disparos contra las lanchas del vapor New-York de la línea Clyde en Monte Cristi y el acuerdo de depositar su carga en Puerto Plata, y que los insurgentes ocupan La Vega y la península del sureste mientras la ciudad de Santo Domingo está estrechamente sitiada por unos 1,200 hombres.

records.summary_en: The *New-York Tribune* reported allegations by General Francisco Leonte Vásquez that Dominican insurgents deliberately targeted Americans to provoke armed United States intervention. Vásquez claimed government troops discovered incriminating letters at Santiago de los Caballeros written by revolutionary Governor Desiderio Arias to rebel leader Juan Isidro Jimenes. According to Vásquez, these documents explained the deadly attack on machinist Johnson of the USS *Yankee* and the gunfire directed against the American steamer *New York*.
records.summary_es: El *New-York Tribune* informó sobre las denuncias formuladas por el general Francisco Leonte Vásquez en el sentido de que los insurgentes dominicanos atacaban deliberadamente a estadounidenses para provocar una intervención armada de los Estados Unidos. Vásquez afirmó que las tropas del gobierno hallaron cartas incriminatorias en Santiago de los Caballeros escritas por el gobernador revolucionario Desiderio Arias al líder rebelde Juan Isidro Jimenes. Según Vásquez, estos documentos explicaban el ataque mortal contra el maquinista Johnson del USS *Yankee* y los disparos dirigidos contra el vapor estadounidense *New York*.

WANT U. S. TO INTERVENE. Statement of General Vasquez as to San Domingo Insurrectionists.

That the Dominican insurrectionists are waging a war against Americans and American Interests for the express purpose of causing the intervention of the United States In the affairs of San Domingo was the direct accusation made yesterday by General Francisco Leonte Vasquez, who has just returned to this city from the scene of conflict. He brings with him, he says, documentary proof in substantiation of his assertions, and [in?] these might be found the explanation for the killing of the machinist, Johnson, of the United States gunboat Yankee, and the firing on the Clyde Line steamer New-York by the revolutionists. The documents on which General Vasquez bases his charges are two letters addressed to General Juan Isidro Jiménez, chief of the rebellion, by General Desiderio Arias, one of his subordinates, which were intercepted at Santiago de los Caballeros by the government army, of which General Vasquez was in command until a few weeks ago.

records.summary_en: The *Wahpeton Times* reported that Captain Miller of the USS *Columbia* refused to permit Dominican President Morales to blockade domestic ports against American shipping after the gunboat *Presidente* turned away the American schooner *W. R. Perkins*. In San Pedro de Macorís, insurgents seized and armed the Clyde Line tugboat *Burro*, while the steamer *Cherokee* received a naval convoy from the USS *Hartford*. The report also noted domestic arrests and the deportation of several Dominican political figures to Cuba.
records.summary_es: El *Wahpeton Times* informó que el capitán Miller, del USS *Columbia*, se negó a permitir que el presidente dominicano Morales bloqueara los puertos nacionales al comercio marítimo estadounidense, luego de que el cañonero *Presidente* rechazara a la goleta estadounidense *W. R. Perkins*. En San Pedro de Macorís, los insurgentes incautaron y artillaron el remolcador *Burro* de la Clyde Line, mientras que el vapor *Cherokee* recibió escolta naval del USS *Hartford*. El informe dio cuenta asimismo de detenciones internas y de la deportación de varias figuras políticas dominicanas hacia Cuba.

President Morales, of the Dominican republic, has been refused permission to blockade his own ports to keep out the revolutionists, as shown by the following report, to the navy department by Capt. James E. Miller, commanding the cruiser Columbia: "This morning (Feb. 18) the American three-masted schooner W. R. Perkins came in from the eastward and our boarding boat went alongside. The captain informed me that he had been warned off Macoris and not allowed to enter by the gunboat Presidente, and was told that he must proceed to this port. "Immediately upon receipt of this information I communicated with the minister, requesting him to communicate with President Morales and inform him that I would not recognize his right to blockade Macoris and refuse entrance to vessels flying the American flag. The minister informs me that the president demurred at first, but finally agreed to the fact." Rebels Seize American Tug. San Domingo. March 3. United States Minister Powell has been informed that the insurgents at San Pedro de Macoris have seized the tug boat Burro, belonging to the Clyde line of New York, and armed her. The Clyde line steamer Cherokee has gone to Azua de Compostela, convoyed by the United States training ship Hartford. Many arrests have been made here and several politicians were sent out of the country yesterday on board the steamer Julia of the Cuba line. Edward C. Reed, United States consular agent at San Pedro de Macoris,

records.summary_en: The *New-York Tribune* recounted political maneuvers during President Buenaventura Báez's historical efforts to annex the Dominican Republic to the United States. The account recalled how Báez jailed political opponents to guarantee passage of the treaty until an American politician persuaded him that a small dissenting vote would look less suspicious. It also detailed an earlier attempt to lease Samana Bay surveyed by Captain George B. McClellan, which collapsed when British and French warships arrived to oppose American acquisition.
records.summary_es: El *New-York Tribune* relató las maniobras políticas durante las gestiones históricas del presidente Buenaventura Báez para anexionar la República Dominicana a los Estados Unidos. La crónica recordó cómo Báez encarceló a opositores políticos para asegurar la aprobación del tratado hasta que un político estadounidense lo convenció de que una pequeña votación disidente resultaría menos sospechosa. Detalló asimismo una tentativa anterior para arrendar la bahía de Samaná, inspeccionada por el capitán George B. McClellan, la cual fracasó al llegar buques de guerra británicos y franceses para oponerse a la adquisición estadounidense.

“Jail methods will ruin the whole business,” he said. “This thing must be done on the square, or it will fall through.” Baez at first shrugged his shoulders, and when he did speak he only said: “But you want it unanimous, don't you? “Not at all. A unanimous vote always creates suspicion. A small minority vote gives a far better impression.” “All right.” said Baez. “You can have that. Anything you want you can have in San Domingo.” Baez summoned several representatives, and there was a hurried conference. The treaty was passed with a “small minority.” Twenty years before the failure of this annexation scheme this government made a treaty with San Domingo to rent in perpetuity the great sheltered Bay of Samana. The father of the present Mayor of New-York accompanied the commission sent to negotiate for the territory, and Captain McClellan, as he was known then, made a survey of that part of the Dominican coast. Just before the treaty could be ratified, however, news of its purpose leaked out. England and France both took alarm, and dispatched warships to Samana Bay. At the sight of European cannon the San Domingo statesmen forgot all about the treaty.

records.summary_en: The *Omaha Daily Bee* reported that departing United States Minister Powell assured the Dominican president that the United States had no intention of annexing the republic and strongly supported its sovereignty under the Monroe Doctrine. Powell urged the government to prevent foreign intervention by honoring debts to foreign creditors, protecting foreign commercial concessions, and governing transparently. The article added that the Dominican gunboat *Independencia* transported government troops to assault Monte Cristi, which remained held by insurgents.
records.summary_es: El *Omaha Daily Bee* informó que el saliente ministro de los Estados Unidos Powell aseguró al presidente dominicano que los Estados Unidos no tenían intención de anexar la república y respaldaban firmemente su soberanía bajo la Doctrina Monroe. Powell instó al gobierno a prevenir intervenciones extranjeras honrando las deudas con los acreedores externos, resguardando las concesiones comerciales foráneas y gobernando con transparencia. El artículo añadió que el cañonero dominicano *Independencia* transportó tropas gubernamentales para asaltar Monte Cristi, ciudad que continuaba en manos de los insurgentes.
records.passage: the future of Santo Domingo. The president expressed hope that the revolutions would cease and that the Dominican family would become united. Neither the government nor the people of the United States had tha least idea of annexation. They desired that San Domingo should remain a sovereign Independent power, and in this the republic would have the support of the United States government. Mr. Powell said his government would not consent to any portion of Domingo passing under the control of any foreign power. The future of the republic rested largely On the keeping of all obligations toward foreign creditors, on respecting the concessions the government made to foreigners, on developing the country's resources and on passage of such laws as would bring prosperity. These considerations and the taking of the whole people into the confidence of the government would be the greatest guard against revolution and anarchy. The minister assured the president that the American people would be at his side If he remained steadfast to the principles of a good republic. Mr. Powell will leave tomorrow. records.summary_en: The *Barre Daily Times* reported that United States Minister Powell delivered a farewell address reaffirming the Monroe Doctrine and denying any American intention to annex the Dominican Republic. Powell warned that the nation's future sovereignty depended upon fulfilling financial obligations to foreign creditors and maintaining domestic peace. The dispatch noted the appointment of Thomas C. Dawson of Iowa to succeed Powell, while the warship *Independencia* moved troops to confront insurgents at Monte Cristi.
records.summary_es: El *Barre Daily Times* informó que el ministro de los Estados Unidos, Powell, pronunció un discurso de despedida en el que reafirmó la Doctrina Monroe y negó cualquier intención estadounidense de anexionar la República Dominicana. Powell advirtió que la futura soberanía de la nación dependía del cumplimiento de las obligaciones financieras con los acreedores extranjeros y del mantenimiento de la paz interna. El despacho señaló el nombramiento de Thomas C. Dawson, de Iowa, para suceder a Powell, mientras el buque de guerra *Independencia* trasladaba tropas para enfrentar a los insurgentes en Monte Cristi.

records.full_text:
U. S. RECEIVERSHIP FOR SANTO DOMINGO

The Novel Scheme Which Roosevelt Will Probably Put Into Effect—Island Would Have Been Annexed to This Country in 1869 But for the Opposition of Chas. Sumner.

By Jacob Waldeck.
WASHINGTON, Jan. 10.—Santo Domingo, torn by revolution, misgoverned and despoiled, is soon to feel the chastening influence of "the big stick." A century of turmoil, bloodshed, robbery and disorder is to be terminated by the intervention of the United States.

Officials of the highest rank in the administration say that such action is inevitable. President Roosevelt is said, on the best authority, to hold that view of the case. It is a question of time, but of months, rather than years. American officials and American marines will inaugurate a reign of good order and a season of debt-paying in the country.

They don't call it that in diplomatic language, but the proposed order of things in Santo Domingo seems to be nothing more or less than a receivership. It will be

Something Brand New
in American history. The republic will bear a relation to this country unlike Porto Rico, which was annexed; unlike the Philippines, which were hitched on behind, and unlike Cuba, which is the object of a benevolent guardianship. Santo Domingo is to be regulated. It is to be told to pay its debts and be good.

The plan is to place men in the custom houses to collect the revenue of the country. They are to see that a fair share of this money goes to the creditors, and that public officials, instead of looting the public treasury, conduct the government on an economical basis. One custom house, that of Puerto Plata, is now in the hands of an American as a result of arbitration, last summer, over a claim of $5,000,000 owned by New Yorkers. They advanced a lot of money about 10 years ago and took a blanket mortgage on the government. The proceeds at Puerto Plata are being devoted to their claim.

Opinion as to the new deal is divided among the people. Creditors, business men and most of the people of the cities favor it. Those living in the interior are, as a rule, opposed to foreign interference. So are the insurgent chiefs, who fear that a settled order of things may interfere with the revolution industry and keep them from digging their hands into the treasury.

A Land of Chaos.
In the past the order of things has been very much unsettled. The country has been in a chronic state of revolution. There have been nearly a dozen presidents in five years.

From the standpoint of novelty it would seem that the people ought to welcome a receivership. The country has had autocratic, monarchial and republican forms of government. It has also had no government; there having been prolonged seasons of anarchy. Te people have been ruled by despots, emperors and presidents. Mostly despots, though, for whatever the title of the man who happened to be ruling for a short period, he has usually paid no attention to law. Men whom he hasn't liked he has caused to be shot. Any money lying around that he fancied he has appropriated. If money was scarce he negotiated loans at extravagant rates from foreigners. The lenders got Chadwick rates in the way of interest and bonuses, and could rest serene in the fact that when the day for settlement came their governments would force San Domingo to pay.

Another class of men who may embarrass the administration, when intervention takes place, are now flocking to Santo Domingo. They are "investors." A lot of them, Americans, are going over to the republic from Porto Rico. They

Scent Rich Profits
and are eager to be early on the ground. Tehir option is to pick up property at anarchy rates and sell at prices incident to American rule. Santo Domingo, in its climate and resources, has been described by all travelers who have visited the country as one of the most attractive and richest spots in the world. It has not been developed because for 100 years there has been little or no respect for personal or property rights. As a result of this condition it has been possible for years to buy the best of sugar land and land covered with magnificent forests at a nominal price. A good many Americans have taken advantage of the opportunity. They have made no attempt to develop their holdings, but have patiently awaited the day when order should be restored in the country. Others are now crowding in to get the benefit of the bargains offered. They are confident that this country will, in some form, soon enforce order, and they are equally confident that when the United States finally withdraws it will exact guarantees for the protection of their interests.

Came Close to Annexation.
The question of adding the territory of the republic to the United States has been raised at intervals for half a century. It confronted Lincoln in the closing days of the civil war, but he was busy with bigger problems, and consigned it to a pigeonhole. Grant took it up in 1869. Men contended in those days that Santo Domingo would be a more valuable acquisition than Cuba, Haiti or Porto Rico. The fine climate, valuable forests, rich soil, sparse population and small public debt were all said to be in its favor. At that time the debt to be assumed by this country would have been only $1,500,000. Now it would be $32,000,000, secured by Dominican bonds, while Spain would put in a claim for other millions that, the dons say, they were to receive if the republic should ever, by consent of its people, become annexed to another country.

De B. Randolph Keim, a Pennsylvania editor who is also an official of the bureau of insular affairs, brought the first proposition of annexation to this country. He went to the island in 1869 as the correspondent of a New York newspaper.

President Buenaventura Baez feared that he was going to be displaced by revolutionists. His predecessor had

In a Similar Predicament
given the country to Spain. The latter held it from 1861 to 1865. Baez thought it would be a good scheme to deliver the republic to the United States. He feared to trust a communication on the subject to the mails. Keim was therefore induced to carry the offer to President Grant. The latter received it with the utmost favor. A commission sent by him to the island spent 40 days in investigation and returned with a favorable report. The Dominicans at an election voted in favor of annexation. A treaty was signed Nov. 29, 1869. Grant submitted it to the senate with a favorable recommendation. It was bitterly opposed by Chas. Sumner, chairman of the committee on foreign relations. He denounced Baez as an adventurer and declared that he was held in power by the United States navy. Sumner defeated the treaty. Soon thereafter he was deposed from the chairmanship of the foreign relations committee and otherwise humiliated by his republican colleagues. In 1872, Samana bay, one of the finest harbors on this side of the world, was ceded to a company formed in the United States, but the cession was cancelled in the following year because of the non-payment of rent. When President Heureaux, in 1893, delivered the custom houses to an American company as security for a loan, there was a great outcry soon there was only one president. There was not and has not been, however, much that resembled a civilized governmetn. Now that the cruiser Detroit, Captain Bernard G. Scott, is on guard. It is believed that only the presence of that vessel has prevented the hatching of new revolutions. While there has been quiet, however, there has been no disposition or an inability to pay the debt held by Americans or Europeans. Conditions are intolerable. Unless among Dominicans that it would lead to annexation. In 1891 President Harrison proclaimed a reciprocity treaty with the republie.

The Detroit on Guard.
The navy department has long been keeping a sharp watch on Santo Domingo. About a year ago, when two men were claiming the presidency and two or three revolutions were going on, a naval squadron was sent down there to restore order. Capt. Richard Wainwright brought up the disturbers with a sharp turn and the United States interferes, some foreign power will probably assert its rights. So the United States will step in as the policeman of the occacation.

records.summary_en: The *Springfield Weekly Republican* argued that foreign capitalists and commercial planters in the Dominican Republic actively encouraged political unrest to terminate indigenous rule. It cited State Department admissions that American firms had supplied money and weapons to opposing Dominican factions while simultaneously petitioning Washington for naval protection. The editorial noted that President Morales, having secured power through United States naval support, signed the customs receivership agreement to align with foreign property interests.
records.summary_es: El *Springfield Weekly Republican* sostuvo que los capitalistas y hacendados comerciales extranjeros en la República Dominicana fomentaban activamente la inestabilidad política para poner fin al gobierno autóctono. Citó admisiones del Departamento de Estado respecto a que firmas estadounidenses habían suministrado dinero y armas a facciones dominicanas rivales mientras pedían simultáneamente protección naval a Washington. El editorial señaló que el presidente Morales, habiendo asegurado el poder mediante el apoyo naval estadounidense, firmó el acuerdo de administración aduanera para alinearse con los intereses de los propietarios extranjeros.

The Dominican planters and all the foreign capitalists concerned in the republic have had a strong economic object in bringing the native rule to a close. records.summary_en: The *San Francisco Call* reported that the Navy Department dispatched 200 marines aboard the *Dixie* to Guantanamo in preparation for possible unrest over the American administration of Dominican customs. records.summary_en: The *Springfield Weekly Republican* detailed the finalized protocol providing for American administration of Dominican customs until foreign creditor claims were settled. The modified convention affirmed the Monroe Doctrine, guaranteed Dominican territorial integrity, and allotted 45 percent of gross customs revenues directly to the Dominican government for its operating budget. The agreement stipulated that future tariff modifications required approval from the President of the United States and prohibited increases in the national public debt.
records.summary_es: El *Springfield Weekly Republican* detalló el protocolo definitivo que establecía la administración estadounidense de las aduanas dominicanas hasta que se saldaran las reclamaciones de los acreedores extranjeros. La convención modificada reafirmaba la Doctrina Monroe, garantizaba la integridad territorial dominicana y asignaba el 45 por ciento de los ingresos aduaneros brutos directamente al gobierno dominicano para su presupuesto operativo. El acuerdo estipulaba que las futuras modificaciones arancelarias requerían la aprobación del presidente de los Estados Unidos y prohibía cualquier incremento de la deuda pública nacional.

The first section is but slightly altered, while the second section is greatly modified, the American government agreeing completely to respect the territorial integrity of San Domingo. The convention or protocol specifically affirms the Monroe doctrine. The customs officials are to be subject to the civil and penal jurisdiction of the Dominican republic without being considered subjects of that government. There is to be paid to the Dominican government 45 per cent of the total gross amount collected in all the custom-houses of the republic, that proportion of the revenues being for the necessities of the administrative budget. The estimate in the protocol of January 20 that this 45 per cent shall be $900,000 for the first year is eliminated, as is. also the agreement “that the extraordinary expenses which may be occasioned in the collection of. the. customs duties shall be made for the account of the creditors of the republic (of Santo Domingo) without assigning to the latter any part thereof.” Any reform of the Dominican tariff is to be subject to approval by the president of the'United States. There shall be no increase of export-duties or of the public debt of Santo Domingo, but export duties may be reduced or abolished by the authority of the American government, on the request of the Dominican government. records.summary_en: This editorial examines the legal basis claimed for American customs operations in Santo Domingo, centered on the arbitration award of July 14, 1904, which authorized the United States Financial Agent to extend his control to Monte Cristi, Sanchez and Samana if the collections at Puerto Plata proved insufficient to meet the monthly installment of $37,500 payable under the award. It reports that Judge Abbott, the Financial Agent, unexpectedly returned to New York saying it had not been necessary to go beyond Puerto Plata for the revenue needed, while Admiral Sigsbee was negotiating with the people of Monte Cristi for their independent adoption of the protocol.

records.summary_en: An Associated Press report from Washington, dated March 17, says Senator Morgan used practically the entire executive-session discussion of the Santo Domingo treaty to charge that William Nelson Cromwell of New York was the prime mover in a scheme to influence the United States in the financial affairs of the Dominican government. Morgan said Cromwell acted to frustrate the Reader syndicate's plan for Dominican concessions and to promote a syndicate holding a mass of claims against Latin-American republics, including a large part of the Dominican debt; the Senate was divided over whether he made his case, and the treaty was expected to be recommitted without a vote.

records.summary_en: The *Springfield Weekly Republican* reported statements from President Morales warning that the Dominican government was powerless to resist European debt enforcement unless the United States intervened to delay creditor demands. Following the United States Senate's failure to ratify the customs treaty, fears spread in Santo Domingo that European nations would seize ports to satisfy unpaid claims. The report noted that while multiple American warships patrolled the coast, local observers argued that European seizures would effectively undermine the Monroe Doctrine.

Tras la falta de ratificación del tratado aduanero por el Senado de los Estados Unidos, se extendió en Santo Domingo el temor de que las naciones europeas incautaran puertos para saldar las reclamaciones pendientes. El informe señalaba que, mientras varios buques de guerra estadounidenses patrullaban la costa, observadores locales sostenían que las incautaciones europeas socavarían de hecho la Doctrina Monroe.

records.summary_en: The *Evening Times-Republican* published President Roosevelt's directive instructing Minister Dawson to implement an interim modus vivendi for collecting Dominican customs revenues while the treaty awaited Senate approval. Under the executive plan, the Secretary of War would nominate port collectors, with unexpended revenues deposited in New York banks pending final legislative action. Concurrently, American warships monitored political movements in Monte Cristi, including the departure of General Barba from Puerto Rico, to prevent revolutionary disruption.
records.summary_es: El *Evening Times-Republican* publicó la directiva del presidente Roosevelt en la que instruía al ministro Dawson a implementar un modus vivendi provisional para recaudar los ingresos aduaneros dominicanos mientras el tratado esperaba la aprobación del Senado. Según el plan ejecutivo, el secretario de Guerra designaría a los recaudadores de los puertos, y los ingresos no devengados se depositarían en bancos de Nueva York a la espera de la resolución legislativa definitiva. Al mismo tiempo, buques de guerra estadounidenses vigilaban los movimientos políticos en Monte Cristi, incluida la salida del general Barba desde Puerto Rico, para evitar disturbios revolucionarios.

The same report sets out the State Department's plan for Santo Domingo's finances, under which American commissioners would collect the customs, with forty-five per cent of the receipts going to the Dominican government and fifty-five per cent deposited in New York for the foreign creditors, pending the Senate's action on the treaty.

records.summary_en: The *Springfield Weekly Republican* reported that the implementation of the Dominican customs receivership awaited President Morales concluding agreements with European creditor nations. The Secretary of War prepared to nominate customs collectors, with President Roosevelt recommending William E. Gould of Baltimore, a linguist and financial editor, for a collectorship. It was also anticipated that George R. Colton, formerly an American revenue collector in the Philippines, would be appointed to assist in administering the Dominican customs service.

records.headline: A travel narrative follows the old Camino Real, the royal road running 150 miles north from Santo Domingo City to Cotui
records.summary_en: A travel narrative follows the old Camino Real, the royal road running 150 miles north from Santo Domingo City to Cotui, La Vega and Moca, describing the ancient Spanish roads as broad paths cut a hundred feet wide through the forest, with no ditching, drainage, macadam or bridges, and the Isabella River crossed in native dugout canoes while the horses swim. It describes the savanna country of red clay loam and an inland town, Savanna Grande, as a row of one-story palm-wood huts thatched with palm leaves around a green central square, and the travelers' night stop at the home of Don Emiliano Tejera, a wealthy power in Dominican politics housed in thatched native houses with dirt floors.
records.summary_es: Una crónica de viaje sigue el viejo Camino Real, la vía real que corre 150 millas al norte desde la ciudad de Santo Domingo hasta Cotuí, La Vega y Moca, describiendo los antiguos caminos españoles como senderos anchos abiertos de cien pies a través del bosque, sin zanjas, drenaje, macadán ni puentes, y el río Isabela cruzado en canoas nativas de un solo tronco mientras los caballos nadan. Describe la región de sabana de arcilla roja y un pueblo del interior, Sabana Grande, como una fila de chozas de un piso de madera de palma techadas con hojas de palma alrededor de una plaza central verde, y la parada nocturna de los viajeros en la casa de don Emiliano Tejera, un hombre rico y poderoso en la política dominicana alojado en casas nativas de techo de palma y piso de tierra.

records.headline: A feature calls Santo Domingo the garden of the western tropics, with soil for cocoa, tobacco, tropical fruits
records.summary_en: A feature calls Santo Domingo the garden of the western tropics, with soil for cocoa, tobacco, tropical fruits, sugar cane, coffee, vanilla and rubber, mahogany forests in its mountainous interior, and constant verdure, and says that freed from its financial incubus it need not lag behind its sister republics. It then traces the career of President Carlos F. Morales, born at Puerto Plata to a prosperous merchant's family, ordained a priest after seminary study, who renounced the priesthood after eight years, edited an opposition newspaper, was arrested and narrowly escaped being shot, lived through revolt and exile, served in Congress and as governor of Puerto Plata, and last year headed the movement that drove out Jiminez and Wos y Gil and assumed control, proclaiming an election for next June.
records.summary_es: Un reportaje llama a Santo Domingo el jardín de los trópicos occidentales, con suelo para cacao, tabaco, frutas tropicales, caña de azúcar, café, vainilla y caucho, bosques de caoba en su interior montañoso y verdor constante, y dice que libre de su peso financiero no tiene por qué quedarse atrás de sus repúblicas hermanas. Después recorre la carrera del presidente Carlos F. Morales, nacido en Puerto Plata en la familia de un comerciante próspero, ordenado sacerdote tras estudiar en un seminario, quien renunció al sacerdocio después de ocho años, editó un periódico de oposición, fue arrestado y escapó por poco de ser fusilado, vivió entre revueltas y exilios, sirvió en el Congreso y como gobernador de Puerto Plata, y el año pasado encabezó el movimiento que expulsó a Jiminez y a Wos y Gil y asumió el control, proclamando una elección para el próximo junio.

records.summary_en: A Washington dispatch reports that, to thwart a revolutionary movement at Macoris against President Morales of Santo Domingo, the State Department has asked the Navy Department to send a warship to that port, and instructions were telegraphed to Rear Admiral Bradford at Guantanamo. It describes Bradford as the American policeman delegated to see that Morales's rule is not disturbed while the Senate acts on the proposed protectorate, and says the department believes the disturbance is fomented by New York interests opposed to the Dominican treaty.

Describe a Bradford como el policía estadounidense delegado para velar por que el gobierno de Morales no sea perturbado mientras el Senado decide sobre el protectorado propuesto, y dice que el departamento cree que la alteración es fomentada por intereses de Nueva York opuestos al tratado dominicano.

records.summary_en: The *Birmingham Age-Herald* criticized President Roosevelt for enforcing the unratified Dominican customs treaty through executive action, using warships to protect Customs Receiver George R. Colton. The editorial argued that neither Roosevelt nor President Morales held constitutional authority to bind their nations without legislative approval, and warned the policy risked committing the United States to guaranteeing debts throughout Spanish America. The article predicted that Senate Democrats would firmly oppose ratification, noting rumors that the administration might seek a congressional joint resolution to validate the receivership.
records.summary_es: El *Birmingham Age-Herald* criticó al presidente Roosevelt por aplicar el tratado aduanero dominicano no ratificado mediante una acción ejecutiva, empleando buques de guerra para proteger al receptor de aduanas George R. Colton. El editorial sostenía que ni Roosevelt ni el presidente Morales tenían autoridad constitucional para comprometer a sus naciones sin aprobación legislativa, y advertía del riesgo de que esta política comprometiera a los Estados Unidos a garantizar deudas en toda Hispanoamérica. El artículo vaticinaba que los demócratas en el Senado se opondrían con firmeza a la ratificación, señalando rumores de que el gobierno intentaría obtener una resolución conjunta del Congreso para validar la administración aduanera.

records.summary_en: The *Free Lance* reported on the repressive governance of Dominican President Morales, stating he had executed approximately 200 political opponents and maintained a coded blacklist of prominent citizens. Meanwhile, the State Department in Washington announced a policy of non-intervention in internal Dominican strife, regarding the conflict as domestic as long as foreign interests remained safe. Officials cautioned, however, that the United States would intervene militarily if violence threatened American lives or interfered with customs collections.
records.summary_es: El *Free Lance* informó sobre la gobernanza represiva del presidente dominicano Morales, afirmando que había ejecutado a cerca de 200 opositores políticos y mantenía una lista negra cifrada de ciudadanos prominentes. Entretanto, el Departamento de Estado en Washington anunció una política de no intervención en las disputas internas dominicanas, considerando el conflicto como doméstico mientras los intereses extranjeros estuvieran a salvo. No obstante, los funcionarios advirtieron que los Estados Unidos intervendrían militarmente si la violencia amenazaba vidas estadounidenses o interfería con la recaudación de aduanas.

An American observer arriving from Monte Cristi, Hugh M. TALE ON SANTO DOMINGO. “Morales Represents Best Element on Island,” Says Observer. Hugh M. Creighton arrived on the steamer [Seminole?], from Monte Cristi, Santo Domingo. Mr. Creighton said:

I was in Santo Domingo three weeks, and was in constant contact with all classes of Dominicans. I became convinced that, unless the government at Washington asserts itself promptly, and with a firm hand sustains President Morales, who is still the constitutional head of the government, the prestige of the United States, with the best element on the island, which is being dissipated by delay, will entirely disappear. The present trouble, as I learned from business men, grows out of the inability of President Morales to respond to the demands made on him by the faction headed by Vice-President Caceres for money. The 4 per cent that is derived from the customs collections, under the supervision of the United States agent, is sufficient for all the legitimate needs of the government, but it affords no margin out of which to pay levies that may be made by political ‘‘grafters.”

records.summary_en: The *Springfield Weekly Republican* reported that former President Juan Isidro Jimenes traveled to Monte Cristi to seek the presidency with the backing of fugitive President Morales and broad northern support. The paper profiled insurgent leader General Demetrio Rodríguez, an American-educated commander who had previously controlled customs revenues in Monte Cristi before being defeated by General Céspedes. It noted that Céspedes, originally a key supporter of Morales, had turned against the president in fierce opposition to the fiscal convention with the United States.

El periódico reseñó al líder insurgente, general Demetrio Rodríguez, un militar educado en los Estados Unidos que anteriormente había controlado los ingresos de aduanas en Monte Cristi antes de ser derrotado por el general Céspedes. Señaló además que Céspedes, quien en un principio fue un firme partidario de Morales, se volvió contra el mandatario en feroz oposición a la convención fiscal con los Estados Unidos.

Gen Jiminez, the former president of San Domingo, has left Puerto Plata for Monte Cristi, and, it is understood, will, with the assistance of Morales, compete for the presidency of the republic against the other candidates for that office. According to the reports brought to Cape Haytien by messengers, a large part of the population of northern San Domingo is in Favor of Gen Jiminez. Gen Demetrio Rodriguez had long been a prominent factor in the affairs of San Domingo. He was a graduate of Fordham college. New York, spoke English fluently, and was described as an affable and scholarly man and a born leader of men. He resided about 25 miles from Monte Christi; and was considered to be one of the most formidable of Morales's opponents. At the close of the last revolution Rodriguez only consented to lay down his arms under the promise of being allowed to collect the customs and other revenues in the province of Monte Christi. Gen Cespedes, who defeated Gen Rodriguez, was one of the leading men in the movement which placed Morales in the presidential chair of San Domingo, but Cespedes quarreled with Morales on account of the latter's transactions with the American government, and when the enemies of Morales became active Cespedes hastened to join issue with them in their opposition to the Morales government and the fiscal agreement between the United States and San Domingo.

Morales, who affirmed that national salvation depended on the ratification of the pending customs convention by both nations. Morales noted that while provisional President Cáceres and various rebel factions had come to endorse the convention, political stability remained precarious under Cáceres's minority government. records.summary_en: The *Springfield Weekly Republican* reported that a peace treaty ending the Dominican insurrection was signed aboard the United States cruiser *Yankee* at Monte Cristi. Foreign Minister Emiliano Tejera stated that the rapid restoration of peace was made possible by decisive military action and the American financial *modus vivendi*, which deprived the insurgents of customs revenues. Under the capitulation terms, Monte Cristi returned to government control, rebel General Desiderio Arias was permitted to go into exile in Puerto Rico, and remaining insurgents were granted amnesty.
records.summary_es: El *Springfield Weekly Republican* informó que se firmó a bordo del crucero estadounidense *Yankee*, en Monte Cristi, un tratado de paz que puso fin a la insurrección dominicana. El ministro de Relaciones Exteriores Emiliano Tejera declaró que el rápido restablecimiento de la paz fue posible gracias a la enérgica acción militar y al *modus vivendi* financiero estadounidense, que privó a los insurgentes de las rentas aduaneras. Bajo los términos de la capitulación, Monte Cristi volvió al control del gobierno, se le permitió al general rebelde Desiderio Arias exiliarse en Puerto Rico y se concedió amnistía a los insurgentes restantes.

Monte Cristi is now in the hands of the constitutional government forces. When Heureaux learned of the practice he decreed that whoever indulged in the sport should be shot. It is interesting to note that when Ricardo Limardo announced his resignation as Governor of Puerto Plata last week the two persons who had been very prominent in the revolution deemed it wise to expatriate themselves, on the theory that the pledges of immunity which Limardo would not violate might not hold good under a successor. Governor Limardo's resignation illustrates the danger of a partisan administration. He has been a consistent Horacist, believing that to be the party representing honesty in politics. After taking office he found that the principal positions under him were to be filled at the dictation of a military officer and in his judgment the men named were notoriously unfit for the duties assigned to them. As his protests were ignored he decided to resign. Few men have more personal friends than he and the administration can hardly afford to lose many such supporters. New President of Brazil. records.headline: 'Rebels killed in Santo Domingo': Nené Cepín, one-armed revolutionary general, and six followers were killed at Guayubín
records.summary_en: 'Rebels killed in Santo Domingo': Nené Cepín, one-armed revolutionary general, and six followers were killed at Guayubín, where he had gone to confer with Governor Camacho of Monte Cristi after taking the field in the Dajabón smuggling district.
records.summary_es: «Rebeldes muertos en Santo Domingo»: Nené Cepín, general revolucionario manco, y seis seguidores fueron muertos en Guayubín, adonde había ido a conferenciar con el gobernador Camacho de Monte Cristi tras alzarse en la zona de contrabando de Dajabón.
records.passage: Cepin was one of the most noted revolutionists in the island. He took sides with Morales in the last outbreak. After the latter's defeat he received guaranty of safety, but with Navarro, took the field in the Monte Christi district with a small party, presumably to assist smugglers at Dajabon, on the Haitian frontier. No duties ever had been paid at Dajabon, tho large quantities of merchandise are received by the customs officers. Cepin visited the town and declared all goods there contraband. While Cepin and his party were fighting many goods were removed inland. After negotiations lasting some days Cepin and Navarro agreed to lay down arms. Cepin was promised the office of military commandant at Dajabon. He went to Guanyubin on a friendly visit to arrange terms. 24th Annual Reduced-Price Sale. The Great Plymouth Clothing House. MILLIONAIRE'S SON TO BECOME A CLERK. Journal Special Service. Chicago, March 10. — Stuyvesant Fish, president of the Illinois Central railroad, and his son, Stuyvesant Fish, Jr., are in Chicago. The son has announced his intention of taking a clerkship in the Illinois Central offices at $60 a month. He purposes to learn the railroad business from the ground up. Young Mr. Fish arrived from New York with his father in a palatial private car. He put up in one of the finest suites on the parlor floor of the Annex and took breakfast yesterday at the Chicago club. This is not the usual program of a working man.

records.headline: Herald correspondence from Santo Domingo, dated March 3, reports that General Ramon Caceres will not resign the presidency
records.summary_en: Herald correspondence from Santo Domingo, dated March 3, reports that General Ramon Caceres will not resign the presidency, because a change of administration would involve internal disturbances, and that the demand for him to remain was almost universal. His cousin Horacio Valdez, head of the Horacist party and the man in whose favor Caceres wished to withdraw, was the first to urge him to reconsider, and after petitions and a mass meeting in Columbus plaza a crowd marched to Caceres's house, where he told them he would postpone his resignation until the danger to the republic ceased, later issuing a public address accepting what he called the new sacrifice.
records.summary_es: Una correspondencia del Herald desde Santo Domingo, fechada el 3 de marzo, informa que el general Ramón Cáceres no renunciará a la presidencia, porque un cambio de administración implicaría disturbios internos, y que la demanda de que permaneciera fue casi universal. Su primo Horacio Valdez, jefe del partido horacista y la persona en cuyo favor Cáceres deseaba retirarse, fue el primero en instarlo a reconsiderarlo, y tras las peticiones y una reunión masiva en la plaza Colón una multitud marchó a la casa de Cáceres, donde les dijo que pospondría su renuncia hasta que cesara el peligro para la república, y después emitió un mensaje público aceptando lo que llamó el nuevo sacrificio.

[Special Correspondence of the Herald.] San Juan, P. R., March 21. — In speaking of the present political situation in Santo Domingo, a former high official of Santo Domingo, now residing in San Juan, who is close to former President Morales, makes the following statement: "Judging from the attitude of Congress, there seems to be every possibility that the Santo Domingo convention will not be approved by the United States government, at least not this year. records.summary_en: The Evening Times published a statement from Dominican revolutionists detailing their aims to reform land taxes, modify tariffs, eliminate export duties, and establish habeas corpus protections. The statement asserted that Generals Morales and Jimenez had reached an understanding, while former President Horacio Vasquez had deserted President Caceres. It also alleged that Dominican Minister of Finance Federico Velasquez was seeking to secure half of the $1,300,000 deposited for foreign creditors to fund government war expenses.
records.summary_es: The Evening Times publicó una declaración de revolucionarios dominicanos en la que detallaban sus objetivos de reformar los impuestos sobre la tierra, modificar los aranceles, suprimir los derechos de exportación y establecer garantías de habeas corpus. El manifiesto aseguraba que los generales Morales y Jimenes habían alcanzado un entendimiento, mientras que el expresidente Horacio Vásquez había abandonado al presidente Cáceres. Alegaba además que el ministro de Hacienda dominicano Federico Velásquez procuraba asegurarse la mitad de los 1.300.000 dólares depositados para los acreedores extranjeros con el propósito de costear los gastos bélicos del gobierno.

It is our purpose, if we are victorious, as I am certain we shall be, to establish land taxes, modify the tariff and remove the pernicious export duties, which retard the progress of our industries. We also want the right of habeas corpus, which is unknown in our country. As matters are, the government puts in Jail and exiles citizens without any process of law. The revolution was started without the consent or advice of General Jimenez. General Morales and General Jimenez have come to an understanding. The government has suspended payment of the army and civil employes and seeks to pay preferred creditors, which cannot be done according to the modus vivendi. Of course we recognize the Santo Domingo treaty, and we are anxious for an even better one. It is probably not generally known in this country, but I know that Federico Velasquez, minister of finance, who is now in this city, has come here to get, if possible, half of the $1,300,000 on deposit for the payment of Santo Domingo's foreign creditors, that the money might be used for the expenses of the war. If the United States could guarantee us free elections the revolution would end, but as we are without help we were compelled to protest with arms. records.headline: Exiles arriving at San Juan from Santo Domingo, a couple of them wounded in encounters with government troops, said
records.summary_en: Exiles arriving at San Juan from Santo Domingo, a couple of them wounded in encounters with government troops, said the revolution was in full blast along the northwest line and that towns including Barahona, Azua, Puerto Plata and Monte Cristi were constantly harassed by insurgent bands. A letter from the country printed with the report says public opinion wants ex-President Morales to lead the movement, hopes Morales and Jimenez will unite to retake the government, and reports that Minister of Finances Velasquez had set out hastily for Washington to seek support for his tottering government.

Una carta del país publicada con el informe dice que la opinión pública quiere que el expresidente Morales encabece el movimiento, espera que Morales y Jiménez se unan para retomar el gobierno, e informa que el ministro de Hacienda Velásquez había salido a toda prisa hacia Washington en busca de apoyo para su tambaleante gobierno.

records.summary_en: The Evening Star reported that Dominican representative Mr. Joubert conferred in Washington with Dr. Hollander and other U.S. officials regarding the situation in Santo Domingo. Joubert dismissed reports of a major revolutionary uprising at Monte Cristi as rumors from enemies of President Caceres and denied claims that customs funds held by the United States would be divided before treaty ratification. Joubert and Dominican Finance Minister Velasquez planned to travel to New York, where Velasquez would study American institutions.
records.summary_es: The Evening Star informó que el representante dominicano, el señor Joubert, conferenció en Washington con el Dr. Hollander y otros funcionarios estadounidenses sobre la situación en Santo Domingo. Joubert desestimó los informes sobre un gran levantamiento revolucionario en Monte Cristi calificándolos de rumores de los enemigos del presidente Cáceres, y negó que los fondos de aduanas custodiados por los Estados Unidos fueran a dividirse antes de la ratificación del tratado. Joubert y el ministro de Hacienda dominicano Velásquez planeaban viajar a Nueva York, donde Velásquez estudiaría las instituciones estadounidenses.

Mr. Joubert is of the opinion that the reports of the revolutionary movement are based on Information supplied by enemies of President Caceres, and says he does not think It Is true that 500 revolutionists are opposing the government troops at Monte Christi. No change In the government Is anticipated by Mr. Joubert, who says the negotiations now pending for a settlement eventually of claims against the Dominican government do not contemplate any expenditure of the money the United States Is now holding for the little republic until after the ratification of the Dominican treaty. "Reports that an attempt Is being made to get a division of the funds derived from customs collections are without founda tion," said Mr. Joubert. "The negotiations now pending are for preliminary arrangements, which will make It possible to pay out the money without delay when the treaty shall be ratified. The adjudication of claims and other preliminary work might well be done immediately, and then the funds could be disbursed more speedily when proper authority is granted." Mr. Velasquez and Mr. Joubert will leave Washington Monday for New York, where Mr. Velasquez will continue his study of American institutions by visiting a number of schools and penal institutions. records.headline: This profile presents Ramon Caceres, the present dictator-president of the Dominican Republic, as a big man of fully
records.summary_en: This profile presents Ramon Caceres, the present dictator-president of the Dominican Republic, as a big man of fully six feet and over 250 pounds whose word is law but who rules with a laugh, even, the writer says, when he shot down his predecessor, Ulysses Heureaux, and who is known throughout the land simply as Mon. It relates that Caceres put Morales in the presidential chair because he did not want the job himself, kept him there against his will, and that Morales, feeling himself virtually a prisoner in his own capital, negotiated with the revolutionists and precipitated a revolution against his own government.
records.summary_es: Este perfil presenta a Ramón Cáceres, actual dictador-presidente de la República Dominicana, como un hombre grande, de seis pies cumplidos y más de 250 libras, cuya palabra es ley pero que gobierna con una risa, incluso, dice el autor, cuando mató a tiros a su predecesor, Ulises Heureaux, y a quien en todo el país se conoce simplemente como Mon. Cuenta que Cáceres puso a Morales en la silla presidencial porque él mismo no quería el puesto, lo mantuvo allí contra su voluntad, y que Morales, sintiéndose virtualmente prisionero en su propia capital, negoció con los revolucionarios y precipitó una revolución contra su propio gobierno.

RAMON CACERES is a big man, fully six feet in height, and weighs considerably over 250 pounds. His word is law, but he rules with a laugh, whether it be to order a man shot before breakfast or to take his accustomed cup of coffee after a hearty meal. It is always a laugh. When besieged in the citadel above Santiago City, he looked around at his twenty generals and laughed.

records.summary_en: The article reports a Dominican government proclamation for Monte Cristi province, countersigned by President Caceres, declaring that peace negotiations having failed, the government will end the war however violent and severe the means, placing the district under siege and threatening summary shooting even for women found carrying cartridges. Exiled revolutionist General Berroa, speaking in New York alongside ex-President Jiminez, called the decree simply despotic, said 700 to 1,000 well-armed revolutionists were in the field, and said the revolution would stop only when constitutional rights, political prisoners and the exiles were dealt with justly.
records.summary_es: El artículo informa de una proclama del gobierno dominicano para la provincia de Monte Cristi, refrendada por el presidente Cáceres, que declara que, habiendo fracasado las negociaciones de paz, el gobierno terminará la guerra por violentos y severos que sean los medios, pone el distrito en estado de sitio y amenaza con fusilamiento sumario incluso para las mujeres a las que se encuentren cartuchos. El general revolucionario exiliado Berroa, hablando en Nueva York junto al expresidente Jiménez, calificó el decreto de simplemente despótico, dijo que había entre 700 y 1,000 revolucionarios bien armados en campaña, y afirmó que la revolución solo cesaría cuando los derechos constitucionales, los presos políticos y los exiliados fueran tratados con justicia.

records.summary_en: The Courier-Journal reported that President Roosevelt transmitted a new treaty with the Dominican Republic to the U.S. Senate concerning the administration of Dominican revenues. Under the agreement, contingent on debt arrangements with creditors, the U.S. President would appoint a receiver general to collect Dominican customs funds. Senate leaders aimed for action before congressional adjournment, and while several Democratic senators signaled support, Senator Bacon of Georgia had not yet fully assented.

Los líderes del Senado procuraban actuar antes del receso del Congreso, y si bien varios senadores demócratas manifestaron su respaldo, el senador Bacon de Georgia aún no había dado su total consentimiento.
