records.full_text:
TREATY RATIFIED BY SAN DOMINGO

Departure in United States' Relations to Small Republics

CONTROLS CUSTOM HOUSE

United States Now Becomes Legally a Trustee In a Financial Sense.

Will Discourage Revolutions.

Santo Domingo, May 3.—The new treaty between the United States and Santo Domingo intended to replace the treaty which has been pending before the United States Senate for the last two years was ratified by the Dominican congress today.

The Dominican treaty marks a new departure from the relations of the United States to the smaller republics of the western hemisphere, for in the case of Santo Domingo the United States now becomes legally a trustee in a financial sense, and must go so far in the preservation of order and the accompanying discouragement of revolutions as is incident to the control of the custom house.

The treaty really had its birth in a revolution. While the American government was pressing for a settlement of the claims of its citizens against Santo Domingo in December, 1904, President Morales being beset by revolutionists in the hope of securing the moral support of the United States, entered into an agreement with Captain Dillingham of the American navy by which the Dominican custom houses were to be occupied by the Americans and the foreign indebtedness of the country discharged from the receipts. Rejected at Washington, this agreement gave place March 31, 1905, to a modus vivendi which has operated up to this time. This placed an American collector in charge and provided for the deposit in New York of 55 per cent of the customs receipts for the benefit of the Dominican creditors. The modus vivendi did not save Morales from political destruction, as he was deported by the revolutionists and his vice president, General Caceres, installed as president. But the modus vivendi did lead to the deposit in New York of $3,000,000 which will now be placed to the credit of the Dominican government. That government has had more available money since the modus vivendi was established than any other time in its history. The Dominican government also finds itself in possession of four coast guard cutters built in the United States.

The modus vivendi was formed after a treaty pending before the United States Senate when Secretary Root assumed office. He recast the document, and February 19, last, the treaty which has just been ratified was submitted to the Senate. The way had been paved by an agreement between Federico Velasquez, the Dominican minister of finance, and the creditors of the republic whereby the latter agreed to a 50 per cent reduction in their claims if these were settled in cash.

A New York banking house undertook to advance the money for this purpose, accepting $20,000,000 5 per cent fifty-year bonds, which will now be promptly issued. Thus all of the creditors of Santo Domingo will be embodied in this New York firm.

The new treaty provides in its first article for the appointment by the President of a receiver of customs to collect the Dominican revenues as long as the bonds are outstanding, a period estimated at twenty to forty years. This collector is to pay the expenses of receivership, the interest on the bonds and the annual sums required for a mortization of the bonds, and then turn the balance over to the Dominican government. On the first day of each month he is to pay $100,000 to the fixed agent of the loan. When the customs receipts exceed $3,000,000 annually, then one-half of the surplus shall be applied to the sinking fund.

records.summary_en: The Mena Weekly Star reported that the Dominican treaty originated during a 1904 revolution when President Morales agreed with U.S. Navy Captain Dillingham to allow American administration of custom houses to satisfy foreign debts. Secretary Root later recast the resulting treaty, facilitated by Finance Minister Federico Velasquez securing a 50 percent cash settlement agreement with creditors. A New York banking firm financed the settlement through $20,000,000 in 50-year five percent bonds, while the treaty authorized the U.S. President to appoint a customs receiver.

records.summary_en: The New-York Tribune reported on an interview with the former Dominican president, who described being detained in a palace during a visit to Port-au-Prince. He asserted that the era of Dominican revolutions had ended, praised President Caceres and the American customs receivership, but expressed firm opposition to annexation by the United States. He also stated his desire to return to Santo Domingo once a general amnesty was granted and recounted how political betrayal had forced his past flight.
records.summary_es: The New-York Tribune informó sobre una entrevista con el expresidente dominicano, quien describió haber sido retenido en un palacio durante una visita a Puerto Príncipe. Afirmó que la era de las revoluciones dominicanas había concluido, elogió al presidente Cáceres y a la receptoría de aduanas estadounidense, pero manifestó su firme oposición a una anexión por parte de los Estados Unidos. Declaró además su deseo de regresar a Santo Domingo tan pronto se concediera una amnistía general y relató cómo la traición política había forzado su huida en el pasado.

records.summary_en: The New-York Tribune reported Consul General Medina's statement announcing the surrender of Dominican insurgent General Candelario de la Rosa and the pacification of refractory districts. Medina asserted that American revenue administration had restored national credit, enabling debt payments and attracting American capital into central pine forestry and railroad construction. He maintained that the government was fully prepared to counter any revolutionary efforts from Dominican exiles in Puerto Rico.

Medina afirmó que la administración aduanera estadounidense había restaurado el crédito nacional, posibilitando el pago de deudas y atrayendo capital estadounidense hacia la explotación forestal de pinares centrales y la construcción de ferrocarriles. Sostuvo que el gobierno estaba plenamente preparado para contrarrestar cualquier tentativa revolucionaria proveniente de los exiliados dominicanos en Puerto Rico.

He says that the hopes of the revolutionists are vain: that the government is prepared to meet every contingency, and that he is keeping a sharp watch on the Dominican exiles residing in Porto Rico. In referring to the actual condition in Santo Domingo, Consul General Medina makes the following statement:

At no time has the Dominican Republic been in such a favorable condition as at present. The fact that honest, strong and intelligent men are at the head of public affairs has raised the credit of the country. American control of the revenues has been the means of insuring a steady income, thus enabling the government not only to attend to its own needs but also to pay off the heavy debt that weighed down the country. With the assurance of lasting peace, capital is flowing into the republic. records.headline: A Washington report describes a new plan to settle the Dominican Republic's debt after the original bond sale to a New York firm
records.summary_en: A Washington report describes a new plan to settle the Dominican Republic's debt after the original bond sale to a New York firm fell through because of the money market. Foreign creditors recognized in the original project would receive an immediate pro rata cash payment from the $3,500,000 accumulated in the National City Bank from 55 per cent of the republic's customs revenues over two years, with the bond sale postponed or bonds issued directly by the Dominican government for the remainder, in a settlement to be discussed with Senor Velasquez at the State Department.
records.summary_es: Un informe de Washington describe un nuevo plan para saldar la deuda de la República Dominicana después de que la venta original de bonos a una firma de Nueva York fracasara por la situación del mercado monetario. Los acreedores extranjeros reconocidos en el proyecto original recibirían un pago inmediato en efectivo, a prorrata, del fondo de $3,500,000 acumulado en el National City Bank procedente del 55 por ciento de las rentas aduaneras de la república durante dos años, y la venta de bonos se pospondría o los bonos serían emitidos directamente por el gobierno dominicano por el resto, en un acuerdo que se discutiría con el señor Velásquez en el Departamento de Estado.
records.passage: public who were recognized in the original project and are willing to agree to accept the other features of the new scheme will receive an immediate cash payment of part of the money owing to them by a division on a pro rata basis of the fund of $3,500,000 which has accumulated in the National City Bank of New York as the result of the segregation of 55 per cent of the republic's customs revenues for the last two years. In consideration of this payment the sale of the bonds of the republic to some syndicate which will advance the cash to settle the remainder of the debt will be postponed until a more opportune time. A variation of this plan, which also will be considered by a conference to-morrow at the State Department between the officials and Senor Velasquez, the Dominican Secretary of Commerce and Finance, looks to the distribution of the accumulated cash as in the first case, but provides for the immediate issue to the creditors of bonds for the remainder of the obligation, which will be issued directly by the Dominican government. In either case it is contemplated that the Morton Trust Company and Speyer Co., who have acted as the fiscal agents for the Dominican government, will continue in that capacity and aid in carrying out the terms of the new agreement. records.summary_en: The New-York Tribune reported on a debt settlement plan proposed by Dominican Finance Minister Velasquez to distribute cash deposited in the National City Bank pro rata and issue $16,000,000 in forty-year 5 percent bonds to foreign creditors. With no New York banking syndicate willing to underwrite the liquidation directly, Velasquez hoped European and American claimants—including the Santo Domingo Improvement Company—would accept the arrangement. The report noted that the United States would continue collecting Dominican customs duties to service the bonds and maintain a sinking fund.
records.summary_es: The New-York Tribune informó sobre un plan de liquidación de deuda propuesto por el ministro de Hacienda dominicano Velásquez para prorratear los fondos en efectivo depositados en el National City Bank y emitir 16.000.000 de dólares en bonos a cuarenta años al 5 por ciento para los acreedores extranjeros. Al no hallarse ningún sindicato bancario neoyorquino dispuesto a suscribir la liquidación directamente, Velásquez esperaba que los acreedores europeos y estadounidenses —incluida la Santo Domingo Improvement Company— aceptaran el arreglo. El informe señaló que los Estados Unidos continuarían recaudando los derechos aduaneros dominicanos para atender el servicio de los bonos y mantener un fondo de amortización.
records.passage: [illegible] cash which Santo Domingo has to her credit in the National City Bank pro rata among the creditors of the republic and to pay off the remainder of the indebtedness, about $16,000,000, with the bonds of the republic at 98%; bearing 5 per cent interest, maturing in forty years, and practically guaranteed by the United States. No syndicate has been found in New York which cared to undertake the liquidating of the debt, but Señor Velasquez hopes that the creditors, in view of the cash payment he is prepared to offer and the gilt edge character of the securities, will accept his new proposition. The creditors include citizens of Belgium, France, Italy and the United States. The largest known American creditor is the Santo Domingo Improvement Company, with an adjudicated claim of $4,000,006. It is understood that a number of the foreign claims have been purchased by American bankers, and there is some suspicion that American interests have been at work to prevent the liquidation of this debt as originally planned, but it is hoped by the Dominican and American authorities that the new plan will be accepted by the creditors and that the entire liquidation may thus be accomplished. The United States, to all intents and purposes, will continue to collect the Dominican customs and supervise the payment of interest and the accumulation of a sinking fund to meet the maturity of the securities. records.summary_en: The New-York Tribune reported that the U.S. Secret Service arrested Giordani in New York, uncovering his role as the financial agent of a Haitian revolutionary movement under General Fermin. Giordani had previously contracted the printing of 1,500,000 "Deux Gourdes" banknotes, half of which had been stored in a New York warehouse after an earlier failed uprising. Federal authorities intervened to prevent the remaining currency from being shipped to finance active insurgent forces in Haiti.

Giordani había contratado previamente la impresión de 1.500.000 billetes de «Deux Gourdes», la mitad de los cuales se hallaban almacenados en un depósito neoyorquino tras un fracasado levantamiento anterior. But before the golden bills arrived in the southern republic the revolutionary movement had met with failure, and. according to information in the possession of the federal authorities, the consignment of revolutionary currency was burned upon its arrival. records.summary_en: The Alexandria Gazette reported on revolutionary turmoil in Haiti, where government officials sought refuge at the American consulate as fighting approached the Dominican border. The arrest of insurgent agent Giordani in New York thwarted an arms shipment linked to Dominican rebel leader General Jimenez, protecting recently negotiated creditor adjustments from disruption. The U.S. State Department took precautions while monitoring the border region, though it did not anticipate the unrest spreading further.

records.summary_en: The Topeka State Journal, quoting the Chicago Tribune, contrasted the revolutionary unrest marching toward Port-au-Prince in Haiti with the peace prevailing in Santo Domingo. The article attributed Dominican stability to the U.S. supervision of customs houses, which prevented ambitious politicians and exiles from seizing revenues to finance rebellions. It argued that without access to customs funds for a war chest, successful insurgencies in the Dominican Republic were no longer possible.

records.summary_en: The New-York Tribune reported on Major McIntyre's inspection of the Dominican customs receivership for the U.S. Bureau of Insular Affairs, noting steadily increasing revenues despite economic downturns. Under Receiver W. E. Pulliam, the receivership paid $100,000 monthly to the Morton Trust Company in New York while transferring the remainder to the Dominican government. McIntyre reported that nearly $5,000,000 had been deposited since 1905, with approximately $2,000,000 already distributed from the sinking fund to settle creditor claims.

Pulliam praised President Ramon Caceres upon his inauguration for a six-year constitutional term, describing him as a respected, military-trained leader from a prosperous agricultural region. records.summary_en: The Semi-Weekly Herald reviewed the outcome of the 1905 Dominican customs arrangement instituted by President Roosevelt to avert foreign military intervention over unpaid debts. Despite initial domestic controversy and Senate delays over Roosevelt's executive authority, the system transferred 45 percent of collections to the Dominican government and 55 percent to debt liquidation. The paper noted that the policy achieved a total transformation in the country, stabilizing public finances and virtually eliminating civil insurrections.

Pese a la controversia nacional inicial y las demoras en el Senado en torno a las atribuciones ejecutivas de Roosevelt, el sistema transfirió el 45 por ciento de la recaudación al gobierno dominicano y el 55 por ciento a la liquidación de la deuda. El periódico destacó que esta política logró una transformación total en el país, estabilizando las finanzas públicas y eliminando prácticamente las insurrecciones civiles.

Realizing that something would have to be done to avert the dangerous complications which were manifestly impending, Mr. Roosevelt instituted negotiations which resulted in the execution in February, 1905, of an agreement whereby officials appointed by the United States government were to collect the customs' receipts and after paying 45 per cent of the same to the Dominican authorities were to apply the remaining [illegible] per cent to the liquidation of the outstanding indebtedness. It will not have been forgotten how bitterly the president was criticised for his action in the premises. He was charged with having exceeded the bounds of his constitutional powers and for months the ratification of the Dominican treaty was delayed by the obstructive tactics of the hostile minority in the senate. Kingston, Jamaica, Nov. 5.—A revolutionary Santo Domingo junta has established headquarters here, and this morning a sloop belonging to it took out clearance papers for Hayti. Her destination, however, is believed to be some point on the Dominican coast. On board the sloop are some of the principal revolutionary leaders. Attempts are being made here to charter a steamer in order to make a descent on Santo Domingo with a President Designate and his staff. ESTRADA DEFEATED. Zelaya's Forces Reported Moving on Rama.

Managua, Nicaragua, Nov. 4 (Delayed in transmission).—Government troops defeated the revolutionists in a sharp engagement to-day, many of General Estrada's followers being killed, wounded or captured. The government lost fifteen men, including General Castillo [Chamorro?]. President Zelaya's forces attacked the rebel general, Fornos Diaz, at Paso las Lajas, capturing that point, which had been defended by four hundred men. The rebels fled in the direction of Rama and were pursued. records.summary_en: The Evening Star detailed extensive public works and infrastructure projects advancing in the Dominican Republic, including the purchase and expansion of the Puerto Plata-Santiago railroad and new branch lines. The Dominican government reduced port fees, dredged the Ozama River, surveyed irrigation systems in Monte Cristi and Azua, and initiated macadamized highway construction between the capital and San Cristobal. The report lauded the country's economic potential, civic improvements, and the hospitality of its citizens.

El gobierno dominicano redujo las tasas portuarias, dragó el río Ozama, realizó estudios para sistemas de irrigación en Monte Cristi y Azua, e inició la construcción de una carretera macadamizada entre la capital y San Cristóbal. El informe alabó el potencial económico del país, sus mejoras urbanas y la hospitalidad de sus habitantes.

records.summary_en: The Evening Star published excerpts from President Taft's message to Congress, reporting that the Dominican customs receivership was operating satisfactorily under the 1907 convention. Taft noted that despite lower customs revenues caused by economic conditions and anticipated tariff revisions, debt service payments were maintained and burdensome private concessions were retired. The message also reviewed U.S. diplomatic interventions regarding corporate claims in Nicaragua and Chile.
records.summary_es: The Evening Star publicó extractos del mensaje del presidente Taft al Congreso, informando que la receptoría de aduanas dominicana operaba satisfactoriamente en virtud de la convención de 1907. Taft destacó que, pese al descenso en los ingresos aduaneros provocado por la coyuntura económica y la expectativa de revisiones arancelarias, se mantuvieron los pagos del servicio de la deuda y se rescataron onerosas concesiones privadas. El mensaje examinó además las intervenciones diplomáticas estadounidenses relativas a reclamaciones corporativas en Nicaragua y Chile.
records.passage: receiver of customs appointed by the President of the United States in accordance with the convention of February [illegible] has proceeded in an uneventful and satisfactory manner. The customs receipts have decreased owing to disturbed political and economic conditions and to a very natural curtailment of imports, in view of the anticipated revision of the Dominican tariff schedule. The payments to the fiscal agency fund for the service of the bonded debt of the republic, as provided by the convention, have been regularly and promptly made, and satisfactory progress has been made in carrying out the provisions of the convention looking toward the completion of the adjustment of the debt and the acquirement by the Dominican government of certain concessions and monopolies which have been a burden to the commerce of the country. In short, the receivership has demonstrated its ability, even under unfavorable economic and political conditions, to do the work for which it was intended. This government was obliged to intervene diplomatically to bring about arbitration or settlement of the claim of the Emery Company against Nicaragua, which it had long before been agreed should be arbitrated. A settlement of this troublesome case was reached by the signature of a protocol on September [illegible], 1909. The Alsop Claim. records.full_text:
WIPING OUT A REPUBLIC'S DEBT

Honest Administration is Saving Santo Domingo. Honduras Asks for Help

NEW TARIFF LAWS HAVE HELPED COUNTRY

WASHINGTON, Aug. 11—The recent suggestion that this government assume a protectorate over Honduras and enter into a joint protectorate with Great Britian, France and Germany over Liberia, makes a review of this country's protectorate of Santo Domingo of timely interest. It will be recalled that the United States in March, 1905, entered into a treaty with the Dominican Republic to arrange its financial difficulties. The republic owed about $20,000,000, and its foreign creditors were pressing hard. Under a treaty, which the Senate reluctantly ratified, an American collector of customs was appointed for the republic, who received all customs receipts and divided them in the proportion of 45 per cent. for the republic and 55 per cent. for the creditors. Under the old Spanish law, which the Dominican republic never repealed, all expenses of the government are paid them for revenues derived from, imports and exports, property paying no taxes whatever.

In the five years that this government has assumed control of the Dominican custom-houses, the republic's debt has been reduced by $7,000,000 and the government, although receiving only 45 per cent. of the revenues has had more money to expend on administration and on public improvements than ever before when all the receipts went into the national treasury. The reason is not far to seek, for the American administration of the customs is honest. There have been naturally several abortive attempts at revolutions from hungry patriots whose souls shudder at the thought that the country's revenues are going into the country's treasury, but behind the American collector of customs, Mr. W. E. Pulliam, stands the American navy, and the net result of these revolutons has been only a decrease in the population of Santo Domingo, for those revolutionists who are not buried where they fall are safely tucked away in Dominican dungeons.

Result of New Tariff.
So well has Mr. Pulliam administered the revenues of the republic that a year ago last month he submitted a new tariff downward by about 15 per cent. Up to that time the Spanish principal of revenue taxation prevailed—namely, placing the heaviest possible duties on the necessities of life and permitting the luxuries to come in with the lightest possible duty. Mr. Pulliam introduced the American idea of letting the necessities of life come in free of duty, or nearly free, while the burden of taxation rested upon the luxuries. It was stipulated that an annual collection of $2,000,000 must be shown if the new tariff should remain in effect for more than a year. The tariff has now been adopted, and after a few months of a transition period, during which the business men of Santo Domingo adgusted themselves to new conditions, the receipts more than surpassed Mr. Pulliam's expectations. For the past three months the custom receipts have passed each month the quarter-million mark. At this rate the revenues for the current year will be at least $3,000,000, or one million more than the stipulated amount.

With this splended display of what American tariff and honesty will accomplish, it is small wonder that Honduras,, whose foreign creditors are pressing her hard for their money, and that Liberia, which faces dissolution as a republic, have appealed to this country for a similar protectorate. Although the State Department is strongly inclined to accede to both requests, it would be premature to say that the request will be granted. The Senate is bitterly opposed to any more such arrangements, although the example of Santo Domingo is encouraging. In the case of Liberia this country has only a sentimental interest, for Liberia owes its inception to American philanthropists.. It was the legislature of Maryland, whose generous appropriations nearly a century ago founded the Province of Maryland and peopled it with freed men from Maryland. The present republic if Liberia is a development of that settlement, but it is acknowledged on every hand that the republic is a failure. If this country enters into a joint protectorate with Great Britain, France and Germany, it will only mean a postponement of the fatal day.

No more Protectorates.
As for Honduras, a protectorate over that little republic would seem to be a logical corollary of the Monroe Doctrine, but the Senate, as already stated, is so bitterly opposed to any more of these treaties that Secretary Knox is at this moment unable to see his way clear to establishing a protectorate there. The Senate holds that if, following the example in Santo Domingo, this country takes up Honduras, it is only a question of time when an American receiver will be in charge of the customs of every petty republic in Central and South America, a condition not to be regarded with toleration.

Catrain, who is a prominent man in Santo Domingan politics and a famous leader, was admiral of the fleet during Morales's presidential term. records.summary_en: The Yorkville Enquirer commented on Dominican political instability and former President Morales's campaign to regain the presidency by force, arguing that the country needed a strong leader comparable to Mexico's Porfirio Diaz. The article questioned whether Morales could improve upon the incumbent administration or justify plunging the nation into civil war. It noted that if threatened, the Dominican government could invoke a treaty clause originally drafted by Morales himself to request American intervention to protect debt obligations.

El artículo cuestionaba si Morales podría mejorar la gestión del gobierno en funciones o justificar que se sumiera a la nación en una guerra civil. Señalaba que, de verse amenazado, el gobierno dominicano podría recurrir a una cláusula del tratado redactada en su momento por el propio Morales para solicitar la intervención estadounidense en salvaguarda de los compromisos de la deuda.

Santo Domingo undoubtedly needs a despotic ruler with a determination to make it progress, a man of the Porfirio Diaz type, who will do for it what Diaz has done for Mexico. Whether Morales is capable of doing this or not can not be surmised. His term of office was too short to permit an influence either in pro or in contra, but his passage was marked by undeniable progress. records.summary_en: The Topeka State Journal reported on President Taft's speech defending his foreign policy against critics of "Dollar Diplomacy," advocating pending treaties with Nicaragua and Honduras modeled on the Dominican arrangement. Taft emphasized that American customs collection in Santo Domingo had ensured debt repayments and fostered national reconstruction. He countered Senate objections that such treaties created entangling alliances for American banking interests rather than promoting regional stability.
records.summary_es: The Topeka State Journal informó sobre el discurso del presidente Taft en defensa de su política exterior frente a las críticas a la «diplomacia del dólar», promoviendo los tratados pendientes con Nicaragua y Honduras diseñados bajo el modelo del arreglo dominicano. Taft destacó que la recaudación aduanera estadounidense en Santo Domingo había asegurado la amortización de la deuda y favorecido la reconstrucción nacional. Replicó a las objeciones del Senado que sostenían que tales tratados forjaban alianzas comprometedoras para los intereses de la banca estadounidense en lugar de afianzar la estabilidad regional.

Broadly speaking President Taft said the proposed treaties with these countries before the senate would secure for them a financial agent in the United States who would settle their existing debts on a just basis and who would point the road to peace and prosperity to two republics, rich in natural resources but torn by strife and revolution. The president pointed out the efficacy of a similar arrangement with Santo Do mingo where this government collects the customs and sees that foreign debts are paid, exercises a benefit supervision that Mr. Taft said has accrued to the upbuilding of Santo Domingo. Objection to the treaties in the United States senate, the president said, was based largely upon the proposition that they would make entangling alliances with republics in this hemisphere for the promotion of a banking contract since the money for the payment of the debts of the two republics would be furnished by American interests. Put into effect on April 1, 1905, the agreement placed customs collection under American officials who distributed funds between the government and foreign creditors. The article observed that civil conflicts ceased almost immediately once revolutionists were unable to seize customs houses and revenues.

records.summary_en: The Salt Lake Tribune discussed political reactions following the assassination of Dominican President Ramon Caceres, noting his past role in killing dictator Ulises Heureaux in 1899. Officials recalled Caceres's rise through cabinet and vice-presidential posts to the presidency in 1905, expressing concern that rival politicians might seize on his death to provoke unrest. The War Department noted that the assassination disrupted an exceptional four-year period of peace in a nation previously plagued by annual revolutions.
records.summary_es: The Salt Lake Tribune analizó las reacciones políticas tras el magnicidio del presidente dominicano Ramón Cáceres, recordando su participación en la muerte del dictador Ulises Heureaux en 1899. Los funcionarios rememoraron el ascenso de Cáceres a través de carteras ministeriales y la vicepresidencia hasta alcanzar la presidencia en 1905, expresando inquietud de que políticos rivales aprovecharan su deceso para provocar alteraciones. El Departamento de Guerra advirtió que el magnicidio truncó un excepcional período de cuatro años de paz en una nación anteriormente asolada por revoluciones anuales.

records.summary_en: The Richmond Virginian reported that war appeared imminent between Haiti and the Dominican Republic amid revolutions in both countries, following the assassination of Haiti's President Leconte and rebel capture of the border town Dajabon. Santo Domingo prepared to declare war after hundreds of Haitians allegedly assisted Dominican insurgents, massing 4,000 troops along the border. records.full_text:
Mexico, Santo Domingo, Nicaragua.

It appears that the criticism of Senor Didapp, the representative of the Mexican revolutionists in Washington, and former Mexican Consul General to Spain, Turkey, and later at Norfolk, Va., is pretty well founded when, in his public utterances, he criticises Secretary Knox’s “dollar diplomacy,” which he maintains is making a mess of it in all Pan-American affairs, especially so in Mexico and Nicaragua.

As regards the former, Senor Didapp says that, unable to protect American lives and property by showing a firm attitude toward Madero, the department has been forced to the expedient of assisting the Mexican government by allowing Mexican troops to cross American territory in their attempt to get closer to the revolutionists. This, adds the senor, under the rules of international law, is equivalent to a declaration of war against the revolutionists on the part of the United States.

While The Herald believes that he is wrong in this contention, because the Mexican revolutionists are not yet recognized as belligerents by the Powers, yet it is a queer way of upholding the laws of neutrality. If this is considered fair on the part of the United States, then it would hardly be a greater violation of neutrality to throw a few brigades of United States regulars across the Rio Grande for the purpose of re-enforcing the Madero armies.

It would seem, therefore, that there is some ground for the contention of Senor Didapp that our government already has “intervened” when it allowed Mexican troops to cross American soil on their way to attack the revolutionists.

Secretary Knox, while away on a mission which an Assistant Secretary could well have fulfilled, leaves Pan-American affairs in a badly muddled condition, and the question may be permitted what good his recent trip to Central America has accomplished. His peace efforts have made a dismal failure of preserving the peace in Nicaragua.

The object of our proposed treaty with that country has been to authorize the executive branch of the United States government, with the consent of Congress, to intervene in Nicaragua, as it did in Santo Domingo in the alleged interest of the protection of American lives and property and the maintenance of public order. We know what that has meant to the Dominicans. Neither was property protected nor order maintained. The natives were overawed by the aid of the American forces. All debts of that republic, since the year one of its existence, were combined into bonds, and these exchanged for pieces of paper called Dominican-American “guaranteed national bonds.” These bonds have the interest guaranteed by the United States, but not the principal, by the collection of customs moneys.

If seriously looked into it will be found that Americans hold large blocks of the old debts of Nicaragua. The State Department had such an easy time in the Senate in the Dominican intervention deal that it also may have given assurances to Nicaraguan professional patriots with bundles of old scrip. But the Senate balked, because, were the United States to side with one faction against another, it would make it quite uncomfortable for American industrial expansionists.

It looks to The Herald that, when the smoke has cleared away, the United States will be found collecting Nicaraguan customs duties in the interest of American pioneers. This is known as “Dawsonizing the Monroe Doctrine,” for it avoids annexing the republics, while it obliterates them from the map as international factors of discord. Despite the fact that the Senate has refused to sanction the grabbing of a neighboring republic's custom-house, it would seem that those interested in the possibilities of spoil possess sufficient power to have the State Department spread United States marines over Nicaragua interior towns. This is apparently evidenced by the fact, quite palpable, that a battalion of American marines had been dispatched to Granada, which is not on the line of communication between Washington and Minister Weitzel, in order to rescue some girls alleged to be held in a French college.

What we should like to know is what these girls, this purely domestic affair, have to do with the Nicaraguan question?

The article credited the American receivership with securing revenues from aspiring revolutionists and providing seven years of uninterrupted domestic peace until disturbances resumed in 1912. Vick's mandate was to preserve the integrity and security of customs collections across all contending political factions.

records.summary_en: The Raymer Enterprise reviewed the history of the Dominican customs receivership, noting that removing customs revenues from political grasp had ended chronic revolutions and established domestic peace between 1905 and 1912. The article recalled that President Roosevelt intervened in 1905 to prevent European creditor nations from seizing Dominican customs to collect $20,000,000 in defaulted debts. Newly appointed Receiver Walter W. Vick was charged with maintaining strict administrative neutrality and safeguarding revenue security.
records.summary_es: The Raymer Enterprise repasó la trayectoria de la receptoría de aduanas dominicana, destacando que sustraer los caudales aduaneros de la codicia política había suprimido las revoluciones crónicas e instaurado la paz interna entre 1905 y 1912. El artículo recordó que el presidente Roosevelt intervino en 1905 para evitar que las potencias acreedoras europeas se apoderaran de las aduanas dominicanas para cobrar 20.000.000 de dólares en deudas morosas. El recién designado receptor Walter W. Vick tenía por misión preservar una rigurosa neutralidad administrativa y resguardar los fondos fiscales.
records.passage: supposed to lie in the American receivership is that the customs revenues are by it removed to neutral hands and are no longer to be preyed upon by aspiring revolutionists or grafting officials. From 1905, when the first temporary arrangement went into effect, until 1912 Santo Domingo had its first long period of freedom from revolution and internal strife. The neutralization of the customs receipts has been regarded as the cause of this peace in the turbulent republic. In 1912 there was continued political disturbance, but even during the revolution the custom houses remained unmolested by either faction in the struggle. It will be Mr. Vick's task to continue this absolute security of the customs receipts and maintain perfect neutrality toward all the contending political factions in the Island. European Intervention in Santo Domingo seemed a certainty when President Roosevelt intervened in behalf of the republic. The Dominican government was saddled with a foreign and domestic indebtedness amounting, with interest, to about [illegible]. Far from paying the interest, the Dominican government was increasing the debt by about a million dollars a year. As a result of centuries of misrule the revenues were being dishonestly dissipated. A succession of revolutions had reduced the government simply to a source of graft for which many factions were contending. records.headline: This article on administering Santo Domingo's finances under the American customs receivership reports that customs
records.summary_en: This article on administering Santo Domingo's finances under the American customs receivership reports that customs receipts, only about $2,000,000 a year before the receivership, reached $3,042,801 in 1912, the highest figure ever attained, with the first four months of 1913 indicating more than $4,000,000 for the year. It credits Receiver-General Pulliam, predecessor of Mr. Vick, with expelling dishonest collectors who had grafted by letting goods in without duty, notes that receipts rose even after export duties were cut by 50 per cent and import duties by 15 per cent, and says the receivership gave the Dominican government more money for its own purposes than it ever had before and built the first real roads in the republic outside the towns.

Atribuye al receptor general Pulliam, predecesor del señor Vick, la expulsión de recaudadores deshonestos que habían lucrado dejando entrar mercancías sin pagar derechos, señala que los ingresos aumentaron aun después de que los derechos de exportación se redujeron en un 50 por ciento y los de importación en un 15 por ciento, y dice que la receptoría dio al gobierno dominicano más dinero para sus propios fines que el que jamás había tenido antes y construyó los primeros caminos verdaderos de la república fuera de las ciudades.

records.summary_en: The New Hampshire Farmer and Weekly Union reported that Minister Sullivan successfully resolved the Dominican civil conflict, announcing a U.S. policy that rejected armed rebellion in favor of electoral remedies and constitutional governance. Following a battle on October 2, Commander Nulton of the Nashville and Receiver Walter W. Vick transported deadlocked peace envoys from Puerto Plata to Santo Domingo City. Negotiations at the capital concluded with a comprehensive peace accord accepted by all factions.

records.headline: This article explains that the United States government is the custodian of the Dominican revenues under a treaty
records.summary_en: This article explains that the United States government is the custodian of the Dominican revenues under a treaty, standing sponsor for the conservation of the public funds and the settlement of the republic's debts, and that President Wilson appointed Mr. Vick to administer the receivership, his salary of $6,500 a year being paid by the Dominican government. It says the removal of the customs revenues to neutral hands gave Santo Domingo its first long period of freedom from revolution, from 1905 to 1912, and recounts how European creditors in 1904 demanded settlement of a debt of about $30,000,000, leading to the modus vivendi, the treaty that took effect on July 8, 1907, and a $20,000,000 bond issue.
records.summary_es: Este artículo explica que el gobierno de los Estados Unidos es el custodio de los ingresos dominicanos en virtud de un tratado, garante de la conservación de los fondos públicos y del arreglo de las deudas de la república, y que el presidente Wilson nombró al señor Vick para administrar la receptoría, con un sueldo de 6.500 dólares al año pagado por el gobierno dominicano. Dice que el traslado de los ingresos aduaneros a manos neutrales dio a Santo Domingo su primer largo período sin revoluciones, de 1905 a 1912, y cuenta cómo los acreedores europeos exigieron en 1904 el arreglo de una deuda de unos 30.000.000 de dólares, lo que llevó al modus vivendi, al tratado que entró en vigor el 8 de julio de 1907 y a una emisión de bonos de 20.000.000 de dólares.

Washington, April 7.—President Bordas of the Dominican Republic has left Santo Domingo City for Santiago to take the field against the insurrectionists. Commander Bierer, on the gunboat Wheeling at Santo Domingo City reported to the navy department today that a Dominican gunboat is carrying Gen. Bordas and 209 government troops to Puerto Plata, from whence they will go overland to Santiago. Dispatches from Commander Bostwick on the gunboat Nashville at Puerto Plata announced the government troops have driven the rebels under Gen. Arias from Santiago. $4128 Claimed for Canadian Detentions. Washington, April 7.—Frederick H. Tarr of Gloucester, Mass., argued today before the International Court of Arbitration the claim of the Tattler, a Gloucester fishing schooner, for $4128 growing out of two detentions, one in 1901 and the other in 1905, of the vessel by Canadian authorities. records.headline: France and Germany Warn Government to Meet Financial Obligations
records.summary_en: France and Germany have warned Haiti that its customhouses will be seized unless arrangements are made to meet its outstanding financial obligations, according to reports reaching Washington. Secretary of State Bryan said no notice of such a step had reached the United States, but the cabinet discussed the situation at length. Officials noted that no treaty or arrangement would allow the United States to take charge of Haitian customs as it did in Santo Domingo, and pointed out that four American warships were already in Haitian waters while the German cruiser Strassburg lay in Dominican waters, within a few hours' sail of Port-au-Prince. Haiti's minister in Washington, Ulrich Duvivier, protested that his country was not a defaulting debtor and that the debts claimed were indemnities demanded by irresponsible foreigners.
records.summary_es: Francia y Alemania han advertido a Haití que sus aduanas serán embargadas si no se toman medidas para cumplir con sus obligaciones financieras pendientes, según informes llegados a Washington. El secretario de Estado Bryan declaró que no había llegado a los Estados Unidos ninguna notificación de tal medida, pero el gabinete discutió la situación extensamente. Las autoridades señalaron que ningún tratado ni acuerdo permitiría a los Estados Unidos hacerse cargo de las aduanas haitianas como lo hizo en Santo Domingo, e indicaron que cuatro buques de guerra estadounidenses ya se encontraban en aguas haitianas, mientras el crucero alemán Strassburg estaba en aguas dominicanas, a pocas horas de navegación de Puerto Príncipe. El ministro de Haití en Washington, Ulrich Duvivier, protestó que su país no era un deudor moroso y que las deudas reclamadas eran indemnizaciones exigidas por extranjeros irresponsables.

Fighting disrupted multiple regions, including Azua, where the national navy destroyed the custom house, and La Romana, where American sugar estates requested protection. records.passage: San Juan, Porto Rico, July 22.—The United States revenue cutter Algonquin arrived here last night from Puerto Plata, Dominican Republic, with 16[illegible] refugees, mostly Porto Ricans, on board. One woman died during the voyage from the effects of starvation. The condition of those remaining in Santo Domingo was reported to be pitiable, as it was almost impossible to obtain foodstuffs, the prices of which were prohibitive. A report was brought here by the Algonquin that an American bluejacket on board the gunboat Machias had been shot in the leg by a bullet from the shore. Solon Menos, the Haitien minister, conferred today with Secretary Bryan and urged that intervention would result in a number of counter revolutions, necessitate the dissolution of the present government, and even the abdication of the president. "I count on the spirit of justice of the American people," said Minister Menos, referring to intervention, "to restrain them from taking the step which would be so harmful to Haiti." Present mobilization of marines in the vicinity of the islands, the minister explained, had been officially explained by the state department as a precautionary step taken to avert possible trouble, and was not, he felt sure, an indication that plans actually existed for the landing of United States troops at Haiti. records.summary_en: The New Hampshire Farmer and Weekly Union contrasted unrest in the Caribbean, noting that while Dominican disturbances were likely to prompt U.S. armed intervention, the country presented fewer military and diplomatic difficulties than neighboring Haiti. European nations maintained smaller financial interests in Santo Domingo, whereas Haitian instability threatened foreign defaults. The Wilson administration sought guarantees that Haitian customs revenues would be managed to satisfy foreign debts in a manner analogous to the Dominican receivership.
records.summary_es: The New Hampshire Farmer and Weekly Union contrastó las revueltas en el Caribe, observando que, si bien era probable que las perturbaciones dominicanas provocaran una intervención militar estadounidense, dicho país planteaba menores dificultades bélicas y diplomáticas que el vecino Haití. Las naciones europeas conservaban intereses financieros más reducidos en Santo Domingo, al tiempo que la inestabilidad haitiana ponía en riesgo moratorias con el exterior. La administración Wilson demandaba garantías de que los ingresos de las aduanas de Haití fueran administrados para cancelar deudas foráneas de modo análogo a la receptoría dominicana.

Witnesses detailed political influence and lobbying efforts involving customs appointments, while Assistant Secretary of State John B. Vick that severely criticized Sullivan's actions.

records.full_text:
'INSIDE INFORMATION' AT SULLIVAN PROBE

Revelations Made by Harry J. Overman, Brother of Senator From South Carolina.

Inside information as to the influences at work on the appointment of American representatives in the Dominican government was brought out yesterday at the first session of the Sullivan hearing here.

Harry J. Overman, file clerk in the office of the Secretary of the Senate and a brother of Senator Lea S. Overman of North Carolina, testified concerning his efforts to obtain appointment as deputy receiver of customs at Santo Domingo under the treaty relations between the Dominican republic and the United States. He declared that he had been urged to apply for the place by a man named Gold, who, he said, suggested that William C. Beer would be a good person to support him for the place. Beer, he said he was told by Gold, could influence Secretary of State Bryan through John H. Grey, of Wilmington, Del.

Md. Overman testified that inasmuch as his own brother was unwilling to use his position to further his candidacy he was compelled to do much of the work himself. He said that he had met Mr. Beer at a hotel in Washington in company with Minister Sullivan.

John E. Osborne, First Assistant Secretary of State, stated that prior to the appointment of Mr. Sullivan, he had gone to Haiti and Santo Domingo on a secret mission for the Government. While there, he stated, he had warned the Dominican government against increasing its indebtedness.

Regarding the Sullivan case, Secretary Osborne said that he knew practically nothing except that he had received personal letters from Mr. Vick, criticising the conduct of the minister.

Others who were present were Joseph P. Tumulty, Secretary to the President; Assistant Secretary of State, Philips; Assistant Secretary of War Breckenridge, and Brigadier General McIntyre, chief of the Bureau of Insular Affairs, War Department.

At the outset of today's session Charles H. Strong, attorney, conducting the examination for Comimssioner Phelan, announced that the entire scope of the investigation was to inquire into the fitness, competence, and conduct of Minister Sullivan.

“The Commissioner intends,” he said, “to run down any legitimate clue bearing on this case without fear or favor for anybody in or out of public office. He means to sift the case to the bottom. Necessarily, inasmuch as the lines upon which this investigation is being conducted are wholly different from court procedure, much hearsay testimony, or even gossip, must creep into the evidence. But as a result of this hearsay evidence we have already been able to unearth things of the utmost importance.”

records.summary_en: The Evening Star reported testimony from presidential secretary Joseph P. Tumulty regarding the inquiry into Dominican Minister James M. Sullivan. Tumulty stated he had instructed Customs Receiver Vick to monitor Sullivan following allegations concerning the Banco Nacional and commercial interests, denying that the White House had ever whitewashed the diplomat. While describing Dominican politics as filled with recrimination, Tumulty defended the administration's scrutiny and dismissed personal criticisms between Vick and Sullivan.

Al calificar el ambiente político dominicano de plagado de recriminaciones, Tumulty defendió la rigurosidad del gobierno y restó importancia a los agravios personales entre Vick y Sullivan.

I asked Mr. Vick to watch Mr. Sullivan closely and keep the White House advised. I also told him to warn Minister Sullivan that the President would be displeased if he heard of Sullivan growing too close to any interests, and would take such action as became necessary." He was inclined to be suspicious of all charges from the Dominican Republic, because Mr. Vick had told him, in relation to accusations against the latter, that the "atmosphere there was charged with recrimination and throat-cutting." Representative Hamill also testified, denying any connection to commercial interests in advocating for Sullivan's appointment.

records.summary_en: The Bridgeport Evening Farmer reported that a violent mob stormed the Dominican consulate in Port-au-Prince, dragging out Haitian General Oscar—who had sought refuge there following palace clashes and the execution of political prisoners—and shooting him dead. The crowd also besieged the French legation, where Haitian President Guillaume had fled after rebels damaged the executive mansion. In response to the breakdown of order, the U.S. cruiser *Washington*, carrying Rear Admiral Caperton and an expeditionary marine force, sailed to intervene.

La multitud sitió también la legación francesa, donde se había refugiado el presidente haitiano Guillaume tras los destrozos causados por los rebeldes en la mansión ejecutiva. Ante el quebranto del orden, el crucero de los EE. UU. *Washington*, con el contralmirante Caperton y una fuerza expedicionaria de infantería de marina a bordo, zarpó para intervenir.

records.summary_en: The Evening Star reported that a mob breached the Dominican legation in Port-au-Prince and executed General Oscar in retribution for his mass killings of political prisoners during a rebel assault on the presidential palace. His corpse remained outside the Dominican mission while demonstrators threatened to storm the French legation to capture fleeing President Guillaume. U.S. Rear Admiral Caperton sailed aboard the cruiser *Washington* with an expeditionary force of marines and sailors to restore security in the Haitian capital.

Su cadáver quedó tendido frente a la misión dominicana mientras los manifestantes amenazaban con irrumpir en la delegación de Francia para apresar al presidente en fuga Guillaume. records.summary_en: The Barre Daily Times reported that American marines established guards in Port-au-Prince following the mob murder of President Guillaume after his removal from the French legation. Prior to the uprising, special commissioner Paul Fuller Jr. reported to President Wilson that Guillaume refused to sign a treaty establishing an American customs receivership out of fear of public revolt. The article noted that the United States had sought to establish financial control in Haiti modeled directly on its Dominican customs administration.

The state department received messages from Charge D'Affaires Davis telling of the assassination of President Guillaume by a mob which broke into the French legation. This violation of the diplomatic immunity which foreign legations enjoy would be regarded ordinarily as a serious affront, but in view of the absence of an established government and the generally turbulent conditions, the incident probably will not complicate the situation. The article detailed how the wife of former President Nord Alexis evaded customs duties by smuggling goods and disguising valuable coffee shipments as untaxed cottonseed. It concluded that establishing an honest, stable administration would allow Haiti to realize its natural agricultural potential.

records.summary_en: The Washington Herald reported that a Haitian rebel commander fled toward Monte Cristi in the Dominican Republic to recruit men and procure arms, raising concerns of renewed destabilization along the border. Officials noted rising unrest and riots within Santo Domingo, where a compromise coalition government instituted under U.S. auspices was widely regarded as failing. American naval forces faced strain, having withdrawn the cruiser *Nashville* from Dominican waters to handle military operations and disarmament efforts in Haiti.

Los funcionarios observaron una creciente conmoción y disturbios en Santo Domingo, donde se consideraba un fracaso el gobierno de concertación auspiciado por los Estados Unidos. La fuerza naval estadounidense se veía exigida tras haber retirado el crucero *Nashville* de aguas dominicanas para atender las operaciones castrenses y de desarme en Haití.

records.summary_en: The Evening Public Ledger reported that Rear Admiral Caperton was authorized to use military force, including landing marines and bluejackets, to maintain the constitutional government of Dominican President Juan Isidro Jimenes. Washington warned Dominican officials that it viewed congressional impeachment proceedings against Jimenes as a veiled revolutionary plot, granting him an eight-day respite to reply. The excerpt also detailed a concurrent constitutional clash in Haiti, where Caperton backed President Dartiguenave against a rebellious parliament.

WASHINGTON, May 5.—Rear Admiral Caperton, commanding the American naval forces in Dominican waters, is under broad instructions to use whatever force is necessary to maintain the constitutional government in the Dominican Republic. The Admiral recently went to the capital with instructions from Washington which declared the United States considered the impeachment of President Jiminez a thinly veiled revolutionary plot. If necessary Admiral Caperton may land bluejackets and marines. PORT AU PRINCE, Haiti, May 5. The Haitian Cabinet has resigned. Parliament has entered a protest with the American Government and Congress against what it declares to be a violation of the rights of the legislative branch of the Government. President Dartiguenave, of Haiti, and his Cabinet have been in controversy with Parliament over the framing of a new constitution to conform with the treaty with the United States. The President and the Cabinet, according to a dispatch from Port au Prince on April 29, threatened to resign if the Deputies and Senators declined to abide by the presidential decree dissolving the Senate, and persisted in continuing to assume legislative powers instead of meeting merely to frame the new constitution. records.headline: At the navy-yard It was learned that five other destroyers, the
records.summary_en: American marines, fully equipped, were landed on the outskirts of Santo Domingo City, first from the cruiser Prairie to protect the American legation after disorders in which several persons were killed or wounded. Advices said the serious situation caused by hostilities between the factions of President Jimenes and General Arias had become quiet after Jimenes resigned, a step he took to prevent threatened armed intervention by the United States. Five additional destroyers and the supply ship Panther were to sail for the Dominican Republic, and the French armored cruiser Marseillaise had arrived in port.
records.summary_es: Infantes de marina estadounidenses, con equipo completo, desembarcaron en las afueras de la ciudad de Santo Domingo, primero desde el crucero Prairie para proteger la legación estadounidense tras desórdenes en los que varias personas murieron o resultaron heridas. Los informes decían que la grave situación causada por las hostilidades entre las facciones del presidente Jimenes y el general Arias se había calmado después de que Jimenes dimitiera, paso que dio para evitar la amenazada intervención armada de Estados Unidos. Cinco destructores adicionales y el buque de abastecimiento Panther debían zarpar hacia la República Dominicana, y el crucero acorazado francés Marseillaise había llegado a puerto.

The French armored cruiser Marseillaise arrived in port Monday morning. The president is said to have taken this action in order to prevent armed intervention with the United States, which previous advices had announced had been threatened unless the hostile factions composed their differences. A Santo Domingo dispatch on Friday said that marines were landed that day from the American converted cruiser Prairie for the protection of the American legation following the outbreak of disorders in which several persons were killed or wounded. Unsettled political conditions in the Dominican Republic, caused by the Arias revolution against the Jimenez government, have forced indefinite postponement of election of a successor to former President Jimenez, according to a report from Rear Admiral Caperton to the navy department today. BOOM FOR GENERAL WOOD IS STARTED. Name of Former Chief of Staff May Be Presented at Republican Convention as Compromise Candidate in Event of Deadlock. Chicago, May 20. — Friends of Gen. Leonard Wood are said to be planning to present his name to the republican national convention as a compromise candidate for the presidency. They believe that if there is a prolonged deadlock he will have a chance to win. John A. Stewart, former secretary of the League of Republican Clubs of New York state, said to be in charge of the work in that interest of General Wood, arrived in Chicago today. Political literature for General Wood's candidacy has been sent to the convention delegates and it was said headquarters for him will be opened in Chicago next week. Merce Vernon, of Washington, D. records.summary_en: The *Buffalo bulletin* reported that American Minister Russell announced U.S. marines would be distributed to strategic points in Santo Domingo to protect American sugar plantations and interests, while warships were stationed at key ports. The State Department declared it would not recognize the election of Federico H. Carvajal as provisional president following the impeachment of President Jimenes. Officials expressed confidence that Rear Admiral Caperton had the revolutionary movement under General Arias well under control.

Carvajal) como presidente provisional tras la destitución del presidente Jimenes. Los funcionarios manifestaron seguridad en que el contralmirante Caperton mantenía plenamente controlado el movimiento revolucionario acaudillado por el general Arias.

American Minister Russell, reporting today that the marines soon would be distributed to strategic points in the republic, said he had received many requests for such action in protection of American sugar plantations and other American Interests. American warships already are stationed at all the important ports. The arrangement for continued cooperation of the American forces in policing Santo Domingo probably will not be as far reaching as that in force in Haiti, officials say, but will be broad enough in scope to prevent any repetition of the present complicated situation. records.summary_en: An arrangement for the disarmament of Santo Domingo revolutionists was virtually perfected by a peace conference of the Dominican factions, according to a dispatch from Rear Admiral Caperton, paving the way for a suspension of hostilities while the future form of government was negotiated. Officials regarded it as the collapse of the revolution led by General Arias and expected a new regime with American supervision similar to that in Haiti, including American direction of revenue collection and disbursements.

Los funcionarios lo consideraron el colapso de la revolución dirigida por el general Arias y esperaban un nuevo régimen con supervisión estadounidense similar a la de Haití, incluida la dirección estadounidense del cobro y desembolso de ingresos.

records.headline: This feature calls the Dominican Republic, and indeed the whole island, naturally one of the richest spots in the world
records.summary_en: This feature calls the Dominican Republic, and indeed the whole island, naturally one of the richest spots in the world, with remarkably fertile soil: cotton near Monte Cristi backed by American and English capital, Puerto Plata linked by railway to the cacao and tobacco towns of the Cibao, Samana Bay with the town of Samana and the port of Sanchez, and San Pedro de Macoris as the sugar port, where thousands of acres of cane and millions of dollars of American capital are worked with modern machinery. It also tours the capital's relics, including the ruins of the first church of San Nicolas, the bones Dominicans claim are those of Christopher Columbus, and the ruins of the house of Diego Colon.
records.summary_es: Esta crónica califica a la República Dominicana, y en verdad a toda la isla, como naturalmente uno de los lugares más ricos del mundo, con un suelo notablemente fértil: algodón cerca de Monte Cristi respaldado por capital estadounidense e inglés, Puerto Plata unida por ferrocarril a las ciudades del Cibao productoras de cacao y tabaco, la bahía de Samaná con la ciudad de Samaná y el puerto de Sánchez, y San Pedro de Macorís como puerto azucarero, donde se trabajan miles de acres de caña y millones de dólares de capital estadounidense con maquinaria moderna. Recorre también las reliquias de la capital, incluidas las ruinas de la primera iglesia de San Nicolás, los huesos que los dominicanos afirman que son los de Cristóbal Colón y las ruinas de la casa de Diego Colón.

Automobiles are plentiful and the ride from the capital to San Cristobal along the new macadam boulevard is most attractive. Automobiles can be procured for $1 an hour. There are several hotels in the city, of which the Hotel Francis is the best known. There is quite a large foreign colony at the capital and in Macoris and Puerto Plata. The whole trip from New York, including a stop at all ports, is about eight or nine days. A very erroneous impression prevails that the climate of Santo Domingo is unhealthy. From its geographical position it cannot be unhealthy. The winds have a clean sweep across the island, and there has been no serious epidemic there since the cholera outbreak some time in the early sixties.

records.summary_en: The *Perth Amboy evening news* reported on U.S. intervention in Santo Domingo, stating that severe unrest in 1914 and 1915 forced the United States to deploy marines and warships to restore quiet. The article asserted that Dominicans reluctantly accepted external peace enforced under the Monroe Doctrine after customs administration alone failed to prevent renewed revolutions. It characterized the military interventions in Santo Domingo, Haiti, and Nicaragua as costly, altruistic sacrifices made for regional security rather than territorial gain.
records.summary_es: El *Perth Amboy evening news* informó sobre la intervención de los Estados Unidos en Santo Domingo, indicando que los graves disturbios acaecidos en 1914 y 1915 obligaron a Washington a movilizar infantes de marina y escuadras navales para restaurar la calma. El artículo aseveraba que la población dominicana aceptaba a regañadientes una paz exterior impuesta al amparo de la Doctrina Monroe, luego de que la sola administración aduanera resultara ineficaz para evitar la reaparición de revueltas. Calificaba los desembarcos militares en Santo Domingo, Haití y Nicaragua como sacrificios onerosos y altruistas en favor de la seguridad continental antes que en búsqueda de engrandecimiento territorial.
records.passage: still left a greater net Income for the use of the government than It had ever had before. "For a long time it was thought that, deprived of the opportunity of securing customs house revenues through the seizure of ports, revolution could not support themselves. But after six or seven years of peace trouble broke out again, and during 1914 and 1915 it became so serious that the United States was forced to Intervene in behalf of peace and to demand, with marines on shore and naval guns trained and pointed on the ports, that the country return to a state of quiet. And so today the Dominicans, realizing that the Monroe doctrine is determined to afford them protection, from their own excesses, their own bitter passions and blind purposes, have accepted the inevitable and have secured the blessings of peace from without when they could not attain that end themselves. It is a reluctant acquiescence they yield, but a wholesome one, none the less. 'It has not been without effort or without expense, nor yet without the actual sacrifice of blood and life that our country has stepped in to play the role of Good Samaritan to the people of Santo Domingo, Haiti and Nicaragua, who had lost the blessings of peace and were unable to regain them. In Haiti alone we lost one officer and six marines and had a number wounded. But out of this altruistic effort are growing results of which a nation that covets no territory, that seeks only its own security and the welfare of its unfortunate neighbors may well be proud.

Approximately 1,800 American marines were tasked with maintaining order and supervising native government operations until January elections, including the disbursement of $600,000 in accumulated export duties. The intervention followed the overthrow of President Jiminez by General Arias and Washington's refusal to recognize the newly chosen government of Frederico Enriquez.

records.summary_en: The *Norwich bulletin* recounted the chronic political instability and recurring civil wars in Santo Domingo that left the republic heavily indebted to foreign creditors. When foreign warships threatened bombardment to enforce debt claims, Dominican authorities entered into an agreement with the United States in 1905 to take over the collection of customs. Under this treaty, American authorities restructured the nation's tariffs to tax luxuries and guaranteed payments to satisfy European claims.
records.summary_es: El *Norwich bulletin* rememoró la crónica inestabilidad política y las constantes guerras civiles en Santo Domingo que abocaron a la república a un pesado endeudamiento con acreedores extranjeros. Al amenazar cañoneros extranjeros con bombardear los puertos para hacer efectivas sus reclamaciones, las autoridades dominicanas celebraron un acuerdo con los Estados Unidos en 1905 para confiarles la recaudación aduanera. Bajo este convenio, los funcionarios estadounidenses modificaron los aranceles nacionales gravando los artículos de lujo y aseguraron pagos para saldar los reclamos europeos.
records.passage: bulletin. "Revolution had followed revolution almost with clocklike regularity. There were assassinations, there were betrayals, there were conspiracies, there were wars within and wars without — war with Haiti over boundary questions and civil war over the control of the government. Debts were piled up without thought of the day of payment or even provisions for meeting the interest charges. "So long and so steady was the orgy of revolution, speculation, debt making and interest-dodging that the nation's credit grew worse than that of its individual citizens. Finally, the day of reckoning came. Foreign warships approached the ports whose harbors had given refuge to the great discoverer Columbus and whose capital city contains what undoubtedly are his ashes, and demanded that the claims of their subjects be satisfied — claims for money advanced, claims for property wantonly destroyed — and they demanded it at the point of big naval guns. "In a predicament from which they were powerless to extricate themselves, the Dominicans were ready enough to negotiate a treaty turning over the control of the country's customs to the United States, if, in return therefor, the United States would protect them from angry European creditors and rejuvenate their treasury. "And so it was that in [illegible] the United States undertook to serve as treasurer of Santo Domingo and to vouch for her debts. The tariff was quickly revised, the American authorities urging that duties be laid on luxuries rather than upon necessities.

records.full_text:
U. S. MARINE DIES IN FIGHT

One American Is Killed and One Severely Wounded by Santo Domingo Bandits.

Washington, Jan. 24.—A night fight between native bandits and American marines in the Dominican republic, resulting in the death of one marine and the severe injury of another, was reported to the navy department.

Captain Knapp, commanding the American cruiser forces, reported the fight occurred Saturday night in the vicinity of the Porvenir sugar plantation, near Macoris, the scene of two similar encounters recently. Private J. R. Olson of the Fiftieth company was killed and Corporal George Wilson of the Fifty-second company was shot in the neck.

records.headline: An Associated Press correspondent writing from Santo Domingo on February 13 reports that peace, expected by everyone
records.summary_en: An Associated Press correspondent writing from Santo Domingo on February 13 reports that peace, expected by everyone to be permanent, has at last been established through the intervention of the United States in a country that has had approximately fifty presidents in seventy years, not one chosen without revolution. Captain Knapp, head of the temporary military government, faces the work of establishing good government, a sound educational system, agriculture and transportation, with an education commission headed by Archbishop Adolfo Nouel already appointed and a great highway of more than 200 miles planned across the Cibao to Monte Cristi.
records.summary_es: Un corresponsal de la Associated Press que escribe desde Santo Domingo el 13 de febrero informa que la paz, que todos esperan permanente, se ha establecido por fin mediante la intervención de los Estados Unidos en un país que ha tenido aproximadamente cincuenta presidentes en setenta años, ninguno elegido sin revolución. El capitán Knapp, jefe del gobierno militar temporal, enfrenta la tarea de establecer un buen gobierno, un sistema educativo sólido, la agricultura y el transporte, con una comisión de educación encabezada por el arzobispo Adolfo Nouel ya nombrada y una gran carretera de más de 200 millas proyectada a través del Cibao hasta Monte Cristi.

In the matter of education a start has been made by the appointment of a commission headed by Archbishop Adolfo Nouel, Catholic primate, Federico Velasquez and other prominent Dominicans, empowered to make an exhaustive study of the educational needs of the people. There is a so-called school system in existence, but those in a position to know say there is not a public school building in the republic and estimates of illiteracy run as high as 90 per cent. Teachers have drawn salaries from the government when they had no pupils to teach and subventions are said to have been granted to private schools which existed only in name. Great Highway Planned. One of the principal public improvements planned by the military government is a great highway crossing the island and connecting Santo Domingo [illegible] Monte Cristi, the most westerly port on the north coast. records.summary_en: An Associated Press dispatch from Puerto Plata reports that extensive repairs have begun on the Dominican Central railroad between Puerto Plata and Santiago, in line with the wishes of the United States military government, including new deviations that will reduce the grade from twelve percent to a maximum of three percent. Tons of tobacco, coffee and cacao have accumulated unmoved at Santiago, and other work described includes a new wharf and customs house at Puerto Plata, a hydro-electric project to serve Santiago, Moca, La Vega and Puerto Plata, rebuilding the bridges on the Santiago to Monte Cristi road that revolutionists burned last spring to check the advance of United States Marines, and a macadam road from Macoris to Santo Domingo City.

records.summary_en: The *Richmond times-dispatch* reviewed U.S. relations with Santo Domingo, describing how the 1907 customs receivership had functioned continuously despite ongoing revolutions and mounting debt. Following a fresh uprising, Admiral Caperton and General Pendleton broke the rebel forces and briefly restored President Jimenez to power. However, President Jimenez refused American demands to permit the United States to organize and command a native constabulary to police the republic.
records.summary_es: El *Richmond times-dispatch* examinó las relaciones entre los Estados Unidos y Santo Domingo, describiendo la continuidad operativa de la administración aduanera de 1907 frente a las sucesivas revoluciones y al endeudamiento creciente. records.summary_en: The *Omaha daily bee* detailed the natural and mineral wealth of the Dominican Republic, highlighting the gold placers worked in the Cibao range and San Cristobal region. It also pointed to extensive unused forests of valuable timber and mountains of pure rock salt located in Barahona province. The report concluded that the country's lack of coal and poor overland transit routes posed the greatest obstacles to its industrial development.
records.summary_es: El *Omaha daily bee* detalló las riquezas naturales y minerales de la República Dominicana, destacando los placeres auríferos explotados en la cordillera del Cibao y la región de San Cristóbal. Hizo notar asimismo los extensos bosques vírgenes de maderas preciosas y las montañas de sal gema pura ubicadas en la provincia de Barahona. El informe concluía que la escasez de carbón y las deficientes vías de transporte terrestre representaban las principales trabas para el desarrollo fabril del país.

The most famous of Dominican resources, and the one about which the American consul receives the most inquiries, is its gold. In the Cibao range and in the San Cristobal region there are placers which have been known and worked for centuries. In the days of the Spanish occupation it is said that the invaders gathered great stores of this treasure by trading with the Indians little silver hawkbells for their fill of gold. Nowadays the peon women wash gold out of these same streams with wooden bowls, making a few dollars a week, and by a law of the land the common people are protected in their right to work these placers. The forest resources are another example of unused wealth. One of the largest Dominican imports is lumber, and yet there are extensive forests of pine, oak and chestnut, as well as mahogany, satinwood, lignum vitae and rosewood. The most serious lack in Santo Domingo is coal, which will probably limit the future industrial development of the island more than anything else. There is an abundance of iron ore and also lead and copper, but no mineral fuel has so far been discovered except lignite. Another striking and so far undeveloped resource is two mountains of rock salt, said to be remarkably pure. They are in Barahona province. records.summary_en: The *Omaha daily bee* reported that many Dominicans accepted American intervention to re-establish law and order, though they remained firmly opposed to annexation. The article analyzed the country's social structure, explaining that approximately twenty elite families controlled virtually all political offices and land while avoiding property taxes. It observed that pervasive political corruption and sinecures had long characterized native governance prior to the American occupation.
records.summary_es: El *Omaha daily bee* informó que numerosos dominicanos aceptaban la intervención estadounidense para restaurar el orden y la ley, aun oponiéndose resueltamente a una anexión. El artículo examinó la estructura social dominicana, señalando que una veintena de familias pudientes acaparaba prácticamente las tierras y los destinos públicos mientras eludía el pago de impuestos prediales. Subrayó que la corrupción inveterada y las prebendas políticas habían sido el rasgo distintivo de la gobernación local con anterioridad a la ocupación estadounidense.
