A large percentage of the Dominicans, then, welcome the American intervention and accept it in a good spirit. They recognize that some stronger power must restore confidence in law and government and initiate the reconstruction of the country. They are not, however, looking toward annexation. Most of them will not hear of this. They are willing for us to help them because they trust the altruism of our motive and the good faith of our professions. It is easy to prove that the Dominicans are a lazy, disorderly people, and also hard to see how they could be anything else under present conditions. As in most small Latin-American countries, there are just two native classes — the very rich and the very poor. The upper class here is said to consist of not more than twenty large families. These hold all the political offices and own nearly all the land. They are wealthy, intelligent and well educated. Every law is designed to benefit them. There is scarcely any tax on land because they own it, but there are two or three taxes on everything else. Political salaries are large and numerous, and many of the political berths include no duties at all. Jimenez subsequently departed the country to lecture in Latin America against American despotism in Santo Domingo. The article noted that Knapp's proclamation established a military government intended as a temporary measure, keeping native courts and municipal administrations intact while imposing press censorship.

Acto seguido, Jimenes abandonó la nación para dictar conferencias por Hispanoamérica denunciando la opresión estadounidense en Santo Domingo. El artículo apuntaba que la proclama de Knapp fundaba un gobierno militar con carácter provisional, manteniendo operando a los tribunales del país y los cabildos locales pero implantando la censura de prensa.

It did not resign, it did not revolt; simply faded and died. To the cabinet officers was tendered the high and chaste honor of serving on without pay, but they unaccountably failed to respond. President Jimenez sent a messenger to Admiral Knapp to explain that his excellency was in a state of financial need and to request that his salary for one month be paid. This was refused. President Jimenez then sailed away and is said to have taken the lecture platform in other Latin American countries and devoted his abilities to an exposition of the greedy and underhand methods by which the eagle of the north is sinking the talons of despotism into the vitals of free and democratic government in Santo Domingo. Higuey is one of the principal inland cities of the Dominican Republic. records.summary_en: The *Richmond times-dispatch* reviewed a book on the history, geography, and administration of Santo Domingo and Haiti written by an author who served with the U.S. financial investigation commission and the Dominican Minister of Finance. The publication traced the republic's development from the Spanish conquest through modern times, detailing its topography, flora, fauna, and population. Additional chapters analyzed Dominican commerce, transportation, national finances, and political prospects.

La obra reconstruía la evolución de la república desde la conquista española hasta la época contemporánea, detallando su topografía, flora, fauna y habitantes. Capítulos complementarios examinaban el comercio dominicano, el transporte, las finanzas públicas y el horizonte político.

The "Days of Conquest," 1492 to 1533, are first considered, after which the important periods in the history of Santo Domingo to date are discussed. Then come chapters on the area and boundary, the topography and climate, the minerals, the flora and fauna, the people, the religion, the education and literature, the means of transportation and communication, the commerce, the government, the politics, the finance and the future of Santo Domingo. records.summary_en: The *sun* reviewed Otto Schoenrich's book on Santo Domingo, highlighting the country's lack of infrastructure, with only 144 miles of railroad and inland roads reduced to muddy trails. The excerpt also examined the historical dispute over the burial place of Christopher Columbus between Spain and the Dominican Republic. Schoenrich concluded from 1877 cathedral excavations that Spain had mistakenly removed the remains of Diego Columbus, leaving Christopher Columbus's body in Santo Domingo.

El extracto examinó asimismo la histórica disputa entre España y la República Dominicana sobre el sitio de enterramiento de Cristóbal Colón. Schoenrich concluía, sobre la base de las excavaciones efectuadas en la catedral en 1877, que España había retirado por error los restos de Diego Colón, quedando el cuerpo de Cristóbal Colón en Santo Domingo.

records.summary_en: The *sun* discussed Dominican efforts to enlist Spanish diplomatic support to secure the withdrawal of U.S. marines, noting historic cultural affinities between the two nations. The piece recalled that Pedro Santana annexed the Dominican Republic to Spain in 1861, which was overturned by a popular revolt that led Spain to recognize Dominican independence in 1865. It added that an 1869 annexation treaty with the United States was ratified by Dominicans but defeated by a tie vote in the U.S. Senate.
records.summary_es: El *sun* trató sobre las gestiones dominicanas dirigidas a concitar el respaldo diplomático de España para lograr la evacuación de las tropas de marina estadounidenses, resaltando los seculares vínculos culturales que unían a ambos pueblos. La nota recordó que Pedro Santana reincorporó la República Dominicana a España en 1861, medida revocada por un alzamiento patriótico que forzó a España a reconocer la emancipación dominicana en 1865. Añadió que el tratado de anexión de 1869 con los Estados Unidos fue respaldado por la población dominicana pero desestimado en el Senado de los EE. UU. por votación empatada.

records.headline: This narrative tells how a Puerto Plata senator chosen as president, on trial for one year after the previous president
records.summary_en: This narrative tells how a Puerto Plata senator chosen as president, on trial for one year after the previous president was killed, announced after some ten months that he intended to hold onto the job, sparking a general uprising against him as a usurper and tyrant. As his forces prepared to shell Puerto Plata unless the city surrendered by two o'clock, and Washington had sent two contingents of Marines to Puerto Plata and Monte Cristi to stand by, the American commander warned him that the first gun fired would result in the landing of Marines and a general cleaning out of the belligerents.
records.summary_es: Este relato cuenta cómo un senador de Puerto Plata escogido como presidente, a prueba por un año tras la muerte del presidente anterior, anunció después de unos diez meses que pretendía quedarse en el puesto, lo que desató un levantamiento general contra él como usurpador y tirano. Mientras sus fuerzas se preparaban para bombardear Puerto Plata si la ciudad no se rendía a las dos en punto, y Washington había enviado dos contingentes de marines a Puerto Plata y Monte Cristi para estar listos, el comandante americano le advirtió que el primer cañonazo disparado provocaría el desembarco de los marines y una limpieza general de los beligerantes.

The soldiers were aching to start something and they could not understand why the President did not order the war to begin. One man after imbibing more than an ordinary man's share of rum began to cry. With tears coursing down his jetty cheeks he begged to know why this and that was so and why there had been no opportunity for himself and his mates to show their bravery, their skill with the big guns. records.summary_en: The *Richmond planet* reported that many U.S. marines in Santo Domingo did not understand why they were stationed there beyond vague rumors about collecting a $20,000,000 debt while running customs. The article criticized the strict military censorship that destroyed letters written by enlisted men and suppressed news from reaching the islands. It highlighted efforts to conceal former President Theodore Roosevelt's public denunciations of President Wilson's military operations in Santo Domingo and Haiti.

El periódico censuró la estricta vigilancia militar que destruía la correspondencia de los soldados e impedía que las noticias arribasen a las islas. Resaltó el empeño puesto en silenciar las condenas públicas formuladas por el expresidente Theodore Roosevelt contra las incursiones militares del mandatario Wilson en Santo Domingo y Haití.

records.headline: One year was the limit if he failed to "make good
records.summary_en: The *Richmond planet* recounted the outbreak of civil war in Santo Domingo after a provisional president, appointed for a one-year trial term, issued a manifesto ten months later refusing to relinquish office. The declaration provoked widespread public outrage, prompting citizens to take up arms under the banner of liberty to remove the administration. While the president armed supporters with government artillery, fighters in Puerto Plata organized resistance, plunging the country into open conflict.
records.summary_es: El *Richmond planet* relató el estallido de la guerra civil en Santo Domingo después de que un presidente provisional, designado para un período de prueba de un año, emitiera un manifiesto diez meses después negándose a dejar el cargo. La declaración provocó una indignación pública generalizada, lo que llevó a los ciudadanos a alzarse en armas bajo el estandarte de la libertad para deponer a la administración. Mientras el presidente armaba a sus partidarios con artillería gubernamental, combatientes en Puerto Plata organizaron la resistencia, sumiendo al país en un conflicto abierto.

If, at the end of that year his administration of affairs had been satisfactory he would be reappointed for the remaining 3 years. However, Dominicans are all ambitious. Give them a taste of power and they are willing to fight for a mouthful of the same. And so it was with the President by accident. After being in office for something like ten months he issued a manifesto announcing that he intended hanging onto the job and that he defied the powers of light and darkness — this meaning all of San Domingo — to oust him. That defiance was the spark that ignited the train leading to the magazine. Immediately the Dominicans were up in arms. records.summary_en: The *Evening star* reported that Dr. Francisco Henriquez y Carvajal rejected assertions that the United States exercised a protectorate over the Dominican Republic, declaring that no treaty akin to the Platt Amendment existed. Henriquez explained that the 1907 convention was limited strictly to customs administration for debt repayment and, as President Roosevelt affirmed, conferred no authority for military intervention. He maintained that the agreement was temporary and would naturally expire once the foreign debt was fully discharged.

records.headline: Our Caribbean Empire
records.summary_en: The *Milwaukee leader* reported sharp criticisms of the U.S. military occupation in Haiti and Santo Domingo, citing findings by Judge Otto Schoenrich and Archbishop Adolfo Nouel. The article reported allegations of despotic military rule, the dissolution of legislative assemblies, arbitrary provost court trials, and the suppression of civil liberties. It also claimed that debt disbursements to native bondholders were suspended under the occupation while New York bankers acquired the depreciated securities.

El artículo dio cuenta de denuncias de un régimen militar despótico, la disolución de asambleas legislativas, juicios arbitrarios ante cortes marciales y la supresión de las libertades civiles. También afirmó que durante la ocupación se suspendieron los pagos de la deuda a los tenedores de bonos nacionales, mientras banqueros de Nueva York adquirían los títulos depreciados.

records.full_text:
OUR CARIBBEAN EMPIRE

The average citizen of the United States is blissfully ignorant of the extent to which this government has established a colonial empire in the Caribbean regions. In Nicaragua the government is practically in the hands of the United States marines. The natives complain not merely that they are ruled without their consent but that they are subject to the whims of our navy department which in this matter is responsible neither to congress nor the people. The American government is also charged with unwarranted interference in Guatemala, Costa Rica and Honduras. At a recent conference at Clark university, Judge Otto Schoenrich, a conservative citizen, born in America, who has held high judicial posts in Porto Rico and is familiar with all the Caribbean countries, read a paper reviewing the record of the American administration of the two island republics, Santo Domingo and Haiti. The first, it will be recalled, is Spanish-speaking and predominantly white; the second French-speaking and Negro. In 1916 our navy took over the government of Santo Domingo, and administers it through the marines against the wishes of the people. “Law and order” have been established. Roads have been built and a beginning has been made at popular education. The reason for our intervention was the failure of the Dominican government to live up to its agreement in the matter of its foreign debt. Foreign bondholders now get their interest regularly! Judge Schoenrich, however, charges that in accomplishing these things the United States government has maintained a censorship so rigid as to apply to every public statement “from the utterances of the chief justice to an advertisement for a servant girl.” Until recently the words, national, revolution, freedom of thought and speech could not appear in a Dominican publication. One unfortunate bookseller was originally sentenced to five years in prison for circulating a speech by the speaker of the Porto Rican house of representatives. Later his sentence was graciously commuted to banishment. Judge Schoenrich also reports serious charges of torture in connection with the administration of the provost courts.

In the neighboring republic of Haiti conditions are even more unsatisfactory. There we intervened on the nominal authority of a treaty, but the Haitian congress only ratified that treaty with 23 reservations which we ignored. In 1916 marines dispersed the congress and in 1917 dispersed a constituent assembly. Tell it not to Trotzky! Judge Schoenrich says there are three governments: the Haitian, the government of the American treaty officials, and the government of the American military. The first is impotent, the second inefficient, and the third indifferent. In the interior districts of the island the officers of the marines exercise despotic powers and the natives charge that a marine can do no wrong to a Haitian. From Haiti also come ugly stories of torture, autocratic and unjust trials of civilians by provost court, and denials of civil liberty. A few months ago armed Haitians, either bandits or revolutionists according to the point of view, actually marched on the capital city where there was vigorous fighting before they were dispersed. The Haitian debt was largely held by the people, who, lacking proper banking facilities, put their savings into national bonds. Under American occupation payment on these was suspended although it was guaranteed in the treaty. The people sold their holdings at low prices. The bonds, it is believed, are now held by New York bankers, and negotiations are under way looking to their payment at par.

It is only fair to say that such criticisms as these were vigorously attacked at the Clark university conference by defenders of the American regime. They are, however, supported by other testimony. Archbishop Nouel of Santo Domingo in a letter to the American minister (we go through the farce of maintaining a minister plenipotentiary in a country ruled by an American rear admiral) complains not only of torture, of the denial of liberty, but of a faulty system of taxation and waste in its expenditure. Emphatically the situation requires investigation. The navy department is ruling three republics without their consent primarily in the interests of their American creditors, with a blissful irresponsibility even as regards congress or the American public. Supposing that conditions in Nicaragua, Santo Domingo, and Haiti prior to our intervention were as bad as their critics assert—it is a sorry world if we can discover no way of helping to educate “backward” people without subjecting them to flagrant economic and political imperialism.

Porto Rico welcomed American annexation and her case is not on all fours with her neighbor’s. Nevertheless, our territorial rule leaves something to be desired. During the year 1917-’18 only 142,846 children out of 427,668 of school age were actually enrolled in the public schools. The total wealth of the island is in the hands of 15 per cent of the population; 14 per cent is in the hands of native Porto Ricans; 67 per cent in the hands of Americans. Wages, housing, and health conditions are wretched. The extension of this sort of thing in Mexico and the Caribbean countries is not our idea of civilizing people.—The World Tomorrow.

records.summary_en: The *Richmond times-dispatch* published a report by Military Governor Rear Admiral Thomas Snowden detailing administrative progress in Santo Domingo. Snowden reported that internal revenue collections had increased from $700,000 to approximately $3,500,000 annually and that regressive taxes were replaced with direct property taxes. He stated that the republic's floating debt was cleared, the 1908 loan was on course to be retired thirty years early by 1926, and administrative savings were funding new schools, highways, and sanitation projects.

Declaró que la deuda flotante de la república había sido liquidada, que el empréstito de 1908 estaba encaminado a cancelarse con treinta años de anticipación para 1926 y que los ahorros administrativos financiaban nuevas escuelas, carreteras y obras sanitarias.

records.summary_en: The *Pine Bluff daily graphic* reported that Julio M. Cestero of the Dominican junta issued a statement asserting that Dominican citizens never sought U.S. intervention and continually demanded the return of their national sovereignty. In a concurrent release, Secretary of State Colby defended American policy, stating that military intervention in Haiti was prompted by chronic bloodshed and the 1915 lynching of President Guillaume Sam in the French legation. Colby maintained that the United States acted under the Monroe Doctrine to restore order and preempt European military intervention.

records.summary_en: The *New-York tribune* reported that the State Department issued a formal denial that the National City Bank of New York received improper government favors in Haiti. The department stated it only provided routine support and had actively intervened to remove monopolistic provisions from the bank's charter when it increased its holdings in the National Bank of Haiti. Furthermore, the statement emphasized that the bank exercised no control over customs revenues, foreign loans, or exchange rates.

Colby confirmed that the State Department was continuing to withhold salaries from Haitian officials until they ceased obstructing the bilateral treaty. Simultaneously, Dominican representative Julio M. Cestero protested that the Dominican people never requested American occupation and consistently demanded the restoration of their freedom and sovereignty.

Al mismo tiempo, el representante dominicano Julio M. records.headline: After a turbulent history, during which the native Indians were exterminated
records.summary_en: The *Evening star* published a historical overview of the Dominican Republic, detailing its initial settlement by Spain, the eradication of indigenous inhabitants, and the importation of enslaved Africans. The article described how an eighteenth-century uprising abolished slavery and expelled colonizers, followed by shifts between Spanish and Haitian rule until the Dominican Republic secured independence in 1844. It observed that despite preserving Spanish language and institutions, the nation experienced frequent political coups and revolutions throughout its history.
records.summary_es: El *Evening star* publicó una reseña histórica de la República Dominicana, detallando su colonización inicial por parte de España, la desaparición de los pobladores indígenas y la importación de africanos esclavizados. El artículo describió cómo un levantamiento en el siglo XVIII abolió la esclavitud y expulsó a los colonizadores, seguido de sucesivas alternancias entre el dominio español y el haitiano hasta que la República Dominicana consolidó su independencia en 1844. Observó que, a pesar de conservar la lengua y las instituciones españolas, la nación experimentó frecuentes golpes políticos y revoluciones a lo largo de su historia.

After a turbulent history, during which the native Indians were exterminated and thousands of African slaves were imported, the latter, assisted by mulatto freemen, rose, in the last years of the eighteenth century, abolished slavery, and drove their oppressors from the island. Though the land of the Dominican Republic reverted for a while to Spanish control, and later was conquered by the Republic of Haiti, with which it shares the island, it established its independence in 1844 and has retained its individuality since. "The territory which now constitutes the Dominican Republic has been subject at different periods to a number of nations. It has been twice under the rule of Spain and has been controlled at other times by French, English and Haitians. records.summary_en: Writer David J. Davies argues that the secrecy surrounding the conduct of United States marines in Hayti and San Domingo is lifting, as Major-General George Barnett's letter calling for a full investigation focuses public attention on the occupation. He recounts stories told by marines who served in both republics, including a former steel worker he met at Santiago de los Caballeros who boasted of orders to kill and burn everything in a valley near Port au Prince and of natives being killed for the fun of it.

records.summary_en: The *New-York tribune* reported on a gathering where James Weldon Johnson and former Dominican President Francisco Henriquez y Carvajal criticized U.S. military occupations in the Caribbean. Johnson characterized the occupation of Haiti as pure economic exploitation, describing native resistance fighters as patriots rather than outlaws. Henriquez y Carvajal explained that Admiral Knapp instituted military rule in 1916 after Santo Domingo rejected an imposed treaty, expressing faith that the American public would eventually repudiate the intervention.
records.summary_es: El *New-York tribune* informó sobre un acto en el que James Weldon Johnson y el expresidente dominicano Francisco Henríquez y Carvajal criticaron las ocupaciones militares de Estados Unidos en el Caribe. Johnson calificó la ocupación de Haití de mera explotación económica y describió a los combatientes de la resistencia local como patriotas y no como forajidos. Henríquez y Carvajal explicó que el almirante Knapp instauró el gobierno militar en 1916 después de que Santo Domingo rechazara un tratado impuesto, manifestando su confianza en que la opinión pública estadounidense finalmente repudiaría la intervención.

records.summary_en: The *Springfield weekly Republican* discussed prospective U.S. withdrawal from Santo Domingo, observing that wartime strategic concerns and foreign debt disputes had prompted military guardianship over the island of Hispaniola. Acting Secretary of State Davis noted that the occupation grew out of the 1907 convention establishing an American customs receivership and barring unauthorized debt expansion. The article observed that Dominican authorities later violated the convention by increasing public debt to finance the suppression of domestic rebellions.
records.summary_es: El *Springfield weekly Republican* analizó la proyectada retirada de Estados Unidos de Santo Domingo, observando que las preocupaciones estratégicas en tiempos de guerra y las disputas por la deuda externa habían motivado la tutela militar sobre la isla de La Española. El secretario de Estado interino Davis señaló que la ocupación derivó de la convención de 1907, la cual estableció la receptoría general de aduanas estadounidense y prohibió el aumento no autorizado de la deuda. El artículo indicó que las autoridades dominicanas violaron posteriormente dicha convención al incrementar la deuda pública para financiar la represión de rebeliones internas.
records.passage: steps looking to its withdrawal suggests an experience in guardianship of an interesting sort. The public would like to hear more about it. It is more than a coincidence, of course, that the period of military occupation has been commensurate with the latter half of the war and the early stage of international adjustment. The possibility that the island of Haiti might become a pawn in the great game explains in part, no doubt, the relation of the United States toward the island's two little republics during the past few years. It was important that they should be assured stable and responsible government of some sort in view of foreign claims upon their resources and foreign appreciation of their strategic location. The present status of Santo Domingo, or the Dominican Republic, is a direct outgrowth, however, of conditions existing long before the war. It was in 1907, in the administration of President Roosevelt, that a treaty was concluded, as Acting Secretary of State Davis explains, by which Santo Domingo agreed to the appointment of an American receiver-general of customs for the purpose of meeting the obligations of the national debt and also agreed that the debt should not be increased without the approval of the United States. This course was held to be desirable because of the danger of European intervention prompted by the Dominicans' failure to pay the interest on their foreign loans. records.summary_en: The *Evening star* reported that the United States initiated steps toward withdrawing forces from Santo Domingo and establishing a native governing commission to restore self-government. The report recounted that naval officers instituted military rule in 1916 after provisional president Francisco Henriquez y Carvajal refused terms of a proposed treaty. Under the occupation, Dominican school enrollment grew from 18,000 to 100,000 pupils, and gross annual revenues expanded from $4,600,000 to over $7,000,000.
records.summary_es: El *Evening star* informó que Estados Unidos inició medidas destinadas a retirar sus tropas de Santo Domingo y establecer una comisión de gobierno nativa para restaurar el autogobierno. La crónica relató que oficiales de la armada impusieron el régimen militar en 1916 luego de que el presidente provisional Francisco Henríquez y Carvajal rechazara las condiciones de un tratado propuesto. Durante la ocupación, la matrícula escolar dominicana aumentó de 18 000 a 100 000 alumnos, y los ingresos fiscales brutos anuales se incrementaron de 4 600 000 dólares a más de 7 000 000 de dólares.

records.headline: It is frequently said that a revolution would follow the departure
records.summary_en: The *Dearborn independent* argued that an immediate withdrawal of American marines from Haiti would quickly lead to revolution and governmental collapse. The article contrasted the French colonial period's agricultural prosperity with the nation's condition following Toussaint L'Ouverture's uprising and Jean-Jacques Dessalines's 1804 declaration of independence. It asserted that more than a century of post-independence conflict and despotic leadership had ruined the country's plantations and civil institutions.
records.summary_es: El *Dearborn independent* sostuvo que una retirada inmediata de los infantes de marina estadounidenses de Haití conduciría rápidamente a la revolución y al colapso gubernamental. El artículo contrastó la prosperidad agrícola del período colonial francés con la situación de la nación tras la sublevación de Toussaint L'Ouverture y la declaración de independencia de 1804 de Jean-Jacques Dessalines. Aseguró que más de un siglo de conflictos y caudillismos despóticos posteriores a la independencia habían arruinado las plantaciones y las instituciones civiles del país.

It is frequently said that a revolution would follow the departure of our occupational forces by a few days and the Marines would scarcely be away long enough to settle down on their battleships before trouble would necessitate their return. For more than a century the Haytian mass have followed the African instinct back to barbarism. Previous to 1804 by fifty years their land under the French had become the richest area in the West Indies. Great plantations of sugar and coffee covered the land. Beautiful cities, built after the French plan, graced the seaports, which were constantly filled with craft carrying the products to Europe. Napoleon looked upon his West Indian possession as the richest under the flag of France. When Toussaint L'Ouverture, an ex-slave, led a revolt against the French land and slave owners in 1798, there started a period of terror which ended in 1804 when Dessalines, the successor of L'Ouverture stood on the seashore at Gonaives, tore the French tricolor into three pieces, cast away the white and ordered the red and blue bars to be fastened together as the flag of independent Hayti. The whites had been expelled. Generations of despotism, revolution and strife have followed. The great plantations of the French, their rich architectural dwellings both in city and country have gone the way of ruin. The ruling class one finds today in Hayti is gathered in the cities. records.summary_en: The *Evening star* reported that President Harding, Secretary Hughes, and Secretary Denby approved a proclamation establishing procedures for withdrawing the military government from the Dominican Republic. The plan directed primary assemblies to convene within a month to choose electors, who would elect senators and deputies and nominate judges under the Dominican constitution. Delegates appointed by the military governor would then negotiate an evacuation convention to ratify military government acts, validate a $2,500,000 public works loan, and extend customs receivership duties.
records.summary_es: El *Evening star* informó que el presidente Harding, el secretario Hughes y el secretario Denby aprobaron una proclama que establecía el procedimiento para retirar el gobierno militar de la República Dominicana. El plan ordenaba convocar asambleas primarias en el plazo de un mes para designar electores, quienes elegirían a senadores y diputados y nominarían jueces conforme a la constitución dominicana. Delegados designados por el gobernador militar negociarían luego una convención de evacuación para ratificar las disposiciones del gobierno militar, convalidar un préstamo de 2 500 000 dólares para obras públicas y prorrogar las funciones de la receptoría de aduanas.

records.summary_en: The *New York herald* reported that the U.S. government conditioned the withdrawal of troops from the Dominican Republic on guarantees that developmental loans and obligations would be respected. During the occupation, the United States oversaw the construction of schools and highways funded through a $2,500,000 loan. Officials warned that American marines would remain and military rule would continue unless the Dominican government provided binding assurances that these financial commitments would be fulfilled.
records.summary_es: El *New York herald* informó que el gobierno estadounidense condicionó la retirada de tropas de la República Dominicana a garantías de que se respetarían los empréstitos y obligaciones de fomento. Durante la ocupación, Estados Unidos supervisó la construcción de escuelas y carreteras financiadas mediante un préstamo de 2 500 000 dólares. Las autoridades advirtieron que los infantes de marina estadounidenses permanecerían y el régimen militar continuaría a menos que el gobierno dominicano brindara seguridades vinculantes de que se cumplirían dichos compromisos financieros.
records.passage: [illegible] by which American troops are to be withdrawn. The Government finds itself in the position of the person who has adopted a ward, has given to it a rudimentary education and has incurred obligations for its further improvement, and desires to assure itself that these obligations will be observed. It might happen that the ward would prove unwilling to carry out the terms of these obligations. That is the situation in which the Government of the United States finds itself. During its occupation the United States started the construction of schools, roads and other improvements, and negotiated a minimum loan of $2,500,000 to insure the completion of those improvements for the advantage of the Dominican people. Before evacuating the republic the Government of the United States wants assurance doubly sure that those obligations will be taken care of. Without such assurances the American marines will remain in the island and the present military Government will continue. It was explained that the proclamation is not in answer to the recent protest made by the Dominicans to the terms of evacuation, but merely to clarify the situation. records.summary_en: The *New-York tribune* reported that while a Senate committee recommended extending Cuban tariff preferences to the Dominican Republic, the Haiti-Santo Domingo Independence Society fiercely condemned the committee's preliminary report. The society denounced the findings as an imperialist endorsement of armed intervention and treaty imposition on smaller republics. It contended that maintaining military garrisons and puppet executives did lasting damage to American prestige throughout Latin America.
records.summary_es: El *New-York tribune* informó que, si bien una comisión del Senado recomendó extender a la República Dominicana las preferencias arancelarias concedidas a Cuba, la Sociedad Pro Independencia de Haití y Santo Domingo condenó enérgicamente el informe preliminar de la comisión. La sociedad denunció las conclusiones como un respaldo imperialista a la intervención armada y a la imposición de tratados a repúblicas más pequeñas. Sostuvo que el mantenimiento de guarniciones militares y gobernantes títeres causaba un perjuicio duradero al prestigio estadounidense en toda América Latina.

records.summary_en: The *Great Falls tribune* reported that a Senate committee led by Senator Medill McCormick unanimously opposed withdrawing American marines from Haiti, declaring their presence essential to preserve peace and order. McCormick stated that the committee's findings on marine atrocity allegations in Haiti would be made public around February 1, with a separate report on Santo Domingo forthcoming. He also urged the immediate appointment of a High Commissioner to unite diplomatic, treaty, and military authorities under single leadership.

McCormick afirmó que las conclusiones de la comisión acerca de las denuncias de atrocidades cometidas por marines en Haití se harían públicas hacia el 1 de febrero, y que próximamente se presentaría un informe por separado sobre Santo Domingo. Asimismo, instó al pronto nombramiento de un alto comisionado para unificar la representación diplomática, las facultades derivadas del tratado y la autoridad militar bajo un solo mando.

records.summary_en: The *Birmingham age-herald* reported that Senator Medill McCormick recommended completing the Dominican North-South highway to stimulate commerce and prevent future insurrections, thereby facilitating American withdrawal. To offset revenue declines caused by the post-war trade depression, the committee advised issuing a new loan to consolidate two outstanding short-term debts. McCormick reported that outside of localized banditry in the east, the military administration had established unprecedented domestic peace while modernizing municipal sanitation, docks, and public education.

A fin de compensar la caída de ingresos provocada por la depresión comercial de posguerra, la comisión aconsejó emitir un nuevo préstamo para consolidar dos obligaciones pendientes a corto plazo. McCormick afirmó que, al margen de partidas aisladas de bandolerismo en el este, la administración militar había instaurado una paz interna sin precedentes a la vez que modernizaba el saneamiento municipal, los muelles y la educación pública.

records.summary_en: Horace G. Knowles said he had been compelled to leave Santo Domingo City under cover of darkness after receiving a letter from Francisco J. Peynado, former Dominican minister to the United States, advising him not to remain an hour beyond the first chance he had to leave. Knowles argued that the treatment accorded him, an American citizen, was an example of the methods of the American military government in Santo Domingo, and asked what it would stop at in the case of natives. He had remained behind to take the testimony of some fifty other witnesses at Senator McCormicks request, and went to the dock with a list of witnesses to deliver to McCormick, only to be informed that he had boarded the Argonne.
records.summary_es: Horace G. Knowles dijo que se había visto obligado a salir de la ciudad de Santo Domingo al amparo de la noche tras recibir una carta de Francisco J. Peynado, exministro dominicano en Estados Unidos, que le aconsejaba no quedarse ni una hora más allá de la primera oportunidad de partir. Knowles sostuvo que el trato que recibió, siendo ciudadano estadounidense, era un ejemplo de los métodos del gobierno militar estadounidense en Santo Domingo, y preguntó hasta dónde llegaría en el caso de los nativos. Se había quedado para tomar el testimonio de unos cincuenta testigos más a petición del senador McCormick, y fue al muelle con la lista de testigos para entregársela, solo para enterarse de que ya había abordado el Argonne.

records.full_text:
THE AMERICAN EMPIRE

[Selected]

In none of the lands that America has guided and protected during the last generation is more interesting than the great island often called Haiti, but more correctly known as Santo Domingo—the island which lies between Cuba and Porto Rico. It is unquestionably the finest of the West Indies—a land of lofty mountains clothed with splendid forests and a rich variety of minerals; a land of spacious plateaus and fertile plains that are capable of producing the finest of sugar, tobacco and other tropical products. Santo Domingo would appear predestined by nature to be the richest and most prosperous of the West Indies. As a matter of fact it lost its early prosperity long ago, and for more than a century has been sunk in a backwardness and misery from which, under recent American guidance, it is only now beginning to emerge. The story of the turbulent past of Santo Domingo and of its new start is a story well worth telling.

As its double name suggests, the island of Santo Domingo, which has an area of some thirty thousand square miles (about half the area of New England), is divided politically into two distinct nations. The western third forms the republic of Haiti; the eastern two-thirds constitutes the Dominican Republic. Haiti is a nation of Negroes; it has only a few mulattoes and no native whites. The people speak a corrupt French and look to France for their culture. The Dominican Republic, on the other hand, is a Spanish-speaking land, much like Cuba and Porto Rico. It has a considerable white or near-white upper class, a peasantry of mixed blood (Indian, white and African) and relatively few full-blooded Negroes.

Christopher Columbus discovered Santo Domingo, and the island was the first Spanish colony in the New World. It had a fine start, for at first the whole colonizing energy of Spain flowed into that relatively small insular area. Within thirty years multitudes of colonists had covered the land with towns of stone. Even now, after four centuries of decay, Santo Domingo, the capital city, still shows those stately mansions proudly described by an early Spanish historian as “so fair and large that they may well receive any lord or noble of Spain.”

During those thirty years the blood of a million Indians paid for the ingots of gold and silver that amazed the Spanish court. But at the end of that exciting period the bloodshed ceased. Mexico and Peru were conquered, the mines of Santo Domingo became insignificant beside the mines of the mainland, and the Indian workers were dead. The restless, fortune-hunting conquistadores who had made up the bulk of the population of Santo Domingo flocked away to the more tempting Spanish Main; and depopulated Spanish Santo Domingo almost sank into oblivion.

So matters stood for perhaps a hundred years. Then, just about the time when our ancestors were settling the Atlantic seaboard of North America, the coming of the French revived the prosperity of Santo Domingo. The Spaniards had colonized only the eastern part of the island—the part now known as the Dominican Republic; they had left the western part, which is today known as Haiti, virtually uninhabited, and the deserted coasts became the haunt of the famous buccaneers. The buccaneers were mainly French, and in time France claimed the region they had occupied, introduced respectable immigrants and made it a colony known as the French part of Santo Domingo. Like the Spaniards, the French devoted themselves to agriculture, and soon showed what marvelous productiveness the island had. During the eighteenth century French Santo Domingo was by far the most flourishing colony in the West Indies. Covered with fine plantations and cultivated to the very mountain crests, the French part of Santo Domingo, though only a trifle larger than the state of Massachusetts, furnished not only France but half Europe with sugar, coffee and other tropical products.

In order to obtain the labor necessary for so many plantations the French brought in multitudes of Negro slaves, who soon vastly outnumbered the white population. When the French Revolution convulsed France and its colonies, the Negroes of French Santo Domingo took advantage of the situation, revolted and after a long struggle succeeded in expelling the whites. Then they declared their independence, and in the year 1804 set up the republic of Haiti, the old Indian name for the land. About twenty years later the eastern part of the island threw off Spanish rule and became the Dominican Republic.

But independence meant neither peace nor prosperity. Having gained their freedom, the Haitians and the Dominicans began to misuse it. Both peoples showed from the first an utter lack of capacity for orderly self-government. The “Black Republic” of Haiti quickly degenerated into an absurd burlesque of France. The government sedulously copied French political forms; and the republic was sometimes styled a kingdom, sometimes an empire. One of the rulers of Haiti especially distinguished himself by creating a whole nobility headed by four princes and fifty-nine dukes; innumerable marquises, counts and barons completed the pompous galaxy that surrounded the “imperial” throne. Meanwhile Haiti itself went to rack and ruin. An endless succession of black and mulatto “generals” at the head of tatterdemalion “armies” fought ferociously for the spoils of office and kept the land plunged in a horrid and interminable anarchy. Revolution succeeded revolution and in those senseless civil wars the fine, well-constructed towns that the French had left were destroyed and replaced by squalid shacks, and the broad plantations and shaded highroads of the countryside again became bush and forest.

In the Spanish (Dominican) Republic colonial prosperity was destroyed because the Haitians repeatedly invaded and conquered it. How the Haitians ruled their own country suggests how they ruled the Dominicans; and finally, when the Dominicans at last succeeded in expelling them, the Dominican Republic continued to flounder in the bog of misgovernment and revolution.

By the beginning of the present century things had become so bad that European intervention seemed certain. Both republics had piled up huge foreign debts that they could not pay. Some of the creditors were Americans, but most of them were Europeans, particularly Englishmen, Frenchmen and Germans.

Now, it soon became clear that whatever the United States might think about its duty in the matter, the European nations would not put up with conditions much longer. In fact, European warships were already appearing off the coast and threatening to bombard the ports unless the money that was due was paid. But if European powers seized the ports of Santo Domingo, what would become of the Monroe Doctrine, one of the corner stones of our foreign policy?

Faced with that critical situation, President Roosevelt succeeded in 1905 in getting the Dominican government to sign an agreement that permitted the United States to adjust the Dominican debt and to administer the customs for the benefit of creditors. The effects of American intervention were instantly felt.

Hitherto the goal of every revolutionist had been the nearest customhouse, because the customs were almost the only source of revenue. If a revolutionist could seize a customhouse, he could maintain an army. But when the United States took charge of the customhouses, the customs officials turned over 45 per cent of the revenue to the Dominican government for its current expenses and applied the remaining 55 per cent to paying the foreign debt. At once the customhouses ceased to be prizes for revolutionists, because an American collector with American naval forces behind him was in charge. Revolutions promptly stopped, and for nearly ten years the Dominican Republic enjoyed unprecedented peace and prosperity. The country developed rapidly; roads, harbors, schools and public buildings were constructed, and the public debt was steadily reduced.

Then came the World War. The withdrawal of American naval vessels to European waters was the signal for fresh revolutions. A series of uprisings threatened to undo all that had been accomplished. In 1916 the United States intervened with armed force. American marines landed, deposed the revolutionary government and set up a military administration headed by an American naval officer. Under American military rule the republic was completely disarmed, banditry was suppressed, and order was firmly established.

Meanwhile, across the border in Haiti, conditions had gone from bad to worse. Between 1908 and 1915 seven presidents were successively overthrown, assassinated or driven into exile. When the World War broke out, German influence in Haiti was strong, and there was danger that Germany might seize a naval base on the island. In July, 1915, after a particularly shocking massacre of political prisoners, American marines landed at Port-au-Prince. A treaty was negotiated between the United States and Haiti under which the United States assumed control of the finances and police of the republic.

Under American supervision the gendarmery was organized, public works were pushed forward, and the country was cleared of the cacos, or mountain bandits, who had terrorized the population for generations. Today both republics on the island of Santo Domingo are peacefully developing their immense natural resources under American guidance and protection.

records.summary_en: The *Great Falls tribune* reported that the Senate committee chaired by Senator Medill McCormick suspended its findings on Dominican affairs due to active negotiations to end military rule in Santo Domingo. Under the arrangement, executive departments would be transferred to Dominican ministers, expenditures would follow established budgets, and American troops would concentrate into select centers while the national police preserved order. records.summary_en: The *Birmingham age-herald* commented that the planned withdrawal of American troops after seven years proved the success of the U.S. mission to stabilize the Dominican Republic and prepare it for self-government. The editorial cited extensive road construction, suppression of banditry, sanitary improvements, and fiscal reforms as permanent benefits of the occupation. It argued that the impending military evacuation refuted accusations that the United States harbored imperialistic designs in Santo Domingo.

El editorial citó la extensa construcción de caminos, la supresión del bandolerismo, las mejoras sanitarias y las reformas fiscales como beneficios permanentes de la ocupación. Sostuvo que la inminente evacuación militar refutaba las acusaciones de que Estados Unidos albergaba designios imperialistas en Santo Domingo.
records.passage: result of the state department's decision to withdraw American troops from the Dominican republic. The American occupation of Santo Domingo lasted for seven years, and while there has been much criticism of the government for its Dominican policy, the task of restoring order and placing the Dominican people in a position to govern themselves has apparently been accomplished. Furthermore, by the building of roads, the protection of private property, the breaking up of banditry, sanitation and government economies, the republic and its people are in far better case than they otherwise would have been. The withdrawal of American troops should put an end to the accusations that the United States was pursuing a high-handed and imperialistic policy in its treatment of Santo Domingo. records.summary_en: The *Washington daily news* published an editorial criticizing American assertions of non-imperialism, pointing to U.S. control across the Caribbean and Pacific, including customs administration in the Dominican Republic and marine occupation in Haiti. The piece derided official claims of purely benevolent motives while exercising regional dominance. It argued that Washington's treatment of its dependencies, particularly the curtailment of self-rule in the Philippines under General Leonard Wood, contradicted its anti-imperialist rhetoric.
records.summary_es: El *Washington daily news* publicó un editorial en el que criticaba las afirmaciones estadounidenses de no ejercer imperialismo, señalando el control de Estados Unidos en el Caribe y el Pacífico, incluida la administración de aduanas en la República Dominicana y la ocupación de la infantería de marina en Haití. El artículo ridiculizó los argumentos oficiales de motivaciones puramente benévolas mientras se ejercía el dominio regional. Sostuvo que el trato que Washington daba a sus dependencias, en particular el menoscabo de la autonomía en Filipinas bajo el general Leonard Wood, contradecía su retórica antiimperialista.
records.passage: "You say you are not imperialistic," it jeers. And reviewing it all, it asks insinuatingly: "What are you up to in all those places?" "Just protecting the interests of the unfortunate peoples," we say. "Oh!" says the world, winking prodigiously! records.summary_en: The *Evening star* reported official statements declaring that the United States did not seek permanent dominion over Santo Domingo, but was actively preparing to evacuate its forces following free elections scheduled for mid-September. The statement explained that American policy in Haiti similarly aimed only to establish stability and competent self-governance following decades of revolution. U.S. authorities emphasized that they harbored no territorial ambitions on the island and would welcome the day American troops could safely withdraw.

El pronunciamiento explicaba que la política estadounidense en Haití aspiraba igualmente a restablecer la estabilidad y un gobierno autónomo competente tras décadas de revoluciones. Las autoridades de Washington hicieron hincapié en que carecían de ambiciones territoriales en la isla y celebrarían el momento en que los efectivos estadounidenses pudieran retirarse de forma segura.

records.summary_en: The *Springfield weekly Republican* published statements by Secretary of State Hughes affirming that the United States was committed to terminating its occupation of Santo Domingo and holding unsupervised elections in mid-September. Hughes maintained that American involvement in Haiti was aimed strictly at promoting stability and order after a century of chronic revolutions, disclaiming any territorial ambitions. He added that the United States maintained a consistent policy of fostering peace and responsible government across Central America and the Caribbean.

records.summary_en: The *Evening star* assessed the outlook for stability in Santo Domingo following the evacuation of American troops, noting general agreement that the nation deserved its opportunity for independent self-government. The article reviewed the background of intervention, recalling that the 1916 marine occupation followed decades of civil strife and the 1905 crisis when foreign creditors threatened naval force over unpaid debts. It described how the United States helped arrange a $20,000,000 refunding loan backed by an American receiver-general collecting customs to make monthly debt payments.
records.summary_es: El *Evening star* evaluó las perspectivas de estabilidad en Santo Domingo tras la evacuación de las tropas estadounidenses, destacando el consenso general de que la nación merecía su oportunidad de autogobierno independiente. El artículo recapituló los antecedentes de la intervención, recordando que la ocupación de los marines en 1916 siguió a decenios de contiendas civiles y a la crisis de 1905, cuando acreedores extranjeros amenazaron con recurrir a la fuerza naval por deudas impagas. Describió cómo Estados Unidos facilitó la gestión de un empréstito de refinanciamiento de 20 000 000 de dólares respaldado por un receptor general estadounidense encargado de recaudar las rentas aduaneras para efectuar pagos mensuales de la deuda.
records.passage: to support his government, or will it be undermined and hampered by political conspiracies and insurrections like those of the past? There are some familiar with the West Indies who feel a good deal of doubt on this question. But all agree that Santo Domingo should have its trial at domestic tranquillity — its chance to make good as an independent, responsible nation. When United States marines were landed on the island in 1916 it was to restore order out of a political and economic chaos that had lasted for many long years. As early as 1905 repeated revolutions had left the affairs of the Dominican government in such a hopeless state that the United States was compelled to come to its assistance in order to preserve the Monroe doctrine. A large group of foreign creditors, each ready to present his bill with a gunboat, clouded the horizon. Another large group of native creditors, each planning to enforce his claims against the government by insurrection, agitated the country's interior. Clearly something had to be done to reestablish Dominican credit, and the United States did it. Through its offices the republic was enabled to secure a loan of $20,000,000 with which to refund its foreign debts. This was arranged by a bond issue, with the understanding that the bonds were to be paid off in monthly installments from the customs revenues. Although Dominican authorities promised fiscal restraint and agreed not to increase public debt without U.S. consent, recurring revolutions diverted revenues into military operations and generated massive unpaid debts. The article explained that the resulting financial collapse and threats to custom houses prompted the United States to deploy marines in 1916.

Aunque las autoridades dominicanas prometieron moderación presupuestaria y convinieron en no aumentar la deuda pública sin el consentimiento de Estados Unidos, sucesivas revoluciones desviaron los fondos hacia gastos bélicos y generaron deudas impagas colosales. records.summary_en: The paper recounted a struggle of more than eight years by the people of Santo Domingo to regain the sovereignty they contended was taken from them when the United States placed the country under a large military force and set up a military government. After repeated Dominican efforts for a withdrawal, former American minister Horace G. Knowles started a campaign in 1920 to secure sovereignty for the Dominicans, and a United States Senate committee then inquired into the occupation in Santo Domingo, which was followed by an agreement for withdrawal of the forces. Sovereignty was restored and an election was held on March 15, with General Vasquez elected President, while about 1,800 marines remained in Santo Domingo and transports had begun evacuating the troops.
records.summary_es: El diario relataba una lucha de más de ocho años del pueblo de Santo Domingo por recuperar la soberanía que, según sostenía, le fue arrebatada cuando los Estados Unidos pusieron el país bajo una numerosa fuerza militar y establecieron un gobierno militar. records.full_text:
The Day in Washington

The house passed a bill to promote production and conservation of helium.

A bill for a new American embassy and consulate general in Tokio passed the house.

The senate rejected a proposal to withhold funds to maintain marines in Haiti.

A senate elections sub-committee recommended the seating of Senator Mayfield, democrat, Texas.

The senate called on Secretary Hughes for information on the Paris reparations agreement.

Heber H. Votaw, brother-in-law of the late President Harding resigned as superintendent of prisons.

The naval bill, containing a request that President Coolidge call an arms conference, passed the senate.

Members of the senate foreign relations committee and others were invited to a night dinner at the White House.

The senate ratified treaties with the Dominican republic on evacuation of American troops and refunding of the Dominican debt.

Senator Shipstead, farmer-labor, Minnesota, charged the increased prices for stocks and bonds were the result of a “stock gambling boom.”

Senator McKellar, democrat, Tennessee, presented a resolution asking President Coolidge to investigate whether England violated the arms treaty in building the battleships Rodney and Nelson.

Justice department took steps to subpoena Senator Wheeler, democrat, Montana, to appear before a grand jury here in connection with the home state indictment against him.

records.summary_en: The *Omaha morning bee* reported details of the treaty ratified by the U.S. Senate refunding the Dominican national debt of $25,000,000. The pact authorized the U.S. president to appoint a general receiver to collect all Dominican customs duties, applying proceeds to receivership expenses, interest, and sinking fund amortization before remitting any surplus to the Dominican government. Under an additional article, the Dominican Republic was prohibited from increasing its public debt without American consent until all refunding bonds were fully paid.
records.summary_es: El *Omaha morning bee* reportó detalles del tratado ratificado por el Senado de Estados Unidos para el refinanciamiento de la deuda nacional dominicana por 25 000 000 de dólares. El pacto autorizaba al presidente estadounidense a nombrar un receptor general para recaudar todos los derechos aduaneros dominicanos, aplicando lo recaudado a los gastos de la receptoría, intereses y amortización del fondo de amortización antes de transferir cualquier remanente al gobierno dominicano. Conforme a un artículo adicional, se prohibía a la República Dominicana aumentar su deuda pública sin consentimiento estadounidense hasta que la totalidad de los bonos de refinanciamiento quedara saldada.
records.passage: the refunding of the Dominican debt totaling $25,900,000. Under the terms of the refunding treaty, the president of the United States will appoint a general receiver of Dominican customs to collect all customs duties in the republic until the payment or retirement of all bonds issued for the refunding of its present obligations. The general receiver will apply the sum so collected first to the payment of expenses of the receivership; second, to payment of interest on all bonds outstanding; third to payment of the annual funds provided for amortization of these bonds, including interest upon all bonds held in the sinking fund and fourth, to purchase and cancellation or retirement and cancellation of any of the new issue of bonds as may be directed by the Dominican government. The remainder would be paid to the Dominican government. Under an additional article of the pact, the public debt of the Dominican republic could not be increased without consent of the United States until all bonds of the present debt have been paid. records.summary_en: The United States and Finland have agreed, by an exchange of notes, to grant each other most-favored-nation treatment on customs duties and other charges relating to commerce, the State Department announced. It warned that careless selections for the few remaining American positions could disrupt the service's success.

records.summary_en: The *Evening Star* reported on political controversy in Haiti surrounding President Borno's eligibility, his decree extending the Council of State to secure reelection, and extended American financial control under the 1915 treaty. The article also noted heavy outward migration among Haitian farmers, with tens of thousands departing for Cuba and the Dominican Republic. An estimated 150,000 natives had emigrated since the American occupation began, resulting in a local labor scarcity.
records.summary_es: El *Evening Star* informó sobre la controversia política en Haití en torno a la elegibilidad del presidente Borno, su decreto de prórroga del Consejo de Estado para asegurarse la reelección y la extensión del control financiero estadounidense bajo el tratado de 1915. El artículo también señaló una intensa emigración de agricultores haitianos, con decenas de miles partiendo hacia Cuba y la República Dominicana. Se estimaba que unos 150 000 naturales habían emigrado desde el inicio de la ocupación estadounidense, lo que provocó escasez de mano de obra local.
records.passage: [A?] new constitution was prepared by Assistant Secretary of the Navy Franklin D. Roosevelt and adopted by Haiti, by decree of its President, acting as dictator. The council of State elected President Borno in 1922. It is claimed that he is ineligible to serve as President, since he was the son of alien French, although he was born in Haiti. The decree establishing the council of state was for a term of 10 years, which term has now expired, but President Borno, a candidate to reelect [himself?] next April 12, has decreed its extension for another 10 years, and it is alleged he has filled several vacancies on it with his own relatives and cabinet officials and expects it to reelect him. In the meanwhile the people have not been permitted to vote for a new Assembly, whose constitutional function it is to elect the President. The treaty of 1915 with the United States has been extended by presidential decree until 1936, without coming before our Senate. This extends our control over Haitian finances. The National City Bank is negotiating an additional loan of $16,000,000 to Haiti, the bids for the loan having been advertised by our State Department. In 1922 the Haitian foreign debt was $6,971,874. Haiti has a population of 3,000,000, mostly small farmers. In 1924 there was an emigration of 21,013 from Haiti to Cuba; in 1925 there were upward of 30,000 emigrated to Cuba, and many more to the Dominican Republic. records.summary_en: The *Evening Star* published an account describing the conditions of Haitian peasants under the American occupation. The report asserted that the occupation protected rural workers from forced military impressment and bandits, allowing them to farm and sell produce freely. It stated that peasants were better fed, clothed, and receiving medical treatment at free clinics, despite widespread illiteracy.
records.summary_es: El *Evening Star* publicó una crónica que describía la situación de los campesinos haitianos bajo la ocupación estadounidense. El reportaje afirmaba que la ocupación protegía a los trabajadores rurales del reclutamiento militar forzoso y de los bandoleros, permitiéndoles cultivar y vender sus productos libremente. Indicaba que los campesinos estaban mejor alimentados, mejor vestidos y recibían atención médica en dispensarios gratuitos, a pesar del analfabetismo generalizado.

By comparison the American Expeditionary Force doughboy, with his rudimentary vocabulary and his amazing pronunciation, would be a wizard in his understanding of French. In addition, the Creole patois rarely sees print. The word man, for instance, is "mouin," possessing not the slightest resemblance to the French word "homme." The peasant, or [illegible], as the American marine dubs him, is not only hopelessly illiterate, but equally inarticulate. Under the influence of our occupation he is no longer the helpless victim of impressment into the armies and bands of robbers who roamed through Haiti, destroying his little garden patch and burning his home while he hid in the hills, but free to work his gardens, and bring its produce into market. records.summary_en: The *Evening Star* reported on efforts to prepare Haiti for eventual American withdrawal by training native personnel across various government departments. Haitian nationals were increasingly staffing public works, sanitary services, customs administration, and agricultural engineering, while Haitians comprised about half the commissioned officers in the gendarmerie. Concurrently, the American military presence had been reduced to an 800-man marine force.
records.summary_es: El *Evening Star* informó sobre los esfuerzos para preparar a Haití para una eventual retirada estadounidense mediante la capacitación de personal autóctono en diversos departamentos gubernamentales. Ciudadanos haitianos se incorporaban de forma creciente a las obras públicas, servicios sanitarios, administración de aduanas e ingeniería agrícola, al tiempo que conformaban cerca de la mitad de los oficiales en la gendarmería. En forma paralela, la presencia militar estadounidense se había reducido a un contingente de 800 infantes de marina.
records.passage: ultimate withdrawal, with all the elements necessary for its self-government. The yearly reports made to the State Department are eloquent in the increasing number and sphere of Haitian participation in the various fields. The department of public works is each year training a growing number of Haitian engineers, architects, artisans, office executives, hydrographic aids, steam gauge readers, telephone and telegraph operators and inspectors. The sanitary service is turning out Haitian physicians, surgeons, nurses, dentists, pharmacists and sanitary inspectors. Practically all the force of the financial adviser and general receiver of customs is purely Haitian. The recently formed office of the chief agricultural engineer is enrolling and training a Haitian personnel. In the ranks of the Haitian gendarmerie there are now approximately 60 Haitians of the best type who are either commissioned, acting or aspirant officers, or practically one-half of its commissioned strength. All these departments are organized into departments with district and subdistrict divisions, so that throughout Haiti the native Haitian is working shoulder to shoulder with Americans in the rehabilitation of the country. Coincident with this sound expansion has gone the gradual reduction of armed American forces to a minimum. The former marine brigade of full strength, with aviation and other attached special units, three years ago was stationed throughout the island. Today it numbers but 800,

records.summary_en: The *Pocahontas Times* recounted the history of U.S. intervention in Haiti, noting that seven revolutions between 1910 and 1915 culminated in the killing of President Sam and the landing of U.S. Marines. Under the 1916 treaty establishing a 20-year protectorate, the article stated that order and prosperity were established with minimal risk of revolution. By October, American military forces had been reduced to 800 marines supporting an armed native constabulary.

Bajo el tratado de 1916 que estableció un protectorado de 20 años, el artículo señalaba que se habían implantado el orden y la prosperidad con mínimo riesgo de revolución. records.passage: West Virginia it is a mountain country, and like West Virginia it has mountains heavily forested clear to the top. It produces for export coffee, sugar, cotton, logwood, and [cacao?]. It is the most fertile island in the West Indies. From the year 1910 to the year 1915, Haiti had seven revolutions, and seven presidents occupied uneasy thrones in that country. The last of the seven, Gen. Sam, was inaugurated March 4, 1915. He lasted until July 26, of that year. That day he took refuge in the French legation, and on that date, 200 political prisoners were massacred in the jail. The funeral services were being held, and the temper of the crowd was so dangerous, that they dragged President Sam out and killed him. Two hours after President Sam had passed, a United States cruiser entered the harbor of Port au Prince and landed marines and restored order. In 1916, a treaty between the United States and Haiti was ratified. By the terms of that treaty, the United States undertook a political and fiscal protectorate for a period of twenty years. Since then Haiti has known a measure of peace and prosperity. At this time there seem to be no danger of revolutions. Last October, there were 800 marines in Haiti with an armed constabulary of 2688 men, and a reserve of 20,000 men. The United States as usual did a good job. records.summary_en: The *New Britain Herald* reported on extensive infrastructure modernization in Haiti under President Borno, including more than 1,000 miles of paved roads, new schools, hospitals, and lighthouses. A concrete highway connecting Port-au-Prince with Santo Domingo had reached the border on the Haitian side, promising to reduce travel time between the capitals from days to hours once the Dominican section was completed. The report also highlighted telephone network expansion, tariff revisions to promote trade with the United States, and the continuing presence of 800 American marines.
records.summary_es: El *New Britain Herald* informó sobre la vasta modernización de infraestructura en Haití bajo el presidente Borno, con más de 1 000 millas de carreteras pavimentadas, nuevas escuelas, hospitales y faros. Una carretera de hormigón que comunicaba Puerto Príncipe con Santo Domingo había alcanzado la frontera del lado haitiano, prometiendo reducir el tiempo de viaje entre ambas capitales de días a horas una vez concluido el tramo dominicano. El despacho destacó asimismo la ampliación de la red telefónica, modificaciones arancelarias para estimular el comercio con Estados Unidos y la continua presencia de 800 infantes de marina estadounidenses.
records.passage: In the last ten years, more than 1,000 miles of paved roads have been laid, replacing highways that had deteriorated until they were little more than trails. A concrete highway connecting Port-au-Prince, the Haitian Capital, and Santo Domingo, capital city of the Dominican Republic, has been completed by the Haitians up to the border. When the Dominican portion is completed, the trip between the two capitals may be done in hours, where formerly it took days. This progress has been particularly notable during the administration of the present chief executive, President Borno, said a report in the booklet made by the Haitian minister of public works. His administration also has seen the construction of fourteen schools, thirteen hospitals and eleven lighthouses; installation of an automatic telephone system, and material progress in irrigation and canals. Since 1921, there has been an increase of 350 per cent in the number of telephones in use and the telegraph system has been augmented and improved. In order to foster trade between the United States and Haiti, the present Haitian Import Customs Tariff is being revised. Some eight hundred American Marines still remain in Haiti, completing their work of reorganizing the native constabulary. records.summary_en: The *Evening Star* reported the arrival in Washington of Dr. Ángel Morales, the newly appointed Dominican Minister to the United States, and his wife. Dr. Morales, who succeeded Dr. José del Carmen Ariza, had previously served as Dominican Minister to Paris, vice president of the League of Nations, and Dominican Secretary of the Interior. The newly appointed legation secretary, Máximo L. Vásquez, a nephew of the Dominican president, also arrived in the capital.
records.summary_es: El *Evening Star* informó de la llegada a Washington del Dr. Ángel Morales, recién designado ministro de la República Dominicana ante Estados Unidos, y de su esposa. El Dr. Morales, quien sucedió al Dr. José del Carmen Ariza, se había desempeñado previamente como ministro dominicano en París, vicepresidente de la Liga de las Naciones y secretario de Interior dominicano. El nuevo secretario de legación, Máximo L. Vásquez, sobrino del presidente dominicano, también arribó a la capital.

Mme. Bostrom is in their Swedish home for the Summer. The newly appointed Minister of the Dominican Republic, Dr. Angel Morales, accompanied by Senora de Morales, have arrived in Washington and taken an apartment at the Wardman Park Hotel. Dr. Morales, who succeeds Dr. Jose del Carmen Ariza, served as Dominican Minister to Paris for one year, and prior to that was one of the vice presidents of the League of Nations at Geneva. An attorney by profession, he has held several governmental posts in the Dominican Republic, serving as secretary of the Interior for one term. The newly appointed secretary of the Dominican legation, Senor Maximo L. Vasquez, also came to Washington last week and, accompanied by Senora de Vasquez, is established at the Roosevelt Hotel. Senor Vasquez is a nephew of President Vasquez of the Dominican Republic. The counselor of the Czechoslovakian legation and Mme. Lipova are expected to arrive Friday aboard the Mauretania, which sailed from Southampton yesterday. M. and Mme. Bonet reported widespread damage to villages and the countryside along the railroad line from Santa Clara Province westward. Several large sugar factories and cigar plants were wrecked or heavily damaged, with multiple casualties reported.

Havana has a plentiful supply of food and medicine, and thus far has been able without difficulty to take care of refugees. Sugar Factories Wrecked. Three large sugar factories in the outlying districts were hard hit by the storm. Central Occidente, a 150-year-old cane grinding plant, was wrecked. Central Fajaro was destroyed, with a loss of eight lives, and Central Toledo was badly damaged. At La Salud [illegible] tobacco curing sheds were demolished. Among the big industries here which suffered from the storm was the Partagas Cigar factory, which was destroyed. It employed 900 cigar makers. The Aguila [illegible] Cigar factory also was destroyed.
