records.summary_en: The Evening Star reported that Cuban Foreign Minister Aureliano Sanchez Arango planned to present evidence to the OAS Peace Committee demonstrating that the Dominican interception of the unarmed vessel *Quetzal* constituted high-seas piracy. Sanchez Arango argued that the ship was seized near Cape San Antonio, far from Dominican territory, and threatened to take the case to the United Nations and the World Court if Cuban crewmen were not freed. Dominican Foreign Minister Virgilio Diaz Ordonez prepared to argue the Dominican case before the committee, amidst reports that Guatemalan prisoners might soon be released.
records.summary_es: El *Evening Star* informó que el ministro de Relaciones Exteriores de Cuba, Aureliano Sánchez Arango, planeaba presentar pruebas ante la Comisión de Paz de la OEA para demostrar que la interceptación dominicana del buque desarmado *Quetzal* constituía piratería en alta mar. Sánchez Arango sostuvo que el barco fue capturado cerca del cabo de San Antonio, lejos de territorio dominicano, y amenazó con llevar el caso ante las Naciones Unidas y la Corte Internacional de Justicia si los tripulantes cubanos no eran liberados. El canciller dominicano Virgilio Díaz Ordóñez se preparaba para exponer los argumentos dominicanos ante el comité, en medio de informes sobre la posible pronta liberación de prisioneros guatemaltecos.
records.passage: Dominicans have since been ac quitted and freed by the Domini can Supreme Court, and the Cu bans’ sentences reduced to 20 years. Diplomatic quarters in Wash ington heard a report yesterday that the Dominican Republic will set the Guatemalans free on Sun day, December 23. Mr. Sanchez Arango said he will present the five-nation Peace Committee of the Organization of American States with “documented proofs that the seizure of' the Quetzal was an act of piracy on the high seas and that no crime had been committed by the crew.’ Says Ship Wasn’t Armed. The Cuban Minister also said he will present Cuban documents to show that the ship was not armed, and that it was taken by a Dominican warship some 50 miles south of Cape San Antonio, while proceeding away from the Dominican Republic about 950 miles distant from its capital, Ciudad Trujillo. If the Cubans are not released as the result of suggestions by the Peace Committee, Mr. Sanchez Arango said, Cuba will carry the case before the United Nations—the Security Council or General Assembly, or both—and perhaps to the World Court of Justice. Foreign Minister Virgilio Diaz Ordonez will present the case of the Dominican Republic to the Peace Committee. Basis for Closing Case. The foreign minister said Cuba would consider the case closed if the imprisoned Cubans were released. Mr. Sanchez Arango said he expects to fly back to Cuba Sunday. It also enumerated countries that had established or restored official relations with the Holy See during the reigning pontificate.

records.summary_en: The News and Views reported on the Dominican Republic's expansion of state-sanctioned nightlife and gambling casinos aimed at attracting American tourists. Four major casinos operated in Ciudad Trujillo, Boca Chica Beach, and San Cristobal, offering roulette, dice, and lavish floor shows. The article noted that Dominican authorities rebuffed attempts by American gambling syndicates to muscle into operations, choosing instead to import gaming equipment directly from Florida and Louisiana.

Cuatro grandes casinos funcionaban en Ciudad Trujillo, la playa de Boca Chica y San Cristóbal, ofreciendo ruleta, dados y suntuosos espectáculos de variedades. El artículo señaló que las autoridades dominicanas rechazaron los intentos de sindicatos del juego estadounidenses de infiltrarse en las operaciones, optando en su lugar por importar equipos de juego directamente desde Florida y Luisiana.

records.summary_en: The News and Views reported on a proposed subsidized flight package called the 'Sportsmen's Week-end Special' linking Miami and Ciudad Trujillo for $150 per passenger. The plan featured in-flight gambling with card games, slot machines, and race betting, along with lodging at the Hotel Jaragua and excursions to local sporting and casino venues. Miami travel promoters organized the charter venture with financial subsidies and betting concessions backed by Dominican interests.

El plan incluía juegos de azar a bordo con naipes, tragamonedas y apuestas de carreras, además de alojamiento en el Hotel Jaragua y excursiones a centros deportivos y casinos locales. Promotores turísticos de Miami organizaron el proyecto chárter con subsidios financieros y concesiones de apuestas respaldadas por intereses dominicanos.

Barnett were leading a two-week Caribbean tour visiting Haiti, Puerto Rico, Jamaica, the Dominican Republic, and Cuba. records.summary_en: A columnist in The News and Views commented on promotional circulars distributed by the Dominican Republic explaining that domestic gambling profits were directed toward cultural programs and public relations. The writer satirically suggested that European debtor nations might follow the Dominican example of using casinos, sports, and tourism revenue to eliminate foreign debt. The article noted Dominican claims of agricultural diversification, industrial expansion, and successful debt-free national development.
records.summary_es: Un columnista de *The News and Views* comentó sobre folletos promocionales distribuidos por la República Dominicana en los que se explicaba que las ganancias del juego nacional se destinaban a programas culturales y relaciones públicas. El articulista sugirió de modo satírico que las naciones deudoras europeas podrían seguir el ejemplo dominicano de emplear ingresos de casinos, deportes y turismo para saldar la deuda externa. El artículo hizo mención a las afirmaciones dominicanas de diversificación agrícola, expansión industrial y un exitoso desarrollo nacional libre de deudas.

records.full_text:
SERVICE BY KEFAUVER

For a long time, I have been wondering about that Kefauver television show. Did it really accomplish something constructive? Obviously, it made Rudolph Halley a figure in New York politics and encouraged Estes Kefauver himself to run for President on the Democratic side.

Was that all?

Apparently, it is not so. I have received a circular from the Dominican Republic Information Center which is devoted to advertising the aforesaid Republic where Christopher Columbus is buried. According to the circular, the Dominican Republic is progressive and takes advantage of every opportunity. Therefore, as Kefauver drove gambling out of the United States, the Dominican Republic made gambling the cultural tie between the United States and the other Republic. The circular says:

“Gambling-in-the-sky via slot machines will feature a four-hour plane flight by the ‘Sportsmen’s Special,’ between Miami and Ciudad Trujillo, Dominican Republic—the ‘Monte Carlo of the Caribbean’ where four legal gambling casinos flourish, if final flight negotiations are completed this week. Three of the casinos have opened since the Kefauver Crime Investigation closed many illegal gambling places in the U.S.

“Service by the 50-passenger chartered plane ‘Lady Luck’ is scheduled to commence on or about March 7 from Miami. The plane, though owned by the (CDA) Compania Dominicana de Aviacion, a Pan-American subsidiary, would be chartered to a sponsoring promotion group to begin the week-end round-trips between Miami and the West Indies country. The Dominican Government itself is not sponsoring the project but approves of it.”

In addition to approving of the slot-machines and other devices, the Dominican Government sends me this circular through the mails. If any American sent a similar circular through the mails, he would probably go to jail. But then Americans no longer count in the United States except to pay taxes and to have their sons conscripted for United Nations police actions.

I forgot to save the envelope in which this circular came and therefore I cannot tell you whether it used a paid-for stamp or came as diplomatic mail, free of charge. I get a lot of that kind of mail, all free, the object of which is always to educate me to love some foreign country. But if anyone wants to send some mail about loving America, a paid-for stamp is essential. It is a fine point, this business of who pays to have mail delivered advocating love.

Police enforced regulations barring demonstrations within 500 feet of the hotel, and the peaceful picketers displayed placards accusing Trujillo of political murders during his presidency. Trujillo was serving as Dominican minister of finance and chief United Nations delegate, while his brother Hector B. Trujillo held the presidency.

records.summary_en: The Evening Star reported that stateless traveler Michael Patrick O'Brien arrived in Ciudad Trujillo after receiving an invitation of resettlement from the Dominican government. records.summary_en: The Evening Star reported that the Dominican government stripped Porfirio Rubirosa of his diplomatic post as embassy counselor in Paris and revoked his diplomatic status citing scandalous personal conduct. Rubirosa's dismissal followed his naming as co-respondent in high-profile divorce litigation in London and the United States. His history of celebrity marriages included unions with Generalissimo Rafael Trujillo's daughter Flor de Oro, French actress Danielle Darrieux, and American heiress Doris Duke.

La destitución de Rubirosa se produjo luego de ser señalado como codemandado en sonados litigios de divorcio en Londres y Estados Unidos. Su historial de matrimonios con celebridades incluía enlaces con la hija del generalísimo Rafael Trujillo, Flor de Oro, la actriz francesa Danielle Darrieux y la heredera estadounidense Doris Duke.

records.summary_en: The Evening Star reported international reactions to Guatemalan accusations alleging a foreign conspiracy against President Jacobo Arbenz's government. The Dominican Foreign Ministry dismissed the charges as communist fabrications, denying any involvement with Guatemala or the Arbenz regime. Other accused figures, including Nicaraguan Colonel Anastasio Somoza Debayle and General Miguel Ydigoras Fuentes, ridiculed the conspiracy claims, while Panama dismissed an attache named in the Guatemalan communique.

records.summary_en: The Tribune recounted a travelogue by visiting members of the Pan American Medical Association touring historic and medical sites across Ciudad Trujillo, including the Alcazar de Colon and the Cathedral of Santa Maria la Menor. The physicians met with Dominican medical colleagues at a modern hospital facility before being received at the presidential palace by President Hector Trujillo. Today, a woman in her 30’s she is credited with being the first person to grow human cancer in animals. The result of her work may speed up science's efforts to find a cure for the dread malady. Dr. Helene Wallace Toolan, a small, pretty woman with curly brown hair and grey eyes, is an associate at the Sloan-Kettering Institute research unit of the Memorial Center for Cancer and Allied Diseases. records.summary_en: The Catholic Times reported that the Holy See and the Dominican Republic signed a historic concordat during a ceremony in the Vatican Palace. The agreement was executed by Monsignor Domenico Tardini on behalf of the Vatican and former President General Rafael Leonidas Trujillo on behalf of the Dominican Republic. Trujillo stated that the treaty affirmed his government's dedication to the Catholic Church as the bulwark of order and Christian civilization.

records.summary_en: The Evening Star reviewed the history of Caribbean political conflicts, tracing how Venezuelan exiles and Romulo Betancourt helped form the Caribbean Legion to invade Rafael Trujillo's Dominican Republic. Following the collapse of those invasion attempts, legion remnants aided Jose Figueres in establishing power in Costa Rica during the 1948 revolution. Dictators Trujillo and Anastasio Somoza accused Figueres of harboring communist conspirators and reforming the legion to attack their regimes, charges Figueres dismissed as dictatorial paranoia.
records.summary_es: El *Evening Star* repasó la historia de los conflictos políticos del Caribe, reseñando cómo los exiliados venezolanos y Rómulo Betancourt colaboraron en la formación de la Legión del Caribe para invadir la República Dominicana de Rafael Trujillo. Tras el fracaso de aquellas intentonas de invasión, los remanentes de la legión ayudaron a José Figueres a afianzarse en el poder en Costa Rica durante la revolución de 1948. Los dictadores Trujillo y Anastasio Somoza acusaron a Figueres de cobijar a conspiradores comunistas y reorganizar la legión para atacar a sus regímenes, señalamientos que Figueres desestimó considerándolos paranoia dictatorial.

When the old military regime was overthrown, its leaders obtained territorial asylum in the Dominican Republic. There, under the tutelage of President Rafael Trujillo Molina, they plotted a counter-revolution. Learning about this, Betancourt and party helped organize an expedi tionary force of asylees from Carib bean totalitarian regimes to invade the Dominican Republic. This force, named the Caribbean Legion, trained in Cuba and failed at two attempts to invade Trujillo's land. It then disintegrated. Costa Rican Adventure Remnants of the legion figured in a revolution that broke out in Costa Rica late in 1948. A conserva tive invalidated the free election of a liberal president. Jose Figueres mobilized a group of young liberals and forced the Conservative-Com munist coalition out, set himself up as provisional president, and even tually turned the government over to the constitutionally elected presi dent. Betancourt is in Costa Rica, with his friend, Figueres. records.summary_en: This is the continuation of the published itinerary of Haitian President Paul E. Magloire's North American tour: after official activity in Washington from January 26 to 28, a visit to the United States Military Academy at West Point and five days in New York, the party travels to Chicago, Boston and Ottawa, Canada. The itinerary lists receptions, luncheons and visits day by day, and ends with the party leaving Canada on February 14 for Kingston, Jamaica, then continuing by boat to Ciudad Trujillo in the Dominican Republic and on to Port-au-Prince. The members of the presidential party, Haitian and American, are named in full, including Secretary of State Mauclair Zephirin, Ambassador Jacques Leger and the United States ambassador to Haiti, Roy Tasco Davis.

Medics Say Smoking Bad For Heart;Whiskey No Antidote BY EDWIN DIAMOND CHICAGO—(I N S)—The American Medical Association declared on Thursday “there seems to be direct evidence” that smoking cigarettes causes heart damage. And the long-held notion that drinking whiskey “protects” the heart against the effects of ciga rettes was rejected as “purely an il lusion.” Two articles and an editorial were devoted to the effects of smoking and drinking in the current Journal of the AMA. Timothy V. Hartnett, chairman of the Tobacco Industry Research Committee, commented: “From time to time, reports can be expected that may seem either favorable or unfavorable to the use of tobacco. It is impossible to at tempt to evaluate each specific re port as it appears in the scientific or lay press. The Tobacco Industry Research Committee is convinced the vast majority of the American public agree that all questions of tobacco in relation to human health need much more thorough and com plete investigation than has been made up to now.”

Any person in that age bracket who is unable to prove ability to read and write is subject to punishment for not reporting to one of the 18,000 schools which have been set up. Dr. Joaquin Balaguer, minister of education, has said that in two more years “we will have no more illiteracy in the Dominican Republic.”’ A government census in 1950 disclosed that there were 830,537 illiterates. A major problem was the recruiting of teachers; a majority of the educators employed in the present campaign are those who are working toward full-time teachers certificates and who volunteered their services to gain experiences. In addition to the professional teacher candidate, a large number of voluntary non-professional teachers are helping in the classrooms. records.headline: Hurricane Katie beat a path across the Dominican Republic, slamming into the south shore with 115-mile winds the night
records.summary_en: Hurricane Katie beat a path across the Dominican Republic, slamming into the south shore with 115-mile winds the night before, but the mountains of Hispaniola distorted the storm and weakened her winds to about 40 or 50 miles an hour. At noon her center was near Puerto Plata, moving northeast at about 14 miles an hour, and she was expected to regain hurricane force over the open Atlantic without threatening the United States mainland.

Al mediodía su centro estaba cerca de Puerto Plata, moviéndose hacia el noreste a unas 14 millas por hora, y se esperaba que recobrara fuerza de huracán sobre el Atlántico abierto sin amenazar el territorio continental de los Estados Unidos.

WASHINGTON —(UP)— A group of Cuban businessmen left for Toledo, Ohio, continuing their tour of a number of United States industrial centers in the interest of promoting greater commerce between the two countries. records.headline: Dominican Ship Boilers Searched, No Galindez Murder Clues Found
records.summary_en: New York detectives searched the Dominican freighter Fundación in Brooklyn for four hours after the Dominican revolutionary leader Nicolás Silfa charged that Jesús de Galíndez, a foe of Generalissimo Rafael Trujillo, had been thrown alive into a steaming boiler aboard the ship. The detectives questioned the 36 crew members and found not a single solid clue to Galíndez's fate, though the boilers' openings were large enough to squeeze a man through. A representative of the Ward Lines, which controls the Dominican Steamship Line, said opening a boiler door while it was fired would burn a man to a crisp, and Silfa, in a statement afterwards, repeated his charge that Galíndez's body was thrown into the firebox on Trujillo's orders.

It also says that “1957 will bring the culmination of important jointly achievements between the two sister nations and a direct inter KNOW THY NEIGHBOR By ANTONIO RUIZ HAITI In all the seaports, the chief cities of the Republic of Haiti, beautiful green mountains form the background of the charming landscape. Of the total area of the country of 10,700 square miles, 8,000 square miles are mountains. There are three principal ranges with several large plains lying be tween them and along their out er fringes. One range, including large groups known as La Horte and La Selle, extends from east to west along the lower peninsula, while the other two stretch from the southeast to the northeast across the mainland an northern peninsula. The highest mountain in Haiti is Morne La Selle in the southeast, which reaches an altitude of 8,700 feet above sea level. There are four plains of major importance in the country: the North Plain, lying along the northern east coast be tween the mountains and the sea; the Central Plain, a large interior flatland, bordering the Dominican Republic, and the Artibonite and Cul-de-Sac Plains, which spread eastward from the Gulf of Gonave. Haiti has numerous rivers, most of them short, rapid streams coursing down the mountain slopes into the sea. The Artibonite River, however, which drains the Arti bonite Plain on its way to the Gulf of Gonave, has a length of 200 miles from its headwaters in the Dominican Republic to its mouth.

records.full_text:
U. S. Government Rejects
Dominican Statements on
Murphy’s Disappearance

WASHINGTON, March 16 (UP) The United States rejected today the Dominican government explanation about the mysterious disappearance of the North American aviator Gerald L. Murphy, in the Dominican Republic.

23 years old Murphy disappeared in the Dominican Republic on December 3rd. last.

In official note, delivered by the United States Embassy in Ciudad Trujillo, the U. S. government rejected the explanation offered by the Dominican government that Murphy was assassinated by the Dominican pilot Octavio de la Maza, who later committed suicide at Ciudad Trujillo, leaving a letter in which he confessed his crime.

A copy of the note delivered in Ciudad Trujillo was handed today to the Dominican Ambassador in Washington, Dr. Joaquín Salazar.

The note urges the Dominican Government to continue “vigorously” the investigation on the disappearance of Murphy, who was said to have been the pilot who took to the Dominican Republic professor Jesús de Galíndez, who disappeared in New York on March 12, 1956. It has also been said Murphy was murdered because he talked too much.

Last January, the Dominican Government delivered to the State Department an alleged letter-confession of pilot de la Maza and other documents, all of which have been carefully examined by the FBI.

The note delivered today by the U. S. Government says:

“Upon examination of these documents and evidence, this Government has reached the conclusion that, if the handwriting samples submitted by Dominican authorities as belonging to Maza are really his, that means the suicide note was not written by de la Maza.”

Other points rejected by the State Department over the explanation are:

1. That Murphy did not know any person with political influence in the Dominican Republic. The U. S. investigation, says the Department of State, shows that Murphy had “good relations” with high Dominican officials, including the then Undersecretary of the Army, now Consul General in New York, Arturo Espaillat.

2. That Murphy’s income while in the Dominican Republic was $350 per month. The investigation shows, the note says, that the missing pilot had a capital substantially bigger than what Dominican authorities say.

“The Government of the United States is gravely concerned by the disappearance of one of its citizens in the Dominican Republic — the note says — and assumes this concern is shared by the Dominican Government.”

Murphy, as de la Maza, worked for the Dominican Air Line, and disappeared when he had announced his intention to return to the United States for good.

As soon as the contents of the note were revealed, Rep. Charles O. Porter, who has realized a personal investigation on Murphy’s disappearance, said the note shows the need of a Congress investigation of the relations of the United States with the Dominican Republic.

records.summary_en: The *Peninsula Enterprise* reported that the Dominican government enacted legislation banning the missionary and educational activities of Jehovah's Witnesses. Under the directive enforced by Security Minister Arturo Espaillat and signed by President Héctor Trujillo, Kingdom Halls were shuttered, foreign missionaries ordered to leave, and dozens of adherents arrested.

It was announced that over $1 million had been appropriated by the Dominican government to enforce the ban. records.summary_en: The wife and four small daughters of deposed Venezuelan President Marcos Pérez Jiménez arrived in Miami on Friday night, aboard a Dominican Republic airliner from Ciudad Trujillo. They refused to discuss their trip to the United States from the Dominican Republic, where Pérez Jiménez has been in exile since he was removed as dictator of Venezuela in January. Accompanying the family were an aide, a governess and a nurse for the children, and it could not be learned whether or when Pérez Jiménez expects to follow his family to the United States.

records.full_text:
Rebels Seize
Army Station
In Venezuela

By ARISTEDES MOLEON

CARACAS, Venezuela (AP) — Rebels seized control of an army regiment’s headquarters at San Cristobal near the Colombian border today in an attempt to set off nationwide revolt against President Romulo Betancourt’s government.

Betancourt ordered soldiers to San Cristobal to quell the uprising, and pledges of support came to him at once from military, political and civilian sources.

The moderate Venezuelan President announced he would use all constitutional powers to crush the rebellion, but would not suspend constitutional guarantees in this oil-rich nation.

The strong military garrison at Caracas announced its support at once for Betancourt’s government.

Leaders of the nation’s three major political parties spoke over a national radio network, appealing to their followers in San Cristobal to vigorously oppose the insurrection.

The rebels seized control of the Simon Bolivar army regiment’s headquarters at San Cristobal.

Gen. Pedro Jose Quevado, commander of the Venezuelan armed forces, urged “my companions in arms to set an example of common sense and maturity” and support the constitutional government.

The head of the Central Workers Organization, Jose Gonzalez Navarro, called for its 1,200,000 members to go on strike. He said this would be a demonstration of opposition to the “criminal” insurrection which, he declared, was counting on the support of the Dominican Republic.

The government had announced last Saturday that it had smashed a plot for an armed invasion of Venezuela from Colombia by officers who were dismissed from the army for their support of former dictator Gen. Marcos Perez Jimenez.

Venezuelan naval craft and air force planes were patrolling the coast today on the lookout for two fishing boats which the minister of defense, General Jose Lopez Henrique, said had sailed from Spain with arms for the plotters.

Betancourt, a moderate with a reputation as a social reformer, has faced a series of minor uprisings, threats and harassments since he took office early in 1959. He was elected a year after the overthrow of Perez Jimenez, now in exile in Florida.

Venezuela, a tropical country, lies on the northern hump of South America facing the Caribbean. It has about six million people, and because of the nation’s rich resources, has the highest per capita income in South America.

records.full_text:
Change For Better Hoped
U.S. Watches Trend In D.R.

WASHINGTON (AP)—Secretary of State Dean Rusk set out today on his delayed trip to join President Kennedy in Europe, signalling a belief that the assassination of Dominican dictator Rafael L. Trujillo will not result in the immediate turmoil officials had feared.

Rusk had been scheduled to leave Wednesday to back up Kennedy in his talks in Paris with French President Charles de Gaulle and later in Vienna with Soviet Premier Khrushchev. Instead he was held here to take personal charge of dealing with the Dominican situation.

That decision underscored the anxiety with which American officials were watching for clues as to which way the Caribbean country will shift.

Rusk’s plane was due in Paris at 9 a.m. Paris time Friday.

Just before takeoff, Rusk told newsmen at National Airport that there is no way of knowing at this time what kind of government will finally take over in the Dominican Republic.

U.S. authorities said information seeping out from tightly censored Ciudad Trujillo indicated the Trujillo group, under figurehead President Jouquin Balaguer, still was in control.

President Kennedy and Rusk, in telephone contact between Paris and Washington, were said to be agreed that the Dominican situation was of such top priority that Rusk could do more by setting the U.S. course as the situation clears than by speeding off to the summit talks.

Informed sources said both the President and the secretary of state had the recent Cuban invasion fiasco very much in mind and were determined to avoid any mistake on the neighboring Caribbean island. They feel the outcome will affect the whole of U.S.-Latin American affairs.

Balking Washington strategists was a scarcity of solid information. Officials said they did not yet know who engineered the assassination or who might be behind the figurehead president who continued in office, Joaquin Balaguer. They said their evidence did not point to pro-Communist Cuba or other foreign manipulators.

The only post-assassination communication from the U.S. Consulate in Ciudad Trujillo reported by late Wednesday was a brief message from Consul General Henry Dearborn saying the capital was calm and he knew of no injury to the 5,200 citizens in the country.

Some U.S. authorities foresaw a struggle for power, both within the Trujillo group and between it and the large elements of Dominican society persecuted during the dictator’s 31-year rule. A continued harsh rightwing regime without Trujillo’s personal leadership, they reasoned, would set off revolt—perhaps pro-Castro the next time.

The United States had several lures to attract Trujillo’s successors down the democratic path, a main aim of Kennedy’s “alliance for progress” Latin American program.

One is resumption of U.S. aid, cut off when Washington joined the other American Republics last year in breaking diplomatic relations and normal commercial ties with Trujillo. Another is a boost in U.S. sugar purchases. The Dominican economy has been sagging.

The United States could also take a leading role in a move by the hemisphere organization, the Organization of American States, in readmitting a progressive Dominican regime to the American family.

Washington congressional reaction was mixed.

Sen. George Smathers, D-Fla., recommended that U.S. Marines be landed in the Dominican Republic to prevent a Communist takeover.

Sens. Homer E. Capehart, R-Ind., Olin D. Johnston, D-S.C., and Allen J. Ellender, D-La., saw a Red Castroite takeover in prospect as a result of Trujillo’s death.

records.passage: CIUDAD TRUJILLO, Dominican Republic, Nov. 22 (AP).—President Joaquin Balaguer says the Dominican armed forces have lined up solidly behind him and that threats by antidemocratic diehards to topple his government have been eliminated. Mr. Balaguer, in a radio address last night, claimed the government had emerged in full control from the crisis prompted by the return of two Trujillo family leaders last week. Their return raised speculation of a resurgence of Trujillo rule and brought a covey of United States warships hovering offshore. Mr. Balaguer declared that the crisis was created by the "ambitious and senselessness of some men of rural mentality.” He said they included two cabinet members but offered no further identification. Mr. Balaguer’s address on the state of the nation obviously was intended in part to squelch reports of rumblings in military ranks over some of his military appointees named to succeed exiled Trujillos. He said there was “propaganda tending to create a false impression” that threats of a coup d’etat remained but warned Dominicans not to take stock in such reports. records.headline: This Spanish-language essay argues that the immense majority of the Dominican people accept Trujillo's tyrannical regime
records.summary_en: This Spanish-language essay argues that the immense majority of the Dominican people accept Trujillo's tyrannical regime only out of an imperative need for collective survival, hate and fear it, and should be regarded as the despot's passive victims rather than held responsible for it. It says three things should not be counted against that majority: having enrolled in Trujillo's political parties, whose membership the regime tied to civil rights, having held public employment, which is service to the state and not to the regime, and having worked in a business of Trujillo or his followers, given the persecution system known as the 'lepra'.
records.summary_es: Este ensayo en español argumenta que la inmensa mayoría del pueblo dominicano acepta el régimen tiránico de Trujillo solo por una imperiosa necesidad de supervivencia colectiva, lo odia y le teme, y debe ser considerada víctima pasiva del déspota en lugar de hacérsele responsable de él. Dice que tres cosas no deben contarse en contra de esa mayoría: haberse inscrito en los partidos políticos de Trujillo, cuya militancia el régimen vinculó a los derechos civiles, haber servido un empleo público, que es servir al estado y no al régimen, y haber trabajado en una empresa de Trujillo o de sus secuaces, dado el sistema de persecución conocido como la «lepra».

records.summary_en: The *Evening Star* reported that OAS Secretary General José A. Mora and Inter-American Development Bank President Felipe Herrera scheduled missions to Santo Domingo to assess reconstruction aid under the Alliance for Progress. Mora planned discussions with President Joaquín Balaguer and incoming interim leader Rafael Bonnelly to prepare substantial technical and financial assistance programs.

Mora, y el presidente del Banco Interamericano de Desarrollo, Felipe Herrera, programaron misiones a Santo Domingo para evaluar la ayuda a la reconstrucción en el marco de la Alianza para el Progreso. Mora tenía previsto mantener conversaciones con el presidente Joaquín Balaguer y con el mandatario interino entrante Rafael Bonnelly a fin de estructurar cuantiosos programas de asistencia técnica y financiera.
records.passage: This group has been described as a “pre-planning” mission to investigate what aid the Dominican Republic needs under the inter-American Alliance for Progress sponsored by the Kennedy administration. Bank Chief to Visit Felipe Herrera, president of the Inter-American Development Bank, also is scheduled to make a personal visit to investigate the possibility of low cost loans for Dominican reconstruction. The Inter-American Development Bank, with assets of over $1 billion, is the hemispheric institution which also administers a $394 million Social Progress Trust fund voted by Congress for the Alliance for Progress. Secretary General Mora’s visit is to last four days. Sources close to him say he will meet with Dominican President Joaquin Balaguer and Rafael Bonnelly, the chief representative of the democratic opposition on the new Council of State. President Balaguer, who is a holdover from the Trujillo regime, has said he will resign once the OAS sanctions are lifted. OAS sources expected, therefore, that most of Secretary General Mora’s dealings would be with Mr. Bonnelly. who will become interim President, and members of his group, the National Civic Union. Experts Gather Data In his statement here, Mr. Mora noted that experts of the OAS are busy collecting data which will be used in planning a technical co-operation program in both economic and social fields. A source close to Mr. Mora said a major aim of his visit is to lend more prestige to these efforts of the experts.

Armed forces chief General Pedro Rodríguez Echavarría announced the installation of a civilian-military junta to govern the country, while arresting council members who refused to cooperate.

Pedro Rodriguez Echavarria, the armed forces chief who thwarted an attempted coup d'etat by the brothers of former dictator Rafael Trujillo last November, emerged grimfaced from the Presidential Palace and announced the change of government. Opposition crowds have been accusing him of dictatorial ambitions and have demanded his resignation. It was clear he led the discussions which resulted in the change of government. City Now Quiet The center of Santo Domingo was quiet this morning. Many stores were closed. Shattered glass littered some streets, Many store fronts were shattered in the night of violence. Conditions through the interior also were reported quiet. The official announcement said four members of the old council, besides Mr. Balaguer, resigned. Informed sources said, however, that they refused to go along with creation of a new civilian-military junta and were placed under arrest. records.summary_en: The *Evening Star* published a profile of Dr. Rafael Bonnelly as he prepared to lead the Dominican transitional government toward general elections. The profile traced his career as a university rector, diplomat, and cabinet minister during the Trujillo era, noting his efforts to maintain professional independence before joining the democratic opposition.

Long in Government The late Dominican dictator, Generalissimo Rafael Trujillo, exerted various forms of economic pressure to bring the country’s influential citizens into his service. For the first 10 years of the Trujillo regime, Dr. Bonnelly stayed clear of any association with the govern ment, but in the 1940s he joined the official family. Among the high posts he held were Secretary of the Interior, Ambassador to Spain and to Venezuela. He was also rector of Santo Domingo University, a job in which he still takes pride since it gave him a chance to teach and direct what Dominicans consider the hemisphere’s oldest institution of learning. During this career, Dr. Bonnelly says he was able to avoid identification with the regime except in a purely professional capacity. Balaguer at Home Mr. Balaguer was at his comfortable home on the city’s western outskirts. Mr. Balaguer became president in 1960, under dictator Trujillo, and his hesitancy to make good his promise to resign was considered the spark that set off the violent street fighting Tuesday that preceded the military takeover. Mr. Balaguer told an interviewer he had refused to yield to earlier demands for his resignation because he feared just such a military move. records.summary_en: The *Evening Star* reported that the Dominican Council of State headed by Rafael Bonnelly implemented significant economic reforms, including doubling sugar workers' minimum wages and launching public works. The transitional government confiscated the extensive holdings of the Trujillo family—redistributing an estimated 40 percent of the nation's wealth—while counting on pledged United States assistance for economic recovery.

El gobierno de transición confiscó los cuantiosos bienes de la familia Trujillo —redistribuyendo cerca del 40 por ciento de la riqueza nacional— mientras confiaba en la asistencia prometida por Estados Unidos para la recuperación económica.
records.passage: form in April.” he added. "Everything is being planned now for the period of renovation." This careful, step-by-step approach is the creed of the new order. It is the creed of basically conservative men with social consciences, men who believe in evolution, not revolution. Rather than drama, they want stability. They have already raised the basic wage of sugar workers 100 per cent—to a minimum of $3.25 per day. These and other lesser wage increases—plus confiscation of the huge Trujillo holdings—are estimated to have redistributed 40 per cent of the wealth of the country already. An emergency public works program emphasizing manpower more than scarce materials is also making the first minor dent in widescale unemployment. “We are open for foreign investment,” affirmed Mr. Bonnelly, “and we want it. But that investment must benefit both the Dominican people and the investors. It will be channeled through our new planning commission.” U. S. Aid Important It was a gentle—but clear—slap at the small trickle of North American “businessmen” who have arrived to speculate on the Dominican future. They check in at the best hotel in town and then pursue new officials with a high-pressure sales pitch. But the new leaders are far more intent on how the United States Government lives up to its commitments of all-out aid. This potential aid is the third and by far the strongest trump in government hands. By general consensus the aid is essential to swift economic recovery.

records.summary_en: The *Evening Star* published an editorial urging the United States to adopt stronger measures against Haitian dictator François Duvalier, suggesting economic boycotts and clandestine support for anti-Duvalier insurgents. The commentary argued that Washington's official reluctance to intervene disregarded past precedents like Guatemala and the Bay of Pigs, warning that inaction could allow Communist influence to expand next to Cuba.

El artículo sostenía que la renuencia oficial de Washington a intervenir ignoraba precedentes pasados como Guatemala y Bahía de Cochinos, advirtiendo que la inacción podría permitir la expansión de la influencia comunista junto a Cuba.

Obviously we take the position nowadays that armed intervention cannot be undertaken in this hemisphere, barring a spectacular threat to our security like the presence somewhere of Soviet rockets. There are ways, however, of accomplishing these things. For one thing, as we pointed out the other day, there is economic pressure. Our purchases from Haiti are not extensive. But, for instance, could we not get along without Haitian coffee while Duvalier remains in power? Duvalier could be toppled, as he should be, by the Haitians themselves— relatively few of them. The men to topple him are there and, sooner or later, one of them will organize the job. They need guns, grenades and explosives. If the United States remains a spectator, growling only when its na tionals seem to be menaced, the next leader of Haiti will owe us even less than the present one. records.headline: IAPA Will Again Protest Discrimination by Brazil
records.summary_en: At its mid-year meeting in Santo Domingo, the Inter American Press Association resolved again to protest Brazilian government discrimination against Copley News Service correspondent Louis Stein, whose foreign office accreditation Brazil has refused to restore for a year. The board wound up its meeting in a flurry of activity, passing hard-hitting resolutions that included a fresh denunciation of Fidel Castro's dictatorship in Cuba. The association directed its president, John R. Reitemeyer, to communicate the protest to the government of Brazil once again and to request that Stein's credentials be restored without further delay.

records.headline: Santo Domingo
records.summary_en: George L. Rosenblatt's travel feature opens on Santo Domingo, the oldest city in the New World, founded by Christopher Columbus's brother Bartholomew, with the celebrated founding date set at August 4, 1496. A few hours' stroll through the Colonial Zone shows the firsts of the hemisphere: the first cathedral, the first hospital, the first university and the first commercial street. Foremost among the sights is the Cathedral of Santa María la Menor, the first cathedral established in the New World, which the article presents as the last resting place of Christopher Columbus, whose ornate tomb stands inside the cathedral and whose coffin is traditionally opened to view on Columbus Day.
records.summary_es: El reportaje de viajes de George L. Rosenblatt se abre con Santo Domingo, la ciudad más antigua del Nuevo Mundo, fundada por Bartolomé, hermano de Cristóbal Colón, con la fecha de fundación celebrada fijada el 4 de agosto de 1496. Unas pocas horas de paseo por la Zona Colonial muestran las primicias del hemisferio: la primera catedral, el primer hospital, la primera universidad y la primera calle comercial. Entre los lugares se destaca la Catedral de Santa María la Menor, la primera catedral establecida en el Nuevo Mundo, que el artículo presenta como el último descanso de Cristóbal Colón, cuya tumba adornada se encuentra dentro de la catedral y cuyo ataúd se abre tradicionalmente a la vista el Día de Colón.

It has been suggested, for example, that a bone from his skeleton or similar relic may have been buried in Seville, Spain, thus giving rise to claims that Seville is Columbus' eternal home. But one knowledgeable guide in Seville says that Santo Domingo is where Christopher Columbus is buried. If you happen to be here on Columbus Day (Oct. 12), you may be able to glimpse Old Chris, since the coffin traditionally is opened to view on the anniversary of his discovery of the New World. These most Columbian of relics were brought to Hispaniola in the mid-1540s from Spain, where Columbus died in 1506, then were buried in a secret vault within the cathedral. records.headline: Santo Domingo
records.summary_en: In the next stretch of George L. Rosenblatt's Santo Domingo feature, the walk continues to the Ozama Fort and its Tower of Homage, both built in the first decade of the 1500s, a short block from the cathedral. From the top of the tower visitors can scan a panorama of the old city: the Ozama River and the port to the east, the bridges to the north, the harbor mouth where the Ozama empties into the Caribbean Sea to the south, and the rooftops of the old city to the west. The feature then passes the Casa de Bastidas, a sprawling sixteenth-century home now a museum and crafts outlet, and notes the sun clock on Calle Las Damas, an eighteenth-century device that still keeps fairly good time.
records.summary_es: En el siguiente tramo del reportaje de George L. Rosenblatt sobre Santo Domingo, el paseo continúa hacia la Fortaleza Ozama y su Torre del Homenaje, ambas construidas en la primera década del siglo XVI, a una manzana de la catedral. Desde lo alto de la torre los visitantes pueden contemplar un panorama de la ciudad vieja: el río Ozama y el puerto al este, los puentes al norte, la desembocadura del puerto donde el Ozama desemboca en el mar Caribe al sur, y los tejados de la ciudad vieja al oeste. El reportaje pasa luego por la Casa de Bastidas, una amplia casa del siglo XVI hoy convertida en museo y tienda de artesanías, y menciona el reloj de sol de la calle Las Damas, un artefacto del siglo XVIII que todavía da la hora con bastante exactitud.

records.headline: Santo Domingo
records.summary_en: The final stretch of George L. Rosenblatt's page-one feature carries the walk north along Calle Las Damas to the Columbus Castle, built by Christopher Columbus's son Diego and now a museum of sixteenth-century court life. Descending the stairs at the northern edge of the castle, the reader reaches La Atarazana, the oldest shopping street in the New World, which dates from the 1500s. The feature pauses at the Casa de Bastidas, with its shaded garden courtyard, and at the eighteenth-century sun clock on Las Damas, described as simple and more remarkable for having survived intact than for any intrinsic quality.
records.summary_es: El tramo final del reportaje de primera página de George L. Rosenblatt lleva el paseo hacia el norte por la calle Las Damas hasta el Castillo de Colón, construido por Diego, hijo de Cristóbal Colón, y hoy museo de la vida cortesana del siglo XVI. Al bajar las escaleras del extremo norte del castillo, el lector llega a La Atarazana, la calle comercial más antigua del Nuevo Mundo, que data del siglo XVI. El reportaje se detiene en la Casa de Bastidas, con su patio ajardinado sombreado, y en el reloj de sol del siglo XVIII de Las Damas, descrito como sencillo y más notable por haber sobrevivido intacto que por cualquier cualidad intrínseca.

records.headline: La Atarazana Shopping Street Dates from 1500s
records.summary_en: In this continuation of George L. Rosenblatt's Santo Domingo feature, the walk resumes on La Atarazana, where a lunch at the Fonda de la Atarazana ends in a tropical downpour that traps the writer in the restaurant, watching the rain on the brick tiles of the patio. The feature continues to the Casa del Cordón, built in 1503 and believed to be the first stone house in the Americas, and to Puerta del Conde, where the flag of the Dominican Republic first flew in 1844. Through the gate stands the shrine of La Trinitaria, where the three Founding Fathers — Juan Pablo Duarte, Francisco del Rosario Sánchez and Ramón Mella — are entombed. The writer closes with his impressions of the Dominican people, whom he finds gentle and unobtrusive, and with a long taxi ride driven by Victor, a man who spoke no English but with whom he talked baseball, and who charged about eleven dollars for a two-hour excursion.
records.summary_es: En esta continuación del reportaje de George L. Rosenblatt sobre Santo Domingo, el paseo se reanuda en La Atarazana, donde un almuerzo en la Fonda de la Atarazana termina en un aguacero tropical que retiene al escritor en el restaurante, observando la lluvia sobre los ladrillos del patio. El reportaje continúa hasta la Casa del Cordón, construida en 1503 y considerada la primera casa de piedra de las Américas, y hasta la Puerta del Conde, donde ondeó por primera vez la bandera de la República Dominicana en 1844. Tras la puerta se encuentra el santuario de La Trinitaria, donde están sepultados los tres Padres de la Patria —Juan Pablo Duarte, Francisco del Rosario Sánchez y Ramón Mella—. El escritor cierra con sus impresiones del pueblo dominicano, al que encuentra amable y discreto, y con un largo viaje en taxi conducido por Víctor, un hombre que no hablaba inglés pero con quien conversó de béisbol, y que cobró unos once dólares por una excursión de dos horas.
